artemisia-absinthium.summary: Absinthium is a perennial herb with silvery leaves and small yellow flower heads. Also called absinth wormwood, it comes from Eurasia and has been grown for its aromatic foliage. Outside gardens, it can become established in pastures, along roads and on disturbed ground. A plant can return from its roots for several years, while its seeds allow it to spread farther. Its strong scent and pale leaves are useful clues, but other wormwoods can look similar. Identifying the leaves carefully matters before removing a plant, especially where native species grow nearby.

launaea-intybacea.summary: Despite the name achicoria azul, this member of the daisy family has pale yellow flowers. Its branching stems rise above a cluster of larger leaves close to the ground; the leaves become smaller farther up the plant. Small flower heads sit along the slender branches. Kew recognizes Launaea intybacea as an accepted species native across tropical and subtropical parts of the Old World. Regional floras describe it as an annual or biennial of seasonally dry places. Its presence in a catalog does not, by itself, show that a particular population is causing ecological harm.

convoluta-convoluta.summary: This tiny marine animal lives among seaweeds and other growth on the seafloor. Usually only a few millimeters long, it has an oval body whose sides curl downward. Algae living inside it contribute to its greenish or yellow-brown appearance and provide food through photosynthesis; the animal also eats small organisms. Convoluta convoluta is an acoel, a group distinct from the true flatworms despite the familiar flatworm label. Smithsonian records describe a northeastern Atlantic native range and introduced records in the Gulf of Maine. Those records describe observations at particular places and times, not its presence along every nearby coast.

eulachnus-rileyi.summary: The active gray pine needle aphid is a small, slender insect that feeds on pine needles. A thin wax coating can give its olive-green or gray body a pale appearance. Like other aphids, it releases sugary honeydew, which can leave surfaces sticky and support a dark fungal coating called sooty mold. Feeding may cause needles to yellow or fall, but these symptoms can also have other causes. Finding the aphids themselves is more useful than diagnosing a tree from discoloration alone. Lady beetles, lacewing larvae and other natural enemies can reduce their numbers as the weather warms.

kilifia-acuminata.summary: Acuminate scale is a small sap-feeding insect found on plant leaves. Adult females are flat, pale green to yellow-green, with a body that narrows toward the head and rounds toward the back. That shape can help you notice them, but closely related scales look very similar. USDA's identification guide records this species on a range of cultivated plants, including mango and gardenia. A scale found on one of those plants is not automatically acuminate scale: both its features and the host need to be checked. Published interception records also describe where infested material was encountered, not proof that the insect is established in every listed place.

pineus-boerneri.summary: A patch of white, wool-like material on a pine twig may be hiding Pineus boerneri. This adelgid, a close relative of aphids, feeds on pine trees beneath a protective covering of wax. Its youngest stages can crawl to a feeding site; after settling, they remain attached. Heavy infestations can damage shoots and cause needles to yellow or fall. Researchers have documented these effects in pine plantations, but the amount of damage depends on the tree and growing conditions. Other pine adelgids make similar white coverings, so the wax alone cannot tell you which species is present.

erysimum-cheiri.summary: Aegean wallflower is a familiar garden plant that can also grow in rocky crevices and cracks in old walls. Its fragrant flowers usually have four petals and are often yellow or orange, while cultivated varieties offer other colors. Narrow green leaves grow along stems that become woody near the base. It is a short-lived perennial, although gardeners often grow it over two seasons. Modern references may list it as Erysimum x cheiri, reflecting its treatment as a hybrid. That name and the older name Cheiranthus cheiri are useful when comparing garden labels or botanical records.

amaranthus-muricatus.summary: African amaranth comes from South America, despite its common name. It is an inconspicuous herb with spreading or partly upright stems, narrow leaves and small flowers gathered near the stem tips. Its tiny fruits become strongly wrinkled as they mature, giving rise to another name, roughfruit amaranth. Regional floras describe it in disturbed places such as roadsides and cultivated ground. It may live for one season or persist as a short-lived perennial, so lifespan alone is not a reliable identifying feature. Neither a common name nor an overseas weed record establishes the status of a population near you.

asparagus-asparagoides.summary: African asparagus fern climbs through other vegetation on thin, twisting stems. Despite its name, it is a flowering plant in the asparagus family, not a fern. Its glossy oval 'leaves' are flattened stems; small pale flowers are followed by berries that turn red as they ripen. Below ground, thickened roots store reserves while connected underground stems allow the plant to spread and return after its shoots die back. It is also widely known as bridal creeper. Outside its African native range, dense growth can shade nearby vegetation, while its underground network makes an established patch difficult to remove completely.

cynodon-nlemfuensis.summary: African bermudagrass spreads across the ground on runners that take root at their joints. Also called African stargrass, this warm-climate perennial is grown for forage and ground cover, but it can extend beyond the place where it was planted. Its flowering stems carry several narrow branches spreading from near the tip like a star. Common names have been applied inconsistently within this group, so the scientific name matters when comparing references. Unlike common bermudagrass, Cynodon nlemfuensis lacks underground spreading stems called rhizomes. Its above-ground runners are nevertheless capable of establishing new growth when moved.

sarotherodon-melanotheron.summary: African blackchin tilapia is a coastal African fish that can live in fresh, brackish and salt water. Adults often have dark patches beneath the mouth and across the lower head, although their coloring varies. It belongs to the cichlid family and is established in parts of Florida and Hawaii. The male shelters developing eggs and young in his mouth, a behavior called mouthbrooding. In Hawaii, introduced populations raise concerns about competition with native fish and changes to aquatic vegetation. Those concerns describe particular environments; they do not tell us how many fish are present or what effects they have in every recorded location.

sansevieria-cylindrica.summary: African bowstring hemp grows a fan of stiff, rounded leaves that taper to sharp points. It is a succulent from Angola, often sold as a houseplant under the names African spear or cylindrical snake plant. Current botanical references usually call it Dracaena angolensis; Sansevieria cylindrica is the older name used in this catalog. Its leaves arise from connected underground stems, allowing new shoots to appear beside an established plant. Braided leaves in a shop are arranged by growers, not a natural growth form. A cultivated plant and a self-sustaining population outside a garden are different kinds of observations.

lycium-ferocissimum.summary: African boxthorn is a densely branched shrub from southern Africa, with rigid thorns and small clusters of fleshy leaves. Pale flowers give way to shiny orange-red berries. It was planted as a living hedge in some regions, but birds can carry its seeds beyond those boundaries. Established shrubs can form difficult-to-cross thickets and compete with nearby vegetation. In Australian landscapes, dense growth has also blocked livestock access to water. Those documented effects help explain why the plant is managed there; local records and conditions are still needed to understand a particular United States population.

setaria-sphacelata.summary: African bristlegrass forms lasting clumps topped by narrow, bristly flower heads. It has been grown for livestock forage, and some forms also establish along roadsides and in other disturbed ground. The species includes several varieties that differ considerably in height, leaf width and how they spread. Some produce abundant seed, while others spread mainly when stems fall over and root where they touch the ground. That variation matters when interpreting a record or planning removal. Its use as a pasture grass does not mean every stand is harmless, and its inclusion in a catalog does not mean all varieties behave alike.

xenopus-laevis.summary: African clawed frogs spend most of their lives in water. Their flattened bodies, upward-facing eyes and broad webbed hind feet suit that way of life, while their small front feet help push food into the mouth. They come from sub-Saharan Africa and have been moved around the world for research and the pet trade. Released or escaped animals have established populations in some United States watersheds. They eat a wide range of small aquatic animals and can threaten native species through predation and disease transmission. An isolated sighting, however, is different from evidence that a population is reproducing locally.

chasmanthe-floribunda.summary: African cornflag is a South African perennial grown for its orange-red, sometimes yellow, flowers. It grows from a corm, a swollen underground stem, and produces long, strap-shaped leaves. Flowering stems rise above the leaves and carry tubular flowers in two opposite rows. Plants can spread through seed and small new corms, including when garden soil or discarded plants are moved. Its presence in a garden does not establish that it has escaped nearby; a record of plants growing beyond cultivation is a separate finding.

cenchrus-macrourus.summary: African feathergrass is a tall, clump-forming perennial with narrow, bristly flower heads. The underground stems, called rhizomes, let an established patch spread beyond the original clump and grow back after the leaves are cut. It has been planted as an ornamental and can move with soil, garden waste and machinery. You may find it listed as Pennisetum macrourum. Some current references, including Kew, place Cenchrus macrourus under Cenchrus caudatus; this profile retains the name used by our catalog so its records remain traceable.

zaprionus-indianus.summary: African fig fly is a small fruit fly with pale stripes bordered in black along its head and thorax. It can enter figs through their natural opening and is also found around damaged or overripe fruit. Its behavior varies with the crop: recent University of Kentucky guidance also reports infestation of ripening berries, so it should not be described as feeding only on fruit that is already damaged. It may occur alongside spotted-wing drosophila. Finding both flies near a crop does not, by itself, show which one caused the original injury.

hemichromis-letourneuxi.summary: African jewelfish is a small predatory cichlid established in Florida, where it lives in habitats including canals, creeks and marshes. Its colors change: a tan fish with blue speckles can become much redder during breeding. Older Florida records often called it Hemichromis bimaculatus, which makes careful identification important when reading historical reports. More recent references use Rubricatochromis letourneuxi for the species covered here. Research has documented its expansion beyond the Miami area and effects on native fish communities in the Everglades; those findings do not imply equal effects at every location.

hemarthria-altissima.summary: African jointgrass, often called limpograss in forage references, is a perennial grass that spreads through creeping stems and underground growth. It is grown as livestock forage in parts of Florida, especially on moist, poorly drained ground. Stems can root at their lower joints, allowing a planting to extend outward. In suitable climates it can keep growing later into the cool season than some other warm-season forage grasses. Its agricultural use and its behavior beyond a managed pasture are different questions; an occurrence record alone does not show that it is causing harm.

strigosella-africana.summary: African mustard is a small annual with pink to violet flowers and slender seedpods. Its branches may spread low across the ground rather than stand upright. The lower leaves are broader and usually lightly toothed; those farther up are smaller. Fine, branching hairs cover much of the plant. It grows on open, disturbed ground and in dry habitats, including desert scrub. Older records may call it Malcolmia africana. An introduced roadside mustard is not automatically this species: flower color, leaf shape, pods, and hairs need to agree.

elaeis-guineensis.summary: African oil palm is a robust, single-trunked palm from tropical Africa, widely grown as a crop in warm regions. Palm oil comes from the flesh of its fruit; palm-kernel oil comes from the seed inside. Each heavy bunch holds many closely packed fruits. Long, feather-shaped leaves make a broad crown, and spines line their stalks. Younger trunks retain old leaf bases, while older trunks can become relatively bare. A planted crop tree and seedlings spreading beyond a planting are different situations; documenting where young palms appear helps distinguish them.

olea-europaea-ssp-cuspidata.summary: African olive is an evergreen shrub or small tree with a dense crown, opposite leaves and small dark fruits carried by birds. Escaped stands can shade out other vegetation, as documented in New South Wales. Its scientific name needs care: older accounts used Olea europaea subsp. cuspidata for both African and Asian brown olives. A recent revision separates the African plants as subsp. africana and retains subsp. cuspidata for Asian plants. A familiar common name therefore does not settle which subspecies a record represents. Leaf photographs, planting history and the identification source all help clarify that distinction.

lepidium-africanum.summary: African pepperwort is a mustard-family herb with tiny flowers and small, flat seedpods. Its lower leaves are broader and toothed, while the upper leaves become narrow. It grows in gardens, roadsides, and other disturbed places and can persist beyond one growing season. Published floras describe considerable variation, including both hairless and hairy plants. The inconspicuous flowers are easy to overlook; a close view of mature pods and the hairs on their stalks usually provides more useful identification evidence. The name pepperwort is not a reason to taste an unidentified plant.

python-sebae.summary: African rock python, also called the northern African python, is a large, muscular constrictor from sub-Saharan Africa. Irregular dark markings cover a tan or gray-brown body, helping it blend into vegetation. It is nonvenomous, but a large snake can bite severely when disturbed. Its prey includes birds and mammals. Florida wildlife agencies monitor a localized introduced population in western Miami-Dade County. A single sighting elsewhere should be documented and investigated, not treated as proof that the species has established throughout that area.

senna-didymobotrya.summary: African senna, often sold as popcorn cassia, is a tropical African shrub with bright yellow flower spikes and dark unopened buds. It may stay small in a cold-climate summer garden but grow into a substantial woody plant where winters are mild. That difference matters when considering escapes. UF/IFAS classifies it as a high invasion risk in Florida using a predictive assessment. This is a warning about its potential to spread, rather than proof that every planted shrub has already harmed nearby habitat.

tamarix-africana.summary: African tamarisk is a Mediterranean shrub or small tree with slender branches and sprays of tiny pale flowers. In its native range it grows around estuaries, coastal wetlands and waterways that may dry seasonally. Its fine foliage can make an entire tree look feathery from a distance. Several other tamarisks have spread extensively in the western United States, but their distribution and impacts cannot simply be assigned to this species. A report needs a checked identification before it can tell us where African tamarisk itself is growing.

spathodea-campanulata.summary: African tuliptree is a tropical African tree widely planted for its large orange-red flowers. In Hawaii it has also spread into wet forests and pastures, where dense growth can crowd native vegetation. Its many winged seeds travel away from the parent tree, and a cut trunk can send up new shoots. A striking garden tree can therefore become an ongoing management problem in a suitable climate. The evidence from Hawaii is especially useful, but it should not be treated as a description of every place where this tree is cultivated.

phacochoerus-africanus.summary: The common warthog is an African wild pig adapted to open grassland and savanna. It grazes, digs for underground food and uses burrows for shelter. Escapes from exotic-animal ranches have established free-ranging populations in southern Texas, where researchers have studied it alongside wild pigs and native collared peccaries. These animals share parts of the landscape but are not the same species. A warthog sighting is useful information about an introduced animal; it does not by itself demonstrate a particular disease or the scale of local ecological damage.

dioscorea-bulbifera.summary: Air yam, also called air potato, climbs into shrubs and trees on fast-growing vines. Its most noticeable means of spread is the potato-like bulbil formed above ground where a leaf joins the stem. Fallen bulbils can start new vines, including very small ones, while underground parts can survive after the shoots are cut. In Florida and other warm parts of the United States, this growth can cover surrounding vegetation. The name is misleading: this is a yam relative, not a potato, and wild bulbils should not be treated as food.

melampsoridium-hiratsukanum.summary: This rust fungus infects alder leaves, producing orange-yellow spore patches and sometimes causing early leaf loss. Repeated heavy attacks can weaken trees, although a rusty leaf does not mean an alder is about to die. Its full life cycle alternates between alder and larch, and researchers have confirmed that cycle in the eastern Alps. The fungus can also spread repeatedly between alder leaves without a nearby larch being obvious. Several similar rusts occur on alder, which makes careful diagnosis particularly important when checking older records.

pinus-halepensis.summary: Aleppo pine is a Mediterranean evergreen widely planted in warm, dry landscapes. Young trees can be fairly upright, while older crowns often spread into irregular shapes with open spaces between branches. Its tolerance of heat and poor soil helps explain its popularity in California and the Southwest. A planted tree and a self-sown population are different things, however. When seedlings appear beyond a planting, check how far they have spread and what is growing around them. Their presence alone does not tell us how they are affecting that habitat.

ptychosperma-elegans.summary: Solitaire palm is a single-stemmed rainforest palm from Queensland, Australia, also grown in warm American landscapes. Its slender trunk and compact crown can make it seem a modest garden plant, but reproduction beyond a planting still deserves attention. The 2026 UF/IFAS assessment recommends caution and management to prevent escape in central and southern Florida. Northern Florida has a different assessment, reflecting its different conditions. Those regional distinctions are more useful than treating every cultivated palm as either harmless everywhere or equally invasive everywhere.

calophyllum-inophyllum.summary: Alexandrian laurel is a broad-crowned coastal tree with glossy leaves and fragrant white flowers. It is native across parts of the Indian Ocean and tropical Asia into the Pacific, and has been planted elsewhere for shade and other uses. Its round fruits can float, helping seeds travel along shores. The Florida assessment does not currently label it a problem species, although the southern assessment remains incomplete. Its inclusion here should therefore not be read as a claim that every tree is damaging nearby habitat.

medicago-sativa.summary: Alfalfa is a perennial forage legume that can persist along roadsides and field margins after escaping cultivation. Its deep root system and growing crown allow it to recover after cutting, which makes it valuable as a crop and explains why a roadside patch may return after mowing. Bacteria associated with its roots help supply nitrogen. An escaped plant is not automatically evidence of serious ecological harm: the Canadian biology review distinguishes survival outside cultivation from invasiveness. Local land use and the behavior of the actual patch still matter.

medicago-sativa-ssp-sativa.summary: This record concerns the cultivated alfalfa subspecies, rather than every plant in the wider Medicago sativa group. It is a perennial with a deep taproot and stems that regrow from the crown after cutting. Plants can survive beyond farm fields, including along roads and ditches. Distinguishing the subspecies matters because yellow-flowered relatives and fertile hybrids also occur. A county record identified only as Medicago sativa cannot automatically be made more precise by assigning it to this subspecies without supporting features or a checked specimen.

gracilaria-vermiculophylla.summary: This red seaweed grows as branching tangles in sheltered bays and estuaries, including muddy places where many seaweeds cannot attach easily. It originated in the northwestern Pacific and has reached both coasts of the United States. Genetic research points to northeastern Japan as an important source of introduced populations and oyster movements as a likely pathway. Its effects depend on the setting: heavy growth can alter existing habitat, but a Chesapeake Bay study also found young blue crabs using its mats as shelter. Neither outcome describes every bay.

grateloupia-doryphora.summary: Grateloupia doryphora is a red seaweed associated with the southeastern Pacific coast. Its name also appears in older accounts of an introduced seaweed in the northeastern United States, but that history needs care. The Rhode Island population first called G. doryphora was later identified as Grateloupia turuturu. These are different species, so records and impacts reported under the older name cannot all be carried into this profile. Such an American introduction record needs a checked specimen or documented reassessment. Independent Peruvian collections document the true species attached to rock in intertidal and subtidal habitats.

limonium-ramosissimum.summary: Algerian sea lavender is a perennial plant that can spread through the upper edges of salt marshes. In the San Francisco Bay area, research has documented dense stands in the transition between tidal marsh and drier ground, where native plant cover can decline. That transition provides important room for marsh vegetation to move as conditions change. This plant produces many seeds, particularly in the less salty, less frequently flooded part of the marsh. A patch near a path or levee therefore deserves attention even when it is not growing in the wettest ground.

alternanthera-philoxeroides.summary: Alligatorweed spreads across water and damp ground on stems that can root wherever their joints touch a suitable surface. Floating mats can fill the edges of ponds and channels, while plants on land form lower, tougher growth. A broken piece is enough to help it move to another site, making careless cutting or disposal part of the problem. Established infestations often need repeated, coordinated work. The same plant can look rather different in water and on a bank, so a small terrestrial patch should not be dismissed because it lacks a large floating mat.

phytomyza-gymnostoma.summary: Allium leafminer is a small fly whose larvae feed inside onions, leeks, garlic and related plants. Adults make neat rows of punctures in the leaves, and the larvae tunnel downward toward leaf bases and bulbs. Damaged plants may become distorted, and injured tissue can spoil. The insect has spread through parts of the eastern United States, with separate spring and fall activity periods documented in affected areas. The timing changes with location and weather, so a calendar from another state is a guide to monitoring rather than a dependable treatment date.

pimenta-dioica.summary: Allspice is an evergreen tropical tree grown for its aromatic berries, which are harvested unripe for the familiar spice. It comes from the Caribbean and Central America and is also planted in warm gardens elsewhere. A cultivated tree and a self-sown population are different records: the first shows where someone planted it, while the second can help document escape. Young plants establishing beyond a garden are worth recording. Whether they are displacing other vegetation needs a closer look at that site, rather than an assumption based on the tree's introduced origin.

cadra-cautella.summary: The almond moth is a stored-food pest also known as the tropical warehouse moth. Its caterpillars feed in dried fruit, nuts, seeds, grain products and other dry foods, leaving silk and waste that can spoil more material than they eat. Adults do not feed. In cooler climates, heated storage buildings can provide conditions that outdoor winters do not. Finding a moth in a kitchen is a reason to inspect food supplies, not proof that every package is infested or that the insect is definitely this species.

aloephagus-myersi.summary: The aloe aphid lives in sheltered parts of Aloe and Haworthia plants, where a colony can be easy to overlook. Its whitish wax makes it resemble a mealybug rather than a typical exposed, pear-shaped aphid. Reports from imported aloes in Korean greenhouses show how infested plants can carry it into new growing areas. Feeding can damage leaves, while sticky honeydew supports sooty mold. This is primarily a plant-health concern in the evidence checked here; a greenhouse finding does not establish an outdoor infestation across the surrounding county.

trifolium-hybridum.summary: Alsike clover is a perennial forage plant associated with cool, moist ground, including poorly drained pastures. Its pale flower heads often become pink as they age. Although it has been included in pasture mixtures, it needs particular care where horses graze. Veterinary guidance associates it with sunlight-related skin injury and, in some cases, liver disease. The substance and circumstances responsible are not fully understood. That uncertainty is a reason to identify the clover and assess the feed, not to assume that every clover has the same risk.

alyssum-strigosum.summary: This small, hairy mustard has pale yellow flowers and rounded seed pods. It is associated with dry, open places in the Mediterranean region and southwestern Asia. Its North American history is much less straightforward: Flora of North America reports that most records assigned to Alyssum strigosum were actually the similar Alyssum simplex. The treatment does not confirm that A. strigosum is established in the region. A name on an old specimen label therefore needs checking before it becomes evidence of a current local population.

aphis-amaranthi.summary: Pigweed aphid feeds on amaranths and can hide around their roots and stem bases rather than forming an obvious colony at the top of the plant. Florida researchers documented it on spiny amaranth and found that some older specimens had been given a different aphid's name. A later nursery record located a colony several inches below ground. These records make careful host and specimen identification worthwhile. They do not, by themselves, establish a major crop loss, a particular plant-virus risk or a need to treat every amaranth nearby.

pterygoplichthys-pardalis.summary: Amazon sailfin catfish is an armored, bottom-dwelling fish from South America that is traded for aquariums. Aquarium releases are a likely route into waters outside its native range. Introduced sailfin catfish populations have been recorded in the United States and elsewhere, but some contain hybrids or have uncertain species identifications. That matters when interpreting a map: a report of an armored catfish may be sound even when the exact species name needs revision. Evidence about a mixed population should not automatically be attributed to pure Pterygoplichthys pardalis.

cecropia-pachystachya.summary: Ambay pumpwood is a tropical South American tree with large, deeply lobed leaves. It readily occupies open or disturbed places, and researchers have documented self-sustaining populations along waterways and abandoned ground in parts of Indonesia and Singapore. Some of those trees were previously called Cecropia peltata, a related species. Checking the name changes how we understand both the introduction history and the appropriate response. The overseas evidence is informative, but it does not establish the same distribution or ecological effects in the United States.

anisandrus-maiche.summary: Anisandrus maiche is a tiny Asian ambrosia beetle now recorded in parts of North America. Like other ambrosia beetles, it tunnels into wood and grows fungi inside its galleries as food for its young. Researchers in central New York found it overwintering as mature larvae inside those galleries and producing two generations in a year. That local study helps explain when beetles may emerge from infested wood. It does not mean that every tree with a pinhole is infested by this species or that the same flight dates apply throughout the country.

euwallacea-similis.summary: Euwallacea similis is a small ambrosia beetle associated with wood, especially weakened trees and cut material. It is presumed native to parts of Asia and the Pacific and has established outside that region, including the southern United States. Reports of timber damage come mainly from tropical areas. Finding this beetle deserves an accurate identification, but it does not establish that a tree has the destructive disease associated with polyphagous or Kuroshio shot-hole borers.

syngonium-podophyllum.summary: American evergreen, often sold as arrowhead vine, changes dramatically as it grows. A small houseplant with arrow-shaped leaves can become a thick-stemmed climber in a warm, shaded landscape. In Florida, escaped vines spread across the ground and climb trees, where heavy growth can cover other vegetation. Stem pieces readily form new plants, making dumped cuttings an important escape route. Keeping a plant indoors is a different situation from allowing it to spread into a nearby wooded wetland.

caprella-scaura.summary: Caprella scaura is a marine amphipod often called a skeleton shrimp. Its thin, jointed body clings to seaweed and branching growth on ropes, docks, and boat hulls. Those surfaces give it shelter and opportunities to travel between harbors. Its original native range remains uncertain, although several recent expansions are well documented introductions. An Italian lagoon survey found strikingly different abundances among sites, a useful reminder that one occupied dock does not tell us how the animal behaves throughout a coastline.

phellodendron-amurense.summary: Amur corktree is a deciduous tree brought from eastern Asia for streets and gardens. Its deeply ridged, corky bark is memorable, but the seedlings beneath and beyond a planted tree often matter more to a woodland manager. Female trees bear dark fruit that birds carry away, and seedlings can establish in forest shade. In parts of the northern United States, escaped trees suppress native tree regeneration. A mature ornamental can therefore become a continuing seed source even when its own crown looks well contained.

rhinogobius-brunneus.summary: Amur goby is a small fish associated with the bottom of streams, but its name carries a complicated history. Rhinogobius brunneus once covered several related forms. Modern morphological and genetic work recognizes a more narrowly defined species in Japan and southeastern Korea. Older reports from Washington and Oregon used the broader name. Those reports are valuable historical records, yet they do not by themselves confirm that the introduced fish belong to the species as it is understood today.

lonicera-maackii.summary: Amur honeysuckle is a broad, densely branched shrub that can turn a woodland edge into a shaded thicket. Its leaves appear early and often remain after many neighboring plants have lost theirs. That long leafy season, combined with heavy branching, leaves less light for woodland flowers and young trees. Birds carry seeds from the red fruit into new places. Introduced from Asia, it is a significant forest invader in places such as Illinois, rather than simply a shrub found occasionally beyond a garden.

lernaea-cyprinacea.summary: Anchorworm is a crustacean, despite the thin, wormlike strand visible on an infected fish. The adult female embeds an anchoring structure in the fish while much of her body projects into the water. Lernaea cyprinacea infects many freshwater fishes, including carp, koi, and goldfish. Attachment wounds can become inflamed and allow secondary infection. Warm ponds are especially favorable settings, and introducing an infested fish can expose an entire connected system rather than just its nearest tank mate.

eichhornia-azurea.summary: Anchored waterhyacinth is a tropical American aquatic perennial that grows with its roots in the mud and long stems extending across the water. Flowers rise above the surface, while submerged and emergent leaves give a single plant two different appearances. It favors shallow, quiet or slow-moving water. Dense growth can obstruct waterways, but the Florida account describes limited North American occurrences rather than a widespread continental problem. Plant fragments carried on equipment provide a practical reason to recognize it early.

brugmansia-suaveolens.summary: Angel's tears is a soft-wooded shrub or small tree best known for its enormous hanging trumpets. Brugmansia suaveolens originates in Brazil and has been cultivated widely in warm gardens, with escapes recorded beyond its native range. In cooler climates it needs protection from frost. The flowers are striking, but the plant contains toxic alkaloids and should never be treated as an edible garden herb. An escaped shrub also needs a location-specific assessment; cultivation history alone does not demonstrate ecological damage.

opuntia-microdasys.summary: Bunny ears cactus, also called angel's-wings, makes low branching clumps of flattened pads. New pads often appear in pairs, giving the plant its familiar rabbit-ear outline. It lacks the obvious long spines of many cacti, but its clusters of tiny barbed bristles are readily detached and can injure people and animals. Garden material is an important spread route because detached pieces can root. In New South Wales it forms invasive thickets; that regional evidence should not be turned into a claim that every US occurrence is introduced.

dichanthium-aristatum.summary: Angleton bluestem is a warm-season perennial introduced into several regions as a pasture grass. It forms clumps, while some forms also spread through short underground stems or stems that root along the ground. Different forage selections can look and behave somewhat differently. It has naturalized in the southern United States and elsewhere. Its usefulness in a managed pasture does not make it suitable for a native grassland restoration, particularly where grazing and disturbance give introduced grasses opportunities to expand.

sitotroga-cerealella.summary: Angoumois grain moth hides its damaging stage inside a grain kernel. A young caterpillar enters the grain, feeds within it, and remains concealed through pupation. The emerging moth leaves a small exit hole. Wheat, corn, and other cereal grains can be affected, including stored material. Adults do not feed on the grain. In ear corn held in storage, the problem can continue from an old lot into a new one, which makes careful inspection and removal of residues especially valuable.

cowpea-mild-mottle-virus.summary: Cowpea mild mottle virus infects legumes, including cowpea and soybean, and is associated with the bean disease name angular mosaic. Whiteflies can carry it between plants. Infection does not always produce an obvious mottled leaf: experimental work in Brazilian soybean cultivars found infected plants with few visible symptoms as well as reductions in crop performance. Work in China also showed that infection alongside soybean mosaic virus can change the symptoms. A healthy-looking plant and a visibly damaged one therefore both need careful interpretation.

avena-sterilis.summary: Animated oat, also called sterile oat, is an annual wild grass with large seed units and long, twisted awns. The name sterilis is misleading: the plant produces seed and can be a serious contaminant of cereal crops. Its growing cycle fits many annual cropping systems, helping it persist in cultivated fields as well as roadsides. Contaminated seed, machinery, straw, and other farm material can move it. At the same time, this wild relative of cultivated oats has value to crop breeders as a source of useful traits.

myrrhis-odorata.summary: Myrrhis odorata is a perennial herb known as sweet cicely and, in some references, anise. It comes from mountainous parts of Europe and has escaped gardens in parts of North America. Soft, finely divided foliage, creamy-white flower clusters, and an anise-like scent give it a distinctive appearance. It can self-seed and regrow from root pieces. The familiar culinary name needs care: true anise is Pimpinella anisum, while several native North American plants called sweet cicely belong to Osmorhiza.

rapistrum-rugosum.summary: Annual bastardcabbage is a branching mustard that starts with leaves near the ground and later raises numerous small yellow flowers. It grows from a taproot and completes its cycle by producing distinctive, two-part fruits. Roadsides, railway margins, and other disturbed places are characteristic settings. It is introduced in regions including Texas and Australia. A flowering stand may be conspicuous, but its name and yellow color are not enough to establish either its identity or the effect it is having on a particular site.

poa-annua.summary: Annual bluegrass is the small, light-green grass that often produces pale seed heads in a closely mown lawn. It grows quickly in cool weather and can return through repeated flushes of seedlings. Despite its name, some forms persist for more than one season, especially in favorable turf settings. Its shallow roots make summer heat and drying difficult, which can leave uneven patches in a lawn or putting green. The management problem is closely tied to the site and the grass already being maintained there.

phalaris-canariensis.summary: Annual canarygrass is grown commercially for the seed used in birdseed mixtures. Plants also turn up along roads and other disturbed places, including sites near spilled seed. It grows as an annual tuft with fibrous roots, then produces compact heads that look rather like small striped eggs. This is Phalaris canariensis, a different species from perennial reed canarygrass. A few plants beneath a feeder should therefore be identified on their own merits, without importing the wetland-invasion history of their better-known relative.

iberis-amara.summary: Annual candytuft is a small garden flower with a distinctive uneven blossom: two of its four petals are noticeably larger than the others. Clusters begin compact and lengthen as fruits develop along the stem. Native to parts of Europe and northern Africa, it sometimes appears outside cultivation. NC State describes these US escapes without treating the species as invasive. Its appearance beyond a border is a reason to check where it is spreading, rather than proof that nearby habitat is being damaged.

vulpia-myuros.summary: Annual fescue, more often called rattail fescue, is a fine-leaved grass with long bristles that give its narrow head a tail-like outline. It can be an easily overlooked component of disturbed ground and a difficult weed in Pacific Northwest wheat systems. Experimental work found that newly formed seeds need a period of afterripening before germinating readily, while cool conditions and winter exposure help shape its annual cycle. These details explain why a field may produce another flush after the first visible plants have disappeared.

stachys-annua.summary: Annual hedge-nettle is a modest member of the mint family with pale, two-lipped flowers above paired leaves. In North American field guides it is treated as an annual, returning through seed rather than forming the conspicuous long-lived patches associated with many familiar hedge-nettles. Its native range extends across Europe into parts of Asia. Scattered introduced records include fields and disturbed ground in New England. In these records it is mainly a plant of managed or disturbed ground; the effect of a particular patch should be assessed locally.

mercurialis-annua.summary: Annual mercury is a branching green herb whose small flowers are easy to miss. It occupies cultivated or disturbed ground and has scattered introduced records in North America. Many plants carry male and female flowers on separate individuals, but the name has also been used broadly for related forms with different reproductive systems. That distinction matters when reading weed reports: a US risk assessment deliberately combined annual mercury with forms sometimes recognized as Mercurialis ambigua. Its conclusions cannot all be assigned to narrowly identified M. annua.

polypogon-monspeliensis.summary: Annual rabbitsfootgrass earns its name from the soft-looking outline of its flowerhead. Fine bristles crowd a dense pale-green head that becomes straw-colored as it matures. This grass grows in damp, open places, including ditches, pond edges, irrigated fields, and disturbed ground. It returns through seed. Its seasonal timing varies with climate: in mild regions it often grows as a winter annual, while colder areas can support a summer cycle. A wet garden corner and a natural wetland therefore call for different responses.

lolium-multiflorum.summary: Annual ryegrass, also called Italian ryegrass, is a fast-growing grass used for forage, cover crops, and temporary winter cover. It usually behaves as an annual or biennial, but the common name should not substitute for observing the actual plants. The same growth that is useful in a planned planting can make it a troublesome weed in small-grain fields or an unwanted component of turf. Whether it belongs at a site depends on the crop, intended use, and ability to prevent unwanted reseeding.

diplotaxis-muralis.summary: Annual wallrocket is a small yellow-flowered mustard associated with fields, paths, walls, and other disturbed places. Despite its common name, botanical accounts describe both annual and biennial plants. Most leaves cluster low on the plant, while slender flowering stems rise above them. Its native range includes Europe and neighboring regions, and it is introduced in many parts of North America. The useful starting point is a sound identification and an understanding of the site, rather than assuming that every roadside mustard has the same impacts.

melilotus-indicus.summary: Annual yellow sweetclover has leaves divided into three leaflets and narrow clusters of tiny yellow flowers. These develop into small, rounded pods with visible veins. It grows in disturbed ground and cultivated settings, including orchards, vineyards and grain fields. Its modest flower size helps distinguish it from larger sweetclovers, though a close look at the pods is often useful.

tapinoma-litorale.summary: Tapinoma litorale is a tiny ant that often nests above the ground in hollow twigs and vines. Small colonies can be easy to miss until their nesting material is disturbed. Available research places it within the native fauna of Florida and the West Indies. Its appearance in an invasive-species catalog should therefore not be treated as evidence that it is introduced or harmful everywhere it occurs.

anoecia-vagans.summary: Anoecia vagans is an aphid whose seasonal life connects dogwoods with the roots of grasses. Root-feeding forms can be yellowish, pale green or olive, while the spring founding female on dogwood is much darker. Different generations can therefore look quite unlike one another. Close relatives use similar plants, so the host and season are useful clues, but a reliable identification requires examination of the insects themselves. Reports of winged specimens alone do not establish a damaging local population.

aphis-eugeniae.summary: Aphis eugeniae is a small aphid that feeds on several kinds of shrubs and trees. Older Asian accounts emphasize spurge-family hosts, while Florida records show a preference for rose-family plants, including apples, pears and especially loquat. Some Florida colonies can damage these hosts. It closely resembles the spirea aphid, so color and host plant alone are unreliable guides. Specialists distinguish it using fine features of the legs and other appendages.

asiphonella-dactylonii.summary: Asiphonella dactylonii feeds on the roots and lower parts of grasses, including bermudagrass. Its pale body may be covered with bluish-white wax, and colonies can remain hidden near or below the soil surface. That makes it less conspicuous than aphids clustered on shoots. Records establish its association with grasses, but do not by themselves show that it causes serious damage wherever it is found.

cerataphis-lataniae.summary: Cerataphis lataniae is an aphid that can look surprisingly like a scale insect. Its body is flattened and oval, with a fringe of white wax around the edge. It feeds on palms and belongs to a group whose members are easily confused, especially with Cerataphis brasiliensis. A photograph may show the waxy outline clearly without revealing enough detail to identify the species confidently.

dysaphis-crataegi.summary: Dysaphis crataegi belongs to a difficult group of aphids associated with hawthorns and carrots. This profile follows the named carrot-associated species while keeping its close relatives separate. In spring, some populations make reddish curled-leaf galls on hawthorn, then move to feed around the base and roots of herbaceous hosts. The wingless aphids are pale yellowish to gray-green and dusted with wax. Colonies can hide near the soil surface. Several close relatives look much the same, so the host and a close examination matter when identifying them.

eucallipterus-tiliae.summary: Eucallipterus tiliae feeds in groups beneath linden leaves. The small aphids are greenish with dark side markings, and winged forms have dusky areas on their wings. A colony may first draw attention through sticky honeydew on leaves, sidewalks or parked cars; dark sooty mold can grow on this sugary coating. Established trees often tolerate the feeding, although saplings can suffer reduced growth. The insect stays with lindens through its seasonal cycle.

geoica-setulosa.summary: Geoica setulosa is a pale aphid that feeds on grass roots. Ants tend its colonies for honeydew and may build small soil mounds around them. In turf, these mounds can be more noticeable than the aphids themselves and may cover or smother nearby grass. Understanding the relationship between the two insects helps explain damage that might otherwise be attributed entirely to root feeding.

geopemphigus-floccosus.summary: Geopemphigus floccosus is a root-feeding aphid associated with morning-glories in the genus Ipomoea. Wingless individuals are pale greenish yellow with tufts of white wax; winged forms can look grayer and have dark bands across the abdomen. Much of its feeding takes place out of sight below ground. Its complete life cycle remains uncertain, so an apparent association with a second host should not be treated as a proven seasonal migration.

greenidea-ficicola.summary: Greenidea ficicola feeds on young leaves and shoots of figs, including ornamental Ficus plants. Its green to brown body has unusually long, hairy tubes that curve outward from the rear, a useful clue for recognition. Researchers have documented colonies on several fig species in Florida. Another introduced Greenidea also feeds on figs, so confirming the species requires closer attention to the surface pattern of those tubes and other small features.

hyalopterus-amygdali.summary: Hyalopterus amygdali is a slender, green aphid often covered with pale, mealy-looking wax. It is associated with almonds and can use reeds during part of its seasonal cycle. Closely related aphids look very similar and may occur on related host plants. For that reason, the host alone is not a reliable identification, and specialists sometimes use genetic evidence to distinguish members of this group.

hyperomyzus-lactucae.summary: Hyperomyzus lactucae can curl and yellow currant leaves in spring before moving to sowthistles, where it feeds on stems and flower shoots. In warmer regions, colonies may remain on these herbaceous hosts. It is a green aphid and can transmit certain plant viruses. Finding the insect is not the same as confirming a virus infection, since leaf symptoms can have several causes.

hyperomyzus-picridis.summary: Hyperomyzus picridis is a glossy yellow-green aphid associated with alpine currant, oxtongues and hawksbeards. Colonies can gather just below flower heads, where they feed on tender growth. Host plants and small anatomical details help distinguish it from similar aphids. It also forms part of a wider insect community: a field study in France reared several kinds of parasitoid wasps from this aphid. Those observations describe its ecology without establishing damage at other locations.

macrosiphoniella-tanacetaria.summary: Macrosiphoniella tanacetaria feeds on tansy, gathering in loose colonies around the tips of shoots. A controlled study found that its performance changed with the growing conditions of the host: fertilizer and competition from goldenrod affected plant growth and the aphids. This helps explain why colony size should be considered alongside the condition of the plant, rather than interpreted as a fixed measure of damage.

macrosiphum-lilii.summary: Macrosiphum lilii is an aphid associated with lilies. It can be pale yellow or orange, sometimes with a purple patch, and has long, dark legs and tubes at the rear of its body. Feeding colonies produce honeydew, which can make nearby plant surfaces sticky. Its seasonal life cycle is not well documented in the available accounts, so host and appearance provide a better starting point than assumptions about its movements.

melanaphis-sorini.summary: Melanaphis sorini is an aphid associated with Miscanthus grasses. Florida records include plants arriving from California and subsequent observations in the ornamental trade. Florida observers have not considered it a pest of Miscanthus grown for biomass there. This specific regional experience matters: the genus also contains important crop pests, but those relatives do not automatically describe what a colony on an ornamental grass is doing.

metopolophium-festucae.summary: Metopolophium festucae is a grass-feeding aphid that may be green, yellow or pink. Winged individuals can have dark bands on the body. It belongs to a group in which the subspecies matters: the cereal-feeding form, Metopolophium festucae cerealium, has its own records and research history. A broad identification to species should not automatically be treated as evidence for that particular crop-associated form.

metopolophium-festucae-cerealium.summary: Metopolophium festucae cerealium is a pale, elongated aphid found on cereal crops such as wheat and barley. Winged individuals have dark markings on the back. It has been recorded in the Pacific Northwest and Kansas. Greenhouse studies found that feeding can harm wheat, while field work documented substantial populations in parts of the Northwest. Those findings do not establish the same level of crop loss in every field.

myzaphis-rosarum.summary: Myzaphis rosarum is a small aphid associated with roses and shrubby cinquefoil. Colonies can occur along the midribs of young leaves. A modern revision compared specimens to distinguish it from related Myzaphis, using details of the antennae, body surface and other fine structures. These features are difficult to see in a casual garden photograph, so a host name and a greenish color are useful clues rather than a complete diagnosis.

myzus-varians.summary: Myzus varians feeds beneath peach leaves, which may roll tightly lengthwise and turn reddish around its colonies. Wingless adults are pale green; winged adults are darker. In its seasonal cycle it can move between peach and clematis, overwintering as eggs near peach buds. Experiments have shown that it can carry plum pox virus from peach to clematis. Finding the aphid or a curled leaf alone does not confirm that a plant is infected.

pleotrichophorus-chrysanthemi.summary: Pleotrichophorus chrysanthemi is a pale yellow-green aphid found beneath chrysanthemum leaves. Feeding may be associated with yellowing, including on plants grown under greenhouse conditions. Its identity is complicated by questions about how it differs from the closely related P. glandulosus. Specialists compare tiny body hairs and other structures, together with the host plant. A careful identification is therefore important before treating similar aphids on chrysanthemums as the same species.

rhopalomyzus-lonicerae.summary: Rhopalomyzus lonicerae has different-looking colonies at different points in its life cycle. Dark green aphids feed on honeysuckle in spring, where leaves may roll around them. Later, paler colonies can occur on grasses, including reed canarygrass in wet places. This seasonal change in host and appearance is useful context: two colonies that look different may still belong to the same species.

rhopalosiphum-rufiabdominalis.summary: Rhopalosiphum rufiabdominale is commonly associated with roots, where its colonies are easily missed. The aphids are greenish to brown, sometimes with a rusty area toward the rear, and use grasses and other plants, including greenhouse crops. Their hidden feeding habits can complicate diagnosis. Poor root growth alone is not enough to identify them; the insects themselves need to be found and examined.

sipha-glyceriae.summary: Sipha glyceriae is a tiny aphid most often found on grasses in damp places, with some records from sedges and rushes too. Wingless adults are usually dull green, sometimes reddish, and may have a paler stripe along the back. They are only about two millimeters long. Unlike aphids that move between trees and grasses through the seasons, this species completes its cycle on herbaceous plants. Identifying it confidently requires a close look: specialists compare its body hairs and minute surface features with those of related grass aphids.

sipha-maydis.summary: Sipha maydis is a dark, glossy aphid with stiff hairs, often found near the bases of grass leaves. It feeds on grasses and cereal crops, including wheat, barley, oats and corn. Colonies can injure leaves, and the species can also transmit plant viruses. Its nearly black or brown appearance helps distinguish it from some common green aphids, though a close examination is still important.

tinocallis-ulmiparvifoliae.summary: Tinocallis ulmiparvifoliae is an aphid associated with Chinese elm. Winged individuals have pale blue-green bodies with white wax stripes and spots, and colonies feed on the leaves. Originally associated with Asia, it has also been recorded in Florida as an introduced insect. Its host is a useful clue, but fine anatomical features are needed to distinguish it confidently from other elm-feeding aphids.

tuberocephalus-sakurae.summary: Tuberocephalus sakurae is a tiny aphid associated with cherry trees. Feeding can turn the leaves red or yellow and curl them into sheltered spaces for the insects. Wingless adults on cherry are dark green to black, with brighter young nearby. The species also alternates to underground parts of Artemisia plants. Distorted leaves may be easier to notice than the aphids themselves, but similar damage can have other causes and does not establish the species on its own.

uroleucon-picridis.summary: Uroleucon picridis is a shiny reddish-brown aphid associated with oxtongues in the genus Picris. Colonies may gather on stems just below the flowers. Dark antennae and rear tubes contrast with a paler, yellowish tail-like projection at the end of the body. These details help specialists distinguish it from related aphids. Host identification matters too: some older records from other plants involve similar species, so color alone is not enough for a reliable identification.

aphidius-ervi.summary: This aphid parasite is a tiny wasp that uses aphids as a nursery for its young. A female Aphidius ervi lays an egg inside an aphid; the developing wasp eventually leaves a dry, swollen shell called a mummy and emerges through a round hole. It attacks aphids including potato and foxglove aphids and is used in biological control. Its presence can therefore reflect pest management rather than a new pest problem.

aphis-pomi.summary: Apple aphid gathers on young leaves and shoots, including the vigorous upright shoots of apple trees. The green insects feed on plant sap and produce sticky honeydew that can support sooty mold. Heavy colonies may weaken young growth, while predators can help limit their numbers. The aphid survives winter as dark eggs on woody growth, ready to hatch as fresh leaves become available.

cassia-javanica.summary: Apple blossom, Cassia javanica, is a tropical tree grown for generous clusters of pink flowers. Its leaves are divided into pairs of leaflets, and its fruit develops into long, cylindrical pods. The tree has a spreading crown and can lose some or all of its leaves seasonally. Several botanical forms differ in their leaves and flower clusters, so a precise identification benefits from photographs of both. Despite its common name, it belongs to the legume family.

cassia-javanica-var-indochinensis.summary: This form of apple blossom belongs to the Cassia javanica group of tropical flowering trees. Botanical references place the older name var. indochinensis under Cassia javanica subsp. agnes. It has paired leaflets and pink flowers, with branching flower clusters at the ends of young leafy shoots. Pink flowers alone cannot separate it from related forms. A comparative study identifies leaflet details, shoot hairs, stipules and flower structures as useful clues, so a confident identification needs a closer look than flower color.

phenacoccus-aceris.summary: Apple mealybug is a soft-bodied insect covered in white wax. It feeds on several woody plants, not just apples, and may hide in bark crevices where colonies are easy to miss. White egg sacs and sticky honeydew can reveal its presence. Orchard sources report insects identified under this name as vectors of little cherry virus 2. This finding should not be assigned automatically to every lookalike in the species group, making accurate diagnosis particularly important in fruit-growing areas.

mentha-suaveolens.summary: Applemint is a perennial herb with rounded, wrinkled, hairy leaves and a fruity scent. Small, pale flowers grow in spikes above the foliage. It spreads through underground stems, which can carry it beyond the edges of a garden bed. Native to parts of Europe and the Mediterranean region, it also grows outside cultivation in moist ground. Its soft leaves help distinguish it from smoother-leaved mints.

nicandra-physalodes.summary: Apple of Peru has pale blue, bell-shaped flowers followed by fruit enclosed in a papery covering. This annual member of the nightshade family comes from South America and can grow quickly in fertile, disturbed ground. It spreads by seed and may appear as a garden escape or field weed. Despite the familiar-looking fruit covering, it should not be confused with edible groundcherries.

jasminum-sambac.summary: Arabian jasmine is an evergreen shrub or scrambling climber with glossy, oval leaves and strongly scented white flowers. The flowers may turn pink as they age, and cultivated forms can have one or several layers of petals. Despite its name, its native range includes areas from Bhutan to India. It is widely grown in warm climates for its flowers and fragrance.

schismus-arabicus.summary: Arabian schismus is a small annual grass with fine leaves and a short, compact flower head. It grows in dry, open places and disturbed desert ground. Southwestern U.S. studies of mixed Schismus stands show that dry growth can connect fine fuels between shrubs; wet seasons can increase annual-grass cover. It closely resembles Schismus barbatus, another introduced desert grass. Small differences in the flower parts are more dependable for separating them than a photograph of their leaves.

brachyrhynchus-membranaceus.summary: Brachyrhynchus membranaceus is a flat bug associated with fungi and decaying wood. Its flattened body suits the sheltered spaces used by these insects. Originally known from the Old World, it has also been documented in the Caribbean and Central America. It feeds on fungal growth and has sometimes damaged cultivated bracket fungi. Finding this insect around wood does not by itself show that a healthy tree is being attacked; its documented food is fungal tissue.

neophyllaphis-araucariae.summary: Araucaria aphid feeds on young growth of Araucaria trees, including around the bases of needles on fresh shoots. Wingless individuals are broadly oval and bright yellow to orange, measuring only about one to one and a half millimeters long. Their tiny size makes a close look worthwhile. The species has been recorded in several tropical and subtropical regions, but that wide distribution does not clearly identify its original home. The host and color are useful clues rather than a complete diagnosis.

lindingaspis-rossi.summary: Araucaria black scale can look like a dark speck attached to a leaf. The female shelters beneath a nearly circular, flattened brown-black cover with darker shed skins near its center. Despite the name, its hosts extend well beyond Araucaria: palms, olives and many other woody plants have been recorded. This broad host range makes examination of the insect especially useful. A dark spot on a familiar plant can suggest an armored scale, but it does not establish this species.

opuntia-leucotricha.summary: Arborescent pricklypear is a Mexican cactus that can grow into a large shrub or small tree. Its gray-green pads carry white hairs and spines, while older growth develops a trunk. Yellow flowers are followed by fleshy fruit. Broken pads can take root, allowing plants to spread from discarded garden material. It has escaped cultivation in places including Australia, where dense growth can become a management problem.

linepithema-humile.summary: Argentine ants are small brown ants often seen moving in long, busy trails. They form networks of shallow nests with multiple queens and can spread through gardens, buildings and natural areas. Native to South America, they have become established in many other regions. They collect sugary honeydew from sap-feeding insects and can displace other ants where their colonies become dominant.

salvator-merianae.summary: Argentine black and white tegu is a large, strong-bodied lizard with a banded tail. Young animals often have greenish heads. It eats a wide range of foods and can shelter in burrows during cold weather. Established populations in Florida are a concern because tegus eat native wildlife, including eggs and young animals; documented prey include alligator eggs and young gopher tortoises.

lepidium-bonariense.summary: Argentine pepperweed is a hairy member of the mustard family with divided lower leaves and simpler leaves higher on the stem. Its small white flowers develop into flattened pods with a notch at the tip. The lower leaves may disappear as the plant matures, changing its overall appearance. Looking at both the remaining leaves and the seed pods helps distinguish it from other pepperweeds.

aonidiella-taxus.summary: Aonidiella taxus is an armored scale found on yews, plum-yews and Podocarpus. A pale, partly transparent cover hides the reddish female beneath it, often on the underside of a leaf. Feeding can leave yellow patches around the insects. Its life also involves much smaller visitors: researchers in Japan found several kinds of tiny wasps parasitizing this scale. The cover and host plant offer useful clues, but related scales can look alike and a confident species identification requires microscopic examination.

dynaspidiotus-pseudomeyeri.summary: Arborvitae scale is a tiny armored insect associated with arborvitae, junipers and other conifers. Its cover can be oval or almost round, with a dull greenish-yellow color that becomes paler and browner with age. Infestations may accompany discolored foliage and dying twigs. A Pennsylvania study found a small parasitic wasp attacking this scale, and predatory mites sheltering in the empty scale covers afterward. Those observations reveal a small community around the insect, but do not establish a tested treatment for an infested tree.

gymnaspis-aechmeae.summary: Gymnaspis aechmeae is a tiny armored scale sometimes called flyspeck scale. Its dark covering can resemble a speck of dirt on bromeliads and other ornamental plants, including those grown in greenhouses. The female remains within the skin from an earlier growth stage and produces live young that can crawl to new feeding sites. Infested plants provide a route for it to move between locations.

howardia-biclavis.summary: Mining scale can be easy to miss because plant tissue often partly hides its pale, rounded cover. The cover may be white, gray or yellow and is roughly three millimeters across at most. Howardia biclavis feeds on many kinds of woody plants. Researchers studying Mexican avocado orchards found it singly or in very small groups on branches, sometimes alongside other armored scales. Despite its common name, the exact way it becomes covered by plant tissue is not well understood, so it is better described as concealed than as a proven tunneling insect.

lepidosaphes-pinnaeformis.summary: Lepidosaphes pinnaeformis leaves small brown, mussel-shaped covers on the leaves and sometimes stems of its hosts. Orchids are frequent hosts, and dense colonies can leave a patchwork of discolored feeding spots. The insect is not restricted to orchids: a Mexican orchard study also found it on avocado branches. Its covers can look much like those of other Lepidosaphes scales. A close view helps locate the insects, while microscopic features of the female are needed to distinguish similar species reliably.

lepidosaphes-yanagicola.summary: Fire bush scale often shelters between the corky ridges on winged euonymus twigs. Its female has a small brown, oyster-shaped cover with a pale body underneath. Lepidosaphes yanagicola also uses other deciduous trees and shrubs, including willow, maple and elm. Adult females can survive the winter and produce eggs the following summer. Heavy infestations sometimes accompany early leaf fall and twig dieback, although damage varies among locations. This is a different insect from Unaspis euonymi, another scale associated with euonymus.

neopinnaspis-harperi.summary: Harper scale can blend into bark even when several insects are present. Its narrow, nearly flat tan covers are only about one to two millimeters long, with darker shed skins at one end and a pink or red female underneath. It feeds on a variety of woody plants and often settles in bark cracks. A specialist comparing specimens from California, Japan and Taiwan confirmed how widely the same species had been recorded. Its sheltered position and resemblance to other scales make microscopic examination important for a reliable identification.

parlatoria-camelliae.summary: Parlatoria camelliae is an armored scale found on camellias and other hosts. Its pale to gray covering has a darker patch made from earlier shed skins. Colonies can occur on either side of a leaf, often near veins, and feeding may discolor the foliage. Reports from places such as Galicia document its presence, but identification still requires attention to the insect rather than leaf discoloration alone.

rutherfordia-major.summary: Rutherfordia major is an armored scale associated with lychee and other tropical woody plants. Its initially pale covering may become covered by plant tissue and appear reddish or dark, helping it blend into bark. It has been introduced to places including the Galapagos. Movement of host plants is relevant to its spread, while the full history of its original distribution remains less certain.

selenaspidus-albus.summary: Selenaspidus albus is an armored scale with a small white disk for a cover. Slightly off-center, yellow-brown remains of earlier growth stages form a contrasting patch. The female's cover is usually less than two millimeters across, making a single insect easy to overlook. Euphorbia is a documented host, and crowded colonies have been reported on cultivated plants. A British botanical-garden report also found a heavy infestation on an imported Euphorbia kept in a heated glasshouse.

selenaspidus-articulatus.summary: West Indian red scale forms thin, partly transparent disks on leaves, often on the upper surface. Each female's cover has a pale edge and an off-center patch of darker shed skins. Citrus is a frequent host, but Selenaspidus articulatus feeds on many other plants, including rubber trees. Dense populations can cause yellowing and damaged leaf or fruit tissue. A field study in Brazil found that numbers on rubber trees changed with the season and differed among tree clones, so infestation levels should be assessed in their local setting.

unaspis-citri.summary: Unaspis citri is often noticed as a snowy white coating on citrus trunks and branches. That appearance comes largely from the white covers of immature males; females have darker, shell-shaped covers. Heavy feeding can weaken trees, contribute to branch dieback and cause bark to split. Its concentration on woody parts of the tree helps distinguish citrus snow scale from some scales found mainly on leaves.

andaspis-punicae.summary: This armored scale is listed as Andaspis punicae, though newer references also place it in Lepidosaphes. Its brown, elongated covering resembles a small shell on woody hosts, including lychee. Heavy populations may reduce plant vigor or damage branches. Changes in the scientific name can make records harder to connect, so both names are useful when checking the research behind an identification.

fiorinia-proboscidaria.summary: Snout scale is a tiny armored insect found on citrus and other plants. The female remains enclosed within a shed skin from an earlier stage, producing a brown, elongated covering with a conspicuous ridge along its back. Dense colonies may also leave white secretions on the leaves. The 'snout' is a much smaller feature of the female's head, visible with close microscopic study. Several related Fiorinia species look similar in the field, so the shape of a brown cover alone is not a reliable identification.

dichrostachys-cinerea.summary: Aroma is a thorny shrub or small tree with finely divided leaves and hanging, two-tone flower heads. Pink or mauve sterile flowers contrast with the yellow fertile end, and clustered pods twist as they mature. Dichrostachys cinerea can establish from seed and spread through shoots arising from its roots, sometimes forming dense thickets. That growth occurs even within its native African range. A South African field study found root suckers among young plants under several fire and grazing regimes, showing why its spreading habit needs local context.

paspalum-paniculatum.summary: Arrocillo is a coarse perennial grass that forms leafy clumps. Its broad blades may feel hairy or rough, while the flowering head opens into many slender, spreading branches. Tiny rounded spikelets sit in paired rows along those branches, a useful detail for identification. Paspalum paniculatum grows in disturbed clearings and other open ground. Its home range includes tropical America, while regional floras record it as introduced elsewhere, including the United States and Australia; a local record needs that regional context.

pseudosasa-japonica.summary: Arrow bamboo has upright canes and long, broad leaves that make it popular as a screen. Beneath the soil, spreading stems can carry new shoots well beyond the original planting. It can form dense patches where it escapes cultivation. Records from places including Maryland and New Zealand illustrate why its underground growth matters when assessing a planting near neighboring gardens or natural vegetation.

xanthosoma-sagittifolium.summary: Arrowleaf elephant ear has large, arrow-shaped leaves held on long stalks that meet the leaf at its base. Thick underground growth and new shoots help it expand into patches. It favors warm, moist places and can grow along streams. In parts of Florida, escaped plants are considered invasive, where their large leaves and dense growth can crowd other vegetation.

caladium-bicolor.summary: Artist's pallet is grown for its heart- to arrow-shaped leaves, patterned in combinations of green, white, pink and red. It grows from underground tubers and produces small flowers grouped on a fleshy spike within a pale surrounding leaf-like structure. Native to tropical America, it is widely cultivated. Its colorful foliage is ornamental rather than edible, and the plant's tissues can cause irritation.

diplosoma-listerianum.summary: Diplosoma listerianum is a name used for closely related colonial sea squirts that form thin, soft sheets over submerged surfaces. Many tiny filtering animals share the same gelatinous covering. Colonies grow on docks, boat hulls and natural surfaces, giving them opportunities to travel with marine traffic. They can cover other organisms as they spread, but the long history of transport makes the species' original native range difficult to establish.

polyandrocarpa-zorritensis.summary: Polyandrocarpa zorritensis is a colonial sea squirt made up of small, club-shaped individuals connected by root-like strands. Each has its own outer covering and two openings used in filter feeding. Colonies occur on docks, boats and natural surfaces such as mangrove roots, and can overgrow neighboring organisms. It was described from Peru, but that alone does not establish where it originally evolved.

siphoninus-phillyreae.summary: Ash whitefly feeds beneath the leaves of trees and shrubs, including pears, pomegranates and citrus. Adults are small and white; immature insects have distinctive waxy structures and may carry tiny droplets. Feeding and honeydew can harm foliage and encourage sooty mold. In California, introduced natural enemies greatly reduced a once-serious outbreak, making this species a notable example of successful biological control.

potentilla-inclinata.summary: Ashy cinquefoil has small yellow flowers and leaves divided into five to seven toothed leaflets. Pale hairs on the undersides give the foliage a grayish cast, and hairy stems rise above the lower leaves. It favors dry, open places, including roadsides, grasslands and disturbed ground. This Eurasian plant has been introduced to parts of North America. Several yellow-flowered cinquefoils look similar, so the leaflet shape, gray undersides and hairs around the flowers are more useful together than flower color alone.

sphaerodactylus-elegans.summary: Ashy geckos are tiny lizards that shelter in leaf litter, beneath bark and among rocks or woody debris, often near buildings. Young animals have bold bands and bright reddish tails; adults become tan to rusty brown with pale speckling. Sphaerodactylus elegans has been introduced to Florida, where other small geckos can complicate identification. Observations from Cuba also describe these geckos hunting flies and ants around a house during daylight. Their changing colors and secretive habits make a clear photograph more useful than a fleeting glimpse.

eriocaulon-cinereum.summary: Ashy pipewort forms a small tuft of very narrow leaves in wet ground. Slender stalks lift rounded, button-like flower heads above the foliage; these may look gray, yellowish or greenish rather than showy. Eriocaulon cinereum occurs in damp valleys and rice fields, including introduced populations recorded in California and Louisiana. Before flowering, its leaves can resemble a small grass. Mature heads are much more useful for recognition, although their tiny flowers still need close examination to distinguish this plant from other pipeworts.

polypogon-fugax.summary: Asia minor bluegrass, Polypogon fugax, is a loosely tufted annual with a compact flower head that may be pale green or tinged purple. Fine, short bristles edge the tiny flower clusters. Its stems can bend near the base and sometimes root at lower joints, while the leaves are often rough to the touch. It grows in moist places, including disturbed ground and farmland margins. Despite its common name, it belongs to Polypogon rather than Poa, and mature spikelets help separate it from similar grasses.

aedes-japonicus.summary: Asian bush mosquito has pale-banded legs and golden markings on its back. It uses small pools of water, including rock pools, tree holes, tires and other containers, and can thrive in relatively cool, wooded settings near homes. Its ability to use artificial containers helps it spread. The species can carry pathogens under some conditions, but finding it does not establish local disease transmission.

dryocosmus-kuriphilus.summary: Asian chestnut gall wasp causes rounded swellings on the buds, leaves and shoots of true chestnut trees. These galls start green or pink and later become woody and brown, sometimes remaining after the wasps have left. Heavy infestations can reduce shoot growth and nut production. The adult wasp is tiny, so the galls are usually the first sign people notice.

diaphorina-citri.summary: Asian citrus psyllid is a small sap-feeding insect often seen with its body tilted upward as it feeds on tender citrus growth. Young insects are yellow-orange and produce curled, waxy tubes. Feeding can distort new leaves, but its greater importance is its ability to transmit the bacteria associated with citrus greening disease. Identifying the insect accurately helps distinguish that risk from ordinary leaf damage.

blattella-asahinai.summary: Asian cockroach usually lives outdoors in leaf litter, mulch and similar sheltered places.
