It closely resembles the German cockroach, but flies readily and is attracted to lights, especially around dusk. Adults may enter buildings from outside. That behavior matters when interpreting a sighting: one flying into a lit room does not necessarily indicate the kind of indoor infestation associated with its lookalike.

acalypha-australis.summary: Asian copperleaf is an annual plant with upright stems and toothed, oval leaves. Young growth may be reddish. Broad, heart-shaped structures surround the small flowers and developing fruit, providing a useful identification feature. Native to Asia, it has been recorded as a weed in parts of the American Midwest, where it can grow and produce seed beneath a crop canopy.

ocinebrellus-inornatus.summary: Asian drill snail has a thick, ridged shell, commonly about one to two inches long. It lives among shells, gravel and mud around oyster beds, where it bores through the shells of its prey. Small oysters are especially vulnerable, although it also eats other shellfish. Native to the northwestern Pacific, it has traveled with oyster shipments. Clusters of bright yellow, bottle-shaped egg capsules can offer another clue to its presence.

cyperus-microiria.summary: Asian flatsedge is an annual sedge of muddy river margins, ditches and fields. Its narrow leaves grow below branched flower clusters surrounded by longer, leaf-like bracts. The small yellow-brown scales in those clusters have green, pointed midribs. Originally associated with East Asia, it has also been recorded as a field weed in Europe. Close flower details help distinguish it from similar sedges.

undaria-pinnatifida.summary: Asian kelp is the brown seaweed widely known as wakame. It has a broad blade with a clear central rib and a ruffled reproductive structure near the base. It grows on rocks as well as ropes and boat hulls, which can help it reach new coasts. Cultivated as food, it is also invasive in some temperate regions, where dense growth can change the habitat available to other marine life.

asian-longhorned-beetle.summary: Asian longhorned beetle is a large, glossy black beetle with white spots and long, banded antennae. Its pale larvae feed beneath the bark of hardwood trees, then tunnel deeper into the wood. Maples are among its hosts, and heavy feeding can eventually kill a tree. Round exit holes, chewed egg-laying marks and coarse sawdust-like material are useful signs. Native to Asia, it most likely reached the United States in wood packaging.

assiminea-parasitologica.summary: Asian marsh snail is a tiny brown snail with a blunt, cone-shaped shell, reaching only about five millimeters. It lives among vegetation high in salt or brackish marshes, where the ground is not continuously underwater. A field study in Japan found it concentrated in middle and upper tidal areas. Native to Japan and Korea, it has also been recorded in Oregon. Smithsonian reports no observed Oregon impacts, which does not establish that impacts are absent.

limnophila-sessiliflora.summary: Asian marshweed looks quite different above and below the water. Its submerged leaves are finely divided and arranged in whorls around the stem; leaves emerging into the air are firmer and toothed. Small pink to violet flowers appear above the surface. This Asian aquatic plant has been sold for aquariums and apparently escaped cultivation in the southeastern United States. Some stem fragments can root and regrow, while dense stands can shade and crowd other aquatic plants.

brassica-tournefortii.summary: Asian mustard begins as a rough-leaved rosette before sending up branching stems with small, pale yellow flowers and long seed pods. In southwestern North America, it can grow quickly after winter rain and compete with native desert wildflowers. It comes from the Mediterranean region and nearby parts of Asia. Its ability to spread through open desert habitat makes it more than an ordinary roadside weed in affected areas.

colubrina-asiatica.summary: Asian nakedwood is a sprawling evergreen shrub with shiny, toothed leaves, small greenish-yellow flowers and rounded seed capsules. Its seeds can float and tolerate salty conditions, helping it move through coastal environments. Native to parts of the Old World tropics, it has become invasive in Florida's coastal habitats, where its climbing and spreading growth can cover other vegetation.

pachycondyla-chinensis.summary: Asian needle ant is a dark ant with paler legs and antenna tips. It often nests in damp wood, leaf litter or beneath stones and feeds on termites and other small animals. Established in parts of the eastern United States, it can displace native ants, including species that disperse plant seeds. It also has a painful sting. Newer references usually call it Brachyponera chinensis.

clitoria-ternatea.summary: Asian pigeonwings is a tropical vine with striking blue flowers that have pale centers. Its leaves are divided into oval leaflets, and flat pods follow the flowers. Widely known as butterfly pea, it is grown ornamentally and for flowers used to color foods and drinks. It can live as a perennial in warm climates, climbing over nearby supports and vegetation.

dichondra-micrantha.summary: Asian ponysfoot forms a low green carpet of small, rounded to kidney-shaped leaves. Its creeping stems root as they spread, while tiny greenish-white flowers sit close to the ground and are easy to miss. Fine hairs, especially beneath the leaves, help with identification. Despite the common name, Kew places its native range in the Caribbean. It has been grown as a lawn substitute and can occur among lawn grasses. Related Dichondra species look similar, and regional references warn that this scientific name has sometimes been applied inconsistently.

hemigrapsus-sanguineus.summary: Asian shore crab has a square shell with three small teeth along each front side. Lifted rocks in the intertidal zone reveal the sheltered spaces it uses between tides. It eats both plant material and small animals, including shellfish. Native to the western Pacific, it has established along parts of the eastern United States. Some invaded rocky shores support dense populations, where its feeding and competition can affect other members of the shore community.

phakopsora-pachyrhizi.summary: Asian soybean rust is a fungal disease that can cause tan or reddish leaf spots and tiny spore-producing bumps, especially on leaf undersides. Wind carries the spores between living host plants, including soybean and kudzu. Warm areas with suitable hosts can help the fungus survive between crop seasons. Under favorable wet conditions, severe infections can cause early leaf loss and reduce seed production.

arivela-viscosa.summary: Asian spiderflower is a sticky, hairy annual with bright yellow flowers and leaves usually divided into five leaflets, though some have three. The slender stems can reach about three feet, with long, narrow seed pods developing among the upper leaves. Glandular hairs give the plant its noticeably sticky surface and help distinguish it from other yellow-flowered herbs. Older botanical accounts call it Cleome viscosa; this catalog retains Arivela viscosa for the same species.

monopterus-albus.summary: Asian swamp eels historically grouped as Monopterus albus have long, smooth, scaleless bodies, small eyes and greatly reduced fins. They breathe air and shelter in muddy wetlands, ponds and slow-moving waters, feeding on small aquatic animals. Research has revealed several genetically distinct forms within this group. This overview describes their shared biology; it does not establish the identity of individual U.S. populations. Florida records now assigned to M. javanensis should not automatically be attributed to M. albus.

nephrolepis-brownii.summary: Asian swordfern has long, arching fronds made up of many narrow leaflets. Flat, dark brown scales on the leaf stalks are among the features used to distinguish it from similar ferns. It can form dense stands in sheltered places and spreads through spores. In Florida, introduced populations can displace native vegetation, making accurate identification important where several swordferns grow together.

schyzocotyle-acheilognathi.summary: Asian tapeworm is a parasite that lives in the intestines of freshwater fish. It infects carp, minnows and many other hosts, and can reduce growth or harm young fish. Moving infected fish, including bait, can help it reach new waters. It is not identified by the fish's appearance alone; examining the parasite or using genetic methods is needed to distinguish it reliably.

aedes-albopictus.summary: Asian tiger mosquito is black with white-banded legs and a single white stripe down its back. It bites during the day and breeds in small water-filled containers such as tires, buckets and plant trays. Eggs laid just above the waterline can survive dry periods. That combination has helped this Asian species travel with goods and establish around homes in many other regions.

penaeus-monodon.summary: Asian tiger shrimp is a large shrimp with bold bands across its body. Young animals use estuaries and mangroves, while adults breed in marine waters and feed near the bottom, often at night. Native to the Indo-Pacific and widely farmed for food, it has been found along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts of the United States. Its presence raises questions about effects on native species, which require local evidence.

elatine-ambigua.summary: Asian waterwort is a tiny, creeping herb of wet mud and shallow water. Its delicate, branching stems carry small leaves and can produce roots at the joints, helping it spread over damp ground. Field observations describe it in rice fields, irrigation channels and other persistently wet cultivated places. It closely resembles other waterworts, especially Elatine triandra. The stalks beneath its flowers and fruits, together with other small botanical details, are more reliable identification clues than its low-growing shape alone.

corbicula-fluminea.summary: Asiatic clam has a rounded, roughly triangular shell marked by strong concentric ridges, usually yellowish to brown. It filters tiny particles from freshwater and can also feed on organic material in the sediment. Rapid growth and reproduction can build dense populations that alter food and nutrient conditions. Large numbers may clog water intakes. Effects on native mussels vary among places, so the presence of this clam alone does not establish why a native population has declined.

commelina-communis.summary: Asiatic dayflower opens vivid blue flowers that usually last only a day. Each flower has two large blue petals and a much smaller pale one. Its leaves wrap around the stems, which can take root where they touch the ground. Native to East Asia, it grows in disturbed places and can become a crop weed, spreading through patches of moist, suitable soil.

rumex-confertus.summary: Asiatic dock has large lower leaves and upright flowering stems that rise above the surrounding vegetation. It grows along rivers, in meadows and in disturbed ground, where seeds and spreading underground stems can help it form patches. Research in Central Europe found that light and shallow burial strongly influenced seedling emergence, helping explain establishment in gaps and disturbed soil. It has expanded in parts of Europe, but those regional findings do not establish its effects in every place it occurs.

maladera-formosae.summary: Asiatic garden beetle is a small, cinnamon-brown beetle with a rounded shape resembling a coffee bean. Adults hide during the day and feed on leaves at night. Underground, the pale, C-shaped grubs feed on roots and can damage seedlings. Introduced from Asia, it occurs in the United States, where the larvae have also become a concern in some corn-growing areas.

striga-asiatica.summary: Asiatic witchweed is a parasitic plant that attaches to the roots of grasses, including crops such as corn and sorghum. Its narrow, hairy leaves and small flowers appear above ground, while the connection to its host remains hidden below. Seeds can persist in soil for a long time. That persistence helps explain the long-running monitoring and control efforts around infestations in the Carolinas.

crioceris-asparagi.summary: Asparagus beetle is a small, dark beetle with pale spots and reddish edges. Both adults and grayish larvae feed on asparagus. Dark eggs are often laid upright on the plant, and feeding can scar spears or strip foliage. It differs from the orange, spotted asparagus beetle, so noticing the adult's color pattern helps connect damage with the correct species.

asparagus-densiflorus.summary: Asparagus fern is a flowering plant with fine, feathery-looking growth. The narrow green structures that resemble leaves are modified stems; its true leaves are much smaller. True Asparagus densiflorus has upright, closely branched growth, with small white to pinkish flowers that can develop into red berries. It grows naturally on sandy ground in southeastern Africa. Garden names are often mixed with Asparagus aethiopicus, so an arching plant sold as a Sprengeri asparagus fern may represent that related species instead.

phyllonorycter-apparella.summary: Aspen leafblotch miner spends its larval life inside the leaves of aspens and cottonwoods. Young larvae feed on sap, while later stages remove internal leaf tissue and leave a visible blotch. Silk can draw the mined area into a raised fold. The insect also pupates within its mine before emerging as a tiny moth. These altered patches on leaves are often easier to notice than the adults; a leaf mine still needs careful identification because other insects make similar marks.

conyza-bonariensis.summary: This asthmaweed, Conyza bonariensis, is an annual or short-lived plant with narrow, hairy, gray-green leaves. Its many small flower heads release seeds carried by fine, fluffy hairs. Originally from South America, it grows in fields, orchards and along roads in other regions. Wind dispersal helps it reach newly disturbed ground, where a small plant can develop into a much-branched seed producer.

conyza-floribunda.summary: Asthmaweed develops upright, leafy stems carrying many tiny flower heads in a broad, branching cluster. Narrow leaves and the nearly hairless bracts around the heads help distinguish this species from some similar fleabanes. Its small fruits carry fine, pale bristles. It grows in disturbed places, including roadsides and river margins. Modern treatments place Conyza floribunda in Erigeron as Erigeron floribundus; older records sometimes mix it with E. sumatrensis, so those records need a name check.

tamarix-aphylla.summary: Athel tamarisk is a large evergreen tree with fine, jointed-looking branches and tiny, scale-like leaves. Its deep roots and tolerance of dry, salty conditions have made it useful for shelter plantings. Outside cultivation, it can spread along waterways. In parts of Australia, dense stands have altered river habitats and soil conditions, showing how a tree valued for protection from wind can become a problem in the wrong setting.

hedera-hibernica.summary: Atlantic ivy is an evergreen vine that can carpet the ground or climb trees. Young growth has lobed leaves, while mature flowering growth has less-divided leaves and produces fruit eaten by birds. Stems can also root as they spread. Introduced populations in the Pacific Northwest can dominate forest ground cover and add weight to trees. It is closely related to, but distinct from, English ivy.

aleuroclava-aucubae.summary: Aucuba whitefly is a tiny sap-feeding insect that uses many host plants, including citrus and ivy. Its dark, oval immature stages sit on leaves and are easier to examine with magnification. Plants moved through trade can carry it between locations. A California assessment reported no significant known impacts at that time, so detection should be distinguished from evidence of serious damage.

geranium-homeanum.summary: Australasian geranium is a low-growing herb with hairy, rounded leaves divided into lobes. Its small pink flowers have paler centers and usually appear singly or in pairs. Thickened roots support the plant in moist places such as gullies, creek margins and forested ground. The modest flowers and creeping or spreading growth can make it less conspicuous than familiar garden geraniums.

aedes-notoscriptus.summary: Australian backyard mosquito has white-banded legs, a pale ring on its mouthparts and lyre-shaped markings on its back. It breeds in small water collections, including tree holes and containers around homes. Adults may bite during the day in shaded places. Originally associated with Australasia, it has also been detected in California, where container habitats can provide suitable places for it to reproduce.

pteris-tremula.summary: Australian brake is a fern with large fronds divided into many narrow green segments. Brown stalks rise from a short base, and lines of spore-producing structures form along the undersides of the leaf edges. It grows naturally in Australasian forest and stream habitats and is also cultivated. Looking beneath a mature frond can reveal features that are less obvious from its overall shape.

pittosporum-undulatum.summary: Australian cheesewood is an evergreen tree with glossy, wavy-edged leaves and fragrant white flowers. Orange capsules open to expose sticky seeds that birds can carry away. Native to eastern Australia, it has become weedy in some places outside its natural range. Its attractive foliage and scent explain its garden use, while bird-dispersed seeds help it move beyond planted sites.

vallisneria-australis.summary: Australian eelgrass is a freshwater plant with long, ribbon-like leaves rooted in the bottom. It spreads through runners and can form dense underwater beds. Female flowers reach the surface, and their stalks coil after pollination. Despite the common name, it is not a marine seagrass. Introduced populations occur in places including California's Delta, where its underwater growth can change the structure of aquatic habitat.

chloris-truncata.summary: Australian fingergrass is easiest to recognize by its little windmill-shaped seed heads. Usually six to nine slender branches spread almost horizontally from the top of a stem, with the florets turning dark as they mature. Narrow leaves form a low, dense clump beneath flowering stems that can reach about knee height. Native to Australia, it grows on varied soils and flowers in response to rain. The detached seed heads can tumble in the wind, helping scatter seed.

eragrostis-leptostachya.summary: Australian lovegrass is a loosely tufted perennial with narrow leaves and open, branching flower heads. Small, layered flower clusters sit along the fine branches, and hairs near the leaf joints can help with identification. It is native to eastern and southeastern Australia, where it grows in woodland and pasture settings. It should not be confused with other lovegrasses that have different ranges and impacts.

toona-ciliata.summary: Australian redcedar can become a very large rainforest tree, with leaves divided into pointed leaflets and new growth often tinged red or pink. Older trees develop rough bark and may have broad buttresses at the base. Woody fruits release winged seeds. Its valuable timber led to extensive historical logging, and trees growing in open sites can look quite different from tall forest-grown specimens.

cherax-quadricarinatus.summary: Australian redclaw crayfish is a large freshwater crayfish, often blue-green, with a distinctive red patch on the claws of mature males. It comes from northern Australia and nearby regions, using streams, lakes and seasonally changing waters. Widely farmed for food, it can escape cultivation. It eats a variety of plant and animal material, making its establishment relevant to the waters and species it encounters.

atriplex-semibaccata.summary: Australian saltbush is a low, spreading plant that can form a mat over dry or salty ground. Its gray-green leaves have a fine coating, especially beneath, and its seed-bearing structures become fleshy and red. It has been planted for forage and erosion control. Animals can spread its seeds, and it has established outside cultivation in places including coastal California.

leptospermum-laevigatum.summary: Australian teatree is a shrub or small tree with gray-green leaves, white flowers and persistent woody seed capsules. Older plants may have twisted trunks and textured bark. Native to coastal southeastern Australia, it has been planted as a screen and windbreak and has become invasive in some other regions. Newer botanical references may list it as Gaudium laevigatum rather than Leptospermum laevigatum.

trachymela-sloanei.summary: Australian tortoise beetle is a rounded brown beetle, often mottled with darker marks, that feeds on eucalyptus. Adults and larvae chew the leaves, leaving curved or semicircular notches along the edges. Adults commonly feed at night and shelter beneath loose bark during the day, a habit also documented in Chilean field collections. Introduced populations occur in California. Established, well-cared-for trees often tolerate feeding, although heavy defoliation can add stress; finding beetles does not by itself show how seriously a tree is affected.

ficopomatus-enigmaticus.summary: Australian tubeworm lives inside a hard, pale tube attached to a submerged surface. A feathery crown reaches into the water to collect tiny food particles, then withdraws into the tube when disturbed. It favors sheltered brackish places such as estuaries, lagoons and docks. Many generations can build tangled, reef-like colonies, although reefs do not form everywhere it occurs. It also grows on boat hulls and structures. Despite its common name, an Australian native origin remains uncertain.

cotula-australis.summary: Australian waterbuttons is a small, low-growing plant with finely divided leaves and tiny flower heads that look like buttons. The heads are cream to pale yellow and lack the showy outer petals of many daisies. Slender stems may lie along the ground or turn upward, and can root where they touch suitable soil. Look for it in lawns, roadsides, open grassland and other disturbed places. Its modest size can make the button heads easier to notice than the plant beneath them.

pinus-nigra.summary: Austrian pine has stiff, dark green needles held in pairs. Young trees are often roughly pyramid-shaped, while older trees develop broader crowns, deeply furrowed bark and brown cones. Native across parts of Europe, northwestern Africa and western Asia, it has been widely planted for screens and windbreaks. Its paired needles and mature bark are useful features when comparing it with other planted pines.

rorippa-austriaca.summary: Austrian yellowcress is an upright perennial with small, four-petaled yellow flowers and toothed leaves that clasp the stem. Rounded seed pods follow the flowers. It can spread through both seeds and creeping roots, allowing patches to expand in damp fields, pastures and river margins. In parts of the western United States, dense growth can compete with other vegetation, including desirable pasture plants.

elaeagnus-umbellata.summary: Autumn olive is a spreading deciduous shrub with silvery foliage, fragrant pale flowers and small red fruits dotted with pale scales. Native to Asia, it was widely planted in the United States for landscaping and erosion control. Birds and small mammals carry its seeds into fields, roadsides and woodland edges. Its roots can add nitrogen to the soil, helping it grow on poor ground. In North Carolina and other affected regions, dense growth can crowd surrounding vegetation.

zephyranthes-candida.summary: Autumn zephyrlily is a small bulb-forming perennial with narrow green leaves and white, crocuslike flowers. Blooms rise above the grassy foliage in summer and autumn, often following rain. It comes from South America and is grown widely as an ornamental in borders and containers. The plants form compact clumps, and offsets develop around the original bulbs. In mild climates the leaves may remain green; in colder places the bulbs need protection from winter freezing.

chenopodium-hircinum.summary: Chenopodium hircinum is an annual herb from South America and a wild relative of quinoa. Its upright stems branch near the base, carrying alternate leaves that often have three uneven lobes. A pale, mealy coating and an unpleasant smell are useful supporting clues. The tiny whitish-green flowers grow in clusters along narrow spikes. Leaf shape varies considerably, so a familiar-looking leaf alone is not enough to separate it from other goosefoots; mature seeds can be important for identification.

persea-americana.summary: Avocado is an evergreen tree from tropical America, grown for fleshy fruits with a single large seed. Its broad leaves form a dense crown, while small greenish-yellow flowers appear in branching clusters. Fruit size, skin texture and ripening season vary considerably among cultivated varieties. The trees grow best in warm, sunny places with good soil drainage. Avocados have been cultivated in the Americas since before European contact and remain an important orchard crop in tropical and subtropical regions.

pseudacysta-perseae.summary: Avocado lace bug is a tiny leaf-feeding insect whose translucent wing covers resemble fine lace. Adults and spiny young gather beneath avocado leaves, where their feeding creates pale patches that can turn brown. Dark specks of waste and clusters of eggs are useful clues on the lower leaf surface. The insect also uses some other plants in the laurel family. Heavy infestations can cause early leaf drop, exposing fruit and branches to sun; small populations may cause little lasting damage.

fiorinia-fioriniae.summary: Avocado scale is a small armored scale insect found on avocado, palms, tea and many other plants. Females sit beneath narrow, light-brown covers, often lined up along veins on the undersides of leaves. Their feeding can leave yellow spots, and heavy infestations may weaken foliage. Young mobile stages move to new feeding sites, while infested nursery plants can carry established colonies farther afield. Several related scales look very similar, so a microscope is usually needed to confirm the species.

froggattiella-penicillata.summary: Froggattiella penicillata is a small armored scale insect associated with bamboo and other grasses. Females live beneath elongated protective covers, often tucked under leaf sheaths where they are easy to overlook. A Korean study found colonies on the stems of Sasa bamboo and described yellow covers with a darker yellow tip. Closely related scales can look similar without magnification. Its life history and economic effects remain poorly understood, so a sighting alone does not establish that it is causing serious plant damage.

scirtothrips-perseae.summary: Avocado thrips is a small, straw-yellow insect that feeds on tender avocado leaves and young fruit. Fine dark lines cross the adult's abdomen, and the young are pale yellow. Feeding may bronze the leaves and leave rough brown scars on fruit as it grows, reducing its market quality even when the flesh remains usable. In California the insect became a major orchard pest after discovery in 1996. It often builds up during cooler periods when suitable young growth is available.

sagina-subulata.summary: Awl-leaf pearlwort, often sold as Irish moss, is a low flowering perennial that forms dense green mats. Its slender stems root where they touch the ground, and pairs of fine leaves give it a mosslike appearance. Tiny white flowers rise just above the foliage in summer. It grows best in cool, moist conditions and is often planted between paving stones or in rock gardens. It is a flowering plant rather than a true moss. The garden plant historically called Sagina subulata (Sw.) C.Presl was given the replacement name S. alexandrae because an earlier author had used subulata for a different plant.

axis-axis.summary: Axis deer is a spotted deer native to the Indian subcontinent, also known as chital. Adults retain white spots on a reddish-brown coat, and mature males usually carry three-pointed antlers. These social animals use woodland with grassy openings and access to water, feeding mainly on grasses but also browsing other vegetation. Introduced herds occur in places including Texas and Hawaii. In Texas, their ability to use limited forage can bring them into competition with native white-tailed deer.

stephanitis-pyrioides.summary: Azalea lace bug is a tiny insect with patterned, lace-like wings that feeds beneath azalea and rhododendron leaves. The upper surface develops pale speckles, while dark waste spots and shed skins collect underneath. Young bugs lack full wings and become dark and spiny as they grow. Eggs can remain in leaves through winter, allowing new generations to appear the next growing season. Heavy feeding can turn foliage almost white or brown, although visible damage does not always mean the shrub is dying.

myosotis-azorica.summary: Myosotis azorica is a forget-me-not native to the Azores, where it is a conservation concern. This upright, branching herb has simple, fleshy leaves covered with hairs and clusters of small dark-blue to violet flowers at the ends of its stems. Each flower has five petals. It grows in moist places, including rough slopes near waterfalls. Grazing can threaten its remaining habitat. This rare native plant warrants protection in its home range. A 2025 Hawaiian specimen review reassigned former local records to Myosotis latifolia, underscoring the need to check older names.

tagetes-erecta.summary: Aztec marigold is an upright annual from Mexico and Guatemala, widely grown for its large flower heads. Cultivated forms often have rounded clusters of yellow, orange or cream flowers above divided, aromatic leaves. Plant height varies greatly with the variety, from compact bedding plants to taller cut-flower types. It favors sunny, well-drained places and flowers through much of the warm season. The familiar names African marigold and American marigold refer to the same species and do not describe its native range.

nicotiana-rustica.summary: Aztec tobacco is an annual tobacco plant with broad, rounded leaves and relatively short, yellowish tubular flowers. Its foliage is noticeably wider than that of several other tobacco species. Native to Peru according to Kew's botanical account, it has been introduced across many regions, including parts of North America. It has a long history of ceremonial and medicinal use among some Indigenous peoples. Those cultural uses are part of its history, rather than advice to smoke, eat or prepare the plant.

gypsophila-paniculata.summary: Baby's breath is a branching perennial best known for the many tiny white flowers used in bouquets. Its open flower clusters rise above a leafy base and give the whole plant a rounded outline. Native across parts of Europe and temperate Asia, it favors sunny, well-drained sites and occurs along roadsides, fields and sandy ground. Garden escapes have become troublesome in some North American regions, including Great Lakes landscapes. The large, fleshy root helps established plants persist from year to year.

renibacterium-salmoninarum.summary: Bacterial kidney disease is a slow-developing infection of salmon, trout and related fishes caused by Renibacterium salmoninarum. It can affect wild fish as well as those raised in hatcheries. Some infected fish show swollen organs, skin sores or bulging eyes, while others carry the bacterium without obvious illness. Infection can pass between fish and from parents through eggs. Because these signs resemble other diseases and healthy-looking carriers occur, laboratory testing is needed to identify the cause reliably.

bagrada-hilaris.summary: Bagrada bug is a small shield-shaped insect, black with orange and white markings. Both adults and young feed by piercing plants, with cabbage, broccoli and other mustard-family crops especially vulnerable. Feeding on seedlings can leave pale patches, distort developing leaves or destroy the growing tip. The bugs also use wild plants around fields, moving into crops as conditions change. Originally from parts of Africa and Asia, this species has become an agricultural pest in California and other introduced regions.

paspalum-notatum-var-saurae.summary: Paspalum notatum var. saurae is a name used for a perennial South American pasture grass, including the familiar Pensacola bahiagrass. Pensacola has narrow leaves, produces seed readily and can persist under heavy grazing. These traits helped make it a useful pasture grass in Florida. The name needs care: some botanical sources treat this variety as the separate species Paspalum saurae. Descriptions of broad-leaved bahiagrass cultivars should not automatically be applied to this narrower-leaved form.

bromus-racemosus.summary: Bald brome is a short-lived grass that grows as a loose tuft or sometimes as a single upright stem. Its leaves and lower sheaths are hairy, while the flower clusters carry several pale-green, many-flowered spikelets with slender bristles. It is native across a broad temperate range from the Azores and Europe into Asia, and has been introduced elsewhere. Although its common name suggests a hairless plant, the floral details, rather than the absence of leaf hairs, are important for identification.

impatiens-balfourii.summary: Balfour's touch-me-not is an annual with upright, branching stems and two-toned pink and white flowers. Each flower has a narrow spur extending behind it, and the pointed leaves have regularly toothed edges. Native to the western Himalayas, it has been grown as a garden ornamental and sometimes escapes into disturbed ground. In Victoria, Australia, botanical accounts describe localized dense stands near old gardens. Its smooth stems and modest flower size help separate it from some larger, more familiar balsams.

neslia-paniculata.summary: Ballmustard is an annual mustard-family plant of fields, meadows and disturbed ground. Small yellow flowers are followed by rounded fruits, giving the seed-bearing stems their distinctive beadlike appearance. Native to Eurasia, it has spread into parts of northern North America, including New England. The seeds can be difficult to separate from harvested canola or mustard because they are similar in size. That makes it relevant as an agricultural weed even where it is less conspicuous than larger flowering plants.

cardiospermum-halicacabum.summary: Balloon vine is a tendril-climbing plant named for its inflated, papery fruit capsules. The green capsules become brown as they mature, enclosing black seeds with a pale heart-shaped mark. Divided leaves and small white flowers grow along branching stems that scramble over nearby plants. It occurs across tropical and subtropical regions in thickets, river margins and disturbed ground. In parts of the southeastern United States, introduced growth can cover surrounding vegetation, but its native and introduced status varies around the world.

platycodon-grandiflorus.summary: Balloon-flower is a perennial grown for buds that swell like small balloons before opening into broad, five-pointed bells. The flowers face outward or upward above leafy stems, appearing in late spring and summer. Native to eastern Asia, the plant returns from a fleshy root system that can be easily damaged by disturbance. It is commonly grown in sunny or partly shaded borders with well-drained soil. Its unusual unopened buds are usually the easiest feature to recognize.

adelges-piceae.summary: Balsam woolly adelgid is a tiny sap-feeding insect hidden beneath white, woolly wax on true fir trees. Colonies settle on bark and branches, where their feeding can cause swollen twigs, distorted growth and declining crowns. Susceptibility varies among fir species: Fraser fir in the southern Appalachians and subalpine fir in the western United States can suffer severe damage. Introduced from Europe, the insect reproduces without mating in North America. Its small size means an infestation may go unnoticed until tree symptoms develop.

momordica-charantia.summary: Balsampear, also called bitter melon, is a fast-growing annual vine with curling tendrils and deeply lobed leaves. Yellow flowers develop into bumpy or ridged fruits that change from green to orange when ripe. The mature fruit splits open, exposing seeds wrapped in bright red flesh. Cultivated varieties are familiar vegetables in many warm regions, while smaller-fruited forms may grow outside gardens. The plant thrives in heat and humidity and can climb supports or spread across the ground.

phyllostachys-reticulata.summary: This bamboo, also known as timber bamboo or Phyllostachys bambusoides, is a tall woody grass native to central and southern China. Its green canes carry long branches and pointed leaves that are bright green above and blue-green beneath. Young cane sheaths can be pinkish with purple mottling, a useful seasonal detail. It has a long history in cultivation, and its eventual size varies greatly with climate and growing conditions.

poliaspoides-formosana.summary: Bamboo armored scale is a small scale insect that can remain well hidden on its host. Recorded colonies occupy the tight space between a bamboo leaf stalk and the stem, so an ordinary glance at the leaves may miss them. The species was originally described from Asian bamboo and has since been reported in other regions, including Saint Lucia. Closely related scales require microscopic comparison, making the host and concealed feeding site useful search clues rather than a complete identification.

bambusaspis-bambusae.summary: Bamboo pit scale is a tiny sap-feeding insect found on bamboo leaves and stems. Females are elongated and yellowish, sheltered beneath a translucent cover that can blend into the plant. A fringe of pale wax may help reveal a colony. Colonies occupy both leaf surfaces as well as stems, so an inspection should cover more than the most visible leaves. A Danish report records occasional problems in botanical-garden greenhouses. Its importance therefore depends on plant condition and setting, not simply the number of visible scales.

dinoderus-minutus.summary: Bamboo powderpost beetle develops inside cut bamboo, where both adults and larvae make feeding tunnels. The insects can attack culms during processing, storage or use, turning internal tissue into fine powder and reducing the material's strength. Eggs are laid inside the bamboo, and the young remain concealed as they grow. Fresh powder and small exit holes may reveal an infestation before the beetles themselves are noticed. Research in Japan documents it as an important pest of dried bamboo products.

stigmaeopsis-celarius.summary: Stigmaeopsis celarius is a tiny bamboo-feeding spider mite that lives beneath silk shelters on leaves. The dense, oval roofs cover small colonies and help protect them from predators. Experiments observed nest defense by adults, but its effectiveness differed between sexes and behaviors. Several related bamboo mites look similar and older reports used this name more broadly. Webbing beneath a bamboo leaf is therefore a useful place to look, but microscopic examination is needed to identify the species reliably.

pentalonia-nigronervosa.summary: Banana aphid is a small, shiny brown to nearly black insect that feeds on banana sap. Colonies produce sticky honeydew, which can attract ants and support black sooty mold. Its greatest importance is as a carrier of banana bunchy top virus, rather than the feeding injury alone. Winged forms can disperse to other plants. Older accounts assigned aphids from ginger and several other hosts to this species, but modern research separates many of those populations as Pentalonia caladii.

opogona-sacchari.summary: Banana bud moth is a small brown moth whose caterpillars tunnel inside stems and other plant tissues. Despite its name, it attacks many plants, including palms, dracaenas, bananas and other tropical ornamentals. The pale caterpillars have a brown head and produce piles of fine plant waste held together with silk. Infested stems may weaken or collapse, and empty pupal cases can project from the tunnels. Damaged or stressed plants are especially attractive places for the nocturnal adults to lay eggs.

pestalotiopsis-disseminata.summary: Pestalotiopsis disseminata is a fungus reported from many kinds of plants, sometimes causing blight, cankers or fruit decay and sometimes living within apparently healthy tissue. Symptoms depend on the host and growing conditions, so a spotted leaf alone does not identify it. Reports include banana fruit rot and a Thai field survey that attributed large banana leaf spots to this fungus. That survey adds a real leaf association, but its available methods do not establish modern genetic confirmation of the isolates. Microscopy and suitable DNA comparisons are important because closely related fungi can be confused.

passiflora-tarminiana.summary: Banana passionflower is a climbing vine with three-lobed leaves, hanging pink flowers and elongated fruits that ripen yellow. Often called banana poka in Hawaii, it can climb high into forest vegetation and spread across tree crowns. Birds and pigs disperse its seeds there. The vine is native to the Andes and was long confused with another banana passionfruit, Passiflora mollissima. Its vigorous growth is a serious problem in some Hawaiian forests, where it can smother the plants supporting it.

heros-severus.summary: Banded cichlid is a deep-bodied South American fish from the upper Orinoco and upper Negro river regions. Dark vertical markings cross the body, but the pattern must be interpreted carefully because several related fishes are sold as severums. In the modern identification of Heros severus, one middle body bar is shortened rather than extending fully between the upper and lower fins. Older aquarium and biological accounts can mix it with other Heros species, making confirmed identity especially important.

scolytus-schevyrewi.summary: The banded elm bark beetle is a small Asian beetle that now occurs in North America. Adults are reddish brown with a darker band across the wing covers. Its pale, legless larvae tunnel beneath the bark of stressed elms, interrupting the tissues that move food through the tree. The beetle can also carry the fungus responsible for Dutch elm disease. Tree condition matters: in Utah, attacks on the common Siberian elm often cause little damage when disease is absent.

aloe-vera.summary: Barbados aloe is an evergreen succulent with a rosette of thick, pointed leaves edged with small pale teeth. The leaves store water and contain the clear gel familiar from cosmetic products. Mature plants can send up tall stalks bearing tubular yellow to orange flowers, while young offsets form beside the parent plant. It is widely grown in pots and warm-climate gardens, where freely draining soil is important. The yellow latex near the leaf surface differs from the inner gel and should not be casually consumed.

pereskia-aculeata.summary: Barbados gooseberry is a climbing cactus with ordinary-looking, slightly fleshy leaves. Paired hooked spines help its branches catch surrounding plants, while older stems carry clusters of longer spines. Fragrant white or pale-yellow flowers are followed by round yellow to orange fruits. Native to tropical America, it has escaped from gardens in places such as eastern Australia, where heavy, tangled growth can smother other vegetation. Broken stems and even leaves can regrow, making dumped garden material a source of new plants.

jatropha-curcas.summary: Barbados nut is a spreading shrub or small tree native to tropical America. Its broad leaves have three or five pointed lobes, and small yellow-green flowers develop into rounded capsules that split as they mature. The dark seeds contain oil used in industrial products and investigated as a fuel source. The plant tolerates drought and relatively poor soil, which has encouraged cultivation far beyond its native range. Despite the common name, its seeds are not edible nuts and can cause poisoning.

opuntia-ficus-indica.summary: Barbary fig is a large, branching cactus grown for its fleshy fruit. Its flattened, oval pads are stems, often forming a small tree with a distinct trunk. Many cultivated plants lack long spines, but small irritating bristles can still be present. Yellow flowers develop into rounded fruits that change color as they ripen. The species comes from Mexico and has been carried widely in cultivation. In New South Wales it sometimes escapes into surrounding vegetation, spreading through seeds and fallen stem pieces.

aegilops-triuncialis.summary: Barbed goatgrass is a winter annual grass closely related to wheat. Its stiff, narrow leaves and short seed heads become especially noticeable when the very long bristles spread from the developing seeds. Native from the Mediterranean region into central Asia, it grows in California grasslands, rangelands and oak woodlands, including some dry, shallow soils. The bristles catch on clothing and animal fur, helping seeds travel. They can also lodge around livestock mouths or eyes, reducing the usefulness of affected pasture.

gerbera-jamesonii.summary: Barberton daisy is a perennial from southern Africa with bold daisy-like flower heads held above a low rosette of leaves. The leaves are elongated and often deeply lobed, while the flowers usually have red outer rays surrounding a darker center. This species helped give rise to the many hybrid gerberas sold as bedding plants and cut flowers. It favors bright conditions and moist but well-drained soil; saturated soil can damage its roots. In colder climates it is commonly grown seasonally or protected from frost.

cryptocarenus-heveae.summary: Cryptocarenus heveae is a very small, dark-brown bark beetle recorded in South America. At roughly two millimeters long, it is difficult to recognize without a microscope. A specialist key uses details of the forehead, including a shallow depression and small central bump, to separate it from similar beetles. Researchers have caught it in ethanol-baited traps in a mixed Brazil-nut and rubber plantation in the southern Amazon. That finding documents its presence there, but does not by itself show which trees it was using.

xylosandrus-germanus.summary: The black stem borer is a tiny ambrosia beetle from eastern Asia that has become a pest of orchard and nursery trees in North America. Females are shiny black and about two millimeters long. They bore into trunks or branches and grow a fungus inside their tunnels as food for themselves and their young. Stressed trees are especially attractive. Small entry holes, sometimes with thin toothpick-like strands of sawdust, may be easier to notice than the beetles themselves. Heavy attacks can accompany wilting and decline.

echinochloa-crus-galli.summary: Barnyardgrass is a variable annual grass common in damp, disturbed ground and cultivated fields. Its flattened stems may spread near the ground before turning upward, carrying broad, flat blades. The branched seed head is crowded with small spikelets and may have a purplish cast. One useful clue is the absence of a small membrane or fringe where the leaf blade meets its sheath. Introduced from Eurasia into North America, it is a familiar agricultural weed of irrigated fields, ditches and rice-growing areas.

peronospora-belbahrii.summary: Basil downy mildew is caused by Peronospora belbahrii, a microscopic water mold that infects basil. Leaves often turn yellow between the main veins, while gray to purple downy growth develops underneath. Symptoms may begin low on the plant and spread upward, making a healthy-looking crop decline quickly in humid conditions. The pathogen can arrive on seed or infected plants, and its spores travel through the air. Yellowing alone can resemble a nutrient problem, so the leaf underside provides an important clue.

callisia-fragrans.summary: Basket plant is a fleshy perennial from Mexico that forms clusters of broad, glossy leaves. Long flowering stalks rise from the upper leaf bases and carry small, fragrant white flowers. Some cultivated forms have pale or purple markings, so leaf color alone is unreliable. Grown as an ornamental groundcover, it has escaped into hammocks and disturbed places in central and southern Florida, where it can displace existing vegetation. A plant growing outside cultivation should be assessed in its local setting before removal is planned.

thrips-calcaratus.summary: Basswood thrips is a small, brown insect associated mainly with lindens and basswoods. Adults have narrow wings, and identifying them precisely requires microscopic details such as a tiny curved claw on the front foot. The insect feeds on young developing buds and leaves. Native to Europe, it has become a forest pest in the upper Midwest, where outbreaks can cause extensive loss of basswood foliage. Its early-season feeding can leave damage that is mistaken for frost injury rather than insect activity.

sphagneticola-trilobata.summary: Bay Biscayne creeping oxeye, also called wedelia, is a fast-spreading groundcover with fleshy leaves and bright yellow daisy-like flowers. Its rounded stems creep along the ground and can form dense mats. Native to tropical America, it was planted widely for its flowers and rapid cover. In Florida, garden escapes now occur beside streams, roads and other disturbed places, where thick growth crowds neighboring plants. Runners and broken pieces are particularly important in its spread, so cutting a patch can scatter material capable of growing again.

bean-common-mosaic-necrosis-virus.summary: Bean common mosaic necrosis virus is a plant virus that affects beans and related legumes. It can produce mottled, distorted leaves, but the result depends strongly on the bean variety. In some varieties, infection triggers darkening veins, wilt and widespread tissue death; in others it resembles ordinary bean common mosaic. Infected seed can introduce the virus, and aphids spread it between plants during brief feeding visits. Because related viruses can cause similar symptoms, laboratory testing is needed to distinguish them reliably.

bean-common-mosaic-virus.summary: Bean common mosaic virus infects beans and several other legumes. Affected leaves may show an uneven light-and-dark green pattern, puckering or curling, and plants infected early can remain small. The virus travels in infected seed and can be carried between plants by aphids during short feeding visits. Symptoms vary with the plant variety and virus strain, and some infections are easily confused with other bean viruses. Starting with tested seed is therefore more reliable than judging seed health by its appearance.

batrachochytrium-dendrobatidis.summary: Bd chytrid fungus is a microscopic fungus that infects amphibian skin. It releases swimming spores into water, allowing infection to pass through wet environments. Some amphibians carry it without obvious illness, while others develop chytridiomycosis, with abnormal skin shedding, weakness or loss of normal movement. Severe outbreaks have contributed to amphibian declines around the world. A skin swab can reveal infection, but visible illness is not specific enough to identify the fungus, and detecting it does not always mean the animal has developed disease.

casuarina-equisetifolia.summary: Beach sheoak is a tall flowering tree whose fine, drooping branchlets can make it look like a pine. Its true leaves are tiny scales arranged in rings around those jointed branchlets, and the fruits form small woody, cone-like clusters. Native across parts of Asia and the western Pacific, it has been planted widely in tropical regions. In Florida, it is one of several introduced Casuarina species that have spread into native plant communities. Counting the leaf scales helps distinguish it from related sheoaks.

crepis-vesicaria.summary: Beaked hawksbeard is a leafy herb with yellow, dandelion-like flower heads and toothed or lobed leaves. The outer rays can be reddish underneath, a useful detail when similar yellow-flowered plants grow together. Mature seeds narrow into a slender beak before the tuft of hairs used for wind dispersal. Native to parts of Europe, the Mediterranean and nearby Atlantic islands, it has been introduced elsewhere. North American records include disturbed places, meadows and fields, although its local abundance varies considerably.

aphis-fabae.summary: Bean aphids are small, dark sap-feeding insects that gather on tender growth, leaves and stems. Adults are usually dull dark green to purplish black with lighter legs; both winged and wingless forms occur. Dense colonies can curl foliage and weaken young bean plants, while their sugary honeydew leaves surfaces sticky and encourages sooty mold. They can also carry plant viruses. Lady beetles, lacewings and tiny parasitic wasps often reduce colonies naturally, so the presence of aphids does not always mean treatment is needed.

megalurothrips-usitatus.summary: Bean flower thrips is a small insect most often found inside legume flowers. Adults are dark brown, with pale areas on the narrow wings, while males can be smaller and lighter. Feeding and egg laying can damage flowers and developing pods, reducing crop quality. The species is associated with tropical Asia and has more recently been recorded in Florida. Several thrips can share the same bean crop, so an insect in a damaged blossom needs microscopic examination before it can be confidently named.

smynthurodes-betae.summary: Bean root aphids are small, pale insects that feed on the roots of beans and many other plants. The wingless root-feeding forms are yellowish white with a dusting of wax and a light brown head and legs. Their life cycle can also involve Pistacia trees, where colonies develop inside swellings formed from leaf tissue. In places without those tree hosts, populations may remain on roots. This broad choice of hosts means the name describes only part of the aphid's way of life.

acanthoscelides-obtectus.summary: Bean weevil is a small seed beetle that develops inside dry beans. Adults have mottled brown, black and gray wing covers and lack the long snout associated with true weevils. The larvae chew within seeds, often remaining hidden until an adult leaves a neat round exit hole. Infestations can begin in the field and continue through repeated generations in warm storage. Moving infested seed has carried the beetle widely, and apparently intact beans can already contain developing larvae.

acanthus-mollis.summary: Bear's breeches is a clump-forming perennial with large, glossy leaves cut into deep lobes. Tall flower spikes rise above the foliage, carrying white flowers surrounded by purple-toned, spiny structures. The leaf shape is familiar from classical architectural decoration. Native around parts of the Mediterranean, it is grown widely as an ornamental in sun or partial shade. Underground stems allow an established clump to spread, and pieces left in the soil can make it difficult to remove completely.

polypogon-viridis.summary: Beardless rabbitsfoot grass is a moisture-loving grass that forms loose tufts and can spread through creeping stems that root where they touch the ground. Its narrow, flat leaves rise beneath dense, branched flower heads, usually green and sometimes tinged purple. Unlike the conspicuously bristly heads of some related grasses, its tiny flower clusters lack long awns. It grows beside ditches and waterways and on other damp ground, with a native range spanning parts of southern Europe, Africa and Asia.

cimex-lectularius.summary: Bed bugs are small, blood-feeding insects that hide in narrow spaces close to where people rest. Unfed adults are flat, oval and brown, roughly the size of an apple seed; after feeding they become fuller and redder. Young bugs are smaller and much paler. They shelter in mattress seams, bed frames, furniture and other cracks, and can travel with luggage or belongings. Finding the insect itself, shed skins or dark spotting is more useful for identification than a pattern of skin bites.

phyllaphis-fagi.summary: Beech aphids are tiny sap-feeding insects most easily noticed through the white, woolly wax that gathers beneath beech leaves. The insects underneath are pale yellow, and their feeding can curl leaves downward. Sticky honeydew may fall onto lower foliage and support dark sooty mold. On European beech, eggs spend winter in bark crevices before colonies develop on new leaves. Infestations can spoil the appearance of leaves, although established, healthy trees often tolerate them without lasting harm.

neonectria-coccinea.summary: Neonectria coccinea is a fungus associated with bark disease in European beech. It can live in beech tissues without obvious symptoms, but it has also been recovered from declining trees and shown experimentally to cause substantial bark lesions. These injured patches can be part of more complicated tree decline involving stress and other fungi. The species is closely related to fungi involved in North American beech bark disease, so an affected tree's appearance alone cannot establish which fungus is present.

neonectria-faginata.summary: Neonectria faginata is one of the fungi involved in beech bark disease in North America. The disease develops through an interaction between beech scale insects and fungi: scale feeding damages the bark, creating entry points for infection. Affected American beeches develop sunken or swollen areas of dead bark that may merge into larger cankers. The white, woolly material often seen earlier on the trunk belongs to the scale insects. Fungal identification requires closer examination than the tree's outward symptoms.

beech-leaf-disease.summary: Beech leaf disease is caused by a microscopic leaf nematode, Litylenchus crenatae subsp. mccannii. A distinctive early sign is dark banding between the veins of beech leaves, especially when viewed against the light. More affected leaves may become thick, curled or misshapen, while damaged buds produce fewer leaves and the crown gradually thins. The nematodes spend winter in buds and affect developing foliage. American, European and Oriental beeches can develop the disease, so host species alone does not rule it out.

litylenchus-crenatae-ssp-mccannii.summary: The beech tree nematode is a microscopic roundworm that causes beech leaf disease. It lives in developing buds and leaves, where its presence is linked to dark bands between leaf veins and to thickened, distorted foliage. Heavy damage can prevent buds from opening normally and leave the crown sparse. Researchers distinguished this North American subspecies from the previously described Japanese Litylenchus crenatae using body features and DNA, and reproduced disease symptoms by introducing nematodes into beech buds.

perilla-frutescens.summary: Beefsteakplant is an aromatic annual in the mint family, native to Asia and introduced in many parts of North America. It has opposite, toothed leaves on square stems, with small flowers grouped along upright spikes. Common ornamental forms have broad, crinkled, purple to reddish leaves. Plants produce abundant seed and may appear beyond gardens along roadsides or in other disturbed ground. Despite its history of cultivation, it can be troublesome in pastures because the plant is toxic to livestock.

spodoptera-exigua.summary: Beet armyworm is a moth whose caterpillars feed on many vegetables, field crops and weeds. Young larvae gather together and scrape leaf surfaces, sometimes leaving thin, windowlike patches and loose webbing. Older caterpillars spread out, chew irregular holes and may enter developing fruit. They are usually green with lengthwise stripes and a small dark spot near the second pair of true legs. Adults are mottled gray-brown moths, while eggs occur in clusters beneath a covering of pale, hairlike scales.

lonicera-x-bella.summary: Bell's honeysuckle is a dense, many-stemmed shrub produced by crosses between Morrow's and Tatarian honeysuckles. It bears opposite, oval leaves and paired tubular flowers, often pink when fresh and yellow as they age. Red or orange berries follow and can be carried by birds. The hybrid is variable, with leaves and twigs ranging from nearly hairless to lightly downy. In parts of the northeastern and midwestern United States it grows along woodland edges, roadsides and old fields, sometimes forming dense stands.

polygonum-patulum.summary: Polygonum patulum is a slender annual knotweed with upright stems that branch near the base. Narrow, pointed leaves are larger low on the plant and become much smaller toward the flowering branches. Tiny greenish or pink flowers gather around the stem joints, with many crowded near branch tips. Thin, papery sheaths surround the joints below the leaves. Native across parts of Europe and Asia, it occurs in fields, gardens and other open ground, including seasonally flooded places.

jatropha-gossypiifolia.summary: Bellyache bush is a branching tropical shrub with leaves divided into three to five pointed lobes. Leaf stalks and margins carry sticky, gland-tipped hairs, and the foliage may be green or reddish purple. Small red to purple flowers develop in clusters, followed by rounded seed capsules. Native from Mexico through tropical America, it has escaped cultivation elsewhere. In northern Australia it forms dense stands around waterways and disturbed land. Its toxicity makes it a concern where people or livestock might consume it.

ptinus-bicinctus.summary: Belted spider beetles are small beetles that sometimes occur in stored products and buildings. Adults are roughly two to four millimeters long, with patches of pale scales near the front and rear of their wing covers. Males are more parallel-sided, while females look rounder. The species is native to Europe and North Africa and has been introduced to North America. Canadian records include warehouses and homes, and an early United States report documented it breeding in bags of stored flour.

thunbergia-grandiflora.summary: Bengal trumpet is a long-lived climbing vine with large, pale blue to violet flowers and pale throats. Its opposite leaves are variable, often bearing broad teeth or shallow pointed lobes, and young stems are square in cross-section. Thickened underground roots help the plant persist. Native to southern Asia and grown for its flowers, it can become an environmental weed in warm regions such as Queensland. The blossoms attract bees, including large carpenter bees, and flowers may be followed by distinctly beaked capsules.

anguina-agrostis.summary: Bent-grass nematode is a microscopic roundworm that develops inside abnormal growths in grass flower heads. These elongated galls replace developing seeds and can be concealed by the surrounding flower parts. Bentgrasses are the best-known hosts, and a modern study also confirmed the species in fowl bluegrass beside a Wyoming river. Older accounts assigned many other grasses to this nematode, but some of those records belong to different species. Accurate identification therefore depends on examining the nematodes, not just noticing damaged seed heads.

agrostis-castellana.summary: Agrostis castellana is a perennial bentgrass with fine, gray-green leaves and upright flowering stems. It forms tufts linked by slender underground stems, while its flower head spreads into a delicate branching shape and often narrows as it ages. The tiny flower clusters may be greenish or purple, with some bearing slender awns and others lacking them. Native around the Mediterranean and nearby Atlantic islands, it has been introduced elsewhere, including New Zealand, where it is known as dryland browntop.

lachnagrostis-filiformis.summary: Lachnagrostis filiformis is a fine-leaved grass native to Australia, often growing on poorly drained or seasonally wet ground. Its loose, airy flower head branches widely above a tuft of narrow leaves, and the small green or purplish flower clusters carry bent bristles. At maturity, the stem commonly breaks beneath the flower head, allowing it to move away from the parent plant. Plants may behave as annuals or persist longer, and closely related grasses can be difficult to separate.

oxalis-pes-caprae.summary: Bermuda buttercup is a bulb-forming perennial from southern Africa, with bright yellow flowers held above a loose cluster of leaves. Each leaf has three heart-shaped leaflets, often dotted with purple. Despite its common name, it is a wood sorrel rather than a true buttercup. In California it grows during the cooler, wetter part of the year and retreats to underground bulbs as weather warms. Those bulbs allow patches to return and can spread the plant when contaminated soil is moved.

cynodon-dactylon.summary: Bermudagrass is a low, wiry perennial grass that grows most actively in warm weather. It spreads through runners above ground and underground stems, both able to root and form new plants. Narrow leaves and fingerlike branches radiating from the tip of each flower stalk help distinguish a flowering patch. It is widely grown as turf, yet the same spreading growth makes it a persistent weed in gardens and planting beds. In cooler conditions the foliage turns brown as the grass becomes dormant.

pinus-wallichiana.summary: Bhutan pine is an evergreen mountain tree from the Himalayan region, also known as Himalayan pine. Its long, gray-green needles grow in bundles of five and hang downward on older shoots, giving the branches a soft, drooping appearance. Long, resinous cones hang from stalks, while bark changes from smooth gray-green on young wood to darker, fissured scales with age. The species is grown as an ornamental beyond its native range and generally favors sunny sites with well-drained soil.

monomorium-floricola.summary: Bicolored trailing ants are tiny, shiny ants with a dark head and abdomen contrasting with a much lighter middle section. Workers are less than two millimeters long and often forage on trees, shrubs and around buildings in warm climates. Colonies occupy small cavities, including spaces in twigs and bark, and may contain several queens. The ants take insects and sweet foods, including honeydew from plant-feeding bugs. Their small nests can travel with nursery plants and other material moved by people.

cerastium-fontanum-ssp-vulgare.summary: Mouse-ear chickweed is a low, spreading perennial with small paired leaves and white flowers. Its softly hairy growth can blend into lawns until the flowers appear, each with five notched petals. Originally from Europe, it now grows widely in North America in fields, roadsides and other open, disturbed places. The flowers are small, with petals about as long as the green sepals beneath them. Those details help separate it from similar chickweeds.

briza-maxima.summary: Large quaking grass has flower clusters that hang like little paper lanterns from fine stalks. The overlapping scales can turn brown or purple, and the loose clusters give this annual grass its distinctive nodding look. Native to the Mediterranean region, it grows in disturbed ground and has become established beyond its original range. Narrow, flat leaves form loose tufts beneath the flower stems. Its conspicuous clusters make it easier to recognize than many grasses.

lotus-uliginosus.summary: Big trefoil is a perennial member of the pea family, with yellow flowers gathered in clusters above its leaves. Each leaf has five leaflets, though the lower pair sits close to the stem and can be easy to overlook. Hollow stems and creeping shoots help distinguish its growth. Native to Eurasia and North Africa, it has become established elsewhere, including moist disturbed ground in southwestern British Columbia. You may also find it listed as Lotus pedunculatus.

hypophthalmichthys-nobilis.summary: Bighead carp are large freshwater fish with oversized heads, low-set eyes and irregular dark blotches along their bodies. Rather than hunting larger prey, they strain tiny organisms and other food from the water. Introduced from Asia for pond management, they escaped into rivers and now occur in parts of the Mississippi River system. Their appetite for plankton can put them in competition with native fish, including paddlefish and young fish that depend on the same food.

centaurea-macrocephala.summary: Bighead knapweed is a sturdy perennial topped with large, bright yellow flower heads. Beneath each head, overlapping brown, papery scales form a rounded cup. Once grown as a garden ornamental, it has escaped cultivation in parts of Washington, where it can compete with grasses. Its rough, pointed leaves become smaller farther up the stems. The showy flowers are followed by seeds that help it spread, making an escaped patch worth identifying before those heads mature.

pheidole-megacephala.summary: Bigheaded ants get their name from the unusually large heads of their larger workers, which forage alongside many smaller ants. These small brown ants nest in soil, lawns and sheltered spaces beneath paving or pots, often leaving loose piles of sand. They feed on insects and sweet liquids such as honeydew. Established in many warm regions, including Florida, their large colonies can displace other ants and become a persistent household nuisance. Related native ants make careful identification important.

setaria-megaphylla.summary: Broadleaf bristlegrass is a tall, clump-forming perennial whose broad, pleated leaves can look quite different from ordinary lawn grasses. Its flowering stems carry long, branching clusters with fine bristles beside the small spikelets. It favors moist, sheltered places, including forest edges and stream margins, and has become established in Florida. Large rootstocks help the plant persist between growing seasons. A close look at the leaves and flower clusters is useful when separating it from other broad-leaved grasses.

vinca-major.summary: Bigleaf periwinkle is an evergreen groundcover with trailing stems, broad paired leaves and blue-violet flowers. Planted in gardens for its dense cover, it can spread beyond beds when stems take root wherever they touch moist ground. Broken pieces can also travel in dumped garden waste or flowing water. Along shaded creeks and woodland edges in places such as California, established patches can crowd out native plants. Its larger, often heart-based leaves help distinguish it from small periwinkle.

fenusa-pumila.summary: Birch leafminer is a small sawfly whose young feed between the upper and lower surfaces of birch leaves. Their feeding creates pale blotches that later turn brown, sometimes making a tree look badly scorched. Adults resemble tiny dark flies rather than wasps. Introduced to North America from the Old World, this species is one of several insects that mine birch leaves. Healthy, established trees often tolerate the damage, so brown foliage alone does not mean a tree is dying.

vicia-cracca.summary: Bird vetch is a climbing perennial with rows of small leaflets, curling tendrils and clusters of purple flowers gathered along one side of a stalk. It grows through meadows, roadsides and other open or disturbed places, using neighboring plants for support. Underground stems and seeds both help it spread. In Alaska, researchers have observed dense growth overtopping herbs and climbing shrubs at forest edges. Those tangled patches can change the space available to the vegetation beneath them.

lotus-corniculatus.summary: Birdsfoot trefoil is a low perennial with clusters of yellow pea-shaped flowers and slender seedpods that spread out like a bird's toes. Introduced as forage and for erosion control, it now grows along roadsides and in open grasslands. Its branching stems may lie close to the ground or rise above surrounding vegetation. In Minnesota and some other areas, it can crowd native prairie plants. Seeds can remain in the soil for years, allowing patches to return after the visible plants are removed.

sagina-procumbens.summary: Spreading pearlwort is a tiny perennial that forms low patches of slender stems and narrow leaves. It often grows in moist ground, lawns and cracks in paving, where its size makes it easy to overlook. The flowers are very small, with white petals that may be shorter than the surrounding green sepals or absent altogether. Some stems root where they touch the ground. This plant is native in parts of North America but introduced elsewhere, so its local status matters when interpreting a record.

veronica-persica.summary: Persian speedwell is a small annual with trailing, hairy stems and bright blue flowers marked with darker lines and a pale center. It often appears in gardens, crop fields, lawns and disturbed ground, flowering close to the soil surface. The rounded leaves have toothed edges, while individual flowers sit on thin stalks. It reproduces by seed and can grow through cool weather where conditions allow. Although easy to miss among larger weeds, a close look at the flowers usually reveals its distinctive pattern.

aegopodium-podagraria.summary: Goutweed is a spreading perennial often planted as a leafy groundcover, including forms with creamy white leaf edges. Beneath the surface, branching rhizomes help it form dense patches that can be difficult to contain. Its leaves are divided into toothed leaflets, and small white flowers gather in broad, flat clusters above them. Originally from Europe and Asia, it has escaped gardens into shaded edges and woodlands. Dense growth can displace native herbs and leave less room for young trees to establish.

zingiber-zerumbet.summary: Shampoo ginger is a tropical perennial with upright leafy stems and cone-shaped flower heads on separate, shorter stalks. The overlapping bracts begin green and become red as they mature, with small pale flowers emerging between them. It spreads from creeping rhizomes and favors moist, sheltered places. Known as awapuhi in Hawai'i, it was brought there by early Polynesian voyagers and has a long cultural history. Its leafy growth can die back seasonally, while the underground stems remain ready to grow again.

cichlasoma-bimaculatum.summary: Black acara is a small, deep-bodied freshwater fish with two dark blotches, one near the middle of its side and another near the tail. Native to northern South America, it has become established in southern Florida, especially in shallow ditches and other disturbed waters. It eats a mixture of small animals and plant material, and both parents guard their young. Similar-looking chanchita have sometimes been mistaken for this species, so color and body shape alone are not enough for a confident identification.

phyllostachys-nigra.summary: Black bamboo is a tall evergreen grass best known for canes that emerge green and darken as they mature. Narrow leaves form light, arching sprays above the distinctive stems. Native to China, it is widely grown as an ornamental screen or garden feature. Although a planting may initially stay in a tight clump, underground rhizomes can send shoots farther out, particularly in warm, moist conditions. That spreading habit matters more for containment than the color of the canes.

brachyplatys-subaeneus.summary: Black bean bug is a small, shiny black insect that often gathers with others on plant stems and leaf stalks. Despite its beetle-like appearance, it is a true bug that feeds by sucking plant fluids. Pale yellow markings on its head and shoulders help distinguish it from other dark insects. Native to Asia and confirmed in southern Florida, it is associated particularly with legumes, including crop plants. Finding it on a plant does not necessarily mean it can complete its life cycle there.

fallopia-convolvulus.summary: Black bindweed, also called wild buckwheat, is an annual vine with pointed, arrow-shaped leaves and slender stems that trail or climb through nearby plants. Its tiny greenish flowers are easy to miss, especially beside the showier flowers of field bindweed, a different species. Introduced from Eurasia, it grows in crop fields, gardens, roadsides and other disturbed ground. It reproduces by seed, producing small, dark, three-sided fruits, and can become a troublesome tangle among crops.

mylopharyngodon-piceus.summary: Black carp is a large, dark fish with broad scales and powerful teeth deep in its throat that can crush snails and mussels. Brought from Asia for use in fish farming, it escaped into waterways and now reproduces in the Mississippi River basin. Its appetite raises concern for native freshwater mollusks, many of which already face other threats. Young black carp closely resemble grass carp, making careful identification important when unfamiliar fish are caught or moved.

attagenus-unicolor.summary: Black carpet beetles are small, dark, oval beetles whose young have a very different appearance and appetite. The narrow, brown, hairy larvae carry a long tuft at the rear and feed on wool, fur, feathers and other animal materials. Adults visit flowers for pollen and nectar and may enter buildings to lay eggs. Indoors, larvae can remain hidden in lint, stored textiles or insect collections; shed skins and irregular damage are often easier to find than the beetles themselves.

myzus-cerasi.summary: Black cherry aphids gather on tender cherry growth, where their glossy dark bodies stand out against the leaves. Feeding can curl sweet-cherry leaves tightly around the colony and distort young shoots. The aphids also leave sticky honeydew that can support dark sooty mold. Eggs spend the winter on cherry twigs, while later generations commonly move to plants in the mustard family for summer. Lady beetles, lacewings and other predators help limit their numbers in orchards.

aphis-aurantii.summary: Black citrus aphid is a small, dark sap-feeding insect found on soft new growth of citrus and many other plants. Coffee, cacao and ornamental shrubs are among its hosts. Colonies can curl or distort young leaves and deposit sticky honeydew, on which sooty mold grows. Despite its name, it is not restricted to citrus. Predators and tiny parasitic wasps often keep colonies in check, and the importance of this aphid varies with the crop and region.

hyoscyamus-niger.summary: Black henbane is a sticky, unpleasant-smelling member of the nightshade family that grows as an annual or biennial. It occurs along roadsides, fences and disturbed pastures, sometimes forming dense patches. Originally brought to North America for ornamental and medicinal use, it now grows outside cultivation in many areas. Its historical use should not suggest a safe household remedy: every part contains toxic alkaloids. A plant may spend its first season as a low rosette before producing an upright flowering stem.

solenopsis-richteri.summary: Black imported fire ants live in colonies with conspicuous soil mounds and workers of several sizes. Workers are mostly brownish black, sometimes with a reddish patch on the abdomen, and can deliver a painful sting. Introduced populations are established in parts of the southeastern United States. This species is closely related to the red imported fire ant and can hybridize with it, so color alone is not a reliable way to separate them. Specialist examination may be needed for a firm identification.

medicago-lupulina.summary: Black medick is a low, spreading member of the pea family often seen in lawns, field edges and disturbed ground.
