Its leaves have three small leaflets, giving it a clover-like appearance, but the central leaflet has a short stalk of its own. Rounded clusters of tiny yellow flowers develop into dark seedpods, which explain the common name. It often grows where turf is thin or soil is poor, and its taproot supports a mat of stems close to the ground.

mimosa-pigra.summary: Black mimosa is a prickly, woody shrub with finely divided leaves that fold when touched. Rounded pink to mauve flower heads are followed by clusters of bristly brown pods. It favors wet ground, including floodplains, stream edges and abandoned fields. Native to tropical America, it has become a major wetland invader in northern Australia, where dense stands replace open vegetation and obstruct access. Its sensitive foliage resembles that of smaller sensitive plants, but mature black mimosa forms a substantial shrub.

brassica-nigra.summary: Black mustard is an upright annual with bright yellow flowers and a loose rosette of lower leaves. The lower leaves are lobed, while leaves higher on the stem become narrow and undivided. Its short, slender seedpods stand close against the flowering stem, a useful distinction from several other yellow-flowered mustards. Mature plants can rise well above surrounding low vegetation. The plant is widely known under the name Brassica nigra, although modern taxonomic treatments sometimes place it in another genus.

solanum-nigrum.summary: Black nightshade is a branching herb with small white flowers and clusters of berries that change from green to black or purplish black. It grows in sunny, disturbed places such as fields, gardens and roadsides. Birds can spread its seeds after eating the fruit. Identification deserves care: several closely related nightshades look alike, and New England records have often used this name too broadly. The leaves and unripe fruit contain toxic compounds, so appearance alone is no basis for treating it as food.

jacaranda-mimosifolia.summary: Black poui, better known in many places as jacaranda, is a South American tree grown for its blue-purple flowers and fine, fern-like foliage. Its spreading branches create light shade, and the flowers can form a colorful carpet beneath the canopy. Rounded, woody seed capsules persist after flowering. It does best in warm conditions with sunshine and well-drained soil; frost limits where it can thrive. Its presence as a planted ornamental should be distinguished from evidence that it has escaped cultivation.

rattus-rattus.summary: Black rats are slender, agile rodents also called roof rats or ship rats. Their long tails help them balance as they climb trees, fences and buildings. They often nest above ground in dense vegetation, attics or wall spaces and forage mainly at night. Fruit and nuts are important foods, but their diet also includes small animals and eggs. Human transport has carried them far beyond their original range, and around buildings they can contaminate food and damage materials by gnawing.

parasaissetia-nigra.summary: This black scale, also called nigra scale, is a sap-feeding insect found on many tropical and subtropical plants. Adult females look like dark brown or glossy black bumps; they are broader on leaves and often narrower on twigs. Citrus, coffee, mango, avocado, hibiscus and figs are among its hosts. The young crawlers move to new feeding sites, while older stages are usually still. Feeding produces honeydew, and natural enemies can provide substantial control of colonies.

saissetia-oleae.summary: Black scale is a soft scale insect whose mature females resemble dark raised bumps on woody stems. A ridge shaped like the letter H is a particularly useful clue. Young stages settle on leaves and twigs, feeding on plant sap and releasing sticky honeydew. Sooty mold grows on that coating, and heavy colonies can weaken trees. Olive and citrus are familiar hosts, along with many ornamentals. Dense, sheltered foliage can favor the insect, while parasitoid wasps help restrain it.

ctenosaura-similis.summary: Black spiny-tailed iguanas are large lizards with a long tail ringed by sharp scales. Adults are commonly gray or tan with dark bands, while young animals may retain green coloring. They bask in open places and shelter among rocks, walls or burrows. Young iguanas eat many insects; adults take more plant material but still consume animal prey. Native to Mexico and Central America, the species has established populations in Florida, where local wildlife impacts have been documented.

tubastraea-micranthus.summary: Black sun coral builds branching, tree-like colonies with dark green to black living tissue over a hard pale skeleton. Unlike many familiar reef corals, it lacks the symbiotic algae that supply energy from sunlight. Its polyps capture food carried by the water, and its strong skeleton suits places exposed to currents. Native to the Indo-Pacific, it has also been recorded growing on offshore platforms in the northern Gulf of Mexico. It is a stony coral, despite the name suggesting precious black corals.

vincetoxicum-nigrum.summary: Black swallow-wort is a perennial climbing plant that winds around neighboring vegetation or trails across the ground. Its opposite, oval leaves are glossy green, and its small dark-purple flowers have five triangular lobes. In summer, slender pods develop and later release seeds with silky hairs. The plant comes from southwestern Europe and has established dense patches in parts of North America. Its twining stems and nearly black flowers help distinguish it from the more familiar upright milkweeds.

ischnaspis-longirostris.summary: Black thread scale is an armored scale insect with an unusually long, narrow protective cover. Adult females have yellow bodies hidden beneath shiny dark-brown to black covers that look like tiny dashes on a leaf or stem. It feeds on many tropical and subtropical plants, with palms among its common hosts. The yellow young crawlers disperse before settling to feed. Female reproduction does not require mating, and males have not been reported.

xylosandrus-compactus.summary: Black twig borer is a tiny beetle that tunnels into small branches of many trees and shrubs. Females make pin-sized entrances, often on the underside of a twig, and establish a chamber where their young develop. Fungi growing inside provide food for the beetles. Leaves beyond an attack may wilt and turn brown, making a dead twig the first obvious sign. Unlike many related ambrosia beetles, it can attack healthy plants as well as stressed ones.

otiorhynchus-sulcatus.summary: Black vine weevil is a dark, broad-snouted beetle that feeds at night and hides by day. Adults leave rounded notches around leaf edges, but the more serious damage usually happens below ground. Its pale, legless grubs eat roots and can cause container plants to wilt or die. Many ornamental plants and some fruits are hosts. Adults cannot fly, yet they climb well, and movement of infested plants can make this a persistent nursery and garden problem.

acacia-mearnsii.summary: Black wattle is an Australian shrub or tree with finely divided leaves and rounded clusters of pale-yellow or cream flowers. The foliage gives the canopy a soft, feathery appearance, while its seedpods are narrow and often pinched between the seeds. In its native southeastern Australian range it grows in forest, woodland and coastal scrub, including creek banks and hillsides. It has been widely cultivated for tannin and timber products, so a planted tree does not by itself establish a local invasion.

iris-domestica.summary: Blackberry lily is a perennial in the iris family, despite its lily-like common name. Fans of upright, sword-shaped leaves rise from underground stems, and wiry flowering stems carry orange blooms marked with red spots. Later, the seed capsules split open to show shiny black seeds clustered like a blackberry. Native to eastern and southeastern Asia, it is widely grown as an ornamental. The showy black clusters are seeds rather than edible berries, an easy distinction to miss.

thunbergia-alata.summary: Blackeyed susan vine is a twining plant with soft, triangular to heart-shaped leaves and flowers that usually have a dark central eye. Wild forms commonly flower in yellow or orange, while garden selections offer additional colors. Native to tropical and southern Africa and Madagascar, it grows in varied habitats from woodland edges to disturbed vegetation. In gardens its stems climb supports or trail from baskets. It is distinct from the upright North American Rudbeckia flowers that share the black-eyed Susan name.

acacia-melanoxylon.summary: Blackwood is an Australian tree with dark, deeply furrowed bark and a leafy crown that can reach forest-tree proportions. Its mature foliage consists of flattened leaf stalks, called phyllodes, with several strong lengthwise veins. Pale cream to yellow flower balls are followed by twisting brown pods; each dark seed is partly surrounded by a bright orange or reddish thread. In its native range it grows in moist forests, including wet eucalyptus forest and cooler rainforest.

silene-latifolia.summary: White campion, Silene latifolia, also called bladder campion in some references, is a familiar white-flowered herb of open ground. This short-lived perennial has soft, hairy leaves in opposite pairs and white flowers with five deeply notched petals. Behind each flower is a swollen, veined green cup. Male and female flowers grow on separate plants. Native to Europe and introduced in North America, it grows in fields, meadows and disturbed ground. It can hybridize with red campion, producing plants with pink flowers.

silybum-marianum.summary: Blessed milkthistle is a large annual or biennial thistle whose glossy green leaves are boldly marbled with white. Sharp spines line the leaves and the broad bracts surrounding its pink-purple flower heads. Young plants begin as ground-level rosettes before sending up tall flowering stems. Originally from southern Europe, it has been cultivated as an herb and can escape into disturbed ground and pasture. Its conspicuous foliage helps separate it from many other thistles even before it flowers.

papaver-dubium.summary: Blindeyes, also called long-headed or field poppy, is a slender annual with hairy stems, divided leaves and delicate orange-red flowers. Its four petals may have little or no dark marking at their bases. The fruit is especially useful for recognition: a smooth, elongated capsule rather than the short, rounded capsule of some other poppies. Fine hairs lie flat against the upper flower stalk. A taproot anchors the plant, while its dry capsules release many small seeds.

calliandra-haematocephala.summary: Blood red tassel flower is a tropical shrub or small tree grown for round, bright red flower clusters that resemble powder puffs. The showy threads are the flowers' long stamens. Its leaves are twice divided into small leaflets, giving the spreading crown a fine texture. Firm brown pods follow the flowers. It is native to Bolivia, while cultivated plants are familiar in warm gardens, where moist, well-drained soil and sun or partial shade suit its growth.

asclepias-curassavica.summary: Bloodflower is a tropical milkweed with narrow, opposite leaves and clusters of red-orange flowers topped by yellow or orange crowns. Its upright stems release milky sap when damaged, and slender pods eventually open to release silky-haired seeds. It stays leafy in warm conditions but is often grown as an annual where winters are cold. Monarch caterpillars feed on it, yet persistent winter growth in warm regions can encourage parasite buildup, making locally native milkweeds a better garden choice there.

geranium-sanguineum.summary: Bloody geranium is a low, spreading perennial often grown in gardens for its magenta-pink flowers. Each flower has five broad petals marked with darker veins, while the leaves are deeply divided into narrow, fingerlike lobes. Underground stems allow a clump to widen over time. Native to Europe and western Asia, it favors well-drained ground in sun or partial shade. Garden escapes have been documented in parts of North America, including disturbed sites and meadows in New England.

hemimysis-anomala.summary: Bloody red shrimp is a tiny freshwater crustacean with prominent black eyes and a partly transparent body speckled red or orange. Its color changes with light and temperature, so some individuals look almost colorless. Swarms shelter around rocks, docks and other shaded structures, emerging to feed on small aquatic organisms. Native to the Ponto-Caspian region, it has spread to the Great Lakes. Its flat-ended tail, with a long spine at each corner, is more useful for identification than redness alone.

chrysomya-rufifacies.summary: This blow fly is often called the hairy maggot blow fly because its older larvae carry fleshy, spiny projections that give them a bristly appearance. Adults are metallic green with a bluish sheen and resemble several other blow flies. The larvae develop in animal remains, where older stages may also prey on other maggots. The species is important in forensic research and livestock health; in some regions it can infest existing animal wounds as well as carrion.

acyrthosiphon-kondoi.summary: Blue alfalfa aphid is a soft-bodied, blue-green insect that feeds on alfalfa and other legumes. Long legs, antennae and paired rear tubes give it a slender appearance. Colonies often gather on young shoots and stems, especially in cool weather. Feeding can stunt plants, while sticky honeydew supports dark sooty mold. It closely resembles the pea aphid and may occur alongside it, but its antennae darken gradually toward the tips instead of carrying distinct dark bands at the joints.

sherardia-arvensis.summary: Blue fieldmadder is a small annual that can spread into a low, rough-textured mat. Narrow leaves and leaflike structures form rings around its square stems, making it resemble a miniature bedstraw. The tiny flowers set it apart: they are pinkish mauve, with a short tube opening into four spreading lobes, clustered near stem tips. Native across parts of Europe, North Africa and Asia, it also grows beyond that range in fields, grassland and other open, disturbed places.

selitrichodes-globulus.summary: Blue gum galling wasp is a small insect whose larvae develop inside swollen growths on blue gum eucalyptus. The damaged shoots can look distorted and discolored, making the galls easier to notice than the adult wasps. The species was described scientifically in 2009 after infestations were found in Los Angeles County, California. Published accounts associate it with the blue gum complex; unusual eucalyptus galls on their own do not prove that this particular wasp is present.

panicum-antidotale.summary: Blue panicum is a tall, coarse perennial grass that grows in dense clumps and spreads by short underground stems. Its sturdy stems have conspicuous joints, while the long leaves show a strong middle vein and often wavy margins. Loose, branching seed heads become drooping as they mature. Native to Asia and planted as a forage grass elsewhere, it can escape into open or disturbed ground. Texas records describe it in fields and other open sites, especially on clay loam soils.

crotalaria-verrucosa.summary: Blue rattlesnake is a bushy tropical legume, also known as blue rattlepod. Unlike many relatives with divided leaves, it has broad, simple leaves on angular, branching stems. The pea-shaped flowers are pale blue, lavender or whitish, with a darker keel, and are followed by short, inflated, softly hairy pods. Its native range extends from tropical and subtropical Asia to northern Australia. Elsewhere in the tropics it occurs in open places, including pastures and sandy roadsides.

ophiostoma-tenellum.summary: Ophiostoma tenellum, now called Jamesreidia tenella, is a fungus associated with wood. It is a microscopic wood-associated fungus recorded from North America, including collections connected with bark beetles in spruce logs. It has also been isolated from logs used to grow shiitake mushrooms, where it can interfere with mushroom growth. Blue stain is a broad type of wood discoloration that can involve different fungi; it cannot establish this species by itself. Identifying this fungus requires examination of its microscopic structures and, when needed, DNA evidence.

oreochromis-aureus.summary: Blue tilapia is a deep-bodied freshwater fish with a small mouth and an olive to bluish-gray back. Its tail usually has irregular markings and a pink-red outer edge; young fish show a dark spot near the rear of the dorsal fin. It occupies varied waters, from canals and vegetated lakes to rivers and springs. Females shelter eggs and young in their mouths. Introduced populations occur in Florida, where similar tilapias make careful identification important.

billardiera-heterophylla.summary: Bluebell creeper is an evergreen climbing shrub from Western Australia, with slender twining stems and narrow green leaves. Small, nodding blue flowers hang in clusters and are followed by elongated purple fruits. It is grown ornamentally in mild climates and can climb through nearby vegetation. The name needs care: the similar Billardiera fusiformis is also sold and described as bluebell creeper. Older accounts under Sollya heterophylla may include both species, so identification should use a modern botanical treatment.

passiflora-caerulea.summary: Bluecrown passionflower is a vigorous climbing vine from South America. Tendrils help it grip supports, while deeply lobed leaves surround striking white flowers with a ring of blue, white and dark purple threads. Raised reproductive parts stand above the flower's center. Oval fruits ripen from green to yellow-orange. The vine remains leafy in warm winters but may lose its leaves in colder conditions. It is widely grown on fences and trellises in sunny, well-drained places.

atriplex-nummularia.summary: Bluegreen saltbush, often called old man saltbush, is a large Australian shrub with silvery-gray foliage. Tiny scales give the leaves their pale appearance; leaf shapes can vary from oval to nearly round even on one plant. Male and female flowers usually grow on separate shrubs, and the developing seeds are enclosed by enlarged, leaflike bracts. It naturally occupies inland dry country, often on heavy soils near floodways, and tolerates both drought and occasional flooding.

ageratum-houstonianum.summary: Bluemink is the familiar garden ageratum, a small annual grown for clusters of soft-looking flowers. The heads are usually blue or lavender, though cultivated forms may be pink or white. Its broad, softly hairy leaves have shallowly toothed edges, and the stems can be green or reddish. Native to Central America, it favors sunny or partly shaded, well-drained sites. It sometimes escapes cultivation, but North Carolina's flora notes that many records there represent planted specimens rather than wild populations.

agrilus-cyanescens.summary: The bluish borer beetle is a metallic wood-boring beetle whose adults vary from blue to green. Native to Eurasia, it is established in parts of North America. Larvae develop in woody stems of honeysuckles; a confirmed Oregon discovery involved damaged twinberry shrubs and beetles emerging from their branches. Its appearance can resemble other Agrilus beetles, so color alone is unreliable. Published assessments describe limited overall economic impact, even though individual ornamental shrubs can suffer noticeable damage.

tradescantia-spathacea.summary: Boatlily is a tropical perennial that forms clumps of stiff, sword-shaped leaves, usually green above and purple underneath. Its small white flowers sit inside pairs of folded purple bracts that resemble little boats, explaining several of its common names. Short, thick stems keep the leaf rosettes close to the ground. Often grown as a houseplant or warm-climate groundcover, it can spread beyond gardens in suitable climates. The sap may irritate skin, so handling deserves care.

ficus-religiosa.summary: Bodhi tree is a large fig tree recognized by heart-shaped leaves that taper into unusually long, narrow tips. Its small figs grow near the leaf bases and turn purple to black when ripe. Native to parts of South Asia, it is widely cultivated and holds religious importance in Buddhism and Hinduism. The tree may begin life on another tree before roots reach the ground. In Singapore, birds and small mammals eat its fruits and help disperse the seeds.

schoenoplectiella-mucronata.summary: Bog bulrush is a wetland sedge with upright, spongy stems that are distinctly three-sided. Its leaves are reduced largely to brown sheaths around the stem bases, so the green stems do most of the visible work. Clusters of small, cone-shaped flower spikelets produce dark brown seeds. It grows in waterlogged ground and wetlands, with a broad native range across the Old World and Australia. The names Scirpus mucronatus and Schoenoplectus mucronatus appear in older accounts of the same species.

fuchsia-boliviana.summary: Bolivian fuchsia is a large shrub or small tree from the Andes of Peru, Bolivia and northwestern Argentina. Long clusters of narrow, hanging flowers end its arching branches, usually combining scarlet tubes and petals. Broad leaves have hairy red stalks, and elongated berries darken to purple or nearly black. It is cultivated for its abundant flowers in mild, moist conditions. Some garden forms have white flower tubes with red petals, so flower color alone does not define the species.

paraleyrodes-bondari.summary: Bondar's nesting whitefly is a tiny plant-feeding insect that leaves circular white wax deposits on foliage. Adults are about a millimeter long, with gray-brown wing bands that form an X when viewed from above. Young stages produce fine wax threads and a skirtlike fringe, eventually sitting inside a white waxy nest. Heavy infestations can coat leaves with honeydew and dark sooty mold. It has been recorded on several tropical crops and ornamentals, but related nesting whiteflies can be difficult to distinguish.

chrysanthemoides-monilifera.summary: Boneseed is a woody South African shrub with yellow daisy-like flowers and small fruits that turn black when ripe. The name usually refers to Chrysanthemoides monilifera subspecies monilifera, whose leathery leaves have toothed edges and whose dry seeds are pale and bone-colored. The broader species also includes bitou bush, a more spreading form with rounder, smoother-edged leaves. Introduced boneseed can form dense stands in parts of Australia and New Zealand, so the subspecies matters when describing its appearance and local behavior.

croton-bonplandianus.summary: Bonpland's croton is a branching, partly woody plant with narrow, pointed leaves and small, inconspicuous flowers. The leaves have blunt teeth along their edges. Male and female flowers share the same flowering stem, and the rounded, three-lobed fruit separates into single-seeded sections when ripe. Native to southern South America, it has spread into many tropical regions. In India's Eastern Ghats it is naturalized in disturbed places, including clearings, village margins and fallow ground.

ligustrum-obtusifolium.summary: Border privet is a spreading, many-stemmed shrub often planted as a hedge. Small oval leaves grow in opposite pairs, and narrow clusters of white flowers are followed by black fruits that can persist into the colder months. Its branches spread broadly, giving an untrimmed plant a loose, layered shape. The leaves may turn reddish-purple in autumn, with some retained in mild conditions. This Asian shrub has escaped cultivation in Connecticut, where it can establish in lightly managed areas.

parthenocissus-tricuspidata.summary: Boston ivy is a deciduous woody vine from eastern Asia, familiar on walls and other vertical surfaces. Branched tendrils end in adhesive pads that anchor the stems firmly. Mature leaves are usually broad and three-lobed, turning red or burgundy in autumn; young growth can carry three separate leaflets. Small blue-black fruits, often on red stalks, attract birds. Although commonly cultivated, it also grows outside gardens in disturbed places and on rocky ledges in parts of New England.

saponaria-officinalis.summary: Bouncingbet, also called soapwort, is an upright perennial with smooth stems and opposite, lance-shaped leaves marked by several strong veins. Clusters of pale pink or white flowers bloom at the stem tips. Each flower usually has five slightly notched petals emerging from a long, narrow green or reddish tube; double-flowered garden forms also occur. Originally from Eurasia, it was widely cultivated. Its soapwort name recalls the saponins in the leaves, which were formerly used to make a washing liquid.

cydalima-perspectalis.summary: Box tree moth is an Asian moth whose caterpillars feed on boxwood. The larvae are green with black heads and contrasting dark and pale lengthwise stripes. They tie foliage with silk, leaving webbing, droppings and chewed leaves inside the shrub. Heavy feeding can strip the leaves and damage bark. Adults usually have white wings bordered broadly in dark brown, though a darker form also occurs. Hidden caterpillars among dense foliage make careful inspection of the plant's interior useful.

monarthropalpus-flavus.summary: Boxwood leafminer is a tiny fly whose young live and feed inside boxwood leaves. Infested leaves develop yellowish spots and swollen, blisterlike mines that later turn brown; heavy attacks can thin a shrub as damaged leaves fall early. The orange to reddish adults resemble small gnats and appear around boxwoods in spring. Several larvae may share one leaf. Because the insects are concealed between the leaf surfaces, checking the leaves themselves is more useful than looking only for flying adults.

centaurium-pulchellum.summary: Branched centaury is a small annual with delicate pink flowers above pairs of oval leaves. It often branches near the base and may stay only a few inches tall. Unlike some other centauries, it does not form a lasting rosette of leaves at ground level. Its tiny flowers have short stalks and a narrow tube that opens into spreading lobes. Native across parts of Europe, Asia and northern Africa, it occurs in North American fields and other disturbed ground as an introduced plant.

schizoporella-errata.summary: Branching bryozoan is a colony of tiny marine animals that builds a hard crust over rocks, shells and harbor structures. Older portions can become thick, dark brown or purplish, while growing edges are paler; some colonies develop folded sheets or hollow branches. Its animals collect suspended food with fine tentacles. Originally described from Naples, it is associated with warm coastal waters. Similar bryozoans have often been confused with it, so older reports from distant coastlines need careful checking.

begonia-hirtella.summary: Brazilian begonia is a small, soft-stemmed tropical plant with green leaves covered in fine hairs. It can flower while still only a few centimeters tall, producing small white blossoms above the foliage. Its papery brown fruits hold numerous dustlike seeds. The species is native to tropical parts of the Americas and favors moist tropical settings. It is also found outside that range; Singapore records it as a casual nonnative plant rather than assigning it a broad invasive status.

jasminum-fluminense.summary: Brazilian jasmine is a woody, evergreen climber with opposite leaves divided into three leaflets. Its white, tubular flowers open into narrow spreading lobes and have a noticeable fragrance. Despite its common name, the species comes from Africa and the Arabian Peninsula. Introduced as an ornamental, it has escaped cultivation in southern Florida, where it can climb into forest canopies and cover other vegetation. Birds and mammals carry its seeds, helping it spread away from planted vines.

alternanthera-brasiliana.summary: Brazilian joyweed is a long-lived herb or small shrub often grown for its purple or reddish foliage. Leaves grow in opposite pairs, and small whitish flowers gather into rounded or slightly elongated heads on slender stalks. Shaded plants may be much greener than plants in sun. Native from Mexico through tropical America, it has been planted elsewhere as an ornamental. Stems can root where they touch the ground, and discarded cuttings can help it spread beyond gardens.

solanum-seaforthianum.summary: Brazilian nightshade is a sprawling perennial shrub or climber grown for loose clusters of mauve-blue, star-shaped flowers. Its leaves are deeply divided, and the flowers are followed by small, bright red berries. The stems lack prickles, a useful feature when comparing it with other nightshades. It has escaped ornamental plantings into moist sites in parts of Australia. In Florida, current guidance varies by region, with central and southern areas advised to manage plantings to prevent escape.

schinus-terebinthifolia.summary: Brazilian Peppertree is an evergreen shrub or small tree with dense branches, glossy compound leaves and clusters of small red fruits. The leaves have several leaflets along a central stalk, which may be narrowly winged. Native to South America, it was widely planted as an ornamental and now forms dense thickets in parts of Florida and Hawaii. Birds help disperse its single-seeded fruits. It grows in many disturbed and natural habitats, including relatively dry ground within otherwise wet landscapes.

schinus-terebinthifolia-var-raddianus.summary: Brazilian peppertree is sometimes recorded under the older name Schinus terebinthifolia var. raddiana, also written var. raddianus. That name is now treated as a synonym of the typical variety rather than a reliably separate kind of tree. Brazilian peppertrees are evergreen shrubs or small trees with compound leaves, small pale flowers and clusters of red fruits. Those familiar features help recognize the broader species, but they do not establish the older variety name on a living plant.

verbena-brasiliensis.summary: Brazilian vervain is a tall, rough-haired herb with branching stems and slender spikes of tiny bluish-purple flowers. Opposite, toothed leaves sit directly on the angular stems. Native to South America, it grows in fields, roadsides, damp grassland and stream margins where introduced, including North Carolina. It is easily confused with other tall verbenas. The small flower size and the bracts projecting among the flowers are more useful clues than its overall silhouette alone.

eichhornia-paniculata.summary: Brazilian water hyacinth is an aquatic herb that holds its leaves and branching flower clusters above the water. Its broad leaves have heart-shaped bases and long, slender stalks that are not swollen. Upright flowering plants have many blossoms in each branched cluster, making a different outline from a floating rosette. Current botanical references place it in Pontederia as Pontederia paniculata. It is a separate species from the familiar floating water hyacinth, so that plant's growth habits and impacts should not be assumed here.

egeria-densa.summary: Brazilian Waterweed is a submerged freshwater plant with long, branching stems and dense rings of bright green leaves. Rooted near the bottom, it grows upward and often concentrates its foliage close to the surface. White flowers rise to the water surface during warmer months. Native to South America, it became familiar through ponds and aquariums. In invaded Washington waters, thick growth can crowd other aquatic plants, slow water movement and interfere with recreation.

poranopsis-paniculata.summary: Bridal bouquet is a vigorous climbing vine with broad, heart-shaped leaves and large sprays of tiny white flowers. The undersides of its leaves are covered in pale, silvery hairs, giving foliage a two-tone appearance. Native from the Indian subcontinent to Myanmar, it has been cultivated in other warm regions. Hawaiian specimens document vines spreading across fences, shrubs and trees, sometimes reaching well into the canopy. The small flowers may have a faint sweet fragrance.

campanula-cervicaria.summary: Bristly bellflower is a rough-haired wildflower with pale blue to lilac bells packed into rounded clusters. Its lower leaves are narrow, and the upright stem is thick and angular. Plants often begin as a leafy rosette before flowering in a later season. It grows around woodland edges, open woods and other partly open habitats in Europe. Its status deserves local attention: conservation work in Bavaria aims to support remaining populations, showing why a catalog listing alone cannot establish that a plant is unwanted.

cynosurus-echinatus.summary: Bristly dogstail grass is an annual grass with a dense, egg-shaped flower head covered in long, stiff bristles. Its narrow leaves are flat, and its upright stems may grow alone or in small tufts. Each head contains a mixture of fertile and sterile flower units, which contributes to its distinctive bristly outline. In British Columbia it occurs in disturbed ground, dry forest edges and thin-soiled Garry oak habitats, where managing seed production can help protect sensitive native vegetation.

leontodon-hispidus.summary: Bristly hawkbit is a dandelion-like herb whose leaves form a rosette close to the ground. Flower stalks rise above it with yellow flower heads, while the leaves vary from lightly toothed to deeply divided. Many plants carry forked or branching hairs, although hairiness varies among forms. A familiar grassland plant in parts of Europe and the Alps, it is also recorded as an introduced plant in New England fields, lawns and roadsides. Mature fruits help distinguish it from similar hawkbits.

persicaria-longiseta.summary: Bristly Lady's Thumb is a low, often sprawling annual with slender spikes of tiny pink flowers. Its smooth stems bear alternate leaves, sometimes marked with a faint dark blotch. A papery sheath circles each leaf base, with conspicuously long bristles along its upper edge. Native to Asia, the species is introduced in much of eastern North America. At Fontenelle Forest in Nebraska it is common along trails, where its loose growth and small flower spikes can be easy to overlook.

helminthotheca-echioides.summary: Bristly oxtongue is a coarse herb with yellow, dandelion-like flower heads and conspicuously rough leaves. Many of its hooked hairs arise from small raised bumps, giving the plant a prickly appearance. Beneath each flower head, several broad outer bracts surround a narrower inner set. It grows in fields, gardens, roadsides and other disturbed ground. Native around the Mediterranean region, it has been introduced elsewhere, including North America, and older references often call it Picris echioides.

najas-minor.summary: Brittle Waternymph is a submerged freshwater plant with narrow, curved leaves and teeth visible along their edges. Leaves grow in pairs, though crowded shoots may look whorled. Its flowers and seeds are tiny and sit near the leaf bases. Native to parts of Europe, Africa and Asia, it has spread in North America through seeds and fragments. Some invaded waters develop dense growth, but effects vary: Wisconsin reports that nuisance-level growth has not been observed there.

galeopsis-tetrahit.summary: Brittlestem hempnettle is an annual in the mint family with square, bristly stems and opposite, coarsely toothed leaves. Clusters of tubular pink, purple or white flowers sit where the upper leaves meet the stem. Each blossom has an arched upper lip and a spreading lower lip with darker markings near its base. Native from Europe to southwestern Siberia, it is introduced in North America, including British Columbia. Its nettle-like foliage can disguise its distinctive flowers until they open.

rumex-obtusifolius.summary: Broadleaf Dock is a sturdy perennial that starts as a rosette of large leaves with heart-shaped bases. Later it sends up a tall, ribbed flowering stem, with smaller leaves above and branching clusters of tiny greenish flowers. These clusters turn reddish brown as the fruits mature, and older foliage may also become reddish. A large fleshy taproot supports repeat growth. It is a familiar plant of disturbed ground and occurs along waterways in places such as Arizona.

epipactis-helleborine.summary: Broadleaf helleborine is a terrestrial orchid with an upright stem, broad leaves and a loose line of small flowers. Its leaves alternate up the stem, with parallel veins and lower bases that partly wrap around it. Flowers combine green, pink or purplish tones and have a shaped lower lip rather than a long spur. Native across much of Europe and Asia and parts of North Africa, it has become established in North America, sometimes appearing in disturbed garden or woodland settings.

juncus-planifolius.summary: Broadleaf rush is a tufted perennial that can look like a small clump of grass until its branched flower clusters develop. Flat leaves gather at the base, while the stems carry an open, umbrella-like arrangement of small rounded flower heads. Brown capsules follow the flowers. It favors open, damp ground, including exposed clay and track or drain margins. Native in parts of the Southern Hemisphere, including New Zealand and Australia, it is introduced in places such as Hawaii and Oregon.

lepidium-latifolium.summary: Broadleaved pepperweed is a tall perennial in the mustard family, with smooth green to gray-green leaves and dense sprays of tiny white flowers. New shoots begin as low rosettes before sending up stiff stems. Underground, an extensive root system stores energy and produces more shoots. Introduced from southeastern Europe and Asia, it forms persistent stands in parts of the western United States, especially around waterways, wetlands and irrigated ground. Seeds and root pieces can move it into new areas.

vulpia-bromoides.summary: Brome fescue is a small annual grass with slender stems, narrow leaves and a compact, bristly flower cluster held clear of the uppermost leaf sheath. Its spikelets contain several flowers, each with a fine projecting awn. It grows in a wide range of open habitats, from coastal ground to dry inland sites, and is introduced from Europe in Washington. Some current references call it Festuca bromoides, while regional floras continue to use the catalog name Vulpia bromoides.

thaumastocoris-peregrinus.summary: Bronze bug is a tiny, flattened brown insect that lives on eucalyptus foliage. Adults and orange young insects may gather on the same leaves, alongside clusters of black eggs. Feeding can turn leaves reddish, then yellow-brown, giving affected crowns their bronze appearance; heavy infestations may thin the canopy. Native to Australia, it has spread to eucalyptus plantings in several other regions. Its small size and similarity to related bugs make a close examination more dependable than leaf discoloration alone.

odontites-vulgaris.summary: Odontites vulgaris, usually called red bartsia, is a downy annual of open grassland. Slender, branching stems carry narrow, toothed leaves and small pink flowers with two lips. Plants can reach about half a metre tall. They make their own green growth while also drawing resources from grass roots, a habit called partial parasitism. Native in Britain and Ireland, red bartsia also appears in Canadian floristic records. Unlike the pale, leafless plants often called broomrapes, red bartsia keeps conspicuous green foliage.

anolis-sagrei.summary: Brown anoles are small, quick-moving lizards often seen basking on low fences, tree trunks and sunny garden edges. Their brown or gray bodies commonly show pale stripes, spots or diamonds, and males display an orange-red throat fan with a pale border. They hunt insects and other small animals, usually close to the ground. Native to Caribbean islands, they are widespread introductions in Florida. Native green anoles can also turn brown, so body color alone is not a reliable identification.

bugula-neritina.summary: Brown bryozoan forms branching, purplish-brown tufts that may look like miniature seaweed bushes. Each tuft is a colony of tiny animals that draw food particles from seawater. Colonies attach to rocks, pilings, floats, hulls and other submerged surfaces, sometimes becoming part of heavy marine fouling. The name Bugula neritina covers several genetically distinct forms with very similar appearances. Some have spread widely through human transport, while the origins and status of particular populations require closer investigation.

cyperus-fuscus.summary: Brown flatsedge is a small annual sedge that forms tufts on damp, open ground beside ponds, streams and ditches. Smooth stems and narrow leaves support clusters of flattened flower spikes, often dark reddish-brown but sometimes yellow-green. It takes advantage of muddy or sandy margins exposed as water levels fall. The species is native across much of Europe and parts of Africa and Asia, with introduced records in North America. Its local status matters: in Germany, it is a native conservation concern.

cornu-aspersum.summary: Brown garden snail carries a rounded, coiled shell patterned with brown bands and pale flecks. Adults are often about three centimetres across, although size and markings vary. Most feeding happens at night or in damp weather, when snails leave shelter to rasp leaves, flowers and soft fruit. Silvery trails can reveal visits after the animals have hidden again. Long transported with plants and for food, this European snail became a troublesome garden and crop pest in California after its nineteenth-century introduction.

hoplosternum-littorale.summary: Brown hoplo is a dark, armored catfish with two rows of hard plates along each side and two pairs of long whiskerlike barbels. It searches muddy bottoms for small invertebrates and decaying material in slow rivers, ponds, marshes and canals. Gulping air helps it cope with oxygen-poor water. Males make floating bubble nests mixed with vegetation and defend them during breeding. Native to South America, it has established in Florida, where its unusual nests have been documented in shallow lake marshes.

halyomorpha-halys.summary: Brown marmorated stink bugs are broad, shield-shaped insects with mottled brown bodies and pale bands on their antennae. Adults are roughly the size of a fingernail. They feed on many fruits, vegetables and ornamental plants, and their feeding can leave fruit distorted or damaged. Native to eastern Asia, they have become important crop pests in parts of North America. In autumn, adults often gather on buildings while looking for winter shelter; finding them indoors does not mean they are breeding in the house.

brassica-juncea.summary: Brown mustard is a leafy mustard crop grown for pungent greens and seeds used in condiments and oil. Plants usually grow as annuals, producing clusters of yellow, four-petaled flowers followed by slender seed pods that split when dry. Leaves vary greatly among cultivated forms, from green to purple and from relatively smooth to deeply lobed. It grows best in cool weather with adequate moisture. Widely introduced beyond its Eurasian origins, it can also occur as a weed, so cultivated plants and wild escapes need different context.

lyctus-brunneus.summary: Brown powderpost beetle is a small, flattened reddish-brown beetle associated with hardwood timber and wooden objects. Its cream-colored larvae tunnel through starch-rich sapwood, sometimes reducing the interior to very fine, flourlike powder. Round exit holes appear when adults emerge, making damage easier to notice than the insects themselves. Infested wood can carry the beetle between countries. The amount of damage depends on the wood and its sapwood content; powder and holes deserve identification before assumptions are made about structural danger.

lecanosticta-acicola.summary: Lecanosticta acicola is a fungus that causes brown spot needle blight in pines. Small discolored spots can expand into brown bands, and infected needles may die at the tips or fall early, leaving a thin-looking crown. Wet needles and humid weather favor infection, while rain and wind spread spores. In New England, eastern white pine is a frequent host, though other pines are susceptible. Similar symptoms can come from other needle diseases, so the pattern of damage alone does not confirm this fungus.

septoria-glycines.summary: Brown spot of soybean is a leaf disease caused by the fungus Septoria glycines. Small brown patches usually appear low on the plant, often surrounded by yellowing tissue. The patches can merge and affected leaves may fall early. Warm, wet weather helps the disease develop, while infected crop remains can carry the fungus into the next season. Brown spot is common in soybean fields and often has little effect on yield; more serious damage is possible when it moves into the upper canopy.

salmo-trutta.summary: Brown trout are introduced freshwater fish familiar to many anglers. Stream fish often have a golden-brown body with dark and reddish spots, while fish living in large lakes can look much more silvery. They eat aquatic insects and other small animals, including fish as they grow. Brought to the United States for fishing, they now live in many rivers and lakes. Their role depends on the waterway: some populations support managed fisheries, while others compete with native trout that conservation programs are working to protect.

latrodectus-geometricus.summary: Brown widow spiders often make their webs in sheltered places around buildings, plant pots and outdoor furniture. Many are mottled tan or brown with an orange hourglass beneath the abdomen, but their colors vary enough to make identification tricky. Young black widows can look similar. A round egg sac covered in little silk spikes is a particularly useful clue. This nonnative spider is established in parts of the southern United States and Southern California. It can bite if pressed against the skin, so identification is best done without handling it.

niditinea-fuscella.summary: The brown-dotted clothes moth is a small, easily overlooked moth with mottled brown wings and a tufted head. Its larvae feed on dry plant and animal material, often in bird nests or poultry houses where feathers and other remains collect. Despite its name, it is only occasionally associated with damage to clothing. Stored animal specimens can also provide food. Adults resemble other small nest moths, so finding one indoors does not by itself show that fabrics are being damaged.

ruellia-blechum.summary: Browne's blechum is a low herb with paired leaves and upright flower spikes. The overlapping green bracts around those spikes are often more noticeable than the tiny pale flowers, giving the plant its other name, green shrimp plant. Its stems can spread along the ground and root where they touch the soil. Native to tropical parts of the Americas, it has become established beyond that range and is listed as invasive in Florida. The square-looking flower spikes are a useful starting point for recognizing it.

centaurea-jacea.summary: Brown knapweed is a perennial wildflower with purple-pink flower heads on upright, branching stems. Beneath each head are overlapping bracts with broad, brown, papery tips that look unevenly torn. Native to Europe, it has become established in North America in fields, meadows and disturbed ground, and can form large patches. It also crosses with black knapweed, producing plants that blur the usual identification clues. A close look at the bracts is more useful than flower color alone.

euproctis-chrysorrhoea.summary: Browntail moths have white wings and a tuft of brown hair at the tip of the abdomen. Their caterpillars feed on trees and shrubs, including oaks, apples and cherries, and spend winter together in silk nests that hold dead leaves on branch tips. Established in parts of New England after introduction from Europe, they can strip foliage during outbreaks. The caterpillars' tiny hairs are also an important concern: they can irritate skin and breathing, even when carried on wind or left on surfaces.

watersipora-arcuata.summary: Watersipora arcuata is a marine animal that grows in colonies, often as dark crusts with reddish growing edges. A colony is made up of many tiny connected individuals and can develop overlapping, curled layers. It attaches to hard surfaces such as rocks, docks and boat hulls, which can carry it between harbors. Records from Southern California and Hawaii reflect its history of introductions, although its original native range remains uncertain. Similar Watersipora species are hard to separate without examining their tiny skeletal features.

plantago-lanceolata.summary: Buckhorn plantain grows as a clump of narrow, strongly ribbed leaves close to the ground. Slender, leafless stalks rise above them, ending in short flower heads ringed with pale, projecting stamens. Originally from Eurasia, it is now a familiar plant in lawns, paths, fields and other disturbed places across much of North America. Its low-growing leaves help it persist under mowing. Compared with broadleaf plantain, the leaves are much narrower and the flowering heads are usually shorter and more compact.

aphis-nasturtii.summary: Buckthorn aphids are tiny, soft-bodied insects that feed on plant sap. They are usually pale yellow or green, and colonies can gather on the undersides of potato leaves. In colder regions they spend winter as eggs on buckthorn, then move to other plants during the growing season. Their importance in crops is not just the sap they take: they can carry potato viruses between plants. Several aphids look alike, making a careful identification useful before deciding how to respond.

fagopyrum-esculentum.summary: Buckwheat grows quickly into a soft, branching annual with arrowhead-shaped leaves and clusters of small white or pink-tinged flowers. Although its seeds are used like grain, it belongs to the knotweed family rather than the grasses. Farmers also grow it as a short-season cover crop, where its dense growth shades weeds and its flowers draw bees and other beneficial insects. Plants sometimes appear outside cultivation, especially on disturbed ground; that alone does not establish an invasive impact.

tandonia-budapestensis.summary: The Budapest slug is a slender, ground-dwelling slug often found around gardens, cultivated fields and other disturbed places. Its brownish-gray body is densely speckled, with a pale yellow ridge running down the tail. A dark stripe along the otherwise pale underside is especially useful when separating it from similar keeled slugs. It can feed both above and below the soil surface, damaging root crops, bulbs and newly sown seed. A curled, horseshoe-like resting posture is another helpful clue.

nipaecoccus-nipae.summary: Buff coconut mealybugs look rather like tiny wax-covered cushions on their host plants. Adult females are orange to reddish brown, with yellowish wax and pointed tufts around the edge and across the back. Despite the common name, they feed on many plants, including palms, avocado and ornamental flowers. Their sap feeding produces sticky honeydew that can support black sooty mold, and ants may tend the colonies. Close inspection of a mature female is often needed to confirm the species.

cenchrus-ciliaris.summary: Buffelgrass forms coarse perennial clumps with rough leaves and fuzzy, bottlebrush-shaped seed heads. Originally planted as forage in dry regions, it is a serious problem in the Sonoran Desert, where it fills the spaces between native shrubs and cacti. Those connected patches carry fire through vegetation that is poorly adapted to burning. The seed heads change from reddish or purplish tones to tan as they mature, and seeds can travel on shoes, clothing, animals and moving water.

fallopia-baldschuanica.summary: Bukhara fleeceflower, also called silver lace vine, can cover a fence with a cloud of tiny pale flowers in late summer. This deciduous, twining climber has heart-shaped leaves and woody older stems. Its speed is part of its appeal in gardens, but also the reason it needs careful placement: shoots can scramble across nearby shrubs and quickly outgrow their support. Small winged fruits develop after flowering, often taking on a pink or reddish tint.

rhopalosiphoninus-latysiphon.summary: The bulb and potato aphid lives in places that are easy to overlook: around roots, inside stored bulbs and on potato tubers. It feeds on a wide range of plants, including ornamental bulbs such as tulips and gladiolus, and can affect crops both in the field and in storage. It is also associated with transmission of plant viruses. Because colonies may remain hidden below ground, careful inspection of planting material is more useful than looking only at the leaves.

watsonia-meriana.summary: Bulbil bugle-lily sends tall spikes of curved, trumpet-shaped flowers above fans of tough, swordlike leaves. This South African perennial grows from underground corms and is familiar in gardens for its salmon, pink, red or pale blooms. The bulbil-producing form develops small brown cormlets along the flower stems, each capable of starting another plant. In invaded open habitats, dense clumps can crowd out other vegetation; moving soil or dumping garden waste can carry the corms to new sites.

poa-bulbosa.summary: Bulbous bluegrass is a small, cool-season grass that gets an early start in spring and dries out early as conditions warm. It grows in tufts, with narrow leaves ending in the little boat-shaped tips typical of bluegrasses. Many plants carry an unusual flowering head full of tiny leafy bulblets, rather than an ordinary-looking spray of seeds. These bulblets and the swollen bases of the shoots help it persist and spread. It occurs on disturbed ground and has also been used to stabilize eroding soil.

phalaris-aquatica.summary: Bulbous canarygrass, often called Harding grass, is a robust perennial that forms tall, leafy clumps topped by dense cylindrical flower heads. Slightly swollen shoot bases give it its other common name. Introduced from Mediterranean Europe as a forage grass, it has escaped into fields, ditches and streamside habitats. In affected western landscapes, established clumps compete with native vegetation for water and space. Most new plants arise from seed, although pieces of its short underground stems can also regrow.

cirsium-vulgare.summary: Bull thistle starts as a low rosette of prickly leaves, then raises a branching stem with pinkish-purple flower heads. Unlike creeping thistles, it has a taproot and spreads by seed. The leaves are rough and hairy above, woolly beneath, and tipped with sharp spines; spiny wings also run down the stems. Originally from Eurasia, it readily colonizes disturbed soil and heavily grazed ground. Its prickles discourage grazing and can make neighboring forage harder for animals to reach.

anthriscus-caucalis.summary: Bur chervil has delicate, fernlike leaves, but its small hooked fruits are its most useful calling card. This Eurasian herb commonly grows as an annual, with hollow, branching stems and little clusters of white flowers beside the upper leaves. The burrlike fruits catch on animals and help the plant travel beyond the parent patch. In parts of the western United States it can form dense growth along waterways and beneath shrubs, although it also survives in drier grassland.

medicago-polymorpha.summary: Burclover spreads low across the ground, with three-parted leaves that can easily be mistaken for an ordinary clover. Small yellow flowers give way to tightly coiled pods, often armed with hooks that cling to fur and clothing. It grows in lawns, fields, roadsides and other disturbed places, and is also grown as forage or a cover crop. The same burrs that help disperse its seeds can become tangled in sheep's wool, reducing its value.

oplismenus-burmannii.summary: Burmann's basketgrass is a low annual grass with spreading stems and relatively broad leaves. The blades can look gently rippled across their width, a useful clue when the plant is not flowering. Its flower head is arranged as several short branches along a central stalk, with slender, often pinkish-red bristles extending well beyond the tiny spikelets. It can grow beside paths and in other disturbed places. Similar basketgrasses need careful comparison, especially when assessing a plant outside its familiar range.

caryota-mitis.summary: Burmese fishtail palm gets its name from the jagged, fan-shaped leaflets that resemble little fish tails. Several slender trunks grow together in a clump, with new shoots arising at the base. Flowering follows an unusual sequence: a trunk flowers near its top first, then progressively lower down, and dies after its final flowering. The rest of the clump continues growing. Native to tropical Asia, this palm is widely cultivated in warm climates; its small fruits contain irritating material and should not be handled casually.

python-bivittatus.summary: Burmese pythons are large, muscular snakes patterned with dark, irregular patches on a tan background. They are comfortable in water and can be remarkably difficult to notice among wetland plants. Native to Southeast Asia, they have an established invasive population in southern Florida, where they eat a wide variety of mammals, birds and reptiles. Their broad diet is well documented: one study of digestive contents from more than 1,700 Florida pythons identified 76 prey species.

cayratia-japonica.summary: Bushkiller is a vigorous vine that uses tendrils to climb over shrubs, trees and garden structures. Its leaves have five toothed leaflets, and the small flowers are orange or salmon colored. The fleshy roots send up new shoots, particularly after they are disturbed, helping a patch recover even when the visible vines have been cut back. Native to Asia, Australia and nearby Pacific regions, it has escaped cultivation in the southern United States and is considered invasive in North Carolina.

eucalyptus-lehmannii.summary: Bushy yate is an evergreen eucalypt from Western Australia that grows as a bushy small tree or a many-stemmed mallee. Its smooth bark varies from pale pink and gray-brown to reddish tones, sometimes with older bark collected around the base. Cream, greenish or yellow flowers add a softer contrast to the foliage. In its native landscape it grows on exposed slopes, rocky outcrops, coastal dunes and creek beds; it is also planted as an ornamental tree elsewhere.

linaria-vulgaris.summary: Butter and eggs is the familiar yellow toadflax, with pale yellow, snapdragon-shaped flowers and a deeper orange-yellow center. Slender leaves line its upright stems, and each flower carries a long spur at the back. Once grown as an ornamental and dye plant, it now occurs along roadsides, in fields and in other open ground across much of temperate North America. A spreading root system lets it form persistent patches, making a few flowering stems part of a much larger plant.

bauhinia-purpurea.summary: Butterfly tree is also known as purple orchid-tree, and both names fit: its rounded leaves are split into two lobes, while its showy flowers range from pink to deep purple. This small to medium tree comes from India and Myanmar and is widely planted in warm regions. Long, flat seedpods follow the flowers and may remain on the branches through winter. In Florida it has escaped cultivation and is considered invasive, so its ornamental appeal needs to be weighed against local spread.

ophiognomonia-clavigignenti-juglandacear.summary: Butternut canker fungus attacks the bark of butternut trees, creating dead, sunken areas that can gradually encircle branches and trunks. Early damage may appear around leaf scars or wounds; older cankers become long cracks or open, dark-stained patches edged with ridges of living bark. As the disease advances, branches die back and the crown thins. Spores move between trees in rain splash and by other carriers. The disease has caused severe losses of butternut across its eastern North American range.

soliva-anthemifolia.summary: Button burrweed stays close to the ground, forming small patches of finely divided, fernlike leaves. Its flowers are easy to miss because the heads sit together near the plant's center rather than rising on showy stalks. As the fruits mature, the clusters become buttonlike and woolly, with stiff pointed tips. This South American annual has become established in disturbed ground and pastures elsewhere. Mature fruit is especially useful for separating it from other small burrweeds with a similar leafy appearance.

impatiens-walleriana.summary: Busy lizzy is a soft-stemmed tropical perennial best known as a colorful bedding plant for shady gardens. Compact mounds of glossy foliage carry flowers in white, pink, red, orange and many cultivated combinations, often from late spring until frost. In colder climates it is usually grown as an annual. Ripe capsules release their seeds suddenly, giving the genus its 'impatient' name. Common garden impatiens can suffer from downy mildew, which yellows the leaves and may leave plants nearly bare.

brassica-oleracea.summary: Cabbage belongs to a remarkably varied species that also includes kale, broccoli, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts and kohlrabi. Centuries of cultivation have emphasized different parts of the same basic plant: leaves, flower buds or swollen stems. The leaves are usually thick and waxy, often blue-green, and flowering plants carry yellow, four-petaled blossoms followed by long pods. Wild cabbage and garden forms may look quite different, so a tight leafy head is only one possible expression of this species.

hellula-undalis.summary: Cabbage webworm is a small moth whose caterpillars feed on cabbage and other mustard-family plants. The larvae are pale gray-yellow with several darker stripes running lengthwise, and they shelter in silk among the young leaves. Feeding near the growing point is particularly damaging: young plants may be stunted or develop several small heads instead of one normal head. The adults are brownish moths with pale wing markings, but closely related webworms can look very similar.

pieris-rapae.summary: The small white butterflies visiting a vegetable patch may be the parents of imported cabbageworms. Their velvety green caterpillars blend into cabbage, broccoli, and related crops, often resting along a leaf vein before chewing holes between the veins. Older larvae do most of the damage and can work their way into developing heads. A regular look beneath the leaves can catch them early; handpicking caterpillars and using well-fitted row covers are useful options for a home garden.

psylliodes-chrysocephalus.summary: Cabbage-stem flea beetles feed on wild and cultivated members of the mustard family. Adults chew the leaves, while their larvae tunnel inside leaf stalks and stems, so the same pest can cause damage in two quite different places. The beetles are usually shiny metallic blue with orange-red legs, although pale and mixed-color forms occur. They are especially important in oilseed rape, where heavy feeding on newly emerged seedlings can destroy the growing point before plants have a chance to recover.

cactoblastis-cactorum.summary: Cactus moth caterpillars live together inside prickly pear pads, hollowing them out as they feed. Older larvae are bright orange-red with dark bands, a striking contrast to the unobtrusive gray-brown adult moth. Females stack eggs into slender sticks that can resemble cactus spines. Introduced from South America to control unwanted cacti in some countries, the moth became a threat where native prickly pears are important parts of the landscape. Infested pads may yellow, ooze fluid and shed piles of insect droppings.

tenebroides-mauritanicus.summary: Cadelle beetles live among stored grain and other dry foods, where both the insects and the places they hide deserve attention. The shiny dark adults have a noticeable narrow waist behind the front part of the body; the pale larvae have a black head and dark markings. Feeding damages grain kernels, especially the germ. Larvae can also bore into nearby wood or plaster, creating sheltered places that make an infestation harder to clear. Old grain residues and damaged storage surfaces are useful places to inspect.

urena-lobata.summary: Caesarweed has small pink flowers that look like miniature hibiscus blooms, but its hooked fruits are often the more memorable feature. They cling to clothing and animal fur, carrying seeds away from the parent shrub. Rough, sometimes lobed leaves and hairy stems help distinguish it before fruit forms. This widespread tropical plant grows in disturbed places, pastures, and forest openings; Florida treats it as invasive. Brush seeds from clothing and equipment before leaving a patch, and keep seed-bearing cuttings contained during removal.

acorus-calamus.summary: Sweet flag grows at wetland edges in clumps of upright, sword-shaped leaves. A short, fleshy spike of tiny flowers appears to project from the side of a leaflike stalk, an unusual feature worth photographing. Names matter here: introduced Acorus calamus has often been confused in North American records with the native American sweet flag, Acorus americanus. The introduced North American form spreads through rhizomes and is sterile. Have a wetland plant specialist confirm the identification before removing a stand or moving divisions.

eulecanium-cerasorum.summary: Calico scale earns its name from the white patches on a dark, rounded adult female. These sap-feeding insects settle on deciduous trees, and their sticky honeydew can leave leaves and objects beneath the tree coated with black sooty mold. Young scales spend part of the season on leaves, then move onto twigs to overwinter. A few scales may do little harm, so check the tree's condition as well as the insects. If treatment is needed, monitoring for tiny moving crawlers helps identify the useful window.

ligustrum-ovalifolium.summary: Oval-leaved privet is a dense hedge shrub with glossy leaves, fragrant white flower clusters, and small fruits that ripen dark purple-black. Its foliage usually remains through mild winters, giving an escaped plant the same tidy-looking greenery as a garden hedge. The species comes from eastern Asia and is recorded outside cultivation in regional floras. Young shoots are nearly hairless, a useful clue alongside the broad oval leaves. Where seedlings appear beyond a planting, remove them early and prune unwanted flowers before fruit develops.

aonidiella-aurantii.summary: California red scale can look like a scattering of tiny reddish-brown disks on citrus leaves, twigs, or fruit. Each disk shelters a sap-feeding insect; newly hatched crawlers move before settling and building their own protective cover. Heavy infestations weaken plants and blemish fruit, but parasitoid wasps often provide valuable control. Look closely before treating a tree, because scale covers can remain after the insect dies. A local crop adviser can help check whether scales are alive and time any treatment to the vulnerable crawler stage.

zantedeschia-aethiopica.summary: The white 'flower' of a calla lily is a curved leaflike spathe wrapped around a yellow spike of many tiny flowers. Large arrow-shaped leaves rise from thick underground rhizomes, forming lush clumps in moist ground. This southern African plant is widely grown for gardens and cut flowers. Its ability to grow from rhizomes matters when a planting is removed: leftover pieces should not be dumped beside streams or wetlands. Wear gloves when handling it, and keep the irritating plant material away from children and pets.

pyrus-calleryana.summary: Callery pear is conspicuous in spring when clusters of white flowers cover the branches before or around leaf-out. Glossy, rounded leaves follow, along with small hard fruits that birds can carry beyond planted trees. Familiar cultivars such as Bradford belong to this species, and crossing between compatible trees has helped escaped populations spread. Wild seedlings may develop formidable thorns and form dense growth in fields and disturbed places. Replacing a planted tree with a locally appropriate alternative helps reduce seed sources; removal also needs a plan for sprouts.

lepidosaphes-camelliae.summary: Camellia scale hides beneath small brown, oystershell-shaped covers on the undersides of leaves. Camellias, sasanquas, and hollies are among its hosts, and heavy infestations can make foliage drop. Tiny crawlers briefly move about before settling to feed, while older insects remain protected under their covers. It is easy to confuse this species with other armored scales, so a close photograph or sample is useful. Inspect incoming plants and preserve the lady beetles and parasitic wasps that help keep scale populations down.

alhagi-maurorum.summary: Camelthorn is a thorny perennial with an underground reach far greater than its modest height suggests. Its stiff branches carry small gray-green leaves and pink to maroon pea flowers; the pods narrow between the seeds like a string of beads. Deep roots and spreading underground stems help it persist in dry ground and colonize irrigated fields or ditch banks. Cutting the top is rarely the end of the job. Keep soil and root fragments from moving to clean areas and plan follow-up with a local weed specialist.

aspidiotus-duplex.summary: Camphor scale is an armored scale that can hide in plain sight as small brown bumps on ornamental plants. The female's rounded, raised cover usually has a yellow-orange spot toward one side, while the male's cover is more elongated. Despite the common name, its hosts include camellias, citrus, and many other plants as well as camphor trees. Older references call it Aspidiotus duplex; modern accounts use Pseudaonidia duplex. Inspect new plants carefully, and have a sample identified before choosing a scale treatment.

cnestus-mutilatus.summary: Sometimes called the gas-can beetle, this small ambrosia beetle is drawn to ethanol odors, including those released by stressed trees. Females bore into wood and cultivate fungi that feed their young. The dark adults are only a few millimeters long, so fresh entry holes and boring dust may attract attention first. Its unusual habit of also boring into some plastic fuel containers explains the nickname. In a landscape, investigate the condition of affected trees and obtain an identification before assuming every tiny hole has the same cause.

cinnamomum-camphora.summary: Camphor tree is a broad evergreen with glossy leaves that release a distinctive camphor scent when crushed. Three strong veins often stand out near the leaf base, and small dark fruits attract birds that carry the seeds. Originally from Asia, it can become a large shade tree; in Florida, escaped trees invade disturbed ground and forests. Small seedlings are easier to address than mature trees, which can resprout after cutting. Where it is invasive, choose another shade tree and check nearby woodland for young plants.

poa-compressa.summary: Canada bluegrass is a low, spreading perennial whose flattened stems give it another helpful name: flat-stemmed bluegrass. It forms loose turf through underground rhizomes and carries compact, branched seed heads above narrow leaves. Poor, disturbed ground often suits it better than the richer soils favored by some other pasture grasses. Despite its common name, it originated in Eurasia and was introduced to North America. For an unfamiliar patch, photograph the stem, leaf junction and seed head before deciding how it fits a lawn or restoration site.

cirsium-arvense.summary: Canada thistle builds patches from a spreading root system, so the shoots above ground show only part of the plant. Spiny leaves and clusters of small purple flower heads help identify it, but its persistent underground buds explain why a single mowing or digging rarely succeeds. It competes in crops, pastures, and disturbed ground, and livestock often avoid grazing around prickly patches. Prevent seed production, keep root-contaminated soil from moving, and combine repeated follow-up with healthy competing vegetation to gradually weaken an established stand.

phoenix-canariensis.summary: Canary Island date palm makes a striking silhouette: a stout trunk topped by a broad crown of long, arching feather leaves. Mature trunks show diamond-shaped scars from old leaf bases, while female trees bear clusters of small yellow-orange dates. Native to the Canary Islands, it is widely planted in warm climates and can naturalize where conditions suit it. The sharp spines at the base of each leaf deserve respect. Leave work high in the crown to a qualified arborist and watch for seedlings beyond the intended planting.

hypericum-canariense.summary: Canary Island St. John's wort is a woody shrub with narrow leaves and clusters of bright yellow flowers. Unlike the low-growing St. John's worts many gardeners know, it can reach several meters tall. In coastal California, escaped plantings form dense stands in disturbed grassland and scrub, crowding native vegetation. Both underground spread and abundant seed complicate removal. Photograph the flowers, leaves and stem shape before acting, then work with local land managers to prevent seed production and revisit treated patches for new growth.

delphinium-elatum.summary: Tall delphinium brings upright spires of blue to purplish flowers above a clump of deeply divided leaves. This perennial comes from Europe and Asia and is the source of many garden selections, so cultivated plants can vary markedly in height and flower color. Its tall stems appreciate shelter and support, especially in wind or heavy rain. Remove spent spikes if you do not want seed, and keep all parts away from grazing animals or curious pets: this beautiful member of the buttercup family is toxic if eaten.

aleurites-moluccanus.summary: Candlenut, or kukui, is a broad-crowned tropical tree whose pale green foliage can stand out across a wooded valley. Younger leaves are often lobed, while older leaves may be more oval. Small pale flowers give way to rounded fruits enclosing hard, dark seeds rich in oil, the source of the name candlenut. Long valued in Pacific cultures, it is naturalized in Hawaii and holds special cultural significance there. Fallen seeds readily produce seedlings, so watch planting boundaries and avoid distributing unwanted fruit or soil containing seeds.

rhinella-marina.summary: Cane toads are large, warty amphibians that often appear around gardens, buildings, and water after dark. Their broad glands behind the eyes can release a milky toxin when threatened, making an encounter dangerous for a pet that bites one. Introduced populations are a management concern in Florida and other warm regions. Smaller native toads can look similar, so size alone is not enough for identification. Keep pet food indoors, supervise pets outside, and photograph an unfamiliar toad before seeking local wildlife guidance.

rhabdoscelus-obscurus.summary: The New Guinea sugarcane weevil spends its most damaging stage hidden inside a plant. Pale, legless larvae tunnel through sugarcane and palms, often leaving a plug of fibers at a tunnel entrance. Feeding can weaken palm trunks or damage the growing tip, so the first visible sign may be a declining or unstable plant. The species has moved among tropical islands, with transported palms providing a pathway. Keep suspect plants on site and ask an agricultural or plant-health specialist to identify the insect before moving or treating them.

pouteria-campechiana.summary: Canistel is a tropical fruit tree best known for its golden-yellow fruit and rich, sometimes egg-yolk-like flesh. The glossy leaves are simple and smooth-edged, and small cream flowers sit in their axils. Fruits vary from rounded to spindle-shaped, often ending in a point; several glossy brown seeds lie inside. Garden trees benefit from room to grow and good drainage. Pick fruit at the appropriate mature stage and let it soften before eating, and keep an eye on self-sown seedlings around a planting.

cucumis-melo.summary: Cantaloupes, honeydews, and several less familiar melons all belong to Cucumis melo, a warm-season vine with tendrils, rough leaves, and small yellow flowers. Fruit shape, rind and flesh vary greatly among cultivated groups, so a netted orange-fleshed melon is only one version of the species. Bees and other insects help flowers set fruit. In a garden, give the vines sun, space and well-drained soil, and avoid excess nitrogen that produces lush growth at the expense of fruit.

campanula-medium.summary: Canterbury bells usually spends its first year as a leafy rosette, then sends up a tall stem lined with generous bell-shaped flowers. Blue, pink, purple and white garden forms make this European biennial a familiar cottage-garden plant. The lower leaves are long and toothed, with smaller leaves along the flowering stem. Seed escapes through small openings in the dry capsules, allowing new plants to appear nearby. Deadhead before capsules mature if you want to keep the display within its chosen bed.

nymphaea-capensis.summary: Cape blue waterlily holds its fragrant flowers above a raft of broad floating leaves. Although blue is the familiar color, named forms and cultivated relatives can also flower pink or mauve. The leaves have a deep notch and a wavy edge, while a short upright, tuberous rhizome anchors the plant below. It comes from Africa and grows in still or slow water. Keep pond plants and discarded rhizomes out of natural waterways, and use more than flower color to distinguish this species from waterlily hybrids.

tecoma-capensis.summary: Cape honeysuckle is a scrambling southern African shrub with clusters of bright trumpet flowers. It belongs to the trumpetvine family, and its compound leaves, usually with five to nine toothed leaflets, help distinguish it from true honeysuckles. Orange-red is typical, with yellow and other colors available in garden selections. Long capsules release winged seeds, and stems can be propagated by layering or cuttings. Give a planting room, prune it to the intended space, and keep rooted trimmings from being dumped beyond the garden.

plumbago-auriculata.summary: Cape leadwort is a loose, scrambling shrub covered in clusters of pale blue flowers, with white-flowered selections also grown. Its small light-green leaves have little ear-shaped appendages near the base, a useful detail behind the name auriculata. Native to southern Africa, it is widely planted in warm gardens and can become a broad mass without pruning. Sunny conditions and good drainage suit it well. Keep a planting within its intended area and collect trimmings rather than dropping them at the edge of natural vegetation.

crassula-multicava.summary: Fairy crassula spreads as a low succulent mat, with fleshy rounded leaves and airy clusters of small pale pink stars. Tiny plantlets may form among the flowers, drop to the ground, and become new plants; creeping stems also root where they touch soil. That easy propagation makes garden waste an effective way to start another patch. The South African species has become an environmental weed in parts of Australia and New Zealand. Collect every loose piece during removal and revisit the site for rooted fragments or fallen plantlets.

stipa-capensis.summary: Cape ricegrass is easiest to notice when its seed heads develop long, twisted awns.
