These bristles give the annual grass a tangled appearance and help its sharp seeds catch on clothing or animal fur. Narrow leaves and a compact seed head support identification, but flowering material is especially useful. In southern California desert areas, it can form dense patches and is a concern for native wildflowers and fire potential. Brush seeds from footwear before leaving a patch and report unfamiliar stands to the local land manager.

delairea-odorata.summary: Cape ivy can drape a streambank or woodland edge in a thick green blanket. Its fleshy, lobed leaves resemble ivy, but clusters of tiny yellow flower heads reveal its place in the daisy family. In invaded coastal California habitats, the vine climbs over shrubs and trees and shades the plants beneath. Even small stem and underground pieces can start again after removal. Keep cut material out of waterways, collect fragments carefully, and expect repeated visits to clear regrowth rather than a single successful pull.

arctotheca-calendula.summary: Fertile capeweed spreads a rosette of deeply lobed leaves close to the ground, then lifts yellow daisy heads with dark centers above it. Turn a leaf over to see the pale, woolly underside. This seed-producing species is an agricultural and environmental weed in parts of Australia and has established in coastal California. Its seeds travel with soil, equipment, footwear, and animals. Remove small plants before seed ripens and check the identification carefully: the creeping ornamental capeweed, Arctotheca prostrata, has different spreading habits and yellow flower centers.

arctotheca-prostrata.summary: Creeping capeweed was planted as a groundcover for its low rosettes and cheerful yellow daisies, but its runners can cross the intended boundary. Stems root as they creep, allowing a patch to expand even where the cultivated plants produce no fertile seed. California records describe escapes into coastal prairie and nearby urban ground. It is often confused with fertile capeweed, Arctotheca calendula; longer creeping stems and yellow flower centers help separate it. During removal, collect rooted runners and fragments so the cleared patch can stay clear.

hydrochoerus-hydrochaeris.summary: Capybaras are the largest living rodents, with sturdy brown bodies, blunt muzzles, and short legs adapted to life beside water. Partly webbed feet and eyes, ears, and nostrils set high on the head help them swim while keeping watch. In their South American range, they live socially and graze on grasses and aquatic plants. An animal seen far outside that range may be an escape or release. Observe from a distance, keep pets away, and report the location to wildlife authorities rather than feeding or relocating it.

wigandia-urens.summary: Wigandia is a large-leaved shrub or small tree from tropical America, with showy lavender flowers above coarse, hairy foliage. The hairs are a reason to admire it without brushing past: they can irritate skin and sometimes provoke a stronger allergic reaction. Plants described from the Santa Monica Mountains have escaped cultivation into dense colonies near homes. Their big, toothed leaves and curling flower clusters give a useful starting point for identification, although local forms and older botanical names need careful comparison.

carum-carvi.summary: Caraway is the familiar kitchen spice grown on a delicate-looking member of the carrot family. Finely divided leaves form below branched stems topped with small white or pink-tinged flower umbels; the aromatic, ridged fruits are commonly called seeds. It often grows as a biennial and can self-sow freely where conditions suit it. In a herb bed, harvest or remove ripening heads to limit volunteers. Wild carrot-family plants can be difficult to tell apart, so do not use a casual resemblance as a basis for foraging.

cynara-cardunculus.summary: Cardoon brings the artichoke family's bold outline to open ground: a broad rosette of deeply cut, gray-green leaves sends up tall stems topped with purple flower heads. This Mediterranean perennial is cultivated as a vegetable and ornamental, but wild plants also occupy California grasslands and other disturbed habitats. Its spiny leaves and substantial taproot make established plants awkward to remove. Seed and surviving root pieces can renew a patch, so a single cut rarely settles the problem.

saissetia-neglecta.summary: Caribbean black scale can look like a row of small dark bumps along a fruit stem or twig. Mature females develop a tough, rounded covering with an H-shaped ridge; younger scales are paler and less distinctive. This sap-feeding insect uses many plants, including citrus, mango and guava. On citrus, its sugary honeydew supports sooty mold that can reduce fruit quality. Tiny natural enemies help limit populations, making a close inspection more useful than an automatic spray.

anastrepha-suspensa.summary: Caribbean fruit fly is a yellow-brown fly whose patterned wings offer a useful first clue to its identity. Females place eggs beneath the skin of mature or overripe fruit, and the pale larvae feed inside before dropping to the soil to pupate. Guava, loquat and many other cultivated or wild fruits can serve as hosts. Because related fruit flies look similar and have different management implications, a suspected find deserves expert identification before fruit is moved.

tabebuia-aurea.summary: Silver trumpet tree pairs golden, funnel-shaped flowers with foliage that catches the light in a silvery sheen. Native to South America, it is planted as a warm-climate ornamental. The leathery leaves spread from a single point like fingers, with five to seven leaflets and a silvery underside. Corky bark gives an established trunk a distinctive texture. Several yellow-flowered trumpet trees share this general silhouette, so a whole leaf and a close view of the bark are useful alongside the flowers.

caucalis-platycarpos.summary: Small white flower clusters make bur parsley easy to overlook until its hooked fruits catch your attention. This annual has finely divided leaves and only a few rays in each flower cluster. It belongs to the flora of Europe, northern Africa and parts of Asia, where it often grows in dry cultivated ground and field margins. Its conservation context matters: Switzerland regards it as vulnerable. A plant found among crops is therefore not automatically a candidate for removal.

cupaniopsis-anacardioides.summary: Carrotwood's glossy, leathery leaflets give this evergreen tree a tidy appearance, but its orange capsules reveal the feature that helps it travel: dark seeds wrapped in a bright aril that attracts birds. It is native to coastal eastern Australia, including rainforest near the sea and estuaries. In Florida, escaped trees invade a wide range of habitats and alter the understory. Young seedlings are much easier to tackle than the established trees they can become.

tinea-pellionella.summary: The casemaking clothes moth's most revealing sign is often a tiny moving case rather than a moth. Its caterpillar builds a portable shelter from silk and fibers, feeding on vulnerable animal-based materials such as wool as it carries the case along. The adult is a small, buff moth with narrow, fringed wings and dark forewing spots. Stored textiles and the sheltered undersides of wool rugs deserve attention, especially when they have gone undisturbed for a long time.

senna-spectabilis.summary: Spectacular cassia earns its common name with broad clusters of bright yellow flowers above a rounded crown. This tropical American tree has compound leaves and long pods that darken as they mature. Its appeal as an ornamental has carried it beyond its native range; in parts of East Africa and India, it has spread into forest edges, gaps and degraded land. Dense growth can hinder forest recovery, so seedlings near vulnerable habitat merit attention before they become seed-bearing trees.

manihot-esculenta.summary: Cassava is a tropical crop grown for its large, starch-rich storage roots, also familiar as the source of tapioca. Above ground, it forms a woody shrub with long-stalked, deeply divided leaves and milky sap. Farmers commonly propagate it from stem cuttings, a useful reminder that discarded stems can remain planting material. Although cassava is an important food plant, its raw parts contain toxins and require proper processing; the appearance of an edible crop does not make it safe to sample.

ricinus-communis.summary: Castor bean is hard to miss: huge, star-shaped leaves rise on fast-growing stems, followed by clusters of prickly capsules. In warm climates it can become a substantial shrub, while frost-prone gardens often grow it as an annual. Escaped plants favor disturbed ground and waterways, and mature capsules scatter seeds that can establish new plants. Those attractive, mottled seeds are highly poisonous, so this is a plant to identify visually and keep away from children and animals.

dolichandra-unguis-cati.summary: Cat's-claw creeper climbs with tiny, three-pronged hooks that grip bark and other supports. Its yellow trumpet flowers may look inviting, but the woody vine can spread across forest floors and climb over trees, smothering vegetation in invaded areas. Underground tubers make it persistent after the visible stems are cut. Winged seeds travel by wind and water, while detached stems and tubers can also restart growth. Early identification is especially valuable around streambanks and woodland edges.

kalanchoe-pinnata.summary: Life plant has an unusual way of making a new generation: tiny plantlets can grow from the scalloped margins of its fleshy leaves, particularly after a leaf falls. This Madagascar succulent becomes an upright, shrubby perennial, with simple lower leaves and divided leaves farther up the stems. Drooping, bell-shaped flowers hang in branching clusters. Its easy propagation explains both its popularity and its tendency to become weedy; a discarded leaf can be more than garden litter.

nepeta-cataria.summary: Catnip's gray-green, aromatic leaves are familiar to many cat owners, but this mint-family perennial also attracts a lively mix of flower visitors. Small white flowers, often marked with pink or purple, crowd the tops of its square stems. Native to Europe and Asia, it has naturalized widely in temperate regions, especially along roadsides and field margins. It readily seeds around gardens and can become a nuisance, although that does not make every patch an ecological invasion.

bothriochloa-bladhii.summary: Caucasian bluestem forms dense clumps of pale green grass that turn straw-colored as they mature. Its branched seed head has a central axis extending beyond the shorter side branches, a helpful clue when comparing it with other bluestems. This warm-season perennial occurs under several regional common names, including forest blue grass in Australia. In Kansas, introduced stands have spread into native sites. Identification deserves care because the name "bluestem" also belongs to valuable native prairie grasses.

phedimus-spurius.summary: Two-row stonecrop makes a low carpet of fleshy leaves, with creeping stems that root as they spread. Clusters of star-shaped pink or white flowers rise just above the mat, and many garden forms develop reddish foliage as the season changes. This perennial comes from the region around the Caucasus, northeastern Turkey and northern Iran, and is often sold under its older name, Sedum spurium. It tolerates dry, rocky ground well, which helps explain its popularity in rock gardens and planted roofs.

stachytarpheta-cayennensis.summary: Nettleleaf porterweed holds small blue-purple flowers along slender, curved spikes that rise above its wrinkled green leaves. Only part of a spike blooms at once, leaving a patterned stem behind as flowers fall. This tropical American shrub is grown ornamentally, but can spread through disturbed ground and degraded pasture in warm, moist regions. Seeds travel with contaminated soil, hay, equipment and garden waste. Other porterweeds are similar, making leaf texture and growth habit useful starting points rather than a final diagnosis.

colombian-datura-virus.summary: Colombian datura virus can hide in an apparently healthy angel's trumpet, then show itself as pale mottling, wrinkled leaves or stunted growth. Brugmansia plants are important hosts, and moving infected cuttings helps carry the virus between collections. Aphids and transferred plant sap can spread it too. Related ornamental and crop plants can also be infected, including tomato. Because these symptoms overlap with other problems and some infected plants show none, reliable identification depends on laboratory testing.

acacia-elata.summary: Cedar wattle is a tall Australian tree with unusually large leaflets for a feathery-leaved acacia. Sprays of pale yellow or cream flower balls appear above the foliage, followed by flat pods. In its native New South Wales range, it grows in rainforest and wetter eucalypt forest. Planting has carried it farther afield: it can escape into adjacent bushland and is documented as naturalized in South Africa. Its location matters when deciding whether a seedling belongs or needs attention.

chelidonium-majus.summary: Greater celandine brings small yellow flowers to shady edges, gardens, and disturbed woodland. This leafy herb lives for more than one season or behaves as a biennial, spreading readily by seed where conditions suit it. Its deeply divided leaves and orange-yellow sap help separate it from other yellow-flowered plants. Originally from Eurasia, it has become established beyond its native range. The sap can irritate skin, so this is a plant to recognize without breaking its stems by hand.

pholcus-manueli.summary: This cellar spider belongs to the long-legged spiders that hang beneath loose webs in sheltered corners. Pholcus manueli has been recorded in cellars and other buildings, including a garage from which it was first described. Although its name was established from American specimens, the World Spider Catalog treats it as an Asian species introduced to the United States. Several cellar spiders look similar, so a web in a basement is a useful clue, not enough to identify this particular species.

eremochloa-ophiuroides.summary: Centipedegrass is the pale-green, low-growing lawn grass often planted in warm parts of the country. It creeps across the soil on aboveground runners, gradually forming a coarse-textured turf rather than an upright clump. Its leaves alternate along the runners, giving them the appearance that inspired its common name. This grass is adapted to acidic, relatively low-fertility soils. Because it is widely cultivated, a patch beside a lawn should be described in that context rather than automatically labeled a harmful invasion.

epipremnum-pinnatum.summary: Centipede tongavine is a tropical climbing plant whose leaves change dramatically as it grows. Young shoots creep or climb with relatively simple leaves; older shoots supported by a tree or another surface can produce much larger, deeply divided leaves. Aerial roots help the vine hold on as it climbs. Native across parts of Asia and the Pacific, it is grown ornamentally beyond that range. Its changing leaf shape makes identifying mature and juvenile plants together especially useful.

actinocyclus-normanii-f-subsala.summary: This microscopic diatom is known from freshwater plankton and is associated with the smaller freshwater forms of Actinocyclus normanii. Viewed through a microscope, its round silica shell has a patterned surface of pores that specialists use for identification. Its history in the Great Lakes is less straightforward than an introduction date might suggest: older sediment evidence has raised questions about whether it arrived recently at all. Even the boundary between named forms is uncertain, making careful identification more useful than a simple invasive label.

skeletonema-potamos.summary: Skeletonema potamos is a tiny diatom that drifts in fresh and slightly brackish water, often as short chains of cells. Its delicate silica walls are so small that it can be overlooked even under a light microscope. Researchers studying the Danube found that it became a larger part of the river's plankton community as water temperatures rose. Its original range remains uncertain, and finding it in a water sample does not by itself establish a harmful bloom or a recent introduction.

heterodera-avenae.summary: Cereal cyst nematode is a microscopic roundworm that feeds inside the roots of wheat, barley, oats, and other grasses. Damaged roots have more difficulty supplying the plant with water and nutrients, which can leave uneven patches of weak or stunted crop. After a female dies, her hardened body becomes a cyst that shelters eggs in the soil. Those persistent cysts make the problem longer-lived than one growing season, while the symptoms above ground can easily be mistaken for other crop stresses.

oulema-melanopus.summary: The cereal leaf beetle is a small insect with metallic blue wing covers and an orange-red area behind its head. Its larvae are easier to notice by what they leave behind: narrow strips of damaged tissue on cereal and grass leaves. A dark coating of their own waste often hides the larvae's pale bodies. Heavy feeding can reduce the leaf area a grain crop needs to fill its seeds, but natural enemies also help keep populations in check, making field monitoring important.

secale-cereale.summary: Cereal rye is an upright annual grass grown for grain, forage, and soil cover. Its tall stems carry dense, bristly seed heads that may lean as they mature, while a network of roots helps hold the soil. It is a familiar agricultural plant that can also appear outside the places where it was sown. Despite the similar name, cereal rye is not the same as the ryegrasses used in many lawns and pastures. Identifying the seed head helps tell those grasses apart.

dianella-ensifolia.summary: Cerulean flaxlily forms clumps of long, sword-shaped leaves, with small pale flowers followed by glossy blue berries. Although its foliage may look grasslike at first glance, it spreads from underground rhizomes and carries its flowers on branching stalks above the leaves. Birds can disperse its fruit. Native across parts of the Old World tropics, it has also been grown as an ornamental. In Florida, UF/IFAS assesses it as invasive, so its attractive appearance should not be the only consideration when choosing a landscape plant.

cucumber-green-mottle-mosaic-virus.summary: Cucumber green mottle mosaic virus affects crops in the cucumber family, including cucumbers, melons, pumpkins, and squash. Infected plants may develop mottled or distorted leaves, poor growth, or damaged fruit, although symptoms vary with the crop and conditions. The virus travels with contaminated seed and plant material and can also move on hands, tools, and other surfaces. That combination makes clean planting material and careful hygiene especially important in gardens, greenhouses, and farms where susceptible crops are grown.

phyllanthus-urinaria.summary: Chamberbitter is a small warm-season annual that can appear among garden plants, in lawns, and in other disturbed ground. Its neat rows of little leaves make a branch look like a miniature mimosa leaf, but those are individual leaves rather than leaflets. Turn a branch over and the round seed capsules underneath become a useful clue. Plants can make seed while still quite small, which is why repeatedly mowing the tops may leave the next generation ready to grow.

houttuynia-cordata.summary: Chameleon plant is a spreading perennial with heart-shaped leaves and a strong scent when its foliage is crushed. Garden forms may have brightly patterned leaves, but the plant can also be plain green. What look like four white petals surround a short spike of tiny flowers. It thrives in moist ground and spreads through creeping underground stems, which can carry it well beyond a garden bed. Those hidden stems also make an established patch more persistent than its soft leaves might suggest.

kalanchoe-delagoensis.summary: Chandelier plant is a succulent with narrow, mottled leaves and clusters of hanging orange-red flowers. Tiny plantlets develop at the leaf tips, detach, and become new plants, helping explain its other name, mother of millions. This Madagascar native has been grown ornamentally and can establish in warm, open habitats beyond gardens. Its ability to reproduce from small pieces makes garden waste an important concern. The plant is poisonous to livestock and pets, so identification matters around grazing land and homes.

myosotis-discolor.summary: Changing forget-me-not earns its name as its tiny flowers age from pale yellow or cream to blue. Several colors can appear on the same curling flower cluster, a helpful detail when this small plant blends into grassy ground. It is a hairy annual with slender stems and narrow leaves, originally from Europe and now established elsewhere. Roadsides, ditches, open pasture, and other disturbed places can provide suitable habitat. A close view of the flowers is much more useful for identification than a distant patch of blue.

pomacea-canaliculata.summary: The channeled apple snail is a large freshwater snail that grazes on aquatic plants and can damage crops grown in wet fields. Its rounded shell has deep grooves between the coils, while conspicuous pink egg masses are laid above the waterline. Originally South American, it has been moved to other regions through human activity. In Hawaii, it became a serious pest of wetland taro. Several apple snails look alike, so shell color or a pink egg mass alone cannot settle the species identity.

sinapis-arvensis.summary: Charlock mustard, also called wild mustard, is an annual plant with clusters of bright yellow, four-petaled flowers. It often grows in cultivated fields and other disturbed ground, where its broad leaves and upright stems compete with crops for space and resources. Long seed pods follow the flowers, and seeds left in the soil can supply later generations. It belongs to the same plant family as many familiar vegetables, so recognizing its leaves, flowers, and pods together is more reliable than identifying it by color alone.

mytella-strigata.summary: The charru mussel is a small, thin-shelled mussel found in estuaries, lagoons, and other sheltered coastal waters. Its shell can range from greenish to nearly black, with a purple inner surface. It filters suspended food from the water and can gather on shells, roots, docks, and aquaculture structures. Introduced populations have become locally abundant, but abundance alone does not measure their effects: field research has found that competition with other mussels needs more careful study than some broad claims suggest.

sechium-edule.summary: Chayote is a vigorous climbing vine best known for its pale-green, pear-shaped vegetable, also called mirliton or vegetable pear. The fruit contains a single large seed, and the vine uses supports to lift its cucumber-like leaves and developing crop above the ground. Separate male and female flowers grow on the same plant and attract pollinators. This tropical American crop is cultivated in warm regions around the world. Its presence in a garden is therefore different from a vine growing independently beyond cultivation.

bromus-tectorum.summary: Cheatgrass is an annual grass that often starts growing in fall, spends winter as a small plant, and produces seed early the following season. Its soft, hairy leaves give way to drooping, bristly seed heads, then dry vegetation as the season warms. In many western landscapes, this early-drying growth adds fine fuel between larger plants and can help fires spread. Repeated disturbance can favor more cheatgrass, making prevention of seed production and recovery of perennial vegetation important parts of long-term management.

malva-parviflora.summary: Cheeseweed mallow gets its name from its round, segmented fruits, which look like tiny wheels of cheese. This annual herb grows in gardens, cultivated ground and other disturbed places, with rounded, shallowly lobed leaves and small pale flowers tucked beside the leaf stalks. Its deep taproot becomes woody as the plant matures. Seeds have tough coats and can remain in the soil, so removing young plants before they fruit is much easier than tackling an established patch.

rosa-laevigata.summary: Cherokee rose is a vigorous scrambling shrub whose long, hooked canes climb through nearby vegetation. Large white flowers with golden centers stand out against glossy leaves, usually divided into three leaflets; bristly orange-red hips follow. Despite its common name, the plant is native to parts of Asia and was brought to North America during colonial times. It can spread aggressively in the southeastern United States, where a locally native climbing plant is often a better garden choice.

enarmonia-formosana.summary: Cherry bark tortrix is a small, intricately patterned moth whose caterpillars live beneath tree bark. Cherries, plums, apples and other members of the rose family can serve as hosts. Eggs are laid on bark, often near wounds, and the larvae tunnel below the surface, causing cracking and sometimes conspicuous gum. The insect is established in parts of the Pacific Northwest. An adult moth may be easy to overlook; damaged bark near the base of a tree can be the first useful clue.

prunus-laurocerasus.summary: Cherry laurel is a dense evergreen shrub or small tree with broad, glossy leaves and upright clusters of fragrant white flowers. Its dark fruits attract birds, which carry the seeds beyond planted hedges. In the Puget Sound region, escaped plants can thrive in forest shade and crowd native shrubs and tree seedlings. Branches touching the ground can also take root. Cutting a large plant once seldom finishes the job, because both roots and cut stems can produce new growth.

prunus-cerasifera.summary: Cherry plum is a small deciduous tree that flowers early, often as its first leaves unfold. The species has green leaves and white blossoms, although familiar garden cultivars may have deep purple foliage and pink flowers. Small, smooth-skinned plums range from yellow to red and attract birds. Native to southeastern Europe and parts of Asia, it has escaped cultivation in several regions, including parts of the United States and southeastern Australia. A purple leaf alone identifies neither the species nor its local ecological impact.

cryphonectria-parasitica.summary: Chestnut blight is caused by a fungus that grows in the bark of chestnut trees. Infection can expand around a branch or trunk, interrupting its supply of water and nutrients and leaving wilted brown leaves above the damaged area. Sunken or cracked cankers may carry tiny orange fruiting bodies. The disease transformed eastern North American forests by devastating American chestnut. It also affects European sweet chestnut; ongoing breeding work seeks useful resistance, but an apparently healthy tree is not proof of lasting protection.

gnomoniopsis-smithogilvyi.summary: Chestnut brown rot can hide inside a nut that looks ordinary from the outside. This fungus damages chestnut kernels, which may become brown, chalky or sponge-like, reducing the quality of the harvest. It can also live in apparently healthy flowers and shoots, and has been associated with twig cankers. Research in Portugal confirmed that isolates caused disease in several sweet-chestnut varieties. Because other fungi produce similar symptoms, a cut nut or bark lesion is a starting point for diagnosis rather than a reliable identification on its own.

sphenoclea-zeylanica.summary: Chickenspike is an annual wetland herb with soft, upright stems and narrow flower spikes that rise above its leaves. The tiny white flowers are packed closely together, followed by small capsules containing numerous seeds. It grows in shallow water, ditches and flooded ground, and is familiar as a rice-field weed. Its native range spans tropical Africa, Asia and northern Australia. The fleshy lower stem and dense, tapering flower spike are useful clues when examining a plant at the water's edge.

astragalus-cicer.summary: Chickpea milkvetch, also called cicer milkvetch, is a long-lived perennial legume grown for forage and soil stabilization. Its leafy stems carry many paired leaflets and clusters of pale yellow to white pea flowers. The inflated pods darken as they mature, and loose seeds may rattle inside. Native to Europe and the Caucasus region, it spreads through underground shoots as well as seed. Its agricultural usefulness is well documented; its presence in this catalog should not be read as proof that it is invasive everywhere.

cichorium-intybus.summary: Chicory brings clear blue flowers to many roadsides and old fields, opening its flower heads along stiff, branching stems. Young plants begin as a rosette of leaves that can resemble a dandelion, above a substantial taproot with milky sap. This Eurasian plant has a long history of cultivation for leaves and roots, and is now naturalized widely in North America. Wild chicory favors disturbed ground and usually does not move far into undisturbed habitats. Its flowers often close around midday.

oenothera-stricta.summary: Chilean evening primrose opens yellow flowers that take on orange or reddish tones as they age. It begins with a rosette of narrow leaves, then sends up a leafy flowering stem from a stout taproot. Usually annual or biennial, it comes from Chile and Argentina and has naturalized in disturbed places beyond that range. Flowers open toward evening and may remain open into the following day. The long floral tube and slender, upright seed capsules help distinguish it from other yellow-flowered plants.

gunnera-tinctoria.summary: Chilean gunnera makes a striking clump of enormous, rough-edged leaves on stout, prickly stalks. Despite the nickname giant rhubarb, it is not culinary rhubarb. Its leaves die back seasonally, leaving large buds on thick rhizomes ready for new growth. In invaded areas of Ireland it forms dense colonies in wet ground, along waterways and on coastal sites, shading smaller plants. Other large gunneras, including garden hybrids, can look similar, so the familiar umbrella-shaped leaf is only the beginning of an identification.

cestrum-parqui.summary: Chilean jessamine is a woody shrub with narrow, glossy leaves and clusters of slender yellow-green flowers. Dark, egg-shaped berries follow the blooms, and birds or water can carry them away from the parent plant. It often grows along disturbed ground and waterways in regions where it has escaped gardens. This plant is particularly troublesome around livestock because its leaves and berries are poisonous, and cut or wilted material remains hazardous. Its soft green stems can develop into a substantial, persistent shrub.

loxosceles-laeta.summary: The Chilean recluse is a brown spider native to South America that has also been introduced elsewhere. It favors sheltered spaces, and established populations outside its native range are sometimes confined to buildings. Its body and legs may be yellowish, reddish brown or darker, with a violin-like marking that can be less obvious than that of the familiar brown recluse. Reliable separation from related recluses requires closer examination than color alone. In quiet corners, its web and secretive habits can make it easy to miss.

melia-azedarach.summary: Chinaberry is a deciduous tree with a spreading crown, finely divided leaves and fragrant lilac-colored flowers. Yellowish fruits often remain on bare branches through winter, making the tree conspicuous after leaf fall. Native across parts of Asia and Australia, it was widely planted for shade and ornament. It now grows along roads, fields and forest openings in the southeastern United States, where it can spread aggressively. The attractive fruits are poisonous and should not be mistaken for something to eat.

ficus-microcarpa.summary: Chinese banyan can begin life perched on another tree, then develop into a broad evergreen with hanging aerial roots. Some of those roots reach the ground and become pillar-like supports. Its smooth gray bark, leathery leaves and small rounded figs are familiar features of warm-climate plantings. The species is also widely grown as a houseplant and bonsai. Seed production depends on a tiny associated fig wasp, so the arrival of a pollinator can change how a cultivated tree reproduces outside its original range.

catalpa-ovata.summary: Chinese catalpa is a deciduous tree with broad, often three-lobed leaves and airy clusters of pale yellow flowers. Purple markings decorate the flowers, which are smaller than those of the two familiar American catalpas. Long, narrow seed capsules follow and can resemble green beans while young. Native to China, the tree has been cultivated well beyond its home range and sometimes self-sows in the United States. Its large leaves and hanging capsules give it a distinctive appearance even when the flowers are gone.

cunninghamia-lanceolata.summary: Chinese fir is an evergreen conifer with a tall, tapering crown and spreading branches whose tips often droop. Its stiff, pointed leaves sit closely along the shoots, giving the foliage a flattened, layered look. Small cones mature from green to brown, while older bark breaks into flakes that reveal warmer reddish tones beneath. Native to China, it is grown as an ornamental tree elsewhere. Old brown foliage may stay attached for years, so interior browning is not by itself evidence of a new disease.

pyracantha-fortuneana.summary: Chinese firethorn, in the traditional regional-flora sense of Pyracantha fortuneana used here, is a spiny shrub grown for its clusters of white flowers and bright red fruits. Its leaves are broadest toward the tip, with rounded or slightly notched ends and small teeth along the edges. Plants cultivated under this name have occasionally naturalized in Australia. The name itself needs care: some floras retain Pyracantha fortuneana, while Kew currently places it within P. crenulata. That disagreement matters when comparing photographs, records or management advice published under different firethorn names.

koelreuteria-elegans.summary: Chinese flame tree is grown for bright yellow flowers and colorful, papery seed capsules. The Taiwanese form, subspecies formosana, has large, twice-divided leaves and three-sided capsules that turn from red or pink to brown as they mature. That ornamental form has escaped in southeastern Queensland and northeastern New South Wales, where it is treated as an environmental weed. The species also includes a Fijian subspecies, so accounts of the Taiwanese garden tree should not automatically be applied to every population.

celtis-sinensis.summary: Chinese hackberry is a fast-growing deciduous tree with smooth gray bark and a broad, spreading crown. Its glossy leaves have teeth mostly toward their tips, and small round fruits ripen through orange and red. Birds help carry its seeds away from planted trees. In parts of eastern Australia, dense stands form along creeks and disturbed forest openings, preventing native vegetation from regenerating. The tree is native to eastern Asia, and its local behavior depends on climate and setting.

holmskioldia-sanguinea.summary: Chinese hatplant is a scrambling woody shrub named for the small, colorful saucers around its flowers. A curved red flower tube emerges from each broad orange-red calyx, creating the hat-like outline. Oval leaves grow along the loose, climbing stems. Native from the Himalayan region toward Myanmar, it is grown as an ornamental in warm climates and can be trained over a support. The showy calyx is part of the flower's outer structure, rather than a flat petal.

cynoglossum-amabile.summary: Chinese hound's tongue is often sold as Chinese forget-me-not for its sprays of small sky-blue flowers. The plant is bushy, with softly hairy, gray-green leaves, and may behave as an annual or biennial depending on the climate. Garden selections also have white or pink flowers. It can flower in its first year and reseed freely, which explains why it sometimes appears beyond its intended bed. It favors cooler growing conditions and may lose vigor during long, hot summers.

eragrostis-unioloides.summary: Chinese lovegrass is a small tuft-forming grass whose open seed heads carry flattened clusters of tiny flowers. These spikelets can turn purplish red as they mature, giving the airy heads a subtle wash of color. Its stems may rise from a leaning base, and plants grow as annuals or short-lived perennials. Native across tropical and subtropical Asia into parts of Queensland, it occurs in grasslands and along roadsides. Similar lovegrasses are difficult to separate, so close views of mature spikelets are more useful than a distant photograph.

tenodera-sinensis.summary: Chinese mantis is a large, slender hunter that waits among leaves and stems with its grasping forelegs folded. Adults range from green to tan or brown, often with a green line along the wings. The head swivels to follow nearby movement. Introduced to North America, it feeds on a broad range of animals it can overpower, including other beneficial insects. Its rounded, foam-like egg case remains on twigs after the adult season and can be mistaken for a small brown growth on the plant.

eriocheir-sinensis.summary: Chinese mitten crab is named for the dense bristles that cover its claws like fuzzy gloves. It spends much of its life in rivers and other freshwater habitats, then moves toward saltier water to reproduce. Originally from coastal China and Korea, it has been carried to other regions through human activity. Where abundant, its burrows can undermine banks, and its feeding and migrations can interfere with native wildlife and fisheries. Small juveniles may lack the obvious hairy claws seen on adults.

cipangopaludina-chinensis.summary: Chinese mysterysnails carry a rounded olive-brown shell with deep seams between its coils and a hard door that closes the opening. These freshwater snails graze on algae and decaying material in ponds, lakes and slow-moving water. Females give birth to live young, a feature behind the 'mystery' name. Introduced from Asia through human transport, they can move again with aquarium releases or aquatic equipment. Keep unwanted snails out of waterways and check boats and gear before leaving the water.

parlatoreopsis-chinensis.summary: Chinese obscure scale is a tiny armored insect found on woody plants, including crabapple. Females live beneath protective covers, and their identity usually depends on microscopic examination. Historical observations in Missouri describe overlapping generations and fertilized females surviving winter. A Korean import study also found the species on a tree brought from China, showing why nursery inspections matter. Older accounts sometimes confused it with a related scale, so an extension diagnosis is a better starting point than treating every crust-like patch on a branch as this species.

firmiana-simplex.summary: Chinese parasoltree has an unusual green trunk and large, lobed leaves that cast a broad patch of shade. This fast-growing deciduous tree carries loose clusters of small pale flowers, followed by distinctive pods and round seeds. Leaves turn yellow before falling, leaving the green bark especially noticeable in winter. Long cultivated outside eastern Asia, it can produce abundant seedlings and has become invasive in several southeastern states. The seedlings around a mature planting are often the clearest sign that it is spreading.

stranvaesia-davidiana.summary: Chinese photinia is an evergreen shrub or small tree whose clusters of red fruits can brighten the branches well into winter. Small white flowers precede the fruit, and its narrow leaves may have gently wavy edges. It comes from China and nearby parts of Asia, where it grows on slopes, in thickets and along riverbanks. Gardeners also know it as Photinia davidiana. The two names refer to the same plant in the accounts used here, rather than to two different red-berried shrubs.

ligustrum-sinense.summary: Chinese privet is a densely branching shrub that often keeps its small leaves through winter in mild climates. Clusters of white flowers are followed by dark fruits that birds and mammals carry into new places. Introduced as an ornamental, it has become a major invader in parts of the eastern and southern United States. Seeds and root suckers both help it form thickets, which can replace a more varied layer of native plants. An old hedge can therefore be a continuing source of new plants beyond the garden.

gonocarpus-chinensis.summary: Chinese raspwort is a small perennial of wet tropical regions, native from southern China through parts of Southeast Asia and the Pacific to Australia. It is easy to overlook beside larger wetland plants. The New South Wales form has rough, four-ribbed stems, narrow toothed leaves and tiny flowers followed by ribbed fruits. Its Australian subspecies is treated separately in this collection, so a close look at the fruit matters when putting a precise name to a plant.

gonocarpus-chinensis-ssp-verrucosus.summary: This Australian subspecies of Chinese raspwort is a slender perennial of damp, open ground. Its small toothed leaves sit mostly in opposite pairs on rough, four-ribbed stems, and the flowers are tiny enough to need a close look. The rounded fruits carry eight ribs, small bumps and short curved hairs, useful details for a careful identification. Native to eastern Australia, it has also been introduced to California and Hawaii; that history alone does not establish how it affects a particular wetland.

lepadoretus-sinicus.summary: Chinese rose beetles often reveal themselves through the lace-like holes they leave between leaf veins. Adults emerge after dusk to feed on many kinds of plants, including garden ornamentals and crops. They are small brown scarabs covered with pale hairs, while their whitish grubs develop underground. The beetle is usually called Adoretus sinicus in modern identification guides. Because a close relative looks almost identical, feeding damage and a photograph can suggest an identification but may not settle it.

miscanthus-sinensis.summary: Chinese silvergrass forms tall, arching clumps topped by airy flower plumes. Familiar from ornamental plantings, this Asian perennial can send windborne seeds beyond the garden and establish along roadsides and other disturbed ground. Older clumps develop a substantial underground mass that makes removal difficult. Cultivars differ in size, leaf pattern and fertility, so a garden label is worth keeping, but it does not replace checking for seedlings nearby. In regions where it spreads, a locally appropriate native grass is a better planting choice.

triadica-sebifera.summary: Chinese tallow is often noticed for its autumn color and clusters of white seeds that resemble popcorn. The deciduous tree has broadly rounded leaves drawn out into slender tips and produces yellow flower spikes in spring. Brought from Asia as an ornamental and potential crop, it now invades wetlands, prairies and forests in the southeastern United States. Birds and water carry its seeds, while cut trees can sprout again. Removing seedlings early and planning follow-up for larger trees helps prevent a return.

asystasia-gangetica.summary: Chinese violet is a creeping perennial with opposite leaves, trumpet-shaped flowers and seed capsules that spring open when ripe. Garden forms can spread quickly in warm climates. The name covers more than one subspecies: the small white flowers with purple markings belong to subsp. micrantha, a serious smothering weed in parts of Australia, while other forms have larger, differently colored flowers. Stems can root where they touch moist soil, making dumped cuttings an effective way to start a new patch.

wisteria-sinensis.summary: Chinese wisteria's fragrant spring flower clusters can be beautiful, but the woody vine grows with enough force to overwhelm trees and shrubs. It climbs by twining and can also spread across the ground, where touching stems take root. The hanging seed pods are velvety, unlike those of native American wisteria. Escaped vines can shade woodland plants and tighten around their supports. Successful removal usually takes follow-up because cutting an established vine commonly produces fresh shoots.

dioscorea-oppositifolia.summary: Dioscorea oppositifolia is a tuber-forming climbing yam native to the Indian subcontinent and Myanmar. Its name has often been applied incorrectly to Chinese yam in North American writing. That distinction matters: descriptions of the invasive Chinese yam cannot simply be transferred to this species. The exact botanical identity therefore matters before interpreting a field sighting or choosing any removal method intended for the Chinese yam.

rorippa-cantoniensis.summary: Chinese yellowcress is a small annual mustard native to eastern Asia. Its lower leaves are divided into lobes, while the smaller leaves higher on the stem clasp it at their bases. Small flowers give way to short, slender cylindrical seed pods. A close look is worthwhile because several yellowcresses share this modest appearance, and leaf shape changes as the plant grows. Photographs showing both the low leaves and mature pods are much more useful than a single flower portrait.

pinus-roxburghii.summary: Chir pine is a tall Himalayan pine with notably long needles carried in bundles of three. Its elongated, egg-shaped woody cones are another useful feature, especially when compared with the shorter cones of some familiar landscape pines. Native from Pakistan through the Himalaya and northern India, it has long been valued as a source of resin. A planted tree is not by itself evidence of an invasion; seedlings growing beyond cultivation deserve a separate, locally informed assessment.

ephestia-elutella.summary: The chocolate moth, also called the cacao or tobacco moth, is a small moth associated with stored goods. Its larvae feed in products such as cocoa, tobacco, cereals and dried foods, so an indoor sighting is a reason to inspect supplies rather than assume the moth came from the garden. Adults have a wingspan of roughly 15-20 millimeters and resemble several related warehouse moths. Warm storage conditions allow populations to develop more quickly, and a precise identification may require an expert.

akebia-quinata.summary: Chocolate vine has five smooth leaflets arranged like the fingers of a hand and small, dark, fragrant flowers in spring. This woody climber comes from eastern Asia and can grow rapidly over shrubs and other vegetation. Its unusual purple fruits may split open to reveal pale pulp and dark seeds, which birds can carry elsewhere. In mild climates it keeps much of its foliage through winter. Once established, repeated pruning may not be enough to contain it, making early attention to escapes worthwhile.

melochia-corchorifolia.summary: Chocolateweed is a small upright herb or subshrub with toothed leaves and tight clusters of little flowers. Despite its common name, the flowers may be white, pink or purple, with regional variation described in botanical floras. Rounded, hairy capsules follow the blooms. The plant occurs widely across warm parts of the Old World and Australia, including damp or seasonally wet places. Its name should not be taken as proof that every population is unwanted: it is native in parts of its range.

leonotis-nepetifolia.summary: Christmas candlestick stands out for the rounded clusters of orange flowers spaced along its upright stems. Also called lion's tail, it has opposite toothed leaves and can grow taller than a person in warm conditions. Botanical accounts place its native range in Africa and the Indian subcontinent. Introduced populations can form large colonies; a Queensland management account describes displacement of native vegetation along riverbanks and floodplains. Seeds can travel in water or muddy equipment, so keeping them on site matters during removal.

themeda-arguens.summary: Christmas grass is a tufted tropical grass whose seed heads reward a closer look. Small groups of spikelets sit within papery bracts, and each fertile unit carries a conspicuous bent, twisted bristle. Most leaves arise near the base of the plant. Native across parts of tropical Asia to northern Australia, it belongs to the same genus as other grasses that can look similar from a distance. Mature flowering material is therefore much more useful for identification than a photograph of the leaves alone.

macrosiphoniella-sanborni.summary: Chrysanthemum aphids gather around tender shoots, buds and leaf undersides, where they feed on plant sap. The small adults are dark reddish brown to nearly black; younger aphids are often dull brick red. Colonies can build quickly because females give birth to live young, and infested plants can carry them between greenhouses. Feeding may distort or stunt growth, while sticky honeydew supports black sooty mold. Regularly checking new shoots and incoming plants helps catch a colony before it becomes dense.

lasioderma-serricorne.summary: Cigarette beetles are tiny, rounded, reddish-brown insects that can turn up in far more than tobacco. Their larvae feed in dried products, including spices, grains, pet food and other stored plant material. The adult's head is tucked beneath its thorax, giving it a hooded appearance from above. Fine details help separate it from the similar drugstore beetle: cigarette beetles have saw-toothed antennae and lack rows of pits on their wing covers. Finding the infested material is more useful than treating a wandering adult.

cinnamomum-verum.summary: True cinnamon is the Sri Lankan tree whose bark supplies the familiar spice. Fresh leaves often emerge red before turning glossy green, and several strong veins run from near the leaf base toward the tip. Small pale flowers are followed by dark, fleshy, single-seeded fruits. In tropical gardens the tree can become a substantial evergreen. Because other cinnamon relatives share aromatic leaves and bark, a scent alone is a poor identification test; leaf arrangement, veins and fruit provide a better starting point.

dynaspidiotus-tsugae.summary: Circular hemlock scale is a tiny armored insect that settles mainly beneath conifer needles. Females sit under rounded, dark brown covers with a raised center; heavy infestations can coat much of a needle. Feeding removes plant fluids and may lead to yellowing and premature needle loss, particularly on hemlocks. Also called shortneedle evergreen scale, it has a mobile crawler stage before the insects settle. Inspecting the lower crown with a hand lens can reveal a problem before thinning foliage becomes obvious.

coccus-pseudomagnoliarum.summary: Citricola scale is a sap-feeding insect that can leave citrus foliage sticky with honeydew and darkened by sooty mold. Its appearance changes as it grows: young scales are flat and translucent beneath leaves, while mature females become oval, grayish bumps on twigs. Heavy populations can weaken trees and reduce fruit production. Ants, sticky leaves and black mold are useful clues, but checking the insects themselves matters because several other citrus pests leave the same signs.

zephyranthes-citrina.summary: Citron zephyrlily is a small bulb-forming perennial with bright yellow flowers held above a tuft of very narrow leaves. Each flower sits on a slender, upright stalk, giving the plant a light, grassy appearance between blooms. Native to parts of Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean, it is also cultivated well beyond that range. A garden planting and a self-sustaining wild population are different situations, so location and evidence of seedlings are useful details when recording it.

phyllosticta-citricarpa.summary: Citrus black spot is a fungal disease that marks citrus fruit with several kinds of blemishes, from tiny dark speckles to sunken spots with pale centers and dark borders. Severe infections can cause fruit to drop before harvest. The fungus can reproduce in infected fallen leaves, helping the disease persist around a tree. Because symptoms vary with the fruit's age and can resemble other problems, a photograph is a starting point for diagnosis rather than a reliable confirmation.

aleurocanthus-woglumi.summary: Despite its name, citrus blackfly belongs to the whitefly family. Adults are dark and sooty-looking, and their young form conspicuous black, spiny patches beneath leaves. Feeding removes plant sap and produces honeydew, which can support a coating of sooty mold. Citrus is an important host, though many other woody plants can carry it. Natural enemies can keep populations low, so finding a few insects does not automatically mean a tree needs treatment.

xanthomonas-campestris.summary: Older citrus canker names need careful interpretation because bacterial species names and pathovar names carry different meanings. Xanthomonas campestris is a recognized bacterial species, while older citrus literature used the more specific name Xanthomonas campestris pv. citri for the canker pathogen now placed in Xanthomonas citri. Dropping that final pathovar name changes the meaning. Resolving the original identification will help ensure that citrus symptoms and reporting advice are attached to the right organism.

xanthomonas-citri.summary: Citrus canker is caused by a citrus-infecting pathovar of Xanthomonas citri, a bacterium that attacks leaves, shoots and fruit. Its raised, corky lesions often have a yellow halo and can make fruit unsaleable; severe disease also causes leaf and fruit drop. Wind-driven rain helps bacteria reach young tissue and wounds. Nursery plants can carry infection between places, including before clear symptoms appear, making careful diagnosis and plant-movement precautions especially important.

liberibacter-asiaticus.summary: Huanglongbing, often called citrus greening, is a serious citrus disease associated with the bacterium Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus. Infected trees may develop unevenly mottled leaves, yellow shoots and small, misshapen fruit that remain partly green. The Asian citrus psyllid carries the bacterium between trees, and infected propagation material can also spread it. Symptoms may take time to appear, so a healthy-looking tree is not proof of freedom from infection. Confirmed disease has no cure.

phyllocnistis-citrella.summary: Citrus leafminer leaves a delicate silver trail as its larvae tunnel just beneath the surface of new citrus leaves. The narrow, winding mine often contains a dark line of waste, and damaged leaves may curl around the developing insect. Young trees can lose valuable new growth, while established trees usually tolerate the injury. Feeding wounds can also make citrus canker infection easier where that disease occurs. The tiny adult moth is much less noticeable than its handiwork.

planococcus-citri.summary: Citrus mealybug looks like a small moving fleck of white cotton, often tucked into a leaf joint, fruit cluster or other sheltered spot. Beneath its waxy coating is an oval sap-feeding insect with short filaments around the body. It attacks many ornamentals as well as citrus, including plants grown indoors. Colonies can weaken growth and leave sticky honeydew that encourages sooty mold. New plants deserve a close inspection because small colonies are easy to overlook.

phyllocoptruta-oleivora.summary: Citrus rust mite is so small that the damage usually catches your eye before the animal does. Feeding on rind cells can leave oranges rusty brown and lemons silvery, changing the fruit's appearance. These pale, wedge-shaped mites also feed on leaves and green stems. In home gardens, light injury is often mainly cosmetic, but heavier infestations can matter in commercial production and may contribute to fruit drop. The similar pink citrus rust mite is a different species.

hediste-diadroma.summary: This clam worm lives out of sight in the mud of brackish estuaries, where its segmented body moves through a burrow. Native to the northwestern Pacific, Hediste diadroma has also been identified in estuaries on North America's Pacific coast. It gathers food from sediment and can filter suspended particles through a mucus net. Its resemblance to native worms makes casual sightings difficult to interpret, and the ecological effects of its introduction remain uncertain.

dysphania-pumilio.summary: Clammy goosefoot is a low, spreading herb whose small leaves and tiny flower clusters are easy to miss underfoot. Fine glandular hairs give it an aromatic, somewhat sticky character. The flowers sit close to the stems in the leaf axils, later producing minute dark seeds. Native to Australia, it has become established in other regions, often around disturbed or cultivated ground. Its modest appearance means close-up details are more useful than a distant photograph.

heliotropium-amplexicaule.summary: Clasping heliotrope forms low, sprawling patches topped with curved clusters of blue-purple to pink flowers, each with a small yellow center. Its hairy, wavy-edged leaves sit close to the stems. This South American perennial can persist through a deep root system and regrow after its shoots die back. In introduced pasture settings it can compete with useful vegetation, and its toxicity to livestock makes a confirmed identification especially important around grazing land.

lepidium-perfoliatum.summary: Clasping pepperweed has an unusual contrast between its leaves: the lower ones are finely divided, while the upper ones are broad and wrap closely around the stem. Small yellow flowers appear above them, followed by little rounded seed pods. This short-lived mustard comes from Eurasia and is introduced in North America, where it often grows on dry, disturbed ground. Seeing both the lower foliage and the flowering stem makes identification much easier.

microthlaspi-perfoliatum.summary: Claspleaf pennycress is a small annual mustard with pale green foliage, tiny white flowers and flattened seed pods with a noticeable notch at the tip. Upper leaves clasp the stem, while lower leaves form a loose rosette. It occurs in dry, often lime-rich soils and can grow among crops and orchard vegetation. Botanical references may call it Microthlaspi perfoliatum, Thlaspi perfoliatum or Noccaea perfoliata, so matching the plant's features is more useful than relying on one name alone.

cotton-leaf-curl-gezira-virus.summary: Cotton leaf curl Gezira virus is a plant virus associated with leaf-curl disease in cotton and other members of the mallow family, including okra. Affected leaves may curl and develop thickened veins, but those changes are not unique to this virus. Reports from ornamental mallows have added another layer of uncertainty because findings in one host do not establish the same disease behavior in another. Reliable identification depends on a professional plant-health diagnosis.

fallopia-dumetorum.summary: Climbing false buckwheat is an annual vine that threads its way through nearby vegetation with slender, twining stems. Its leaves are triangular to heart-shaped, and the small flowers are much less showy than those of a morning glory. As fruits develop, the surrounding flower parts form pale wings. Native across temperate Eurasia, it also occurs in disturbed North American habitats. It closely resembles native climbing false buckwheats, making mature fruit an important part of a useful record.

solanum-dulcamara.summary: Climbing nightshade scrambles through shrubs and fences, especially in moist places. Its purple flowers have petals that curve backward around a bright yellow center, and its berries ripen through several colors before turning glossy red. This perennial vine is native to Eurasia and has become established in North America, where it can spread through underground stems as well as seed. The attractive berries are not edible; all parts of the plant are toxic to people and domestic animals.

ficus-pumila.summary: Climbing fig can turn a wall into a dense covering of small, heart-shaped leaves. This woody evergreen vine, native to eastern Asia, attaches itself with short roots along its young stems. As it matures, it develops thicker branches with much larger, leathery leaves and may produce pear-shaped figs. That change can make the adult plant look surprisingly different from its familiar juvenile form. Its strong attachment to surfaces also deserves consideration wherever it is planted near buildings.

gonionemus-vertens.summary: Clinging jellyfish are small enough to overlook among seagrass and seaweed. Their transparent bells carry a conspicuous orange-brown cross, and sticky pads on the tentacles help them hold onto submerged vegetation. They occur in sheltered coastal waters such as bays, estuaries and ponds, rather than behaving like large jellies drifting conspicuously offshore. Contact can cause a painful sting, with reactions varying between people and populations. A clear photograph taken without touching the animal is the safest useful observation.

cuscuta-epithymum.summary: Clover dodder makes a fine tangle of yellowish, red or purple threads over other plants, with tiny rounded clusters of flowers along its stems. It draws nourishment directly from its hosts, which include clovers, heather and gorse, rather than supporting itself with ordinary green leaves. Its role depends on the setting: it can trouble agricultural crops, yet it is also a native part of European heathland. The identity of both the dodder and its host helps explain a sighting.

sitona-hispidulus.summary: The clover weevil, also called clover root curculio, is a small mottled brown beetle associated with clover and alfalfa. Adults nibble small semicircular notches along leaf edges, but the more serious injury happens underground. Pale larvae feed on roots and can leave scars or deep gouges that weaken plants. A thinning patch of forage may therefore reflect damage that is not visible above ground, although disease and poor nutrition can produce similar symptoms.

cotton-leafroll-dwarf-virus.summary: Cotton leafroll dwarf virus can be associated with curled or puckered leaves, distorted new growth and changes in the way cotton plants develop. Some affected plants become stunted, while others show elongated shoots with poor boll production. Symptoms vary with the cotton variety, growing conditions and the stage at which disease develops; some infected plants show little obvious change. Similar leaf distortion can result from insects or herbicide injury, so appearance alone cannot establish the diagnosis.

begonia-cucullata.summary: Begonia cucullata forms a soft mound of fleshy stems and glossy green leaves, with small white or pink flowers held above the foliage. The leaves have a wavy, finely toothed edge, and the seed capsules are unevenly winged. Native to South America, this begonia is grown ornamentally and has escaped cultivation in some warm regions, including parts of the southeastern United States. Its many garden relatives and hybrids make a flowering, fruiting specimen more informative than a familiar garden name.

malva-verticillata.summary: Cluster mallow carries small pale flowers close to the stem, tucked into tight groups where the leaf stalks join it. Its broad, rounded leaves usually have shallow lobes and scalloped edges, giving a leafy plant a much larger presence than its flowers suggest. It has a long history of cultivation and also grows in fields, roadsides and disturbed ground. Several mallows look similar, and published records themselves sometimes reflect misidentification, so mature fruit is especially valuable for checking a sighting.

trifolium-glomeratum.summary: Clustered clover is a small annual that spreads low over the ground or lifts its stems slightly above surrounding vegetation. Its pink to purplish flowers gather in tight, rounded heads nestled directly against the stem at the leaf joints. Each leaf has the familiar three leaflets, but the almost stalkless flower heads help distinguish it from more familiar garden and pasture clovers. Native around Europe, North Africa and the Middle East, it has also become naturalized elsewhere.

rumex-conglomeratus.summary: Clustered dock is a slender perennial with branching upright stems and small flowers arranged in separated whorls. Many of those clusters have a little leaf beneath them, giving the flowering stem a more leafy appearance than some other docks. It grows in damp places as well as cultivated and pasture ground, and has been introduced well beyond its native Old World range. The modest flowers are easy to overlook, but the mature fruit coverings provide useful identification details.

erechtites-minimus.summary: Coastal burnweed is an upright, short-lived herb with narrow, regularly toothed leaves and clusters of small cylindrical flower heads. Unlike a showy daisy, its heads lack a ring of spreading ray petals. Botanists now commonly treat this plant as Senecio minimus, while Erechtites minimus remains a name used in older records. It occurs naturally in Australia and New Zealand, including moist forest settings, so its presence there should not automatically be interpreted as an alien invasion.

acacia-cyclops.summary: Coastal wattle is a dense shrub or small tree with narrow, leathery leaf-like structures and round golden flower heads. Its most striking feature appears when the pods open: each dark seed is surrounded by a fleshy orange to scarlet loop. Native to coastal Western Australia and South Australia, it has been planted elsewhere for shelter and dune stabilization. Outside its native range it can become invasive; South African conservation assessments identify it as a threat to sensitive coastal plant habitat.

tridax-procumbens.summary: Coatbuttons carries little daisy-like heads on long, wiry stalks above a low tangle of hairy stems and coarsely toothed leaves. A yellow center is bordered by just a few short white, cream or pale yellow rays, giving each head its button-like appearance. The plant is native to tropical America and is now widespread in warm regions elsewhere. It readily occupies bare and disturbed soil, where sprawling stems can form small patches between taller plants.

nopalea-cochenillifera.summary: Cochineal cactus grows into a branching shrub or small tree, with flattened green pads and slender scarlet flowers. Despite its often nearly spineless appearance, the pads can carry tiny irritating bristles. Native to Mexico, it has been planted widely in warm regions and sometimes grows beyond cultivation. It also has a long history as a host for insects used to produce cochineal dye. Its presence in a garden is different from an established wild population, so records need that context.

solanum-capsicoides.summary: Cockroach berry is a prickly, short-lived member of the nightshade family, with broad leaves, white star-shaped flowers, and round fruits that turn orange-red. It grows in disturbed ground in warm, moist regions, including places outside its native tropical American range. The bright fruit can make it conspicuous along a roadside or neglected patch, but appearance alone is not a safe guide to edibility. Similar prickly nightshades have often been confused with it, making careful identification especially useful.

erythrina-crista-galli.summary: Cockspur coral tree brings clusters of vivid red, pea-shaped flowers to a branching shrub or small tree. Its leaves are divided into three leaflets, and the branches carry prickles. Native to South America, it is grown as an ornamental in warmer regions and has been introduced well beyond its original range.

colocasia-esculenta.summary: Taro is the plant behind a familiar tropical food crop and many garden elephant ears. Its large, heart- to arrow-shaped leaves rise from a thick underground corm. In warm wetlands, escaped plants can spread into dense patches along streams, ditches, and marshes, shading smaller vegetation. Pieces of the underground plant can help establish new patches when moved. Its value in cultivation and its ability to invade some waterways are both part of the story; the local setting matters.

cocos-nucifera.summary: Coconut palms are a familiar part of tropical coastlines, with a ringed trunk, long feather-like fronds, and large fibrous fruits. People have carried them widely for food, fiber, and useful materials. They also grow outside cultivation in suitable coastal habitats, where their ecological role depends on the place. Florida's assessment, for example, treats the palm differently across the state and identifies invasive behavior in the south with limited approved uses. A coconut record therefore needs more context than a garden label.

aspidiotus-destructor.summary: Coconut scale is a tiny sap-feeding insect that can gather in pale, closely packed patches on leaves. Coconut and banana are familiar hosts, but it also feeds on many other tropical crops and ornamental plants. Heavy infestations yellow and weaken foliage. Young insects, called crawlers, move before settling beneath a protective covering; infested nursery plants can carry them to new places. Predators and tiny parasitic wasps help suppress populations, so visible scales do not automatically mean broad insecticide treatment is needed.

cydia-pomonella.summary: Codling moth is best known for the caterpillar that tunnels into an apple or pear and feeds around the seeds. Adults are small, mottled moths that blend into bark; the damage inside fruit is usually more noticeable than the moth itself. It also attacks walnuts and some other fruit crops. Several generations can develop during a growing season, depending on climate. Successful management combines watching for moth activity with timely fruit protection and removing infested fruit before more insects emerge.

epilobium-hirsutum.summary: Hairy willow-herb is a tall perennial with fuzzy stems and pink-purple flowers, often growing where the soil stays moist. Introduced from Eurasia, it can form dense patches along wetlands, ditches, and stream edges in North America. Underground stems help a patch expand, while silky-haired seeds travel on the wind. Its flowers can be attractive, but a crowded stand can leave less room for other wetland plants. Native willow-herbs and fireweeds make careful identification worthwhile before any removal.

imperata-cylindrica.summary: Cogongrass is a spreading perennial grass that can turn varied vegetation into dense stands. Its extensive underground stems help it survive disturbance and move outward, while fluffy seeds and contaminated soil or equipment carry it farther. In the southeastern United States, it invades roadsides, pastures, and natural areas. The buildup of dry grass also increases fire danger and can change how habitats burn. Because a patch can regrow from underground pieces, controlling it usually takes a coordinated effort and repeated follow-up.

citrullus-colocynthis.summary: Colocynth, sometimes called bitter apple, is a trailing relative of watermelon adapted to dry landscapes. Its rough, deeply divided leaves and small yellow flowers spread close to the ground, followed by round fruits that change from mottled green to yellow. Unlike a sweet watermelon, the fruit has intensely bitter flesh. The plant is native across parts of Africa and Asia and adjacent regions. Its desert ecology is well documented, but a record outside that range does not alone establish local invasive damage.

cuphea-carthagenensis.summary: Colombian waxweed is a small, branching herb with rough, hairy leaves and tiny purple to pink flowers. It can be easy to overlook among grasses in a damp, disturbed patch. Native from Mexico through tropical America, it has become established in other warm regions, including parts of the southeastern United States and Hawaii. The flower's narrow tube and the plant's sticky hairs help distinguish it from superficially similar weeds. Its introduced presence alone does not tell us how strongly it affects a particular habitat.

agrostis-capillaris.summary: Colonial bentgrass, also called Rhode Island bentgrass, is a fine-leaved perennial introduced from Europe and nearby regions. Its airy flower clusters can give an unmown patch a soft haze. It has long been used in lawns, but also grows in fields, roadsides, and other open ground beyond cultivation. In some regions it becomes an invasive grass rather than staying a lawn plant. Separating it from related bentgrasses takes a closer look at the flowering branches and the small membranous flap where a leaf blade meets its sheath.

didemnum-perlucidum.summary: This colonial sea squirt forms thin living sheets over surfaces such as dock structures, ropes, rocks, and shellfish. Each sheet contains many tiny animals that filter food from the water. Colonies often look pale or marbled, but their appearance changes with conditions. It has spread through warm-water ports and can overgrow other organisms, creating concerns for aquaculture and some natural habitats. Its original home remains uncertain in parts of the scientific literature, even though introductions are documented in several regions.

symplegma-reptans.summary: Symplegma reptans is a colonial sea squirt that spreads as a low covering of many small animals joined within a shared outer layer. Native to the Indo-West Pacific, it has established in Southern California harbors, where it grows on docks, hulls, and other submerged surfaces. Colonies expand by producing new individuals through budding. At some sites they can cover large areas and potentially compete for space with other attached organisms. Its resemblance to related sea squirts has complicated identification and some early records.

tussilago-farfara.summary: Coltsfoot sends up yellow, dandelion-like flower heads before its broad leaves unfold. Later, the leaves form a low cover, with a pale, woolly underside that helps distinguish them from dandelions. Native across parts of Eurasia and North Africa, this perennial grows in moist disturbed ground and can spread into nearby habitats. Underground stems allow it to form persistent patches, while its fluffy seeds provide another route of dispersal. Removing only the visible leaves often leaves the living network below intact.

hyptis-pectinata.summary: Comb bushmint is a branching, aromatic herb whose tiny pale flowers line curved clusters like the teeth of a comb. It can grow tall enough to look like a small shrub, with toothed, hairy leaves and angular stems. Native to tropical America, it now occurs in other warm regions, often around disturbed ground, thickets, and moist edges. Although it appears in weed records, Florida's assessment does not document it as a problem species there. Its local behavior deserves attention without assuming severe impacts everywhere.

combretum-indicum.summary: Rangoon creeper is a woody climber best known for fragrant flowers that change from white through pink to red as they age. Hooks formed from leaf stalks help it climb over supports, and its broad leaves grow in opposite pairs. Its native range includes Tanzania and tropical and subtropical Asia through northern Australia. Widely cultivated in tropical gardens, it has also been introduced elsewhere. The mix of flower colors on a single vine makes it especially distinctive when in bloom.

asparagus-setaceus.summary: Common asparagus-fern looks soft and fern-like, but it is a flowering climber rather than a true fern. Its fine green sprays are familiar in houseplants and floral arrangements. Outside cultivation in warm regions, thorny shoots can climb through other vegetation, and birds carry seeds from its dark berries. Persistent underground growth makes established plants difficult to remove completely. Native to eastern and southern Africa, it has escaped cultivation elsewhere; Florida guidance recommends preventing escape and managing existing plants carefully.

melissa-officinalis.summary: Lemon balm is a perennial herb with wrinkled, toothed leaves that release a lemon scent when bruised. A member of the mint family, it produces small pale flowers visited by pollinators and has long been grown for kitchen and garden use. Native from the Mediterranean toward Central Asia, it has become established well beyond that range. Plants can spread and self-seed around gardens, so keeping an eye on seedlings is useful. Its familiar usefulness and occasional weedy behavior are both worth recognizing.

bambusa-vulgaris.summary: Common bamboo forms large clumps of tall, jointed canes topped by leafy branches. Native to parts of Asia and widely planted in warm regions, it supplies material for buildings, tools, and crafts as well as garden screens. It is a clumping bamboo, so its growth differs from the long-running bamboos familiar in some gardens. That distinction matters when evaluating a sighting or planning management. Florida's completed assessment for its southern region does not document an invasive problem there; other regions need their own assessment.

berberis-vulgaris.summary: Common Barberry is a deciduous shrub with branched spines, hanging yellow flower clusters, and red berries that can remain into winter. It grows in woodland, pasture, hedgerows, and disturbed ground, tolerating both sun and shade. Dense stands can crowd other vegetation, while birds carry its seeds to new sites. The shrub also serves as an alternate host for black stem rust, a disease of cereal crops. Its persistence comes from both long-lived seed and underground stems that send up shoots, so removing the visible branches alone rarely settles an established infestation.

hordeum-vulgare.summary: Common barley is the cultivated cereal familiar from grain fields, brewing, and livestock feed. This cool-season annual sometimes appears along roadsides or in disturbed ground after seed escapes cultivation. Such plants should not automatically be described as a damaging invasion: the USDA guide describes volunteers as generally not persistent. The compact seed head often carries long bristles, although some cultivated forms lack them. Two-row and six-row barley differ in how many spikelets develop grain, a useful reminder that variation within this crop can change its appearance without indicating another species.

ornithopus-sativus.summary: Common bird's-foot is a small annual legume also called French serradella. Its softly hairy stems spread along the ground or rise above it, carrying leaves divided into many small leaflets. Small pink or whitish pea flowers develop into slender, jointed pods. Each pod segment holds a seed, giving mature fruits a beaded appearance. It is native to southwestern Europe and has been introduced elsewhere. The mature pods provide a useful way to recognize an unfamiliar patch after the flowers fade. A nearby planting or seed mixture may help explain an occurrence, but the plant itself still needs identification.

borago-officinalis.summary: Common borage is an annual garden herb with bristly leaves and bright blue, star-shaped flowers. Native to the Mediterranean region, it is grown in herb and flower gardens and attracts bees. Plants often return through self-sown seed, rather than surviving as the same individual from year to year. Escapes beside a garden may therefore reflect ongoing seed production.
