The dark central cone of each nodding flower is especially distinctive against the blue petals. Flowers open in sequence as the curled clusters unfold, extending the display through summer. A persistent garden escape deserves attention without assuming that every volunteer damages surrounding habitat.

cotula-coronopifolia.summary: Common brassbuttons is a low wetland plant named for its small yellow flower heads, which resemble buttons without surrounding petals. Fleshy stems can creep and root where they touch the ground. It occurs along streams and in both fresh and salty marshes, so a coastal location is helpful context but not a requirement. Introduced populations are widespread, though the Smithsonian account does not describe it as a highly aggressive invader. Local abundance and the plants growing alongside it matter when judging an occurrence. Its wetland setting also makes careless trampling or soil disturbance a concern during investigation.

reichardia-picroides.summary: Common brighteyes is a Mediterranean daisy-family herb with yellow flower heads and somewhat fleshy, often lobed leaves. The useful clue is beneath the flower: small bracts have a distinctive broad shape and pale, thin margins. It occurs in disturbed places such as field edges and roadsides in its native region. A familiar-looking yellow flower is not enough to identify an introduced occurrence, because many unrelated daisies look similar from above. Descriptions of related annual and perennial forms require care, especially when matching a plant found far from the area covered by a particular flora.

rhamnus-cathartica.summary: Common Buckthorn is a large shrub or small tree that can form a dense understory in woodland and along forest edges. It opens its leaves early and retains them late, extending the period when it shades plants beneath it. Female plants produce dark fruits eaten by birds, which carry the seeds elsewhere. Introduced as an ornamental and hedging plant, it has become a significant woodland invader in parts of North America. It also provides an overwintering host for soybean aphids. Removing a mature patch is a continuing project because cut stems can resprout and new seedlings can appear.

arctium-minus.summary: Common Burdock begins as a cluster of large, heart-shaped leaves, then sends up a branching flowering stalk. Its purple flower heads develop into the familiar hooked burs that cling to fur and clothing. This is an effective way for seeds to travel beyond the original patch. The plant commonly occurs in pasture, fence lines, and other disturbed ground, where its broad leaves can shade neighboring plants. A deep taproot supports its growth. Finding young rosettes before burs develop makes management easier and helps prevent painful tangles in animals' coats.

cyprinus-carpio.summary: Common Carp is a large, deep-bodied fish introduced to North America from Eurasia. It often feeds in shallow water, sucking material from the bottom and sorting out food. Where populations are abundant, this activity can uproot aquatic plants and stir sediment, reducing water clarity and changing habitat for other fish and waterfowl. It lives in lakes, rivers, ponds, and wetlands. Cultivated forms vary in color and scale coverage. Ornamental koi may belong to the related Amur carp rather than this species, so color alone cannot settle an identification. An unfamiliar capture should be identified carefully before any management decision.

silene-gallica.summary: Common catchfly is a small annual of fields, roadsides, and other disturbed ground. Its narrow flowering stems carry white, pink, or occasionally red-marked flowers above opposite leaves. The plant is introduced from Europe and has been recorded in scattered parts of North America. Short sticky hairs and longer ordinary hairs occur together around the flowers, a useful clue that is easy to miss in a distant photograph. Records of introduction do not by themselves demonstrate substantial ecological damage; the practical concern at a garden or restoration site is whether an unwanted patch is producing seed and expanding.

stellaria-media.summary: Common Chickweed is a low annual that often makes bright green mats in gardens, lawns, and other moist ground. It grows particularly well during cool, wet weather and can complete a generation quickly. Its tiny white flowers appear to have ten petals, but each of the five petals is deeply divided. Seeds allow repeated flushes of growth during favorable weather, so a patch can return after a quick weeding. Young plants may flower while still quite small. In vegetable beds it competes for space, nutrients, and light.

symphytum-officinale.summary: Common comfrey is a perennial garden escape with broad leaves and hanging tubular flowers. It can persist around old homes, ditches, and damp disturbed ground long after a planting is abandoned. Pieces of its substantial root system can produce new plants, making soil movement and incomplete digging important routes of persistence. Garden plants sold as comfrey may also be hybrids or other species, so the familiar name does not settle identification. Historical medicinal use explains some cultivation, but it should not be presented as evidence of safety: extension sources warn that comfrey is unsafe to consume.

agrostemma-githago.summary: Common corncockle is a slender annual with large pink to purple flowers, once a frequent weed of grain fields. Improved crop-seed cleaning and other farming practices have made it much less common in many agricultural areas. It also occurs in disturbed ground and may be grown as a flower. Long green points extending beyond the petals give the blooms a recognizable outline. The plant produces numerous seeds and is poisonous to people and livestock, making contamination of harvested grain or feed a more relevant concern than its attractive appearance suggests.

crupina-vulgaris.summary: Common crupina is a winter annual of open grassland and rangeland. It starts as a low rosette, then produces upright branching stems with narrow purple flower heads. Dense infestations can replace desirable forage and reduce plant diversity. Its seed is relatively large and carries a dark ring of bristles. Two named varieties occur in North America; their differences are most useful on mature fruits, not in a distant photograph. Preventing seed production and movement is central to containment because the species reproduces by seed.

crupina-vulgaris-var-brachypappa.summary: Common crupina variety brachypappa is one of the named forms of a purple-flowered annual that grows in rangeland and other open sites. It shares the divided leaves and small flower heads of Common crupina as a whole. The main reported distinction lies in the mature fruits: their attached bristles are shorter than those assigned to variety vulgaris. A 2023 genetic study of western US populations corroborated the two named varieties. Photographs of leafy plants alone cannot establish either one. A botanist may need mature fruit and a carefully chosen identification key.

crupina-vulgaris-var-vulgaris.summary: Common crupina variety vulgaris is a named form of the same purple-flowered annual found in rangeland and other open sites. It has divided leaves, small flower heads, and fruits bearing bristles. North American treatments distinguish this variety mainly by the relatively long bristles attached to mature fruits. Older literature uses the name variety typica for a longer-bristled form, while newer material uses variety vulgaris. A 2023 genetic study supports the two varieties in contemporary US usage. Historical labels should still be checked before reassignment. The shape and color of a young rosette do not reliably resolve its variety.

taraxacum-officinale-ssp-officinale.summary: Common dandelion is treated here in the broad officinale aggregate used by many references; its exact subspecies boundaries differ among floras. The familiar plant has a basal leaf rosette, yellow flower heads, a deep taproot, and wind-carried fruits. Its flowering stalk rises directly from the rosette, and the rounded seed head breaks apart as individual fruits drift away. That general appearance can identify a dandelion without proving this exact subspecies. Native North American dandelions are treated differently by different authorities, so applying an introduced label to every dandelion in a natural area would be misleading.

erucastrum-gallicum.summary: Common dogmustard is a yellow-flowered mustard of fields, roadsides, railway margins, and other disturbed ground. Introduced from Europe, it can be a weed of cereal and oilseed crops. Its flower stalks often have small leafy bracts beneath them, a useful difference from several superficially similar mustards. Plants usually complete their life cycle in one season, although some floras include biennial behavior. Like many crop weeds, it spreads through seed. A new occurrence near a planting deserves identification and attention to seed movement, without assuming that every roadside plant causes the same level of harm.

linum-usitatissimum.summary: Common flax is the cultivated annual grown for linen fiber and linseed oil. Escaped plants can occur in fields, along roads and railways, and around disturbed places where seed has been moved. Its slender stems carry narrow leaves and blue flowers with five petals, followed by rounded capsules. An introduced crop volunteer is not automatically a major ecological invader; a few plants beside a grain-handling site may have a different significance from repeated establishment in natural vegetation. Other blue-flowered flaxes are perennial and can look similar, making life history and small flower details important when checking an unfamiliar plant.

hydrocharis-morsus-ranae.summary: Common frogbit is a floating aquatic plant that resembles a miniature water lily. Rounded to heart-shaped leaves collect in rosettes, and small white flowers may rise above them in summer. Plants can form crowded surface mats among other shallow-water vegetation. Besides growing shoots, the plant produces compact overwintering buds that detach and start new plants. These buds help it persist even when much of the visible foliage disappears. It is often called European frogbit, which helps distinguish it from American frogbit and other plants sold under similar common names.

gomphrena-globosa.summary: Common globe amaranth is a warm-season garden plant with rounded pink, purple, or white flower heads. Most of the visible color comes from firm, papery bracts surrounding tiny flowers. Those bracts retain their color when dried, explaining the plant's popularity in arrangements. Hairy opposite leaves and stiff branching stems complete its appearance. It is usually grown as an annual and may produce self-sown seedlings. A garden volunteer is not necessarily a damaging invasion. Watch whether new plants remain within the bed or repeatedly establish in surrounding unmanaged ground.

ulex-europaeus.summary: Common gorse is a dense evergreen shrub with stiff spines and golden-yellow pea flowers. Mature plants can form nearly impenetrable stands that displace grassland vegetation. Older bushes often accumulate dead material inside the living outer growth, and their oily foliage contributes to a serious fire hazard. Hairy pods split open and throw seeds away from the branches. Seeds can remain viable in soil for decades, so an apparently cleared patch may keep producing seedlings. Introduced for ornamental use, gorse is especially challenging where a long-established seed supply has built up beneath a thicket.

senecio-vulgaris.summary: Common Groundsel is a fast-growing annual of garden beds, nurseries, and disturbed soil, especially during cool conditions. Its small yellow flower heads soon open into white seed tufts carried by wind. Plants can flower when quite small, and several generations may develop in a favorable year. A particularly important detail is that flowers on pulled plants can still produce viable seed. Groundsel competes with young garden and crop plants, and it is also a livestock hazard because eating it can cause liver poisoning. Removing it promptly matters more than letting a patch reach a conspicuous size.

hieracium-vulgatum.summary: Common hawkweed is a yellow-flowered perennial whose scientific name is used differently among North American references. Some authorities recognize Hieracium vulgatum, while the Pacific Northwest flora uses Hieracium lachenalii and regards the former name as misapplied. These treatments may refer to different taxonomic boundaries rather than a simple spelling change. The plant described in the regional key has toothed basal leaves, several leaves along the flowering stem, and a group of small yellow heads. Native hawkweeds can look similar, so an unfamiliar plant needs both close examination and a clear choice of identification reference.

cynoglossum-officinale.summary: Common Houndstongue is a biennial or short-lived perennial whose long hairy leaves form a low rosette before a flowering stem develops. Dull reddish-purple flowers produce four small hooked fruits that cling firmly to fur, clothing, and equipment. This makes trails, livestock movement, and contaminated material important opportunities for spread. It grows in pasture, roadsides, and other disturbed ground and can compete with forage. The plant is poisonous to livestock, including when dried in hay. A soft-looking rosette is therefore worth identifying before a mowing or haymaking operation carries it farther.

hemidactylus-frenatus.summary: Common house gecko is a small nocturnal lizard often seen on walls near lights, where insects gather. Broad toe pads let it climb smooth surfaces, and its pale gray to brown coloring can make it difficult to notice by day. Native to Asia, it has established introduced populations in parts of the United States and on many islands. Several other house geckos share buildings and look similar, so a gecko near a porch light is not automatically this species. Cargo and transported belongings are practical places to watch for accidental movement.

mesembryanthemum-crystallinum.summary: Common iceplant is a spreading succulent with broad fleshy leaves covered in clear, bead-like cells. These cells catch the light and give the plant its crystalline appearance. It often grows on disturbed coastal or salty ground, forming a low mat that may turn reddish as it ages or dries. In invaded coastal habitats, accumulated salts and persistent dead material can hinder other plants. This species differs from the large, familiar iceplants with thick triangular leaves. It usually completes its life cycle quickly, although its lifespan varies with conditions.

kochia-scoparia.summary: Common kochia is a bushy summer annual of crop fields, roadsides, and other open disturbed places. It tolerates dry and salty soils, helping it establish in arid and semiarid landscapes. The plant was grown ornamentally before spreading beyond cultivation, and modern sources commonly call it Bassia scoparia. Narrow leaves and many branches create a dense outline, sometimes becoming reddish late in the season. It competes with crops for light, water, and nutrients. Some populations resist several herbicide groups, so preventing seed production and maintaining plant competition are especially valuable.

syringa-vulgaris.summary: Common lilac is a deciduous shrub best known for fragrant spring flower clusters. Long cultivated around homes, it can persist at former garden sites and spread locally through shoots arising around the base. Its flowers vary widely among cultivars, including white, pink, and purple forms. A surviving old shrub is not evidence by itself of rapid invasion, but expanding suckers can move it beyond an intended planting. The plant prefers climates with substantial winter chilling, which helps explain its familiar presence in cooler gardens. Records beyond cultivation should distinguish an old planting from newly established growth.

malva-neglecta.summary: Common Mallow is a spreading annual or biennial with rounded leaves and small pale flowers. Its flattened ring of fruits resembles a tiny wheel of cheese, giving it the alternate name cheeseweed. Young plants can be easy to overlook, but they soon develop a strong taproot that becomes difficult to pull. The plant reproduces by seed, and the hard seed coat allows some seeds to persist for years. It occurs in gardens, disturbed soil, and cultivated ground, where larger patches can compete with desired plants and replenish a lasting seed supply.

schismus-barbatus.summary: Common mediterranean grass is a small annual grass that can be easy to overlook until many plants cover the spaces between desert shrubs. Its narrow leaves and short, pale or purple flower clusters grow close to the ground. Plants dry to straw color as moisture disappears. Originally from the Old World, it now occurs in disturbed dry ground in parts of the western United States. It is often discussed with the closely related Arabian schismus because the two grasses look similar and share habitats. Management deserves particular care in deserts, where disturbing the soil can create more opportunities for annual weeds.

cerastium-fontanum.summary: Common Mouse-ear Chickweed forms low green mats with small leaves covered in conspicuous hairs. Unlike the annual Common Chickweed, established plants often persist for several years and can spread as creeping stems take root. Small white flowers rise above the foliage, each with five notched petals. It grows in lawns, gardens, fields, and other disturbed places, especially where conditions stay cool and moist. Much North American weed guidance concerns the widespread subspecies vulgare within this species. A patch may remain green through winter in mild conditions, then resume growth before many neighboring plants become active.

verbascum-thapsus.summary: Common Mullein starts as a broad rosette of thick, soft, gray-green leaves. Later it sends up a tall stalk topped with closely packed yellow flowers, often becoming one of the most noticeable plants along a sunny roadside. It usually flowers in its second year, though conditions can delay flowering. Introduced from Europe, it favors open disturbed ground, pastures, and waste places. A mature plant produces numerous tiny seeds, and the soil seed bank can outlast the visible stand. Preventing fresh seed and restoring dense vegetation are therefore more useful than simply removing old brown stalks.

lapsana-communis.summary: Common nipplewort is a leafy herb with many small yellow flower heads on a branching stem. The lower leaves often have one broad end lobe and smaller side lobes, giving the plant a different outline from a lawn dandelion. It is native to Europe and Asia and has been introduced widely in North America, where it grows in fields and other disturbed places. Plants generally complete their lives as annuals, although short-lived perennial growth is also reported. The pale yellow heads contain only strap-shaped flowers; there is no contrasting central disk.

avena-sativa.summary: Common oat is the familiar cereal and forage crop, with loose, branching seed heads rather than the compact ears of wheat or barley. Plants may also appear outside fields after grain is spilled or cultivation ends. These escapes occur along roadsides and on disturbed ground across North America. Common oat is an annual, so management of unwanted plants centers on preventing another seed crop and identifying the source of new seed. Its presence alone does not show that a habitat is being invaded or damaged; an isolated volunteer and a deliberately planted cover crop need different responses.

littorina-littorea.summary: Common periwinkle is a marine snail found on rocky shores, pilings, and other surfaces exposed by the falling tide. It holds tightly with a muscular foot and scrapes algae with a ribbon of microscopic teeth. A small hard lid seals its shell opening when the animal withdraws, helping it retain moisture. Originally European, it is well established along much of northeastern North America; scattered Pacific-coast records have not always represented reproducing populations. Dense populations can change seaweed communities through grazing. Its empty shells also provide homes for hermit crabs and shelter for other small shore animals.

vinca-minor.summary: Common Periwinkle is a creeping evergreen groundcover with glossy dark leaves and blue to lavender flowers. Long stems take root where their joints touch soil, allowing a small planting to become a connected mat. Native to Europe and the Caucasus, it has been widely planted around homes, old gardens, and cemeteries. Escaped patches can spread into nearby natural areas and crowd low-growing vegetation. Flowers are most noticeable in spring and early summer, but the persistent foliage makes patches visible in other seasons too. Cultivated forms may have pale-edged or golden leaves rather than solid green.

plantago-major.summary: Common Plantain grows as a low rosette of broad leaves with strong curved veins. Slender upright stalks carry tiny flowers and later crowded seed capsules. It is familiar in lawns, paths, gardens, and other frequently disturbed places, particularly where soil is compacted and stays moist. A tough crown at ground level allows an established plant to survive mowing and produce new leaves. Although unwanted in many lawns, a few plants do not automatically justify treatment. Accurate identification matters because other broad-leaved plantains, including native species, can occupy the same kinds of sites.

opuntia-monacantha.summary: Common pricklypear is a shrubby to tree-sized cactus with flattened green stem segments that often droop toward their tips. Older plants can develop a woody trunk, while yellow flowers and reddish-purple fruit form around the edges of the segments. Native to South America, it has escaped cultivation in warm regions elsewhere. Broken segments can root when they reach soil, so garden waste and moved plant pieces can start new patches. Its spines and tiny barbed bristles make handling difficult. The name “prickly pear” covers many different cacti, including native North American species, making exact identification especially important.

ruta-graveolens.summary: Common rue is a small aromatic shrub with blue-green divided leaves and clusters of yellow flowers. Young stems are soft and green, becoming woody as the plant ages. It has long been grown in herb and ornamental gardens and can reseed around the parent plant. The foliage also serves as food for several swallowtail butterfly species. Common rue is associated with southeastern Europe and the Balkan region, but has been cultivated and naturalized elsewhere. It is not appropriate to assume that every garden planting causes ecological harm. Wear gloves and long sleeves when handling Common rue: skin contact followed by sunlight can cause a severe skin reaction.

mesapamea-secalis.summary: Common rustic moth is a small, stout, night-flying moth whose brown forewings often show a conspicuous pale kidney-shaped mark. Adults rest among vegetation by day and may come to outdoor lights after dark. The caterpillars feed on grasses, including cereal crops. A Eurasian species, it was first documented in North America in the Pacific Northwest in 2016 and has since been recorded more widely in that region. European crop damage is known, but the regional university account does not currently recognize it as a North American pest. New records are therefore useful for tracking its spread without assuming damage.

rumex-acetosella.summary: Common Sheep Sorrel is a low perennial with slender stems and leaves that often resemble small arrowheads. Groups of shoots can belong to the same spreading underground system, so a patch may persist long after its original crown has died. Tiny flowers and developing fruits can give a stand a reddish-brown cast. Introduced from Eurasia, it is widespread in temperate North America in fields, pastures, roadsides, and other open places. It tolerates acidic, low-fertility soils particularly well, but its presence does not prove that soil needs lime. Existing vegetation and growing conditions strongly influence how troublesome it becomes.

sonchus-oleraceus.summary: Common Sowthistle is an upright annual with yellow flower heads, lobed leaves, and a hollow stem that releases white sap when damaged. It often begins as a ground-level rosette before growing taller and branching near the top. The flower heads later release small fruits carried by tufts of fine white hairs. It grows in gardens, crop fields, roadsides, and other disturbed places, and can complete its life cycle in either cool or warm seasons. In mild climates, plants may be present through much of the year. Seed prevention is especially useful because established plants reproduce by seed rather than a spreading perennial root system.

veronica-officinalis.summary: Common Speedwell is a low perennial with trailing stems, opposite leaves, and short clusters of small pale blue to violet flowers. Its stems can rise at their tips while the lower portions remain close to the ground. It occurs in fields, woodland openings, and disturbed places, with early-summer flowering documented in northern climates. Regional floras describe it as introduced from Europe in New England and the Pacific Northwest. The name "speedwell" is shared by many species, including annual lawn weeds and other perennials, so a management decision should begin with the actual plant rather than the common name alone.

hypericum-perforatum.summary: Common St. John's Wort is a perennial with branching stems and clusters of bright yellow flowers. Held to the light, its small leaves show translucent gland dots that can look like pinholes. It grows particularly well in open disturbed places, including pastures, roadsides, and grasslands. Introduced from Europe, western Asia, and North Africa, it can spread through seeds and underground growth. Grazing animals that consume enough may become unusually sensitive to sunlight, making pasture infestations a practical concern. The name is also used loosely for ornamental Hypericum shrubs, so yellow flowers alone do not identify this particular species.

sigesbeckia-orientalis.summary: Common St. Paul's wort is an upright annual with paired leaves and small yellow flower heads surrounded by conspicuous spreading green bracts. The bracts carry sticky gland-tipped hairs, a useful feature when the tiny flowers are hard to see. It belongs to the daisy family and is unrelated to the familiar yellow-flowered St. John's Wort. Its broad native range includes parts of Africa and Asia, with differing historical interpretations in Australia, and it has been introduced elsewhere. It often grows in disturbed ground. Site conditions and local records matter more than the word “weed” in one of its alternate names.

tanacetum-vulgare.summary: Common Tansy is a tall perennial with finely divided leaves and dense, flat-topped clusters of yellow button-like flower heads. Several stems rise from a spreading underground system, and established plants can form substantial clumps. Originally from Eurasia, it was introduced as an ornamental and herb and now occurs along roads, fields, streambanks, and other open sites. Its foliage has a strong odor when disturbed. Dense stands can displace desirable pasture plants and other vegetation. Although the plant has a long history of use, it can be toxic to livestock and should not be treated as forage or a home remedy.

retithrips-syriacus.summary: Common thrip is a minute leaf-feeding insect more widely described in specialist sources as black vine thrips or castor thrips. It feeds and breeds on many plants, including grapevines, roses, castor bean, and tropical landscape trees. Older leaves are especially important feeding sites. The species is associated with the Old World tropics and has been recorded in Florida, the Caribbean, and Brazil. Its tiny size makes it easy to overlook on moved plants and cuttings. Leaf injury alone cannot establish which thrips species is present, and a confirmed identification is more useful than treating every damaged leaf as the same pest.

holcus-lanatus.summary: Common Velvetgrass is a perennial grass covered in short, soft hairs that give its leaves and stems a pale gray-green appearance. Its branching flower clusters can be silvery green, pink, or purplish, changing shape as they open and mature. It often grows in moist meadows, pasture, lawns, and disturbed ground. Introduced to North America through forage seed and related pathways, it is more widespread in coastal regions than in the continental interior. Established patches can become dense, and seed left in the soil can complicate removal. The soft texture is useful for recognition, but it should be checked alongside the flower and leaf-junction features.

echium-vulgare.summary: Common viper's bugloss is a bristly plant with vivid blue flowers and conspicuous projecting pink to red stamens. It usually spends its first year as a rosette of narrow leaves, then produces upright flowering stems before dying after seed production. Originally from Europe and central Asia, it occurs along roads, in pasture, and on other dry disturbed ground. Its coarse hairs can irritate skin, and dense growth can reduce more palatable forage. Each flower can produce four small nutlets. Preventing those seeds is an important part of managing an unwanted patch, especially where wildflower seed mixtures or moved soil could introduce it.

podarcis-muralis.summary: Common wall lizard is a small European lizard that now lives in several introduced North American populations. Sunny stone walls, rock piles, and similar sheltered places provide basking surfaces and hiding spaces. Its brown or gray colors can blend closely with masonry, although the sides often carry conspicuous dark markings. A sighting does not by itself establish damage to local wildlife: Indiana's wildlife agency describes ecological effects there as uncertain. The useful first step is documenting where the lizards occur, especially when a population appears well away from an already known introduction.

triticum-aestivum.summary: Common wheat is the familiar cereal grown for grain, but plants also appear outside cultivation when spilled or surviving seed germinates. These volunteers occur in fields, roadsides, and other disturbed ground. Domestication favored large grains and seedheads that stay together for harvesting, helping explain why a wheat head looks different from many wild grasses. An escaped plant should not automatically be described as an ecological threat. Its importance depends on the setting: unwanted wheat can interfere with another crop, while a few roadside plants may simply mark a recent source of grain.

bromus-madritensis.summary: Compact brome is a small annual grass introduced from the Mediterranean region. It grows in disturbed grassy places and produces bristly seedheads that may turn reddish purple before the seed is ripe. Its name needs care: some references combine it with red brome as two subspecies, while others recognize separate species. This profile uses Compact brome for Bromus madritensis in the narrower sense. Studies about red brome alone should not be transferred automatically to this plant, particularly claims about desert fire, abundance, or effects on native vegetation.

pseudococcus-comstocki.summary: Comstock mealybug is a sap-feeding insect that gathers on leaves, stems, bark, and fruit. Its white wax covering can make a colony look like small bits of cotton caught on a plant. Feeding can contribute to fruit drop, while the sticky honeydew it produces supports dark sooty mold. Ants attracted to that honeydew can provide a useful clue when the insects themselves are hidden. Fruit trees and ornamental plants deserve close inspection, but a white insect colony is not enough to name the species: several mealybugs and scale insects look similar.

trachelospermum-jasminoides.summary: Confederate jasmine is an evergreen woody vine known for glossy leaves and strongly scented white flowers. Despite its common name, it belongs to the dogbane family rather than the true jasmine genus. Twining stems can climb a support or spread across the ground, which explains its use on fences, trellises, and garden banks. Established plants tolerate periods of dry weather. Where it grows beyond a planting, evaluate the actual spread and nearby vegetation rather than assuming every cultivated vine is harmful. Its ability to root from stems makes garden cleanup important when containment is needed.

dynaspidiotus-abietis.summary: Conifer needle scale is an armored scale insect that feeds on conifer needles and twigs. The insect lives beneath a small protective cover, so an infestation may first look like scattered gray bumps rather than moving insects. Heavy feeding can lead to early needle loss and drying branches. Infested cut trees and ornamental greenery can transport it: Minnesota inspectors documented this species on Christmas trees in 2023. That finding illustrates a pathway, not a nationwide instruction to destroy conifers. Identification matters because several different scales occur on these hosts.

cyathea-cooperi.summary: Cooper's cyathea is an Australian tree fern with a single trunk topped by very large, finely divided fronds. Often sold as Australian tree fern, it can become a substantial plant rather than remaining a compact garden fern. It reproduces through spores, which are much smaller than seeds and can travel on the wind. In Hawaii, escaped plants compete with native forest vegetation, including native tree ferns. That documented impact should be distinguished from an assumption of equal harm everywhere it is planted. Escapes near moist natural areas deserve particular attention.

acacia-baileyana.summary: Cootamundra wattle is a small Australian tree or large shrub grown for its gray-blue foliage and masses of yellow flowers. The leaves are divided twice into many narrow leaflets, giving them a fernlike outline. Escaped plants can grow in woodland, scrub, and disturbed ground. Seeds can persist in soil and germinate after heat or disturbance, so removing a mature plant may not end an infestation. Its ornamental origin helps explain many occurrences outside its native range; management should focus on places where it is reproducing beyond plantings or affecting valued habitat.

cyclops-strenuus.summary: This copepod, Cyclops strenuus, is a freshwater crustacean requiring microscopic identification. Its reported North American distribution is difficult to interpret because several similar species have been confused. USGS explains that some Great Lakes specimens previously called Cyclops strenuus were later identified as Cyclops sibiricus, while other recent material proved to be Cyclops divergens. Earlier research also questioned whether some northern records belonged to Cyclops canadensis. These are consequential identification changes: records, native status, and impacts assigned to one species cannot simply be carried over to another.

harpacticella-paradoxa.summary: This Copepod, Harpacticella paradoxa, is a minute freshwater crustacean that mainly crawls on surfaces or lives among bottom sediments. It is known from Asian freshwater habitats and has been recorded in western North American reservoirs and estuaries. Smithsonian researchers consider the timing and separated distribution of those records evidence of introduction. Unlike larger conspicuous invaders, this animal is found through specialist sampling. The Smithsonian account reports no demonstrated ecological or economic effects, so its presence should not be presented as proof that a particular waterbody has been damaged.

limnoithona-tetraspina.summary: This Copepod, Limnoithona tetraspina, is a tiny crustacean that drifts in estuarine water and feeds on microscopic organisms. First recorded in the San Francisco Estuary in 1993, it quickly became abundant in the low-salinity zone and largely replaced another introduced species, Limnoithona sinensis. Its small size matters to food-web research because a community dominated by tiny prey differs from one containing larger copepods. Researchers continue to examine those consequences. A dense population is evidence of establishment, but it should not be used alone to explain changes in fish populations.

mesocyclops-pehpeiensis.summary: This Copepod, Mesocyclops pehpeiensis, is a small freshwater crustacean native to Asia. Introduced populations have been found in rice fields, ponds, and facilities growing aquatic plants. It has also been studied and moved for mosquito-control experiments, which should not be taken as encouragement for private releases. Older records may use Mesocyclops ruttneri, a name later placed in synonymy with this species. The connection with transported aquatic plants is especially useful for prevention: water accompanying an ornamental plant can carry organisms that are almost invisible during a casual inspection. Laboratory experiments show it suppresses populations of small freshwater prey, but these results do not measure damage in a particular lake.

nitokra-hibernica.summary: This Copepod, Nitokra hibernica, is a tiny crustacean associated with bottom surfaces and aquatic vegetation. Native to Eurasia, it tolerates both fresh and brackish water and has been recorded in the Great Lakes region. Its lifestyle makes nearshore plant beds and sediment samples more informative than a casual look at open water. This is a microscopic identification problem, not an animal most visitors will notice from shore. Older records may use the spelling Nitocra hibernica. Researchers have recovered this species from ballast water carried by ships within the Great Lakes, showing a route for transport between waterbodies.

oithona-davisae.summary: This Copepod, Oithona davisae, is a small estuarine crustacean thought to originate in East Asia. It was formally described from introduced California material, a reminder that the place where a species receives its scientific name is not necessarily its native home. Ballast water can move it between ports. It feeds on microscopic food and can become very abundant, but the Smithsonian account separates possible food-web effects from demonstrated species-specific impacts. Small size and similar-looking relatives have complicated both historical records and efforts to determine its full distribution.

tortanus-dextrilobatus.summary: This Copepod, Tortanus dextrilobatus, is a small predatory crustacean native to Asian coastal waters. It eats smaller copepods rather than relying only on microscopic plants. Introduced populations were discovered in the San Francisco Estuary in 1993, and transport in ships' ballast water is considered the likely pathway. Its predation can change the numbers of other plankton, although the full consequences for the food web require further study. This is an animal identified through plankton sampling and microscopy, so an unaided observation from the shore is unlikely to establish its presence.

malephora-crocea.summary: Coppery mesemb is a trailing South African succulent that can form a low, dense mat. Fleshy leaves store water, and bright flowers stand above the spreading stems. It has escaped ornamental plantings in California and other regions with suitable climates. Stems can root where they touch the ground, while seeds provide another means of spread. Water helps disperse the seeds. These traits make discarded garden pieces and runoff worth watching around an escaped patch. Its presence outside its native range does not by itself establish the same level of harm at every planted site.

antigonon-leptopus.summary: Coral vine is a perennial climber with heart-shaped leaves and long clusters of pink flowers. Tendrils let it grip fences and neighboring plants, and vigorous growth can cover vegetation at disturbed sites and forest edges. Below ground, enlarged roots store reserves that allow the vine to return after cutting or frost damage. It also produces seeds that can travel in water. Those two routes of persistence explain why cutting away the visible growth is often only a first step. In warm places where it escapes, preventing seed production and following regrowth are central to containment.

jatropha-multifida.summary: Coralbush is a tropical ornamental shrub with deeply cut leaves and clusters of bright coral-red flowers. The narrow leaf divisions give the foliage a distinctive open outline, while the flowers stand on long stalks above it. It belongs to the spurge family and produces sap when damaged. Plants and seeds should not be eaten, and sap can irritate skin. Reports of cultivation or escape outside its native tropical American range do not establish severe ecological effects everywhere. A useful local assessment asks whether seedlings are appearing beyond the garden and spreading into surrounding vegetation.

spartina-x-townsendii.summary: Cordgrass here refers specifically to Spartina x townsendii, the sterile hybrid between smooth cordgrass and small cordgrass. It is not the same taxon as the fertile species Spartina anglica that arose through chromosome doubling. That distinction is important because older literature sometimes combined the two, making invasion histories easy to misread. Both are salt-marsh grasses with spreading underground stems. A confirmed identification therefore requires more than recognizing a tall cordgrass patch. Records that lack evidence for the hybrid's identity should remain provisional rather than inheriting the distribution and seed-spread claims of Spartina anglica.

sporobolus-alterniflorus-x-foliosus.summary: Cordgrass hybrid is the cross between introduced smooth cordgrass and native California cordgrass, also widely written as Spartina alterniflora × Spartina foliosa. In San Francisco Bay, fertile hybrids and their descendants form a variable population rather than one uniform-looking plant. They can spread into tidal habitat and complicate restoration because the native parent must be protected during control. The current Sporobolus wording reflects a change in genus classification, not a different hybrid. Accurate identification and coordinated management are especially important here: a broad label of nonnative cordgrass can conceal both native plants and mixed ancestry.

coriandrum-sativum.summary: Coriander is an annual culinary herb whose fresh leaves are commonly called cilantro and whose ripe fruits supply the spice called coriander. The same plant changes noticeably as it grows: broad lower leaves give way to finer leaves on flowering stems. Warm conditions can bring early flowering, followed by rounded seed-bearing fruits. Plants sometimes grow outside cultivation after seed escapes or remains in a garden. That makes unwanted volunteers possible, but the sources reviewed do not justify treating every escaped plant as a serious ecological invader. Managing seed production is usually the practical issue.

quercus-suber.summary: Cork oak is an evergreen Mediterranean tree best recognized by its thick, deeply ridged bark, the source of commercial cork. Its leathery leaves stay green through winter and have pale, hairy undersides. Mature trees produce acorns and can persist for a long time in parks and older plantings. Occasional self-sown trees are documented outside its native range, but cultivation and escape are not equivalent to a demonstrated ecological threat. For a tree growing outside its native range, useful questions are whether seedlings are spreading beyond a planting and whether they are displacing vegetation at that particular site.

rigidoporus-vinctus.summary: The name Rigidoporus vinctus does not by itself establish a cause of corm dry rot. Older references describe a crust-forming wood-decay fungus and use names including Junghuhnia vincta. A recent taxonomic revision found that material called Rigidoporus vinctus included several distinct fungi, and treats the type-linked species as Lividopora vincta. This name history makes an old disease label an uncertain guide to the organism present today. Decayed corms alone cannot establish the species or show that a nearby wood-decay fungus caused the problem.

bromus-squarrosus.summary: Corn brome is an annual Eurasian grass found outside cultivation in fields, roadsides, and other disturbed places. Its relatively large, drooping flower clusters and outward-spreading bristles become most apparent as the seedhead matures. It can arrive with grain or other transported seed, which helps explain scattered occurrences away from established populations. Closely related bromes can look nearly identical, so records based only on a loose grass head deserve checking. Local abundance and behavior matter more than the common name: finding one Corn brome plant does not by itself establish a large invasive infestation.

ranunculus-arvensis.summary: Corn buttercup is a small annual buttercup of cultivated and disturbed ground. Its yellow flowers are familiar in outline, but the developing fruits provide a stronger clue: each has conspicuous spines. Leaves also change along the plant, from broader lower leaves to narrow divisions higher on the stems. It can occur as a crop or field weed outside its native range. Because several native and introduced buttercups share yellow flowers, a patch should be identified before broad removal. Corn buttercup's annual habit means preventing a new seed crop is a useful management goal.

anthemis-arvensis.summary: Corn chamomile is an annual, sometimes short-lived biennial, herb of fields, roadsides, and disturbed open ground. White outer flowers surround a yellow center, and the leaves are cut into many narrow segments. It resembles several plants called chamomile or mayweed, which makes the common name a poor basis for identification or use. The small dry fruits and the structures inside the flowerhead provide better evidence than the familiar daisy outline. Where it is an unwanted field or garden weed, recognizing plants before they shed seed makes removal more useful.

buglossoides-arvensis.summary: Corn gromwell is a small annual or winter annual herb with narrow leaves and tiny pale flowers. It often grows in fields, pastures, lawns, and other disturbed ground, where the modest blooms can be easy to overlook. The plant belongs to the borage family and develops small hard nutlets rather than a showy seed capsule. Older references call it Lithospermum arvense; that name is useful when following historical records. Its use in modern oilseed development does not make an unidentified roadside plant appropriate for eating or home remedies.

rhopalosiphum-maidis.summary: Corn leaf aphid is a small sap-feeding insect found on corn, sorghum, barley, and other grasses. Colonies can shelter inside developing leaves and around tassels, where sticky honeydew may become more obvious than the insects themselves. Heavy infestations can interfere with plant growth or pollination, and the aphid can transmit cereal viruses. Effects depend on the crop and conditions: UC IPM notes that direct damage in small grains is usually minor and treatment is seldom needed. Checking plant condition and natural enemies is more informative than reacting to every visible colony.

papaver-rhoeas.summary: Corn poppy is an annual flower associated with fields, gardens, and disturbed ground. Its thin red petals and dark center are familiar, but ornamental forms can vary in color and petal number. The plant reproduces by seed, with capsules developing after the brief flowers fall. Introduced occurrences may reflect old plantings or seed mixtures rather than a spreading ecological problem. Its annual life cycle makes seed management the practical focus where volunteers are unwanted. A patch of red poppies should still be identified, because several poppy species and cultivars can look alike in bloom.

veronica-arvensis.summary: Corn Speedwell is a low annual weed whose small blue flowers can appear among grass before taller spring plants draw attention. It often grows in lawns, fields, and disturbed edges, particularly where turf is thin. Plants commonly begin growth in the cool season, then flower and set seed as conditions warm. The lower and upper leaves differ in shape and arrangement, which helps distinguish it from other speedwells. Its presence is often a ground-cover or maintenance issue rather than evidence of serious habitat damage. Addressing repeated bare spots can matter as much as removing the visible plants.

spergula-arvensis.summary: Corn Spurry is an annual plant with narrow leaves clustered around its stems and small white flowers. It grows particularly well in disturbed, sandy ground and can become troublesome among crops when many plants form a dense cover. An introduction once grown as forage in North America, it now occurs in fields, roadsides, and cultivated places. Its small size can disguise how quickly it replaces itself: plants can flower and set seed within a single growing season, and buried seed can survive for a long time. Preventing fresh seed is more useful than judging a patch only by its height.

glebionis-segetum.summary: Corndaisy is a yellow-flowered annual associated with cultivated fields, disturbed ground, and occasional garden plantings. Both the outer ray flowers and the central disk are yellow, giving each flowerhead a single strong color. Its fleshy, often blue-green leaves vary from toothed to lobed, so different parts of one plant may look surprisingly different. The species is native around the Mediterranean and has spread beyond that range. An escaped plant may simply be a short-lived visitor, while repeated seedlings can become a crop or garden weed. Records under Chrysanthemum segetum refer to the same species under an older scientific name.

gladiolus-dalenii.summary: Cornflag is a perennial with upright, sword-shaped leaves and a tall stalk of red, orange, or yellow flowers. Each flower has a prominent upper hood, often above a contrasting yellow throat. The plant survives between growing seasons in a corm, a compact underground stem that stores reserves, and can produce smaller corms around it. Native to a broad part of Africa and extending into Arabia, it has long been cultivated and sometimes escapes gardens. It also contributed to garden gladiolus breeding, which makes a colorful roadside flower worth checking carefully before assigning it to this wild species.

lyctus-linearis.summary: Cosmopolitan powderpost beetle is a small beetle whose larvae develop inside dry hardwood. An infestation may first become visible as fine wood dust and tiny round exit holes in flooring, furniture, or stored timber. The adult beetles do little of this damage; the hidden larvae tunnel through suitable wood while feeding. This species has been recorded from a range of hardwoods, including oak, ash, and walnut. A hole in an old piece of furniture is not proof that beetles are still active, however. Other wood-boring beetles leave similar signs, and the insect itself is needed for a reliable species determination.

oxycarenus-hyalinipennis.summary: Cotton seed bug is a small, dark insect that gathers around the seeds of cotton and related plants such as hibiscus and okra. Adults have pale, translucent wings, while young bugs have reddish abdomens and no developed wings. Feeding can reduce cotton seed quality, and crushed bugs can stain cotton fibers during processing. The species can also hide on non-host plants, packing materials, and other objects between feeding periods. That ability makes transported plants and cargo important routes of spread. Finding a cluster on a garden plant is a reason to obtain an identification, especially where the insect has not previously been recorded.

pulvinaria-floccifera.summary: Cottony camellia scale is a sap-feeding insect found on camellias, hollies, yews, and numerous other woody plants. Its most noticeable sign is a white egg sac on the underside of a leaf, often with a small tan female at one end. Sticky honeydew and black sooty mold may draw attention before the insects themselves are noticed. Heavy, persistent populations can yellow foliage and reduce growth, but a few scales do not necessarily require treatment. Old egg sacs also remain after the female dies, so checking for living insects and newly hatched young is more useful than counting white patches alone.

icerya-purchasi.summary: Cottony cushion scale feeds on the sap of citrus and many ornamental shrubs and trees. The insect is best known for the long, white, ridged egg sac attached behind its orange-brown body. Large populations can weaken plants, while the sticky honeydew they release supports black sooty mold. Its history also includes a notable success in biological control: the vedalia beetle helped suppress severe citrus infestations after being introduced from Australia. Today, predators and parasitic flies can still keep populations low where they are established. Protecting those natural enemies is often more effective than reacting to every visible egg sac.

pulvinaria-vitis.summary: Cottony grape scale is a soft scale insect that spends part of its life on grape canes and part on leaves. Mature females produce conspicuous cottony egg masses, while younger stages can be easy to overlook against the bark. Their honeydew can attract ants and leave fruit or foliage coated with sooty mold. The significance of an infestation is not limited to direct feeding: this species can transmit certain grapevine leafroll viruses. A healthy vine with a few scales may tolerate their feeding, but scales near known virus infections deserve a different response. Accurate identification and the condition of neighboring vines both matter.

pulvinaria-elongata.summary: Cottony grass scale is an elongated soft scale associated especially with grasses, including sugarcane. Living adult females can be pinkish with two red lines running along the back, a feature reflected in the alternate name red-striped sugar-cane scale. Unlike scales with large, conspicuous white tails, this species produces only a short egg sac beneath and around its body. Published accounts describe it as a minor sugarcane pest in many circumstances. More serious sugarcane damage has been reported in colonies associated with the tawny crazy ant, Nylanderia fulva. Its presence on a plant should therefore prompt a check of the population and damage, rather than an assumption of severe harm.

pulvinariella-mesembryanthemi.summary: Cottony pigface scale feeds on the fleshy leaves of iceplants and related succulents. Young adult females are greenish, then become reddish brown as they mature and produce a white egg sac. On a dense groundcover, infestations may be hidden among growing tips before damaged patches become obvious. Historical outbreaks affected iceplant plantings, and natural enemies introduced in a coordinated biological control program helped reduce them. The name Pulvinariella mesembryanthemi appears in older studies, while current taxonomic catalogs place the same insect in Pulvinaria. This name change does not make every cottony scale on an iceplant this species.

ficus-altissima.summary: Council tree is a large evergreen fig with broad, glossy leaves and pale gray bark. It can begin life on another tree or a stone surface, then develop roots that reach the ground and support a substantial trunk. Small yellow to orange figs enclose its flowers, as in other members of the fig family. Native to tropical Asia, it is planted for shade and as an ornamental, but has escaped in some warm regions. Its effects depend on local conditions: Florida assessments identify concern in the south, while the presence of a cultivated tree elsewhere does not establish the same ecological risk.

cenchrus-setiger.summary: Cow sandbur is a tufted perennial grass adapted to hot, dry conditions. Its short, dense seedheads contain small burrlike units rather than the long, spreading spines familiar from some other sandburs. It has been used as forage in dry regions because established plants withstand drought and grazing, yet it can also spread beyond plantings and become a weed in suitable environments. Rain can prompt rapid growth and seed production. You may also find it under the scientific name Cenchrus setigerus; that different ending does not mean it is a separate grass.

vaccaria-hispanica.summary: Cow soapwort is an annual with smooth, blue-green foliage and small pink flowers on branching stems. The green cup around each flower has five pronounced ridges, giving it an angular, almost inflated appearance that remains useful for identification after the petals fall. Native to Europe and neighboring regions, the plant occurs as an introduced weed in cultivated and disturbed ground in North America. It is also grown ornamentally, so a few plants may mark a past planting rather than a spreading infestation. Its life cycle centers on seed, making mature capsules and returning seedlings the main things to watch.

striga-gesnerioides.summary: Cowpea witchweed is a small parasitic plant that attaches to another plant's roots and draws resources from it. Its own leaves are reduced to tiny scales, and clusters of short flowering stems may be the first visible sign above ground. Different forms use different broadleaf hosts, including cowpea and several wild or introduced legumes. This host specialization matters: damage documented on cowpea elsewhere should not automatically be assigned to every population. Florida records include plants associated with hairy indigo and alyce clover. A suspected new occurrence deserves expert attention because tiny seeds and an underground phase make casual removal an incomplete response.

salix-x-fragilis.summary: Crack willow is a large deciduous willow associated with moist ground, riverbanks, and planted landscapes. The multiplication sign in Salix x fragilis identifies the hybrid between white willow and the willow treated as Salix euxina in current regional floras. Its branches can break at their bases, and detached pieces may root on wet ground. That allows a tree to spread along waterways without relying on seed. Older sources have used the name crack willow for different parts of this willow group, so records and management advice need to be checked against the hybrid concept rather than matched by common name alone.

duponchelia-fovealis.summary: This Crambid moth, Duponchelia fovealis, is widely known as European pepper moth. Its caterpillars feed on many kinds of plants, including bedding ornamentals and vegetables, and can hide near the soil surface, among damp debris, or inside damaged stems. A greenhouse plant may therefore decline before the feeding caterpillar is noticed. Adults are small brown moths with pale curved lines across the wings. Although peppers are one host, the common name should not narrow an inspection to that crop. The species can also use decaying plant material, making sanitation and careful inspection of incoming plants important parts of nursery management.

lamprosema-charesalis.summary: This Crambid moth is recorded in current North American sources as Nacoleia charesalis; Lamprosema charesalis is an older combination for the same named species. It is a small brown moth native to the Asian and Australasian tropics and first detected in Florida in 2012. Caterpillars feed in decaying vegetation and have also been recorded boring into turmeric stems in their native range. Those habits do not establish that every adult near a garden is causing damage. The insect resembles several other crambids, including a related banana pest, so an identification should come before conclusions about affected plants.

lagerstroemia-indica.summary: Crapemyrtle is a deciduous shrub or small tree familiar for summer clusters of crinkled flowers and bark that peels to reveal smooth patches beneath. Cultivars range widely in height and flower color, from compact garden shrubs to small shade trees. The species comes from Asia and has been planted extensively beyond its native range. It sometimes persists or produces volunteers near old plantings, but introduced status alone does not make it a damaging invader. Regional assessments describe it as a limited escape in some areas. Many modern landscape plants are hybrids, so a familiar garden appearance does not always establish pure Lagerstroemia indica.

narcissus-tazetta.summary: Cream narcissus is a bulb-forming perennial that produces clusters of fragrant flowers above upright, strap-shaped leaves. A short yellow or orange cup sits in the center of each flower, usually surrounded by pale outer segments. The bulbs can survive for years at old home sites and garden edges, making a spring clump a possible trace of former cultivation. This species is widely grown and sometimes naturalizes, but persistence alone is not evidence of aggressive spread. Names used for cultivated narcissus can be loose: some plants called paperwhites belong to another species, while garden hybrids further complicate identification.

lepidium-campestre.summary: Cream-anther field pepperwort is a small mustard-family plant that often begins as a low rosette, then sends up flowering stems in spring. Its tiny pale flowers give way to crowded, oval seedpods that are easier to notice than the blossoms. The stems and leaves carry short hairs, and upper leaves clasp the stem with pointed bases. Native to Europe and western Asia, it is introduced in North America and occurs in disturbed ground, gardens, orchards, and fields. It reproduces by seed and may behave as an annual or biennial, so preventing mature pods is the central task where it is unwanted.

agrostis-stolonifera.summary: Creeping Bentgrass forms low, fine-leaved patches linked by stems that travel across the soil surface. Each rooted joint can extend the patch, which explains why pulling a few blades seldom removes it. This perennial is cultivated for turf but also occupies disturbed ground and damp margins. It tolerates a wider range of soils than its association with wet lawns suggests. Its presence alone does not show that a natural area is being damaged; the practical concern is whether the patch is expanding into vegetation that the landowner wants to retain.

ranunculus-repens.summary: Creeping Buttercup is a perennial of damp lawns, pasture edges, and other moist ground. Its yellow flowers rise above spreading leaves, while runners put down roots at their joints and create new plants. Seed adds another route of spread. A patch can therefore persist even when its flowers are cut off. It is especially noticeable in spring and early summer, when flowering makes scattered plants easier to find. Dense patches can crowd thin turf. In grazing areas, identification matters because fresh buttercup material can be harmful to livestock.

potentilla-reptans.summary: Creeping cinquefoil is a low perennial that spreads through long, slender runners. Where each runner roots, another leafy plant can establish, allowing a small patch to stretch through grass or a garden bed. Its yellow flowers open in bright weather and close at night or in dull conditions. Native across parts of Europe and Asia, it has been introduced to North America. It can be unwelcome where it displaces desired planting, but it is also valued in wildlife gardens within its native range. An introduced record alone does not establish local ecological damage.

euchiton-gymnocephalus.summary: Creeping cudweed, treated here in the broad Euchiton japonicus complex that includes the historical gymnocephalus names, is a small perennial with a basal rosette and clusters of tiny flowerheads above the leaves. Plants described under the closely associated name Euchiton japonicus spread by runners, with green upper leaf surfaces and pale, densely hairy undersides. The name Euchiton gymnocephalus has been used in different ways, so observations carrying that name need careful checking. Several cudweeds share a low, leafy habit and inconspicuous flowers. A useful record includes a complete plant, its connections to neighboring shoots, and mature flowerheads, rather than only a close photograph of the pale underside of one leaf.

callisia-repens.summary: Creeping inchplant forms low mats of small, fleshy leaves on branching stems that trail over pot rims or creep across soil. A stem joint can take root where it touches damp ground, making loose trimmings a ready source of new plants. Its tiny white flowers are easy to overlook among the leaves. This tropical American plant is widely grown in hanging baskets and warm gardens. Escape is a regional concern: Florida's assessment calls for preventing its spread from cultivation in central and southern parts of the state.

indigofera-spicata.summary: Creeping indigo is a low perennial with small compound leaves, reddish flowers and narrow pods that point downward. Its stems can lie among pasture grasses, making a scattered plant easy to miss. It grows from a persistent woody base and occurs in open, disturbed ground. Authenticated plants have caused serious poisoning in grazing ponies, so suspected patches deserve prompt attention around horses. A closely related species, Indigofera hendecaphylla, shares the common name and was included in many older records. The distinction matters for identification, even though both deserve caution around grazing animals.

liriope-spicata.summary: Creeping liriope resembles a small ornamental grass, but it belongs to the asparagus family. It was planted widely as a durable groundcover and spreads through underground stems that connect neighboring shoots. In suitable conditions those connections build dense patches and carry the plant into adjacent beds or woodland. Pale summer flowers are followed by dark, rounded fruits. The same spreading habit that fills a landscape bed can make an escaped patch difficult to remove. A border planting should therefore be assessed by its expansion beyond the intended area, especially near natural vegetation.

alopecurus-arundinaceus.summary: Creeping meadow foxtail is a long-lived pasture grass that forms thick sod on wet ground. Underground stems spread outward, and its light seeds travel with water or wind. It supplies forage on sites too wet for many other pasture grasses, but can escape into waterways and wetlands. In an Idaho wet meadow, researchers linked greater cover of the Garrison cultivar with lower survival of native common camas, particularly in wetter areas during some years. That finding concerns one cultivar and study site. A landowner's practical question is whether a forage stand is expanding into neighboring vegetation.

holcus-mollis.summary: Creeping velvetgrass is a perennial grass with soft leaves and pale flowerheads. Beneath the surface, spreading stems connect shoots and help the plant occupy moist disturbed ground. Flora of North America records it as a European introduction and describes problems in some ungrazed pastures, prairie remnants, and oak savannas of the Pacific Northwest. That regional evidence should not be stretched into a claim of equal harm everywhere it occurs. Its close resemblance to common velvetgrass makes checking the lower stem and underground growth more useful than judging a patch by its softness.

rorippa-sylvestris.summary: Creeping yellowcress is a yellow-flowered perennial that can arrive in a garden hidden among the roots of purchased plants. Its white, fleshy roots spread sideways and produce fresh shoots; even small broken pieces can start again. This makes an apparently simple weeding job surprisingly persistent. It occurs on damp disturbed ground as well as in nursery and garden settings. Hostas and daylilies are documented pathways for root fragments. Prevention starts with checking incoming plants, because moving an infested root ball may carry the problem to a new bed before any flowers appear.

elsholtzia-ciliata.summary: Crested latesummer mint is an annual herb introduced from Asia. It appears in yards, roadsides, railroad margins, and other disturbed places, where its short purple flower spikes provide a useful identification clue. Unlike a perennial mint patch that returns from surviving roots, an annual population depends on a new generation of plants. Native Plant Trust notes that this species can become invasive, but a scattered garden occurrence does not establish the size of its local impact. Watch whether it keeps producing seedlings and moves from disturbed ground into neighboring vegetation.

barleria-cristata.summary: Crested philippine violet is an upright shrub with dark green leaves and funnel-shaped flowers, usually lavender or purple but sometimes white. Leaves grow in opposite pairs, and their deeply marked veins can give them a puckered surface. Small, stiff points on the green parts surrounding each flower are useful identification clues. The plant is native to Asia and grown in warm gardens for its late-season flowers. It can produce many seedlings around an established planting. Watching those seedlings makes it easier to keep a garden clump within its intended space.

agropyron-cristatum.summary: Crested wheatgrass is a cool-season perennial introduced from Eurasia for forage and land rehabilitation. Its drought and cold tolerance helped make it a familiar grass in planted western rangelands. The name also covers a complicated group of related cultivated grasses in older literature, and commercial hybrids add to that difficulty. The exact species in this entry, Agropyron cristatum, is often called the fairway type. Its value in a pasture does not establish its suitability for restoring native plant communities. Management should distinguish a maintained forage stand from unwanted expansion beyond it.

pteris-cretica.summary: Cretan brake is a fern with a few long leaf divisions spreading from each central stalk. Its open shape is quite different from the finely divided fronds of many familiar garden ferns. New fronds arise from a short, creeping underground stem, and fertile fronds carry spores along their leaf margins. It is widely cultivated and has escaped in warm regions, including parts of the United States. Several related ferns share its general shape, and nursery names can be misleading. Checking how the upper leaf divisions join the central stalk is especially useful.

metaltella-simoni.summary: Cribellate spider, Metaltella simoni, is a small South American spider established in parts of the southern United States. Females and young spiders make tangled silk retreats beneath bark, boards, logs, and other sheltered surfaces; males may be found wandering. It also occurs around buildings and ornamental plants. A Florida account raised concern about possible competition with a native spider, but did not demonstrate a measured displacement trend. That distinction matters: encountering this introduced spider is useful distribution information, not by itself proof of ecological damage or a reason for broad spraying.

callistemon-citrinus.summary: Crimson bottlebrush is an Australian evergreen shrub or small tree with bright red flower clusters shaped like bottle-cleaning brushes. Their showy parts are long stamens, and the narrow leaves have a lemon scent when bruised. Woody seed capsules can stay closed on branches for years, then release seed after branches are cut. Many garden forms have been selected, and some are hybrids. The name Melaleuca citrina refers to the same species in sources that place bottlebrushes in Melaleuca. Florida's university assessment rates it a high invasion risk; that prediction should not be mistaken for measured damage at every planting.

trifolium-incarnatum.summary: Crimson clover is a cool-season annual often planted as a cover crop, forage, or flowering groundcover. Its upright red flowerheads are much more elongated than the rounded heads many people picture when they think of clover. Like other legumes, it can contribute to soil fertility through its association with nitrogen-fixing bacteria. It also protects bare ground while growing. Some cultivars readily reseed, allowing plants to persist beyond a planned sowing. Its agricultural usefulness and its potential to become weedy both deserve mention; an introduced clover is not necessarily causing ecological damage wherever it occurs.

cenchrus-setaceus.summary: Crimson fountaingrass forms upright clumps topped by long, bristly flowerheads. It was introduced as an ornamental and has escaped into dry landscapes, including parts of the southwestern United States. Dry foliage can carry fire, and repeated burning can favor the grass rather than eliminate it. Seeds are its main natural means of spread and can move on wind, water, animals, clothing, or vehicles. The common name is also used loosely in horticulture, so a reddish nursery grass should not automatically be assigned to this species without checking its botanical identity.

chorispora-tenella.summary: Crossflower is a small mustard with pale purple flowers and a strong, often unpleasant odor. It commonly begins as a low rosette in fall, then branches and flowers early the next spring. This timing lets it produce seed before a neglected bare patch receives much attention. Its narrow pods break into short seed-bearing sections, helping carry the next generation into new ground. It is a weed of disturbed dry sites and cultivated land in western North America. The same plant is frequently described by extension services as blue mustard or purple mustard.

allium-vineale.summary: Crow Garlic often first announces itself when a mower releases an onionlike smell from its leaves. It is a cool-season perennial that grows from bulbs, with foliage appearing in fall and dying back after flowering as summer temperatures rise. Aboveground, the flowering stalk may carry a cluster of tiny bulbs instead of many flowers. Underground bulb offsets add another means of persistence. This combination explains why a lawn patch can disappear for summer and then return. It is a common introduced weed of disturbed ground, but native onions must be distinguished before removal.

matricaria-chamomilla.summary: Crown mayweed is the annual herb more often sold as German chamomile. Slender, divided leaves surround branching stems topped by white-and-yellow flowerheads. The raised yellow center becomes especially noticeable as a head matures. Plants grow readily from seed, and spent flowers can produce another generation in nearby bare ground. It is cultivated for flowers and fragrance and also occurs along roadsides and in fields and meadows. Its ability to reseed makes it a garden weed in some settings; the practical concern is whether seedlings are spreading into spaces where other plants are wanted, rather than the mere presence of a cultivated herb.

securigera-varia.summary: Crown Vetch is a spreading perennial legume once planted extensively to cover road banks and other exposed ground. Its pink-and-white flower clusters rise above trailing stems and many small leaflets. Underground stems help a colony expand, while persistent seed creates a longer-term source of new plants. Dense growth can shade neighboring vegetation and spread into grasslands, forest edges, and other open habitats. Despite its name, it is not a true vetch and has no climbing tendrils. Its old use for erosion control means removal on a slope should include a plan to maintain soil cover.

phyllotreta-cruciferae.summary: Crucifer flea beetle is a tiny, dark beetle that chews small holes through cabbage-family crops. Newly planted seedlings are particularly vulnerable because a little feeding can remove much of their leaf area. Adults leap when disturbed and also fly between food plants. Their larvae develop belowground, while adults cause the familiar scattered holes in leaves. Broccoli, cabbage, kale, arugula, radish, and related crops can all be affected. The species is introduced in North America, but gardeners usually encounter it as a crop pest requiring early protection and close monitoring rather than an eradication campaign.

aspidiotus-cryptomeriae.summary: Cryptomeria scale is an armored scale insect that lives beneath the needles of several conifers. Its small protective cover makes an infestation easy to overlook until the upper needle surfaces become yellow and mottled. Heavy feeding can lead to needle loss and weakened branches, with particular concern in nurseries and Christmas-tree plantings. The insect does not roam about once the female has settled; the tiny newly hatched stage, called a crawler, moves to new feeding sites. Old covers can remain after insects die, so visible scales do not automatically mean a tree needs another treatment.

osteopilus-septentrionalis.summary: Cuban treefrog is a large Caribbean treefrog that has established populations in parts of the southeastern United States. It climbs plants and buildings using broad toe pads and often shelters in tight spaces during the day. Adults eat insects and other small animals, including native frogs. Warm rains stimulate breeding, and even water held in a bucket or other artificial container can serve as a nursery. Plants, vehicles, and boats can accidentally carry frogs to new places. Its changing color makes identification less simple than matching a photograph of one green or brown individual.

monopterus-cuchia.summary: Cuchia swamp eel is an air-breathing freshwater fish native to southern Asia. Its long, brown body resembles an eel, but it belongs to a different fish family and lacks the paired fins of a true eel. It shelters in muddy water and burrows, feeding on small aquatic animals. Live-food imports have provided a pathway into the United States, where established populations have been documented. Recent sources use the name Ophichthys cuchia. Its ability to survive difficult water conditions makes preventing releases important, although the effects of introduced populations remain incompletely studied.

diaphania-indica.summary: Cucumber moth is a warm-climate moth whose caterpillars feed on cucumbers, melons, squash, pumpkins, and related crops. Young larvae scrape leaf tissue; larger ones shelter in folded leaves and may damage flowers or enter fruit. That hidden feeding can make a small caterpillar more consequential than the adult moth first suggests. The species originated in southern Asia and now occurs across many tropical and subtropical regions, including Florida. Infested plants and produce can transport immature stages. Its presence matters most in cucurbit plantings, where watching tender growth and folded leaves can reveal trouble before fruit damage becomes obvious.

allium-sativum.summary: Cultivated garlic is the familiar bulb crop grown for its strongly flavored cloves. It is a perennial plant, although gardeners normally harvest it after one growing season. Each bulb contains several cloves, and an overlooked clove can produce another plant. Hardneck types also make a flowering stem that may carry small bulbs; softneck types usually do not. Garlic can persist around old gardens or appear in moved soil, but a volunteer plant is not by itself evidence of ecological damage. Where it is unwanted, understanding how cloves survive is more useful than simply cutting the leaves.
