persicaria-wallichii.summary: Cultivated knotweed is a large perennial also widely called Himalayan or garden knotweed. Long pointed leaves and pinkish flower clusters give it a different appearance from the broad-leaved Japanese knotweed relatives. Beneath the surface, spreading underground stems allow a clump to expand and return after the tops die back. It has escaped ornamental plantings into roadsides, wet ground, and stream corridors, where dense stands can displace other vegetation. Small pieces moved in soil, floodwater, or garden debris can start new plants. That ability makes preventing fragment movement an essential part of any removal effort.

raphanus-sativus.summary: Cultivated radish is an annual or biennial vegetable grown in many forms, from small red garden radishes to long white roots and crops harvested for leaves or pods. Plants that escape harvest can send up branching flower stems and set seed along garden edges, roadsides, and disturbed ground. The thick edible root varies greatly among cultivars, so an escaped plant may look unlike a supermarket radish. It is widely recorded outside cultivation in North America. Whether it needs attention depends on where it is growing and whether it is reproducing beyond the intended planting.

nicotiana-tabacum.summary: Cultivated tobacco is a large-leaved member of the nightshade family grown around the world for its leaves. In gardens it may also be kept for its clusters of tubular flowers. It usually behaves as an annual in colder climates, while plants can persist longer where winters are mild. Capsules produce numerous tiny seeds, allowing volunteers to appear near previous plantings. A cultivated or escaped tobacco plant is not automatically an invasive stand. Its more immediate household concern is its poisonous foliage, which should be kept away from children, pets, and grazing animals.

eragrostis-cumingii.summary: Cuming's lovegrass is a small, tuft-forming grass native across parts of Asia and Australia and recorded as a weed in Florida. It grows in open or lightly shaded disturbed places, including lawns, roadsides, and fields. Fine leaves and branched seedheads give it an inconspicuous appearance among other small grasses. It is usually annual, although botanical treatments also describe longer-lived plants. Its many small flower clusters eventually break apart to release seed. A few plants in a lawn and an expanding patch in a natural area present different management questions, so note the setting and extent when recording an occurrence.

rumex-crispus.summary: Curly Dock is a perennial of pastures, roadsides, gardens, and other disturbed ground. Its long leaves form a low cluster before a tall flower stalk rises above them. Green flowers develop into conspicuous reddish-brown seed clusters that often remain standing after surrounding plants have faded. A substantial taproot lets an established plant return after mowing. Wet ground and excess irrigation can favor it, so repeated top removal may leave the underlying conditions unchanged. In agricultural settings it can compete with desirable plants; in cherry orchards it also hosts a leafhopper involved in spreading X-disease.

carduus-crispus.summary: Curly plumeless thistle is a Eurasian thistle found in disturbed ground, pastures, roadsides, and fields. It grows as an annual or biennial, producing purple flower heads above spiny stems and leaves. The name is easy to confuse with the much more frequently reported spiny plumeless thistle, Carduus acanthoides. Botanical authorities caution that some North American records of curly plumeless thistle may belong to that other species. A careful identification therefore matters more than assuming that any small-headed, wing-stemmed thistle is this one. Preventing seed production is a reasonable first aim where a confirmed plant is unwanted.

potamogeton-crispus.summary: Curly-Leaf Pondweed is a rooted underwater plant with leaves that resemble narrow, rippled ribbons. It often starts growing earlier than many native pondweeds and can form dense growth near the water surface in spring. As summer advances, it makes hard resting buds and often dies back. Those buds remain in the sediment and produce later growth, so a summer disappearance does not mean the population has been eliminated. Dense stands may hinder boating or swimming and alter nutrient cycling, although their effects vary among waterbodies. In some degraded waters, the plant also provides habitat that would otherwise be scarce.

agrilus-ribesi.summary: Currant stem girdler is a small metallic beetle whose larvae develop inside currant and gooseberry stems. Feeding tunnels interfere with water movement, causing affected shoots to wilt, weaken, and dry. Repeated attacks can seriously damage a shrub. The beetle is native to Eurasia and was recognized in North America only after specimens previously assigned to a similar species were reexamined. Its scientific name matters: gardening references also use currant stem girdler for the unrelated sawfly Janus integer. A wilted currant shoot therefore provides a reason to investigate, but does not by itself identify Agrilus ribesi.

macrohomotoma-gladiata.summary: Curtain fig psillid is a tiny sap-feeding insect of ornamental curtain fig, Ficus microcarpa. Colonies gather around tender new shoots, where feeding curls leaves and can stop normal shoot development. White, wool-like wax around the growing tips is often noticed before the insects themselves. Sticky honeydew can also support dark sooty mold on nearby foliage. Native to Asia, this psyllid has established outside its original range, including California and Hawaii. Infested nursery plants provide a practical reason to inspect new figs carefully. The host identity is important because other fig-feeding insects create somewhat similar symptoms.

rubus-laciniatus.summary: Cutleaf blackberry is a vigorous bramble recognized by leaflets cut into narrow, jagged lobes. Its long, arching canes can build dense thickets, and tips that touch the ground may root into new plants. Birds and other animals also spread seeds after eating the fruit. The plant has escaped cultivation in North America and is particularly troublesome in parts of the Pacific Northwest, where it can overtop streamside vegetation. Its black fruit is familiar, but the deeply divided leaves distinguish it from many other blackberries. Removing visible canes alone leaves a substantial root crown capable of sending up replacements.

geranium-dissectum.summary: Cutleaf geranium is a small annual or biennial with hairy stems, finely divided leaves, and modest pink flowers. It grows in disturbed grasslands, gardens, roadsides, orchards, and open woodland. After flowering, its pointed fruits split and scatter seeds nearby; some seeds can remain viable in soil for years. That persistence helps explain why seedlings may return after an apparently thorough cleanup. Introduced from Europe, it is widespread but generally described as a minor wildland weed rather than a uniformly severe invader. In dense local patches it can still compete with smaller plants and complicate restoration or garden maintenance.

dipsacus-laciniatus.summary: Cutleaf Teasel spends at least one season as a low cluster of leaves before sending up a tall, prickly flowering stalk. It flowers once and dies, leaving stiff seedheads that can remain conspicuous through winter. The heads contain many seeds, and moving them in dried arrangements or mowing mature stands can spread the plant. Introduced from Eurasia, it can form colonies in roadsides, fields, prairies, and other open habitats. Its large leaves shade the ground, giving later seedlings space around the dying parent. Preventing seed production and removing young plants are central to limiting a patch.

scorzonera-laciniata.summary: Cutleaf vipergrass is a taprooted herb with yellow flower heads and leaves that often divide into narrow, fingerlike lobes. Native to parts of Europe, Asia, and the Canary Islands, it has become established in disturbed ground in several western and central states. It usually lives for one or two growing seasons, although some plants persist longer before flowering. The flower heads open above a low rosette, then develop conspicuous tufts that carry the seeds. Its presence in a field or roadside does not by itself establish that it is causing ecological damage; the size and spread of the patch matter.

hypena-subidalis.summary: Cutworm moth, Hypena subidalis, is a moth placed in the family Erebidae. The original 1991 report documents specimens from Long Key and Bahia Honda in the Florida Keys; Mississippi State University's resource illustrates museum and specialist specimens. Older scientific names include Hypena pilosalis and Hypena triangularis. The broad name "cutworm" should not be taken as evidence that this particular species is damaging a lawn or crop. A moth seen near a damaged plant may simply be resting there; connecting an adult moth to feeding damage requires identification of the larvae and evidence from the affected plant.

aspidiotus-excisus.summary: Cyanotis scale is a tiny armored scale insect associated with many kinds of plants, including ornamental Aglaonema, Hoya, and palms. It was described from Cyanotis in Sri Lanka, which explains its common name; it is not restricted to that host. The insect lives beneath a thin, pale cover that can be mistaken for a small blemish or bit of debris. Moving infested plants can carry scales into new collections. Because several armored scales look very similar on a leaf, a photograph may establish that a plant has scale insects without establishing that they are Cyanotis scale.

aulacaspis-yasumatsui.summary: Cycad aulacaspis scale is an armored scale insect that can seriously injure cycads, including the plants often sold as sago palms. These plants are cycads rather than true palms. Dense infestations form a white crust on leaves, while feeding causes yellowing, browning, and eventual leaf death. The scale can also occupy stems and roots, where it is easily missed during an inspection. Native to Thailand, it was detected in Florida in 1996 and has spread through the movement of infested plants. White covers can remain after the insects die, so a white leaf is not by itself a measure of how many living scales remain.

cyclaneusma-minus.summary: Cyclaneusma needle cast is a fungal disease of pines that causes older needles to yellow and fall prematurely. The fungus Cyclaneusma minus affects several pine species, including Scots and Austrian pine. Repeated infection can leave a tree carrying mainly its youngest needles, giving the crown a thin appearance. Spores are released from infected needles still on the tree and from fallen needles, and spread with wind and rain. Symptoms may appear well after infection, making the timing confusing. Normal autumn shedding also removes older pine needles, so yellowing alone is not enough to diagnose this disease.

megacyclops-viridis.summary: Cyclopoid copepod, Megacyclops viridis, is a very small freshwater crustacean often found among aquatic plants near shore. It feeds on a range of microscopic organisms and small animals, including mosquito larvae, and is itself food for fish. Records from the Great Lakes have prompted discussion about whether it arrived in ship ballast water or was overlooked as part of a wider northern distribution. Its environmental effects there remain insufficiently understood. This is an animal for careful microscopic study, not something a pond owner can reliably recognize as a moving speck in the water.

euphorbia-cyparissias.summary: Cypress Spurge forms low colonies of upright stems clothed in soft, narrow leaves that resemble miniature conifer branches. Yellow-green floral leaves brighten the stem tips in spring and may turn reddish as they age. This perennial was brought from Europe and nearby western Asia as an ornamental, including for cemetery plantings. It can spread through underground growth and, in fertile populations, seed, allowing a small planting to expand into nearby fields or open ground. Its milky sap irritates skin and eyes, and livestock should not eat it. Established colonies can be difficult to remove because shoots return from surviving underground parts.

ipomoea-quamoclit.summary: Cypressvine is a fast-growing annual climber with finely divided green leaves and small scarlet flowers. Its slender stems twine around nearby supports, making it a familiar garden vine on fences and trellises. Hummingbirds and butterflies visit the tubular flowers, which can continue from early summer until frost. Native to tropical America, it has become naturalized beyond gardens in some parts of the United States. An annual vine can still be persistent in a planting: dry capsules release seeds that produce a new generation the following year. Whether it needs control depends on where it is growing and how readily it escapes the intended space.

erigeron-sumatrensis.summary: Daisy (Erigeron sumatrensis) is a tall fleabane with many small flower heads rather than a few large, showy daisies. A leafy stem grows upward before branching into a broad cluster of heads, which later release seeds with fine bristles. Native to Mexico and tropical parts of the Americas, the species has become established in many other regions. It occurs in California and parts of the southeastern United States, where older records sometimes used the names of other fleabanes. It is especially associated with disturbed ground, cultivated places, and roadsides. Confirming its identity matters because several close relatives share the same general appearance.

glebionis-coronaria.summary: Daisy (Glebionis coronaria) is an upright annual with deeply divided leaves and yellow-centered flower heads. Often called crown daisy or garland chrysanthemum, it has been grown as both an ornamental and a leafy vegetable. Plants can escape cultivation into disturbed ground. In parts of coastal California, dense stands occupy dunes, scrub, and streamside habitats and can interfere with the return of native vegetation. That regional experience does not mean every cultivated plant has the same effect. The flowers may be entirely yellow or have white tips, depending on the form and the taxonomic treatment used.

hedypnois-rhagadioloides.summary: Daisy is a small Mediterranean annual with yellow flower heads and a loose rosette of toothed or lobed leaves. The very broad common name can be misleading: this plant belongs to the dandelion-like part of the daisy family, and its heads contain only strap-shaped flowers. It grows in disturbed ground, field margins, and open grassland. As the heads mature, the surrounding bracts harden and curve around some of the fruits. This unusual fruit arrangement offers a much better identification clue than flower color alone.

paspalum-dilatatum.summary: Dallisgrass is a coarse perennial grass that grows in expanding clumps, often standing above the surrounding lawn. Introduced from South America for forage, it also establishes along wet roadsides, ditch banks, and other managed ground. Short underground stems allow an established clump to survive from year to year, while abundant seed helps it reach new sites. In turf, the hard, uneven clumps can interfere with walking and mowing. Its seed heads can also carry an ergot fungus that makes affected material hazardous to livestock.

linaria-dalmatica.summary: Dalmatian Toadflax has yellow snapdragon-like flowers above broad, waxy leaves that clasp its upright stems. This perennial was grown as an ornamental before spreading into roadsides, rangeland, and other open habitats. A patch can expand through an extensive root system as well as by seed, so removing the flowers does not remove the plant. Disturbed or sparsely vegetated ground gives seedlings an opening. Established stands can displace other vegetation, making early detection and protection of healthy surrounding plant cover especially useful.

syzygium-nervosum.summary: Daly river satinash is a tropical tree with glossy, aromatic leaves and clusters of small fruits that become purple to black. It is native across parts of tropical Asia and northern Australia, where it occurs in forests and near freshwater wetlands and streams. Its flower clusters form on older twigs below the leaves, giving the branches a distinctive appearance in bloom. The tree can become substantial, so an escaped seedling and a mature planted specimen present very different management questions. Its presence alone does not establish that it is causing ecological damage.

rosa-x-damascena.summary: Damask rose is an old garden hybrid valued for strongly fragrant flowers, usually in shades of pink. Its prickly, open-growing branches and gray-green foliage give it a less compact appearance than many modern bedding roses. Most traditional forms flower in spring or early summer, while Autumn Damask forms can bloom again. Some cultivars have a long history in perfume production. A rose persisting beside an old homesite may be a remnant planting rather than a newly spreading population, and flower color alone cannot establish which old garden rose is present.

plutella-porrectella.summary: Dame's rocket moth is a small, slender moth whose caterpillars feed on dame's rocket and related host plants. The larvae can curl or join leaves with silk, and the moth's pale, streaked wings make it easy to overlook when resting on vegetation. It resembles the better-known Diamondback moth, but the two should not be assigned the same crop-pest behavior simply because they look alike. Research in Ontario found two generations in a year and young larvae surviving winter inside the host plant's growing tips.

hesperis-matronalis.summary: Dames rocket is a biennial or short-lived perennial with fragrant clusters of white, pink, or purple flowers. It was brought into gardens from Europe and can spread into woodland edges, roadsides, and open ground through plentiful seed. First-year plants form a leafy rosette; flowering stems rise in a later season. The blossoms attract insects, but the plant can still crowd other vegetation where it escapes. It is often mistaken for native phlox, a confusion that can lead to both accidental planting and removal of the wrong flower.

campanula-glomerata.summary: Dane's blood is a perennial bellflower with tight clusters of upward-facing purple, blue, or sometimes white blooms. The flowers sit together at the top of an upright stem, explaining its more familiar name, clustered bellflower. Native to Europe and parts of temperate Asia, it is widely cultivated in borders and can form expanding clumps through underground stems. Cultivars differ in height and flower color. A garden clump is not automatically a harmful invasion, but seedlings or expanding growth beyond a planting are worth tracking near sensitive habitat.

brachymyrmex-patagonicus.summary: Dark rover ant is a tiny brown ant that can nest outdoors and enter buildings as workers or winged adults. It feeds on sweet resources such as nectar and honeydew, and may appear around kitchens, bathrooms, irrigated landscaping, and other moist places. Its small size makes it easy to confuse with several other household ants. Infestations can persist because nearby nests or separated parts of a colony may supply more ants after treatment. The main documented household concern is nuisance activity, rather than the conspicuous stings associated with fire ants.

lolium-temulentum.summary: Darnel ryegrass is an annual grass historically associated with cereal crops and contaminated planting seed. Its upright seed spike can blend into a grain field, and its seeds were once difficult to separate from harvested wheat. Some seed lots carry fungi associated with toxicity, so suspected contamination belongs in a grain or forage assessment rather than a home food experiment. Modern seed cleaning has greatly reduced the plant in some regions. Occasional plants in disturbed ground should therefore be documented without assuming that an old account of severe crop infestation describes local conditions today.

berberis-darwinii.summary: Darwin's berberis is an evergreen shrub with small, glossy, spiny leaves and hanging clusters of orange-yellow flowers. Purple to nearly black berries follow the flowers and can carry its seeds beyond a hedge or garden when birds eat them. Native to Chile and Argentina, it has formed dense colonies in some regions where it was introduced. The combination of sharp spines, shade tolerance, and regrowth after damage can make established patches difficult to manage. Its attractive flowers therefore need to be considered alongside any observed spread into surrounding vegetation.

phoenix-dactylifera.summary: Date palm is the familiar cultivated palm that produces dates. Its crown of long, blue-gray feather-shaped leaves can rise high above a stout trunk, while shoots from the base sometimes form a clump. Male and female flowers occur on separate plants, so only female palms produce fruit. Cultivated for thousands of years in hot, dry regions, it is also planted ornamentally. Seedlings or basal shoots may need attention where they spread beyond a maintained planting, but the presence of a crop or landscape palm alone does not establish ecological harm.

cestrum-diurnum.summary: Day jessamine is an evergreen shrub with glossy leaves and clusters of small, fragrant white flowers. Despite its name, flower scent is not a dependable identification test: accounts differ on when it is strongest. Its dark berries are more useful, and birds can spread their seeds away from planted shrubs. The plant has escaped cultivation and formed thickets in warm regions, including parts of Florida. The berries are poisonous to people and other mammals, so a fragrant garden shrub should not be treated as a source of edible fruit.

contarinia-quinquenotata.summary: Daylily gall midge is a tiny fly whose larvae develop inside unopened daylily flower buds. Affected buds become unusually short and swollen, then fail to open or rot, while the leaves may remain normal. The damage is chiefly a loss of flowers rather than a decline in the whole plant. Early-flowering varieties are more exposed because their buds coincide with the fly's activity. Mature larvae leave the buds and enter the soil, where they survive until the next season, making prompt removal of affected buds especially useful.

codium-fragile-ssp-fragile.summary: Dead man's fingers is a green seaweed with soft, spongy branches that repeatedly fork like thick fingers. This subspecies has spread beyond its northwest Pacific origin on marine equipment, shellfish, and other transported material. It attaches to hard surfaces, including rock and shells, and fragments can establish elsewhere. Dense growth can overgrow other organisms, including shellfish, although effects vary among sites. The name has changed in much of the literature: records called Codium fragile subsp. tomentosoides commonly refer to the same introduced subspecies treated here.

amanita-phalloides.summary: Death cap is a mushroom that can cause fatal poisoning if eaten. It grows from a fungus living underground in association with tree roots, so removing visible mushrooms does not remove the whole organism. Caps can be greenish, yellowish, pale brown, or nearly white, and young mushrooms may remain enclosed in a rounded outer covering. The familiar green cap is therefore not a reliable safety test. Cooking, drying, and freezing do not make it safe to eat, and serious poisoning can begin only after a delay.

blaberus-craniifer.summary: Death's head cockroach is a large tropical cockroach named for the dark, face-like pattern on the shield behind its head. It normally shelters beneath decaying wood and vegetation, and is also kept in insect collections and captivity. Young insects lack the adults' full wings and spend much of their time concealed. Its imposing size and name do not establish that it is a typical kitchen pest. An isolated indoor sighting may involve a transported or escaped animal, so identifying its source matters before planning a household treatment.

lipoptena-cervi.summary: Deer ked is a flattened, blood-feeding fly that mainly lives on deer and related mammals. Newly emerged adults have wings and search for a host; after settling on one they shed the wings and can look surprisingly tick-like. People often encounter flying adults in fall or find wingless insects while handling deer. Bites can cause persistent skin irritation. Finding microbes in a ked does not by itself prove that it transmits disease to people, and that distinction remains important when interpreting alarming reports about these insects.

dianthus-armeria.summary: Deptford Pink is a slender annual or biennial with small, deep pink flowers dotted with white. Several blooms sit together at the tip of a wiry stem, surrounded by long, pointed green bracts. It grows in open grassland, roadsides, and disturbed ground, and has become established outside its European and Asian range. The plant's status differs greatly by region: it is an introduced wildflower in much of North America but a conservation concern in parts of its native range. A scattered occurrence should be assessed in its local habitat.

phradonoma-nobile.summary: Dermestid beetle here refers specifically to Phradonoma nobile, a small patterned beetle in the same family as carpet beetles. The common name covers a much larger family and does not identify this species by itself. Published records include stored-grain environments and associations with insect material, but those observations do not establish that every household sighting represents a damaging infestation. A 2009 Arizona specimen formed the basis of the first published North American record. Correct identification is particularly useful when an unfamiliar dermestid appears in stored goods or a collection.

volutaria-tubuliflora.summary: Desert knapweed is a winter annual that starts as a low rosette and later sends up branching stems with small pink, purple or whitish flower heads. Plants can reach about five feet, but dry conditions may produce flowering plants only a few inches tall. That size difference makes small plants easy to miss. Desert knapweed can produce thousands of seeds, and California observations indicate that seeds remain viable in soil for at least five years. Its ability to grow in dry, sparsely vegetated ground makes early detection especially useful around desert roads, disturbed ground and nearby natural areas.

agropyron-desertorum.summary: Desert wheatgrass is a long-lived grass introduced for forage and soil protection in dry rangelands. It grows in dense bunches, usually one to three feet tall, and begins growth during the cool part of the year. Its narrow, flattened seed heads distinguish it from many grasses with open, branching flower clusters. Desert wheatgrass tolerates drought and grazing, qualities that made it useful in planted pastures. Those same qualities can make it difficult to combine with less competitive native plants. Whether a stand needs management depends on the site's purpose: a seeded grazing field presents different choices from a native grassland restoration.

monomorium-destructor.summary: Destructive trailing ant is a very small ant also known as Singapore ant. Workers are pale brown to reddish yellow, with a distinctly darker rear section of the body. Their slow trails may lead to food, cracks or concealed indoor nests. The name reflects a particular household concern: colonies can occupy electrical equipment and damage wiring. Destructive trailing ant is now commonly placed in the genus Trichomyrmex, so searches under both scientific names are useful. Color and size provide an initial clue, but other small indoor ants look similar; a confirmed identification is helpful before choosing a control approach.

sargassum-horneri.summary: Devil weed is a large brown seaweed native to waters around Japan and Korea that has become established along parts of the eastern Pacific coast. It attaches to hard surfaces, including rock, docks and boats. Young plants have a compact, fernlike appearance; older plants develop long branching stems and gas-filled floats that hold them in the water. Detached, buoyant plants can travel and remain capable of reproduction, making boat gear and drifting material important pathways. Research is still examining how Devil weed affects different marine communities. Its presence does not mean every nearby native seaweed is being displaced in the same way.

kalanchoe-daigremontiana.summary: Devil's backbone is a succulent whose leaf edges carry rows of tiny plantlets. Each plantlet can develop roots, drop to the ground and begin a new plant, which explains why it can spread beyond a pot without flowering. The upright stems bear broad, pointed leaves often marked with purple beneath, and mature plants may produce hanging pink or lavender flowers. Devil's backbone comes from Madagascar and is grown as an ornamental. It is easily confused with related plants sold under the same common names, especially a hybrid with narrower leaves. All parts should be kept away from animals and children who might eat them.

achyranthes-aspera.summary: Devil's horsewhip is a variable herb with opposite leaves and long, narrow flower spikes. The small flowers are inconspicuous, but their stiff, pointed coverings become memorable when they catch on clothing or animal fur. Plants may live for one season or persist longer, sometimes developing a woody base. Devil's horsewhip occurs across warm regions of the world in disturbed ground and other habitats. The species includes several varieties with different histories and ranges, so a species-level record alone does not establish that a particular population is introduced or harmful. Mature flowers help resolve that finer identification.

achyranthes-aspera-var-pubescens.summary: Devil's horsewhip variety pubescens is the pointed-leaved form of a plant best recognized by its long, prickly flower spikes. Its flowers are small, but noticeably longer than those of the typical variety when examined closely. The name pubescens refers to hairiness, although hair alone is not a reliable way to recognize it. Kew treats this variety as native from southern Florida and the Caribbean into parts of tropical America, and introduced in Maryland and Texas. That regional distinction matters: finding Devil's horsewhip does not by itself justify removing a plant from natural vegetation.

alstonia-macrophylla.summary: Deviltree is a tropical evergreen tree with a straight trunk, leaves arranged in groups around the twigs, and clusters of small white flowers. Its long, slender fruits release small hairy seeds that can be carried by wind. Deviltree has been planted for timber and landscaping outside its Asian range, and seedlings can appear away from planted trees. Regional assessments differ: some Florida resources identify it as an invasive concern, while an older university assessment records limited documented problems and a reassessment in progress. Local observations of escape and regeneration are therefore more useful than assuming every planted tree has the same impact.

triumfetta-rhomboidea.summary: Diamond burbark is a hairy herb or small shrub with yellow flowers and round fruits covered in hooked spines. Its lower leaves often have three shallow lobes, while the smaller upper leaves can be much narrower. That change in leaf shape on a single plant can make it look more variable than expected. Diamond burbark grows in disturbed tropical and subtropical places, including roadsides, and has become established outside its original range. The burrs are its most practical recognition feature: they can cling to clothing and carry seeds away from the parent plant.

plutella-xylostella.summary: Diamondback moth is a small moth whose caterpillars feed on cabbage-family plants, including broccoli, kale and many mustards. The caterpillars often feed from beneath a leaf, leaving thin, translucent patches before larger holes develop. Despite their small size, numerous larvae can damage seedlings and spoil developing heads. Adult moths usually show a pale zigzag band that forms diamond-like marks when the wings are folded. Diamondback moth can arrive on infested transplants as well as by adult movement. It has developed resistance to many insecticides, making careful scouting, exclusion and protection of natural enemies especially valuable.

stephanodiscus-binderanus.summary: Diatom, in this entry, means Stephanodiscus binderanus, a microscopic freshwater alga with a silica shell. Its round cells can join into chains and drift in the water. It can become abundant in nutrient-rich conditions, and historical blooms have clogged water-treatment equipment and affected water's taste or smell. Its North American origin is less straightforward than older invasive-species lists suggest. Researchers found its remains in Lake Simcoe sediments dating to the late seventeenth century, challenging the idea that it arrived on the continent only during twentieth-century shipping. Abundance and water-quality effects should therefore be assessed separately from assumptions about introduction.

centaurea-diffusa.summary: Diffuse Knapweed begins as a low rosette and develops a branching flowering stem, often about one to two feet tall. Small heads usually carry white flowers, although purplish flowers also occur. The name refers to its spreading arrangement of branches, which can give a mature plant a rounded outline. Diffuse Knapweed reproduces by seed and can spread through disturbed grasslands and roadsides, particularly where competing vegetation is sparse. Preventing seed production is therefore central to management. Plants may flower in their first year, live for two years, or persist a little longer, so a fixed two-year schedule can miss some individuals.

centaurea-x-psammogena.summary: Diffuse-spotted knapweed hybrid results from crosses between Diffuse Knapweed and spotted knapweed. It is fertile, so finding a plant with mixed features does not mean it is a reproductive dead end. The hybrid can combine the branching habit of Diffuse Knapweed with darker flower-head bracts associated with spotted knapweed. Flowers may be white or purple, and individual plants vary considerably. Researchers have documented hybrid traits and genetic evidence in North American populations. That variation is useful to recognize in the field, but it also means an intermediate-looking plant needs closer examination before it is assigned this hybrid name.

ichthyocotylurus-pileatus.summary: Digenean fluke, here Ichthyocotylurus pileatus, is a small parasitic flatworm with a life cycle involving snails, fish and fish-eating birds. In fish it occurs as an immature stage that becomes enclosed in a tiny capsule within internal tissues. Studies have found it in organs including the kidneys and swim bladder, and Great Lakes records extend back to the early twentieth century. A fish may carry more than one closely related fluke, so finding a cyst does not establish this species. The parasite's movement between hosts also means that identifying an infection is a fish-health task rather than a shoreline visual survey.

neascus-brevicaudatus.summary: Digenean fluke, here listed as Neascus brevicaudatus, is a microscopic fish parasite historically reported from the eye. Other literature links this name to Posthodiplostomum brevicaudatum, a fluke whose immature stages occur in fish and whose adults develop in fish-eating birds. The name needs care because records identified only as Neascus cannot be assigned to this species. The current Great Lakes account treats the reported introduction as probably unsuccessful, with no further reports after the 1990s. That is different from an established, expanding infestation. Eye abnormalities or dark spots on a fish are not enough to show that this particular parasite is present.

digitaria-eriantha.summary: Digitgrass is a perennial African grass widely used for grazing and hay. Its flower head has several slender branches spreading from near the stem tip like fingers. The species includes quite different forms: some make upright bunches, while others spread through above-ground runners that root as they grow. That distinction matters when managing an escape from a planted pasture. Some cultivars produce seed, while the familiar pangola type is sterile and spreads through runners. Digitgrass is not considered a serious weed everywhere it is grown; management should respond to its behavior at the site and the vegetation it is entering.

anethum-graveolens.summary: Dill is a familiar annual herb with finely divided leaves and broad clusters of tiny yellow flowers. Its leaves and mature fruits are used as seasoning, and its flowers attract bees and other beneficial insects. Dill also supports black swallowtail caterpillars where that butterfly occurs. Garden plants often reach two to three feet, with taller cultivars approaching five feet. Because Dill readily reseeds, seedlings may appear beyond the original bed the following year. That tendency calls for ordinary garden containment where volunteers are unwanted; it does not by itself show that Dill is damaging nearby natural habitat.

blaberus-discoidalis.summary: Discoid cockroach is a large tropical cockroach frequently kept as a feeder insect or laboratory animal. Adults have well-developed wings, although husbandry guides describe them as flightless, and females produce live young after retaining the developing egg case. Outdoor records include sheltered places beneath dead plant material and stones. Historical accounts also document occasional transport with tropical plants and temporary greenhouse populations. A single Discoid cockroach indoors therefore calls for checking its source, such as a feeder colony or incoming plant, rather than assuming it behaves like a common kitchen pest. Similar Blaberus species can be difficult to tell apart.

fimbristylis-schoenoides.summary: Ditch fimbry is a small, narrow-leaved sedge of wet or seasonally moist ground. Instead of a large branching flower cluster, it usually carries one oval spikelet at the stem tip, sometimes with one or two additional spikelets. This spare outline can make it resemble a spikerush. In the southeastern United States it occurs on moist sand or peaty soil in ditches, roadside clearings and other low, open places. Regional floras describe it as annual or perennial, so a single life-span rule is unreliable. Its presence identifies a wet-ground plant, but does not alone demonstrate substantial ecological harm.

solanum-nigrescens.summary: Divine nightshade is a perennial herb with small star-shaped flowers and clusters of berries that darken as they mature. It may stand upright or sprawl, and larger plants can become shrub-sized. The species belongs to the black-nightshade group, whose members are often confused with one another. Divine nightshade is native across parts of the southeastern United States and tropical America, so it should not automatically be treated as an introduced invader. Although some regional traditions use related nightshades as food or medicine, an uncertain identification is no basis for eating the berries or leaves.

hibiscus-mutabilis.summary: Dixie rosemallow is a large flowering shrub whose blooms can change color during a single day. Many open white or pale pink and deepen to rose as they age, so one plant can carry several shades at once. Broad, lobed leaves and hairy young growth give it a different texture from many familiar garden hibiscus plants. Native to China, it has been widely cultivated for its late-season flowers. Some plants persist or spread beyond gardens, but an old planted shrub alone does not show that a population is expanding.

pityrogramma-calomelanos.summary: Dixie silverback fern forms upright tufts of finely divided fronds, dark green above and often strikingly white beneath. That pale underside is a natural waxy coating, not a disease. Its fronds arise from a short, scaly stem near the ground, and the spore-producing structures lie across the lower leaf surface. Originally from tropical America, it is cultivated and naturalized in many warm regions. It often occupies disturbed places such as rocky openings, road edges and cracks in paving. Finding it outside a pot warrants documenting the location, without assuming every occurrence causes ecological damage.

rosa-canina.summary: Dog rose is a thorny shrub with arching branches, pale pink or white flowers and red rose hips. It is native to parts of Europe and western Asia and has become established outside cultivation in North America. Its compound leaves and curved prickles are familiar rose features, but distinguishing it from other wild and escaped roses takes a closer look. In some places it forms large shrubby patches in grassland. A rose growing along a fence may be a planted survivor, an escape or another species, so identification should come before control.

pseudelephantopus-spicatus.summary: Dog's-tongue is a small perennial herb with broad lower leaves and narrow, upright clusters of tiny white flowers. Despite belonging to the daisy family, it has no showy ring of petals around a yellow center. Several small flower heads sit together along the flowering branches, each accompanied by narrow leaflike bracts. It comes from tropical America and has been recorded as introduced in Florida, including open sandy places. The common name is shared with unrelated plants, so a label saying dog's-tongue is not enough to identify it or infer its effects.

discula-destructiva.summary: Dogwood anthracnose is a disease caused by the fungus Discula destructiva, especially on flowering and Pacific dogwoods. It can begin as leaf spots and blight, then kill shoots and damage larger branches through cankers. Cool, moist, shaded conditions favor infection, which often starts low in the crown and progresses upward. Some trees decline severely, while other dogwood species and resistant cultivars tolerate infection better. Brown leaves alone are not proof of this disease: several leaf-spot fungi and growing conditions can produce similar symptoms, making examination of branches as well as leaves important.

felis-catus.summary: The domestic cat is familiar as a house pet, but some cats live with little or no direct human care. Their coats vary enormously, but the quiet stalking approach and quick pounce are recognizable behaviors. Cats hunt birds, small mammals and other animals even when people provide food, so feeding alone does not prevent wildlife predation. An outdoor sighting cannot tell you whether a cat is lost, regularly allowed outside or living independently. That distinction matters: preventing roaming, finding an owner and arranging appropriate care can protect both the cat and nearby wildlife.

canis-lupus-familiaris.summary: The domestic dog is a domesticated canid whose many breeds reflect a long association with people. Dogs serve as companions and working animals, and their size, coat and behavior vary widely. When allowed to roam, they may chase wildlife or provoke defensive responses from deer, elk and other animals, putting themselves and people nearby at risk. A dog alone outdoors may be a lost pet or escaped working animal rather than part of a feral population. Keeping dogs under reliable control is therefore both a wildlife precaution and an important part of responsible care.

capra-hircus.summary: The domestic goat is a social browsing animal kept in many breeds for milk, meat, fiber and companionship. Goats readily eat leaves and shoots from shrubs and trees, and their climbing ability helps them reach vegetation above ground level. Those same habits make secure fencing especially important. Escaped or independently living goats can repeatedly browse young plants and strip bark; the effects depend on the habitat and the number of animals. A goat beyond a fence may still belong to a nearby farm, so observations should help locate its keeper before anyone assumes it is feral.

equus-asinus.summary: The donkey is the domestic descendant of the African wild ass, familiar for its long ears, upright mane and strong association with people as a working animal. Donkeys have been carried far beyond their ancestors' range. In parts of the American Southwest, escaped or released animals contributed to the free-ranging burro populations present today. A donkey seen outside a pasture may instead be an owned animal that has escaped. These situations call for different responses, but both begin with keeping a safe distance and identifying the responsible owner or land manager.

rumex-longifolius.summary: Dooryard dock is a tall perennial with broad, long leaves and upright clusters of small flowers that develop into brown fruits. It occurs in disturbed ground, fields, roadsides and some moist shore habitats. Introduced populations are documented in northeastern North America, but finding one plant does not establish that it is displacing nearby vegetation. Like other docks, it is easiest to recognize after flowering, when the thin structures surrounding each fruit have expanded. Those fruit details matter because several docks look very similar as leafy plants, and hybrids can further complicate an identification.

cryptodiaporthe-populea.summary: Dothichiza canker is a fungal disease of poplars that often becomes most damaging when trees are stressed. Small twigs may die first; larger cankers can then interrupt the living tissue beneath the bark, killing branches or young stems. Newly planted trees and nursery stock deserve particular attention because transplanting and dry conditions can leave them vulnerable. The fungus has several older names, including Dothichiza populea, which still appears in forestry literature. Its presence on a damaged poplar does not mean that every nearby tree will suffer the same outcome.

allantophomopsiella-pseudotsugae.summary: Douglas fir canker is associated with a fungus that can live on dead conifer tissues and extend into living shoots after injury. Frost-damaged young growth is an important starting point in forestry accounts. Affected shoots turn brown, and a canker that completely surrounds a small stem can kill everything beyond it. Damage is often limited, although recently planted or weakened trees may suffer more seriously. The fungus also occurs on other conifers, including pines. Older references call it Allantophomopsis pseudotsugae or Phomopsis pseudotsugae; the currently used genus is Allantophomopsiella.

geranium-molle.summary: Dovefoot Geranium is a small annual with soft, rounded leaves and pink flowers whose petals have deep notches. It often grows in open, disturbed ground, including thin turf and cultivated places. Plants can germinate in spring or establish in autumn and survive the winter, so a patch may contain seedlings and flowering plants at different times. The familiar cranesbill name refers to the long, beaklike fruit. Its importance depends on the setting: it can compete in some crops, while a few plants in an informal garden may simply be unwanted volunteers.

betula-pubescens.summary: Downy birch is a deciduous tree with pale bark, fine branches and small toothed leaves. The name points to the soft hairs on young shoots, one of its useful distinguishing features. It grows well in cool, moist settings and can occur on wet or peaty ground. Mature trees may reach about 65–80 feet, although exposure and growing conditions strongly affect their form. Downy birch has a broad, botanically complex range, including parts of the North Atlantic region. A tree's identity and local origin matter before an occurrence is treated as an unwanted introduction.

potentilla-intermedia.summary: Downy cinquefoil is a yellow-flowered plant of roadsides, open disturbed ground and other relatively dry sites. Its leaves usually have five separate leaflets, and its branching stems carry many small flowers. Unlike the silvery underside of some other cinquefoils, the leaves remain green or gray-green beneath their soft hairs. Botanical treatments differ in how they present its origin: Kew recognizes it as Potentilla × intermedia, a named hybrid involving silver and Norwegian cinquefoils. That history helps explain why careful comparison with related cinquefoils is more useful than relying on a single familiar-looking leaf.

phyllostachys-flexuosa.summary: Drooping timber bamboo is a woody bamboo from China that spreads through long underground stems. These stems, called rhizomes, can send up new canes beyond the visible edge of a planting. The canes are often slightly bent near their bases and commonly reach about 16–20 feet, with taller growth possible. Its narrow leaves and arching growth can make an effective screen, but the planting needs room and continuing containment. The common name alone is not a reliable identification: several green-stemmed running bamboos look much alike once their new shoots have matured.

fumaria-officinalis.summary: Drug fumitory is a small annual with finely divided, blue-green leaves and rows of pink flowers tipped with dark purple. Its slender stems branch freely and may stand upright or lean among neighboring plants. It is familiar in cultivated soil, gardens and other disturbed places, where it completes its life cycle through seed. A patch can look delicate while still producing a substantial seed crop. Its agricultural importance varies with density and the crop involved. The name reflects historical medicinal use, but identifying a garden plant is not a basis for preparing or using it as a remedy.

stegobium-paniceum.summary: Drugstore beetle is a tiny brown pantry pest whose larvae develop inside dried foods and other stored materials. Its name comes from its history of infesting herbal medicines and pharmaceutical products. Flour, spices, dry pet food, seeds and dried flowers can all provide food, so the source may be less obvious than an open cereal box. Adults can fly and often gather near windows or lights, some distance from the infested item. Finding the breeding material matters more than chasing individual beetles: a forgotten packet can keep producing adults after the surrounding shelves look clean.

cryptotermes-brevis.summary: Drywood termite in this profile refers specifically to Cryptotermes brevis, also called the West Indian drywood termite. Its colonies live inside wood and obtain enough moisture there without maintaining a connection to soil. That allows infestations in furniture, frames and structural timber to remain hidden for years. Small pieces of wood can carry a colony when moved, and more than one colony may occupy the same building. Piles of dry pellets or shed wings can be the first visible clue. These signs deserve investigation, but they do not identify this species by themselves.

ottelia-alismoides.summary: Ducklettuce is a rooted freshwater plant whose broad underwater leaves have a conspicuous pattern of crossing veins. Young leaves are narrow, then broaden as the plant develops. It grows in shallow, slow-moving or still water, including ditches, ponds and rice-growing areas. Some flowers can fertilize themselves without opening, allowing seed production even when conspicuous surface flowers are absent. Introduced populations are documented in the United States, but evidence of their actual ecological impacts remains limited in the federal risk assessment. Preventing new introductions is sensible without assuming that every occupied waterbody has suffered the same damage.

dieffenbachia-seguine.summary: Dumbcane is a tropical evergreen grown for its large leaves, often marked with cream, white or yellow patches. Thick, fleshy stems carry most of the foliage toward their tips, giving older plants a cane-like appearance. It is native to the Caribbean and tropical South America and is widely familiar as a houseplant. The common name refers to the painful mouth and throat irritation that can follow chewing the plant. Microscopic calcium oxalate crystals in its tissues are responsible for much of that irritation. An attractive indoor specimen therefore needs placement that keeps it away from children and pets.

agriotes-obscurus.summary: Dusky wireworm is the soil-dwelling larval stage of a click beetle. The slender, hard-bodied larvae feed on underground plant parts, including roots, seedlings and potato tubers, and can remain in the soil for several years. Damage may appear as missing seedlings, weakened plants or holes that reduce a harvested crop's quality. Long-established grass and recently converted pasture can provide favorable conditions. The adult beetle is a different-looking stage, small and brown, with the clicking mechanism characteristic of its family. Several wireworm species occur together, so crop damage alone cannot establish which one is present.

ophiostoma-novo-ulmi.summary: Dutch Elm Disease associated with Ophiostoma novo-ulmi is the more aggressive of the two major fungal forms behind the loss of many elms. The fungus enters the tree's water-conducting tissues, and the tree's response to infection further restricts water movement. Leaves wilt, branches die and a susceptible tree may decline rapidly. Elm bark beetles carry the fungus between trees, while joined roots can pass it directly between neighboring elms. This species drove the later, more destructive disease pandemic. A diagnosis of Dutch Elm Disease does not by itself identify which fungal species caused an individual tree's symptoms.

ophiostoma-ulmi.summary: Dutch elm disease was first associated with Ophiostoma ulmi, the fungus responsible for the earlier twentieth-century epidemic. A related, more aggressive species, O. novo-ulmi, later became the dominant cause in many affected regions. Both infect elm water-conducting tissues and can spread through bark beetles or connections between roots. The older fungus remains an important part of the disease's history and taxonomy, but an old report using its name may not follow today's species distinction. For a homeowner with a wilting elm, prompt diagnosis and management are more useful than guessing the pathogen from the tree's rate of decline.

lonicera-xylosteum.summary: Dwarf honeysuckle is a deciduous shrub with soft gray-green leaves, paired pale flowers and paired red berries. Despite its name, it can grow several feet tall and form a substantial shrub along woodland edges, roadsides or old plantings. It is native to Europe and western Eurasia and has escaped cultivation in parts of North America. Birds disperse its fruits, helping new plants appear beyond the original garden. It resembles several other introduced bush honeysuckles closely, so naming it correctly often requires flowers as well as leaves. Its modest size does not make every small honeysuckle this species.

urtica-urens.summary: Dwarf nettle is an annual nettle with toothed leaves and stinging hairs on its stems and foliage. It often appears in cultivated, nutrient-rich ground, including gardens, farmyards and crop fields. Unlike the larger perennial nettles that spread through underground stems, it completes its life through seed. Its compact size can be misleading: brushing a small plant can still cause a sharp sting. Growing seasons vary with climate, and sheltered plants may survive mild winters. It can be troublesome where people work or crops establish, although its presence alone does not justify clearing all nearby vegetation.

chaenorhinum-minus.summary: Dwarf snapdragon is a small annual that grows in open, disturbed ground, often among gravel or along roads and railway beds. Its pale lavender flowers resemble miniature snapdragons, but the mouth remains slightly open and a short, blunt spur projects from the back. Narrow leaves and fine gland-tipped hairs give the plant a modest appearance that is easy to overlook between stones. It is introduced from Europe and nearby regions in much of North America. A scattered plant in rough ground is a different management situation from a patch interfering with a garden or maintained surface.

marsilea-minuta.summary: Dwarf waterclover is a creeping aquatic fern whose four leaflets can make it look like a tiny clover. It grows in shallow water and on wet mud, changing its leaf size and stalk length as water levels change. Underground or surface-running stems allow a patch to expand, while spores develop inside small protective structures near the leaf bases. Plants carrying this name occur in the aquarium trade and in introduced populations. The boundary between this species and some related waterclovers remains disputed among botanical sources, so a familiar four-leaf shape cannot establish an exact identity.

genista-tinctoria.summary: Dyer's greenweed is a small woody shrub with many slender branches and bright yellow, pea-shaped flowers. It was grown as a source of yellow dye, a use reflected in both its common and scientific names. Plants favor sunny, well-drained ground and may occur in meadows, pastures or disturbed places after escaping cultivation. Narrow, simple leaves help distinguish it from several larger broom shrubs. The seed pods change from green to brown as they mature. Its regional status varies, so decisions about retaining or removing it should take account of nearby natural habitat and local observations.

rubia-tinctorum.summary: Dyer's madder is a scrambling perennial best known for the red dye obtained from its roots. Small backward-pointing hooks on the stems and leaves let it catch against neighboring vegetation as it grows. The leaves form rings around the stem, and small yellow-green flowers are followed by dark, fleshy fruits. Beneath the surface, creeping stems can extend the planting beyond the original crown. It has a long history of cultivation, so an occurrence may be a surviving dye-garden plant or an escape. Local spread and the surrounding habitat matter more than the historical use when deciding what to do.

isatis-tinctoria.summary: Dyer's woad has a long history as a source of blue dye, but its yellow flowers and dark hanging seed pods are the features you will see outdoors. It usually spends its first year as a low cluster of leaves, then sends up branched flowering stems. Originally from parts of Europe, Asia, and northern Africa, it has escaped cultivation into western North American rangelands. Dense stands can reduce the forage available to grazing animals. Rocky, well-drained ground suits it, and old stems may keep their distinctive pods well into winter.

acacia-auriculiformis.summary: Earleaf acacia is a tropical tree with curved green foliage, yellow flower spikes, and seed pods that twist into an ear-like shape. What look like adult leaves are actually flattened leaf stalks that take over the work of leaves; seedlings have true leaves first. Native to northern Australia, New Guinea, and parts of Indonesia, it has been widely planted for shade and other uses. In Florida it can establish beyond plantings and crowd native vegetation. Its seeds and young trees around a mature planting are worth watching, especially beside natural areas.

solanum-mauritianum.summary: Earleaf nightshade is a fast-growing shrub or small tree with large, softly hairy leaves and clusters of violet flowers. Small leaf-like flaps beside the larger leaf stalks explain the name. Round berries change from green to dull yellow and are carried by fruit-eating animals, helping the plant reach disturbed ground and woodland edges. It comes from South America and has become troublesome in several warm regions outside that range. The hairs can irritate skin and breathing passages, and the plant should not be treated as an edible nightshade. Cutting it back may be followed by vigorous regrowth.

echinochloa-oryzoides.summary: Early water grass is an annual grass adapted to wet ground, especially rice fields and irrigation channels. Its name refers to flowering ahead of late watergrass; in California rice guidance, it can flower roughly 40 days after flooding. That early start helps it replenish the soil's seed supply before the crop is harvested. It belongs to a closely related group of grasses that compete strongly with rice and can be difficult to distinguish when young. Some modern research treats it as a variety of barnyardgrass, while several floras continue to recognize Echinochloa oryzoides as a species.

helodrilus-oculatus.summary: Earthworm in this entry refers specifically to Helodrilus oculatus, a slender worm associated with saturated soil and the margins of fresh water. European records include stream banks, ditches, ponds, and wet caves. A 2016 study documented it at Dyke Marsh near Washington, D.C., reporting the first known North American record at that time. Its preference for wet habitats makes it different from the familiar picture of a large nightcrawler in a lawn. Possible competition with native wetland worms has been raised, but that report did not demonstrate ecological damage caused by this species.

setaria-barbata.summary: East indian bristlegrass is a leafy tropical grass with broad, pleated blades and a branched flower head. Its slender bristles remain visible after the small seed-bearing units fall away. Unlike the dense, bottlebrush-shaped heads of many familiar foxtails, its flowering branches are more distinct. Plants can grow into tall clumps, while lower stems may spread along the ground and root at their joints. It is an annual in the botanical treatments reviewed here. Its presence in a cultivated or disturbed place deserves a closer look, but does not by itself demonstrate ecological damage.

digitaria-setigera.summary: East indian crabgrass is a spreading grass whose flowering branches rise like slender fingers above the leaves. Lower stems can root where they touch the ground, helping a plant form a loose mat. Its height, leaf hairiness and number of flowering branches vary considerably. It grows in tropical and subtropical settings, including fields, roadsides and other disturbed ground. Its origin in Hawaiʻi remains debated: Bishop Museum lists it as indigenous, while historical research suggests an accidental introduction by Polynesian voyagers. A local record therefore needs geographic context before it is treated as a new arrival or a removal priority.

ptinus-raptor.summary: Eastern spider beetle is a tiny stored-product beetle named for the spiderlike outline made by its long legs and rounded body. It is an insect, with six legs and antennae, rather than a spider. The species has been recorded in cereal products in warehouses and in cargo containing grain or flour. A beetle found walking across a shelf may have come from food hidden elsewhere, so locating the source matters more than treating the visible insect. Several closely related spider beetles occur in buildings, and a household photograph rarely establishes which species is present.

lobelia-erinus.summary: Edging lobelia is a low flowering plant commonly grown along garden borders and in hanging baskets. Its small flowers often have blue or violet lobes around a pale throat, although cultivated forms also come in white, pink and other shades. Some plants form compact cushions while others trail over a container edge. Native to Africa, it is widely grown as an annual where winters are cold, even though it can persist longer in suitable climates. An isolated garden escape is not evidence of widespread harm; the useful question is whether plants are repeatedly establishing beyond cultivation.

ficus-carica.summary: Edible fig is a spreading deciduous shrub or small tree with broad lobed leaves and the familiar fleshy figs. Its flowers are hidden inside the developing fig rather than displayed as an open blossom. Many cultivated varieties can form a crop without pollination, but fruit production and viable seed production are different processes. The tree also sends up shoots from its roots, and discarded branches can take root. In parts of California it forms dense patches along waterways. An established fruit tree in a garden should be assessed by its local spread, not by fruiting alone.

gyrodactylus-anguillae.summary: Eel pest, here referring to Gyrodactylus anguillae, is a small parasitic flatworm associated with the skin and gills of eels. Its common name is also used for other eel parasites, making the scientific name important. Researchers have identified it on more than one eel species, and movement of live eels has helped carry parasites between regions. Infection does not automatically explain a sick or dying fish: a study of affected young European eels found several parasites together and could not attribute the deaths to this species alone. Diagnosis therefore needs an examination of the fish and its surroundings.

pseudodactylogyrus-anguillae.summary: Eel pest, in this entry Pseudodactylogyrus anguillae, is a small flatworm that attaches to eel gills. It shares its common name and its host fish with several other parasites, including Pseudodactylogyrus bini. The two can occur together, but they differ in their attachment structures and some habitat tolerances. P. anguillae has been studied on eels in both fresh and brackish water. Live-fish movements are an important concern because an eel can carry small parasites without an obvious external change. A fish-health examination is more informative than assuming that clear-looking skin means the gills are parasite-free.

pseudodactylogyrus-bini.summary: Eel pest, here Pseudodactylogyrus bini, is a gill-dwelling flatworm best known from studies of cultured eels. It anchors to the delicate gill tissue and can interfere with breathing when infections become severe. Young eels may be especially vulnerable, while an infected fish can show little change on its outer body. The parasite lays eggs and develops without needing a different animal as an intermediate host. That life cycle makes the movement of eels and their holding environment important. The shared name “Eel pest” should always be paired with the scientific name when discussing a laboratory result.

solanum-melongena.summary: Eggplant is a warm-season crop grown for its smooth, fleshy fruits, which range from familiar dark purple forms to white, green, striped, round and slender varieties. The plants have broad leaves and violet, star-shaped flowers with a yellow center. They are sensitive to cold and are commonly grown for a single season, though they can live longer in warm conditions. A volunteer beside a garden or discarded fruit is not evidence that the crop is invading natural habitat. Confirming the plant and observing whether it persists beyond cultivation is more useful than treating every cultivated food plant as a removal target.

phelipanche-aegyptiaca.summary: Egyptian broomrape is a parasitic flowering plant that obtains water and nutrients from another plant's roots. Much of its development happens underground; the yellowish or purplish shoots become noticeable when they emerge to flower beside the host. It has tiny scale-like leaves rather than ordinary green foliage. Agricultural hosts include tomato and other broadleaf crops. Its numerous minute seeds make accidental movement in soil a concern. Native broomrapes are also part of North American vegetation, so an unfamiliar parasitic plant needs expert identification before it is disturbed or treated as this agricultural pest.

alopochen-aegyptiaca.summary: Egyptian Goose is a sturdy waterbird with pink legs, a dark eye patch and a pale gray-brown body. It grazes beside ponds and lakes, often in pairs or family groups, but also feeds in shallow water. Despite its name, it belongs closer to shelducks than to the familiar true geese. Native to Africa, it has established introduced populations in parts of the United States. Pairs can use tree holes, ledges or abandoned bird nests as well as ground sites, and may defend the nest vigorously. A bird standing well above the water is therefore no surprise.

dactyloctenium-aegyptium.summary: Egyptian grass is a low, spreading annual whose seedheads resemble small crow’s feet. Several short branches radiate from the top of a stalk, each lined with tightly packed spikelets. The lower stems can lie along the ground and root at their joints, producing mats in disturbed soil. It grows especially well in warm conditions and occurs in fields, paths and other open ground. Its origin is in Africa and Asia, and its behavior varies by place: Florida’s assessment distinguishes greater invasion concerns in the central and southern regions from a caution rating in the north.

pentas-lanceolata.summary: Egyptian starcluster brings clusters of small, five-pointed flowers to warm-season gardens. Each apparent star ends a slender floral tube, and the clusters attract butterflies and hummingbirds. Red, pink and white forms are familiar, with other colors available among cultivars. The plant is a tropical shrub from eastern Africa and southern Arabia, but gardeners often grow it as a seasonal bedding plant where winters are cold. In warm places it can persist for several years. Its presence in a garden is not, by itself, evidence of harmful spread; plants appearing independently beyond cultivation are the observations worth distinguishing.

inula-helenium.summary: Elecampane inula is a tall perennial with broad leaves and yellow flowerheads surrounded by many narrow rays. A leafy rosette can occupy a substantial patch before flowering stems rise above it in summer. The plant comes from Eurasia and has become established along roadsides, in fields and around former plantings in North America. Its large leaves and sunflowerlike heads make it conspicuous, but neither feature alone identifies it. The roots have a long history of human use, which helps explain its cultivation; that history should not be treated as advice to prepare or consume a wild plant.

aristolochia-elegans.summary: Elegant dutchman's pipe is a twining vine best recognized by its cream-colored flowers densely marked with purple. Their bent tube opens into a broad, heart-shaped face, giving the bloom its unusual outline. Native to South America, it was widely planted as an ornamental and has escaped in warm regions, including parts of Florida. Established vines can climb over and weigh down surrounding vegetation. The flower’s unpleasant odor attracts flies that pollinate it. References also use the scientific name Aristolochia littoralis for this plant. Its striking flowers do not make it safe to eat or use medicinally.

cenchrus-purpureus.summary: Elephant grass forms towering, bamboo-like clumps with long leaves and dense, bristly flowerheads. This African perennial was brought to the United States as a forage crop and has escaped into warm landscapes. Its rapid growth can produce useful biomass in managed settings, but unmanaged stands can crowd other vegetation and obstruct access along waterways. Pieces of mature stems and underground growth can establish new plants, making careless clearing a route of spread. Many older publications call it Pennisetum purpureum; that name refers to the same species now placed in Cenchrus.

platycerium-bifurcatum.summary: Elkhorn fern grows attached to trees or rocks, using its support as a place to live rather than drawing food from it. It makes two very different kinds of fronds: rounded shields that cover the base and long, repeatedly forked fronds that resemble antlers. The shields catch fallen material and help direct rain toward the roots. Often cultivated on boards or tree trunks, the fern can develop into a substantial colony. Brown areas beneath mature fertile fronds contain spore-producing structures; they are part of the fern’s life cycle, not automatically a disease or insect problem.

ochrosia-elliptica.summary: Elliptic yellowwood is a tropical shrub or small tree with glossy leaves arranged around the stem and striking pairs of red fruits. Those paired fruits are the origin of another common name, bloodhorn. Small pale flowers precede them, and broken tissues release white sap. The species comes from coastal parts of northeastern Australia and nearby Pacific islands and is grown ornamentally in warm climates. Its attractive fruit should not be tasted: both fruit and sap are reported as poisonous. A planted tree and seedlings growing independently beyond a garden represent different situations when evaluating its local establishment.

xanthogaleruca-luteola.summary: Elm Leaf Beetle feeds on elm foliage, with adults and larvae leaving different signs. Adults chew holes through leaves, while larvae scrape away the softer tissue and leave a network of veins. Heavy feeding can turn a canopy brown and repeated severe defoliation can weaken a tree. This damage should be distinguished from Dutch elm disease, which has a different cause and management response. The beetles also enter buildings to shelter, sometimes in large numbers. Finding them indoors does not mean they are eating the house; the feeding stages depend on elm leaves.

rubus-ulmifolius.summary: Elmleaf blackberry is a scrambling bramble with arching canes, pale-backed leaflets and pink flowers followed by black fruit. Its canes can root where their tips touch soil, extending a patch without waiting for new seedlings. Native to Europe and northwestern Africa, it is one of several introduced blackberries recorded in California. Brambles provide food and cover, but dense growth can also block access or overtake wanted vegetation. The name blackberry covers many species, including native ones, so a thorny thicket should not be assigned to this species from its fruit alone.

fiorinia-externa.summary: Elongate Hemlock Scale is a tiny sap-feeding insect that spends much of its life sheltered beneath a protective cover on conifer needles. Hemlocks and firs are important hosts, with other conifers also affected. Infested foliage may develop yellow blotches, lose needles or look unusually white where male scales produce waxy threads. A light infestation can be easy to miss because the insects sit mostly on needle undersides, including older growth inside the canopy. Introduced from Asia, this pest can weaken trees when abundant, but discoloration alone is not enough to identify it.

emerald-ash-borer.summary: Emerald Ash Borer is a small metallic-green beetle whose hidden larvae cause the most serious damage. They feed beneath ash bark, disrupting the tissues that move water and nutrients through the tree. A tree may carry an infestation before the canopy shows obvious decline. Native to Asia, the beetle has killed large numbers of North American ash trees and can attack otherwise healthy trees. Adults fly locally, while infested firewood, logs and nursery trees can carry it much farther. Early reporting and careful decisions about ash wood are therefore important even when only one tree appears affected.

senna-alata.summary: Emperor's candlesticks is a large tropical shrub with upright columns of yellow flowers. Orange bracts cover the unopened buds at the top, while flowers open farther down, creating the candlelike shape behind its name. Its long leaves carry rows of broad, rounded leaflets, and winged pods follow the blooms. Native to tropical America, it is widely grown as an ornamental and has naturalized in warm regions. In Hawaiʻi it can form dense pasture stands. Its history as a cultivated medicinal plant helps explain its spread, but does not establish that home preparations are safe or appropriate.

sitobion-avenae.summary: English grain aphid is a small, soft-bodied insect that feeds on cereal crops and grasses. Its color varies from green to reddish brown, but its long dark rear tubes are a useful clue. Colonies occur on leaves and stems and often gather on wheat heads as grain develops. Feeding can matter when numbers are high, and the aphid can transmit barley yellow dwarf virus. The importance of those two risks differs with crop, growth stage and region. Predators and parasitic insects often keep colonies in check, so finding a few aphids is a reason to inspect more closely rather than automatically spray.

ilex-aquifolium.summary: English holly is an evergreen shrub or tree familiar from its glossy leaves and winter decorations. Many leaves have sharp marginal spines, while female plants can carry red fruits after pollination. Birds eat the fruits and move the seeds beyond gardens. Native to Europe, northern Africa and western Asia, the species has become established in parts of the United States and can spread through forest understories, particularly in the Pacific Northwest. A well-kept hedge and a self-sown woodland stand deserve different assessments. Escaped plants can persist in shade and grow into substantial woody plants.

hedera-helix.summary: English Ivy is a woody evergreen vine that can spread across the ground or climb high into trees. Its familiar lobed leaves belong to the juvenile stage. Older flowering shoots have a different outline and produce dark berries that birds carry away. Long used as a groundcover, it has escaped into woodlands, with serious effects documented in the Pacific Northwest. Dense ground cover can prevent other plants from establishing. Climbing growth brings heavy vegetation into tree crowns, making early attention easier than dealing with an established canopy infestation.

juglans-regia.summary: English walnut is the familiar cultivated walnut tree, grown for its nuts, shade, and wood. A broad crown and large divided leaves give it a substantial presence in a garden or orchard. Green husks enclose the nuts through summer. People have moved and cultivated this tree for thousands of years, making the edges of its original Eurasian range difficult to reconstruct. Finding an English walnut outside cultivation shows that it has established there; it does not by itself establish that the tree is damaging the surrounding habitat.

torilis-japonica.summary: Erect Hedgeparsley is a slender member of the carrot family whose small fruits cling to clothing and animal fur. That hitchhiking habit helps it move along paths, woodland edges, and disturbed ground. Plants commonly begin as low rosettes before sending up branched stems with white flower clusters. Native to Europe and Asia, it has spread outside that range and can form troublesome stands in parts of North America. Its fine leaves and modest flowers can be overlooked until burr-like fruits start catching on a passing sleeve.

cynodon-aethiopicus.summary: Ethiopian dogstooth grass is a robust perennial that spreads by thick surface runners. Its stiff flowering branches often form several tiers and may be red or purple. It has been moved from tropical Africa for forage and ground cover, and has escaped cultivation. Older records can be difficult to interpret because related stargrasses were often confused. Some current authorities combine this name with Cynodon nlemfuensis, while regional floras still distinguish it. A 2024 Hawaiian study also identified hybrids between these grasses, making a pasture label an unreliable species determination.

crotalaria-brevidens.summary: Ethiopian rattlebox is an upright branching legume with three narrow leaflets and yellow flowers marked with reddish veins. Long narrow pods follow the flowers. Native to tropical Africa, it has been cultivated and introduced elsewhere.
