It is among the rattleboxes used as leafy vegetables in parts of East Africa, but that history is not a safe guide to eating an unfamiliar roadside plant. Related species look similar, and the genus includes plants with important toxicity concerns. Its presence outside cultivation should be assessed in its local setting.

chrysophtharta-m-fuscum.summary: Eucalyptus leaf beetle is a small, rounded Australian beetle that feeds on eucalyptus foliage. Adults chew older leaves, while groups of larvae concentrate on tender growth, leaving ragged edges that can look like caterpillar damage. It has become a pest of some landscape trees and cut-foliage plantings outside Australia. Several different beetles share the name eucalyptus tortoise beetle, so that common name alone can be misleading. This species is also placed in the genus Paropsisterna, a name increasingly used in taxonomic references.

phoracantha-recurva.summary: Eucalyptus longhorned borer is an Australian beetle whose larvae feed beneath eucalyptus bark. Here the name refers to Phoracantha recurva, one of two closely related borers established in California. Freshly cut wood and stressed trees provide breeding opportunities, especially when drought has weakened a planting. Larval tunnels can interrupt the tissues carrying water and nutrients, causing branch decline or killing a heavily attacked tree. An adult beetle is much easier to identify than a fading crown, since wilting and bark leakage can have several causes.

gonipterus-platensis.summary: Eucalyptus snout beetle is a leaf-feeding weevil associated with eucalyptus. This entry concerns Gonipterus platensis, one member of a group formerly treated as a single widespread pest. Adults chew leaf edges, while larvae scrape or consume young foliage. Repeated heavy feeding can reduce tree growth and leave a thin crown. The species originated in Tasmania and has spread with eucalyptus plantings to other regions. Older reports under Gonipterus scutellatus need careful interpretation because they may refer to this species or to a different, very similar weevil.

trioza-eugeniae.summary: Eugenia psyllid is a name with an important scientific mix-up. The insect widely reported from ornamental eugenia in the United States as Trioza eugeniae was shown by a taxonomic study to be Trioza adventicia. True T. eugeniae is a separate Australian species. The familiar garden pest makes young foliage blistered and pitted, but those observations should not automatically be assigned to the scientific name in this entry. Both insects are tiny sap feeders; separating their identities requires more than seeing a damaged hedge.

planchonia-stentae.summary: Euphorbia pit scale is a small sap-feeding insect found on many ornamental plants, especially succulents. Despite its common name, its host range extends well beyond Euphorbia. Mature females remain fixed to the plant beneath a close-fitting cover, while young crawlers can move to new feeding sites. Heavy infestations may produce pits or raised calloused areas and weaken stems. Originally described from South Africa, it has been recorded in the Americas and elsewhere. Movement of infested cuttings and plants is an important way it reaches new collections.

streptopelia-decaocto.summary: Eurasian collared dove is a pale, fairly large dove often seen walking beneath feeders or calling from wires above towns and farms. Its thin black neck collar and broad, squared tail distinguish it from the familiar mourning dove. Introductions in the Bahamas preceded its spread into Florida and across much of North America. Grain and other seeds are important foods, and developed landscapes provide both feeding places and nesting trees. Its expansion is well documented; the presence of this introduced bird does not by itself establish that a particular yard needs wildlife control.

grapholita-delineana.summary: Eurasian hemp moth is a small moth whose caterpillars feed inside hemp stems and developing flower or seed structures. The hidden feeding can leave swollen stems, wilted shoots and damaged buds even when few insects are visible on the leaves. Originally described from Asia, it is established in parts of North America, but its importance varies among growing regions. Several generations can occur in a season. Crop remnants matter because larvae can survive between crops in plant material, making this a pest for which careful inspection and residue management are particularly useful.

melampsora-larici-populina.summary: Eurasian poplar leaf rust pathogen is a fungus that produces yellow-orange spore patches on poplar leaves. Susceptible trees can lose foliage early, and repeated severe infections reduce growth and may contribute to dieback. Wet conditions favor infection, so damage can differ greatly among sites and years. The fungus has a life cycle involving poplars and larches, although repeating infections on poplar can also sustain it under suitable conditions. Poplar varieties differ in susceptibility, and a variety that once resisted the disease may become vulnerable as the rust population changes.

myriophyllum-spicatum.summary: Eurasian Watermilfoil is a rooted aquatic plant with finely divided leaves arranged around long underwater stems. Shoots can reach the surface and form dense growth that interferes with boating and changes habitat, although not every occupied lake develops a severe infestation. Small broken pieces can root and start new plants, which explains why fragments caught on boats and equipment deserve attention. This perennial survives from its rooted base and spreads readily within suitable waters. Its resemblance to native watermilfoils makes careful identification important before anyone begins removal.

alnus-glutinosa.summary: European Alder is a fast-growing deciduous tree associated with wet ground, stream margins and pond edges. Rounded leaves and small woody, cone-like fruits make it recognizable through much of the year. Microbes in root nodules help it obtain nitrogen, allowing growth on some relatively poor soils. It has been planted outside its native European, western Asian and northern African range and has spread into natural areas in parts of North America. Water carries its small seeds, while rooting branches and new shoots can help a stand expand locally.

ammophila-arenaria.summary: European beachgrass grows in tight clumps on coastal sand and spreads through buried stems called rhizomes. It was widely planted to hold dunes in place along the Pacific coast. That ability also changes the habitat: dense stands trap sand, alter dune shape and replace open areas used by native plants and animals. It is adapted to accumulating sand and can send new shoots upward as burial continues. On the Pacific coast, identifying the grass correctly matters because American beachgrass, their hybrid and native American dune grass can grow in similar settings.

prunus-padus.summary: European bird cherry is a small deciduous tree with fragrant white flower clusters in spring and dark cherries later in the year. Also called Mayday tree, it has been planted as an ornamental well beyond its northern European and Asian range. Birds eat the fruit and carry the seeds into surrounding vegetation. In Alaska, escaped trees can form dense thickets in natural areas, making garden trees an important source to watch. Cutting alone can encourage a flush of new shoots from trunks and roots, so successful removal requires more than taking down the visible crown.

ribes-nigrum.summary: European black currant is a deciduous shrub grown for dark berries used in juices, preserves and other foods. Its leaves and branches carry aromatic glands, giving the plant a distinctive scent. Native to Eurasia, it occurs in cultivation and as an introduced plant elsewhere; that history alone does not make every planted shrub an ecological problem. A particularly important consideration in North America is white pine blister rust. Susceptible black currants can serve as an alternate host for the fungus, whose most serious damage occurs on five-needle pines.

rubus-vestitus.summary: European blackberry is a prickly, scrambling shrub with arching canes, soft-looking hairy foliage and clusters of dark fruit. It belongs to a difficult group of closely related European brambles, several of which have become established outside their native ranges. In the Pacific Northwest it occurs in scattered disturbed places and woodland edges. Dense growth can obstruct access and compete with surrounding vegetation, but species-specific impact information is less complete than for Himalayan blackberry. Correctly naming the plant helps keep local records and management expectations from being confused with those of its better-known relatives.

lycopus-europaeus.summary: European bugleweed is a perennial of wet margins, ditches and marshy ground. Its upright stems carry toothed leaves in opposite pairs and small white flowers crowded where the leaves join the stem. Although it belongs to the mint family, it lacks the familiar mint scent. Seeds can travel in water or on muddy footwear and machinery, while spreading stems help patches expand. It is introduced in parts of North America and has become troublesome around some New Zealand lakes; those observations do not establish the same level of impact at every North American site.

centaurium-erythraea.summary: European centaury is a small upright herb with pink flowers held above a basal cluster of leaves. It grows in grasslands, roadsides and other open, disturbed places, sometimes becoming much more conspicuous in favorable seasons. Native across parts of Europe, western Asia and northern Africa, it has been introduced on several other continents. A flowering patch can look striking without necessarily being a high-priority invasive problem. Local abundance, the plants it is growing among and the purpose of the site are more useful management guides than its introduced status alone.

castanea-sativa.summary: European chestnut is a large deciduous tree grown for its nuts, shade and timber. Long, sharply toothed leaves and densely spiny fruit husks are its most familiar features; older trunks develop deep grooves. The tree's cultivation outside its native range does not by itself call for removal. Tree health is often the more immediate concern: chestnut blight and chestnut gall wasp can damage it, and moving affected shoots or planting material can help pests travel. A well-identified, healthy tree and an escaping seedling present different management questions.

cerastium-pumilum.summary: European chickweed is a small, hairy annual that flowers in spring on open, sandy or gravelly ground. Its white, shallowly notched petals and opposite leaves give it the familiar mouse-ear chickweed appearance, but identifying the exact species requires a closer look. North American floras have included quite variable plants under this name, including material also treated as the glutinosum subspecies or variety. A roadside patch therefore should not be assigned a narrow taxonomic identity from flower color alone. The available accounts describe an introduced plant of disturbed ground rather than establishing severe harm at every site.

phragmites-australis-ssp-australis.summary: European common reed is the introduced lineage of a very tall wetland grass also represented in North America by native relatives. Its dense stands can replace diverse marsh vegetation and obstruct shorelines or drainage routes. Upright canes carry long leaves and large purple-brown flower plumes that fade as the season ends. Buried stems and fragments help it spread, so moving soil or mowing equipment between sites can create new problems. The native common reed is not the target of this profile: confirming the lineage is an essential part of deciding what to do.

ostrinia-nubilalis.summary: European Corn Borer is a moth whose caterpillars tunnel into corn stalks and other sturdy plant stems. Feeding can weaken stalks, damage ears and leave broken tassels or wilted shoots. Corn is an important host, but peppers, potatoes, beans and some ornamental plants can also be attacked. The pest survives winter as a larva inside plant material. The number and timing of generations vary with region and weather, so a calendar date that works in one place may miss the vulnerable stage elsewhere. Local scouting is more useful than assuming every damaged stalk needs treatment.

rubus-caesius.summary: European dewberry is a low, trailing bramble whose dark fruit often carries a pale blue-white coating. Its slender prickly canes can root where their tips touch the soil, gradually extending a patch. White flowers and usually three-part leaves distinguish its appearance from many taller blackberries. It is native across a broad Eurasian region and occurs outside that range in scattered introduced populations. In a garden, the main practical issue may be keeping rooted canes within their intended space; an occurrence does not automatically carry the same impact as a large Himalayan blackberry thicket.

forficula-auricularia.summary: European earwig is the familiar brown garden insect with conspicuous pincers at the end of its body. It feeds at night and shelters in tight, damp spaces by day. Earwigs can damage seedlings, flowers and soft fruit, but they also eat aphids and other small insects, so their presence is not automatically a reason to control them. The scientific name has historically covered a complex of very similar species. Recent research separates several of those species, which means older North American records and garden advice do not always refer to Forficula auricularia in the narrow modern sense.

eriococcus-spurius.summary: European elm scale is a sap-feeding insect that can make the area beneath an elm sticky long before the insects themselves are noticed. Its honeydew, a sugary waste, supports black sooty mold on leaves and branches. Heavy infestations can cause yellowing, early leaf fall and twig dieback. Mature females sit on bark with a distinctive white fringe around a darker body, while young stages may feed along leaf veins. The insect is also widely called Gossyparia spuria in current references; those accounts concern the same elm pest.

sphaerium-corneum.summary: European fingernail clam is a tiny freshwater bivalve that lives among bottom sediments and aquatic vegetation. Unlike the larger mussels familiar from riverbanks, it is only about the width of a fingernail. It filters suspended food from water and occurs in lakes, ponds and slower-flowing waters. North American records have been treated as introductions from Eurasia, but the extent of ecological harm remains poorly documented. A recent U.S. risk assessment calls the evidence insufficient to determine invasion impacts; uncertainty should not be turned into either a claim of serious damage or a guarantee of harmlessness.

myrmica-rubra.summary: European fire ant is a small reddish ant that can form dense colonies in damp gardens, lawns and other sheltered places. Disturbing a nest can provoke painful stings, and the ants may make heavily occupied areas unpleasant to use. Nests are often hidden beneath stones, wood or roots rather than marked by obvious soil mounds. Colonies can spread locally by splitting into new nests, while moved soil, mulch and potted plants can carry them farther. Native to Europe and parts of Asia, the species has established troublesome populations in parts of North America.

parthenolecanium-corni.summary: European fruit lecanium scale feeds on the sap of many woody plants, including fruit trees and maples. The rounded brown females can look like little swellings in the bark. Large populations may slow growth or contribute to twig dieback, while sticky honeydew supports black sooty mold on leaves and surfaces below. An infestation does not automatically call for spraying: natural enemies often keep this soft scale in check. Its appearance changes with its host and age, which makes identification less straightforward than the common name suggests.

diaspidiotus-ostreaeformis.summary: European fruit scale is a small armored scale that lives on the bark of fruit trees and other woody hosts. Apple, pear, cherry, peach, and plum are among the plants it can infest. A gray cover protects each settled female, so colonies may resemble roughened bark rather than insects. Heavy feeding can weaken a tree, and feeding on leaves may produce reddish marks. This species is especially easy to confuse with San Jose scale, sometimes on the same plant; a reliable diagnosis matters before choosing a treatment.

ribes-uva-crispa.summary: European gooseberry is a thorny, deciduous fruit shrub with lobed leaves and berries that may ripen green, yellow, pink, or red. Many cultivated forms have been selected for cooking or fresh eating, so fruit color and sweetness vary widely. Outside gardens it can persist or become naturalized, including in parts of New England. Its presence does not by itself demonstrate ecological harm. The flowers and spines are more useful for identifying a stray shrub than the familiar grape-sized fruit alone, especially where native gooseberries grow nearby.

nemapogon-granella.summary: European grain moth is a small, mottled moth whose larvae can spoil stored grain and other dry foods. Damp conditions are especially favorable, and the insect also uses fungi and decaying material. In grain, caterpillars feed near the surface and bind material with silk, leaving clumps of grain and waste. Its interests extend beyond cereal stores: a study in Italian wine cellars documented larvae tunneling into bottle corks. Finding a moth therefore calls for a search for the breeding material, rather than assuming that the nearest flour bag is the source.

carcinus-maenas.summary: European green crab is a coastal crab that can live in sheltered bays, tidal marshes, eelgrass beds, and river mouths. Its tolerance of changing salinity helps it use habitats where freshwater and seawater meet. In invaded areas it can threaten native shellfish and damage eelgrass habitat. Despite its name, a green crab may be brown, orange, or reddish as well as green. The most dependable visible clue is the set of five points along each side of the shell behind the eyes. Prompt, well-documented reports help coastal managers locate newly occupied sites.

lepus-europaeus.summary: European hare is a long-legged mammal of open fields, grasslands, and farmland. Unlike a rabbit, it rests above ground in a shallow hollow rather than living in a warren. Its young, called leverets, are born furred and with open eyes, ready to move soon after birth. Introduced populations can damage crops and young trees, particularly by clipping stems or gnawing bark. That agricultural role varies by place: in parts of its European range, declining populations are a conservation concern. A sighting alone is not a reason to begin control.

heliotropium-europaeum.summary: European heliotrope is a gray-green annual that grows in open, disturbed ground and agricultural fields. Its small white flowers line a curled stalk that gradually straightens as they develop. In warm weather a plant can flower within weeks of germination, allowing seed production to continue through the growing season. It is a serious pasture concern in parts of Australia because eating it can cause cumulative liver damage in livestock. Seed can travel in contaminated fodder, on equipment, or with animals. Keeping new patches from setting seed is more useful than waiting for a dense stand.

larix-decidua.summary: European larch is a large conifer that turns yellow and drops its needles in autumn. This seasonal change is normal, not a sign that the tree has died. Native to European mountain regions, it is a light-demanding pioneer that can establish after disturbance. It has also been planted widely for timber and ornament, including in northeastern North America, and sometimes seeds beyond cultivation. Its ecological behavior depends on location: naturalization alone does not establish that a particular planting is causing harm. The soft spring needles and persistent small cones make it recognizable through much of the year.

lachnellula-willkommii.summary: European larch canker is a fungal disease that damages the living tissue beneath the bark of larch trees. Cankers can deform trunks, kill branches, and eventually kill a tree. The pathogen affects native larches as well as planted European larch, so the disease name does not restrict its hosts. In North America it has been documented in parts of eastern Canada and Maine. Tiny orange-centered fungal cups may appear around infected bark, but other fungi on larch look similar. A suspected case needs specialist confirmation before it is treated as a new outbreak.

sorbus-aucuparia.summary: European mountain ash is a deciduous tree grown for white spring flowers, divided leaves, and conspicuous clusters of orange-red fruit. Birds eat the fruit and carry its seeds beyond gardens, allowing seedlings to establish in woodland and along disturbed forest edges. It has escaped cultivation in parts of northern North America and is a management concern in some regions. Despite its name and ash-like foliage, it belongs to the rose family rather than the true ashes. Native mountain ashes can look very similar, especially when young, making identification important before removing a volunteer tree.

olea-europaea-ssp-europaea.summary: European olive is the evergreen olive of Mediterranean orchards, valued for its fruit and oil. The subspecies includes cultivated and wild forms, so trees vary in fruit size and habit. Long-lived plantings can also supply seed to surrounding vegetation when birds and mammals carry the fruit away. In parts of southern Australia, escaped olives form dense stands that crowd out native plants. That regional invasion history should not be applied automatically to every orchard or garden. The silvery undersides of the leaves are a useful first clue, but other olive subspecies need to be considered.

neodiprion-sertifer.summary: European Pine Sawfly larvae feed together on pine needles, sometimes raising their heads in unison when disturbed. Although they look like caterpillars, they belong to the same insect order as bees and wasps. They usually eat older needles, leaving the current season's growth at the branch tips. This can make a pine look stripped and untidy without killing it, though repeated attacks reduce growth and fullness. Mugo pine is a familiar garden host; Scots, red, and several other pines are also used. Small colonies are often manageable without treating an entire tree.

rhyacionia-buoliana.summary: European Pine Shoot Moth is a small moth whose caterpillars feed inside pine buds and shoots. A damaged terminal bud can force a side branch to take over, leaving a permanent bend in the tree's leader. Nursery stock, Christmas trees, and ornamental pines may lose shape and vigor even when the whole tree survives. Larvae begin near needles and then shelter within buds, often surrounded by silk and resin. That hidden feeding makes early detection more useful than waiting until many shoot tips have browned and died.

contarinia-baeri.summary: European pineneedle midge is a tiny fly whose larvae feed near the bases of pine needles. Affected needles bend down, discolor, and may fall, reducing the appearance of nursery or Christmas trees. Michigan research found one generation per year, with larvae spending winter in cocoons on the ground and adults appearing in spring. European studies also associate it with Scots pine and other pines. It is generally described as a minor pest in Europe, although conspicuous injury can occur. Bent needles warrant examination; they do not by themselves demonstrate a serious outbreak.

prunus-domestica.summary: European plum is the familiar cultivated fruit tree that supplies many plums, prunes, and related garden selections. White blossom appears in spring, followed by fruit that varies greatly in skin color, shape, and sweetness. Animals eating the fruit can carry seeds beyond cultivation, and trees sometimes persist around old homesteads or establish along woodland edges. A volunteer plum is not automatically an invasive plant. Cultivated varieties and different botanical treatments make this group unusually variable, so its identity is best judged from flowers, leaves, fruit, and planting history together.

ligustrum-vulgare.summary: European privet is a densely branched shrub long used for hedges. Clusters of small white flowers are followed by dark fruits that birds eat, carrying seeds into nearby woods and field edges. Plants can also recover strongly after cutting. In parts of eastern North America, escaped privets form persistent thickets and compete with surrounding vegetation. Several introduced privet species grow together, so a patch identified only as 'privet' may contain more than one species. The leaves and fruit are not food for people or pets, even though birds use the berries.

oryctolagus-cuniculus.summary: European rabbit is the species from which domestic rabbits were bred. Wild-type animals are compact, gray-brown grazers, but escaped domestic rabbits may be white, black, spotted, long-haired, or much larger. Groups often shelter in connected burrows called warrens. Where introduced populations become numerous, grazing can damage crops and prevent young plants from establishing, while burrowing changes the ground around them. A rabbit seen outdoors in North America may instead be a native cottontail or an escaped pet. That distinction should guide the response, rather than assuming every rabbit is an invasive wild animal.

rubus-idaeus-var-idaeus.summary: European red raspberry is the Eurasian form of red raspberry, familiar from fruit gardens and sometimes found beyond cultivation. The perennial root system sends up canes and new shoots, allowing a patch to widen over time. Its red fruit is made of many small fleshy segments and comes away from the plant with a hollow center. Native American red raspberry is closely related and is treated as either a separate species or another variety or subspecies. Red berries alone cannot separate them, and a spreading raspberry patch should not be cleared before that distinction is checked.

limonium-duriusculum.summary: European sea lavender is a small Mediterranean plant that has established in California coastal wetlands and nearby habitats. A low rosette of leaves supports branching stems carrying tiny pale pink to purple flowers. It spreads by seed and can form persistent stands among native marsh plants. Because it resembles both other introduced sea lavenders and the native California sea lavender, some populations were initially overlooked or misidentified. Its local importance comes from where it grows: even a short plant can occupy space needed by native salt-marsh vegetation.

veronica-beccabunga.summary: European speedwell is a fleshy wetland perennial that creeps along muddy stream edges and other wet ground. Its stems can root where they touch the soil, producing connected patches with rounded leaves and small blue flowers. Introduced populations occur in northeastern North America. Dense local stands may affect neighboring vegetation, but USGS finds the evidence insufficient for a full assessment of its environmental impact in the Great Lakes. It closely resembles native American speedwell, so both identification and the actual extent of spread matter when deciding whether a patch needs attention.

gilpinia-hercyniae.summary: European spruce sawfly feeds on spruce needles, with larvae usually taking older foliage first. Its introduction once caused major forest damage in northeastern North America, but viruses and parasitic insects subsequently reduced those outbreaks. A few larvae on a tree therefore do not predict widespread decline. The adults are small, wasp-like insects; the caterpillar-like feeding stage is more likely to attract attention. Spruces with thinning foliage deserve a closer look because several unrelated insects can cause similar damage.

sturnus-vulgaris.summary: European starling is the short-tailed, pointed-billed bird often walking briskly across a lawn or gathering in a noisy flock. Its dark feathers show green and purple reflections in good light, while fresh winter plumage carries many pale spots. Introduced to North America, it now uses farms, towns and other open landscapes extensively. It eats insects as well as fruit and grain, and nests inside cavities. Competition for nest sites and large concentrations around buildings or livestock feed are more useful concerns than the presence of a single bird.

lappula-squarrosa.summary: European stickseed is a rough, hairy annual whose tiny blue flowers give way to fruits armed with hooked prickles. Those fruits readily catch on clothing and animal coats, carrying seeds away from roadsides, fields and other disturbed ground. Plants may grow as summer annuals or start as autumn rosettes. A patch can return from seeds even after the standing plants disappear. Its presence is especially worth noticing along routes where people, pets or equipment can carry the fruits into cleaner ground.

quercus-cerris.summary: European turkey oak is a large deciduous tree from southern Europe and western Asia, often recognizable by the shaggy cups around its acorns. Planted trees can grow well beyond a garden's scale, reaching 20 m or more. Their leaves vary considerably, so a single unusually lobed leaf can be misleading. Look for the buds and acorns as well as the crown. A cultivated tree is not by itself evidence of harmful spread; seedlings establishing beyond planting sites provide more useful information about local behavior.

alisma-plantago-aquatica.summary: European water plantain grows at shallow-water margins, lifting broad leaves and branching flower stems above a basal clump. Small three-petaled flowers develop into rings of dry fruits that can float away. The name needs care in North America: older accounts used Alisma plantago-aquatica for plants now treated as native species such as A. triviale and A. subcordatum. A water plantain beside a pond therefore should not be assumed to be the introduced European species from its general appearance or an old label.

marsilea-quadrifolia.summary: European waterclover looks like a four-leaf clover growing in shallow water, but it is a fern. Four fan-shaped leaflets stand on slender stalks or float at the surface, while creeping underground stems connect the plants. It can also occupy exposed mud as water levels fall. Expansion within a pond is often vegetative. The clover-like leaves are a useful first clue, but several native waterclovers have a very similar appearance, so an unfamiliar patch should be documented before removal.

betula-pendula.summary: European white birch is a deciduous tree with pale bark, slender hanging twigs and small, sharply toothed leaves. Commonly planted forms include deeply cut leaves and strongly weeping branches. Its trunk changes with age: dark fissures can become prominent enough that an older tree looks much less white than a young one. A planted birch should be assessed for its actual local spread and health. In warm or dry settings, stress and bronze birch borer can be a more immediate concern than seedling establishment.

nymphaea-alba.summary: European white waterlily is a rooted aquatic perennial with rounded floating leaves and large flowers, usually white around a yellow center. It grows from substantial horizontal underground stems in the mud of still or slow water. Garden waterlilies complicate its identification: many cultivars contain ancestry from several species and may resemble this one closely. A white waterlily in a pond can therefore be a native species, a planted cultivar or European white waterlily; flower color alone does not settle the question.

lupinus-luteus.summary: European yellow lupine is a hairy annual with yellow pea-shaped flowers above leaves divided into finger-like leaflets. It has been cultivated as well as occurring wild in its Mediterranean home range, so a roadside plant may originate from a nearby planting. Flowers give way to densely hairy pods containing several seeds. The annual habit matters when considering spread: preventing seed production addresses its next generation, while the presence of a cultivated crop does not establish an ecological problem in every surrounding landscape.

pentaglottis-sempervirens.summary: Evergreen bugloss is a coarse-leaved perennial with small bright blue flowers and a deep, persistent root. It can remain as a dense clump in shaded gardens and escape into nearby disturbed ground. The flowers have pale centers and are visited by pollinating insects, but the plant's size and spread can make it unwelcome among smaller plants. Its other familiar name, green alkanet, refers to the same species. Removing only the leaves leaves its root system capable of producing another season's growth.

clematis-vitalba.summary: Despite its catalog name, evergreen clematis is a deciduous woody climber; Clematis vitalba usually loses its leaves in winter. It is also widely called old man's beard because the pale, feathery seed heads remain conspicuous after flowering. Established vines can climb high into trees and cover shrubs, reducing light and adding weight. Ground-trailing stems and discarded fragments can also establish. The scientific name is especially important here, since other clematis sold as evergreen vines are different species.

archips-fuscocupreanus.summary: Exotic leafroller moth is an East Asian moth whose caterpillars tie leaves and other soft plant parts together into feeding shelters. Apples, crabapples, pears and plums are among its hosts, although its host range is much broader. The visible damage comes from the caterpillars rather than the adult moth. In the northeastern United States it has one generation annually, overwintering as eggs on woody branches. Rolled leaves deserve inspection, but many native leafrollers create similar shelters and need different identification.

heliconia-latispatha.summary: Expanded lobsterclaw is a large tropical perennial with banana-like leaves and upright clusters of orange, yellow or red bracts. The conspicuous colored structures surround much smaller greenish flowers; they are not giant petals. Native to tropical America, it is cultivated for its appearance and has naturalized in parts of Hawai'i. A substantial clump can persist beyond the garden where it began. Knowing whether nearby plants were deliberately planted or have established independently is useful when documenting its local spread.

leontodon-autumnalis.summary: Fall dandelion is a perennial rosette plant that raises several yellow flower heads on branching stems. It often appears in grassland, lawns, road margins and other open ground, flowering later in the season than many familiar spring dandelions. The catalog uses Leontodon autumnalis; many modern references place the same species in Scorzoneroides as S. autumnalis. Its branching flower stems and small stem scales are more informative than the general dandelion-like flower. A scattered plant in managed turf is a different management situation from repeated establishment in a sensitive grassland.

dama-dama.summary: Fallow deer is a medium-sized deer with an unusually variable coat. The familiar form is brown with white spots, but dark and nearly white animals also occur, so spotting is not a dependable requirement. Mature males carry broad, flattened antlers. Introduced populations and captive herds occur far beyond the species' original range. They graze and browse in mixtures of woodland and open ground, and escaped animals can establish locally. A sighting should be interpreted with local herd history rather than assuming every deer of unusual color is wild or introduced.

digera-muricata.summary: False amaranth is an annual herb with slender flower clusters rising from the leaf joints. Its tiny flowers range from pale whitish pink to deeper red, so it can be easy to overlook among other field weeds. The plant occurs in cultivated and disturbed ground across parts of tropical Africa and Asia. A close examination of its small fruits is more useful than its resemblance to an amaranth. Local occurrence and establishment should be documented before assuming that one accidental arrival represents a persistent problem.

galium-mollugo.summary: False baby's breath, treated here in the traditional broad Galium mollugo sense, is a perennial bedstraw with narrow leaves arranged around the stem and many small white flowers. It can sprawl through surrounding vegetation in fields, hedges and disturbed places. Its name should not be confused with garden baby's breath, which belongs to another genus. The scientific name also needs care: Galium mollugo has been used broadly to include plants other floras call G. album. That difference affects records and identification, so a familiar common name does not establish which botanical concept was recorded.

chrysopogon-zizanioides.summary: False beardgrass is the tall clumping grass commonly known as vetiver, grown for its aromatic roots and for erosion-control plantings. Its dense upright leaves and deep roots make an established clump substantial even when it produces little seed. Cultivar identity matters: the sterile cultivar 'Sunshine' is widely used, but that does not mean every plant assigned to the species is sterile. A planted barrier, an abandoned clump and a seed-producing escape should therefore be recorded separately when assessing local spread.

pseudaulacaspis-cockerelli.summary: False oleander scale is a sap-feeding armored scale found on many ornamental plants, not just oleander. Its pale covers can look like flecks of white paint on leaves and green stems. Feeding may produce a yellow patch around each insect, and heavy infestations can weaken plants. The cover remains visible after the insect dies, so a plant with old scale marks is not necessarily undergoing active damage. Nursery movement is an important practical setting for inspection and early containment.

pseudococcus-nakaharai.summary: The catalog's false scale insect is Pseudococcus nakaharai, more specifically known as Nakahara mealybug. It is associated especially with cacti and can occur around their roots, making an infestation easy to miss during a quick inspection of the upper plant. Plant-trade interceptions show why cactus collections deserve careful checking before plants are shared. ITIS treats it as native to the continental US; interceptions and greenhouse occurrences do not establish that every domestic population is introduced.

sorbaria-sorbifolia.summary: False spiraea is a deciduous shrub that produces upright clusters of small white flowers above long leaves divided into many narrow leaflets. Its stems often arise in groups, and new shoots can appear beyond the original plant as root suckers. This habit can turn a single ornamental planting into a colony. The name resembles spiraea, but the compound leaves are an important clue that it belongs to Sorbaria. Local spread from a planted bed is more informative than the size of an individual shrub.

dittrichia-viscosa.summary: False yellowhead is a sticky, strongly scented perennial shrub with numerous yellow daisy-like flower heads. Older stems become woody near the base, helping distinguish a persistent plant from an annual yellow-flowered weed. It grows in disturbed places in its Mediterranean region and has become problematic in some introduced settings. Contact with its sticky oils can irritate skin. Its close relative stinkwort is also sticky and yellow-flowered, so an identification should include the base, leaves and flower size rather than scent alone.

ptilinus-pectinicornis.summary: Fan-bearing wood-borer is a small beetle whose males carry conspicuously branched antennae. Its larvae tunnel within hardwood, including felled timber and occasionally furniture, while adults consume little. Related evidence also records it in exposed dry wood of old broad-leaved trees. Small round exit holes can reveal a past infestation, but holes alone cannot show which beetle made them or whether insects remain active. The distinction matters before treating a building, a piece of furniture or dead wood outdoors.

euchiton-japonicus.summary: Father-and-child plant is a small perennial cudweed with green upper leaf surfaces and densely pale-haired undersides. Short creeping stems can link neighboring rosettes, while upright shoots carry tight clusters of tiny flower heads. Older floras may list it under Gnaphalium japonicum or related historical names. It is native in parts of Australasia, so a foreign source calling it native does not determine its status at a US observation. The useful first task is to distinguish it from the many superficially similar cudweeds.

bithynia-tentaculata.summary: Faucet snail is a small freshwater snail with a smooth brown shell and a hard lid that closes its opening. Introduced from Europe, it occurs in parts of the Great Lakes and other US waters. It can act as an intermediate host for parasites that harm waterfowl, making prevention of further movement important even though individual snails are easily overlooked. Mud, aquatic vegetation and wet equipment can carry it between sites. Established populations are much harder to address than snails caught during equipment inspection.

melanoides-turriculus.summary: Fawn melania is a slender freshwater snail recorded from Florida springs and streams. Its name carries an important uncertainty: some specialists treat it as a form of the variable red-rimmed melania, Melanoides tuberculata, while others provisionally keep it separate. A shell matching the traditional description therefore does not settle the species question. Published accounts describe introduced Florida populations, but their ecological effects are poorly documented. Possible competition with native snails should not be presented as a demonstrated impact of this particular taxon.

celosia-argentea.summary: Feather cockscomb is an annual grown for upright flower heads that retain their color and texture as they dry. The species includes several cultivated forms: feathery garden selections differ from plants with narrow, silvery or pink flower spikes. Escaped plants can occur in disturbed ground and cultivated fields. Each small flower has papery parts surrounding a seed capsule, so a fading head may still be producing seed. Its presence outside a flower bed is worth documenting, but an ornamental escape does not by itself demonstrate serious ecological harm.

azolla-pinnata.summary: Feathered mosquitofern is a tiny floating fern whose branching shoots form triangular pieces at the water surface. It can multiply into dense mats, shading water beneath them. A close association with nitrogen-fixing bacteria helps explain why this small fern can grow vigorously without obtaining all its nitrogen from the surrounding water. Plants may be green or reddish, so color alone is unreliable. Because other mosquitoferns look similar, a floating red or green mat should be identified before it is reported as this introduced species.

cenchrus-longisetus.summary: Feathertop is a perennial grass grown for soft-looking flower heads above arching leaves. The many long bristles give mature heads a broad, pale bottlebrush outline. Outside cultivation it can establish in disturbed places, and its bristled seed units can travel on animals, clothing, and equipment. Garden waste and deliberate planting are avoidable ways to move it further. A decorative grass beside a road still needs identification: several related fountain grasses have similar heads, and their appearance changes as the flowers mature.

dysaphis-foeniculus.summary: Fennel aphid feeds on members of the carrot family, including fennel and related cultivated herbs. Colonies of small sap-feeding insects may be noticed before the individual aphids can be identified. The name deserves care: close relatives share similar appearances, and fennel itself can host more than one aphid. Specialist accounts describe this aphid from temperate regions around the world. Knowing the host plant, the part being fed on, and the colony's appearance is more useful than naming it from a distant photograph alone.

equus-caballus.summary: Feral horse refers to a domestic horse or its descendants living without routine human care. Free-ranging herds can occupy grasslands, marshes, and other open habitats, but their ownership and management differ among places. A horse outside a fence may also be a recently escaped animal. These distinctions matter when deciding whom to contact. Horses are social grazers, often moving and feeding in groups. Their familiarity to people should not be mistaken for an invitation to approach, feed, or handle them.

feral-swine.summary: Feral swine are free-ranging pigs, including descendants of domestic pigs, introduced wild boar, and their crosses. Their rooting can turn over soil and vegetation while they search for food, damaging crops and natural habitats. Groups may be present well before a landowner sees an animal directly. Tracks, wallows, and repeatedly disturbed ground are useful early clues. Because pigs move across property boundaries, effective responses usually require neighboring landowners and wildlife staff to work together rather than treating each sighting as an isolated problem.

idiopterus-nephrelepidis.summary: Fern aphid is a small dark aphid associated with many kinds of ferns, including plants grown indoors and in greenhouses. Colonies often hide on the undersides of fronds. Connecticut's experiment station reports that it seldom causes severe injury on Boston fern, although other observations document distorted leaves on infested plants. This makes inspection more useful than assuming every colony requires treatment. The contrasting pale legs and patterned wings of adults can help draw attention to an insect that is otherwise easy to overlook.

pinnaspis-aspidistrae.summary: Fern scale is an armored scale insect found on ferns and a range of other ornamental plants. The white covers of developing males may be conspicuous against a dark frond, while brown female covers are easier to miss. Feeding can leave pale spots and weaken heavily infested plants. The covers remain after an insect dies or an adult male leaves, so visible specks do not all represent living pests. Moving infested plants or cut foliage is an important way to carry this insect into a new collection.

catapodium-rigidum.summary: Ferngrass is a small annual grass with stiff flowering branches that can resemble a miniature branching spray. It grows in dry, open, disturbed places such as tracksides, gardens, gravel, and sandy ground. Despite its common name, it is a flowering grass rather than a fern. It has become naturalized outside its original Mediterranean and western Asian range. A few plants in a path do not establish a serious ecological impact, but seed-bearing plants can be worth removing where they are spreading into a managed garden or restoration site.

achillea-filipendulina.summary: Fernleaf yarrow is a tall perennial grown for dense, flat clusters of yellow flowers above divided green leaves. Its stiff stems and long-lasting flower heads make it familiar in gardens and dried arrangements. It has naturalized beyond cultivation in parts of North America, but that does not make every planting a spreading problem. University horticultural accounts distinguish its relatively restrained clumping growth from more aggressive forms of common yarrow. Observing whether seedlings or expanding clumps actually appear beyond a bed is a useful starting point.

tanacetum-parthenium.summary: Feverfew is an aromatic perennial with clusters of small white-and-yellow flower heads. It is grown as an ornamental and has a long history as a cultivated herb, but garden plants can also seed into nearby open ground. Its divided leaves give a much fuller outline than the flowers alone suggest. Cultivars include double-flowered forms that look different from the familiar small daisies. Self-seeding can be vigorous under favorable conditions, so whether it stays within a planting depends partly on how spent heads and volunteers are managed.

convolvulus-arvensis.summary: Field bindweed is a perennial vine that trails over bare ground or twines through neighboring plants. White or pink trumpet-shaped flowers can conceal the persistence of the plant beneath them: established roots produce new shoots, and pieces moved in soil can start another patch. Seeds also remain a long-term source of seedlings. It is a troublesome weed in gardens and agricultural ground, where a single round of cutting or pulling seldom finishes the job. Early recognition is much easier to act on than a deeply established infestation.

bromus-arvensis.summary: Field brome is an annual grass with an open, branching flower cluster and slender, awned flower units. It occurs in fields, roadsides, and other disturbed places and has also been grown as a cover crop. Its similarity to other bromes makes a mature flowering plant much easier to identify than a patch of green leaves. Introduced populations may behave differently among habitats, so the name alone does not establish the scale of a local problem. Preventing seed movement is a reasonable focus where it is unwanted.

soliva-sessilis.summary: Field burrweed is a low annual of lawns and other closely managed ground. Its small green flowers are easy to miss, but the sharp points on mature fruits are difficult to ignore under bare feet. In warm-temperate lawns it commonly grows through the cooler part of the year and produces burs in spring. Plants may die as weather warms while the hardened burs remain. That makes finding the young plants more useful than waiting until a lawn has become uncomfortable to walk on.

trifolium-campestre.summary: Field clover is a small yellow-flowered annual whose leaves have three leaflets. Its compact flower heads make it easy to confuse with several other low legumes, especially before the flowers are fully open. It is widely naturalized, including in North America, and can occur among other plants in disturbed grassy places. A yellow clover in a lawn is not automatically evidence of a damaging infestation. Identification and the purpose of the site should guide whether to leave it, monitor it, or prevent further seed production.

myosotis-arvensis.summary: Field forget-me-not is a short-lived herb with tiny blue flowers carried above hairy leaves. As a flowering stem lengthens, older flowers give way to small fruits lower down. It commonly grows in cultivated or otherwise disturbed open ground. Plants in dry, exposed places can be much smaller than those in favorable conditions, which makes overall height a weak identification feature. Its flowers are smaller than those of the familiar woodland forget-me-not, but mature fruiting structures provide useful confirmation when several species are possible.

brassica-rapa.summary: Field mustard belongs to a variable species that also includes familiar cultivated vegetables and oilseed forms. Escaped or volunteer plants can flower in fields, roadsides, and disturbed ground, producing clusters of yellow flowers followed by slender pods. A flowering mustard is therefore not necessarily a separate wild species from a nearby crop. Several related Brassica species look much alike and can complicate identification. The useful first step is to record the whole plant, leaves, flowers, and pods rather than assign the name from a yellow roadside display.

thlaspi-arvense.summary: Field pennycress is an annual mustard best recognized when its broad, flat seedpods develop. Small white flowers continue near the top of the stem while the round pods mature below. Plants may begin in autumn or spring, and early seed production can let them replenish a patch before other garden or field work begins. It grows in agricultural and disturbed ground. The name reflects the coinlike fruits, which are much more distinctive than the young rosette of leaves.

sonchus-arvensis.summary: Field sowthistle is a perennial with yellow, dandelionlike flower heads on upright leafy stems. Its creeping roots can produce new shoots, allowing a patch to persist and expand even when flowering stems are removed. Wind-carried seeds provide another route to new ground. It can compete strongly with crops, especially in dense stands. The plant resembles annual sowthistles, but its persistent underground system changes what successful management requires: preventing seed alone will not eliminate an established patch.

ficus-thonningii.summary: Ficus thonningii, treated here in the broad African species sense, is an African fig tree that can develop a broad crown, multiple stems, and roots descending from branches. Some plants begin growing on another tree before their roots reach the ground. The name has also been applied to several close relatives, including trees called Ficus burkei and Ficus petersii in other treatments. That history matters when reading older records or identifying a cultivated tree. A familiar common name or nursery label alone does not establish which botanical concept a record represents.

lepidosaphes-conchiformis.summary: Fig scale is a small armored insect that feeds on leaves, twigs, and fruit. On figs, feeding on the fruit surface can leave raised, warty areas that reduce quality. The insect's protective cover changes in color and shape with its location and stage, so an infestation need not look uniform. In California fig production, a tiny parasitic wasp often keeps populations under control. That makes preserving natural enemies and checking for active damage more useful than automatically spraying every scale-covered twig.

singhiella-simplex.summary: Fig whitefly is a tiny sap-feeding insect best known for yellowing and leaf loss on ornamental Ficus trees and hedges. A disturbed plant may release a cloud of adults, but an active infestation can also remain when few flying insects are visible. Immature whiteflies stay against leaf surfaces and are easily overlooked. Heavy populations can cause dieback and slow young-tree growth. Leaf loss alone is not a diagnosis, however, and a bare hedge should be checked for live stages and other possible causes before treatment or severe pruning.

chenopodium-ficifolium.summary: Figleaf goosefoot is an annual of cultivated and disturbed ground, with inconspicuous green flower clusters rather than showy petals. Its name refers to the shape of its leaves, not to a relationship with fig trees. Middle leaves commonly have a long central section and two shorter lobes near the base. It resembles common lambsquarters closely enough that records based only on a casual glance may be unreliable. Mature leaves and seeds together give a much better basis for identification, especially where several goosefoot species grow together.

fimbristylis-littoralis.summary: Fimbry is a small tufted sedge associated with wet or seasonally wet ground, including river margins and cultivated wet fields. Numerous tiny brown flower clusters form a branching head above narrow basal leaves. Older publications often call related plants Fimbristylis miliacea, but that name has been applied inconsistently to more than one taxonomic concept. Current US wetland references use Fimbristylis littoralis, while preserving the older name as a historical misapplication. Local identification should therefore be tied to a modern flora rather than to the common name alone.

epidendrum-radicans.summary: Fire star orchid grows on long, leafy stems that lean into surrounding plants. Its orange flowers have a yellow center and gather at the ends of the stems. Native from Mexico to Colombia, it is widely grown as an ornamental and has escaped cultivation in several tropical regions. It often occupies disturbed ground, roadsides, and grassland. Its conspicuous roots help the stems hold onto nearby vegetation; a planting can occupy more space than its small flowers suggest.

odontonema-tubaeforme.summary: Firespike is a tropical shrub with broad, glossy leaves and upright clusters of red tubular flowers. Descriptions of Odontonema tubaeforme place its origin in Mexico and Central America. It can grow roughly 2 m tall or more in favorable conditions and is cultivated for its conspicuous flowers. Escapes have been associated with discarded garden material. The name firespike is also applied to other Odontonema plants, so a familiar garden name does not by itself establish this species.

senecio-linearifolius.summary: Fireweed groundsel is an Australian perennial herb or small shrub with clusters of small yellow daisy-like heads. It often grows in relatively moist forests and can become conspicuous after fire or other disturbance. Plants reach around 1.5 m, with leaves that vary considerably among recognized varieties. That variability matters: a broad, toothed leaf and a narrow, nearly smooth-edged leaf can belong to the same species. Its presence in a species catalog should not turn an Australian native forest plant into a universal removal target.

cercopagis-pengoi.summary: Fishhook waterflea is a tiny predatory crustacean that lives in open lake water. Its body is nearly transparent, but its black eye and long, hooked tail can stand out under magnification. It eats other small drifting animals, potentially competing with young fish for food. Introduced populations occur in the Great Lakes region. Anglers may first notice tangled clusters on fishing lines or other submerged equipment rather than individual animals. Movement of water and wet equipment can carry it between lakes.

tephrosia-purpurea.summary: Fishpoison is a low shrub in the pea family, with many small leaflets, pale to purple flowers, and slender seed pods. It occurs widely in tropical regions and has a long history of cultivation and use. In Hawaii, accounts associate its arrival with early Polynesian settlement. The common name refers to historical use of the roots to stun fish; it is not an invitation to put the plant into a pond or stream. A planted specimen and an unwanted spreading population require different decisions.

nephrolepis-falcata.summary: Fishtail swordfern is an ornamental fern whose arching fronds carry leaflets with divided tips. The repeated forks give the frond its familiar fishtail appearance. It comes from tropical Asia and the western Pacific and is grown in gardens and containers. Florida extension records it escaping cultivation but explicitly distinguishes that history from the invasive status of other introduced swordferns. Its presence therefore calls for correct identification and attention to local spread, rather than assuming that every ornamental fern needs removal.

tamarix-chinensis.summary: Five-stamen tamarisk belongs to the saltcedar group of shrubs and small trees. Slender branches carry tiny scale-like leaves and clusters of small pinkish flowers. Tamarisks can occupy riverbanks, floodplains, and saline ground, where established stands may be difficult to remove. In North America, Tamarix chinensis and T. ramosissima have hybridized extensively. Many familiar saltcedar stands therefore cannot be confidently assigned to a single species from their outline or flower color.

bassia-hyssopifolia.summary: Fivehorn smotherweed is an annual with narrow, softly hairy leaves and tiny flowers that become hooked fruits. It often grows on disturbed or salty ground, including fields, roadsides, and seasonal wetland margins. A mature plant can reach about 1.2 m. The hooks are small enough to miss without a close look, but they give this otherwise inconspicuous plant its name. Dense growth can interfere with desirable vegetation, and livestock should not be allowed to consume large quantities.

urocystis-tritici.summary: Flag smut of wheat is a fungal disease that damages leaves and shoots rather than simply replacing the grain head with spores. Infected plants can be stunted and produce excessive shoots with few or no heads. A study of three DNA regions supports Urocystis tritici as the wheat pathogen, distinct from the narrower U. agropyri concept. Some extension guidance still uses the older, broader agropyri name. Keep that distinction when matching a laboratory result to a species record.

gloriosa-superba.summary: Flame lily climbs with the curling tips of its leaves and bears striking red, orange, and yellow flowers. Its six narrow flower segments bend backward above spreading stamens. The stems die back seasonally, while thick underground parts remain alive and produce new growth. Native to Africa and Asia, it has escaped gardens in warm regions, including coastal habitats in Australia. Every part is poisonous if eaten, including the underground parts that can be mistaken for edible roots.

koelreuteria-elegans-ssp-formosana.summary: Flamegold is a tree grown for yellow flower clusters followed by inflated pink to rose-colored capsules. The papery fruits later turn brown and release dark seeds. This profile concerns the Taiwanese subspecies formosana, rather than the closely related Fijian subspecies. In warm landscapes it can produce many seedlings and has escaped cultivation in the southeastern United States. The showy fruit is a useful recognition feature, but preventing seedlings from establishing beyond a planted tree is the practical management priority.

pyrostegia-venusta.summary: Flamevine is a fast-growing woody climber with clusters of long orange flowers. It grips supports with branched tendrils and can extend over fences, shrubs, and trees. Native to South America, it is cultivated in warm regions and has escaped gardens in Florida and eastern Australia. Florida accounts often note its conspicuous cool-season bloom. Its vigor is the main practical concern in a garden: a small rooted cutting can eventually occupy much more space than the original planting.

aclerda-takahashii.summary: Flat grass scale is a sap-feeding insect associated especially with sugarcane. Colonies can be hidden between the stem and the wrapping leaf sheath, so a plant may carry insects that are not visible from the outside. Young females are pale, while older females become elongated and dark reddish brown. A Florida pest alert documented it on energy cane in 2016 and emphasized that its economic effects were poorly known. Finding scales calls for identification, not an assumption of severe crop loss.

sida-linifolia.summary: Flaxleaf fanpetals is a slender, upright mallow with unusually narrow leaves and pale flowers marked by a dark center. It grows in open tropical habitats, including savannas and disturbed ground. Its native range includes parts of tropical America and Africa, so occurrence outside a garden is not automatically evidence of a harmful introduction. The narrow foliage makes it less obviously mallow-like than broad-leaved relatives, but the small segmented fruit and central column of stamens help reveal the relationship.

abutilon-hirtum.summary: Florida keys indian mallow is a hairy herb or soft-stemmed shrub with broad, heart-shaped leaves. Yellow to orange flowers usually have a reddish or purple center, followed by rounded fruits made of numerous joined segments. Despite its geographic common name, the plant has a much wider tropical distribution. Young shoots may feel sticky because they bear gland-tipped hairs. These details distinguish it more usefully than the general impression of a yellow-flowered mallow.

chrysomphalus-aonidum.summary: Florida red scale is a small armored insect that feeds on leaves, green twigs, and fruit. Its circular coverings can look like dark spots stuck to the plant. Heavy infestations may cause yellowing and leaf loss, but natural enemies often keep populations in check. Citrus, palms, and many ornamentals can host it. The common name does not mean that every red or brown scale found in Florida belongs to this species; several armored scales are very similar.

emilia-fosbergii.summary: Florida tasselflower is a fast-growing annual with small pink to red flower heads above its leaves. The heads later produce many lightweight fruits with fine white hairs that carry them on the wind. It is common in warm disturbed places and can become a nuisance in nursery containers and landscape beds. Its name is easy to confuse with other tasselflowers, and color varies enough that a red bloom alone is not a dependable identification.

glycosmis-parviflora.summary: Flower axistree is a small evergreen shrub or tree in the citrus family. It bears small white flowers and rounded fruits that change from pale colors to red as they ripen. Its leaves vary: some have only one leaflet, while others carry several. Native to parts of eastern and southeastern Asia, it is cultivated as an ornamental and has escaped in southern Florida. The berries can attract birds, making seedlings beyond a planted shrub worth checking.

hibiscus-trionum.summary: Flower of an hour is a branching annual mallow with pale flowers and a dark purple center. Each bloom lasts only briefly, but the plant remains recognizable by its deeply divided leaves and the inflated, veined covering around its fruit. It was introduced as an ornamental and now grows in fields, gardens, and other disturbed places across much of the United States. It reproduces by seed, so removing plants before their capsules mature is more useful than waiting for a long flowering display.

butomus-umbellatus.summary: Flowering Rush is a wetland perennial with narrow upright leaves and rounded clusters of pink flowers. In deeper water it may stay submerged and never flower, making established patches less conspicuous. It spreads through pieces and small buds from its underground stems, and some populations also produce viable seed. Dense growth can crowd shoreline vegetation and obstruct access to water. Small fragments carried on equipment or released during poorly planned removal can establish another patch.

venturia-saliciperda.summary: This forest pathogen causes willow scab, a disease of young leaves and shoots that is most noticeable during wet spring weather. Leaves brown, wither, and fall soon after they emerge, and small twigs may die back. The fungus can survive in infected twigs and fallen leaves, allowing rain to spread spores when new growth appears. Willow scab may occur alongside black canker, so a badly blighted willow can have more than one disease at once.

eucalyptus-tereticornis.summary: Forest redgum is a large Australian eucalyptus with smooth bark that sheds in patches or plates. Mature trees carry long narrow leaves and clusters of white flowers, followed by small woody capsules. It is widely planted outside its native range. The name refers to the horn-like caps on the flower buds in typical forms, a feature worth examining before the flowers open. Several subspecies and related redgums share much of its appearance, so bark alone is a weak identification.

pyracantha-koidzumii.summary: Formosa firethorn is a thorny evergreen or partly evergreen shrub with white spring flowers and dense clusters of orange-red fruit. It is native to Taiwan and widely grown as a hedge or barrier. Birds eat the fruit, and plants sometimes persist or escape beyond old garden sites. Its sharp branch tips make close inspection and pruning awkward, but the shape of the leaves is a useful way to distinguish it from other cultivated firethorns.

lilium-formosanum.summary: Formosa lily sends a leafy upright stem from an underground bulb and bears large white trumpet-shaped flowers. The outside of a flower may be flushed purple, followed by an upright capsule that dries and releases lightweight seeds. Native to Taiwan, it is cultivated widely and has escaped into disturbed ground in several warm regions. The stems die back seasonally, but the bulb remains alive. Removing only the visible flowering stem therefore does not remove the whole plant.

coptotermes-formosanus.summary: Formosan Termite is a wood-feeding social insect whose large colonies can damage buildings and trees. Colonies include pale workers, defensive soldiers, and winged reproductive adults. Although often associated with soil, it can also build nests above ground where moisture is available. Mud shelter tubes and discarded wings are useful warning signs, but old damage alone does not establish that termites are still active. Movement of infested timbers can carry colonies to new places.

membraniporopsis-tubigera.summary: This fouling bryozoan is a colony of tiny animals that share a branching, pale cream structure. Young colonies spread across a surface; older growth rises into thin, curling fronds. Each animal filters food from the water with a crown of tentacles. Large deposits have washed onto beaches in Brazil, where researchers studied blooms involving this bryozoan and other organisms. Its original native range remains uncertain. Historical records from Florida and the Gulf region do not establish that it is introduced or causing damage at every U.S. site.

hydroides-sanctaecrucis.summary: This marine worm lives inside a hard white tube attached to a submerged surface. It extends a tentacled feeding crown into the water, then withdraws and closes the opening with a specialized plug. It belongs to the western Atlantic fauna, including parts of the U.S. coast, and has also been recorded outside that range. A Taiwanese study found it among fouling organisms on ropes and mussels. Boat and equipment movement matters because attached animals can travel with the surfaces they occupy.

livistona-chinensis.summary: Fountain palm grows slowly from a broad cluster of leaves into a palm with one trunk and a rounded crown. The name refers to the hanging tips of its fan-shaped leaves. Young plants may remain close to the ground for years, which can make an eventual tree look like a shrub in a garden bed. It is widely planted for its foliage, but seedlings outside cultivation deserve attention where local guidance identifies an escape risk. Its appearance and mature size depend strongly on growing conditions.

russelia-equisetiformis.summary: Fountainbush makes a low, spreading shrub with green stems that rise and then arch toward the ground. Slender red flowers hang along those stems; yellow and salmon garden forms also occur. Hummingbirds visit the flowers, and flowering can continue through much of the year in warm conditions. Native to Mexico, it is often planted along walls or in large containers. It can root where arching stems touch soil, so a planted clump may gradually occupy more space. Garden vigor alone does not establish that it harms surrounding habitats.

polycarpon-tetraphyllum.summary: Fourleaf manyseed is a small annual weed that can be easy to overlook until its branching stems carry many tiny fruits. It grows in disturbed ground, gardens and other open places rather than forming a tall, conspicuous stand. The leaves often sit in groups of four around a stem, giving the plant its name. The flowers are minute and pale, and the seed capsules are more useful than blossom color for recognizing a mature plant. Although usually annual, some regional accounts describe plants lasting longer.

aulacorthum-solani.summary: Foxglove aphid feeds on many plants, not just foxgloves. In vegetables and greenhouse crops it can remain hidden among young leaves, where small scattered populations are easily missed. Its short life cycle allows numbers to rise quickly, and winged adults can move to new plants. Feeding and the viruses it can transmit are separate concerns: finding aphids does not establish that a plant has a virus. Careful inspection of fresh growth is more useful than waiting for a large, obvious colony.

setaria-italica.summary: Foxtail millet is a cultivated annual grass grown for grain and birdseed. Plants escaping from cultivation can appear around feeding stations, disturbed soil and discarded seed. The dense, bristly flower head gives it the familiar foxtail shape, but that outline is shared by several wild grasses. This profile treats cultivated foxtail millet separately from green foxtail, Setaria viridis. Their close relationship explains why older sources sometimes place them together. A volunteer millet plant does not by itself demonstrate a damaging local invasion.

cordia-dichotoma.summary: Fragrant manjack is a tropical tree with broad leaves, small white flowers and soft fruit around a hard stone. Its sticky fruit pulp explains alternate names such as glue berry. Flowers form branching clusters near the ends of shoots, while young plants may have more strongly toothed leaves than mature trees. It is native across a broad part of Asia and the western Pacific region and is planted elsewhere. A tree's presence outside cultivation should be assessed locally; this description does not imply that all planted or naturalized trees are harmful.

genista-monspessulana.summary: French broom is a leafy shrub whose yellow pea-shaped flowers can make an established patch conspicuous in spring. It keeps many three-part leaves through the year, unlike the comparatively bare appearance of some other brooms. In affected western U.S. habitats, dense stands compete with other vegetation and complicate restoration. Mature plants produce abundant seed, while cut plants can resprout from the crown. That combination makes early removal and follow-up more useful than a single round of cutting.

linum-trigynum.summary: French flax is a slender annual with small yellow flowers held above narrow leaves. It often blends into sparse grass or disturbed ground until the flowers open. The plant grows from seed and finishes with small rounded capsules, rather than forming a woody shrub. Its native range includes the Mediterranean region, and it occurs as an introduced plant in some other regions. The name has also been confused with yellow-flowered ornamental shrubs, so the annual growth form matters when checking a record.

musa-x-paradisiaca.summary: French plantain is used for a group of cultivated bananas, while Musa x paradisiaca covers a broader hybrid background involving Musa acuminata and M. balbisiana. These plants form clumps of large leaves on stems made from tightly wrapped leaf bases. New shoots emerge beside older stems, allowing a planting to persist after a fruiting stem finishes. French plantains form a narrower cultivated group within that hybrid background. The group name does not establish a particular clone.

tamarix-gallica.summary: French tamarisk is a deciduous shrub or small tree with slender reddish-brown branches, tiny scale-like leaves and clusters of pink to whitish flowers. It has been planted well beyond its western Mediterranean homeland, including coastal and dry landscapes. Its fine leaves can give a branch a soft outline, but close inspection reveals ordinary small leaves rather than needles. Several tamarisks are difficult to distinguish, and older records may use names broadly. Identifying the actual species matters before attaching local impact records or a management plan to it.

fredericella-sultana.summary: This freshwater bryozoan forms small branching colonies on submerged surfaces. Each branch contains tiny feeding animals, which extend a circular crown of tentacles into the water. It can occur in water-system fouling, but a colony is not automatically a sign of damaged water quality. The species also participates in the life cycle of a parasite associated with kidney disease in salmonid fish. That association does not mean every colony is infected. Older North American records require particular care because some were later reassigned to Fredericella indica.

lophopodella-carteri.summary: This freshwater bryozoan consists of many tiny animals living together in a soft, clear to yellowish colony. It attaches to submerged wood and other surfaces, where the animals extend tentacles to collect food from the water. Colonies are small enough to escape notice among other aquatic growth. The species also makes durable resting structures that can survive after the soft colony is gone. It has records outside its Asian native range, but occurrence and documented local harm are separate questions.

ruta-chalepensis.summary: Fringed rue is a small, woody-based plant with divided blue-green leaves and clusters of yellow flowers. The petal edges carry fine fringes, which explain the common name and provide a useful clue when the plant is blooming. It is grown in gardens and occurs beyond cultivation in some regions. The foliage has a strong smell, but rubbing it is an unsuitable identification test: contact followed by sunlight can injure skin. Its history of herbal use does not make it safe to eat or handle casually.

fuchsia-hybrida.summary: Garden fuchsias sold as Fuchsia hybrida are a varied group of ornamental hybrids, rather than one uniform wild species. Some grow upright, while others trail from baskets or containers. Their hanging flowers combine a conspicuous outer set of sepals with inner petals, often in contrasting colors. Single and double flowers occur, and plants differ in their tolerance of heat and cold. A garden label or cultivar name can therefore be more informative than the broad hybrid name. This profile does not transfer the behavior of a particular wild fuchsia to every garden hybrid.

aculops-fuchsiae.summary: Fuchsia gall mite is a minute plant-feeding mite that lives among hairs and folds of fuchsia growth. Its feeding makes leaves and growing tips thicken, twist and form irregular swollen growth. Blossoms can also be affected, reducing a plant's display. The mites are much harder to see than the damage they cause, and they move onto fresh growth as a plant develops. Infested cuttings and plants are an important way they reach new gardens. Susceptibility varies substantially among fuchsia species and cultivars.

ophiostoma-piliferum.summary: Ophiostoma piliferum is one of several fungi associated with discoloration inside sapwood. Its microscopic growth can contribute to the blue, gray or dark staining seen in logs and lumber. Such staining can reduce a board's value even when the main concern is appearance. It should not be confused automatically with wood decay or with every other tree disease caused by a related fungus. Laboratory studies have also used nonpigmented strains of this species, illustrating why a fungus name does not predict the color or behavior of every strain.

attagenus-pellio.summary: Fur carpet beetle larvae feed on animal-derived materials such as wool, fur and feathers. They can damage clothing, stored skins and natural-history collections, especially in quiet places where debris accumulates. Adults have a different way of life: they can fly and visit flowers. Finding one adult near a window therefore calls for inspection rather than proving that every textile is infested. Bird-associated debris and concealed animal material can support larvae, so locating the food source is central to managing an indoor problem.

anobium-punctatum.summary: Furniture beetle spends most of its damaging life as a larva tunneling inside seasoned wood. The small round holes people notice are usually exits made by adults, after development has already occurred within the timber. Furniture, floorboards and structural wood can be affected, particularly where moisture favors the insect.
