Old holes can remain long after an infestation ends, so their presence alone does not prove current activity. A useful inspection looks for fresh evidence and the conditions that allowed the attack.

aeromonas-salmonicida.summary: Aeromonas salmonicida is a bacterium associated with serious fish disease. The typical subspecies causes furunculosis in salmon and trout, while other forms can cause ulcers and illness in a wider range of fish. Some infected fish carry the organism without obvious external signs. Outbreaks can therefore involve both visibly sick fish and apparently healthy carriers. The catalog name covers the bacterial species, not just one strain or one pattern of disease, and the risks differ with the fish, strain and conditions.

fusarium-oxysporum-f-sp-canariensis.summary: This specialized form of Fusarium causes a lethal wilt primarily associated with Canary Island date palm, Phoenix canariensis. It colonizes the palm's water-conducting tissues, and symptoms commonly begin in the oldest living leaves before progressing upward. A palm can carry the fungus before recognizable symptoms appear. Contaminated pruning tools are an important route between palms, making pruning hygiene relevant even when a tree looks healthy. The name does not cover every Fusarium disease of palms or the different wilt diseases of commercial edible date palms.

cyperus-pilosus.summary: Fuzzy flatsedge is a wet-ground sedge with narrow leaves and branching clusters of flattened flower units. The name refers to tiny stiff hairs on the axis within those clusters, not a conspicuously furry leaf surface. It grows in wetlands, muddy margins and rice-field settings, and Flora of North America records it as introduced from eastern Asia. Plants can spread through short creeping stems as well as seed. Like many sedges, it is easiest to identify when mature flower and fruit structures are present.

fowlpox-virus.summary: FWPV is the catalog abbreviation for fowlpox virus, a cause of disease especially in chickens and turkeys. Infection can produce scabbed skin lesions, or a more serious form involving the mouth and upper breathing passages. Mosquitoes can carry virus between birds, and contaminated material can also spread it through damaged skin. Fowlpox belongs to a larger group of avian poxviruses; a pox-like lesion on any wild bird does not automatically establish this exact virus. Prevention combines flock hygiene, mosquito reduction and an appropriate vaccination plan.

contarinia-nasturtii.summary: The gall midge in this entry is swede midge, a tiny fly whose larvae feed around the growing points of cabbage-family plants. Broccoli, cauliflower, kale and related crops can develop twisted leaves, brown scars or multiple stems after feeding damages the central shoot. A young heading crop may never form a usable head. The adults are inconspicuous, and the larvae hide within tightly folded growth, so damage often attracts attention first. Soil beneath affected crops can carry resting stages into later seasons.

leptocybe-invasa.summary: This tiny wasp develops inside swellings on young eucalyptus growth. The larvae feed within the plant rather than chewing exposed leaves, and repeated attacks can distort shoots and slow the growth of seedlings and nursery trees. Susceptibility differs among eucalyptus species. A gall on a eucalyptus is worth checking, but it does not by itself identify this wasp or show that a mature tree is in danger.

galinsoga-parviflora.summary: Smallflower galinsoga is a short-lived weed of vegetable beds, nurseries, and other regularly disturbed soil. Its flowers are tiny, but plants can set seed quickly enough to produce repeated generations during a growing season. Letting a few plants mature can therefore undo much of a season's weeding. It is especially useful to recognize this species while it is small, before seed heads blend into the surrounding crop.

aristolochia-ringens.summary: Gaping Dutchman's pipe is a tropical American climbing vine grown for its unusually shaped flowers. It can climb through other vegetation or sprawl across it, and escaped plants deserve attention in warm climates. Florida's assessment identifies a high invasion risk; that is a regional assessment, not evidence that every planting throughout the country is invasive. Its striking flowers should not be taken as a reason to introduce it into natural areas.

centaurea-cyanus.summary: Cornflower, also called bachelor's button, is a familiar garden annual that also grows along roads, railways and field edges. It spreads by seed and can reappear outside the place where it was planted. Its presence in a species catalog does not mean it has the same impacts as the more aggressive perennial knapweeds. When recording it, distinguish an intentional flower strip from plants growing and reproducing without cultivation.

cosmos-bipinnatus.summary: Garden cosmos is an annual flower that readily produces seedlings around plantings. Escaped plants occur along roads and in disturbed fields, but a colorful roadside patch may also have been deliberately sown. This distinction matters when documenting its spread. Garden varieties differ greatly in height and flower form, so an escaped plant may not look exactly like a seed-packet photograph.

cucumis-sativus.summary: Garden cucumber is a warm-season crop that may also appear as a volunteer near gardens, compost or discarded fruit. A plant outside a bed is not automatically an established invasive population: note whether it persists and produces new plants without being replanted. Cultivars range from long climbing vines to compact bush forms, and fruit shape varies considerably.

heliotropium-arborescens.summary: Garden heliotrope is a fragrant South American ornamental, often grown as summer bedding where winters are cold. In frost-free conditions it can live as a small shrub. Its scent and purple flowers make it recognizable in gardens, but the sweet smell does not mean the plant is safe to eat. A record of a cultivated specimen should be kept separate from evidence that it has escaped and established nearby.

lactuca-sativa.summary: Cultivated lettuce sometimes grows beyond vegetable beds, especially on compost heaps and disturbed ground. Once it sends up a flowering stalk, it can look very different from the leafy crop sold for salads. The presence of a stray lettuce plant is not, by itself, evidence of substantial ecological harm. Recording whether plants are tended, recently discarded, or reproducing on their own helps explain what an observation means.

atriplex-hortensis.summary: Garden orache is a tall annual leaf vegetable that can also occur outside cultivation. Its small flowers are easy to overlook, but a mature plant carries many thin, papery fruit coverings. Some garden forms are reddish or purple, while others are green. Because several native and introduced oraches look alike, an unfamiliar plant should not be assigned to garden orache from leaf color alone.

rheum-rhabarbarum.summary: Garden rhubarb is a long-lived vegetable that returns from a substantial underground crown. A clump beside an old home or garden may be a surviving planting rather than a newly spreading population. Garden rhubarbs have a complicated cultivated history, and references use several scientific names for them. Rheum rhabarbarum is commonly used for cultivated hybrids as well as the parental species; a photograph alone may not resolve the ancestry of a garden clone.

rumex-acetosa.summary: Common sorrel is a perennial of fields and roadsides, also grown as a leafy herb. It returns from a persistent rootstock and carries reddish flower clusters above its leaves. Several other sorrels share this general appearance. Understanding which one is present matters more than the common name: some are native, and their habitat and growth habits differ.

rumex-thyrsiflorus.summary: Narrow-leaved sorrel is a perennial Eurasian plant recorded on disturbed ground, roadsides and open grassy sites in parts of North America. It has often been mistaken for common sorrel, so older names and records need care. A well-documented photograph of the mature plant is more useful than a report based only on a few narrow leaves.

thymus-vulgaris.summary: Common thyme is a small woody herb grown for its aromatic leaves. It favors sunny, well-drained ground and can persist around old plantings. It is not interchangeable with every creeping thyme sold for ground cover. A garden clump or occasional escape does not establish that it is causing ecological harm, so observations should explain whether the plant is cultivated or growing independently.

solanum-lycopersicum.summary: Tomatoes can appear as volunteers where fruit or compost has been discarded, as well as in deliberately planted vegetable beds. They are warm-season plants, usually grown as annuals where frost ends the season. A stray tomato is not equivalent to an established invasive population. Useful observations show whether plants are surviving, fruiting and producing another generation without cultivation.

valeriana-officinalis.summary: Common valerian is a tall perennial once widely planted as a medicinal herb. It can escape into meadows, stream edges and woodland openings, returning early in spring from underground growth and spreading by seed. Dense stands can crowd nearby plants. Its ecological significance is regional; Wisconsin, for example, identifies it as an invasive plant of concern. It is different from the purple-flowered ornamental commonly sold as garden heliotrope.

vicia-sativa.summary: Common vetch is an annual legume used as a cover crop and also found growing outside cultivation. Its tendrils let it scramble over neighboring plants, forming a loose tangle rather than standing firmly on its own. Seed production can make it a persistent visitor around fields and gardens. A planted cover crop and an unmanaged escape should be described differently in a sighting record.

vicia-sativa-ssp-nigra.summary: Narrow-leaved vetch is a slender annual member of the common-vetch group, often listed under Vicia angustifolia or a subspecies name. It grows among grasses and along disturbed margins, using leaf tendrils to hold nearby stems. It can spread by seed, but distinguishing it from related vetches is important before assigning a precise name to a record.

lysimachia-vulgaris.summary: Garden loosestrife is a yellow-flowered perennial that spreads through long underground stems as well as seed. In wet ground it can build dense patches that replace other vegetation along shorelines and in marshes. A few visible stems may be connected to a much larger underground system, which is why one round of cutting rarely finishes the job. It is unrelated to purple loosestrife despite the shared common name.

zachrysia-provisoria.summary: The Cuban brown snail feeds on a wide range of cultivated plants and is an established garden and nursery pest in parts of Florida. It can travel unnoticed with potted plants, making inspection of pots and growing media particularly useful. Chewed leaves alone do not identify this snail: slugs, other snails and insects can leave similar damage.

lepidium-sativum.summary: Garden cress is a fast-growing annual cultivated for its young leaves. Plants allowed to mature produce branching stems, small flowers and numerous flat seed pods, and occasional escapes occur around gardens and disturbed ground. It is a terrestrial mustard-family plant, not watercress. A seedling crop in a tray and a self-sown outdoor population represent very different kinds of occurrence.

alliaria-petiolata.summary: Garlic mustard is a woodland plant that usually spends its first year as a low rosette and flowers the following spring. It can crowd out native spring plants and leave a lasting supply of seeds in the soil. Removing a patch is therefore a follow-up project, not simply a matter of pulling the tallest stems once.

euphorbia-terracina.summary: Carnation spurge, also called false caper, is an introduced spurge that can form dense patches in disturbed grassland and coastal habitats. In California it has spread into places such as bluffs, dunes and open woodland. Its small greenish flowers are easy to overlook, so the branching stems and narrow leaves are often what first draw attention.

blattella-germanica.summary: The German cockroach is an indoor pest closely associated with kitchens, food storage and other warm places where food and moisture are available. It can arrive with belongings or deliveries and build a hidden population in narrow cracks. Seeing one does not tell you how many are present, which is why monitoring and removing food, water and shelter matter as much as treating the insects you can see.

iris-germanica.summary: Bearded iris is a long-cultivated perennial that grows from thick, horizontal rhizomes. Garden forms come in many colors and sizes, and an old clump can persist after a garden has disappeared. A surviving planting is different from a population spreading into nearby habitat; recording that context helps explain what an observation means.

scleranthus-annuus.summary: Annual knawel is a small, branching weed of open ground, lawns and fields. Its narrow leaves can make a patch look like thin grass or moss, but it is a flowering plant in the carnation family. It reproduces by seed and often grows through the cool season, though its timing varies with climate.

vespula-germanica.summary: The German yellowjacket is a social wasp that nests in enclosed spaces, including wall cavities and underground sites. Workers hunt insects and also visit human food, which can bring a nest into conflict with people. A wasp visiting a picnic is not necessarily nesting nearby, and its yellow-and-black coloring alone does not distinguish this introduced species from native yellowjackets.

asperugo-procumbens.summary: Madwort is a rough-haired annual that sprawls or scrambles through disturbed ground and field margins. Its tiny blue flowers are less distinctive than the enlarged, leafy structures that later surround the fruits. Those structures make a fruiting plant much easier to recognize than a young seedling.

spiraea-chamaedryfolia.summary: Germander meadowsweet is a deciduous ornamental shrub with white spring flowers and new shoots that can arise from the ground around an established plant. It has been recorded outside cultivation in parts of New England. A persistent garden shrub and an expanding escape are different situations, so a useful report shows both the plant and its relationship to nearby plantings.

veronica-chamaedrys.summary: Germander speedwell is a low perennial with bright blue flowers. It spreads through slender underground stems and stems that root where they touch the ground, which can let it persist in lawns and garden edges. Sometimes sold as ground cover, it is also found outside cultivation. A few flowers can hide a more extensive connected patch.

tapinoma-melanocephalum.summary: Ghost ants are tiny ants whose pale legs and abdomen can seem to disappear against a light surface. They nest both indoors and outside in warm regions, and may occupy small, temporary spaces rather than one conspicuous mound. An indoor trail can therefore come from a hidden nest inside the building or from a nest nearby.

ameiva-ameiva.summary: The giant ameiva is an active, ground-dwelling lizard; older Florida references report introductions under this name through the pet trade. It searches for food during the day and can be seen moving quickly through open or disturbed vegetation. Historical records under this name deserve careful checking because similar ameivas and whiptails can be confused, particularly when young.

pomacea-maculata.summary: The giant applesnail is a large freshwater snail that feeds on aquatic vegetation. Its bright pink egg masses are often the first sign people notice, attached above the waterline to plants or other solid surfaces. It can alter aquatic habitats, but several native and introduced applesnails look similar, so a large shell or pink eggs alone may not settle the species.

blaberus-giganteus.summary: The giant cave cockroach is a large tropical cockroach associated with dark, sheltered places such as hollow trees, caves and decaying wood. It scavenges organic material and is also kept in captivity. A sighting outside a collection should be documented, but it should not automatically be treated as evidence of a widespread household infestation or an established outdoor population.

setaria-faberi.summary: Giant foxtail is a summer annual grass that produces a bristly seedhead and can compete strongly with crops. It spreads by seed rather than a creeping perennial root system. Preventing a new seed crop is important, especially where plants survive along field edges or after an early harvest.

giant-hogweed.summary: Giant hogweed is a very large member of the carrot family whose sap can make skin extremely sensitive to sunlight, causing serious burns. Its size is striking, but young plants may be much smaller and still hazardous. A suspected plant should be photographed from a distance and reported for confirmation, not handled to test its identity.

fallopia-sachalinensis.summary: Giant knotweed is a tall perennial that forms dense stands connected by underground rhizomes. It can crowd out streamside vegetation, and small pieces moved in soil or flood debris can start new patches. Its stems die back seasonally, but the underground system remains alive; a stand that looks cleared in winter may return strongly in spring.

marisa-cornuarietis.summary: The giant ramshorn is an applesnail with a flattened, disk-like shell. It eats aquatic plants as well as other organic material and can change vegetation in waters where it becomes abundant. Although it has been tested for weed control, releasing it to clear a pond can create a new invasive-species problem rather than solve the original one.

arundo-donax.summary: Giant reed is a very tall perennial grass that forms dense, cane-like stands along waterways and other moist ground. Its rhizomes make established patches difficult to remove, and dry stands can contribute to fire hazards. The thick growth can replace more diverse streamside vegetation and complicate access and restoration.

macrobrachium-rosenbergii.summary: The giant river prawn is a large freshwater prawn widely raised in aquaculture. Adults live in fresh water, while early development normally involves brackish water. An animal found outside a farm or aquarium is worth documenting, but an isolated escape does not by itself demonstrate a self-sustaining population.

salvinia-molesta.summary: Giant salvinia is a floating fern that can rapidly cover sheltered water with dense mats. Those mats shade plants below, interfere with access and can reduce oxygen as vegetation dies and decomposes. It spreads through living fragments, so a small piece caught on a trailer or fishing gear can matter.

alocasia-macrorrhizos.summary: Giant taro is a large tropical perennial grown for its dramatic foliage. Its thick stem can persist and produce new growth, so discarded plants or divisions deserve care in climates where they survive outdoors. The name elephant's ear is also used for other plants; a large leaf alone does not establish which species is present.

aleurodicus-dugesii.summary: Giant whitefly feeds on plant sap and can cover leaf undersides with long white wax strands. Sticky honeydew encourages black sooty mold, making an affected plant look worse even when the mold is growing on the residue rather than invading its tissues. Heavy infestations can weaken ornamentals, but the presence of wax does not mean the plant is beyond recovery.

lachnus-tatakaensis.summary: Lachnus tatakaensis is described in specialist aphid literature from willow trunks and branches in Taiwan, while the common name giant willow aphid is usually used for Tuberolachnus salignus. Some databases link the names, but the specialist treatments do not support simply combining all their biology and records.

fusarium-graminearum.summary: Fusarium graminearum causes several cereal diseases, including Gibberella stalk and ear rot in corn and Fusarium head blight in small grains. In corn, weakened stalks can lodge before harvest. The fungus can also produce mycotoxins, so crop quality and feed safety need to be assessed separately from how much mold is visible.

haplorchis-pumilio.summary: Haplorchis pumilio is a tiny parasitic fluke with a life cycle involving snails, fish and fish-eating hosts. It has been found in introduced snails and freshwater fish at sampled sites in southern California. People can be exposed by eating infected fish raw or inadequately prepared, but finding the parasite in fish is not the same as documenting a local human infection.

trogoderma-glabrum.summary: Glabrous cabinet beetles are associated with stored grain, flour mills and, sometimes, food in homes. Their larvae feed on grain and other dry materials; the adults visit flowers for pollen and nectar. An adult near a window does not by itself show where an infestation began, so finding the food source matters more than treating the place where the beetle was noticed.

sacciolepis-indica.summary: Glenwood grass is a small annual grass of damp ground, including muddy edges of freshwater wetlands. Its narrow, compact flower heads can make it easy to overlook among other grasses. Finding it in a wet area is not enough to establish either its identity or an ecological impact; both depend on the plant and the site being documented.

iberis-umbellata.summary: Globe candytuft is a Mediterranean annual grown for rounded clusters of pink, purple or white flowers. It can reseed and occasionally appear outside gardens on disturbed ground. Those escapes should be documented separately from intentionally planted flowers; the references here do not justify treating every garden planting as an invasive infestation.

sphaerolecanium-prunastri.summary: Globose scale is a sap-feeding insect associated with stone-fruit trees, particularly plums. Mature females resemble small dark bumps on branches. Dense colonies can weaken a tree and leave sticky honeydew that supports sooty mold, but a few bumps on bark are not enough to identify the insect or decide whether treatment is needed.

trigonogenius-globulus.summary: Globular spider beetles are small scavengers found in buildings and stored materials. They can matter in museums and collections as well as food-storage areas, where their presence may lead to an overlooked pocket of dry organic debris. Their rounded shape and long legs resemble a tiny spider, but they are beetles with six legs and antennae.

frangula-alnus.summary: Glossy buckthorn is a woody shrub or small tree that can form a crowded understory. It tolerates both sun and shade and occurs in wet places as well as some drier, nutrient-poor habitats. Where it is invasive, a few fruiting shrubs can supply seedlings for years. The same species is also called alder buckthorn; that name does not make it an alder.

ligustrum-lucidum.summary: Glossy privet is an evergreen shrub or tree with thick leaves and clusters of small pale flowers followed by dark fruit. Its size can make an old planting look quite different from a clipped hedge. Birds can carry the seeds away from the original tree, so seedlings beneath perches and along nearby woodland edges are worth checking where this species escapes cultivation.

senna-surattensis.summary: Glossy shower is a large tropical shrub or small tree grown for its yellow flower clusters. Flat hanging pods follow the flowers, making a mature plant easier to recognize than a young seedling. It has escaped cultivation in some warm regions; Hawaii extension describes it shading pasture forage. That regional record does not establish that a garden plant is invasive or present everywhere.

lepidosaphes-gloverii.summary: Glover's scale is a small armored scale insect associated especially with citrus. The conspicuous brown shape is a protective cover over the insect, not a beetle or a plant scar. Colonies can occupy leaves, fruit, twigs and bark. On woody branches the narrow covers often line up with the grain, which helps them blend into the surface and makes a quick inspection easy to miss.

salix-caprea.summary: Goat willow is a deciduous shrub or small tree whose catkins open before its leaves. Male trees carry silvery catkins that become yellow with pollen; female trees have greener, narrower catkins and later release tiny seeds with woolly tufts. Its broad leaves set it apart from the narrow-leaved willow image many people know. It can also hybridize with other willows, making some trees difficult to name confidently.

aceria-kuko.summary: Goji gall mite feeds on goji plants and causes raised blisters in their leaves. The swollen plant tissue is much easier to see than the mites themselves. A plant can arrive with an infestation that becomes noticeable only after new growth develops, so recently purchased goji plants deserve a close look. Similar-looking leaf damage needs examination before it is assigned to this species.

etiella-zinckenella.summary: Gold-banded etiella moth is the adult stage of a caterpillar that feeds inside legume pods. Peas, beans and soybeans are among its hosts. The damaged seeds may remain hidden until a pod is opened, so a crop can look relatively normal from a distance. This sheltered feeding also makes the timing of inspection and any control decision more useful than spraying after damage is already well established.

camelina-sativa.summary: Gold-of-pleasure, also called camelina, is a short-lived mustard-family plant cultivated for its oily seeds. It can appear as an intentional crop or as a volunteer outside cultivation, so the setting matters when deciding whether it is unwanted. Small pale flowers are followed by numerous swollen pods. Those pods are more useful for identification than a distant view of the yellow flowers.

prymnesium-parvum.summary: Golden algae is a microscopic, single-celled organism that can form blooms harmful to fish and other animals that breathe through gills. A bloom may tint water yellow or golden brown, but not every bloom is toxic and cell numbers do not perfectly predict a fish kill. Its common name describes a visual effect; it does not mean that every golden-colored pond contains this species.

cota-tinctoria.summary: Golden chamomile is an herbaceous perennial with divided foliage and yellow daisy-like flower heads. It is grown in borders and for cut flowers, and cultivated forms can differ in height, hairiness and flower color. Older references often call it Anthemis tinctoria. A plant outside a garden should be identified on its leaves and flower-head structure rather than on the word chamomile alone.

trifolium-aureum.summary: Golden clover is a short-lived, upright clover with dense heads of small yellow flowers. It usually grows as an annual, although some floras also describe biennial plants. Its leaves have the familiar three-leaflet arrangement, but the yellow heads can make it easy to confuse with other small clovers. A flowering stem with intact leaves is much more informative than flower color alone.

asterodiaspis-variolosa.summary: Golden oak scale is a tiny sap-feeding insect that sits in shallow pits on oak twigs. The pits are changes in the bark caused by feeding, and their rims may become slightly swollen. Heavy infestations can accompany poor growth and twig dieback, but a few pits do not explain every unhealthy branch. Several closely related oak pit scales look much alike in the field.

allamanda-cathartica.summary: Golden trumpet is a tropical evergreen plant grown as a scrambling shrub or woody climber. Its large yellow flowers and glossy leaves make it a familiar garden ornamental in warm climates. It can escape cultivation in some tropical settings, and cut stems contain milky sap that can irritate skin and eyes. The attractive flowers should not be taken as a sign that the plant is edible.

acacia-pycnantha.summary: Golden wattle is a shrub or small tree best known for rounded golden flower heads. It is native to southeastern Australia and is Australia's floral emblem, while also being a weed in places outside its native range. That contrast makes location important: an Australian name or ornamental use does not establish whether a particular planting is appropriate elsewhere.

aurinia-saxatilis.summary: Golden-tuft alyssum is a low perennial often planted in rock gardens, where its small yellow flowers form dense spring clusters above gray-green foliage. It is also sold as basket-of-gold, and older references use Alyssum saxatile. The plant can remain after the brief mass of flowers has faded, so its foliage and persistent base are useful parts of the identification.

hylurgus-ligniperda.summary: Goldenhaired bark beetle breeds mainly under the bark of recently cut pine logs, stumps and the roots or bases of dead and weakened trees. It is therefore often encountered in harvested wood rather than in a healthy tree canopy. Its presence matters when wood is moved, even where direct wood damage is limited. Finding the beetle in dead material does not by itself show that it killed the tree.

koelreuteria-paniculata.summary: Goldenrain Tree is a deciduous ornamental with compound leaves, yellow flower clusters and papery, inflated seed capsules. The capsules may remain on bare branches, giving a useful winter clue. Seedlings can establish around planted trees and in disturbed ground in regions where the species escapes. A planted adult and a self-sustaining wild population are different observations and should be recorded separately.

lamarckia-aurea.summary: Goldentop grass is a small tufted annual whose compact flower heads turn yellowish or golden as they mature. It is associated with open, disturbed ground and dry sites in regional floras. Its decorative-looking head contains both seed-producing and sterile spikelets, a useful distinction from grasses with a superficially similar soft or brush-like appearance.

channa-aurolineata.summary: Goldline snakehead is an elongated freshwater fish with a flattened head and long fins. It uses quiet or slow-water habitats such as canals, pools and vegetated lakes. Older records may call it bullseye snakehead or identify it as Channa marulius, but modern taxonomic work separates the two. A familiar common name can therefore hide an important identification difference.

cucumis-myriocarpus.summary: Gooseberry gourd is a sprawling or climbing annual with small round fruits, sometimes called prickly paddy melon. It grows through disturbed ground and can trail for a couple of meters. The fruit may resemble a tiny melon, but this is not a reason to taste it. Several wild cucurbits share the name paddy melon, so fruit size and surface details are important.

eleusine-indica.summary: Goosegrass is a tough, low-growing grass that often gains a foothold where traffic has thinned turf and compacted the soil. It is usually a summer annual, although it can persist longer in tropical conditions. Its flattened, pale-centered clumps can survive close mowing and still produce seed. Removing the visible grass without improving the worn patch leaves the same opportunity for the next generation.

eragrostis-ciliaris.summary: Gophertail lovegrass is a tufted grass with a narrow, often woolly-looking flower head. Regional floras describe it chiefly as an annual, with stems that may rise straight or bend upward from the base. Its head can be tightly packed or broken into small lobes, so the outline varies. The name lovegrass covers many species, and a general resemblance is not enough for a confident identification.

flacourtia-indica.summary: Governor's plum is a shrub or small tree with small flowers and rounded red to purple fruit. Many plants have sharp spines, sometimes branching on the trunk. Its leaves, hairiness and overall size vary considerably, and botanical treatments differ in how broadly they define the species. It is cultivated in some places and escapes in others, so a fruiting plant should be assessed in its local setting.

pseudomyrmex-gracilis.summary: Graceful twig ant is a slender, wasp-like ant associated with vegetation and hollow twigs. Its long body and large eyes make it look different from many compact ants seen around kitchens. It can deliver a painful sting if handled or disturbed, but its presence on a shrub does not automatically call for treatment. Nesting location and actual contact with people matter more than a single sighting.

manihot-grahamii.summary: Graham's manihot is a branching shrub or small tree grown for leaves divided into many narrow lobes. Its pale green, striped flowers are less conspicuous than the foliage. It is sometimes called hardy tapioca or ornamental cassava, names that can be misleading if interpreted as food advice. The catalog species is distinct from cultivated cassava, and its ornamental use does not establish that its parts are edible.

eucalyptus-grandis.summary: Grand eucalyptus, also known as rose gum or flooded gum, is a very tall forest tree used in timber plantations. A mature specimen can greatly exceed the scale of an ordinary garden tree. Its trunk usually has a short rough-barked base with smooth pale bark above. Closely related eucalyptus species and planted hybrids mean that bark color alone is not a reliable name tag.

xylosandrus-crassiusculus.summary: Granulate ambrosia beetle is a tiny beetle that tunnels into woody stems and grows fungi inside its galleries. The fungi provide food for the beetles and their young. Young or stressed ornamental and fruit trees can be seriously damaged, and infested nursery plants can carry the problem to another site. The insects are usually hidden by the time a tree begins to wilt.

hypoponera-opaciceps.summary: Granulate mini-ponerine ant is a small, dark ant that is easily overlooked in soil and leaf litter. Museum records include nests in potted plants and piles of bark, which makes movement of planted material a practical concern. It is not usually seen in conspicuous outdoor trails. Workers and queens have a sting, although the species is not described as aggressive.

ctenopharyngodon-idella.summary: Grass Carp is a large freshwater fish that feeds heavily on aquatic plants. It has been stocked to manage vegetation, but too many fish can remove much more plant cover than intended. That can alter habitat for other animals and leave a pond looking very different. Stocked fish therefore need a planned management context; they are not a simple substitute for identifying the plants causing a problem.

stellaria-graminea.summary: Grass-like starwort is a slender perennial whose weak stems weave through grasses and other low vegetation. The narrow leaves can be overlooked until small white flowers appear. Each flower has five petals split so deeply that it may look as though there are ten. It belongs to the chickweed family, but its narrow foliage and open branching flower clusters differ from the common garden chickweed mat.

antonina-graminis.summary: Grass-root antonina is also widely called rhodesgrass mealybug. It feeds in sheltered places on grasses, especially around stem joints beneath the leaf sheaths. Affected turf can yellow and thin in a way that resembles drought, so watering alone may not address the problem. The insect produces honeydew, which can leave grass sticky and support black sooty mold. Ants may visit this sugary material. Several predators and parasitoids attack the mealybug, making their presence useful information when assessing an infestation.

euphorbia-graminea.summary: Grassleaf spurge is a lightly built, branching herb that can appear in gardens and nursery areas. Its name is misleading if you expect every leaf to resemble a grass blade: the main leaves can be quite broad, while the smaller leaves around the flowering branches are narrower. Tiny flowers sit in cup-shaped structures typical of spurges, with small white appendages that are easier to see than the flowers themselves. Published floras describe different plant sizes and life spans in different settings, so neither height nor an assumed annual habit is a safe identification shortcut.

gamochaeta-coarctata.summary: Gray everlasting is treated here in the broad Gamochaeta americana complex that includes historical coarctata names. Older southeastern United States references used Gamochaeta coarctata for a small woolly cudweed with basal leaves and crowded flower clusters. A more recent regional treatment applies the name Gamochaeta impatiens to that plant. Kew, meanwhile, includes both names under a broader Gamochaeta americana. These treatments draw species boundaries differently, so the name on an older record needs to be interpreted alongside the flora that supplied it.

deroceras-reticulatum.summary: Gray field slug is a small slug that often becomes noticeable when young plants develop ragged feeding damage. It is active in moist conditions and can shelter out of sight during the day, so an apparently empty bed may still contain feeding slugs. Color varies considerably: many are pale gray or buff with darker flecks, but some are much more uniformly pale or dark. The species can damage seedlings and crops, although finding one slug does not show that every nearby hole or missing seedling was caused by it.

veronica-polita.summary: Gray field speedwell is a low annual with small blue flowers and rounded, toothed leaves. It grows in cultivated and disturbed ground, including gardens and crop fields. Its stems spread close to the surface, so flowers may be easier to notice than the plant supporting them. The gray-green foliage helps suggest the name, but leaf color changes with light and growing conditions. Related speedwells can occupy the same kind of ground, making a flowering and fruiting plant much easier to identify than a seedling.

populus-x-canescens.summary: Gray poplar is a hybrid between white poplar and European aspen. A mature tree can be substantial, but a patch may instead appear as numerous young stems arising from spreading roots. That distinction matters: several stems close together are not necessarily independent seedlings. The foliage is variable, especially between ordinary branches and vigorous shoots. Its gray leaf undersides can be a helpful clue, although the amount of pale hair changes as leaves age. Published regional accounts document both large trees and dense sucker stands.

casuarina-glauca.summary: Gray sheoak can look like a pine from a distance, but its fine green hanging strands are jointed branchlets. The true leaves are tiny scales arranged around the joints. It can also send up shoots from its roots, creating groups of connected stems around an older planting. The species is native to part of eastern Australia and has been planted elsewhere. Whether a particular stand is appropriate to retain depends on its location and local guidance, not simply on the tree's presence in a catalog.

dysmicoccus-boninsis.summary: Gray sugarcane mealybug feeds in protected spaces beneath the leaf sheaths of sugarcane and other grasses. Its wax coating can make the insects look like pale debris pressed against a stem. Finding the species requires opening those hiding places carefully; a quick look at the exposed leaves may miss it. Other mealybugs occur on sugarcane as well, so host choice alone does not establish identity. Published observations include gray and paler forms, making body color useful but insufficient on its own.

echinops-sphaerocephalus.summary: Great globethistle is a tall perennial with rounded clusters of pale flowers above coarse, spiny leaves. The flower balls are made of many small individual flower heads, a structure that separates globe thistles from the more familiar open-topped thistles. Stems can reach roughly 2 m in favorable conditions. The plant has been grown ornamentally and is recorded outside cultivation in some regions. Its flowers attract visiting insects, but an attractive flowering plant can still need containment where local guidance identifies a problem.

rorippa-amphibia.summary: Great yellowcress is a perennial of wet ground and shallow water edges, with yellow mustard-family flowers and underground rhizomes. A large patch can represent connected growth rather than many separate seedlings. The leaves change shape along the stem, and submerged or low leaves can look different from the leaves held above water. In some populations fruit develops poorly, so a stand without obvious mature pods is not necessarily young or dying. Wetland identification needs particular care because other yellow-flowered mustards may grow nearby.

arctium-lappa.summary: Greater burdock begins with a rosette of large leaves and later sends up a tall, branching flowering stem. The purple flower heads eventually become hooked burs that cling to clothing and animal fur, carrying the enclosed seeds away. Its large leaves can resemble those of unrelated garden plants at first glance, but the woolly undersides and bur-forming flower heads are much more informative. It is usually a biennial, so a nonflowering rosette and a tall flowering plant may be different stages of the same species.

pisidium-amnicum.summary: Greater European pea clam is a freshwater bivalve small enough to be overlooked among sand and fine gravel. Despite its name, a full-grown shell is only about a centimeter long. It is associated particularly with flowing water, although it also occurs in lakes. Its shell has clear concentric ridges, giving it a more strongly sculptured surface than many small freshwater clams. The species is native across parts of Eurasia and North Africa and has introduced populations elsewhere; a local record still requires proper identification.

centaurea-scabiosa.summary: Greater knapweed is a perennial with deeply divided leaves and large purple flower heads on upright branching stems. The outer flowers are often enlarged, giving a head a loose, spreading fringe. It occurs in grassland and other open places, and its status varies substantially across regions. In parts of its native range it is a valued grassland plant; an introduced population elsewhere may receive different management advice. The word knapweed alone is therefore not a reason to remove it.

lepidium-coronopus.summary: Greater swinecress is a low plant that spreads across disturbed or trodden ground. Its small white flowers are easy to miss, but the rough little fruits are distinctive once you look closely. Older books often call it Coronopus squamatus; that name refers to the same species treated here as Lepidium coronopus. It may behave as an annual or a short-lived biennial in different treatments. Compacted paths, field edges and similar open ground are useful places to look, but habitat alone cannot confirm it.

galleria-mellonella.summary: Greater wax moth is chiefly a problem when its caterpillars reach stored comb or comb that a honey bee colony cannot adequately defend. The larvae tunnel through the material and leave silk, debris and damaged comb behind. Adult moths themselves are not the stage chewing through it. Greater and lesser wax moths can occur together, so the presence of moth damage does not automatically identify the species. A damaged hive also deserves a wider health check: weak colonies may be vulnerable for reasons beyond the moths.

hemiberlesia-rapax.summary: Greedy scale is an armored scale insect that can settle on leaves, stems and fruit of many woody plants. The part usually noticed is the small protective cover rather than the soft-bodied insect beneath it. Covers can remain in place after the insects die, so their presence alone does not prove that an infestation is still active. Several similar armored scales share the same hosts, making a host name or a few pale dots on a leaf an unreliable basis for choosing treatment.

aphis-spiraecola.summary: Green citrus aphid also goes by spirea aphid, a reminder that citrus is only one part of its host range. Colonies can occur on fruit trees, spireas and various ornamentals, particularly around growing shoots. Both wingless and winged forms occur, and winged adults can move between plants. It resembles the green apple aphid closely enough that orchard advisers often discuss the two together. Useful management starts with the plant's condition and the insects present, rather than assuming every green aphid is this species.

setaria-viridis.summary: Green Foxtail is a clump-forming annual grass with a narrow, bristly seed head. It can occur in cultivated ground, along roads and in turf, especially where there is room for seedlings to establish. Its green flower heads resemble small bottlebrushes, but several other grasses share that look. The plant grows from seed rather than from a persistent creeping root system, making seed production an important consideration when it is unwanted. A young nonflowering plant is easiest to identify by examining the leaf base as well as the blade.

iguana-iguana.summary: Green Iguana is a large, mainly plant-eating lizard that climbs well and readily enters water. Young animals are often bright green, but adults may be brownish, dark or seasonally orange, so the name does not describe every individual. A long tail makes up much of its total length. In places where it has been introduced, feeding and burrowing can create problems around gardens and built structures. Its native or introduced status depends on location; an observation should be assessed against the local wildlife authority's guidance.

pulvinaria-psidii.summary: Green shield scale is a soft scale insect that feeds on leaves and young stems of many broadleaf plants, including tropical fruit trees and ornamentals. Mature females produce conspicuous white cottony egg sacs that can make a plant look dusted with fluff. Feeding insects also release honeydew, allowing black sooty mold to grow on the sticky surface. Old wax can remain after the scales have died, so white patches do not necessarily indicate a continuing active infestation. The name refers to one stage of an insect whose color changes as it matures.

xiphophorus-hellerii.summary: Green swordtails are freshwater aquarium fish whose wild ancestors come from Mexico and Central America. They give birth to live young and can produce several broods in warm conditions. Released aquarium fish and escapes from outdoor ponds have established populations outside that range. They use vegetated streams as well as ponds, ditches and warm springs, so an apparently isolated ornamental pond can still become a source of fish for nearby water.

acacia-decurrens.summary: Green wattle is an Australian tree with finely divided, dark green foliage and clusters of bright yellow flower balls. It has been planted beyond its native New South Wales range and can establish in open woodland and along disturbed edges. Mature trees can reach about 10-15 m. The fine-looking foliage belongs to a substantial woody plant, so identifying young trees early is more practical than waiting until a dense stand has developed.

eleutherodactylus-planirostris.summary: The greenhouse frog is a tiny ground-dwelling frog that can travel with potted plants and moist garden materials. Its eggs develop on land and hatch directly into miniature frogs, so it does not need a pond full of tadpoles to reproduce. Adults hide in leaf litter and other damp cover and become easier to notice after rain. A quiet series of high, birdlike chirps may reveal a frog that is otherwise almost invisible against brown leaves.

insignorthezia-insignis.summary: Greenhouse orthezia is a sap-feeding scale insect found on leaves and stems of many cultivated plants. Unlike a smooth, stationary-looking armored scale, the female carries conspicuous white wax plates and a long egg sac with her. It can be moved with living plants, making inspection of incoming greenhouse and nursery stock especially useful. Its unusual appearance helps find an infestation, but closely related ensign scales still need careful identification.

milax-gagates.summary: The greenhouse slug is a small, dark slug associated with cultivated ground and plant movement. It is also called the jet slug or black-keeled slug. Like other garden slugs it is easiest to find when conditions are damp, while daytime hiding places can include pots, debris and soil crevices. Leaf damage alone cannot identify it: several unrelated slugs feed in the same settings, and some similar-looking species need anatomical examination.

desmodium-intortum.summary: Greenleaf ticktrefoil is a trailing perennial legume grown as forage in warm, humid regions. Its stems scramble through nearby vegetation and can root where they remain against moist ground. The small jointed pods break into seed-bearing pieces that cling to clothing and animals. A planted forage patch and an unwanted escape therefore need different decisions, but both benefit from recognizing the plant before mature pods are carried elsewhere.

phyllostachys-viridiglaucescens.summary: Greenwax golden bamboo is a vigorous woody grass that can form a tall, dense thicket. Its underground running stems can extend the planting beyond the visible canes. Young growth has a pale waxy coating, while older canes are green to yellow-green. This is a plant to assess by the space it occupies underground as well as the screen it creates above ground, especially near a property boundary or natural vegetation.

ascidia-sydneiensis.summary: The grey sea squirt is a solitary marine animal attached to hard surfaces, including mangrove roots, docks and vessel hulls. Despite its common name, it can be cream, yellow, orange, red or burgundy as well as pale gray. Water passes through the body as the animal filters food. Transport on marine structures and boats helps explain its broad distribution, while its ecological impacts remain poorly documented.

glechoma-hederacea.summary: Ground ivy, often called creeping Charlie, is a low perennial that spreads through lawns and garden beds on trailing stems. The stems root where their joints touch soil, making a connected mat rather than a collection of separate seedlings. Its small violet flowers and rounded leaves can be attractive, but repeated rooting lets it occupy gaps and return when only the leafy tips are removed.

rhizoecus-falcifer.summary: This ground mealybug feeds below the soil surface, where an infestation can remain hidden while a potted plant loses vigor. It has been recorded from roots of many kinds of plants. White wax around roots may be the first useful clue, but yellow leaves or slow growth alone have many possible causes. Looking at the root ball is therefore more informative than repeatedly treating the foliage.

rhizoecus-kondonis.summary: Kondo ground mealybug feeds below ground on plant roots. It has been studied in citrus orchards in Japan and alfalfa fields in California, as well as being included in nursery root-mealybug guidance. In affected alfalfa, declining plants can form roughly circular patches that expand slowly. Current taxonomic sources use Ripersiella kondonis, while many crop references retain Rhizoecus kondonis. Both names are useful when seeking an identification.

caryedon-serratus.summary: Groundnut bruchid is a seed beetle associated with peanuts and tamarind. The damaging stage is the larva, which feeds inside seeds while much of the infestation remains concealed. Adults emerging from stored material can reveal damage that started earlier. Keeping suspect pods or seed lots separate is useful both for protecting clean stores and for tracing where the insects came from.

psidium-guajava.summary: Common guava is a tropical American fruit tree widely grown for its fragrant, seeded fruit. Outside managed orchards it can form thickets in suitable warm climates. Florida's invasive-plant program describes effects on forests and open woodland where dense guava crowds other vegetation. A productive garden tree and an expanding wild stand need different management, so first establish whether the plants are deliberately maintained or spreading beyond cultivation.

greenidea-psidii.summary: Guava aphid gathers on tender shoots and the undersides of young leaves, especially on guava and other members of the myrtle family. It feeds by drawing sap from growing tissues. Its unusually long rear tubes make it easier to notice than many tiny aphids, but another Greenidea species has a very similar appearance. Finding a colony is an opportunity to confirm the insect before plants or cuttings are moved.

megathyrsus-maximus.summary: Guineagrass is a tall, clump-forming tropical grass also known in older guides as Panicum maximum. It has been grown as forage and can become a large, persistent plant around disturbed ground and wet margins. Long leaves and an open, branching seed head give mature stands a much looser appearance than grasses with compact bottlebrush heads. A seedling is harder to recognize, making flowering material useful for confirmation.

echinochloa-crus-pavonis.summary: Gulf cockspur grass is a robust grass of wet ground, stream margins and shallow water. Its stems may bend near the base and root in mud, while a large, loosely branched seed head arches above broad leaves. Regional floras describe both annual and perennial plants. Its resemblance to other barnyard grasses makes a complete mature specimen more useful than a photograph of a single blade.

bidens-pilosa.summary: Hairy beggarticks is a branching annual whose narrow fruits readily hitch a ride on clothing and animal coats. It grows in disturbed places, crops and garden settings in warm regions. The flower heads may be much less showy than those of related Spanish needles, but a mature plant can produce many barbed fruits. Recognizing it before that stage prevents an ordinary weeding job from spreading seeds along the route home.

cardamine-hirsuta.summary: Hairy bittercress is a small mustard that often appears in nursery pots, moist beds and thin turf. It can flower while still quite small, then scatter its seeds when the slender ripe pods spring open. That makes timing more important than plant size: a low plant tucked beneath a shrub may already be ready to seed the surrounding bed. Its growth season varies with climate and moisture.

ranunculus-sardous.summary: Hairy buttercup is a low, conspicuously hairy plant with glossy yellow flowers. It occurs in fields and other open ground and can blend into a mixture of yellow-flowered buttercups. The flowering plant is easier to investigate than an isolated basal leaf, but ripe fruits are valuable when separating close relatives. Its appearance alone should not be used to decide that every buttercup in a field needs removal.

hypochaeris-radicata.summary: Hairy cat's ear is a perennial rosette plant with yellow dandelion-like flower heads. The leaves stay close to the ground while the flowering stems rise above them, allowing a plant to persist in turf even when its flowers are repeatedly cut. Seeds form fluffy heads and can move away from the original rosette. Its low, hairy leaves are often a better starting point for identification than a distant yellow flower.

digitaria-sanguinalis.summary: Hairy crabgrass, also called large crabgrass, is a warm-season annual that spreads outward through open or thinly covered soil. Lower stem joints can root and anchor a broad mat. It reproduces by seed, so a plant that is allowed to flower can leave a new problem even after the current year's growth dies. Gardens, crop fields and worn lawn edges provide the open conditions it readily occupies.

fatoua-villosa.summary: Hairy crabweed is better known to many gardeners as mulberryweed. It can arrive in nursery pots and quickly produce seeds among ornamental plants, especially in moist, shaded beds. Even a small plant can be reproductive, and some seeds are thrown away from the parent. Its resemblance to a young tree sometimes lets it remain in a pot long enough to spread through a plant collection.

eriochloa-villosa.summary: Hairy cupgrass, also called woolly cupgrass, is an annual grass of crop fields, ditches and disturbed ground. Its soft-haired leaves can resemble a foxtail at first, but the mature seed head is built differently. Early plants may compete with a crop before their identity is obvious. Because the next generation comes from seed, finding isolated plants before they mature is particularly useful.

cenchrus-pedicellatus.summary: Hairy fountain grass is a grass of open woodland margins, grassland and disturbed or cultivated ground. Older references call it Pennisetum pedicellatum. It can stand upright or bend at lower stem joints, and published treatments describe both annual and perennial forms. The name fountain grass covers several different species, so a fluffy-looking head or a nursery label is not sufficient to establish this identity.

solanum-villosum.summary: This hairy nightshade is a small, usually annual herb whose ripe berries are orange to red, sometimes yellow. It belongs to the black-nightshade group, where closely similar plants have often been reported under the wrong name. The common name hairy nightshade is also used for other Solanum species. A record with that name alone therefore cannot reliably establish which plant was present.

ptinus-villiger.summary: Hairy spider beetle is a stored-product insect associated with cereal foods, grain and animal feeds. It can live in mills, granaries, warehouses and homes, with damp grain particularly favorable. Larvae feed among food particles and produce silk, leaving webbed granular material. Finding a beetle away from food is a reason to inspect nearby dry stores, not proof that the building itself is being eaten.

vicia-villosa.summary: Hairy vetch is a scrambling legume often grown as a cover crop. Tendrils let its stems climb neighboring plants, and an established planting can form a dense tangle of foliage and purple flowers. Outside its intended area, seed production can create volunteer plants in later crops or nearby vegetation. Recognizing a deliberately managed cover crop is as important as noticing an unwanted escape.

rytidosperma-penicillatum.summary: This wallaby grass is a slender perennial that grows in loose to crowded tufts. It is also called slender wallaby grass, a useful name because the catalog's hairy wallaby grass is shared with another species. Narrow leaves and an elongated flowering head can make it look inconspicuous among other pasture grasses. Species identification depends heavily on the tiny flowering parts rather than the overall amount of hair.

rytidosperma-pilosum.summary: Hairy wallaby grass is a perennial grass whose small flowering parts are more distinctive than its general tufted appearance. The same English name is used for Rytidosperma penicillatum, so using the scientific name prevents two different plants from being combined. Older references may also use other genus names. A mature flowering head is especially useful when confirming a suspected plant outside its known local flora.

merremia-aegyptia.summary: Hairy woodrose is a twining vine with large, five-part leaves and white morning-glory-like flowers. In warm conditions it can climb through shrubs and along fences, covering supporting vegetation. Long coarse hairs on the stems and flower coverings make it distinctive at close range. Some newer references call it Distimake aegyptius, so both names may appear when looking up a plant or an old observation.

hemigrapsus-penicillatus.summary: The hairy-clawed shore crab is an East Asian coastal crab whose identity needs particular care. For many years, two very similar crabs were recorded together under Hemigrapsus penicillatus. Researchers separated Hemigrapsus takanoi in 2005, and later genetic work supported that distinction. Older records, especially reports of an invasion in Europe, cannot automatically be assigned to the species in this profile.

petrorhagia-dubia.summary: Hairypink is a slender annual with small pink flowers and narrow leaves. It grows in open, dry, disturbed ground and can occur in pasture or along tracks. Its flowers are easy to overlook because a tight head may show only one open flower at a time. The brown bracts around that head remain useful for recognizing the plant after the bright petals have disappeared.

carex-hirta.summary: Hammer sedge, often called hairy sedge, is a perennial that can extend through the soil on long rhizomes. A patch may therefore consist of connected shoots rather than separate seedlings. It occurs in grassy and disturbed places, including damp ground. Its place in the local vegetation matters: it is native in parts of its range, so finding it is not by itself a reason to remove it.

rhaponticum-repens.summary: Hardheads is also widely known as Russian knapweed. This perennial can build dense colonies through an extensive root system, with new shoots arising from buds below ground. A patch that appears to have been cleared can return from surviving roots. It is a particular concern in pasture and hay because it is poisonous to horses, making correct identification useful even where only a few stems are visible.

fuchsia-magellanica.summary: Hardy fuchsia is a woody shrub from southern South America, familiar in gardens for its hanging red-and-purple flowers. It can grow into a substantial shrub or scramble through surrounding vegetation. Cultivated plants are variable, and the name fuchsia also covers many hybrids and other species. An escape from a garden needs a closer look before it is recorded as Fuchsia magellanica.

conringia-orientalis.summary: Hare's ear mustard is an annual mustard with unusually smooth, broad leaves clasping the stem. It grows in open disturbed ground and can be mistaken for a young crop mustard before flowering. Mature plants develop long, narrow seed pods above the leaves. Those pods, together with the way the leaves meet the stem, are much more useful for identification than a general impression of yellow flowers.

lagurus-ovatus.summary: Harestail grass is an annual grass with soft, oval flower heads that resemble small pale tails. It is native to the Mediterranean region and is also grown ornamentally. Dry sandy ground, tracks and disturbed coastal places suit it well. The same heads that make it attractive in a dried arrangement contain the structures that produce its next generation, so collecting or moving mature heads can move seed.

peganum-harmala.summary: Harmal peganum, more often called African rue or harmal, is a bushy perennial of dry ground. It can persist beside roads, in disturbed pasture and around heavily used farm areas. A deep root system makes an established plant much harder to remove than its small aboveground size suggests. Seeds and pieces of roots can move with soil or equipment, and the plant is toxic to livestock.

phenacoccus-dearnessi.summary: Hawthorn mealybug is a small sap-feeding insect associated with woody plants such as hawthorn, mountain ash and serviceberry. Colonies can be concealed in bark crevices before becoming obvious on new twigs or leaves. Their sticky honeydew may be noticed before the insects themselves. Heavy populations can weaken twigs, but finding a few mealybugs does not establish the cause of every leaf or branch problem on a tree.

myzocallis-coryli.summary: Hazel aphid is often called filbert aphid in orchard guidance. It feeds on hazel foliage and can leave sticky honeydew beneath a tree. Colonies may be inconspicuous when small, while heavy, sustained infestations can affect nut development. Hazel also supports other aphids, so a sticky leaf or a pale insect is a starting point for inspection rather than a firm identification.

anredera-cordifolia.summary: Heartleaf madeiravine is usually called Madeira vine. This long-lived climber has fleshy leaves and stems that wind through shrubs and trees. Established vines can cover and weigh down other vegetation. Its most important spread structures are the irregular tubers formed along the stems and below ground. A vine can therefore remain a problem after its visible canopy has been cut away.

brachypodium-pinnatum.summary: Heath false brome is a perennial grass that forms tufts connected by wiry underground rhizomes. A spreading patch can become much denser than its individual flowering stems suggest. It belongs to a group of similar grasses, some native in the same regions where it occurs. Checking the species and the purpose of managing the site is essential before treating a patch in a meadow or woodland edge.

calluna-vulgaris.summary: Heather is a small evergreen shrub that can turn open ground pink or purple when it flowers. It is a characteristic native plant of many European heathlands and moors, and also a widely planted ornamental. Outside its native setting it can escape cultivation. Its preference for open, acidic, nutrient-poor soils helps explain why the surroundings are as useful to record as the plant itself.

cucumis-dipsaceus.summary: Hedgehog gourd is an annual climbing or trailing plant in the cucumber family. Its pale green fruit is densely covered in soft bristles and becomes yellow as it ripens. The species comes from tropical Africa and has been carried to other warm regions. It can grow in disturbed ground and cultivated places, where its trailing stems may become mixed with other vines before the distinctive fruits appear.

sisymbrium-officinale.summary: Hedgemustard is an annual of open, disturbed ground, including field margins, roadsides and neglected garden edges. It starts with divided leaves near the ground and later sends up a branching stem with small yellow flowers. Its most distinctive feature appears as the flowers fade: short, slender pods lie tightly against the stem, making a fruiting branch look noticeably different from many other mustards.

myzus-hemerocallis.summary: Hemerocallis aphid is a small, pale aphid associated especially with daylilies, and it also occurs on Agapanthus and some other ornamental hosts. Colonies can feed near the base of leaves, where they are easy to miss during a quick inspection of flowers. Heavy feeding can distort or discolor foliage, buds and flowers, while honeydew leaves affected surfaces sticky. The amount of damage varies, so inspect the insects and new growth together.

phorodon-cannabis.summary: Hemp aphid, also called cannabis aphid, feeds on leaves and stems of Cannabis plants. Colonies can build quickly, leaving honeydew and pale shed skins on the crop. Heavy feeding may cause yellowing, wilting and reduced plant vigor. Both indoor and outdoor plantings can be affected, and moving infested planting material can carry a colony into a new growing area.

senecio-brasiliensis.summary: Hemp-leaf ragwort is a tall, leafy perennial from South America. Its deeply divided leaves and clusters of yellow flower heads can make it stand out above surrounding pasture plants. The species is important in livestock management because poisoning has been documented in cattle, and material mixed into hay is a concern. Wind-carried seeds also make a flowering patch worth noticing before it begins to disperse.

ardisia-crenata.summary: Hen's eyes is more commonly known as coral ardisia. This evergreen shrub was planted for its glossy foliage and hanging clusters of red fruit, but it can escape into moist, shaded woodland. In Florida, dense stands are a recognized invasive-plant problem. Its fruit often remains conspicuous long after flowering, making winter a useful time to look beneath the leaves for an overlooked plant.

lamium-amplexicaule.summary: Henbit is a small annual in the mint family that often appears during cool weather in gardens, thin lawns and cultivated ground. It can flower while still quite low, producing pink-purple tubes among rounded leaves. Many plants establish in autumn and flower the following spring, although spring-germinating plants also occur. Its ability to set seed while growing close to the ground makes early recognition helpful.

descurainia-sophia.summary: Herb sophia, also called flixweed, is a mustard that starts as a low rosette before sending up a slender, branching flowering stem. Its finely cut foliage gives disturbed ground a gray-green, almost fernlike cover. It reproduces by seed and can compete with crops, especially where soil is regularly disturbed. Recognizing the rosette makes removal easier than waiting until the plant has a full crop of narrow pods.

mayetiola-destructor.summary: Hessian fly is a small fly whose larvae feed on wheat stems beneath the leaf sheaths. Infested young wheat may stay short and unusually dark green, while damage higher on older stems can leave plants weak enough to lodge. The adult is easy to overlook. Finding the immature stages at the base of the plant or near a stem joint is more useful than trying to identify a passing fly.

pinnaspis-strachani.summary: Hibiscus snow scale is an armored scale insect that feeds on many kinds of woody and herbaceous plants. A heavy colony can look like white flecks spread over stems and foliage. The white material is the insects' protective covering, not a fungus. Hibiscus is only one possible host, so a plant name alone cannot identify this scale. Several similar Pinnaspis species require close examination to separate.

malva-sylvestris.summary: High mallow is a tall, spreading herb with conspicuous pink to purple flowers. It grows as a biennial or perennial and is associated with gardens, roadsides and other disturbed ground. Its flowers and rounded leaves resemble several other mallows, including low garden weeds. A flowering stem usually gives a clearer identification than a young rosette. A cultivated plant is not, by itself, evidence that the species is spreading locally.

influenza-a-virus.summary: Highly pathogenic H5 avian influenza is a disease caused by particular influenza A viruses. The scientific name Influenza A virus is broader than this disease: it includes many viruses that are not highly pathogenic H5 bird flu. This overview concerns that narrower H5 disease. It can affect wild and domestic birds and some mammals. An animal can carry an avian influenza virus without showing obvious illness, so appearance cannot confirm freedom from infection.

pseudeurostus-hilleri.summary: Hiller's spider beetle is associated with stored products and accumulated food residues. An Australian government assessment describes it as a likely scavenger and a potential minor pest of feed mills and warehouses. That is a narrower claim than saying it routinely damages sound grain. Finding a spider beetle indoors is a reason to look for an infested material or hidden residue, but the exact species still needs confirmation.

impatiens-glandulifera.summary: Himalayan balsam is a tall annual of moist ground, particularly stream margins and other places where water can carry its seeds. Large pink to purplish flowers hang from soft, upright stems. Mature seed capsules burst open, throwing seeds away from the parent. Dense stands can leave little space for other low vegetation, then die back at the end of the season. Preventing another seed crop is central to managing an established patch.

rubus-bifrons.summary: Himalayan berry is a vigorous blackberry that forms tangled thickets of long, prickly canes. It spreads both through seed in its fruit and where cane tips root into the ground. Established patches can block paths and overgrow other vegetation. The name Rubus bifrons is used for Himalayan blackberry by the regional management sources consulted here; blackberry naming has changed across sources, so an older label should be checked against its actual species treatment.

martyringa-xeraula.summary: Himalayan grain moth is a small moth that can use stored grain, but its larvae also feed in decaying organic material. A moth attracted to a porch light does not show that a nearby pantry is infested. The North Carolina species account describes it as a minor stored-grain pest and notes that its outdoor habitats are poorly documented. This is a species for which careful identification matters more than the common name suggests. The accepted name currently includes a provisional synonym, M. ravicapitis; unresolved variation means a specialist should qualify difficult records.

leycesteria-formosa.summary: Himalayan honeysuckle is an upright shrub with drooping clusters of pale flowers framed by dark purple bracts. Its berries ripen through red to purple-black and can be carried away by birds. It is grown ornamentally, but escaped plants can form persistent patches in suitable climates. Despite the common name, it has a distinctive cane-forming habit and is not a twining honeysuckle vine.

hiptage-benghalensis.summary: Hiptage is a woody perennial that can grow as a shrub in open ground or climb high into surrounding trees. Its clusters of fragrant flowers are followed by distinctive winged fruits. In warm, moist settings, climbing growth can cover other vegetation, and wind or water can carry the fruits beyond the original planting. The fruit is often the easiest feature to recognize when a large vine has flowers out of reach.

acanthospermum-hispidum.summary: Hispid starbur is a rough-haired, branching annual whose small yellow flower heads turn into hard, prickly fruits. It grows in disturbed ground and cultivated places, and its burrs can cling to wool, clothing and harvested material. The flowers are easy to miss, while mature fruits can make an unnoticed patch troublesome to walk or work through. Removing plants before those burrs harden helps limit further movement.

berteroa-incana.summary: Hoary alyssum is a grayish, hairy mustard that grows in dry, disturbed ground, pastures and hay fields. Plants may live for one season or persist longer, but spread is through seed. It is especially important to recognize where horses graze or hay is made because it can be toxic to horses, including in dried forage. A small white-flowered plant in a hay field deserves a closer look before cutting.

solanum-physalifolium.summary: The name hoe nightshade has been applied to small, hairy nightshades of cultivated and disturbed ground, and historical scientific-name usage needs careful interpretation. Older regional floras used Solanum physalifolium broadly, including plants now treated as Solanum nitidibaccatum. Recent North American floristic work excludes true S. physalifolium from that region. A useful report should therefore preserve photographs and specimens rather than turn an old name into a confident local identification.

quercus-ilex.summary: Holly oak is a Mediterranean evergreen tree with a dense crown and leathery leaves. Young leaves can be sharply toothed like holly, while older growth may carry nearly smooth-edged leaves on the same tree. Its acorns reveal that it is an oak. It is planted as a shade or street tree in suitable climates, and its presence in cultivation should be distinguished from seedlings establishing beyond the planting.

dynaspidiotus-britannicus.summary: Holly scale is an armored scale that can feed on several ornamental plants, not just holly. Its small covers sit against leaves, twigs or fruit and can be mistaken for harmless surface marks. Feeding may damage tissue around the attachment point and weaken heavily infested growth. The name also appears as laurel scale or bay tree scale, which makes the scientific name useful when requesting a diagnosis. Turkish research also records it on cedar, fir and spruce, so inspect conifers as well as broad-leaved hosts.

alcea-rosea.summary: Hollyhock is a familiar garden plant with tall flowering stalks and large open blooms. It usually grows as a biennial or short-lived perennial, often making a leafy base before flowering. Plants may appear along roadsides or around old gardens after escaping cultivation. Flowers vary widely in color, so the tall habit, leaves and fruit are more useful than expecting one particular shade.

varroa-destructor.summary: Varroa destructor is a parasitic mite of honey bees and a major concern in managed colonies. It feeds on bees and reproduces in capped brood cells, and it can transmit viruses such as deformed wing virus. A colony can carry a damaging mite load before many mites are obvious on adult bees. Routine measurement is therefore more useful than waiting to see mites or visibly deformed bees.

acarapis-woodi.summary: Honey bee tracheal mite lives inside the breathing tubes of adult honey bees. This makes it very different from the larger varroa mites visible on the outside of bees. Heavy infestations can contribute to poor colony performance and losses, but early infestations may go unnoticed. A weak colony or crawling bees can have many causes, so this diagnosis needs laboratory evidence rather than a visual judgment at the hive entrance.

melianthus-major.summary: Honey-flower is a large, spreading shrub grown for its blue-green foliage and tall dark red flower clusters. It can send up new shoots from a persistent root system, so a plant that dies back above ground may return. Birds visit its nectar-rich flowers, but the leaves and roots are poisonous. The attractive foliage and the word honey should never be taken as signs that the plant is safe to eat or feed to animals.

leonurus-japonicus.summary: Honeyweed is an upright herb in the mint family, with deeply divided leaves and rings of small flowers spaced along the upper stems. It can grow in disturbed ground and has also been cultivated. The name Leonurus sibiricus was historically misapplied to this plant in some regions, so older records require care. The two honeyweed entries in this catalog should not be combined simply because their common names match.

leonurus-sibiricus.summary: This honeyweed is the true Leonurus sibiricus, an annual or biennial herb with finely cut leaves and pink to purple-red flowers. It is distinct from Leonurus japonicus, although the latter has often been sold or reported under the same name. Because the catalog contains both species, an identification needs to follow the scientific characters of the plant rather than the label on a seed packet.

phalaris-paradoxa.summary: Hood canarygrass is a tufted annual grass with dense, short flower heads. The uppermost leaf sheath often swells around the base of the head, giving it a partly enclosed appearance. It is documented as a crop weed in Australia, but a dense grass head alone does not identify it. Several canarygrasses share that general shape, and the small units within the head provide the strongest distinction.

setaria-verticillata.summary: Hooked bristlegrass is an annual grass whose bristly seed heads catch on fur, clothing and one another. The tiny hooks point backward, which distinguishes it from many other foxtail grasses. Plants may stand upright or sprawl, forming loose tufts in disturbed ground. The sticky feel is mechanical: it comes from the bristle barbs rather than a coating of sap.

phorodon-humuli.summary: Hop aphid is a small sap-feeding insect that uses hops during the growing season and Prunus trees, including plums, for part of its life cycle. Colonies gather on leaves and can enter developing hop cones. Their honeydew and feeding can make an infestation important even when the individual insects are hard to see. Checking early growth and following the crop into cone development is more useful than inspecting only at harvest.
