barleria-lupulina.summary: Hophead philippine violet is a small, spiny shrub with yellow tubular flowers packed into upright clusters. The overlapping bracts beneath the flowers give the heads a hoplike appearance. It has been grown as an ornamental and can form thorny growth where it escapes in warm climates. Despite the common name, it is neither a true violet nor necessarily a purple-flowered plant.

marrubium-vulgare.summary: Horehound is a gray-green perennial herb of open, disturbed ground and pasture. Its broad, wrinkled leaves and small white flowers can make it look like a soft garden mint, but mature flower cups become hooked burrs. Grazing animals often leave it behind, allowing it to compete with more useful pasture plants. Burrs can then carry its seeds beyond the patch.

haematobia-irritans.summary: Horn flies are small blood-feeding flies that spend much of their adult life on cattle. Large numbers repeatedly bite and irritate an animal, disrupting feeding and contributing to production losses. The larvae develop in cattle dung, so the flies have both an on-animal stage and an off-animal stage. Effective management depends on knowing which fly is present and measuring the pressure on the herd.

trapa-bicornis.summary: Horn nut is an aquatic plant associated with the hard, two-horned fruits sometimes called bat nuts. Floating leaves form a rosette above stems rooted in bottom mud. Trapa taxonomy varies among floras: some recognize Trapa bicornis, while Flora of China includes it within a broad T. natans. This account concerns that horn-nut form, without borrowing distribution claims for the distinct North American two-horned trapa described as T. bispinosa.

osmia-cornifrons.summary: Hornfaced bee is a solitary mason bee introduced from Asia for pollination of spring-flowering fruit crops. Females use nest cavities rather than forming a honey-bee colony. It closely resembles another introduced mason bee, Osmia taurus, and distinguishing them matters when documenting their spread or evaluating purchased nesting material. A bee using a garden nest block cannot be identified simply from the nest structure.

macrochlamys-indica.summary: Horntail snail is a small land snail with a delicate amber shell and a pointed fleshy projection at the end of its tail. It can shelter in moist plant material and nursery settings, making movement with plants a practical concern. Feeding studies show that it can use seedlings and various cultivated plants, although the amount of damage depends on the setting. A chewed leaf alone cannot show which snail caused it.

dopatrium-junceum.summary: Horsefly's eye is a small, soft-stemmed herb of wet ground, including rice fields, pond margins and seasonally wet riverbeds. Its thin branches and reduced upper leaves can make it resemble a tiny rush until the flowers open. It is an annual, so a patch may change greatly as water levels rise and fall. Its occurrence in a wet place is not enough to establish either its identity or an ecological impact.

armoracia-rusticana.summary: Horseradish is a perennial mustard grown for its thick, pungent roots. The large leaves die back in cold weather and new shoots rise from the surviving underground parts. Those roots also make it persistent outside its intended bed: even a small piece left behind can produce another plant. Harvesting a patch and removing a patch are therefore different jobs.

phyllotreta-armoraciae.summary: Horseradish flea beetle is a small leaf beetle associated especially with horseradish and related mustard crops. Adults chew small holes in leaves, while its larvae can burrow in leaf stalks and veins. The adult feeding can resemble damage from several other flea beetles. Checking the beetle itself helps avoid treating every small hole as evidence of this particular species.

moringa-oleifera.summary: Horseradish tree, also called moringa or drumstick tree, is a cultivated tropical tree with finely divided foliage and long hanging fruits. It is unrelated to the familiar horseradish crop despite the shared common name. The leaves and immature pods are used as vegetables in some food traditions, but that does not make every part suitable for use or establish a medicinal benefit. For identification, the long fruits and small leaflets are especially helpful.

carpobrotus-edulis.summary: This plant is also widely called sour fig or highway iceplant. It is a trailing succulent that roots at its joints and forms heavy, dense mats. Native to South Africa, it has escaped coastal plantings in several other regions. Its thick stems and leaves store water, so detached pieces can remain viable long enough to spread in dumped garden waste. Flower color varies with age and hybrid ancestry, which can complicate identification.

mogulones-crucifer.summary: Hound's tongue root weevil is an insect used in Canada to suppress houndstongue, Cynoglossum officinale. Adults feed on the leaves, but larvae inside the roots cause the more consequential damage. It can also use some related native plants, so biological-control benefits and non-target risks need to be considered together. An insect that damages a weed is not automatically appropriate to collect and release elsewhere.

mus-musculus.summary: House mice live around buildings, stored food and farms as well as in fields. They contaminate food, gnaw materials and build nests in sheltered spaces near a dependable food supply. A single mouse indoors can be a sign to inspect the building, but droppings or a fleeting glimpse may not identify the rodent species. Control works best when entry points, food access and the animals already inside are addressed together.

passer-domesticus.summary: House sparrows are stocky, social birds closely associated with buildings, farms and urban food sources. They often feed in groups and use holes in structures or nest boxes. Their status differs greatly across their range: a species introduced in one country may be a declining native bird in another. A useful identification should come before any decision about nest boxes or nuisance birds.

pulex-irritans.summary: Human flea is one of several flea species that can bite people. Its common name does not mean that a flea found on a person is necessarily this species; cat, dog and other fleas can also feed on humans. Adults take blood meals, while immature stages develop in the surrounding environment. Solving a flea problem therefore usually requires finding its animal or environmental source, not just treating the bites.

lablab-purpureus.summary: Hyacinthbean is a twining bean grown for its flowers, pods and other uses. It can behave as an annual or a short-lived perennial, climbing through supports and nearby vegetation on long stems. Cultivated plants vary considerably: flowers can be white, pink, red or purple, and the pods and seeds also differ in color. A plant beside a garden may be cultivated, self-sown or discarded; its location alone does not establish that it is spreading in the surrounding habitat.

hydrilla.summary: Hydrilla is a rooted underwater plant whose branching stems can grow upward and form dense growth near the surface. It can spread when stem fragments are moved between waters, and it also produces resting structures that help populations persist. A patch may therefore return after its visible shoots have disappeared. Its close resemblance to other submerged plants makes careful identification especially important before anyone begins cutting, raking or treating a waterbody.

maeotias-marginata.summary: This hydroid is most likely to be noticed as a small jellyfish in brackish water. Its conspicuous swimming stage is only one part of the life cycle: the attached polyp is minute and has been much harder to observe. Maeotias marginata is associated with the Black Sea and Sea of Azov region and has been recorded in other estuaries. California monitoring has found it during warmer, lower-salinity conditions, but those observations do not establish a universal seasonal schedule.

moerisia-lyonsi.summary: Moerisia lyonsi is a very small hydroid with an attached polyp stage and a free-swimming jellyfish stage. The polyps can grow on shells, stones, debris and other submerged surfaces. Both stages are easy to overlook, and a population may be present without an obvious jellyfish bloom. Its native range is uncertain. Reports using only the name Moerisia cannot automatically be assigned to this particular species.

lythrum-hyssopifolia.summary: Hyssop loosestrife is a small annual of damp ground, including places that are wet for part of the year. It is much less conspicuous than the tall, purple-flowered loosestrifes people may recognize from wetlands. Its narrow leaves and tiny flowers can blend into low vegetation or recently exposed mud. The shared common name does not mean that it has the same life cycle or should receive the same management as purple loosestrife.

sansevieria-hyacinthoides.summary: Iguanatail is a tough, evergreen plant that forms upright clumps of stiff leaves. Thick underground rhizomes allow a clump to expand and connect neighboring shoots. It has been grown as an ornamental and can persist where garden material is discarded. The familiar snake-plant appearance is useful for recognizing the group, but several related species are cultivated and their names are easily confused.

onopordum-illyricum.summary: Illyrian cottonthistle is a large, spiny thistle that begins as a low rosette and later produces an upright, branched flowering stem. Its pale, woolly surface gives a plant a gray-white appearance. In affected pasture, broad rosettes can occupy space needed by other plants, and dense stands of mature stems can obstruct movement. Those effects are documented in regional weed guidance and do not establish its status at an unverified location.

tradescantia-zebrina.summary: Inchplant is a trailing perennial often grown in hanging baskets or as a groundcover. Its jointed stems can root where they touch a suitable surface, allowing a loose piece or an escaped garden planting to become established. The striped foliage is conspicuous, but cultivated varieties differ in how much green, silver and purple they show. A pot on a windowsill and a spreading patch outdoors are different situations and need different responses.

tectaria-incisa.summary: Incised halberd fern is a large fern of moist, shaded places. It produces pale green fronds from a short, stout rhizome and can form substantial groundcover where conditions suit it. It has been cultivated as an ornamental, and Florida accounts identify discarded garden material as a possible route into natural areas. A fern appearing in a wet woodland should still be identified carefully, because related native ferns can look very similar.

duchesnea-indica.summary: India mockstrawberry is a low, creeping perennial that spreads through long runners. New plants root along those runners, gradually forming a patch in lawns, beds and other suitable ground. Its three-part leaves and bright red fruits resemble a strawberry, but the flowers provide a particularly helpful distinction. Whether a patch needs removal depends on the planting and local guidance; its presence alone does not show that it is harming the surrounding habitat.

ficus-benghalensis.summary: A single Indian banyan can become a spreading stand of trunks. Roots hanging from its branches thicken into supports when they reach the ground. Seeds carried into another tree can also start life above ground, with roots eventually surrounding the host. This tropical fig is widely planted for shade, but its large root system and ability to establish outside cultivation deserve attention near buildings and natural areas.

sisymbrium-orientale.summary: Indian hedgemustard is an upright, short-lived mustard of disturbed ground and cultivated places. Its pale yellow flowers give way to long, narrow pods that spread away from the stem. The plant changes shape as it grows: broad, divided lower leaves are replaced by narrower leaves higher up. A flowering plant without mature pods can easily be mistaken for another roadside mustard.

heliotropium-indicum.summary: Indian heliotrope carries a narrow flower spike with a curled tip, rather like a slowly unrolling tail. Only a few tiny flowers open at a time, while the older part develops fruits. This hairy annual grows in open, often damp or disturbed places, including field edges and drains. Its presence in a garden does not tell us how common it is elsewhere in the surrounding county.

ziziphus-mauritiana.summary: Indian jujube is a thorny shrub or small tree grown for fruit and shade. In suitable warm environments it can spread into dense thickets that restrict access and displace other vegetation. Animals eat the fleshy fruits and carry the seeds away. Cutting back an established plant is not necessarily the end of it: damaged roots and the swollen woody base can produce vigorous new shoots.

eragrostis-pilosa.summary: Indian lovegrass is a small tufted annual that can be easy to overlook until its delicate seed heads spread open. It grows in disturbed ground and cultivated places, where fine branches hold many narrow spikelets. Each spikelet contains several tiny flowers. The plant is much less conspicuous than large perennial lovegrasses, and the small hairs around its leaf bases and flowering branches are useful clues.

limnophila-indica.summary: Indian marshweed can look quite different above and below water. Submerged stems carry whorls of finely divided leaves, while shoots above the surface have shorter leaves and small pale flowers. It is a rooted freshwater perennial that can form dense underwater growth. Aquarium labels and a feathery appearance are not reliable identification: several related marshweeds are difficult to separate and have different regulatory histories.

plodia-interpunctella.summary: Indian meal moth is usually a pantry problem rather than an insect feeding on living plants outdoors. Its caterpillars eat stored dry foods and leave silk, shed skins and droppings among them. Flour is only one possible source: nuts, dried fruit, pet food and birdseed can also support an infestation. A caterpillar on a wall may have wandered away from the food to find a place to pupate.

morinda-citrifolia.summary: Indian mulberry, often called noni, is a tropical shrub or small tree with glossy leaves and unusual pale, knobbly fruit. Many small flowers join to form each fruit, which becomes soft and strongly scented when ripe. The plant has a long history of cultivation and transport through the Pacific. That history matters when interpreting a record: a planted noni tree and a self-established population are different observations.

polytrias-indica.summary: Indian murainagrass forms a low perennial mat by sending creeping stems across the ground. Those stems root at their joints, so a patch can persist even when its short flowering shoots are cut. Its seed heads are small and narrow, with golden hairs that become easier to see close up. It is one of several fine tropical grasses whose identity is easily lost when lawns are regularly mown.

ficus-elastica.summary: The familiar rubberplant houseplant can grow into a substantial tree outdoors in a frost-free climate. Its thick shiny leaves and pointed pinkish new-growth coverings are often recognizable long before it develops a trunk and aerial roots. This species is widely cultivated, so a record may represent a planted specimen rather than an escaping population. A large tree and an indoor potted plant also present very different management questions.

santalum-album.summary: Indian sandalwood is an evergreen tree grown for its fragrant heartwood. Its roots connect to other plants and obtain part of their water and nutrients through those connections. It still has green leaves and makes its own food through photosynthesis. That combination makes it a root hemiparasite, rather than a vine growing over another tree. Cultivated trees and plants establishing outside cultivation should be distinguished in a report.

cenchrus-biflorus.summary: Indian sandbur is a tufted annual grass with a seed head made of small, prickly burs. Those burs can catch on fur, clothing and equipment, moving seeds beyond the original patch. They also make a mature infestation unpleasant to walk through. Open, disturbed ground is a useful place to look, but a prickly grass should not be identified from its common name alone: several sandburs have a similar appearance.

canna-indica.summary: Indian shot, or canna lily, is a tall perennial with broad leaves and red or yellow flowers. Beneath the stems are thick, branching rhizomes that let a clump survive and spread. In warm, wet settings, escaped plants can form dense stands along waterways. Garden cannas include hybrids as well as this species, so a conspicuous canna beside a stream still needs a closer identification.

hygrophila-polysperma.summary: Indian swampweed is an aquatic plant that can grow submerged or extend onto damp banks. Its stems break readily, and loose pieces can root and start new patches. That makes aquarium disposal and the movement of plant-covered equipment especially important. Dense growth can crowd other aquatic plants and obstruct use of a waterway, but a photograph of a few underwater leaves is not enough to establish the species.

euphorbia-tirucalli.summary: Indiantree spurge, often sold as pencil tree, is a succulent shrub or tree with a network of slender green branches. It may look like a cactus, but it belongs to the spurge family. Its milky sap is irritating, which matters when someone handles a broken branch or clears discarded cuttings. A cultivated plant in a pot is different from a population growing outside a garden; include that distinction when reporting it.

hemidactylus-garnotii.summary: The Indo-Pacific gecko is a small, mostly nocturnal lizard that catches insects. It can live around buildings and other sheltered places, but its appearance overlaps with several other house geckos. Its original tail has a particularly useful clue: a saw-like edge. A replaced tail may lose that feature, so an apparently smooth-tailed animal should not be ruled in or out from that character alone.

charybdis-hellerii.summary: The Indo-Pacific swimming crab is a coastal crab that has reached parts of the western Atlantic beyond its original range. Its flattened rear feet work like paddles, while stout claws and a spiny shell give it a compact, armored appearance. Researchers consider it a possible competitor and predator of native animals, although the strength of those effects is not equally documented in every invaded location.

thinopyrum-intermedium.summary: Intermediate wheatgrass is a long-lived, cool-season grass planted for pasture, hay and soil stabilization. It spreads through underground stems and can form a dense sod. Selected forms are also grown for the perennial grain sold as Kernza. Those uses are important context: a planted field should not automatically be treated as an invasive infestation, even though the grass is introduced and can spread beyond a planting.

diprion-similis.summary: Introduced pine sawfly larvae feed on pine needles and can make an otherwise healthy-looking branch suddenly appear thin. They resemble caterpillars, but they are the young of a sawfly, a relative of bees and wasps. White pine is an important host, although other pines can also be used. Feeding may involve older needles first and, in later generations, both older and newer needles.

solanum-tuberosum.summary: Irish potato is the familiar food crop grown for its underground tubers. Plants can also reappear from tubers left in a garden, discarded in a pile or missed during harvest. These volunteer plants matter especially around potato production because infected tubers can carry disease into another season. A volunteer potato is not, by itself, evidence of a damaging invasion of nearby natural habitat.

limnoria-quadripunctata.summary: This tiny marine isopod is a wood-boring gribble, not an insect. It lives in submerged timber and excavates narrow galleries near the surface. Repeated attack and erosion can gradually weaken wooden marine structures. The catalog's broad common name, isopod, covers many unrelated-looking crustaceans, so reports need the scientific name and an expert identification rather than a photograph of damaged wood alone.

anchusa-azurea.summary: Italian bugloss is a bristly perennial grown for its bright blue flowers. It produces upright, branching flowering stems above a leafy base and may be found outside cultivation. It is recorded as nonnative in California, but that does not mean every garden plant is causing ecological harm. Describing whether it was planted or growing independently is especially useful for this ornamental species.

epidiaspis-leperii.summary: Italian pear scale is a tiny armored scale insect that feeds on the woody parts of fruit trees. It often hides beneath moss or lichens on older bark, where a small infestation can be easy to miss. Heavy aggregations can weaken a tree or contribute to bark damage, but small populations may cause little noticeable harm. Finding the scale is a reason to inspect the tree carefully, not an automatic reason to spray.

carduus-pycnocephalus.summary: Italian plumeless thistle is a spiny thistle that starts as a low rosette before producing branching flowering stems. In suitable disturbed ground or grassland it can form dense, prickly patches. Its narrow flower heads and spiny stem wings are useful clues, but it is easily confused with slenderflower thistle and other thistles. Native thistles also support wildlife, so getting the identification right matters before removal.

pinus-pinea.summary: Italian stone pine is the broad-crowned pine associated with Mediterranean landscapes and commercial pine nuts. A young tree is much more compact than the umbrella-shaped adult, so age can change the first impression considerably. It is planted as an ornamental in suitable climates. Records of planted trees and records of seedlings establishing away from them should be kept separate when describing its spread.

linaria-angustissima.summary: Italian toadflax is a narrow-leaved perennial with yellow, snapdragon-like flowers and a long spur behind each flower. It belongs to a group that includes the more familiar yellow toadflax. Similar-looking plants should not be assumed to be the same species, especially when an observation would be a new regional record. European accounts place it in dry grasslands, where its slim flowering stems rise above narrow foliage.

rottboellia-cochinchinensis.summary: Itchgrass is a tall, rapidly growing annual grass that can crowd crops, pastures and roadside vegetation. Its stiff hairs are more than a rough texture: they can break off against skin and cause irritation. Plants produce many side shoots, and new seedlings can continue appearing through the warm season. The distinctive jointed seed head is a better identification clue than height alone.

aphis-hederae.summary: Ivy aphids feed on young shoots and foliage of ivy and sometimes related plants. Colonies can be accompanied by sticky honeydew and dark sooty mold. Those signs indicate sap-feeding insects, but they do not identify this particular aphid. A colony on ivy is a useful lead for an identification, not proof that every insect in it is Aphis hederae.

coccinia-grandis.summary: Ivy gourd is a perennial climbing vine that can cover shrubs, fences and other supports. Its persistent underground rootstock lets it regrow after the visible vine is cut. Bright red mature fruits and white flowers help distinguish it from some other climbing plants. In Hawai‘i it is a significant invasive vine, with local reporting priorities that differ among islands.

veronica-hederifolia.summary: Ivyleaf speedwell is a low, spreading annual that often starts growing in the cooler part of the year. Its small flowers can be easy to overlook among the rounded, lobed leaves. Plants may spread into loose mats in disturbed ground, gardens or lawns. Several speedwells occupy similar places, so the leaf shape and fruit are useful companions to a flower photograph.

phytoliriomyza-jacarandae.summary: The jacaranda leaf miner is a small fly whose larvae feed inside jacaranda leaflets. Their tunnels begin as short, brown tracks and widen into blotches. Affected leaflets can fall early, and substantial damage can make a tree's canopy look yellow and sparse. This is different from an insect chewing open holes: much of the feeding takes place between the leaf surfaces.

canavalia-ensiformis.summary: Jack bean is a cultivated legume with large leaves and substantial, flattened pods. Some forms grow as bushy plants while others climb or trail. It has been grown as a crop and cover plant, so a report should explain whether it was intentionally planted or growing beyond cultivation. Its similarity to other Canavalia beans makes mature pods and seeds especially useful for checking the identity.

pseudococcus-jackbeardsleyi.summary: Jack Beardsley mealybug is a sap-feeding insect that can infest leaves, stems and fruit on many kinds of plants. Its waxy covering gives colonies a flour-dusted or cottony appearance. Honeydew can support dark sooty mold, and ants may attend the colonies. Several related mealybugs look very similar, so an apparently matching insect needs specialist confirmation before this species name is assigned.

trioceros-jacksonii.summary: Jackson's chameleon is a tree-dwelling lizard introduced through the pet trade. In Hawai'i, it adds another predator to habitats with native insects, spiders and snails. Its slow, rocking movement and grasping feet are distinctive, but being familiar as a pet does not make releasing or relocating it harmless. Sightings should be interpreted in their local context, especially on islands where response priorities differ. Established populations are reported on Hawaii, Maui and Oahu; other island sightings need local verification.

crassula-ovata.summary: Jade plant is a succulent shrub commonly kept as a houseplant or grown outdoors where winters are mild. Thick branches and fleshy leaves let an old specimen resemble a miniature tree. It is easy to propagate from plant pieces, which is useful in cultivation but a reason not to discard living material in natural areas. A garden specimen and a self-established outdoor patch are different kinds of records.

digitaria-horizontalis.summary: Jamaican crabgrass is a spreading grass of warm, disturbed places, including cultivated ground and roadsides. Its stems can lie along the ground and root, while slender flowering branches rise above the leaves. It resembles other crabgrasses closely. The common name does not establish where a particular population originated, and an ordinary lawn photograph may not contain enough detail to identify the species.

tribulus-cistoides.summary: Jamaican feverplant, also called puncture vine or nohu, is a low, spreading plant with yellow flowers and sharply spined fruits. Its status depends strongly on location. Florida references treat it as nonnative and invasive, while Bishop Museum and the University of Hawai‘i recognize it as indigenous in Hawai‘i. That difference matters: a plant in this catalog should not automatically be removed from a native coastal community.

browallia-americana.summary: Jamaican forget-me-not is a small flowering herb grown ornamentally and sometimes found escaping into disturbed ground. Despite its common name, it is a Browallia in the nightshade family, not a true forget-me-not. The blue, purple or whitish flowers have a slender tube and a paler throat. Its presence beside a garden should be documented separately from a planted bedding display.

aralia-elata.summary: Japanese angelica tree is a spiny shrub or small tree that can spread by both seeds and root suckers. Birds can carry its dark fruits, while shoots from connected roots enlarge an existing patch. In parts of the eastern United States it has escaped ornamental plantings into woodland edges and gaps. It closely resembles native devil's walkingstick, so this is a case where identification should come before clearing.

berberis-thunbergii.summary: Japanese barberry is a dense, thorny shrub introduced as an ornamental. Escaped plants can form thickets beneath woodland canopies and around disturbed edges. Its leaves often appear early and remain late, making it noticeable when many neighboring shrubs are bare. Garden cultivars have different leaf colors, so a purple or yellow-leaved plant may belong to the same species as a green woodland shrub.

callicarpa-japonica.summary: Japanese beautyberry is a deciduous shrub grown for its clusters of purple fruit. Its arching branches and changing autumn foliage make it conspicuous in gardens, but a planted shrub does not by itself demonstrate a population spreading in the surrounding habitat. When reporting it, distinguish a maintained planting from seedlings or shrubs growing without cultivation nearby.

popillia-japonica.summary: Japanese beetles feed on the leaves, flowers and fruit of many plants. Adults often gather on sunny foliage, leaving a lacy network of veins where they eat the softer leaf tissue. Their young are soil-dwelling grubs that feed on grass roots. Finding adults on a rose or fruit plant does not tell you how many grubs are beneath that particular lawn, because adults can fly in from elsewhere.

pinus-thunbergii.summary: Japanese black pine is an evergreen tree widely planted for its rugged shape, dark bark and tolerance of exposed coastal settings. Young trees are often broadly pyramidal, while older ones develop an irregular, spreading crown. Cultivated specimens, including carefully trained trees, can look quite different from one another. A useful observation therefore includes whether the tree was planted and whether seedlings are appearing beyond the maintained area.

bromus-japonicus.summary: Japanese brome is an introduced annual grass that often starts growing in fall and completes its life cycle during the following growing season. It can become part of the vegetation in grasslands and disturbed ground, with its abundance changing as weather and land management change. It should not be confused with a perennial grass simply because seedlings return to the same place each year.

haloa-japonica.summary: The Japanese bubble snail is a small marine snail with a delicate shell partly hidden by its soft body. It grazes on algae in sheltered coastal habitats, including mud, rocks, oyster beds and marina structures. Some North American records were originally published under other names. Keeping the scientific name used by the original source helps reviewers distinguish a renamed record from a newly documented arrival.

cryptomeria-japonica.summary: Japanese cedar, also called cryptomeria, is an evergreen conifer grown in landscapes for its textured foliage and reddish bark. Full-sized forms can become large trees, while selected garden varieties remain much smaller. Its common name does not make it a true cedar. A planted specimen should be distinguished from a tree that has established on its own when documenting its occurrence.

achyranthes-japonica.summary: Japanese chaff flower is a perennial herb that can form dense stands along streams and in woodland habitats. Its seeds catch on clothing and animal fur and can also travel with water, helping it reach new sites. The most useful response to a small new patch is early documentation and a plan that prevents seed movement, especially before people or equipment pass through it. Here, Achyranthes japonica follows North American identification guidance; some global floras include it within A. bidentata.

pittosporum-tobira.summary: Japanese cheesewood is an evergreen shrub or small tree commonly planted as a hedge. Its thick leaves and fragrant spring flowers make it recognizable in landscapes, but other pittosporums can look similar. A record is more informative when it says whether the plant is part of a hedge, a surviving old planting or a seedling beyond cultivation.

lygodium-japonicum.summary: Japanese climbing fern grows upward as well as across the ground, winding through shrubs and trees with long, wiry fronds. In parts of the southeastern United States it can cover surrounding vegetation and interfere with habitat restoration. Unlike a flowering vine, it spreads by spores, so the absence of flowers or berries does not mean a patch is unable to spread.

kummerowia-striata.summary: Japanese clover, often called common lespedeza, is a warm-season annual legume found in lawns and other open ground. Its low, spreading branches can become wiry as the plant matures, making it more noticeable late in the growing season. It returns through seed rather than a perennial root system. The shared name lespedeza covers several different plants, so guidance for a tall perennial species should not automatically be applied to this one.

periplaneta-japonica.summary: Japanese cockroach is a dark cockroach that can live outdoors in conditions too cold for some familiar household species. Researchers confirmed it in New York City using both anatomy and DNA. An insect found outside is therefore worth identifying carefully, but a dark cockroach beside a building is not enough to establish this particular species or an indoor infestation.

cornus-kousa.summary: Japanese dogwood, also called kousa dogwood, is a small deciduous tree valued for a late spring display of pointed white bracts. The actual flowers are the small cluster in the middle. Its branching form, later flowering and rounded, strawberry-like fruits give it a different seasonal character from the flowering dogwood familiar in eastern North America.

deparia-petersenii.summary: Japanese false spleenwort is a fern of damp, sheltered places, with soft green fronds rising from a creeping underground stem. It can appear in disturbed lowland forest and near streams. Its status varies by region: a fern that belongs naturally in one part of its broad range may be introduced elsewhere, so the common name alone says little about a local population.

clerodendrum-japonicum.summary: Japanese glorybower is a tropical shrub with broad leaves and branching clusters of vivid red flowers. The flower clusters stand above the foliage, making a flowering plant much easier to recognize than a leafy shoot. It belongs to a large group of ornamental shrubs with overlapping common names; a label such as glorybower or pagoda flower should be treated as a starting point.

lonicera-japonica.summary: Japanese honeysuckle is a climbing woody vine that can also spread across the ground. Its fragrant flowers open white and age to yellow, so both colors often appear together. In regions where it is invasive, stems climbing through shrubs and low tree branches can build a dense covering. It spreads through seed and through stems that root or send up new growth.

humulus-japonicus.summary: Japanese hop is an annual climbing vine that can cover a surprising amount of ground in one season. It scrambles over neighboring vegetation and forms dense tangles along sunny river margins, roadsides and other disturbed places. Its hooked hairs help it cling to supports. Despite the familiar hop name, an unmanaged patch should not be assumed to be a planted brewing hop.

fallopia-japonica.summary: Japanese knotweed is a tall perennial whose summer stems form a dense screen, then die back while a large underground rhizome system survives. Its jointed canes can suggest bamboo, but it is a flowering broadleaf plant. Along streams and disturbed edges, the underground network and the movement of fragments make established stands especially difficult to manage.

eragrostis-tenella.summary: Japanese lovegrass is a small annual grass with a light, open seed head held above slender stems. Regional floras record it in disturbed grassland, sandy places and other open ground. Its delicate appearance can conceal how difficult small lovegrasses are to identify: several species share fine branching heads, and older publications have not always used the same names consistently.

acer-palmatum.summary: Japanese maple is a small deciduous tree with a layered crown and hand-shaped leaves. Garden selections range from upright trees to low, weeping forms, and from green foliage to deep red or finely divided leaves. That variety is part of its appeal, but it also means that leaf color and overall size are unreliable shortcuts to identifying the species.

lopholeucaspis-japonica.summary: Japanese maple scale is a tiny armored insect that feeds on many woody plants, not just Japanese maples. Heavy colonies can turn portions of the bark pale and lead to weakened growth or dying branches. A light infestation can hide in bark crevices for some time, which is why examining a declining branch closely is more useful than judging the whole canopy from a distance.

mazus-pumilus.summary: Japanese mazus is a small annual herb that can appear in moist, disturbed ground. Its low leaves and tiny purple flowers are easy to overlook until several plants bloom together. It differs from creeping mazus, the perennial groundcover sold for gardens, in both lifespan and growth pattern. That distinction matters when a little flowering patch is being identified or managed.

spiraea-japonica.summary: Japanese meadowsweet, usually sold as Japanese spirea, is a deciduous shrub with clusters of small pink flowers. Many garden forms stay compact and have brightly colored young foliage. Outside cultivation it can establish dense patches in some regions, so a neat nursery plant and an escaping population can look quite different while belonging to the same species.

planococcus-japonicus.summary: Japanese mealybug is the name attached here to Planococcus japonicus, a valid species of plant-feeding scale insect. Published records include several woody and cultivated hosts, and plant material has carried it through international trade. The name needs care because similar mealybugs are readily confused and a common name may be applied differently in horticultural advice. Examined Chinese specimens include insects collected from hackberry relatives and sweet osmanthus.

echinochloa-esculenta.summary: Japanese millet is a cultivated annual grass used for grain, forage and other agricultural purposes. Escaped plants can occur near places where it has been sown or where birdseed has spilled. It belongs to the same difficult grass group as barnyardgrass, so a sturdy grass beside a feeder is not automatically a different species from one growing in a field.

cyrtomium-falcatum.summary: Japanese netvein hollyfern forms a tuft of sturdy, glossy fronds whose broad leaflets look rather like holly leaves. It stays green in mild conditions but can lose foliage in colder weather. This is a fern, so the brown structures beneath fertile fronds are spore-producing clusters rather than flowers, seeds or automatically a sign of insect damage.

styphnolobium-japonicum.summary: Japanese pagoda tree is a large deciduous tree with a rounded crown, divided leaves and creamy summer flowers. It is also called Chinese scholar tree and was long known as Sophora japonica. The familiar Japanese name reflects its cultivation history rather than a simple statement about origin. Mature trees can become much broader and taller than a young nursery specimen suggests.

gymnosporangium-asiaticum.summary: Japanese pear rust is a fungal disease whose life cycle connects susceptible pears and related plants with junipers. Japanese pear is an important host, while infection can persist on juniper for more than one season. The fungus is only one of several Gymnosporangium rusts, so a rusty pear leaf or an orange growth on a juniper does not by itself establish this species.

sagina-japonica.summary: Japanese pearlwort is a tiny, tufted flowering plant that can be mistaken for a little grass or a patch of moss until its white flowers appear. It is an annual or short-lived biennial in botanical treatments. The delicate stems and narrow leaves make it easy to miss in a casual survey, and several other pearlworts share almost the same general appearance.

primula-japonica.summary: Japanese primrose is a moisture-loving perennial with upright flower stems rising from a broad rosette of leaves. Flowers appear in separated tiers around the stem, giving it the candelabra appearance that gardeners recognize. Red-purple is a familiar color, but white and other garden forms occur. A flowering group beside water can be striking without being enough to establish its local ecological status.

ligustrum-japonicum.summary: Japanese privet is an evergreen shrub or small tree often clipped into a hedge. Left to grow freely, it produces clusters of fragrant white flowers followed by dark fruit. Its thick leaves can make it look tidy even when seedlings are beginning to appear elsewhere. The degree of escape and the recommendations for planting vary by region and should be checked locally.

hovenia-dulcis.summary: Japanese raisintree is a deciduous tree with a spreading crown and an unusual fruiting display. The swollen, branching stalks beneath the small fruits give rise to its raisin name. It has been planted as an ornamental in many places and has escaped in some regions. A tree's familiar garden use therefore does not settle whether it is appropriate beside nearby natural habitat.

kerria-japonica.summary: Japanese rose, or kerria, is a deciduous shrub with slender arching stems and bright yellow spring flowers. It is a member of the rose family, but its simple leaves and green shoots give it a different appearance from a typical garden rose. New shoots arising around the clump can gradually create a broad thicket, even when the original plant was small.

carex-kobomugi.summary: Japanese sedge, also called Asiatic sand sedge or calligraphy sedge, is a low perennial adapted to coastal sand. Its underground stems can produce dense mats of stiff leaves on dunes and upper beaches. In parts of the introduced range it competes with dune vegetation, so management needs to consider both the sedge and the fragile ground supporting it.

microstegium-vimineum.summary: Japanese stiltgrass is a summer annual that can form a soft-looking carpet across woodland edges, damp paths and shaded lawns. Its sprawling stems may root at the nodes, allowing a few plants to occupy more ground during the season. The plants die, but seed left in the soil can keep a patch returning for years, especially when disturbed ground remains open.

petasites-japonicus.summary: Japanese sweet coltsfoot, also called giant butterbur, is a perennial that makes a bold patch of broad leaves in moist ground. The flower shoots appear early, before the full summer foliage develops. Underground rhizomes let a planting spread well beyond its original clump. Leaf size varies considerably among forms and growing conditions, so spectacular size is a clue rather than a requirement.

wisteria-floribunda.summary: Japanese wisteria is a woody climbing vine with long hanging flower clusters. Its showy spring display can disguise the scale of its later growth: established stems can climb through trees, while surface runners root wherever they meet suitable ground. In regions where Asian wisterias escape, a flowering canopy may be connected to a much wider network below.

lysimachia-japonica.summary: Japanese yellow loosestrife is a low, branching herb with small yellow flowers and rounded to oval leaves. Regional floras describe it in moist places, including stream margins and damp forest edges. Despite the loosestrife name, it is not purple loosestrife, and advice for that much taller wetland plant should not be assumed to apply here.

podocarpus-macrophyllus.summary: Japanese yew is an evergreen conifer more accurately known as a podocarp or Buddhist pine. It is not a true yew in the genus Taxus. In gardens it may be clipped into a narrow hedge, but unconfined plants can become trees. The long, flat leaves give it a broad-leaved appearance even though it produces cones rather than ordinary flowers.

hyparrhenia-rufa.summary: Jaraguagrass, also called thatch grass, is a tall, tufted grass associated with warm open habitats and pasture introductions. Mature stands can leave substantial dry material. In Hawaii, fire specialists identify it as a fire concern, but the importance of a particular patch depends on local climate, surrounding vegetation and how the land is managed.

syzygium-cumini.summary: Java plum is a large evergreen tree with a dense crown and clusters of dark, oblong fruit. It is also called jambolan and is widely cultivated in warm regions. Animals eat the fruit and carry its seeds, helping explain why seedlings may appear away from an old planting. Invasion assessments vary even within Florida, so local guidance matters.

bischofia-javanica.summary: Javanese bishopwood is a substantial tropical tree with a dense, rounded crown. It has been widely planted for shade and street landscaping, but has also escaped cultivation in places such as southern Florida. Young foliage can have a bronze cast. Its most useful everyday identification feature is the three-part leaf, which should be examined as a whole rather than as separate leaves.

clerodendrum-speciosissimum.summary: Javanese glorybower is a traditional name for a red-flowered tropical shrub usually described with large, hairy, heart-shaped leaves. However, the scientific name has been applied inconsistently. Some institutional sources place Clerodendrum speciosissimum with C. buchananii, while other botanical treatments distinguish them. The traditional speciosissimum concept is used here, with the related buchananii treatment kept explicit.

solanum-pseudocapsicum.summary: Jerusalem cherry is a small ornamental shrub often grown in a pot for its bright orange-red berries. It belongs to the nightshade family and is not an edible cherry or a pepper. Outside cultivation it can persist in suitable moist, disturbed places. The colorful fruit makes the plant conspicuous, but it also makes careful labeling especially useful.

rhodotypos-scandens.summary: Jetbead is a deciduous shrub with a loose, arching outline, white flowers and shiny black fruits. The fruits often remain on the branches after the leaves fall, giving the shrub its common name. It has escaped ornamental plantings in parts of eastern North America. Despite the species name scandens, the plant normally presents as a shrub rather than a climbing vine.

datura-stramonium.summary: Jimsonweed is a robust summer annual with broad leaves, large trumpet-shaped flowers and prickly seed capsules. It can grow rapidly in disturbed ground and crop fields. The flowers may be white or purple, and the stems can also take on a purple color. All parts are poisonous, so this is a plant to identify by observation rather than by tasting or experimenting.

commelina-benghalensis.summary: Jio is the catalog common name for Commelina benghalensis, more widely called Benghal dayflower or tropical spiderwort. It is a spreading herb with broad leaves and small blue to purplish flowers. One especially important feature is hidden: it can produce self-pollinating flowers and seed-bearing capsules underground. A patch with no visible flowers can therefore still deserve attention.

coix-lacryma-jobi.summary: Job's tears is a robust grass best known for the smooth, beadlike structures carried among its flower clusters. Those hard coverings surround the grain and have long been used as beads. The plant grows in warm, moist settings, including stream banks and disturbed wet ground. Its cultivated forms and local life span vary, so a garden label may be useful context.

viola-tricolor.summary: Johnny jumpup, also called heartsease or wild pansy, is a small, short-lived violet that often returns from seed. Its cheerful flowers commonly combine purple, white and yellow, although the balance of colors varies. It is related to cultivated pansies, and a volunteer beside a flower bed may need closer examination before it can be assigned to this species.

sorghum-halepense.summary: Johnsongrass is a tall perennial grass that spreads through both seed and a network of underground rhizomes. It was introduced as a forage plant in some regions but is now a troublesome weed of crops, roadsides and other disturbed land. A patch can expand even when seed production is reduced, because established underground stems continue sending up shoots.

aegilops-cylindrica.summary: Jointed goatgrass is a winter annual grass that closely resembles wheat while young. It is particularly troublesome in winter-wheat systems because its growth timing overlaps the crop and its seed-bearing pieces can contaminate grain. Mature heads make the name easier to understand: they look like narrow cylinders built from a stack of joints.

amaranthus-tricolor.summary: Joseph's-coat puts its color into leaves rather than a conspicuous flower display. Ornamental forms of Amaranthus tricolor combine green, yellow, red, pink, or copper, sometimes making the upper growth look quite different from the leaves below. Other forms are mostly green. This upright annual can become a substantial, branching plant during a warm growing season, so a small nursery seedling does not tell you its eventual size. Cultivar choice makes a considerable difference to both height and color.

ziziphus-jujuba.summary: Jujube is a deciduous fruit tree with shiny leaves, often zigzagging branches, and fruits that change from green to brown as they mature. The brown fruit eventually softens and wrinkles, explaining the familiar name Chinese date, although this tree is unrelated to date palms. Cultivars differ in fruit quality, tree size, and thorniness. A less obvious feature is its ability to send up shoots from roots some distance from the trunk, which matters when choosing a place for it in a garden.

ovachlamys-fulgens.summary: The jumping snail is a tiny land snail whose name describes an unusually energetic escape. When disturbed, it can flick itself away using the rear of its foot and a hornlike structure near the tail tip. It has been recorded on ornamental plants, including orchids, and can be overlooked among pots and moist plant material. Laboratory research found that isolated individuals could produce viable eggs without mating, so finding only one snail does not establish that a plant shipment is free of a reproductive population.

amynthas-agrestis.summary: Amynthas agrestis is one of several earthworms commonly called jumping worms. They live close to the soil surface and can leave a loose, granular layer that resembles coffee grounds. In affected North American woodlands and gardens, their rapid processing of surface organic matter can change the conditions that plants and other soil organisms depend on. They also travel with everyday gardening materials, including soil, mulch, and potted plants. Their presence calls for careful containment, even when the individual worms seem easy to collect.

echinochloa-colona.summary: Junglerice is a warm-season annual grass that takes advantage of moist, disturbed ground, especially where irrigation continues through summer. It forms clumps that may stand upright or spread low across the soil. In rice fields it can resemble the crop before flowering and compete with it; in orchards and garden beds, repeated summer emergence can make a patch seem to return just after it has been cleared. The plant reproduces by seed, so preventing another seed crop is central to keeping a small problem from growing.

fiorinia-pinicola.summary: Juniper fiorinia scale is a minute armored scale insect with a particularly confusing naming history. Fiorinia pinicola is retained as a valid species in ScaleNet and a modern review of United States Fiorinia, but older accounts sometimes placed it under names also used for other scales. Records include conifers and additional woody hosts, so neither the word juniper nor a plant's identity is enough to settle the diagnosis. An infestation may appear as scattered dark flecks on foliage before the insects themselves are recognized.

corchorus-aestuans.summary: Corchorus aestuans is a leafy herb with small yellow flowers and slender, angular seed capsules. It is often called jute, a name that also covers other Corchorus species and can obscure important differences. Floras record it in warm regions, including moist or marshy sites in parts of India. Its ordinary green foliage is easy to overlook, but the details at the base of a leaf and the shape of a ripe capsule are much more informative than its general resemblance to a small mallow.

themeda-quadrivalvis.summary: Themeda quadrivalvis is most usefully called grader grass, although kangaroo grass appears among its common names. It forms upright clumps with cane-like stems and branched seed heads that turn warm reddish-brown or golden as they mature. In parts of Australia it has spread through roadsides, pastures, and other disturbed ground, where dense stands compete with desirable vegetation and add dry fuel. The common-name overlap matters: the better-known Australian kangaroo grass, Themeda triandra, is a different species and should not be removed on the strength of a shared label.

tilletia-indica.summary: Tilletia indica is the fungus responsible for Karnal bunt, a disease of wheat, durum wheat, and triticale. It is often called partial bunt because infection can replace only part of a grain with a dark mass of spores. A crop may look fairly ordinary in the field, with the problem becoming apparent after threshing exposes the affected kernels. Its importance extends beyond the amount of grain visibly damaged: grain movement and export requirements can make even a small confirmed finding significant for a grower or grain handler.

dysphania-carinata.summary: Keeled wormseed, also called keeled goosefoot or green crumbweed, is a small aromatic herb that may spread along the ground or stand upright. Its green leaves and tiny clustered flowers make it easy to dismiss as an ordinary garden weed. That would be a poor assumption everywhere: the Victorian flora describes it as rare there, occurring on sandy or gravelly ground near the Snowy River and its tributaries. The scientific name Dysphania carinata is more useful than its varied common names when checking a local record.

cymbalaria-muralis.summary: Kenilworth ivy makes a low, trailing patch of small leaves and violet flowers, often tucked into the joints of a wall or between paving stones. Despite its name, it is a flowering herb rather than a woody ivy. Slender stems can take root where they touch a suitable surface. Its flower stalks have an unusual habit: after flowering they turn away from the light, helping place developing seeds in sheltered cracks.

poa-pratensis-ssp-pratensis.summary: Kentucky bluegrass is a perennial grass that spreads through slender underground stems and can form a close turf. It is familiar in lawns, parks and pasture, but the name covers considerable variation. This entry concerns the subspecies pratensis. That distinction matters because plants sold or recorded simply as Kentucky bluegrass do not always fit neatly into one subspecies, and some cultivated material combines characters from several groups.

citrus-x-aurantiifolia.summary: Key lime is a small citrus tree or large shrub with glossy evergreen leaves and strongly aromatic fruit. Its thin-skinned limes turn yellow as they ripen, although green fruit is familiar in shops. The tree belongs to warm climates and needs protection from cold. A garden specimen is best understood as a cultivated fruit tree; finding one near a house is not, by itself, evidence that it is spreading through the surrounding landscape.

alternanthera-pungens.summary: Khakiweed is a creeping perennial that makes low, dense mats in disturbed ground, lawns and other frequently used places. Its most troublesome feature is the cluster of sharp burrs that develops around the seeds. Burrs can catch on shoes, fur and equipment, carrying the plant into new patches. Stems can also root where they touch the ground, so a mat may have more than one rooted point.

cenchrus-clandestinus.summary: Kikuyugrass is a vigorous perennial grass that spreads by thick runners above ground and underground stems below it. It can produce a dense, springy mat and push into neighboring lawn or garden beds. In parts of California it is a difficult turf and landscape weed, although it is also managed as turf in some settings. Its small flowers are mostly hidden inside the upper leaf sheaths, an unusual feature for a grass.

persicaria-orientalis.summary: Kiss me over the garden gate is a tall annual grown for its dangling clusters of pink flowers. A mature plant can rise above surrounding border plants and look almost shrubby, but it completes its life cycle through seed. It can reseed freely and turn up on disturbed ground beyond a garden. NC State notes naturalization and invasive behavior in parts of the southeastern United States, a regional concern rather than a universal description.

dichanthium-annulatum.summary: Kleberg's bluestem is a perennial grass with a small fan of slender flowering branches at the top of the stem. It is one of several similar grasses whose common names include bluestem. The name alone is therefore a poor guide to identity. Plants can spread through rooted shoots, and mature flowering material is usually needed to tell this species from neighboring pasture and roadside grasses.

panicum-coloratum.summary: Kleingrass is a perennial grass grown in some places for forage and found elsewhere outside cultivation. It forms leafy tufts or patches with upright flowering stems and a loose, branched seedhead. Its appearance varies enough that a common name or overall color is not sufficient for identification. The individual spikelets and the plant's persistent base provide a better starting point than the silhouette of a flowering clump.

anolis-equestris.summary: The knight anole is a large, tree-dwelling lizard from Cuba that has established in southern Florida. It spends much of its time among trunks and leafy branches, where green coloration can make a substantial animal surprisingly easy to overlook. It eats invertebrates and small vertebrates, and observations also document fruit and other plant material. Its size and predatory behavior make it a different presence in a garden from the smaller anoles often seen nearby.

torilis-nodosa.summary: Knotted hedgeparsley is a small annual in the carrot family, usually noticed when its burrlike fruits catch on clothing. Its branching stems grow close to the ground or rise through nearby vegetation. It occurs in disturbed places such as field edges, pasture and roadsides. The rounded flower and fruit clusters sit close to the stems, giving it a more knotted appearance than hedgeparsleys with broad flower clusters raised on long stalks.

cyprinus-rubrofuscus.summary: Koi are domesticated ornamental carp bred in many combinations of white, orange, gold and black. They can grow into substantial pond fish and live for many years, so buying a small individual creates a long-term care commitment. This catalog follows the name Cyprinus rubrofuscus used by USGS for koi. Older and horticultural sources often call them Cyprinus carpio, reflecting a complicated history of carp classification and breeding.

selaginella-kraussiana.summary: Krauss' spikemoss forms a soft-looking green carpet in damp, shaded places. Despite the name, it is a small vascular plant related to other spikemosses, rather than a true moss. Slender creeping stems branch repeatedly and root as they go. It has been grown as an ornamental, including in containers and terrariums, and can spread beyond cultivation where moisture and shade suit it.

pueraria-montana.summary: Kudzu is a robust climbing plant with large leaves and thick storage roots. This entry uses Pueraria montana at species rank, which includes more than one named variety. The familiar kudzu that blankets trees and roadsides in parts of the United States is generally treated as variety lobata. Keeping that distinction visible avoids turning every report of the broader species into a confirmed record of that particular variety.

kudzu.summary: Kudzu can turn a sunny woodland edge into a continuous layer of leaves, covering shrubs and climbing into trees. This entry concerns Pueraria montana var. lobata, the variety usually meant by kudzu in United States weed guidance. It is a perennial vine with large storage roots, and stems touching the soil can take root at their joints. That combination allows an established patch to persist after its visible growth is cut.

megacopta-cribraria.summary: Kudzu bugs are small sap-feeding insects associated with kudzu and other legumes, including soybeans. They can also become a household nuisance when adults gather on light-colored walls and seek sheltered places for winter. A cluster on a house does not mean the insects are feeding on the building. In fields, their importance depends on the crop, the number present and the stage of growth, so a sighting alone is not a treatment threshold.

eulecanium-kunoense.summary: Kuno scale is a sap-feeding insect that can look like a row of shiny brown beads fixed to a twig. It is a soft scale, and heavy populations can leave sticky honeydew beneath an affected plant. Black sooty mold may grow on that residue, while ants are often attracted to it. UC IPM particularly associates troublesome garden populations with plum trees in parts of northern California, although the insect has other woody hosts.

euwallacea-kuroshio.summary: Kuroshio shot hole borer is a tiny ambrosia beetle that bores into wood and carries fungi used as food inside its galleries. In southern California, this beetle-fungus partnership can damage living trees, including avocado and several landscape and riparian species. The visible problem is therefore more than a small hole in the bark: fungal growth and repeated attacks can contribute to branch dieback and declining tree health.

fusarium-kuroshium.summary: Fusarium kuroshium is a microscopic fungus associated with the Kuroshio shot hole borer. The beetle introduces its fungal partners into woody tissues while making galleries, and the fungi provide food for the insects. Research in California found this species capable of causing disease in young avocado plants. It is one member of the wider beetle-and-fungus problem called Fusarium dieback, rather than a visible mushroom that can be recognized beside an affected tree.

graphium-kuroshium.summary: Graphium kuroshium is a microscopic fungal partner of the Kuroshio shot hole borer. It was described from the beetle-fungus complex affecting woody plants in California. In the original research, inoculation tests showed that it could cause disease in young avocado plants. That result establishes a specific experimental finding; it does not show that every declining tree with beetle holes is infected by this fungus or that the fungus acts alone in the field. Species Fungorum now spells the same name Graphium kuroshio.

ulva-pertusa.summary: Lacy sea lettuce is a sheetlike green seaweed recorded under the name Ulva pertusa and now widely treated as Ulva australis. It grows in shallow coastal settings, including lagoons, and can resemble several other sea lettuces. The change in name reflects taxonomic work, not a visible change in the alga. This profile keeps the catalog identifier while making the newer name available for comparison with current identification resources.

pteris-vittata.summary: Ladder brake is a fern with long, narrow fronds divided once into many slender leaflets. It often appears on lime-rich surfaces, including old mortar and masonry, as well as in disturbed ground in suitable climates. A plant growing from a wall crack may be small, while a shaded specimen can carry much longer fronds. Its spreading units are microscopic spores, so it never produces flowers or seed pods.

persicaria-maculosa.summary: Lady's thumb is an annual smartweed often found in cultivated or disturbed ground. It develops branching stems and compact pink flower spikes, sometimes reaching about a meter tall. The familiar dark mark on many leaves gives the plant its common name, but some leaves lack that mark. A spot is a useful clue, not a reliable shortcut around examining the rest of the plant.

galium-divaricatum.summary: Lamarck's bedstraw is a slender annual that can be easy to overlook among dry grasses and other low vegetation. Fine branching stems spread into a loose, wiry framework, with tiny leaves grouped around the joints. Its flowers and fruits are much smaller than those of many familiar garden weeds. The plant has been recorded in disturbed lowland habitats in western North America, while Australian floras also describe it from dry, open places.

chenopodium-album.summary: Lambsquarters is an upright annual that often appears quickly in cultivated soil, vegetable beds and other disturbed places. Its young foliage commonly has a pale, floury coating, especially underneath. As the plant grows it branches and produces dense clusters of tiny green flowers. Because it reproduces through seed, a small overlooked seedling can become a much larger source of future weeds if left through the growing season.

crotalaria-lanceolata.summary: Lanceleaf rattlebox is an erect annual legume with narrow leaflets and clusters of small yellow flowers. It occurs in disturbed ground, including sandy fields and roadsides, and has also been cultivated outside its African range. As the flowers finish, inflated pods darken and hold the seeds associated with the rattlebox name. Several related plants have similar flowers and pods, making the leaves and flower size important parts of the identification.

lantana-camara.summary: Lantana is familiar as a flowering garden shrub, but the name Lantana camara has also been applied broadly to a complicated group of cultivated and escaped plants. Some current Florida resources distinguish the widespread ornamental weed as Lantana strigocamara. That difference matters when interpreting a photograph or a local invasive-plant record. This account uses the broad cultivated-and-escaped camara complex, rather than assigning every plant to a narrow species.

salix-cinerea.summary: Large gray willow is a deciduous shrub or small tree that often forms a broad, many-stemmed crown. It favors wet ground, including stream edges, swamps and lake margins. In regions where it has escaped cultivation, it can form dense stands and regenerate from seed or surviving woody growth. Its soft early catkins make it attractive, but a wetland planting needs more thought than its appearance alone might suggest.

luziola-subintegra.summary: Large watergrass is a robust perennial grass that can float or rise above shallow water. It spreads into mats, supported in part by its swollen, spongy leaf sheaths. Florida observations document large colonies that crowd other aquatic vegetation. Its size sets it apart from the more delicate watergrasses, but a floating grass mat still needs careful examination before a species name is assigned.

lysimachia-punctata.summary: Large yellow loosestrife is an upright garden perennial that expands through underground rhizomes. Its yellow flowers and leafy stems can make a handsome colony, but the same growth can carry it beyond the space originally intended. It has escaped from gardens in several regions, often around discarded plant material. This is a Lysimachia in the primrose family, rather than the unrelated purple loosestrife often discussed in wetland management.

ludwigia-grandiflora.summary: Large-flower primrose-willow is an aquatic perennial associated with shallow water and wet margins. Creeping stems can first form floating mats, then produce upright flowering shoots. Bright yellow flowers make the patch conspicuous, but they do not settle its identity. The name Ludwigia grandiflora has sometimes been used loosely for a group of similar creeping water primroses, so an exact species record deserves more care than a general report of the weed.

amaranthus-deflexus.summary: Largefruit amaranth often spreads close to the ground, its branching stems weaving through paving edges, garden soil, and other disturbed places. Unlike many familiar upright pigweeds, this species is a perennial with a persistent base. Young growth can be hairy, while the small green flowers gather into narrow, rather inconspicuous clusters. The enlarged fruits are more useful for recognizing it than the flowers, which easily disappear against the foliage.

adiantum-macrophyllum.summary: Largeleaf maidenhair has a simpler, bolder outline than the finely divided maidenhair ferns often grown indoors. Each arching frond carries a small number of broad leaflets, and fresh growth can emerge reddish pink before turning green. Botanical treatments describe it from tropical American forests, including streamside settings. Those habitat records describe where the fern grows; they do not establish that every cultivated or newly observed plant is an environmental problem.

hydrocotyle-bowlesioides.summary: Largeleaf marshpennywort is a small, creeping lawn and disturbed-ground herb whose name can suggest something much larger than the plant itself. Its stalked, lobed leaves sit above slender stems, with conspicuous pale hairs giving parts of the plant a fuzzy appearance. A Louisiana botanical report documented how easily it can be filed under the wrong name: the original specimen had been identified as Bowlesia incana. Careful close-up examination matters more here than the common name.

tomicus-piniperda.summary: The larger pine shoot beetle uses different parts of a pine during its life cycle. Breeding takes place beneath the bark of recently cut material, stumps, or badly weakened trees, while newly emerged adults can feed inside the shoots of living pines. That shoot feeding may leave damaged tips in the crown or on the ground. A fallen pine shoot is a clue worth examining, but several insects and weather events can produce similar damage.

scolytus-mali.summary: The larger shothole borer is a small bark beetle associated with weakened trunks and branches, including those of fruit trees. Its presence can therefore be part of a larger tree-health problem rather than the first cause of decline. Beneath occupied bark, a lengthwise mother gallery gives rise to smaller larval tunnels spreading across the grain. These galleries can help an expert understand the infestation, although they should be examined on already detached or dead material.

centratherum-punctatum.summary: Larkdaisy is a branching herb with small, rounded purple flower heads that stand out against rough-textured leaves. Plants may sprawl or grow upright, and the base can become woody as the season progresses. It is cultivated ornamentally, while botanical records also document it outside gardens in disturbed places and pasture. A flowering plant beside a garden is therefore worth recording in context, without assuming that one escaped individual represents a widespread local problem.

hemiberlesia-lataniae.summary: Latania scale is an armored scale insect that spends much of its life beneath a tiny protective cover attached to a plant. Colonies can look like pale specks or small crusts on leaves, stems, or fruit. The covers remain much easier to see than the insects themselves. Finding a few scales does not automatically mean a plant needs treatment: their importance depends on the host, whether the insects are alive, and whether damage is developing.

erigeron-karvinskianus.summary: Latin American fleabane makes loose cushions of wiry stems carrying small daisy heads, often with white and pink flowers visible together. It is familiar in rock gardens and wall crevices, and botanical records describe escapes into other moist or disturbed settings. Its cheerful flowering habit can make it easy to overlook seedlings outside the original planting. Whether those escapes need action depends on the surrounding habitat and local guidance.

salix-pentandra.summary: Laurel willow is a broad-leaved willow whose glossy foliage can look surprisingly unlike the narrow leaves many people associate with the genus. It grows as a shrub or tree in wet settings, and planted trees occur beyond its Eurasian range. The name needs particular care in North American records: a New Zealand taxonomic treatment notes research assigning North American material previously called Salix pentandra to a hybrid. A garden label or older observation should therefore be checked rather than accepted automatically.

raffaelea-lauricola.summary: Laurel wilt is a tree disease caused by the fungus now called Harringtonia lauricola, formerly Raffaelea lauricola. The catalog retains the older fungal name. The redbay ambrosia beetle can introduce the fungus as it bores into a host, after which the tree's water-conducting tissue becomes blocked. Redbay, sassafras, avocado, and other members of the laurel family can be affected. Susceptible trees may decline rapidly, making an early, well-documented report useful.

kalanchoe-fedtschenkoi.summary: Lavender scallops is a succulent with rounded, fleshy leaves whose blue-gray coloring and scalloped edges give it a soft, patterned appearance. It can stand upright or lean outward as stems lengthen. Hanging, bell-like flowers appear in branched clusters above the foliage. The species comes from Madagascar and is widely cultivated; a flora record of an escaped roadside plant in Zimbabwe shows why garden waste deserves attention, without establishing the same behavior in every climate.

hydrocotyle-sibthorpioides.summary: Lawn marshpennywort is a low perennial whose slender creeping stems can thread through grass, garden soil, or damp litter. Its small, rounded leaves are often only about a centimeter across, so the plant may first appear as a fine green mat rather than a collection of separate stems. Botanical treatments differ somewhat in the amount of hair they describe, and the New South Wales flora notes that its local species concept is under revision. Those details make careful regional identification worthwhile.

bellis-perennis.summary: Lawn daisy, also called English daisy, is the familiar low plant with a yellow-centered flower head surrounded by white or pink rays. Its leaves stay close to the ground, allowing it to persist among regularly mown grasses. It is a perennial, although garden forms may be grown for a shorter season. Whether it counts as a weed is often a matter of the lawn's purpose: Oregon State includes it among plants that can be retained in an ecolawn and provide food for visiting pollinators.

typha-laxmannii.summary: Laxman's bulrush is a cattail, with narrow upright leaves and the familiar brown, cylindrical flowering head. It grows at shallow water margins and in other wet ground, and it is also cultivated as a pond plant. Compared with some larger cattails, the female portion of its flower spike is relatively short. That compact head can be a useful starting point, but cattail identification needs more than a distant view of a brown cylinder.

xanthomonas-oryzae.summary: Xanthomonas oryzae is a bacterial species that includes distinct disease-causing forms in rice. The form called pathovar oryzae causes bacterial leaf blight, while pathovar oryzicola causes bacterial leaf streak. The catalog's broad species name should not be read as a diagnosis of one particular disease. Both can damage leaves, but their early symptoms and biology differ, and late-stage injury can look much alike.

eballistra-oryzae.summary: Leaf smut of rice is caused by Eballistra oryzae, a fungus still called Entyloma oryzae in many crop guides. It produces small dark spots in leaf tissue and is generally treated as a minor disease in the United States extension accounts reviewed here. A heavily spotted leaf may look alarming, but its appearance does not by itself indicate a major yield threat. The first useful step is to distinguish leaf smut from the other leaf and grain diseases that share parts of its common name.

dysaphis-crithmi.summary: Dysaphis crithmi is described in specialist aphid literature as an aphid associated with rock samphire, Crithmum maritimum, particularly around sheltered leaf bases. The common name leaf-curling plum aphid points toward a different insect: university plum guidance uses that name for Brachycaudus helichrysi. Combining the two would give readers the wrong host plant and could lead to an incorrect diagnosis.

centrocoris-volxemi.summary: Centrocoris volxemi is a small true bug in the leaf-footed bug family, documented in Utah and Idaho after its arrival in North America. University of Idaho observations describe it as a possible household nuisance as well as an insect found outdoors. Russian thistle is an important recorded feeding plant. Its appearance on another plant does not necessarily mean that plant is a host, a distinction emphasized in California's pest assessment.

erasmoneura-variabilis.summary: The variegated leafhopper is a tiny grape-feeding insect listed in older vineyard guides as Erythroneura variabilis and placed in Erasmoneura in taxonomic treatments. Both adults and immature stages remove the contents of leaf cells, leaving pale stippling behind. Large populations can reduce leaf function, but a few insects or scattered feeding marks do not automatically call for treatment. Vine condition, population trends, and the activity of natural enemies all matter.

euphorbia-esula-var-esula.summary: Leafy spurge names can conceal an important difference between closely related plants. The name Euphorbia esula has often been applied to the troublesome North American plant now treated as Euphorbia virgata. Montana's botanical guidance explicitly marks that older usage as a misapplication, while European floras distinguish true E. esula by its leaf shape and other characters. This account concerns true variety esula; importing a general North American leafy-spurge account would risk describing the wrong taxon.

euphorbia-virgata.summary: Leafy spurge is a perennial that can turn an open field yellow-green when its flowering shoots rise together. Much of that color comes from modified leaves around the tiny flowers. Beneath the surface, spreading roots connect patches and produce new shoots, so cutting a stem does not remove the plant. In northern North American grasslands, established colonies can crowd other vegetation and complicate pasture management.

acrolepiopsis-assectella.summary: Leek moth is a small moth whose caterpillars feed inside the leaves of leeks and other alliums. Early damage can be easy to miss because the feeding is sheltered within the plant. As larvae grow, they can reach central leaves, stems and bulbs, leaving a crop ragged and reducing its usable quality. A damaged leek deserves a closer look before the injury is blamed on weather or disease.

eragrostis-lehmanniana.summary: Lehmann lovegrass is a perennial bunchgrass with a loose, wiry appearance. Some stems lean outward or lie along the ground, where they may take root. In parts of the southwestern United States, it can spread from scattered clumps into nearly continuous stands.
