Its history as a planted forage grass does not mean it is suitable for every restoration project, especially where conserving diverse desert grassland is the goal.

cymbopogon-citratus.summary: Lemongrass is a warm-climate perennial grown for its citrus-scented foliage and thickened leaf bases. In cooler gardens it is often treated as an annual or kept in a container that can be brought indoors. A small division can become a substantial clump during warm, humid weather. Its familiar culinary name also applies to related grasses, so a nursery label and the plant's structure are more useful than fragrance alone.

corymbia-citriodora.summary: Lemon-scented gum is a tall tree whose pale trunk and narrow canopy leaves give it a distinctive presence. It is planted well beyond its Australian range, so a tree in a park or street may be cultivated rather than evidence of a nearby wild population. The lemon fragrance associated with its foliage is a helpful clue, but trees within the broader taxonomic treatment vary and should be checked against other features.

hordeum-murinum-ssp-leporinum.summary: Leporinum barley, also called hare barley, is an annual grass that forms soft green tufts before producing dense, bristly seed heads. It is often noticed on disturbed ground when the long awns become conspicuous. Sources treat it either as Hordeum leporinum or as a subspecies of H. murinum. That naming difference matters when comparing records, but both names can refer to the same plant represented here.

ranunculus-ficaria.summary: Lesser celandine is a low-growing perennial that appears early in spring, flowers brightly, and then disappears above ground. That summer absence can be misleading: small underground tubers remain alive. In invaded North American woodlands and gardens, the plant can form a dense carpet before many other plants emerge. Modern references commonly call it Ficaria verna; Ranunculus ficaria is the older name retained in this catalog entry.

callosobruchus-chinensis.summary: This small seed beetle is a pest of stored pulses, including several kinds of beans, peas and lentils. The damaging stage lives inside a seed, so an apparently intact batch can contain developing insects. Adults leave neat circular holes when they emerge. Common names vary between countries: the same species is called the southern cowpea weevil or adzuki bean beetle as well as the lesser cowpea weevil.

centaurea-nigra.summary: Lesser knapweed, also called black or common knapweed, is a branching perennial with purple, thistle-like flower heads. Its role depends on location: it is a familiar grassland plant in parts of Europe, while introduced populations elsewhere may need assessment. The dark covering beneath each flower head is more useful for recognizing it than the common name, which is shared loosely across a complicated group of knapweeds.

xyleborinus-saxeseni.summary: The lesser shot hole borer is an ambrosia beetle that develops in wood with the help of cultivated fungi. It often uses weakened, dying or recently cut trees, leaving tiny entrance holes and tunnels. The beetles and their young depend on the fungal growth within these galleries. A hole in a trunk therefore needs investigation, but it does not by itself establish this beetle's identity or prove that the insect caused the tree's original decline.

lepidium-didymum.summary: Lesser swinecress is a low, spreading mustard that fits easily into gaps in lawns, garden beds and disturbed ground. Its small flowers attract little attention, but the finely divided foliage and paired, wrinkled fruits are distinctive at close range. It commonly completes its life cycle as an annual, though some plants persist longer. Older weed guides may list it as Coronopus didymus, a name worth recognizing when comparing advice.

achroia-grisella.summary: Lesser wax moth is associated with honey-bee comb and stored hive materials. Its caterpillars tunnel through the comb and leave silk and waste behind, especially where bees are absent or a colony is already weak. Finding wax moth damage should therefore prompt a look at the colony's underlying condition as well as the moth itself. Strong colonies are usually much better able to defend their comb.

nasonovia-ribisnigri.summary: The lettuce aphid Nasonovia ribisnigri feeds on foliage and often hides among the youngest leaves near the heart of a lettuce plant. An outer leaf can look fairly clean while insects are already sheltered deeper inside. Rapid reproduction and this protected feeding position make established infestations difficult to manage. It is also called the currant-lettuce aphid because some populations alternate between currants or gooseberries and herbaceous hosts.

pemphigus-bursarius.summary: Pemphigus bursarius is more precisely called lettuce root aphid, which distinguishes it from aphids living inside lettuce heads. Its colonies feed underground, interfering with water uptake and leaving plants yellow, slow-growing or wilted. In part of its life cycle it produces distinctive galls on poplar leaf stalks. Those two very different settings belong to one insect, although its life cycle can vary with climate and host availability.

helichrysum-petiolare.summary: Licorice-plant is a soft, spreading shrub grown mainly for its silvery foliage. The rounded leaves and loosely branching stems make it a familiar companion to brighter flowers in garden plantings. It can become a substantial shrub where conditions suit it, rather than remaining a small seasonal accent. The common name is not a reason to treat it as a food plant or substitute it for culinary licorice.

epiphyas-postvittana.summary: Light brown apple moth is a leafroller whose caterpillars use silk to shelter among leaves or between touching plant parts. Despite its name, it can feed on many fruit crops and ornamental plants. The visible injury may be folded leaves or feeding on protected surfaces rather than a conspicuous insect. Because many other leafrollers behave similarly, a suspected sighting should remain provisional until a specialist checks it.

salvia-verticillata.summary: Lilac sage is a perennial with branching flowering stems and repeated rings of small purple flowers. Its bold foliage and airy flower arrangement make it useful to recognize beyond the general label of garden salvia. Cultivars can differ in size and display, so a named garden selection should not be used as the sole model for every plant. Plants found outside a bed also deserve identification before their local significance is judged.

lilioceris-lilii.summary: Lily leaf beetle is a bright red beetle that can strip leaves and damage buds on true lilies and fritillaries. Both adults and larvae feed, so removing only the obvious red insects may leave a damaging population behind. Plants commonly called lilies are not all equivalent hosts: daylilies belong to a different group and are not the breeding hosts described for this beetle.

salpichroa-origanifolia.summary: Lily of the valley vine is a scrambling perennial in the nightshade family. Its small hanging white flowers explain the common name, but it is quite different from the familiar broad-leaved woodland lily of the valley. Long stems can weave over nearby plants and fences, while an extensive underground system allows the plant to return after its top growth has been cut away.

triphasia-trifolia.summary: Limeberry is a thorny evergreen shrub grown for its glossy foliage, fragrant white flowers and small red fruits. It is often maintained as a hedge in warm climates, but can also establish beyond cultivation in suitable places. The name sounds like a familiar citrus fruit, yet identifying the shrub requires attention to its leaves and spines rather than relying on fruit color or scent.

salvia-tiliifolia.summary: Lindenleaf sage is an annual with broad leaves and slender flowering spikes carrying small blue blossoms. It grows in disturbed habitats and can be easy to overlook among larger weeds until flowering begins. Its familiar sage shape does not establish whether it belongs naturally at a particular site; the species has both native and introduced populations, and local context matters when deciding what to do.

misopates-orontium.summary: Linearleaf snapdragon, often called lesser snapdragon or weasel's snout, is a slender annual with small flowers resembling miniature garden snapdragons. It may occur among crops or on disturbed ground, but being found in a field does not automatically make it a harmful invader. Its conservation standing varies geographically, so the most useful first step is to establish the identity and local context.

agriotes-lineatus.summary: The lined click beetle is best understood through its underground young: the wireworms that feed on seeds, roots and tubers. Adults can fly between sites, while larvae remain in soil through a prolonged development period. Damage may appear as poor crop establishment or holes in harvested roots. A field can contain several wireworm species together, so identifying one adult does not explain every damaged plant.

leonotis-leonurus.summary: Lion's ear is a vigorous shrub with tiered rings of orange flowers that stand above its foliage. It has a woody base and softer upright stems, giving it a different character from a low herbaceous sage. In warm gardens it can become tall and broad; in colder climates its winter survival depends on conditions. The tubular flowers provide nectar to visiting birds and insects.

pterois-volitans.summary: Red lionfish is a predatory reef fish with an unmistakable striped silhouette and dramatically spreading fins. In the western Atlantic and Caribbean, introduced lionfish have become an important management concern. Their striking appearance can make them tempting to approach, but several fin spines are venomous. Observations are most useful when the fish is left undisturbed and its location is recorded accurately.

bixa-orellana.summary: Lipsticktree, also known as annatto or achiote, is a tropical shrub or small tree grown for its showy flowers and colorful seed capsules. The reddish coating around its seeds is the source of annatto coloring. Its fruit is visually memorable, often covered with soft-looking bristles, but fruit color varies among plants. A cultivated tree and a self-established population should be recorded separately when assessing its local occurrence.

aceria-litchii.summary: The litchi mite, more often called lychee erinose mite, is a minute plant-feeding mite whose effects are easier to see than the animal itself. Feeding on tender lychee growth triggers dense, feltlike patches called erinea. Damaged leaves become distorted, and severe infestations can affect flowers and fruit. The pest's sheltered position among these abnormal hairs makes early recognition particularly useful.

medicago-minima.summary: Little bur-clover is a small annual legume whose low stems and three-part leaves can resemble other medics or clovers. Its coiled, spiny fruit provides the strongest clue. The plant may be inconspicuous while leafy, then become more noticeable when burs develop close to the ground. The alternative name woolly burr medic reflects the fine hairs that can be especially obvious on young growth.

wasmannia-auropunctata.summary: Little fire ant is a tiny ant capable of forming troublesome populations in gardens, nurseries and other warm habitats. Its small size makes it easy to move unnoticed with plants or materials. Unlike the image many people have of fire ants, it does not need a conspicuous soil mound: colonies can occur in trees, pots and sheltered spaces. Finding it early depends on a deliberate survey rather than waiting for an obvious nest.

cyanthillium-cinereum.summary: Little ironweed is an upright herb with small mauve or purple flower heads at the ends of branching stems. Mature heads turn into little pale tufts as the fruits develop their dispersal hairs. It often appears on roadsides, abandoned ground and other open disturbed sites. Older references may call it Vernonia cinerea, a useful synonym when matching an observation to a flora.

hop-stunt-viroid.summary: Hop stunt viroid is a microscopic plant pathogen that can infect citrus as well as hops and grapevines. In citrus, the consequences depend on both the viroid variant and the variety of tree. Some infections produce little obvious damage, while cachexia-associated variants can affect the bark and wood of susceptible plants. A healthy-looking canopy therefore does not establish that a tree is suitable as a source of grafting material. Little leaf of citrus is a historical name associated with the cachexia naming tradition; it is not a dependable symptom test.

eragrostis-minor.summary: Little lovegrass is a small annual grass that can make a loose, branching tuft in pavement cracks, cultivated ground and other disturbed places. Its airy flower heads are easy to overlook until their many flattened spikelets catch the light. Plants growing in compacted ground may remain quite short, so height alone is a poor guide. The most useful details are close to the leaf margins and stems, where tiny glands help distinguish it from other lovegrasses.

briza-minor.summary: Little quakinggrass has a delicate appearance that becomes especially noticeable when a breeze moves its hanging flower heads. This annual grass forms loose tufts with thin, flat leaves and a much-branched spray of tiny spikelets. In the New South Wales flora it is recorded from disturbed ground and flowers in spring. Its attractive movement does not tell you whether it belongs in a particular planting, so identification and local context are useful before deciding to retain or remove it.

plectranthus-parviflorus.summary: Little spurflower is a soft-stemmed perennial with opposite, rounded leaves and small pale flowers. Older references use Plectranthus parviflorus, while North Carolina State's plant account places it under the newer name Coleus australis. It can spread outward or stand more upright, and established plants may die back to a fleshy base before growing again. That seasonal change is worth recognizing in a garden, where a temporarily bare plant might otherwise be mistaken for one that has failed.

ipomoea-triloba.summary: Littlebell is a slender morning-glory vine whose modest flowers can be hidden among surrounding leaves. It trails over open ground or twines through other vegetation, with pink to purplish funnel-shaped blooms and variable heart-shaped or lobed leaves. The Flora of the Cayman Islands describes it as an annual of sandy ground, pastures, clearings and thickets. Australian rainforest records also place it along roads and in open riverside situations, showing why a single habitat description is not enough to identify it.

camelina-microcarpa.summary: Littlepod false flax is a slender annual in the mustard family. Its pale yellow flowers are easy to miss, but the small swollen seed pods give a mature plant a recognizable texture. It occurs in cultivated and disturbed ground, including cereal fields and vineyard margins in the University of Navarra's weed flora. Plants branch above their lower leaves and can look rather spare when growing among taller vegetation. A fruiting specimen is much more informative than an isolated yellow flower.

phalaris-minor.summary: Littleseed canarygrass is an annual grass with a dense, compact flower head that can resemble a short green brush. It is particularly important to recognize in cultivated ground, where a grass weed may blend into a cereal crop before the heads emerge. The Indian National Institute of Plant Health Management describes it as a winter annual. That seasonal pattern should be interpreted locally, since growth and flowering depend on the climate and the cropping calendar.

paratachardina-pseudolobata.summary: Lobate lac scale is a small sap-feeding insect that can become difficult to notice against woody stems. Colonies may cover twigs and branches, while black sooty mold makes the plant look as though its bark has darkened. In southern Florida it has been recorded on many shrubs and fruit trees, including cocoplum, hibiscus and mango. Heavy infestations can be associated with branch dieback, but neither black mold nor declining growth identifies this scale by itself.

sisymbrium-irio.summary: London rocket is a yellow-flowered mustard that often starts as a low rosette before sending up branching stems. In California, university guidance describes it as a winter annual of fields, orchards, gardens and roadsides. A patch may become conspicuous quite quickly as the stems lengthen and narrow seed pods develop. Its presence in disturbed ground is a useful clue, but many unrelated and closely related mustards share that setting, so the mature plant deserves a closer look.

eragrostis-elongata.summary: Long lovegrass, also called clustered or close-headed lovegrass, forms a tuft of narrow leaves beneath slim flowering stems. Its seed heads look more compressed than the open, cloudlike heads of many other lovegrasses. Australian floras record it in woodland and grassland, with flowering in summer or following rain. Those regional accounts also show variation in lifespan and soil association. It is therefore better understood through its structural features and local setting than through a single rigid description of where it must grow.

pseudococcus-longispinus.summary: Long-tailed mealybugs are small sap-feeding insects that often hide in the protected parts of houseplants and greenhouse plants. Their white wax can make a colony look like scattered bits of lint. Feeding may be accompanied by sticky honeydew and black sooty mold, which sometimes draw attention before the insects themselves are noticed. Warm, sheltered foliage is a useful place to begin an inspection, especially when several plants are crowded together and their leaves overlap.

erodium-botrys.summary: Longbeak stork's bill is a low-growing herb whose fruit becomes much more striking than its small pinkish flowers. Young plants form a leafy base, and later stems may spread close to the ground with a reddish tint. The long, pointed fruiting beaks explain the common name. In Victoria it is recorded from roadsides, pasture, grassland and grassy woodland. A plant without mature fruit can resemble other stork's bills closely, so a confident identification often requires a return visit.

pholcus-phalangioides.summary: The longbodied cellar spider is a familiar resident of quiet corners in houses, garages and sheds. Its very long, slender legs surround a small body, and it usually hangs upside down in a loose, irregular web. It feeds on insects and other spiders that it can capture, sometimes including prey much larger than itself. In a building, its presence often becomes noticeable through the web rather than through any damage to possessions or plants.

oenothera-affinis.summary: Longflower evening primrose is a hairy, upright herb with large yellow flowers carried above remarkably long, slender floral tubes. Its stems may branch, and the yellow petals can become reddish as they age. It has been cultivated and recorded from disturbed sites outside its South American range. The name is especially descriptive when a flower is viewed from the side: much of its apparent stalk is actually part of the flower, extending between the ovary and the open petals.

ehrharta-longiflora.summary: Longflowered veldtgrass, also called annual veldtgrass, is a tufted annual with broad, soft-looking leaves and drooping spikelets on a relatively open flower head. It can be conspicuous on neglected urban ground and on sandy or alluvial soils. New South Wales and Victorian floras describe plants approaching a meter in height, although smaller plants occur. Its large spikelets help separate it from many ordinary lawn grasses, but other veldtgrasses require closer attention.

icosium-tomentosum.summary: Icosium tomentosum is a small longhorn beetle associated with conifers in the cypress family, including junipers, cypresses and thujas. Its larvae develop in woody material, initially beneath bark and later farther into the wood. Adults are active at night and may come to lights, which explains some records made around buildings. Finding one near a tree does not establish that it caused the tree's decline: published accounts emphasize dead or dying branches, and evidence of serious damage to healthy trees is limited.

paratrechina-longicornis.summary: Longhorned crazy ants are small, dark ants whose rapid, wandering movements can make a busy colony look disorganized. They forage through buildings and disturbed outdoor places, searching for food scraps, insects and sugary resources. A nest can be some distance from the workers you see, so the busiest kitchen corner may only be a feeding stop. University field observations describe quick recruitment to household food, a useful clue when investigating how ants are entering a room.

veronica-longifolia.summary: Longleaf speedwell is an upright perennial with narrow, toothed leaves and long spikes of small flowers. Regional floras describe blue flowers. It occurs in moist meadow and waterside settings in parts of its Eurasian range, and garden escapes are recorded elsewhere. A flowering clump can provide a strong vertical accent, but the behavior of a named garden selection should not automatically be applied to every wild population.

deroceras-invadens.summary: The longneck fieldslug, also called the brown field slug, is a small slug often associated with gardens and other disturbed places. Adults are usually only a few centimeters long, and their color can range from pale cream or brown to much darker shades. The John Innes Centre describes it as a minor agricultural and horticultural pest. Its presence beside a damaged plant is worth investigating, but it does not by itself establish which animal made the holes.

sporisorium-cruentum.summary: Loose kernel smut of sorghum is a fungal disease in which developing grain is replaced by masses of dark spores. The fungus is Sporisorium cruentum, also described in older literature as Sphacelotheca cruenta. Affected plants may be shorter and thinner-stemmed than their neighbors and can produce heads earlier. The most useful signs appear as the panicle emerges, when the fragile coverings of the smutted kernels begin to break and expose the black powder inside.

eriobotrya-japonica.summary: Loquat is an evergreen fruit tree with large, textured leaves and clusters of yellow to orange fruit. It is widely planted, but it can also establish outside gardens in suitable climates. Its local status matters: Florida assessments distinguish regions needing caution from regions where it is not currently considered a problem, while Hawaiian references document naturalization and concern for native forest.

amaranthus-caudatus.summary: Love-lies-bleeding is an annual amaranth grown for long, hanging tassels of tiny flowers. It is also associated with grain cultivation, so a plant in a garden or crop plot should not be described in the same way as plants establishing beyond cultivation. It can reseed, making the location of volunteer seedlings useful information when someone reports it.

cyperus-pumilus.summary: Low flatsedge is a small annual sedge also described in botanical references as Pycreus pumilus. It can be easy to overlook among grasses and other short plants. Indian botanical records associate it with marshy ground, rice fields and wetlands. Those habitat observations help explain where to look, but they do not establish its presence or impact in a particular United States county.

malva-pusilla.summary: Low mallow is a small-flowered mallow recorded in disturbed ground, roadsides and waste places. Its rounded fruit resembles a little wheel made of separate segments, a feature shared with other mallows. Common names and older scientific names have been applied inconsistently, so a reliable report needs close photographs rather than a name inferred from a familiar leaf shape.

ardisia-humilis.summary: Low shoebutton, here meaning true Ardisia humilis Vahl, is a woody tropical plant. Modern botanical treatments recognize Ardisia humilis, while several invasion and management publications use that name for shoebutton ardisia, Ardisia elliptica. Those references cannot safely be combined into a single profile without checking which plant they describe. A documented Laos treelet had pink flowers and smooth foliage, independently supporting this true-species account.

thevetia-peruviana.summary: Luckynut, often called yellow oleander, is a flowering shrub or small tree also known as Cascabela thevetia. Its attractive flowers and fruit have encouraged planting, but all parts are poisonous. The word nut in its common name should never be taken as an indication that the seeds are edible. A planted specimen and a population establishing beyond a garden are different kinds of observations.

ptychosperma-macarthurii.summary: Macarthur palm is a clustering palm commonly planted in warm climates. Several slender trunks can rise together from the same planted clump, so a group of stems is not necessarily evidence of many separate seedlings. When documenting possible spread, distinguish that original clump from smaller palms growing away from it without cultivation.

rosa-bracteata.summary: Macartney rose is a thorny, climbing or trailing shrub that can form dense thickets in open woodland and pasture. In parts of the southern United States those thickets displace other vegetation and make ground difficult for people, livestock and wildlife to use. Its historical use as a living fence helps explain why an old hedge and a spreading patch may occur together.

noronhia-emarginata.summary: Madagascar olive is an evergreen tree planted for its tough foliage and tolerance of coastal conditions. It is not the familiar olive grown for olive oil. Botanical records document naturalization in parts of Hawaii, but that history should not be used to assume that every landscape tree is spreading or causing the same effects elsewhere.

catharanthus-roseus.summary: Madagascar periwinkle is a tender perennial commonly grown as a summer bedding plant. It can survive longer in warm climates but is often treated as an annual where frost or disease ends the planting. It is frequently sold as vinca, although true Vinca species belong to a different genus and have different growth and invasion histories.

cryptostegia-madagascariensis.summary: Madagascar rubbervine can grow as a woody shrub or climb over neighboring vegetation on long, flexible stems. It was planted for its pink-purple flowers, but in suitable climates it can cover other plants and spread from cultivation. It is closely related to another rubbervine, Cryptostegia grandiflora, so sources discussing both should not be treated as if every detail applies equally to this species.

kalanchoe-blossfeldiana.summary: Madagascar widow's-thrill is the compact flowering kalanchoe often sold in pots. It is a succulent perennial, with fleshy leaves that help it withstand dry periods. Its presence in cultivation does not make it equivalent to every other Kalanchoe in the catalog: related species differ considerably in their growth, reproduction and behavior outside gardens.

hippobroma-longiflora.summary: Madamfate is a small herb with striking white flowers held at the ends of unusually long tubes. It grows in moist, shaded or disturbed places and is sometimes planted as an ornamental. Its Caribbean origin and regional history matter when interpreting records; being listed in the catalog is not a reason to assume it is introduced or harmful at every location.

euphorbia-helioscopia.summary: Sun spurge, also listed as madwoman's milk, is an annual plant of disturbed ground and cultivated places. Its small greenish flower structures can be less noticeable than the broad leaves clustered around them. It reproduces by seed rather than the persistent spreading roots associated with some perennial spurges, so correct identification changes how a patch should be assessed.

prunus-mahaleb.summary: Mahaleb cherry is a small deciduous tree or large shrub that can escape gardens and old homesteads. Birds move its seeds after eating the fruit, so young trees may appear away from the original planting. Its status is local: Washington places it on a monitoring list rather than treating it as a listed noxious weed, a distinction worth keeping clear.

dianthus-deltoides.summary: Maiden pink is a low-growing perennial often planted for its bright flowers. It can also occur beyond gardens, reproducing through seed and underground stems. A patch may therefore persist after flowering ends. Reports should distinguish a planted border from plants spreading into neighboring open ground rather than treating every colorful garden clump as an invasion.

muehlenbeckia-complexa.summary: Maidenhair vine is a woody climber with slender, interlacing branches that can form a dense tangle without a support. It is native in New Zealand but has been recorded outside cultivation elsewhere, including California. The names wire vine and angel vine are also used for related species, making a nursery name or a small round leaf an unreliable identification by itself.

silene-vulgaris.summary: Bladder campion, also called maidenstears, is a perennial herb recognizable by the inflated greenish or pinkish case beneath each white flower. It occurs in open and disturbed places, including forage ground. It can return through underground stems as well as seed, so a flowering patch is not simply a group of annual plants that disappears permanently after mowing.

syzygium-jambos.summary: Malabar plum, often called rose apple, is an evergreen tree grown for its pale fruit. In some warm, moist regions it has spread beyond cultivation and formed dense stands that shade the vegetation below. It is different from Java plum, Syzygium cumini, so records and advice attached only to the word plum need to be checked carefully.

lindernia-crustacea.summary: Malaysian false pimpernel is a small annual herb of moist ground, gardens and disturbed places. It can creep close to the soil or grow more upright, making its appearance change with the surrounding vegetation. Its common name does not make it a true pimpernel, and a tiny purple flower by itself is not enough to establish the species.

centaurea-melitensis.summary: Maltese star-thistle is a spiny, yellow-flowered plant of disturbed ground, grasslands and other open places. It usually grows as an annual, although some plants live into a second season. It can be confused with yellow starthistle, but the two are different species. A treatment or biological-control result for yellow starthistle should not automatically be applied to this one.

silene-chalcedonica.summary: Maltese cross is a perennial garden flower with dense clusters of bright scarlet blooms. It may also be listed under its older name, Lychnis chalcedonica. A plant beside a house or in a maintained bed may be an intentional ornamental; records outside cultivation should distinguish that setting from a self-established population. Flower color alone is not enough to decide its identity or local impact.

leymus-racemosus.summary: Mammoth wildrye is a coarse perennial grass that spreads through underground stems called rhizomes. It has been planted to hold inland sand and reduce wind erosion. That useful role does not rule out unwanted spread into neighboring vegetation, but neither does its catalog listing mean every established planting should be removed. Site history and local assessment are important parts of a record.

peperomia-pellucida.summary: Man to man, or shiny bush, is a small fleshy herb that grows in moist, sheltered places. It can appear in garden beds, beside walls and in other damp crevices. Its delicate stems and tiny flowers make it easy to overlook until several plants are present. Common names vary widely, so the scientific name and clear photographs are especially useful when reporting it.

thladiantha-dubia.summary: Manchu tubergourd, also called red hailstone or goldencreeper, is a perennial climbing vine that can persist through a network of underground tubers. Shoots can cover fences, shrubs and other vegetation. Those tubers are important to both spread and control: cutting the visible vine does not remove the stored growth below ground, and discarded tubers can start another patch.

juglans-mandshurica.summary: Manchurian walnut is a deciduous tree grown for its large divided leaves and, in some forms, its nuts. The name has been used broadly in some botanical treatments and more narrowly in others. Japanese walnut and heartnut may be included within it or listed separately. That naming history matters when matching a cultivated tree or an older record to this profile.

mangifera-indica.summary: Mango is a widely cultivated evergreen fruit tree. In warm climates it may also grow outside maintained gardens, but a fruit tree in cultivation and a spreading wild population are different observations. Florida assessments distinguish regional levels of concern, so the species should not be described as equally problematic throughout the United States. Record the setting and evidence of recruitment rather than assuming impact from the name alone.

milviscutulus-mangiferae.summary: Mango shield scale is a small sap-feeding insect found on mango and many other host plants. It belongs to the soft scales, which can produce sticky honeydew that supports dark sooty mold. A dirty-looking leaf is therefore a clue to investigate, not a diagnosis: several scale insects and other sap feeders can produce the same effect.

sphaeroma-terebrans.summary: The mangrove-boring isopod is a small crustacean that shelters in burrows in mangrove roots and other suitable material. Its relationship with mangroves is more complicated than a simple damage label. Studies document root injury and altered root growth, but the outcome depends on the site and conditions. Its origin and introduction history are also uncertain in parts of its range.

zoysia-matrella.summary: Manila grass is a warm-season perennial turf grass that forms a close mat through aboveground runners and underground stems. It is intentionally planted in lawns, but those same spreading structures can cross a maintained edge. A lawn planting is not itself evidence of ecological harm. Records outside cultivation should explain where the grass is growing and whether its patch is expanding.

eucalyptus-viminalis.summary: Manna gum is a tall Australian eucalyptus with pale upper bark that sheds in long ribbons. It has been planted beyond its native range. Florida assesses it as a high invasion risk using a predictive tool; that is a warning about potential behavior, not proof that every Florida county has an established population. A useful observation distinguishes a planted tree from seedlings growing beyond cultivation.

mabuya-multifasciata.summary: The many-striped skink is now commonly placed in the genus Eutropis, although older records use Mabuya multifasciata. It is a sturdy, day-active lizard from southern and southeastern Asia. Published observations document introduced populations in southern Florida. Those records establish particular occurrences, not a reason to assume that any brown skink seen elsewhere is this species.

aristotelia-chilensis.summary: Maqui is a many-branched shrub or small tree with dark berries. It is native to parts of southern South America, but its movement to islands illustrates why location matters: research from the Juan Fernández archipelago documents invasion of native vegetation there. That island history should not be presented as proof of the same impact at every United States occurrence.

ranunculus-marginatus.summary: Margined buttercup is a small yellow-flowered buttercup recorded in disturbed places, including roadsides and seasonally moist ground. It can resemble several other annual buttercups. The mature fruits are more informative than flower color, and regional descriptions differ in the fruit forms they report. A yellow blossom alone is not enough to identify this species.

neotoxoptera-oliveri.summary: Neotoxoptera oliveri is a small aphid recorded from several herbaceous hosts, including violets, chickweeds and some onion relatives. The catalog label marigold aphid is not enough to establish the host range or identify an infestation. A Florida inventory published in 2025 reports this species from herb nurseries and herb gardens, illustrating why the plant's identity and growing setting are worth recording.

cannabis-sativa.summary: Cannabis is an annual plant with a long history of cultivation for several purposes. It can also persist as escaped plants in disturbed ground. The names hemp and marijuana do not provide a reliable visual identification of a plant's chemical composition. This profile concerns recognizing and documenting the plant, not determining its legal classification or how it may be used.

membranipora-membranacea.summary: The lacy crust bryozoan is a colony of many tiny animals, often forming a pale, net-like layer across kelp. A colony begins when a swimming larva settles, then grows by budding additional individuals. In parts of the northeastern United States it is an introduced fouling organism that can weaken kelp tissue. Its effects should be described for the affected region rather than assumed everywhere.

eualetes-tulipa.summary: Eualetes tulipa is a marine worm snail: despite its irregular tube-shaped shell, it is a snail rather than a worm. Adults remain attached to hard surfaces and feed from the surrounding water. Records include harbors and other altered coastal habitats. Its native range and identification history are complicated, with older records published under names such as Vermetus alii.

cernuella-virgata.summary: The maritime gardensnail, also called vineyard snail, is a land snail that can gather on vegetation, posts and other objects above the soil. Agricultural concern includes contamination of harvested grain and interference with machinery, not only feeding on plants. It can travel with equipment and goods, so a small cluster on stored material is worth documenting before that material is moved.

pinus-pinaster.summary: Maritime pine is a large Mediterranean pine planted for timber, shelter and ornament. It can establish beyond plantings in suitable environments. Florida identifies invasion risk through a predictive assessment, with recommendations differing by region. That assessment should guide caution about planting and escape, but it does not establish that a particular county already contains a wild population.

ardisia-japonica.summary: Japanese ardisia, also listed as marlberry, is a low evergreen shrub that can spread into a dense groundcover. Its underground growth makes a patch larger than the stems visible above it. Florida guidance identifies particular concern in the north of the state, with different assessments farther south. That regional context matters when deciding whether a planted groundcover has become a management problem.

gnaphalium-uliginosum.summary: Marsh cudweed is a small woolly annual found on damp ground, including pond margins, wet meadows and disturbed places. Its flower heads are much less showy than those of familiar daisies. Regional references differ about whether all North American populations should be considered introduced, so its local origin and ecological role need to be assessed separately from its identity.

cyclospermum-leptophyllum.summary: Marsh parsley, also called slender celery, is a finely divided annual herb found in gardens, roadsides and other disturbed ground. Its airy foliage and tiny white flowers can resemble several members of the carrot family. The common names do not make it an edible herb, and a safe identification should rely on leaves, flowers and mature fruit together.

cirsium-palustre.summary: European marsh thistle is a tall, spiny plant of damp open places, wetland edges and disturbed woodland. It starts as a low rosette and later produces a flowering stem, sometimes after more than two growing seasons. A population can therefore contain inconspicuous rosettes as well as tall plants. Mapping both stages helps reveal the extent of a developing infestation.

persicaria-hydropiper.summary: Marshpepper knotweed, or water-pepper, is an annual of wet ground, ditches and stream or pond margins. It can form groups of plants through repeated seed production, especially where wet soil is disturbed. Its common name reflects a reported peppery taste, but tasting an unknown smartweed is unnecessary and should not be used as an identification method.

trimezia-martinicensis.summary: Martinique trimezia is a yellow-flowered perennial in the iris family, also known as yellow walking iris. That common name can cover more than one garden plant. A recent Florida flora warns that the similar Trimezia steyermarkii has often been called T. martinicensis. This distinction needs resolving before older Florida observations or horticultural descriptions are assigned confidently to this species.

maruca-vitrata.summary: The legume pod borer is a moth whose caterpillars feed inside or around the flowers and pods of beans and other legumes. They can tie plant parts together with silk, making feeding less obvious from a distance. Damage matters most when flowers or developing seeds are affected. Reports from different regions should not be confused with proof of a newly established population at every sighting.

mirabilis-jalapa.summary: Marvel of Peru, or four-o'clock, is a familiar garden plant with flowers that often open late in the day. It can live as a perennial where winters are mild and is grown as an annual in colder places. Both seed production and persistent swollen roots can matter when it becomes unwanted, so removing the visible stems may not finish the job.

phyllanthus-tenellus.summary: Mascarene Island leaf-flower, also called long-stalked phyllanthus, is a small upright plant often found in nursery pots, irrigated beds and disturbed ground. Its tiny leaves can make the side branches resemble compound leaves, but they are separate leaves on a stem. Plants can flower when still small, so waiting for a tall weed can allow seed production to begin unnoticed.

lepidosaphes-pallida.summary: Maskell scale is a tiny armored scale insect that feeds on several conifers, including junipers, arborvitae and Japanese cedar. Infestations can cause yellowing, browning or twig decline, but those symptoms have other causes too. Old scale covers may remain after the insects have died, so the amount of visible debris is not necessarily the size of the living infestation.

amaranthus-blitoides.summary: Mat amaranth, also called prostrate pigweed, is a summer annual that spreads close to the ground in dry fields, roadsides, gardens, and other open places. It is native to part of North America, so its presence does not automatically represent an introduced invasion. In a vegetable bed or newly planted field, however, a spreading plant can compete with the plants someone is trying to establish.

nardus-stricta.summary: Matgrass is a small, tough perennial bunchgrass from Eurasia. Its name describes the dense, wiry clumps it can build rather than a soft lawn. In parts of the western United States it is a concern in grazed grasslands because livestock tend to leave it while eating more palatable grasses. Its quiet appearance makes a small infestation easy to overlook among other pasture plants.

lycium-barbarum.summary: Matrimony vine is the sprawling, sometimes climbing shrub also sold as goji or wolfberry. Long arching shoots, small purple flowers, and orange-red berries can make it conspicuous along old gardens and disturbed ground. Cultivated plants can spread through both seed and root suckers. Whether that spread is an environmental concern depends on the region and setting; a fruit planting is not evidence that the species is invasive throughout the country.

ampelodesmos-mauritanicus.summary: Mauritanian grass is a large perennial bunchgrass native to the western and central Mediterranean region. It has been cultivated outside that range and is recorded as established in parts of California. A mature clump can be substantial, with flowering stems rising well above the leaves. Flora of North America notes that plants dry rapidly in summer, an important consideration where ornamental plantings meet fire-prone vegetation.

furcraea-foetida.summary: Mauritius hemp is a massive rosette-forming succulent grown for ornament and historically for fiber. Despite its common name, a planting can spread through little plantlets produced on the towering flower stalk. Those plantlets, called bulbils, can fall and establish around the parent. Florida assessments identify it as invasive in natural areas, while its behavior and management priority elsewhere need to be checked locally.

parlatoria-pittospori.summary: Mauve pittosporum scale is a tiny armored scale insect found on leaves and small stems of a wide range of woody and ornamental plants. Pittosporum is only one host; records also include pines, apples, and several other plant groups. The insect has been reported in California, but a scale-covered shrub elsewhere should not be assigned this name without examination. Its protective cover can remain visible after the insect underneath has died.

leucanthemum-maximum.summary: Max chrysanthemum is a white-flowered perennial daisy associated with gardens and occasional escapes. The scientific name Leucanthemum maximum is useful here because the familiar label Shasta daisy is also applied to cultivated hybrids. The species is native to southwestern Europe and introduced elsewhere. Its presence in a catalog of introduced species should not be read as a claim that every garden daisy is an invasive plant requiring removal.

phyllophaga-hondura.summary: This May beetle belongs to a large group whose adults and soil-dwelling larvae are often called June beetles and white grubs. Phyllophaga hondura was verified in a Homestead, Florida nursery after larvae found beside pygmy date palm roots in December 2002 were reared to adults and identified by a specialist. A separate Mexican forest-site specimen also documents the species. These observations establish particular records, not a claim that every white grub is this beetle or that it causes widespread crop damage.

cichlasoma-urophthalma.summary: Mayan cichlid is a Central American fish that has established populations in southern Florida. It can occupy fresh and brackish water, which helps explain its occurrence in canals, marshes, and estuarine environments. It feeds on a variety of aquatic animals. Scientific publications have used several combinations for its name, including Cichlasoma urophthalmus and Mayaheros urophthalmus; those naming differences should be checked when comparing records rather than treated as separate fish.

malvaviscus-penduliflorus.summary: Mazapan is a woody ornamental mallow with long, hanging flowers that never open into the broad flat shape familiar from many hibiscus plants. It is also called Turk's-cap mallow, a name shared with related plants. Its regional status deserves care: the University of Florida's current assessment describes it as not a problem species in Florida, while other regional sources report invasive behavior elsewhere. Neither statement establishes its behavior in every landscape.

bromus-commutatus.summary: Meadow brome is an introduced grass of fields, meadows, and disturbed ground. In this profile the name means Bromus commutatus, a species native to Europe and western Asia, rather than every forage grass sold under a similar common name. Correct identification matters because closely related bromes can occur together and differ in agricultural importance. Its presence in a field is a starting point for assessment, not proof that the surrounding habitat needs treatment.

schedonorus-pratensis.summary: Meadow fescue is a perennial forage grass that has become naturalized in the United States. It grows in meadows, grasslands, roadsides, and streamside settings, sometimes within deliberately planted pasture. You may encounter the names Festuca pratensis or Lolium pratense in floras and seed information. Those alternative names make checking a scientific identification more useful than assuming that every plant called fescue has the same behavior or management needs.

alopecurus-pratensis.summary: Meadow foxtail is a perennial grass with a soft cylindrical flower head and a long history of use in hayfields and pasture. It favors moist, fertile ground and can form dense stands. It is native in parts of Europe and introduced in North America. A foxtail-shaped head is not itself a sign of an invasive grass: several unrelated grasses share that silhouette, and their seasonal growth and management differ.

hieracium-caespitosum.summary: Meadow hawkweed is a yellow-flowered perennial that can spread into dense patches in grasslands and other open ground. Modern references often call it Pilosella caespitosa. It belongs to a difficult group of introduced hawkweeds, several of which spread through runners as well as seed. In the Pacific Northwest, distinguishing these plants from native hawkweeds is an essential first step before removal.

centaurea-debeauxii.summary: Meadow knapweed is a common name used for plants in a hybrid complex involving black and brown knapweed. The scientific name Centaurea debeauxii needs careful comparison with that complex: current botanical sources distinguish it from the hybrid also called Centaurea x moncktonii. Confirmed meadow-knapweed hybrids are a management concern in parts of the United States, where they can replace desirable meadow and pasture vegetation. Their control advice should not be applied to an uncertain identification.

lathyrus-pratensis.summary: Meadow pea, also called meadow vetchling, is a scrambling perennial with bright yellow pea-shaped flowers. It uses tendrils to lean through surrounding vegetation rather than standing as a rigid shrub. In New England it is a non-native plant of fields, meadows, and disturbed places. The word pea in its name describes its relationship and flower form; it should not be used as an assurance that an unidentified wild pod is suitable for food.

pyralis-farinalis.summary: Meal moth is a stored-food moth whose caterpillars feed in grain products, animal feed, and other dry provisions. It is especially associated with damp or moldy grain and neglected storage residue. Finding an adult indoors is a reason to inspect stored materials, but the flying moth itself is not the feeding stage. A moth in a distant room may have developed from a caterpillar that wandered away from the food to pupate.

hyalopterus-pruni.summary: Mealy plum aphid is a wax-covered sap feeder associated with plums, prunes, and related fruit trees. Large colonies can weaken growth and produce sticky honeydew that supports black sooty mold. In its seasonal cycle, eggs overwinter near buds, spring colonies build on trees, and winged forms can move to reeds or cattails before returning in autumn. Those movements help explain why populations on a tree change during the year.

dysmicoccus-grassii.summary: Dysmicoccus grassii is a mealybug with a well-documented association with banana production in the Canary Islands. Its naming history also follows plant trade: the original material was found on imported bananas, and an older name, Dysmicoccus alazon, is now treated as a synonym. These records establish a real species and an important crop association, but they do not by themselves demonstrate an outdoor infestation at any United States location.

eriococcus-araucariae.summary: The insect listed here as Eriococcus araucariae is treated in current scale-insect references as Uhleria araucariae, a felt scale associated especially with Araucaria trees. Although Araucaria mealybug is a documented common name, it belongs to the felt-scale family rather than the true mealybug family. It has moved widely with ornamental hosts, and heavy honeydew production can leave foliage coated with dark sooty mold.

ferrisia-malvastra.summary: Ferrisia malvastra is a mealybug recorded from many plant families and from material intercepted in international plant trade. It has a complicated history of confusion with other Ferrisia, particularly the striped mealybug. The original type material came from Malvastrum in Texas, and its origin across the United States is not fully settled. A record needs local context before it can tell us whether the insect is introduced there.

nipaecoccus-aurilanatus.summary: Golden mealybug is a distinctive sap-feeding insect associated with Araucaria and Agathis trees, including ornamental relatives of Norfolk Island pine. It comes from Australia and has also been recorded in New Zealand and California. Unlike many familiar mealybugs that use a wide variety of houseplants, its documented hosts are concentrated in the Araucariaceae. A host record is useful context, but should accompany rather than replace an insect identification.

pseudococcus-importatus.summary: Imported mealybug, Pseudococcus importatus, is strongly associated with orchids in taxonomic and plant-quarantine records. Its original description involved insects on Vanda material; a later Dutch greenhouse record documents it on Maxillaria splendens. That history makes orchid collections and imported planting stock relevant places to investigate a suspected finding. The word imported is a common name, however, and does not prove where a particular insect came from or whether an outdoor population is established.

pseudococcus-odermatti.summary: Odermatt mealybug is a small plant-feeding insect documented on foliage and fruit, including citrus and ornamental plants. It has been recorded in Florida and intercepted on plants moving through international trade. Recent research has also questioned how sharply it is separated from the related Comstock mealybug. That uncertainty does not erase the existing name, but it makes expert identification especially important when interpreting a new record.

pseudococcus-viburni.summary: Obscure mealybug is a wax-covered insect that feeds on grapes, ornamentals, and several fruit crops. It can hide beneath bark and in sheltered plant parts, making an infestation less obvious than the sticky honeydew or contaminated fruit it produces. In California vineyards it is one of several mealybugs that need to be distinguished before management decisions are made. The older names Pseudococcus affinis and Pseudococcus obscurus may appear in records.

amaranthus-graecizans.summary: Mediterranean amaranth is a small annual whose North American history is unusually tangled. Flora of North America warns that the name Amaranthus graecizans was repeatedly misapplied to the common native species A. albus and A. blitoides. Some old reports may therefore refer to a different plant entirely. A record carrying this name needs a specimen-based review before it is used to describe a present-day invasion.

ephestia-kuehniella.summary: Mediterranean flour moth is a stored-product pest best known from flour mills, food-processing facilities, warehouses, and sometimes homes. Caterpillars do the feeding; adult moths do not eat the stored food. Their silk can bind flour and grain residues into masses and, in industrial settings, obstruct handling machinery. An infestation therefore calls for attention to hidden food deposits and storage conditions, not just the moths flying around a room.

ceratitis-capitata.summary: Mediterranean fruit fly, often shortened to Medfly, is a serious agricultural pest whose larvae develop inside many kinds of fruit and vegetables. Infested produce is an important route by which it reaches new areas. It is established in Hawaii, while mainland detections have prompted official response programs. A suspected finding deserves prompt reporting, but neither a small fly near fruit nor a maggot in a damaged fruit identifies this species by itself.

hemidactylus-turcicus.summary: Mediterranean gecko is a small, introduced lizard often seen on building walls after dark. Porch lights attract the insects it hunts, and cracks around masonry and fixtures provide daytime shelter. In much of its introduced range it is closely associated with people and buildings. Its presence should not automatically trigger pest treatment: household guidance emphasizes preventing unwanted indoor entry rather than poisoning these insect-eating lizards.

mytilus-galloprovincialis.summary: Mediterranean mussel is a marine bivalve that attaches to hard surfaces and has been introduced beyond its original range. Genetic surveys established its presence in California, where it can coexist with native bay mussels and their hybrids. It belongs to a difficult complex of blue mussels in which shell appearance, local conditions, and hybridization can make a simple photograph misleading.

orthotomicus-erosus.summary: Mediterranean pine beetle, also called Mediterranean pine engraver, is a small bark beetle associated mainly with pines. It often breeds in recently cut, fallen, or stressed trees, though attacks can contribute to the death of living pines. It was discovered in California in 2004. Wood packaging and bark-bearing wood are important pathways, so finding beetles in delivered wood is a different situation from identifying the cause of decline in a standing tree.

loxosceles-rufescens.summary: Mediterranean recluse spider is a small, inconspicuous spider that has traveled beyond the Mediterranean region, often in human environments. Introduced populations may remain closely associated with buildings. Because several harmless brown spiders are mistaken for recluses, an identification should rest on the animal rather than on fear, a vague violin-shaped marking, or an unexplained skin lesion. The common name does not mean every brown spider indoors is dangerous.

salvia-aethiopis.summary: Mediterranean sage is a woolly biennial that begins as a ground-level rosette and later produces a tall, branching flower stalk. It is a weed of open, disturbed and grazing landscapes in parts of the western United States. Mature plants can break loose and tumble, distributing seed as they travel. Recognizing the first-year rosette gives landowners a chance to act before that mobile seed-bearing stage develops.

parlatoria-ziziphi.summary: Mediterranean scale is more often called black parlatoria scale or ziziphus scale in plant-health references. It is an armored scale insect associated especially with citrus, where dense colonies can mark fruit and cause yellowing or loss of leaves. Florida has documented introductions, and the insect also occurs in other warm regions. A historic pest alert describes a particular event; it does not establish the current status of every citrus-growing area.

taeniatherum-caput-medusae.summary: Medusahead is a winter annual grass that can degrade western rangelands. Its long barbed awns and silica-rich tissues make mature plants poor forage, while slowly decomposing litter builds a dense thatch. It often stays green later than neighboring annual grasses, drawing attention as other vegetation dries. Its impacts are tied to particular landscapes and climates; a careful identification is needed before managing a suspected new patch.

saissetia-miranda.summary: Mexican black scale is a soft scale insect that can settle on the leaves and stems of many kinds of woody plants. Its dark, rounded adult females can look like small bumps attached to the plant. Feeding colonies may attract attention when several life stages occur together, but a common name or a black shell is not enough to identify the species. Florida entomologists have long recognized it among several closely similar black scales. That regional history does not establish which species is present on a particular shrub today.

metamasius-callizona.summary: The Mexican bromeliad weevil threatens some of Florida's native bromeliads, the plants often seen growing on tree branches. First detected in the state in 1989, it spread through infested plant movements as well as the flight of adult beetles. The damaging stage is the larva, which tunnels inside the plant near its base and can destroy the central growing tissues. A bromeliad may therefore be seriously injured before an observer sees an adult weevil. Susceptibility varies among bromeliads; a small air plant should not automatically be treated as an infested host.

washingtonia-robusta.summary: Mexican fan palm is familiar as a tall, narrow silhouette above streets and gardens. Native to northwestern Mexico, it also establishes beyond cultivation in parts of California, including riparian areas and orchards. A deliberately planted avenue and a group of seedlings spreading along a watercourse are different management situations. California guidance identifies escaped populations as a concern, particularly where palms alter vegetation or accumulate dry fronds. Its presence in a landscape elsewhere does not by itself establish the same ecological impact or legal status.

pseudogynoxys-chenopodioides.summary: Mexican flamevine is a tropical climber grown for its vivid orange flower heads. It can climb a support or spread across nearby vegetation when left to its own devices. Its presence in this catalog should not be read as a recommendation to eradicate every garden specimen. The University of Florida assessment reviewed here classifies it as not a problem species in Florida and assigns low invasion risk. That conclusion is specific to the assessment and region, while a vigorous vine may still need ordinary garden containment.

anastrepha-ludens.summary: Mexican fruit fly is a regulated pest whose larvae feed inside fruit, especially citrus and mango. An infested fruit can look reasonably sound while feeding damage develops beneath the skin. The insect matters to home growers as well as commercial orchards because moving fruit can carry hidden life stages into a new area. United States restrictions and response areas change with detections. Use the current USDA or state agriculture notice for the location in question rather than assuming that an older outbreak map still applies.

sciurus-aureogaster.summary: Mexican gray squirrel, also called Mexican red-bellied squirrel, is native to Mexico and Guatemala. An introduced population was established on Elliott Key in Florida in the twentieth century, and Biscayne National Park lists the animal among its nonnative wildlife. That localized history should not be expanded into a claim that every unusual gray squirrel in the southeastern United States is this species. A report needs a precise location and a careful comparison with the squirrels already present in the area. The sources reviewed here do not provide a current population estimate.

physalis-philadelphica.summary: Mexican groundcherry is the name used here for Physalis philadelphica, a husked-fruit plant also associated with cultivated tomatillos. Kew places its native range in Mexico, Central America, and parts of the Caribbean, while floras elsewhere document introduced plants. A vegetable grown in a garden, a volunteer near a compost pile, and a persistent population outside cultivation are different observations. The reviewed sources do not establish that this species causes ecological harm throughout the United States. Records also need care because related names have been used inconsistently. The broad species concept used here includes immaculata in the 2023 Mexican revision, although other authorities place that name with P. ixocarpa.

physalis-philadelphica-var-immaculata.summary: Physalis philadelphica var. immaculata is used here in its historical North American varietal sense; its botanical placement differs among floras. Some North American treatments recognize it as a variety of Mexican groundcherry. Kew instead places the name in the synonymy of Physalis ixocarpa. Those are different ways of delimiting the plant, not simply interchangeable spellings. An occurrence filed under the variety therefore needs its original identification checked before it is combined with species-level records or interpreted as evidence of an invasion.

plectranthus-amboinicus.summary: Mexican mint is a succulent, aromatic herb also sold as Cuban oregano or Indian borage. The catalog retains Plectranthus amboinicus, while current botanical and Florida assessment sources use Coleus amboinicus. Its many geographic common names are not a dependable guide to its origin. Although it is familiar in home gardens, the 2026 University of Florida predictive assessment assigns it high invasion risk and does not recommend it for Florida planting. That is a regional risk assessment, not proof that every cultivated plant has already escaped or caused damage.

hunnemannia-fumariifolia.summary: Mexican tulip poppy is an ornamental perennial valued for bright yellow flowers above finely divided, blue-green foliage. Gardeners in colder climates may grow it as an annual. Its native range includes western Texas and extends south into Mexico, while California floristic records classify it as nonnative there. Location matters when assessing a plant found outside a garden: a yellow-flowered poppy in its native region calls for a different response from an ornamental spreading beyond a planting.

perna-perna.summary: Mexilhao mussel, more often called brown mussel, is a marine bivalve that attaches to hard surfaces with strong byssal threads. Populations can form dense beds, providing structure for other organisms while changing the surfaces they occupy. Smithsonian accounts document introductions beyond its native range, including the Gulf of Mexico, and United States records include historical Texas observations. Those records do not establish that the mussel is currently present at every previously reported site. Its value as food in some regions also does not settle its ecological status or the safety of collecting it elsewhere.

ochna-serrulata.summary: Mickey mouse plant is a southern African shrub whose unusual fruit display helped make it an ornamental. Yellow flowers are followed by glossy dark fruits set against a bright red floral base. Birds can carry the seeds beyond gardens, and discarded garden material is another pathway. New South Wales guidance describes it as an environmental weed where it forms persistent infestations. That documented regional problem is a reason to examine local escapes carefully, while United States status and any removal requirements should be checked with the relevant local authority.

ichthyosporidium-hertwigi.summary: Ichthyosporidium hertwigi is a microscopic fish parasite name that needs specialist review before it can support a confident distribution or impact statement. Modern marine taxonomy links the name with Glugea hertwigi, while fisheries sources often retain Glugea for the parasite reported from smelt. A research paper discussing Ichthyosporidium also describes an old I. hertwigi record from connective tissue of fish gills. These records should be reconciled using the underlying taxonomy and host evidence rather than joined solely because the species epithet matches.

ipomoea-cairica.summary: Mile a minute vine, or Cairo morningglory, is a perennial climber that can spread over shrubs and other vegetation. The common name is shared with unrelated vines, so the scientific name matters when interpreting a report or choosing a response. The University of Florida assessment assigns Ipomoea cairica high invasion risk and does not recommend it for planting in Florida. Australian weed guidance also documents vigorous spread and practical control concerns. Those regional findings should be kept distinct from a claim that every occurrence across the United States has the same status.

mikania-micrantha.summary: Mile-a-minute is a fast-growing perennial vine that can cover shrubs, young trees, and nursery plants, reducing the light reaching the vegetation beneath it. Native to tropical America, it has become a serious weed in several other tropical regions. Florida's documented introduction near Homestead was confirmed after investigations that included DNA analysis. Older publications describe the early response area, but those historical counts should not be treated as a current distribution map. A suspected new occurrence deserves prompt attention because both wind-carried seeds and living stem fragments can spread the plant.

persicaria-perfoliata.summary: Mile-a-minute vine is an annual climber that can turn a sunny stream edge or disturbed woodland into a blanket of triangular leaves. Its thin stems hook onto surrounding plants, allowing one season's growth to cover young trees and shrubs. In the Mid-Atlantic, seedlings emerge from an established seed supply even though the old vines die each autumn. That annual life cycle makes preventing new seed an especially useful part of management.

pterois-miles.summary: Miles' firefish, also called devil firefish, is one of the lionfishes recorded outside their native Indo-Pacific range. In the western Atlantic, agencies often report it together with the very similar red lionfish, Pterois volitans. These predators shelter around reefs, wrecks and other structure and eat small fishes and crustaceans. A record of a lionfish therefore does not automatically establish which of the two species was present.

asterolecanium-miliaris.summary: Miliaris pit scale is a small bamboo-associated insect now treated in authoritative identification resources as Bambusaspis miliaris. Asterolecanium miliaris is an older name retained in this catalog entry. Colonies can occur on bamboo stems and on either leaf surface. The insect's protective covering makes it look more like a tiny attached fleck than a moving garden pest, and a photograph of discolored foliage alone cannot establish its identity.

gomphocarpus-fruticosus.summary: This milkweed is a slender, branching shrub often called narrow-leaf cotton bush or swan plant. It is native to southern Africa and has become a weed in some other warm regions. The familiar word milkweed can be misleading in an American garden: this is not one of the native Asclepias species. Its inflated fruits release silky-haired seeds, allowing a planted shrub to become a source of plants well beyond the original bed.

acizzia-jamatonica.summary: Mimosa psyllid is a tiny sap-feeding insect associated with Albizia trees, including the ornamental mimosa or silk tree. Native to Asia, it has been recorded in North America and Europe. Heavy colonies can dry out new growth, cause leaves to drop early and leave sticky honeydew beneath the tree. Because mimosa itself is invasive in parts of the United States, damage to this tree has a different ecological meaning from damage to a native woodland species.

albizia-julibrissin.summary: Mimosa tree, or silk tree, is a small Asian tree planted for its fine foliage and pink summer flowers. It readily escapes into sunny disturbed places in parts of the southeastern United States, including roadsides and open ground. A spreading crown can be attractive in a yard while the tree's seeds establish beyond it. Its status varies with region, so an ornamental planting and an established wild population should be recorded separately.

homadaula-albizziae.summary: Mimosa webworm is a small moth whose caterpillars tie leaves together with silk and feed inside the resulting shelter. It attacks mimosa and honeylocust, including common landscape honeylocust cultivars. Homadaula albizziae, the name in this catalog, is a synonym of Homadaula anisocentra in the cited insect literature. In Missouri and Kansas, two generations can produce much more conspicuous browning late in summer than early in the season.

cyperus-prolifer.summary: Miniature flatsedge is an African wetland sedge often grown as a compact ornamental beside water. Its upright stems end in rounded sprays of fine rays, creating a small papyrus-like silhouette. The name miniature papyrus in a nursery is not a dependable scientific identification: Cyperus prolifer has been sold under several names, including names misapplied from other sedges. Its presence in a planted pond also does not by itself establish that it is invasive locally.

ambrosiodmus-minor.summary: Minor ambrosia beetle, also called the punky wood ambrosia beetle, lives in wood together with a fungus that serves as food. In Florida, its association with the white-rot fungus Flavodon subulatus is especially noticeable in dead wood and broken branches. The fungus breaks down both lignin and cellulose, leaving pale, softened wood. This is not evidence that every living tree near an occupied log is being killed by the beetle. FDACS documented a separate Florida collection in Marion County in 2018.

mentha-x-villosa.summary: Hairy mint is the hybrid between spearmint, Mentha spicata, and apple mint, Mentha suaveolens. Often called hairy mint or mojito mint, it is a perennial herb grown for aromatic leaves. The multiplication sign sometimes written as an x in its name indicates hybrid origin. Nursery names and mint scents overlap considerably, so a plant labeled simply mint should not automatically be recorded as this hybrid.

longitarsus-ferrugineus.summary: Mint flea beetle feeds on mint in two quite different places during its life. Adults make small holes in leaves, while the pale larvae feed below ground on roots and rhizomes. In Oregon mint fields, root injury can become apparent as weak, patchy spring growth. The older name Longitarsus waterhousei appears in some crop literature, so checking the scientific name is useful when comparing past records or management advice.

miscanthicoccus-miscanthi.summary: Miscanthus mealybug can remain hidden inside an ornamental grass while the plant gradually loses vigor. Colonies occupy protected leaf sheaths near the crown and can also infest roots. Yellowed or twisted leaves, shortened flower stems and reduced flowering may be the first visible signs. Some extension publications use the spelling Miscanthiococcus, but CDFA and the ScaleNet-based ITIS record use Miscanthicoccus for this mealybug. Preserve the scientific name with a submitted sample.

cenchrus-polystachios.summary: Perennial mission grass is a large African grass that can form loose, tall clumps in warm climates. It is also found in older references as Pennisetum polystachios. In northern Australia, its persistence into the dry season and heavy growth make it an important weed-management concern. Florida's assessment also treats this species as prohibited. Those regional findings should not be read as proof that every tall grass beside a road is mission grass.

murraya-paniculata.summary: Orange jasmine is a warm-climate shrub or small tree with fragrant white flowers and glossy foliage. It is also called mock orange, a name shared with unrelated shrubs such as Philadelphus. Murraya belongs to the citrus family, and its connection with Asian citrus psyllid matters near citrus production. A hedge can provide suitable new growth for the insect even when it is being grown purely for ornament.

justicia-spicigera.summary: Mohintli, also called Mexican honeysuckle or muicle, is a small shrub with bright orange tubular flowers. It belongs to the acanthus family rather than the true honeysuckles. Native-range botanical records place it in Mexico and Central America, extending into northwestern South America in some treatments. It is widely cultivated in warm gardens, including the southwestern United States. Garden use in a dry region does not determine its behavior in a moist tropical landscape.

sonchus-arvensis-ssp-uliginosus.summary: Moist sowthistle is a form of perennial sowthistle with underground roots that allow an established patch to survive after the flowering stems are gone. It occurs in disturbed ground as well as damp settings, so its common name should not be used as a habitat test. In Alaska, the subspecies uliginosus is distinguished from the more glandular form of perennial sowthistle. Older references may call it Sonchus uliginosus or use the name glabrescens.

melinis-minutiflora.summary: Molassesgrass is a sprawling African perennial introduced into tropical regions as forage. In Hawaii it can form dense growth in dry to moderately moist open ground, including disturbed natural areas. Its sweet smell explains the common name, but its ecological importance comes from the way a thick grass layer changes vegetation and adds fuel. Established mats can recover after fire, making repeated burning a poor assumption for lasting control.

gryllotalpa-gryllotalpa.summary: The European mole cricket is an underground insect with powerful front legs built for digging. Its North American records have been concentrated in northeastern states and associated with plant nurseries, according to the Mississippi Entomological Museum. It should not be confused with every mole cricket found in a southern lawn. The United States also has native mole crickets and other introduced species whose distributions and management differ.

euphorbia-lathyris.summary: Moleplant is an upright spurge also sold as caper spurge or gopher spurge. Its blue-green foliage and unusually orderly leaves make it recognizable in gardens and on disturbed ground. The common names can suggest a pest-repelling use, but they do not establish that planting it controls moles or gophers. In Washington it is on a monitoring list rather than the state's noxious weed list, an important distinction from a required-control designation.

phymatosorus-scolopendria.summary: Monarch fern is a creeping tropical fern with leathery, lobed fronds and rounded clusters of spores underneath. It is also known as wart fern and appears in sources under Microsorum scolopendria. Its names have often been confused with those of the related Microsorum grossum, especially in Hawaiian horticulture and historical records. For that reason, a familiar local name or a nursery label is not enough to establish the narrow scientific species.

lysimachia-nummularia.summary: Moneywort, often sold as creeping Jenny, makes a low carpet of rounded leaves. It is a perennial groundcover from Europe and temperate Asia that has escaped cultivation in North America. Damp lawns, streambanks and pond margins provide places for its trailing stems to spread. The familiar golden-leaved garden forms belong to the same species, and an attractive planting can require attention when it reaches adjoining natural vegetation.

oeceoclades-maculata.summary: Monk orchid is a small terrestrial orchid with mottled leaves, often growing quietly in leaf litter. Native to tropical Africa, it is established in parts of tropical America and Florida. Its inconspicuous flowers are easy to miss, while the patterned leaves remain noticeable near the ground. Florida assessments vary by region, with caution advised in central and southern Florida; that is more precise than calling every occurrence an equally severe invasion.

myiopsitta-monachus.summary: Monk parakeets are social South American parrots that have established populations in several United States cities after escapes and releases from captivity. They can be surprisingly successful in cold urban climates. Their large communal stick nests provide a home throughout the year, rather than serving only as a temporary breeding site.
