When a colony builds on electrical equipment, the nest becomes an infrastructure issue that needs the utility's involvement.

pithecellobium-dulce.summary: Pithecellobium dulce is a thorny tropical American tree often called Manila tamarind, madras thorn or opiuma. The catalog name monkeypod can cause confusion because that name is also widely used for a different tree, Samanea saman. In Hawaii, P. dulce has established in dry pastures and disturbed natural areas, where dense growth can displace other plants. Its coiled pods and unusually small number of leaflets are better guides than its common name.

monkeypox-virus.summary: Monkeypox virus causes the infectious disease mpox. Recognition and care depend on clinical assessment and laboratory testing. The scientific virus name and the disease name are different: current virus taxonomy places it in the species Orthopoxvirus monkeypox. Infection can spread through close contact with an infected person, contaminated materials or infected animals. A person's identity or appearance does not establish infection.

crocosmia-x-crocosmiiflora.summary: Montbretia is a garden hybrid grown for arching sprays of orange flowers above narrow leaves. It returns from underground corms and can build dense colonies that survive after the foliage dies back. Escaped populations occur in coastal California and other mild regions. Movement of garden waste and soil is especially important because small corms can start a new patch even when no flowers or seeds are visible.

sinomegoura-citricola.summary: Sinomegoura citricola has been reported on many woody and cultivated plants in Asia and from limited detections in the United States. A Florida alert documented it on mango fruit, while a California report described a colony on lemon. Those observations are useful detection records, not proof of a widespread, damaging population throughout either state. The catalog name moon aphid is less consistently used than the scientific name Sinomegoura citricola.

aurelia-coerulea.summary: Aurelia coerulea is one of several closely related animals commonly called moon jellyfish. For many years, moon jellies from widely separated coasts were often grouped under Aurelia aurita. Molecular work has revealed distinct species hidden within that familiar appearance. Smithsonian's invasion account documents A. coerulea in California, while its status in some other regions remains debated. Seeing a moon jelly therefore does not establish either the exact species or its introduction history.

ipomoea-carnea.summary: Ipomoea carnea is a large, woody morning-glory that may grow as a shrub or scramble over surrounding vegetation. This differs from the delicate annual vines many people associate with the name morning-glory. Botanical treatments distinguish an erect form, subspecies fistulosa, from a climbing form, subspecies carnea. Florida references often concern the erect subspecies, so those records should not be silently generalized to every form of the species.

bedellia-somnulentella.summary: Morning-glory leafminer moth is best noticed through the translucent patches its caterpillars make inside leaves. It uses plants in the morning-glory family, including bindweeds and sweet potato. The small moth is recorded widely, and crop significance depends on the host and degree of damage. Mines on an unwanted bindweed have a different practical meaning from substantial mining in a sweet-potato planting.

linaria-maroccana.summary: Moroccan toadflax is a delicate annual flower native to Morocco and widely grown in gardens. Escaped plants have been documented in several regions, including occasional records along trails in southern California. Its presence outside a flower bed deserves an accurate record, but the evidence does not support treating every garden planting as an invasive population. The variety of flower colors sold in seed mixes can make recognition less straightforward than a single photograph suggests.

lonicera-morrowii.summary: Morrow's honeysuckle is an upright deciduous shrub from eastern Asia that has spread through parts of eastern North America. It can occupy woodland edges, abandoned fields and other places where birds deposit its seeds. A dense patch shades smaller plants and is more work to remove than scattered young shrubs. It belongs to the bush honeysuckles, so it should not be confused with the twining growth of Japanese honeysuckle.

dasypyrum-villosum.summary: Mosquitograss is an annual grass native from the Mediterranean region toward Central Asia. The common name is not an indication that it repels mosquitoes. It is a member of the wheat tribe and is also found in older references as Haynaldia villosa or Secale villosum. In its native range it grows in dry pasture, uncultivated ground and disturbed roadside habitats. Those observations establish ecology, not a current impact assessment for every United States locality.

portulaca-grandiflora.summary: Moss-rose is a low, succulent annual grown for bright flowers in sunny gardens and containers. It is native to South America and can reseed around a planting. That garden behavior should not be confused with a demonstrated ecological invasion: NC State's horticultural account explicitly describes self-seeding without treating it as invasive in its garden context. Many named cultivars and related ornamental purslanes are sold together, so the label matters when identifying an escape.

verbascum-blattaria.summary: Moth mullein spends its early life as a leafy rosette before sending up a tall flowering stem. It is a biennial of open disturbed places and can appear along roadsides, in fields and around neglected ground. Its slender stalks and relatively smooth foliage make it look less bulky than common mullein. The name refers to a plant, not the caterpillars of the unrelated moth sometimes called the mullein moth.

soleirolia-soleirolii.summary: This plant is usually called baby's tears or mind-your-own-business. The catalog name mother of thousands is also used for unrelated succulent plants, so it is particularly important to use Soleirolia soleirolii when seeking advice. It forms a fine, green carpet in damp, sheltered places and can spread beyond ornamental plantings. Coastal California botanical records document escapes in moist shade, while garden behavior elsewhere depends strongly on climate and site.

caradrina-morpheus.summary: Mottled rustic moth is a Eurasian species established in parts of North America, including the Pacific Northwest. Adults visit lights, so a porch observation may be the first indication that it is nearby. The larvae feed on a range of low-growing plants. A moth at a light does not show which plant its caterpillars used, and the available regional accounts do not justify treating every encounter as a damaging garden infestation.

euphorbia-lactea.summary: Mottled spurge is a branching succulent often mistaken for a cactus. It is grown as a houseplant and, in frost-free climates, can become a large shrub or small tree. Pale markings along the green stems give it a patterned appearance. Crested forms sold as coral cactus can look very different from the upright plant, and a grafted specimen may combine two species. A pot label therefore needs to be interpreted with the plant's actual growth form.

odontonema-cuspidatum.summary: Firespike, the more familiar name for mottled toothedthread, is a tropical shrub cultivated for upright clusters of red tubular flowers. Its native range extends from Mexico into Central America. Hawaiian herbarium records document plants outside cultivation, including along a stream, alongside a long history of ornamental cultivation. Those different settings are a reminder to describe local behavior rather than assigning one impact level to every planting.

bauhinia-variegata.summary: Mountain ebony, commonly called orchid tree, is an Asian tree with large flowers and distinctive two-lobed leaves. It belongs to the pea family, despite the orchid name. In Florida it has escaped cultivation, and regional assessments distinguish greater concern in the south from other parts of the state. A seed-producing ornamental near disturbed ground can become a source of volunteers beyond the original landscape.

hordeum-murinum.summary: Mouse barley is a cool-season annual grass familiar along western roadsides, pavement cracks, disturbed ground and neglected turf. The name covers a variable species complex, with several subspecies recognized in botanical treatments. Its bristly heads may look harmless while green, but the dry, barbed seed units can catch in fur and clothing and injure animals. Managing it before the heads harden is more practical than dealing with scattered dry fragments later.

arabidopsis-thaliana.summary: Mouseear cress is a small annual mustard often found on disturbed ground, garden edges and other open sites. It is also the laboratory plant widely used in genetics research. A plant with that familiar scientific name is not necessarily an escaped experiment; wild populations occur independently of research cultivation. In North America it is introduced, but that fact alone does not establish serious ecological harm at a particular location.

hieracium-pilosella.summary: Mouseear hawkweed is a low, spreading perennial now commonly treated as Pilosella officinarum. The older name Hieracium pilosella remains widespread in weed literature. It can form mats in open, relatively low-fertility ground, including grasslands and roadsides, where runners allow a small patch to expand. Its status and reporting requirements vary by region, and yellow flowers alone are not enough to distinguish it from the many other plants in the daisy family.

oreochromis-mossambicus.summary: Mozambique tilapia is a cichlid native to southeastern Africa that has been moved widely for aquaculture and other purposes. It can live in fresh and brackish water, and introduced populations occur in warm regions outside its native range. Records need careful interpretation because related tilapias and hybrids have sometimes been reported under this name. A photograph of a dark fish beside a pond is rarely enough to establish a new species record.

genista-aetnensis.summary: Mount Etna broom is a large shrub or small tree associated with Mediterranean landscapes. It is grown for a cloud of yellow flowers on slender green branches. Recent botanical work uses Genista etnensis as the correct spelling, while Genista aetnensis remains common in horticulture and in this catalog. Native populations and introduced populations need to be distinguished: research on expansion around Vesuvius does not make every occurrence elsewhere an equivalent invasion.

atriplex-muelleri.summary: Mueller's saltbush is an Australian herb of low-lying and disturbed habitats, with introduced records in parts of Africa. Bishop Museum records document naturalized plants in Hawaii, including a patch on a Maui beach; these local records do not establish nationwide harm. Descriptions differ in how tall it grows and how long it lives. A local identification and documented location are needed before drawing conclusions about its spread in the United States.

pinus-mugo.summary: Mugo pine is a European mountain pine widely planted as an evergreen landscape shrub. Garden forms range from compact cushions to much larger, spreading plants. The name also sits within a taxonomically variable group, so a small nursery cultivar should not be used as the model for every wild population. A planted specimen or compact nursery cultivar does not by itself demonstrate invasive behavior in the surrounding landscape.

artemisia-vulgaris.summary: Mugwort is a strongly scented perennial that can form persistent colonies in gardens, fields, roadsides and disturbed edges. Its underground rhizomes make it difficult to remove once established. Cutting the stems may tidy a patch for a while without eliminating the plant beneath it. In eastern North American landscapes, identifying a small patch early is usually much easier than disentangling a mature colony from valued plants.

harmonia-axyridis.summary: The multicolored Asian lady beetle is both a predator of plant-feeding insects and a familiar autumn house visitor. Native to eastern Asia, it is now widespread in North America. Adults seek sheltered places for winter and can gather in large numbers around buildings. Indoors they are a nuisance rather than a sign that the house is being eaten: they do not reproduce there or damage structural wood. Their defensive liquid can stain surfaces.

rosa-multiflora.summary: Multiflora rose is a thorny Asian shrub that can turn open ground and woodland edges into dense, arching thickets. It was formerly planted for purposes including hedges and erosion control, but its ability to spread by seed and by rooting cane tips makes it difficult to contain. Birds carry the small rose hips away from parent plants, so seedlings can appear well beyond an old hedge. Local weed status varies, and identification should precede removal.

rumex-alpinus.summary: Munk's rhubarb is a large perennial dock, not the rhubarb grown for pie stalks. Its broad leaves and stout underground rhizomes help it persist around old gardens, roadsides and disturbed meadows. Native to parts of Europe and western Asia, it has been introduced to northeastern North America. Flora of North America describes it as uncommon there and specifically notes that it has not been reported as a serious invasive weed.

lophosceles-frenatus.summary: Lophosceles frenatus is a muscid fly recorded in specialist insect catalogues. The common label 'muscid fly' describes its family rather than a distinctive appearance or a particular kind of damage. A museum collection list records this species from Greenland, and the Palaearctic Diptera Catalogue indexes the name. A separate Russian field account records adults in coastal meadow and tundra. These records do not show that the fly is an introduced pest in the United States.

erodium-moschatum.summary: Musky stork's bill is an aromatic annual or short-lived herb that often begins as a low leafy rosette. Its small pink flowers give way to long, pointed fruits that explain the birdlike common name. Originally Mediterranean, it appears in disturbed ground, cultivated places and other open sites outside its home range. An established patch can contain plants of very different sizes, so the biggest specimen is not necessarily a different species.

tagetes-minuta.summary: Muster John Henry, also called stinking Roger, is a tall annual marigold from South America. It carries small, tightly grouped flower heads rather than the large showy blooms familiar from bedding marigolds. The aromatic foliage and upright stems can become conspicuous in disturbed ground, along roads or near cultivation. Its behavior varies by region, so a garden escape should be documented locally rather than assumed to be a serious weed everywhere.

cygnus-olor.summary: A mute swan can look like a familiar ornamental pond bird while still changing the wetland around it. This large Eurasian waterbird was brought to North America for parks and estates, and escaped or released birds established wild populations. Feeding can remove submerged vegetation used by other wildlife, while territorial pairs may drive other waterbirds away from nesting areas. The scale of those effects depends on the waterbody and number of birds.

klambothrips-myopori.summary: Myoporum thrips is a tiny insect with an outsized effect on the new growth of Myoporum trees and shrubs. Feeding twists tender leaves into swollen, folded shelters where the insects can continue developing. Coastal California landscape plantings have suffered serious damage, and in Hawaii the insect attacks native naio, Myoporum sandwicense. A damaged ornamental and a damaged native forest tree therefore raise different management priorities even when the pest is the same.

polygala-myrtifolia.summary: Myrtle-leaf milkwort is an evergreen South African shrub grown for its mauve, pink or sometimes white flowers. In its native range it occupies several habitats, including dunes, rocky slopes and woodland edges. It can also escape cultivation in mild coastal climates overseas. A flowering garden shrub is not automatically an invasive population, but seedlings spreading into nearby open vegetation deserve attention, particularly where local weed programs already recognize this species.

acanthomysis-aspera.summary: The estuarine mysid in this entry is now usually called Orientomysis aspera; Acanthomysis aspera is its earlier scientific name. Native to coastal East Asia, it was recorded in California's San Francisco Estuary in 1992. It is one of several introduced mysids there. Changes in the estuary's mysid community are well documented, but the effect of this particular species is difficult to separate from that of more abundant introduced relatives.

centrocestus-formosanus.summary: Mystery fluke is a minute parasitic flatworm whose developing stages can injure fish gills. Its life cycle links snails, fish and fish-eating birds or mammals, making movement of live aquatic animals an important concern. In the United States, published fish-health accounts describe infections in warm waters and springs. The parasite is particularly significant when vulnerable native fish share habitat with suitable snail hosts; it cannot be recognized simply by seeing snails in a stream.

heterococcus-nudus.summary: Naked grass-mealybug is a small scale insect with a complicated naming history. Older records may use Phenacoccus nudus, Heterococcus graminicola or Heterococcus occidentalis, which current taxonomic accounts place under Heterococcus nudus. ITIS lists it as native in the continental United States and Canada. That matters: the presence of a mealybug name in an invasive-species catalogue does not, by itself, establish that this particular insect is an introduced threat.

murdannia-nudiflora.summary: Nakedstem dewflower, often called doveweed, can disappear visually into a lawn until a dense patch has formed. This creeping summer annual belongs to the dayflower family, despite its grasslike leaves. It grows especially well in warm, wet conditions and can occupy poorly drained ground where turf is already struggling. Fleshy stems trail across the surface and root at their joints, while seed allows the weed to return in later seasons.

prunus-tomentosa.summary: Nanking cherry is a cold-hardy Asian shrub planted for early spring flowers and small tart cherries. It usually forms a dense, spreading outline rather than the tall trunk of an orchard cherry tree. Birds use its fruit, and some plantings are maintained as hedges or shelter. The sources reviewed describe a cultivated fruiting shrub; they do not establish that every planting or occasional seedling represents a damaging invasion.

bauhinia-monandra.summary: Napoleon's plume is an ornamental shrub or small tree better recognized by its butterfly-shaped leaves and large pink flowers. It has been planted widely in tropical regions and can naturalize beyond gardens. Native to Madagascar, it is one of several orchid trees whose similar leaves can make garden escapes difficult to identify before they flower.

nephrolepis-cordifolia.summary: Narrow swordfern is often sold or recorded under names such as tuberous sword fern and fishbone fern. It spreads with runners and can produce underground tubers, helping established clumps persist after the visible fronds are removed. In Florida it is a nonnative fern capable of forming dense stands in natural areas. The name 'Boston fern' is used loosely in horticulture, so a nursery label does not reliably distinguish this plant from native sword ferns.

cardamine-impatiens.summary: Narrowleaf bittercress is a small mustard whose leafy flowering stems can rise from a low rosette in a second growing season. It has become an unwanted plant in parts of North America, including sites addressed by Minnesota weed programs. The species is easy to overlook among other spring herbs before its stems and slender pods develop. Its modest flowers are less useful at a distance than the way the leaves attach to the stem.

typha-angustifolia.summary: Narrowleaf cattail forms tall stands along wetland margins, with underground rhizomes connecting many shoots. Dense expansion can crowd other marsh plants, and the species can hybridize with broadleaf cattail to produce Typha x glauca. Its North American history is not described consistently: some authorities treat it as native in eastern coastal settings, while others treat it as introduced or emphasize its recent inland expansion. Local ecological context matters more than a blanket label.

logfia-gallica.summary: Narrowleaf cottonrose is a small woolly annual, also known as French cudweed and formerly placed under Filago gallica. It often grows in open, sparsely vegetated ground rather than forming the conspicuous patches associated with larger weeds. Botanical floras describe it in grassland, roadsides and disturbed places. Its pale covering of fine hairs makes the entire plant look grayish, but many unrelated little cudweeds share that appearance.

pyracantha-angustifolia.summary: Narrowleaf firethorn is a spiny evergreen shrub with clusters of white flowers followed by conspicuous orange or yellow-orange fruits. It is widely cultivated, and botanical floras document escape into scrub, roadsides and other open habitats. A hedge can therefore be a seed source beyond its planted boundary. Firethorns include many similar species and garden cultivars, so the common name or fruit color should not be treated as a definitive identification.

crepis-tectorum.summary: Narrowleaf hawksbeard is an annual with small yellow flower heads held on branching stems. Introduced from Europe to North America, it occurs in roadsides, fields, ditches and other disturbed open ground. It begins with basal leaves near the soil, then produces a taller flowering stem whose leaves are much narrower. This change in appearance can make seedlings and mature plants seem unrelated during a casual survey.

lupinus-angustifolius.summary: Narrowleaf lupine is an annual Mediterranean legume also known as blue lupin. It has been cultivated and has naturalized in some regions, but an escaped crop plant and a persistent invasive population are different situations. Botanical accounts describe it in open ground, including sandy soils. Its upright flowering stems and hand-shaped leaves make the genus recognizable, while the particularly slender leaflets help narrow the identification.

tropaeolum-majus.summary: Garden nasturtium is familiar for its round leaves and brightly colored flowers spilling from beds and containers. Some forms remain compact while others scramble over neighboring vegetation. It is commonly grown as a warm-season annual and can spread by self-seeding. Whether it stays within a flower bed or persists beyond cultivation depends on local conditions, so observations of escaped plants should distinguish a planted display from seedlings establishing on their own.

clerodendrum-glabrum.summary: Natal glorybower is an African shrub or small tree also known as tinderwood. Modern Kew taxonomy places Clerodendrum glabrum under Volkameria glabra, while older botanical and horticultural accounts retain the familiar Clerodendrum name. It bears scented flowers and conspicuously odorous leaves, making it memorable when encountered in a garden. The evidence reviewed describes its native-range biology well, but does not establish a clear United States invasion history or species-specific management need.

carissa-macrocarpa.summary: Natal plum is a dense evergreen shrub often planted as a hedge in warm coastal gardens. Glossy foliage, fragrant white flowers and red plumlike fruits make it attractive, but the strong thorns deserve equal attention. It belongs to the dogbane family, not the true plum genus Prunus. Plantings vary greatly in height because dwarf forms are common, so size alone is a poor way to decide whether two shrubs are the same species.

teredo-navalis.summary: The naval shipworm is a clam transformed for life inside submerged wood. Its long soft body looks wormlike, but two small shell valves at the front act as cutting tools. It can tunnel through driftwood, pilings, boats and other timber, leaving damage far more extensive than the small entrance holes suggest. Centuries of transport in wooden vessels have obscured its original range, and its native or introduced status needs regional interpretation.

pheidole-navigans.summary: Navigating big-headed ant is a tiny reddish-brown ant with two noticeably different worker sizes. A minority have oversized heads, while the more numerous small workers look much less distinctive. It is recorded as an introduced ant in the southeastern United States and Hawaii. Older records may call it Pheidole moerens, reflecting a later taxonomic correction. Local abundance does not justify assigning it the severe impacts documented for every other big-headed ant.

dothistroma-septosporum.summary: Dothistroma needle blight is a fungal disease that can thin the foliage of susceptible pines after repeated infections. Dothistroma septosporum is one cause of this disease. Moist conditions favor spore production and infection, so dense plantings and frequently wet foliage can be important parts of the setting. A tree may lose older needles while retaining green growth at branch tips, giving the crown a sparse, tufted appearance rather than killing it all at once.

stigmina-deflectens.summary: Stigmina deflectens is a fungus associated with needlecast of junipers. Symptoms can resemble those caused by other juniper diseases, and a local laboratory assessment is needed to understand an affected plant. It should not be confused with better-publicized Stigmina diseases of spruce simply because the genus name is shared. Browning juniper foliage is a reason to investigate, not evidence that this fungus is responsible.

pyracantha-crenulata.summary: Nepalese firethorn is an evergreen shrub with spiny branches, white flower clusters and bright red fruits. Native to the Himalayan region, it has been cultivated in many mild climates and has escaped into some roadsides, scrub and stream margins. Birds can carry firethorn fruits beyond a hedge, so seedlings may appear well away from the original planting. Regional accounts describe differing levels of spread; the plant is not equally troublesome in every setting.

persicaria-nepalensis.summary: Nepalese smartweed is a low, spreading annual with small rounded clusters of pinkish or white flowers. Its natural range extends through parts of Africa and Asia, so its name captures only a small part of its geography. Stems can root at their lower joints and rise from a sprawling base. Unlike the long flower spikes of many familiar smartweeds, this species presents its flowers in little heads close to the upper leaves.

chenopodium-murale.summary: Nettleleaf goosefoot is a branching annual of disturbed, often nutrient-rich ground. The name Chenopodiastrum murale is used in current botanical treatments, while Chenopodium murale remains common in older references. It can develop a bushy outline and reddish tones as it matures, but lacks the conspicuous flowers of many garden weeds. Its small green flowers and variable toothed leaves make careful comparison more useful than a quick match based on color.

stachytarpheta-urticifolia.summary: Nettleleaf velvetberry belongs to the porterweeds, flowering plants with slender spikes that can look deceptively alike. Kew accepts Stachytarpheta urticifolia as a species native from the Caribbean into northern South America. Other major treatments include it within S. cayennensis. That disagreement matters when interpreting reports of escaped plants: a record under one name may represent a broader group than the plant intended here. A local specimen needs careful identification before information about Cayenne porterweed can be applied to it.

kalanchoe-crenata.summary: Neverdie is a fleshy perennial plant in the stonecrop family. Its thick leaves help it occupy seasonally dry settings, and older plants can become small, upright shrubs. Kew places its native range in tropical and southern Africa and the Arabian Peninsula, with introductions including Florida and several Caribbean islands. An introduced occurrence is not, by itself, evidence of damaging invasion. For an observation near a garden, the useful first distinction is between a maintained planting and plants establishing beyond cultivation.

platydemus-manokwari.summary: The New Guinea flatworm is a land-dwelling predator of snails and other small invertebrates. It shelters in damp places beneath pots, stones and leaf litter, so movement of planted containers and their associated soil deserves attention. Researchers documented Florida and Puerto Rico records in a study published in 2015. Its ecological significance comes especially from predation on land snails, including vulnerable native species; it should never be released as a garden snail-control animal.

cochliomyia-hominivorax.summary: New World screwworm is a fly whose larvae feed on living animal tissue. Livestock, pets, wildlife and people can be affected. The problem begins when females lay eggs around wounds or body openings; developing larvae burrow into the tissue and can rapidly worsen the injury. This is an urgent animal-health and public-health concern, not an ordinary household fly nuisance. Where it occurs and how officials are responding can change quickly. Follow the linked USDA guidance for current information; earlier eradication does not mean there is no present risk.

acaena-magellanica.summary: The name New Zealand burr can be misleading for Acaena magellanica. This creeping perennial occurs in southern South America and on several southern islands; the common name does not describe its full range. Its burrs are useful clues: they can attach to clothing or animals and carry the plant's fruits away. Any proposed US observation should be checked against a regional botanical key and a documented specimen; the reviewed evidence does not establish a US population.

balanococcus-diminutus.summary: New Zealand flax mealybug is associated with Phormium, the ornamental plant with long, strap-shaped leaves. Colonies can remain tucked into the crowded bases of those leaves, making a casual inspection of the foliage misleading. The Royal Horticultural Society reports that this insect can survive outdoors through British winters, unlike many greenhouse mealybugs. Outdoor survival in the United States depends on local conditions. Modern ScaleNet records place the species in Trionymus, while many practical references retain Balanococcus diminutus.

geranium-retrorsum.summary: New Zealand geranium, here the type-matching New Zealand form, is a small perennial cranesbill, not the showy bedding plant commonly sold as a geranium. Its identity needs unusually careful regional checking. New Zealand botanists describe several forms under this name and distinguish the typical native plant from unresolved related forms. Australian treatments also warn that some plants assigned to the name differ from the New Zealand type. A record in a disturbed place therefore does not establish either a foreign origin or the correct species.

hebe-speciosa.summary: New Zealand hebe is a coastal shrub better known botanically today as Veronica speciosa. It is native to parts of New Zealand, where naturally occurring populations belong in a conservation context. The plant is also grown ornamentally for its glossy foliage and rich magenta flower clusters. A garden specimen outside that range is not automatically an invasive population. Nursery plants need extra care in identification because hybrids are frequently sold under the species name.

potamopyrgus-antipodarum.summary: The New Zealand mud snail is a tiny freshwater snail that can travel unnoticed on wet fishing gear, boats and equipment. Introduced populations in North America include females that reproduce without mating and give birth to live young, allowing a small introduction to grow. Some invaded streams support extremely dense populations. Effects vary with the waterbody, but prevention is particularly important because established populations in natural waters are difficult to control.

solanum-aviculare.summary: New Zealand nightshade, also called poroporo or kangaroo apple, is a softly woody shrub native to New Zealand and parts of the southwest Pacific region, including eastern Australia. It often occupies open or disturbed ground, forest edges and coastal settings. Some populations are conservation concerns in their native range. Its presence in a garden or an introduced-range record should therefore be described in its local context, rather than treated as evidence that the plant is harmful everywhere.

tetragonia-tetragonioides.summary: New Zealand spinach is a low, fleshy plant also known as warrigal greens. It has been cultivated as a vegetable, but escaped plants can occupy beaches, dunes and coastal wetland margins. California assessments describe local displacement of native vegetation, including problems on the Farallon Islands. That regional concern should not erase its native coastal role elsewhere. Botanical references also use the spelling Tetragonia tetragonoides for the same familiar name, so both spellings can be useful when checking records.

myoporum-laetum.summary: Ngaio tree is a New Zealand evergreen that has also been widely planted as a screen or ornamental shrub. In coastal California it has escaped into woodland and streamside settings, where dense stands can crowd native vegetation. Its status is different within its native range, and local plantings should be assessed accordingly. The foliage is toxic to livestock, so grazing is not an appropriate way to manage an unwanted stand.

pseuderanthemum-variabile.summary: Night and afternoon, also called pastel flower, is a small perennial herb or low subshrub in the acanthus family. Kew recognizes its native range in eastern Australia and New Caledonia and records introductions in Florida, Puerto Rico and South Carolina. Those records establish occurrence outside the native range, not the degree of ecological harm. In its native region it grows in several coastal habitats, particularly moist forests, which helps explain why a shaded garden observation can be plausible.

cestrum-nocturnum.summary: Night jessamine is a woody shrub whose small flowers become strongly fragrant in the evening. Despite the familiar name, it belongs to the nightshade family rather than the true jasmines. It was introduced to Hawai'i as an ornamental and has naturalized in some wetter forest settings. Its ability to grow in shade makes an escape beneath trees worth checking. A fragrant garden shrub and an expanding forest population require different local responses.

hylocereus-undatus.summary: Nightblooming cactus is one of the climbing cacti grown for dragon fruit. Modern botanical references generally call it Selenicereus undatus, while Hylocereus undatus remains common in horticultural information. Kew places its native range from Mexico to Honduras and records introductions in several warm regions, including Florida and Hawai'i. It can become a substantial mass of fleshy stems on a support. Cultivation or an introduced-range record alone does not demonstrate that every planting threatens nearby habitat.

lumbricus-terrestris.summary: The familiar nightcrawler is a European earthworm introduced to North America, where it is often encountered in lawns, gardens and fishing bait. It makes deep burrows and comes to the surface to collect food. In northern hardwood forests that developed without these worms, removal of the protective leaf-litter layer can alter the ground environment for native plants. This regional effect should not be simplified into a claim that all American earthworms are foreign: North America also has native earthworm species, including western groups documented by the Forest Service.

silene-noctiflora.summary: Nightflowering silene, or night-flowering catchfly, is an introduced annual of fields, roadsides and other disturbed ground in parts of North America. It starts as a low rosette and later produces an upright flowering stem. Its common name reflects flowers that often open in the evening, but an absence of open flowers during a daytime visit does not mean the plant is finished growing. Seed production is the important stage to watch when managing unwanted plants.

solanum-chrysotrichum.summary: Giant devil's fig is a large, prickly nightshade. The intended species is Solanum chrysotrichum described by Schlechtendal, native from Mexico into Central America. A different historical name with the same spelling belongs to another plant, and some older records used Solanum hispidum incorrectly. These naming problems matter when interpreting an observation or a report of weed impacts. Botanical accounts document introduced populations overseas, but the exact US occurrence evidence needs further checking.

varanus-niloticus.summary: The Nile monitor is a large African lizard that has established populations in parts of southern Florida following escapes or releases from captivity. It is an agile swimmer and climber, often seen near canals, ponds and other water edges. Its broad diet includes many small animals and eggs, creating concern for native wildlife where introduced populations occur. A single sighting outside a known population is worth reporting, but it does not by itself demonstrate that a breeding population has become established there.

oreochromis-niloticus.summary: Nile tilapia is an African and Middle Eastern cichlid widely moved for aquaculture. Escape or release can place it in warm natural waters, where its effects depend on the habitat and the other species present. Females protect eggs and young in their mouths, an important part of the fish's reproductive biology. US records require particular care: Nile tilapia has often been confused with blue tilapia, and farmed stocks can contain hybrids that later escape.

gastridium-phleoides.summary: Nit grass is a small annual grass from the Mediterranean region that has become established in disturbed habitats elsewhere. Its narrow flower head can be easy to overlook among other grasses. The important identification details are much smaller than the whole plant, and photographs of a distant patch rarely show enough to separate it from related grasses.

achillea-nobilis.summary: Noble yarrow is a perennial introduced through cultivation, with clusters of small pale flower heads above divided leaves. North American records need context: Flora of North America distinguishes established Montana plants from records elsewhere that represented cultivated specimens. A garden record should not be read as proof that the species has spread into surrounding habitat or become invasive there.

carduus-nutans.summary: Musk thistle, also called nodding thistle, is a prickly plant of pastures, roadsides and other open ground. It usually grows first as a low rosette and later sends up flowering stems. Large plants can produce substantial seed, so preventing another generation matters more than simply cutting down a conspicuous stem after its seeds have dispersed.

synedrella-nodiflora.summary: Nodeweed is a small, branching plant with yellow flower heads tucked close to its leaves. It occurs widely in warm disturbed ground, including cultivated areas and roadsides. Its broad tropical American origin and introductions elsewhere mean that local context matters: being weedy in a garden is not the same as being a nonnative ecological threat in every part of its range.

ventenata-dubia.summary: Ventenata is a slender annual grass that can become abundant in western grasslands and pasture. Its fine appearance can disguise the amount of ground it occupies until the seed heads emerge. It commonly establishes in autumn, then flowers and dries during the following growing season. A useful report catches the plant while its identifying structures are still intact.

centaurea-diluta.summary: North African knapweed is an annual with pink-purple flower heads and a branching habit. California records place it in grassland settings, while agricultural research in southern Spain documents vigorous growth in cereal fields. Those are different settings, not evidence of the same impact everywhere. Its ability to emerge over an extended season makes a single early inspection easy to miss later plants.

leiocephalus-carinatus.summary: The northern curly-tailed lizard is a ground-dwelling Caribbean lizard established in parts of Florida. Sidewalk edges, parking areas and other sunny developed places can provide shelter and feeding opportunities. It eats a range of small animals, including insects, and has also been observed taking other lizards. A record of one individual helps document its location but does not measure its effect on a whole local wildlife community.

meloidogyne-hapla.summary: Northern root-knot nematode is a microscopic plant parasite that feeds within roots. Affected plants may grow unevenly, yellow or wilt, while their roots develop small swellings. Despite its name, it is not confined to northern states: it has also been investigated in Florida strawberry and vegetable production. The host plant and a laboratory diagnosis matter when deciding how to respond.

northern-snakehead.summary: Northern snakehead is an introduced predatory fish found in several U.S. waterways. It has a long, mottled body and can breathe air, an adaptation that helps it survive conditions that challenge many other fish. Its presence deserves careful documentation, but accurate identification comes first because native bowfins are often mistaken for snakeheads and should not be harmed because of that confusion.

acer-platanoides.summary: Norway maple is a Eurasian shade tree widely planted along streets and in gardens. In parts of the United States, its wind-carried seeds establish in nearby woods, where dense shade and abundant seedlings can make it harder for other plants to grow. A planted adult and a spreading woodland population are different observations, so record the seedlings and surrounding habitat as well as the tree.

rattus-norvegicus.summary: Norway rats live around buildings, farms and other places that offer food and shelter. They often use ground burrows, including spaces beneath slabs or beside foundations. Besides damaging stored food and structures, their waste can create health concerns. An effective response removes the conditions supporting the rats while dealing safely with the animals already present.

picea-abies.summary: Norway spruce is a European evergreen widely planted as a landscape and forestry tree. Mature trees can be recognized from their hanging branchlets and long cones, but young trees are less distinctive. A planted spruce is not by itself evidence of an invasive population. When documenting an apparent escape, the useful question is whether young trees are establishing beyond the original planting.

antonina-pretiosa.summary: The noxious bamboo mealybug is a small sap-feeding insect that can remain hidden beneath the sheaths wrapped around bamboo stems. Its waxy covering and sheltered position make an infestation easy to overlook when plants are moved or divided. A 2026 Florida diagnostic circular describes it as common on bamboo in that state. Published records place it on several bamboo genera, but finding wax on bamboo is not enough to name this particular species. Other mealybugs occupy similar protected spaces, and their treatment may differ.

phaius-tankervilleae.summary: Nun's orchid is a large ground-growing orchid cultivated for tall stems of nodding flowers. It has become naturalized in places including Florida, Hawaii and Puerto Rico, where records include wet wooded habitats. A planted orchid and an independently growing woodland population tell different stories, so that distinction matters when reporting it. Some current botanical references place the plant in Calanthe as Calanthe tankervilleae; the older Phaius name remains widely used.

eulecanium-tiliae.summary: Nut scale is a sap-feeding soft scale found on a range of woody plants, including oak, elm, hazel and linden. The name does not mean it is limited to nut trees. Established females can resemble small rounded growths on branches, while the younger stages are much less conspicuous. Heavy colonies can weaken a host, but a few scales do not automatically mean a tree needs treatment or removal.

nutria.summary: Nutria are large semiaquatic rodents introduced to the United States through the fur trade. They feed on wetland vegetation and dig into banks, where established populations can damage marshes, levees and other water-control structures. They are not the same animal as a native beaver or muskrat. Confirming that distinction is especially important in places where agencies are trying to detect and remove new nutria populations.

paratrechina-vividula.summary: Nylanderia vividula is a small brown ant associated with disturbed ground and other human-modified habitats. Older references place it in Paratrechina, which explains the name retained in this catalog entry. It can occur around buildings, but a nuisance trail is not evidence of a broader ecological impact. Its origin and relationship to similar North American ants require careful interpretation rather than assuming that every observation represents a newly introduced population.

myzocallis-castanicola.summary: Myzocallis castanicola feeds on the undersides of chestnut and oak leaves. Although the catalog calls it oak aphid, some references use sweet chestnut aphid, and the host alone cannot establish its identity. Its presence documents a feeding insect on that tree; it does not by itself show that the tree is declining or that a surrounding woodland is being harmed. Other aphids can share the same host trees.

oak-wilt.summary: Oak wilt is a serious fungal disease that interrupts water movement in susceptible oaks. It can spread between nearby trees through connected roots and reach new trees when insects carry the fungus to fresh wounds. Red oaks often decline quickly; white oaks may show a slower pattern. A dying oak needs a diagnosis because drought, root problems and other diseases can produce similar symptoms and call for different responses.

pheidole-obscurithorax.summary: The obscure big-headed ant is a South American ant established along parts of the southeastern United States. Colonies include small workers and much larger-headed workers, a feature shared with other Pheidole ants. Surveys have found it in heavily disturbed habitats, including developed open ground. Its spread is worth documenting, although the extent of its effects on native wildlife is still uncertain. An active colony does not by itself establish severe ecological damage.

brachymyrmex-obscurior.summary: The obscure rover ant is a minute brown ant recorded outside its tropical American range, including parts of the southern United States. Rover ants often go unnoticed until workers appear around a plant, building or disturbed patch of soil. Their small size makes mistaken names common. A record of this ant should distinguish a confirmed identification from a general report of tiny brown ants, especially when decisions about control or distribution depend on it.

ipomoea-indica.summary: Ocean blue morning glory is a vigorous perennial vine that can cover shrubs and climb into tree canopies in mild climates. Its spreading stems can root where they touch the ground, so discarded vines and moved garden material can start new patches. Dense growth may shade the vegetation beneath it. Flowering plants are easier to recognize, but the amount of seed produced differs between regions and should not be assumed from a garden observation.

schefflera-actinophylla.summary: Octopus tree, also called Queensland umbrella tree, is a tropical ornamental that has escaped cultivation in places including Florida and Hawaii. Birds disperse its fruits, and seedlings can establish on the ground or in crevices of other trees. In suitable wet and warm habitats, escaped plants can grow into the surrounding forest. An indoor specimen presents a different situation from a fruiting outdoor tree beside a natural area.

thylodrias-contractus.summary: The odd beetle is a small dermestid beetle associated with stored biological materials and museum collections. It can damage dried specimens and other susceptible organic objects, so a discovery in a collection deserves closer inspection. Its unusual name reflects the very different appearance of males and females. Finding one near a window does not establish that an entire collection is infested; the location of larvae, cast skins and fresh damage helps identify the actual source.

hylotrupes-bajulus.summary: The old house borer develops inside conifer wood such as pine and spruce, where its larvae can damage structural timbers. Despite the name, infestations may first become noticeable in relatively new buildings, and older wood can also be reinfested. An adult beetle found indoors does not prove a structural infestation: it may have arrived with firewood or through an open window. Evidence from the wood is essential before deciding on treatment.

ophioglossum-pendulum.summary: Old World adder's-tongue is a tropical fern that grows on tree trunks rather than producing a typical tuft of divided fern leaves. Its natural range includes Hawaii, while Florida records are treated as introduced. That regional distinction is important: inclusion in this catalog is not a reason to remove a native Hawaiian fern. References differ over whether to call it Ophioglossum pendulum or Ophioderma pendulum, so both names may appear in records.

nerium-oleander.summary: Oleander is an evergreen flowering shrub widely planted in warm regions. It can also occur outside cultivation, so records should distinguish a maintained hedge from seedlings or established plants in surrounding habitat. Its invasive risk varies by place and assessment method. In Florida, the current UF assessment reports a high predicted invasion risk while noting that reassessment is incomplete. Oleander is also highly poisonous, an important consideration when handling or disposing of it.

aphis-nerii.summary: Oleander aphids are bright yellow sap-feeding insects often found in clusters on milkweed and oleander. They favor tender growth and can build up rapidly because females produce live young without mating. Their presence on milkweed can be troubling, but eliminating every aphid is not always the best choice for a plant being grown to support butterflies. The condition of the plant and the other insects using it both matter.

empyreuma-affinis.summary: Spotted oleander caterpillar moth is now generally treated as Empyreuma pugione; Empyreuma affinis is an older name. Its caterpillars feed on oleander, but it should not be confused with the more damaging oleander caterpillar, Syntomeida epilais. Florida extension guidance describes the spotted species as less common and not normally requiring control. A moth feeding on an introduced ornamental is not automatically a harmful invader simply because it appears in an introduced-species catalog.

asterolecanium-pustulans.summary: Oleander pit scale is now usually named Russellaspis pustulans; Asterolecanium pustulans is an older name used in this catalog. It feeds on many woody plants, with fig and oleander among its important hosts. Feeding can leave small pits and distorted growth around colonies on twigs. In cooler climates it may persist in protected plantings rather than outdoors, so the growing conditions should be recorded along with the host.

olea-europaea.summary: The cultivated olive is an evergreen tree valued for its fruit, but escaped plants can establish in nearby grassland and shrubland. Birds and mammals move the fleshy, single-seeded fruits beyond gardens and orchards. California records show naturalized populations, although that does not mean every planted olive has the same ecological effect. The broad species includes different regional forms, so findings about African olive should not automatically be applied to every European olive cultivar.

bactrocera-oleae.summary: Olive fruit fly lays eggs in olives, where the developing larvae feed through the flesh. Damage can make fruit unsuitable for table use and reduce its quality for processing. The fly is established in California, but its status is not the same throughout the United States: interception of an insect in shipped fruit is different from an outdoor population. Both commercial groves and fruiting landscape olives can provide host fruit.

euphyllura-olivina.summary: Olive psyllid is a small sap-feeding insect whose young shelter beneath conspicuous white wax on shoots, buds and flowers. It has been recorded in California and is also familiar in Mediterranean olive-growing regions. Large colonies can affect flowering and new growth, while smaller populations may cause little damage. The visible wax can look alarming, but it should be assessed together with the condition of the tree and the insects beneath it.

parlatoria-oleae.summary: Olive scale is an armored scale insect that feeds on olive twigs, leaves and fruit. It is different from the soft, dark olive scales that produce conspicuous honeydew. Feeding on young olives can distort them, while later feeding can leave purple spots. In California, natural enemies often keep olive scale below damaging levels, so finding a few covers is not an automatic reason to spray an entire tree.

palpita-persimilis.summary: Olive shootworm is a leaf-feeding moth recorded in Florida after specimens previously confused with native Palpita moths were reexamined. Despite the common name, many confirmed Florida host records involve Japanese privet. Caterpillars shelter among leaves held together with silk and feed on foliage. A webbed shoot on olive or privet is useful evidence of feeding, but it does not establish this moth's identity by itself.

nasturtium-microphyllum.summary: One-rowed watercress is a perennial plant of shallow water, seeps, streams and wet ditches. It has been introduced beyond its European and western Asian range and can persist where stems lie along wet ground. The catalog name one-row yellowcress can be misleading because its flowers are white. It is also unrelated to the brightly colored garden nasturtiums in the genus Tropaeolum.

crataegus-monogyna.summary: One-seeded hawthorn is a thorny shrub or small tree planted for flowers and hedges that has spread into natural areas in parts of the United States. Birds and other animals carry its red fruits beyond the original planting. In the Pacific Northwest it can form dense thickets in fields and woodland, crowding other vegetation and restricting movement through the site. Native hawthorns also occur, so identification should come before removal.

neotoxoptera-formosana.summary: Onion aphid feeds on Allium crops, including onions, shallots, leeks and chives, and can also occur on stored bulbs. Its importance varies with the crop and growing conditions. French guidance describes generally modest colonies, while recent experimental work shows that its feeding and development differ among Allium hosts. Neither account establishes the severity of an individual garden infestation without looking at the plants themselves.

asphodelus-fistulosus.summary: Onionweed forms clumps of narrow leaves and branched flowering stems in open, often dry ground. Despite the common name, it is not a true onion. It can spread along roadsides and into pasture or native vegetation, and livestock often avoid it, allowing it to compete with more useful forage. Records in California are especially associated with southern coastal areas, but a local sighting should be verified rather than inferred from a broad distribution map.

papaver-somniferum.summary: Opium poppy is an annual plant with a long history of cultivation and occasional occurrences outside gardens. It grows in disturbed ground and produces conspicuous flowers followed by rounded seed capsules. Cultivated forms vary widely, so a bright flower alone is not enough to identify it. A few plants near a former garden should be documented as such rather than automatically described as a persistent or damaging wild population.

hyperacanthomysis-longirostris.summary: This small mysid is a shrimp-like crustacean introduced to the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta from the northwestern Pacific. It is associated with low-salinity estuarine water and is part of the food supply for fishes. Monitoring has documented its prominence in the Delta's mysid community, but a change in which species is most abundant does not by itself explain every cause of native-species decline. Older reports may call it Acanthomysis bowmani.

cotoneaster-franchetii.summary: Franchet's cotoneaster is an arching ornamental shrub whose small orange-red fruits can be carried by birds beyond gardens and hedges. In suitable habitats, escaped plants can establish among native shrubs and contribute to dense woody growth. Several cotoneaster species share this habit, so records need a species-level check rather than relying on the presence of berries. A maintained hedge and a self-sown population should be documented separately.

tubastraea-coccinea.summary: Orange cup coral forms colonies of brightly colored polyps attached to hard surfaces. Native to a broad Indo-Pacific range, it has become established in parts of the western Atlantic and Gulf region, including artificial structures and some natural habitats. Its arrival and spread can change the community of organisms occupying those surfaces. A photograph should be tied to a particular site and depth rather than treated as evidence that every nearby reef is affected.

hemerocallis-fulva.summary: Orange daylily is a long-lived garden plant that persists around old homesites, roadsides and other places where it was planted or discarded. It spreads into clumps through underground growth and can occupy space beyond the original bed. Its status varies regionally: naturalized does not always mean locally invasive. Florida assessments, for example, do not currently classify it as a problem species in the central and southern zones, while the northern assessment remains incomplete.

buddleja-davidii.summary: Orange-eye butterfly bush is a flowering shrub introduced from China and widely grown in gardens. Its flowers attract adult butterflies and other insects, but that appeal does not prevent the plant from escaping cultivation. In some regions it establishes outside gardens and competes with local vegetation. The risk of a particular planting depends on its location and cultivar, so a garden label should be checked rather than assumed to guarantee that no seed will spread.

hieracium-aurantiacum.summary: Orange hawkweed is a perennial wildflower introduced from Europe that can form dense mats in meadows, lawns, roadsides and forest openings. Its bright flowers have encouraged people to move it into gardens, but spreading runners allow a small patch to expand into neighboring vegetation. In affected pastures and natural areas it can crowd out forage and native wildflowers.

acacia-saligna.summary: Orange wattle is a shrubby Australian tree planted for ornament and revegetation that has naturalized in coastal and southern California and other Mediterranean-climate regions. It can produce abundant seed and regrow vegetatively, allowing established patches to persist. Dense crowns shade the plants below, and fire can be followed by renewed growth and seedling emergence. That response is a reason to plan long-term follow-up, not a reason to burn a patch yourself.

dactylis-glomerata.summary: Orchardgrass is a cool-season perennial grass widely planted for hay and pasture and established beyond cultivation. It grows in dense clumps, which can be useful in managed forage fields but unwanted in lawns, planting beds or restoration areas. Its presence therefore needs context: a deliberate pasture planting is different from expansion into a site managed for native plants. Individual plants enlarge by producing more shoots at the base, while seed allows new plants to establish.

sitobion-luteum.summary: Yellow orchid aphid is a small sap-feeding aphid associated with orchids. Records include cultivated plants and named orchid hosts in insect collections, but an aphid on an orchid is not automatically this species. Several unrelated aphids use orchids, and older references may place this one in Macrosiphum. The extent of damage should be assessed from the affected plant rather than assumed from the insect's common name.

pseudococcus-microcirculus.summary: Orchid mealybug is a sap-feeding insect found on cultivated orchids and documented on wild epiphytic orchids in southern Florida. It can remain around roots before becoming obvious on aboveground growth, making plant movement an important concern for collections and restoration projects. Its origin needs careful review: current databases and published Florida accounts do not describe its native or introduced status consistently. That uncertainty should not obscure confirmed records on sensitive orchid populations.

exomala-orientalis.summary: Oriental beetle is an introduced scarab whose most important damage often happens below ground. Adults visit flowers, but the pale grubs feed on roots of turf, nursery plants and some small fruits. Plants can wilt or yellow even when the leaves show little chewing. Originally from eastern Asia, the beetle is established in parts of the United States. Older and current references may call it Anomala orientalis rather than Exomala orientalis; the alternative genus does not describe a different pest.

celastrus-orbiculatus.summary: Oriental bittersweet is a woody climbing vine that can wrap tightly around trees and load their crowns with heavy growth. Introduced from Asia, it has become a substantial management concern in parts of eastern North America. Birds and decorative arrangements can move its colorful fruits beyond an existing patch. The vine can also spread from established root systems. Because the native American bittersweet is much less common in some regions, accurate identification matters before cutting a vine in woodland.

blatta-orientalis.summary: Oriental cockroach is a dark, moisture-associated household pest sometimes called a water bug. It commonly shelters in cool, damp places such as basements, crawl spaces, drains and the ground around buildings. Finding one near a sink does not necessarily mean that food cleanliness is the only problem: leaking pipes, damp voids and entry routes can maintain an infestation. The insect feeds on decaying organic matter and refuse, and persistent activity deserves a combined inspection and sanitation response.

youngia-japonica.summary: Oriental false hawksbeard is a small-flowered annual that can become abundant in disturbed beds, lawns and nursery containers. A rosette of leaves is followed by a slender, branching flowering stem carrying many yellow heads. The plant is widespread in the southeastern United States, including Florida, where warm conditions can support a long flowering season. Its wind-carried seeds make an overlooked plant a source of new seedlings. Local abundance varies, and a garden weed record alone does not measure its effect on a nearby natural community.

bactrocera-dorsalis.summary: Oriental fruit fly damages fruit from the inside, where its larvae can feed before an infestation is obvious from the outside. It attacks many kinds of fruit and vegetables and is a major agricultural biosecurity concern. Established in Hawaii, it has also triggered detections and response programs on the United States mainland. A previous local outbreak does not establish the current quarantine boundary. Check the latest agriculture-agency notice for the place where fruit was grown, purchased or carried.

teucrium-orientale.summary: Oriental germander is a perennial herb from western Asia and the Caucasus, where it occurs in open, often rocky country. Its many upright, hairy stems carry finely divided leaves and violet flowers. Kew records an introduction in Pennsylvania, but that occurrence should not be read as evidence of a widespread United States invasion. A plant persisting in an old garden and a population expanding into nearby vegetation need to be recorded separately.

trema-orientalis.summary: Oriental trema is a tropical tree that can establish in disturbed ground and produce small fruits eaten by animals. Its range of origin lies in the Old World tropics, while introduced populations occur in places including Florida and Hawaii. Florida's 2026 predictive assessment rates the species as high invasion risk and does not recommend planting it. Some references use Trema orientale instead of Trema orientalis. Checking both names helps connect nursery records with botanical and management information.

misgurnus-anguillicaudatus.summary: Oriental weatherfish, also sold as dojo or pond loach, is an Asian freshwater fish that has been introduced through aquarium and pond pathways. It favors slow or still water with soft bottoms, where it can burrow out of sight. The fish tolerates difficult conditions and can obtain oxygen from swallowed air, so a shallow or poorly oxygenated pool is not necessarily a barrier to survival. United States records occur in several regions, but a historical observation does not prove a population remains present today.

aonidiella-orientalis.summary: Oriental yellow scale is an armored scale insect that can settle on leaves, stems, fruits and the bases of palm fronds. In Florida, palms are particularly frequent hosts, although the insect feeds on many other tropical and subtropical plants. Heavy infestations can produce yellow patches, weaken foliage and reduce plant quality. It travels easily on infested planting material. A small scale colony is easier to investigate before it is carried into a new garden or distributed with nursery stock.

pterygoplichthys-multiradiatus.summary: Orinoco sailfin catfish is one of the armored, suckermouthed fishes often sold as aquarium plecos. Records under this name occur in the United States, but separating introduced sailfin catfishes has proved difficult. Some historical observations may involve related species or mixed populations. The fish's capacity to outgrow a home aquarium is a practical reason to plan long-term care before purchase. It should never be released into a canal, pond or river as a way to solve an aquarium problem.

myzus-ornatus.summary: Ornate aphid is a very small sap-feeding insect found on many kinds of herbaceous plants, including ornamentals and culinary herbs. Colonies may sit low on a plant or on leaf undersides, where they are easily missed during a quick inspection. Direct feeding damage is often limited when colonies remain small, but honeydew and the insect's ability to carry some plant viruses can matter in production settings. The presence of aphids alone does not establish that a plant has a virus infection.

polygala-paniculata.summary: Orosne is a slender, much-branched annual also known under the botanical name Polygala paniculata. Current Kew taxonomy places it in Senega as Senega paniculata. Native to tropical America, it has become naturalized in other warm regions, where it occurs along roads, tracks and disturbed vegetation. Its tiny flowers make it easy to overlook among larger herbs. An observation outside a garden should be documented carefully, because the small milkworts include species that are difficult to distinguish without mature flowers and fruit.

astronotus-ocellatus.summary: Oscar is a large South American cichlid familiar in aquariums and established in southern Florida waters. It does particularly well in canals associated with marsh habitat, where it feeds on small fish, insects and crustaceans. Cold spells can sharply reduce local populations, so its abundance can change considerably over time. The aquarium trade has produced striking color forms, but an attractive captive fish should never be released when it outgrows a tank. Wild records elsewhere need to distinguish a single release from an established population.

polygonum-aviculare-ssp-depressum.summary: Oval-leaf knotweed is a low-growing member of the complicated Polygonum aviculare group. It can form leafy mats in paths, roadsides and other disturbed ground. Flora of North America treats it as an introduced subspecies, while British references use Polygonum depressum or P. arenastrum for this part of the group. This is a small herbaceous knotweed, not one of the tall, bamboo-like invasive knotweeds. A record needs the full botanical name to avoid confusing very different plants and management problems.

leucanthemum-vulgare.summary: Oxeye daisy is an introduced perennial whose familiar white flower heads can hide a persistent weed problem. It spreads by seed and by underground growth, allowing patches to return after flowering stems are cut. In some western meadows and pastures it crowds desirable plants and reduces useful forage. Its presence in wildflower seed mixtures can start new infestations. Regional priorities differ, but choosing a seed mix should include checking the species list rather than assuming every plant sold as a wildflower belongs at the site.

senecio-squalidus.summary: Oxford ragwort is a yellow-flowered herb of disturbed ground, especially in relatively cool, damp settings. Its history is unusual: modern research traces the British plant to hybrid ancestry involving Sicilian ragworts, followed by spread from cultivation. North American floras document historical introductions, including the San Francisco Bay region; a later California review reports the Berkeley population as eradicated. That history makes the name more specific than a casual label for any yellow ragwort. Regional records should be checked carefully before assuming that a similar plant belongs to this species.

lepidosaphes-ulmi.summary: Oystershell scale is an armored scale insect that can cover twigs and branches with tiny, shell-shaped coverings. Heavy colonies can weaken woody plants, causing yellowing, wilting and branch dieback. The insect occurs on many hosts, including fruit trees and ornamentals. Its life cycle includes a brief mobile crawler stage before the young scales settle. That makes timing important: a branch covered with old shells does not necessarily contain a population that is equally vulnerable to treatment at every stage.

miscanthus-floridulus.summary: Pacific island silvergrass is a very tall, clumping perennial grass grown in some gardens for its dramatic foliage and feathery flower clusters. Its native range extends through parts of Asia and many Pacific islands; Kew also records introductions in Hawaii and parts of the continental United States. Those introduction records do not establish that every garden clump is harmful. The first useful question is whether the plant remains within a maintained planting or produces independent plants beyond it.

cryptostegia-grandiflora.summary: Palay rubbervine is a woody climber that can also grow as a shrub when it lacks support. Native to Madagascar, it has been planted for its showy flowers and has become a serious environmental weed in some tropical regions. Dense growth can smother vegetation and obstruct access along waterways. Hawaii programs treat rubbervines as high-risk plants and prioritize responses according to the island. The similar Cryptostegia madagascariensis is also a concern, so a report should not rely on the shared common name alone.

globodera-pallida.summary: Pale cyst nematode is a microscopic roundworm that feeds on the roots of potatoes and some other nightshade-family crops. Its durable cysts can remain in soil, making contaminated soil and planting material important pathways. The pest is the subject of an official United States survey and response program. Poor crop growth can have many causes, and neither a weak potato patch nor a photograph of roots establishes an infestation. A suspected detection needs the plant-health authority's sampling and diagnostic process.

linum-bienne.summary: Pale flax is a slender plant whose small blue flowers can be easy to overlook among grasses. Linum bienne comes from Europe and the Mediterranean region into western Asia and has become established outside that range. A Pacific Northwest flora lists it as introduced, alongside the native Lewis flax. That distinction matters: a blue flax growing beside a trail is not automatically an unwanted exotic. Pale flax is associated with open, disturbed ground, pasture, roadsides and similar grassy places, rather than being evidence by itself of damage to an intact habitat.

alyssum-alyssoides.summary: Pale alyssum is a small Eurasian member of the mustard family that has spread into disturbed places in North America. It is usually an annual or biennial, so a patch may look different from one season to the next. Roadsides, open ground and disturbed meadows provide the kinds of gaps where it can grow. Its modest size and pale flowers make it less conspicuous than many familiar mustards. An introduced record describes where the plant came from; it does not mean every occurrence warrants the same response as a damaging agricultural or natural-area infestation.

vincetoxicum-rossicum.summary: Pale swallow-wort is a perennial twining vine from eastern Europe that can form tangled patches in northeastern North America. It climbs nearby vegetation or trails across the ground, occupying fields, woodland edges, gardens and disturbed sites. Established plants can crowd out other vegetation, while seeds equipped with silky hairs travel beyond the original patch. In Ontario it is commonly called dog-strangling vine. Its close relative, black swallow-wort, creates similar problems, but neither should be confused with the native milkweeds that support many insects.

molineria-capitulata.summary: Weevil lily is often sold or recorded as Molineria capitulata, although some botanical references use Curculigo capitulata. Its broad, pleated leaves can give it the appearance of a young palm, but it grows from a rhizome close to the ground. It has escaped cultivation on Kauai, where a survey documented plants outside gardens and recommended further attention to its distribution. That local evidence is more useful than assuming the plant behaves the same way in every warm region. A cultivated clump and a population spreading through forest understory call for different decisions.

potentilla-collina.summary: Potentilla collina is treated here as the traditional hybrid complex, whose name needs particular care in North America. It belongs to a difficult group of cinquefoils, and current botanical references do not all describe the same taxonomic concept. Kew treats it as a hybrid, Potentilla x collina, with a European native range. Flora of North America discusses the group as possible occasional introductions but notes that some historical North American specimens assigned this name were actually other cinquefoils. A name on an old record therefore cannot establish that this particular plant is present at a new site.

paspalum-fimbriatum.summary: Fringed paspalum is a tropical grass with an unusually useful identification feature: a ragged, papery border around part of each tiny spikelet. Its native range includes southeastern Mexico, parts of South America and the Caribbean, including Puerto Rico. It has also been introduced to Florida and Hawaii. Those different regional histories matter when deciding what a sighting means. A grass that is outside its native range on one island may belong naturally to the flora on another. The plant commonly forms tufts rather than looking like a large, woody reed.

urochloa-panicoides.summary: Liverseed grass is an annual tropical grass associated with disturbed ground, cultivated land and heavily grazed places. Urochloa panicoides is native across parts of Africa and extends into Arabia and southern Asia. In the United States it is listed as a federal noxious weed, and an APHIS assessment records occurrences in Arizona, Maryland, New Mexico and Texas. Its association with contaminated grain and seed makes an unexpected plant in agricultural material worth reporting. It should not be confused with every broad-leaved grass growing in damp soil.

ehrharta-erecta.summary: Panic veldtgrass is a perennial South African grass that has become an established weed in parts of coastal California and the southern Sacramento Valley. It grows in disturbed places but can also enter woodland and streamside vegetation, where dense growth competes with smaller native plants and adds litter. Its ability to produce new seedlings over a long season in mild, moist conditions makes a single cleanup unlikely to finish the job. Small outlying plants are especially worth noticing before they contribute seed to a larger patch.

hypoponera-punctatissima.summary: The Hypoponera punctatissima group, in the historically broad sense used by regional US accounts, usually lives out of sight in soil, leaf litter or decaying wood. Records under this name occur widely around the world, but its United States distribution is not equivalent to that of the familiar, conspicuous household ants. Mississippi State entomologists describe it as uncommon in much of the country and an occasional nuisance in Florida. It has a sting, yet a single small brown ant does not establish either this species or a household infestation. Its relatives include other ants that are difficult to distinguish without magnification.

pachycondyla-stigma.summary: The ant Pseudoponera stigma often goes unnoticed in tropical leaf litter; Pachycondyla stigma is an older combination still found in identification guides. It lives mainly in soil, leaf litter and decaying wood rather than forming the conspicuous feeding trails associated with many household pests. Records from different tropical regions do not by themselves reveal which populations arrived through human transport. Its original range has been debated, and it is not generally described as a major nuisance ant. A careful identification is therefore more useful than assuming that every record represents a harmful invasion.

sesbania-sericea.summary: Silky sesban is a tropical legume with finely divided leaves and small yellow flowers. Sesbania sericea comes from tropical Africa and Arabia and has been introduced to places including Florida, Texas and Puerto Rico. Its presence outside that range does not automatically make it a serious invasive plant. The University of Florida assessment currently describes it as not a problem species, while noting that this conclusion lacks the documentation available for some other assessed plants. Local observations of spread are therefore more useful than assuming that all sesbans have the same behavior.

carica-papaya.summary: Papaya is a familiar tropical fruit plant whose tree-like outline hides a mostly nonwoody stem. Native to tropical America, Carica papaya is widely cultivated and can also grow spontaneously from seed in warm places, including southern Florida.
