A volunteer beside a compost area is a different situation from a fruit crop or a plant established in natural vegetation. Its ability to naturalize deserves attention without turning a useful garden plant into a universal invasive threat. Cold temperatures limit outdoor persistence in much of the continental United States.

paracoccus-marginatus.summary: Papaya mealybug is a small sap-feeding insect that attacks papaya and a range of other tropical fruits and ornamental plants. Paracoccus marginatus was detected in Florida in 1998 and became a concern in several warm regions beyond its likely Mexican or Central American home range. Heavy infestations can distort growing shoots and damage plants. Its common name should not narrow an inspection to papaya alone: hibiscus and other hosts can carry the insect too. Introduced natural enemies have been an important part of organized management programs.

broussonetia-papyrifera.summary: Paper mulberry is a fast-growing East Asian tree planted historically for its useful bark fibers and ornamental appearance. In parts of the southern United States it escapes cultivation and spreads through seed and root suckers. A few stems can become a thicket, and removing the visible trunk may leave living roots behind. Regional guidance differs: North Carolina sources describe invasive tendencies, while the current Florida assessment calls for caution and prevention of escape. Those are reasons to manage the actual tree and its spread, rather than assume every state applies the same recommendation.

polistes-dominula.summary: European paper wasps are slender black-and-yellow social wasps that have spread widely in North America since their first reported detection near Boston in 1978. They hunt insects, including caterpillars, and can compete with native paper wasps. Their habit of nesting in sheltered human-made spaces brings them close to people, but a wasp visiting a flower is not the same situation as an active nest beside a doorway. Correct identification helps separate a nest-management concern from unnecessary disturbance of other wasps and bees.

bougainvillea-glabra.summary: Paper flower is a familiar warm-climate ornamental whose brilliant display comes mostly from colored bracts rather than large petals. Bougainvillea glabra originates in Brazil and is grown widely as a scrambling shrub or climber. Its vigorous growth on a fence does not by itself establish an invasive population. The University of Florida's 2025 assessment lists this species as not currently a problem in the state, with documented support for that conclusion. Conditions elsewhere can differ, and cultivated bougainvilleas may be hybrids or named varieties rather than a reliably identified wild species.

cyperus-papyrus.summary: Papyrus is a tall, clump-forming wetland sedge best known for its use in ancient papermaking. Cyperus papyrus grows naturally in warm wetlands across much of Africa and nearby regions, where large stands provide habitat and have long been used by people. It is also grown in ornamental water gardens. Escapes have been reported in several warm United States states, while in colder climates gardeners commonly keep it in containers or grow it seasonally. Its behavior depends strongly on climate and access to wet ground; a pot on a patio is not equivalent to an expanding shoreline stand.

urochloa-mutica.summary: Para grass is a large perennial grass associated with wet ground, ditches and shallow water. Urochloa mutica was widely moved as forage and has spread beyond plantings in warm regions, including Florida. Dense growth can trap debris and reduce water movement in drainage channels. Its creeping stems can root at the joints, so a stand may expand without an obvious flush of seedlings. This is different from the life cycle of an annual grass, and it helps explain why simply cutting a patch can leave the underlying problem intact.

malus-pumila.summary: Malus pumila is a botanical name historically used for the cultivated apple. Many current references place it under Malus domestica, while older floras retain the earlier name. Apple trees have been planted so widely that a tree along a road or in an abandoned field may be a surviving planting, a seedling or part of a former orchard. That history matters when interpreting an occurrence. A familiar edible crop can grow outside cultivation without every such tree representing a damaging invasion, and native crabapples should not be swept into the same category.

daphne-mezereum.summary: February daphne is a small shrub valued for fragrant flowers that appear in late winter or early spring, often before the leaves. Daphne mezereum comes from Europe and western Asia and can escape gardens into shaded woodland. In Washington it is on a monitoring list rather than the state's listed noxious-weed roster, so reporting an occurrence is distinct from an automatic legal requirement to remove it. Its bright fruits also deserve care around people and animals: this is a poisonous ornamental, not a berry plant to taste.

acacia-paradoxa.summary: Kangaroo thorn is an Australian shrub with stiff spines and bright yellow flower heads. Acacia paradoxa has been planted as a hedge, but it has also established outside cultivation in California's coastal ranges. The California Invasive Plant Council places it on its Watch list, reflecting concern about its potential to spread rather than a claim that it dominates every suitable habitat. Its dense, prickly growth can make a small planting difficult to approach once it expands. A confirmed wild occurrence is worth distinguishing from other yellow-flowered acacias nearby.

acanthospermum-australe.summary: Paraguay burr is a low, spreading plant of the daisy family whose fruits readily draw attention to an otherwise modest weed. Acanthospermum australe is native to tropical South America and part of the southern Caribbean and has been introduced into the southeastern United States and other regions. It occurs in sandy ground and disturbed places. Its hooked fruits can accompany material moved from a patch, so the fruiting stage matters when deciding how to handle plants. Its distribution alone does not establish the level of damage at a particular site.

neoergasilus-japonicus.summary: Neoergasilus japonicus is a tiny freshwater copepod, a crustacean whose adult females can attach to fish. Native to eastern Asia, it has been recorded in several United States waters, including the Great Lakes region. Fish movements and aquaculture have helped it spread internationally. Its presence on a fish does not establish how much harm it causes to the surrounding fish community: the United States Geological Survey notes that evidence is insufficient to assess its Great Lakes environmental impact. Many different fish species can serve as hosts.

myriophyllum-aquaticum.summary: Parrotfeather is an aquatic perennial whose feathery shoots can rise above the surface like miniature green trees. Myriophyllum aquaticum comes from South America and was spread widely through the pond and aquarium trade. In shallow, slow-moving water it can form dense growth that crowds other plants, interferes with recreation and obstructs channels. Even a small patch deserves attention because broken stem pieces can establish elsewhere. Local rules matter: King County, Washington, requires control of this regulated weed, but that requirement should not be assumed to apply identically in every jurisdiction.

petroselinum-crispum.summary: Parsley is a Mediterranean herb grown in gardens for its leaves, usually as an annual even though its natural life cycle is biennial. Petroselinum crispum commonly spends its first season building a leafy rosette, then flowers and produces seed in its second season if it survives the winter. Volunteers around an herb bed are therefore quite possible. A self-sown culinary herb is not automatically an invasive natural-area problem. Parsley also serves as food for black swallowtail caterpillars, an interaction worth recognizing before treating leaf loss as a reason to spray.

atrichonotus-sordidus.summary: Atrichonotus sordidus is a South American broad-nosed weevil recorded outside its home region, notably in Australia and New Zealand. Older work calls it Floresianus sordidus. The concealed, root-feeding stage has been studied in New Zealand pasture, where larvae were found beneath ryegrass and white clover. Those observations explain why a plant may show trouble before the insect is noticed, but they do not establish that this species is responsible for damaged turf in the United States. The US introduction history of the related A. taeniatulus must not be assigned to A. sordidus.

pantomorus-tessellatus.summary: Pantomorus tessellatus is a name that requires caution when reading older accounts of introduced weevils. It has been used in a complicated taxonomic history involving Aramigus and Aracanthus. Recent specialist work explains that the introduced South American weevil long called Aramigus tessellatus is now treated as Aramigus pallidus, while the original species named tessellatus belongs in Aracanthus. As a result, a record carrying the older name cannot safely be assigned the introduced species' host plants, distribution or pest behavior without checking what the author meant.

rumex-patientia.summary: Patience dock is a substantial perennial herb with large leaves and tall, branched flower stalks. Rumex patientia comes from Eurasia and has been grown as a vegetable, later appearing outside gardens in disturbed places. North American records include roadsides and open ground across a broad area, including the Pacific Northwest. Its size can make it conspicuous, but an introduced roadside plant is not necessarily a priority invasive species at every site. Identification matters because several docks overlap in appearance, and their names are sometimes applied incorrectly.

tetramorium-immigrans.summary: Immigrant pavement ants are among the small ants most often encountered around sidewalks and buildings in the northern United States. Tetramorium immigrans arrived from Europe and commonly nests in soil beneath paving, stones or structures. Workers search for a wide range of foods and may enter through cracks. They can be a household nuisance, but they do not excavate structural wood like carpenter ants. Their ecological role is mixed, and their widespread presence does not mean every outdoor colony needs treatment. Older North American references often call them Tetramorium caespitum.

acyrthosiphon-primulae.summary: Acyrthosiphon primulae is associated with primroses, not the pea crops suggested by the familiar name pea aphid. Pea aphid refers to Acyrthosiphon pisum, a different species. This primrose-associated aphid has also been called Microlophium primulae, so both names appear in older horticultural and taxonomic accounts. Blackman and Eastop cite a California museum collection. Published observations describe colonies on cultivated Primula, sometimes with many insects but little visible distortion of the foliage. That host association is a useful starting point, although it does not mean every aphid found on a primrose belongs to this species.

liriomyza-huidobrensis.summary: Pea leafminer is a tiny fly whose larvae feed inside leaves of many crops and ornamentals. Its name hides an important identification problem: older North American records included the closely related Liriomyza langei. Molecular work separated those populations from South American L. huidobrensis. A winding mine in a California leaf therefore cannot establish this species, and historical distribution statements need to be checked against the revised taxonomy.

prunus-persica.summary: Peach is a familiar deciduous fruit tree from Asia, grown in many cultivated forms. Nectarines belong to the same species and differ in having smooth fruit skin. Trees can persist around former gardens and occasionally occur in disturbed places, but a surviving planted tree does not prove that an invasive population is spreading. North Carolina botanists specifically caution that some records may represent persistent trees rather than independent reproduction.

parthenolecanium-persicae.summary: Peach scale is also called grapevine scale or European peach scale. It feeds on a range of woody plants, so its common name does not limit it to peach trees. Colonies are important in some grape-growing regions, where sap feeding and honeydew can reduce plant quality. The same level of damage should not be assumed for every American garden tree. Other soft scales can occur alongside it and complicate identification.

anarsia-lineatella.summary: Peach twig borer is a small moth whose caterpillars damage tender shoots and fruit of peaches and other stone fruits. Early feeding can kill a shoot tip; later generations may enter fruit. It is different from the peachtree borer that attacks the lower trunk and crown. That distinction matters because a treatment aimed at one insect may miss the other entirely. Damage and seasonal importance also vary among growing regions.

anisandrus-dispar.summary: Pear blight beetle, also called European shot-hole borer, is an ambrosia beetle that excavates wood and cultivates fungi inside its tunnels. The common name does not mean it causes bacterial fire blight. It has been investigated in Oregon nurseries, including sites in the Willamette Valley. Tiny entrance holes can be the first visible clue, but holes alone cannot distinguish this beetle from other wood-boring insects.

leucoptera-malifoliella.summary: Pear leaf blister moth is a leaf-mining moth associated especially with apple and also with pear and several other woody hosts. The larva feeds within the leaf, producing a rounded blotch rather than chewing an open hole. Heavy populations can reduce useful leaf area, but scattered old mines are not a measure of current larval numbers. Its common name should not be confused with damage caused by pear leaf blister mites.

taeniothrips-inconsequens.summary: Pear thrips is a minute insect that feeds in developing buds of fruit trees and many deciduous forest trees. Sugar maple is an important host in the Northeast, despite the pear name. When emergence coincides with slow bud opening, feeding can leave distorted or tattered foliage. Outbreaks vary considerably between years, and an otherwise healthy maple may recover without a lasting decline.

gymnosporangium-sabinae.summary: Pear trellis rust is a fungal disease that alternates between susceptible pears and junipers. Bright leaf spots on pear are one phase of a life cycle that also involves persistent infections on juniper branches. It is not the only rust affecting pears: in the Pacific Northwest, another pear rust uses incense-cedar instead. Identifying the rust correctly matters before deciding which nearby plants are involved.

cenchrus-americanus.summary: Pearl millet is a warm-season annual grass grown for grain, forage and ornamental use. Many agricultural references call it Pennisetum glaucum, while Cenchrus americanus is used in newer classifications. A planted field or trial plot is different from a self-sustaining escape. For a plant beyond cultivation, the useful question is whether it produces new generations without being sown again.

acacia-podalyriifolia.summary: Pearl wattle is an Australian shrub or small tree grown for silvery foliage and yellow flowers. It is native to part of eastern Australia and has escaped cultivation elsewhere, including other Australian regions. A documented planted specimen in California confirms horticultural use, not a widespread invasion. When evaluating a tree, the useful distinction is whether it is staying within a managed planting or producing independent seedlings in surrounding vegetation.

mentha-pulegium.summary: Pennyroyal is a perennial mint that occupies seasonally wet ground, including ditches, seeps and wetland margins. In California it can persist in places that once supported native wetland vegetation, although the extent of its ecological effects is not equally well documented everywhere. It spreads by seed and by creeping growth, so a patch may survive after its visible stems have been cut.

symmetrischema-capsica.summary: Pepper flowerbud moth is a small moth whose larvae feed in developing pepper buds and fruit. Ground cherries can also serve as hosts. It has been recorded in the Gulf Coast region and farther north, but the published North Carolina record is sparse. A damaged pepper does not by itself establish this insect, since several caterpillars and other pests can enter similar plant parts.

lepidium-apetalum.summary: This small pepperweed is an annual or biennial mustard from Eurasia. Its name appears in older North American records, but Flora of North America cautions that most such reports represent misidentified Lepidium densiflorum. That distinction is central to any report of an apparent escape. A roadside pepperweed with tiny flowers is not enough evidence to place this species on a local invasive-plant list.

atriplex-suberecta.summary: Peregrine saltbush, also called sprawling saltbush, is an Australian plant recorded as introduced in California and Utah. It often occupies disturbed ground. Depending on conditions it can behave as an annual or persist longer, and its stems may sprawl or rise into a low bush. Those traits describe its occurrence; they do not establish a severe ecological effect at every site where it appears.

centaurea-montana.summary: Perennial cornflower, or mountain bluet, is a European garden perennial that can spread beyond flower beds by both seed and creeping underground stems. It forms persistent patches rather than behaving like an annual bedding flower. Washington places it on a monitor list rather than classifying it as a listed noxious weed. Its local importance therefore needs to be assessed in context, especially near meadows and other open vegetation.

lathyrus-latifolius.summary: Perennial pea is a climbing ornamental that persists through underground growth and can escape along roadsides, abandoned gardens and other disturbed places. Unlike an annual sweet pea, an established plant can return after its stems die back. California reports locally dense stands, while King County, Washington, treats it as a weed of concern. Those regional assessments do not mean every cultivated plant has the same impact.

lolium-perenne.summary: Perennial ryegrass is a widely planted pasture and turf grass that also grows outside cultivation. Its value in a managed lawn does not prevent it from competing with desired plants in a meadow or restoration site. The relevant question is the purpose of the site and which plants should be there. Some botanical treatments combine closely related ryegrasses under broader names, making a precise identification especially useful before control.

ehrharta-calycina.summary: Perennial veldtgrass is a southern African grass introduced for uses including forage and stabilization. In California it can invade sandy habitats and develop dense cover among shrubs. Individual tussocks may eventually merge into an almost continuous grassy layer. Its persistence means that removal is a continuing restoration task, particularly where nearby plants remain a seed source.

diplotaxis-tenuifolia.summary: Perennial wallrocket is a yellow-flowered mustard also grown as wild rocket. Outside cultivation it occupies roadsides, rubble and other disturbed ground, and it is a crop or pasture weed in some regions. It has a persistent root system rather than the purely annual habit suggested by a short-lived salad crop. Australian weed regulations and European agricultural observations should not be read as a blanket statement about its impact across the United States.

passiflora-vitifolia.summary: Perfumed passionflower is a vigorous tropical vine grown for its large red flowers. Its grape-like leaves explain the alternative name grape-leaved passionflower. Hawaiian herbarium records include both cultivated plants and vines recorded along forest trails, so the setting of an observation matters. In a cold-climate conservatory it is a managed ornamental; in a warm landscape, growth beyond the planting deserves closer attention.

oligonychus-perseae.summary: Persea mite is a spider mite best known as a pest of avocado. Colonies feed beneath small silken shelters on the leaves, and heavy infestations can cause premature leaf drop. Loss of foliage can expose fruit and branches to sunburn. The mite also occurs on other plants, but finding it near an avocado does not mean every neighboring tree is a feeding host.

lolium-persicum.summary: Persian ryegrass, often called Persian darnel, is an introduced annual grass that can be troublesome in spring grain crops of the northern Great Plains. It emerges around the same time as the crop and may go unnoticed until seed heads become visible. Preventing seed return is especially valuable because this weed's seed bank is relatively short-lived compared with that of many persistent perennial weeds.

nalanthamala-diospyri.summary: Persimmon wilt is associated with the fungus Nalanthamala diospyri, which older references call Cephalosporium diospyri or Acremonium diospyri. American persimmon is an important susceptible host. In a grafted orchard, the identity of the rootstock matters as much as the named fruiting variety: Florida guidance warns that infected propagation material can threaten susceptible American persimmon rootstocks. Wilting alone cannot identify the fungus.

physalis-peruviana.summary: Peruvian groundcherry, also known as cape gooseberry or poha, is cultivated for its husked fruit and has naturalized in Hawaii. It is a short-lived, softly woody perennial in suitable climates, though cold can limit its persistence elsewhere. The familiar papery lantern is shared by many Physalis species, including native groundcherries, so a garden escape should be identified before it is treated as this particular plant.

schinus-molle.summary: Peruvian peppertree is an evergreen ornamental with a loose, drooping canopy. Although it is often called California pepper tree, it is native to South America. In California it can establish beyond plantings in washes, slopes and other suitable places, with impacts assessed as limited rather than uniform across the state. An old shade tree and an expanding population of seedlings call for different management decisions.

ludwigia-peruviana.summary: Peruvian primrose-willow is a shrubby wetland plant that can form dense stands along shorelines and in drainage areas. Florida programs identify it as an invasive management concern. A 2026 federal review treats southeastern US populations as introduced. Older sources differ over its origin, so local records still need careful interpretation. It is important to separate this upright shrub from the creeping water-primrose complex rather than attaching every floating yellow-flowered mat to the same name.

petasites-hybridus.summary: Pestilence wort is better known as common butterbur, a large-leaved perennial introduced from Europe. It favors moist ground and can spread into dense patches through fleshy underground stems. The broad foliage shades surrounding plants, while fragments can start new growth after disturbance. A patch beside a stream therefore needs attention to both the visible leaves and the material hidden in the soil.

euphorbia-peplus.summary: Petty spurge is a small annual weed of gardens, disturbed soil and nursery containers. It is easy to overlook because its flowers are green and blend into the foliage. Unlike perennial spurges that spread through underground runners, this species depends on repeated seed production. Removing a few plants before they mature can therefore prevent a much larger crop of volunteers in the same bed.

fiorinia-phantasma.summary: Phantasma scale is an armored scale insect affecting palms and other ornamental plants. It has been found in Hawaii and Florida, where nursery movement and landscape plantings make careful inspection important. Dense populations can produce yellowing and leaf loss. The adult female remains enclosed within the shed skin of an earlier stage, which helps explain why an apparently simple surface infestation can be difficult to identify and manage.

monomorium-pharaonis.summary: Pharaoh ants are tiny household ants that can establish persistent colonies in warm indoor spaces. They exploit food and water in buildings and can spread through concealed cavities. Colonies have an unusual management complication: disturbance or repellent treatment may split them into additional nesting groups. Seeing fewer workers immediately after spraying therefore does not necessarily mean the infestation has been resolved.

phialophora-cinerescens.summary: Phialophora wilt is a fungal disease of carnations that can move with infected planting material. It affects the plant's water-conducting tissues and may develop gradually, making a slowly fading greenhouse crop easy to mistake for a watering problem. The pathogen can persist in soil and infected plants, and spores can spread with water. Clean propagation stock is therefore more valuable than waiting for a conspicuous outbreak.

aglaonema-commutatum.summary: Philippine evergreen is a tropical foliage plant widely grown indoors and in shaded warm-climate landscapes. Its silver-marked leaves have also been selected into many ornamental forms, so a nursery label may refer to a cultivar or hybrid rather than a readily recognizable wild species. Introduction records include Puerto Rico, but presence in cultivation does not establish ecological harm. A plant kept alive in a maintained bed is different from seedlings establishing independently in nearby vegetation.

spathoglottis-plicata.summary: Philippine ground orchid is a terrestrial orchid that has escaped cultivation in tropical regions, including parts of the Caribbean, Florida and Hawaii. Its attractive flowers do not make it ecologically interchangeable with native orchids. UF/IFAS assigns it a high predicted invasion risk and does not recommend general planting in Florida. Risk assessments describe potential as well as observed behavior, so local records still matter.

epicoccum-sorghinum.summary: Epicoccum sorghinum is a fungus formerly known as Phoma sorghina. It has been associated with leaf spots, blights and other symptoms on several crops, rather than one uniform disease called Phoma blight. A United States study confirmed it causing leaf spot on rice in Texas. Independent Ethiopian work also identified it among rice sheath-rot fungi. These findings concern particular hosts and tested isolates; they do not identify every spotted rice leaf or every fungus called Phoma.

phytophthora-cinnamomi.summary: Phytophthora cinnamomi is a soilborne water mold that damages roots of many woody and herbaceous plants. On avocado it is a major cause of root rot. It moves with contaminated plants, soil and water, so prevention depends on what enters a site as well as how a sick plant is treated. Wet, poorly drained ground favors disease, and adding more water to a wilting tree can make the underlying problem worse.

cajanus-cajan.summary: Pigeonpea is a cultivated food and agroforestry shrub, often grown as an annual even though it can persist for several years in a suitable climate. It has been moved widely through agriculture. Growing outside its original range does not necessarily make pigeonpea invasive. UF/IFAS currently describes it as not a documented problem species across Florida's assessment zones. Volunteer plants should still be evaluated in their local setting.

belonesox-belizanus.summary: Pike killifish is a predatory livebearing fish introduced to southern Florida. Despite the name and long jaws, it belongs to the livebearer family rather than the true pikes. It eats small fishes and can affect native fish populations. Historical Texas records should not be read as proof of a current population there; USGS describes that introduction as apparently lost, while Florida populations are established.

ernobius-mollis.summary: Pine bark anobiid beetle is associated with dead conifer material that retains bark. Its larvae feed mainly in the bark and the outermost sapwood, so their presence does not automatically mean the deep structural attack associated with some other wood borers. Emerging adults can nevertheless make holes through coverings placed over infested timber. Correct identification can prevent both unnecessary treatment and overlooked secondary damage.

lepidosaphes-pini.summary: Pine oystershell scale, also called Oriental pine scale, is an armored scale associated with pine needles. It is native to Asia and has been introduced to the United States. The common name overlaps with other scales, including Lepidosaphes newsteadi, so a report should retain the scientific identification. Several related pine scales are treated together in risk assessments, but evidence for one should not automatically be assigned to all of them.

pineus-pini.summary: Pine woolly aphid, treated here as the historically named Pineus pini group, is an adelgid associated with pine shoots and bark. White wax around colonies can make an infestation conspicuous, but the name has been used inconsistently for closely related Pineus species. International forestry accounts warn that some records combine P. pini, P. boerneri and older names without preserved specimens. A cottony patch on a pine therefore deserves identification before it is assigned a particular distribution or damage history.

dysmicoccus-brevipes.summary: Pineapple mealybug is a small sap-feeding insect that often stays hidden at the base of a pineapple plant. It also uses other bromeliads and many unrelated plants. In Hawaii, where it occurs on the major islands, its importance includes its association with pineapple mealybug wilt. Feeding can also leave pale patches and damage the base of developing fruit. Ants often attend colonies, collecting honeydew while protecting the mealybugs from their natural enemies.

matricaria-discoidea.summary: Pineapple weed is a small aromatic annual commonly noticed along worn paths, pavement edges, and disturbed garden soil. It can also grow in turf and nursery beds. Its name comes from the pineapple-like scent of the foliage and flower heads. Flora of North America treats it as native to northwestern North America and spread elsewhere, including eastern parts of the continent. A weed catalog entry therefore does not make it a foreign invader everywhere. Local abundance and the purpose of the site help determine whether removal is useful.

linaria-pinifolia.summary: Pineneedle toadflax is a North African plant also known as Linaria reticulata; the New England treatment describes it as annual, while a later herbarium account gives a conflicting perennial description. Its spurred flowers resemble miniature snapdragons. Reports from North America need particular care: a New England flora lists Connecticut, but a published voucher audit found no certain specimen and reported that reviewed North American material belonged to Moroccan toadflax instead. That disagreement leaves the identity of historical escapes unresolved. A garden label or old county record should therefore be checked against the actual plant.

bromelia-pinguin.summary: Pinguin is a large terrestrial bromeliad native to tropical America, including parts of the Caribbean. Its tough rosettes have been used as living barriers, a role made effective by the sharply hooked teeth along the leaves. In Florida it is a nonnative ornamental escape that can form dense colonies. A plant's status therefore depends strongly on location: a Florida escape and a population within its Caribbean native range require different decisions.

erythricium-salmonicolor.summary: Pink disease is a fungal disease of woody plants in humid tropical environments. The fungus, Erythricium salmonicolor, also appears in older literature as Corticium salmonicolor. It can infect citrus and many other trees and shrubs, producing cankers that kill bark and may girdle a branch. Warm, wet conditions and dense canopies favor disease development. The name describes fungal growth on affected wood, not a pink discoloration of leaves or fruit. Its significance in a particular US planting needs local diagnosis and disease-history context.

maconellicoccus-hirsutus.summary: Pink hibiscus mealybug feeds on tender growth of many tropical and subtropical plants, including hibiscus. Its feeding saliva can distort leaves and shorten the spaces between them, producing crowded, bushy shoot tips. This damage can be much more conspicuous than the insects themselves. The species was detected in southern Florida in 2002 and has also established in parts of other warm US regions. Local biological control programs are important, so an infestation does not automatically call for repeated broad insecticide treatment.

tarenaya-hassleriana.summary: Pink queen, often sold as spider flower or cleome, is a tall South American ornamental grown for airy clusters of flowers. The plant has circulated under several names, including Cleome hassleriana, Cleome houtteana, and Tarenaya houtteana. Current authorities differ in the genus used: Kew places the hassleriana name within Cleome houtteana, while some regional floras use Tarenaya houtteana. In Florida, UF/IFAS displays a high predicted invasion risk while marking the assessment incomplete. That combination calls for care when choosing new plantings, rather than a blanket claim that every garden plant is already causing ecological damage.

oxalis-debilis.summary: Pink woodsorrel is a bulb-forming perennial that can turn a small garden introduction into a persistent colony. Native to South America, it has been introduced in several US regions and grows in yards, flower beds, roadsides, and other disturbed habitats. Its ability to leave many small bulblets behind makes removal more demanding than its delicate flowers suggest. Florida's completed 2025 UF/IFAS assessment does not classify it as a documented problem species statewide, although individual gardeners may find dense patches difficult to manage.

persicaria-capitata.summary: Pinkhead smartweed is a low, trailing perennial grown as a ground cover for its patterned leaves and small pink flower balls. Native to Asia, it has escaped cultivation in several warm regions. Hawaiian field surveys document it along roads, on lava, and in forest settings, where managers have worked to limit its spread into selected native habitats. It is sometimes called Japanese knotweed, but that common name can cause confusion with the much taller invasive knotweeds. Use the scientific name when seeking advice.

pollinia-pollini.summary: Pit scale, Pollinia pollini, is a tiny sap-feeding insect associated especially with olive trees. It shelters around buds, branch junctions, and cracks in bark, where colonies can be difficult to notice until shoots decline. Reports from Mediterranean olive-growing regions describe leaf distortion, loss of leaves, and drying branches. California has historical introduction records, but published accounts disagree about the extent of eradication and do not establish its present pest importance. A suspected US finding deserves identification rather than an assumption based on the common name.

fusarium-circinatum.summary: Pitch canker is a fungal disease of pines caused by Fusarium circinatum. It can affect seedlings as well as established trees, and its appearance changes with the stage of infection. Monterey pine has been especially affected in coastal California. Douglas-fir can also carry infections, usually with more limited visible damage. Infected planting stock and wood are important reasons to keep suspected material from moving to another site.

mnesithea-granularis.summary: Pitscale grass is a small annual grass whose beadlike flowering structures are much more distinctive than its leaves. Botanical works also call it Hackelochloa granularis. It occurs across warm regions, and Flora Neomexicana records introduced plants on dry plains and foothills in the southwestern bootheel of New Mexico. That regional record does not mean that every rough-haired grass in an American pasture belongs to this species.

bothriochloa-pertusa.summary: Pitted beardgrass, also called Indian bluegrass, is a warm-season perennial that spreads through creeping stems. It has been used as pasture and groundcover in tropical regions. Its ability to form a close mat and tolerate grazing can also change the balance of vegetation where it spreads beyond a planting. A pasture recommendation from Australia does not establish that it is suitable for an American restoration site.

planchonia-arabidis.summary: Pittosporum pit scale is a sap-feeding insect that settles on stems and leaves and can distort new growth. In California it particularly favors pittosporum and ceanothus, although its host list is much wider. Heavy infestations may leave swollen, misshapen twigs and smaller leaves. The insect has also appeared under the older combination Asterolecanium arabidis, a useful name when comparing extension references.

plantago-asiatica-mosaic-virus.summary: Plantago asiatica mosaic virus, usually shortened to PlAMV, is a plant virus of particular concern in commercial lilies. It also infects other plants, including the plantain from which its name comes and heavenly bamboo. Infected bulbs can carry it into new plantings. Unlike several other familiar lily viruses, no biological vector is known for PlAMV; contaminated sap, handling and growing media are important concerns.

rhinacloa-cardini.summary: Rhinacloa cardini is a small member of the plant-bug family, Miridae, with a broad Neotropical distribution. Published Florida records date to 1999, and reported host associations include two species of Enterolobium, trees in the pea family. Those records establish the insect's occurrence and associations; they do not by themselves demonstrate damaging feeding or a need to treat every tree on which it is found.

urochloa-plantaginea.summary: Plantain signalgrass is an annual grass also called creeping signalgrass or Brachiaria plantaginea. It is associated with disturbed ground and crops, and Florida botanical guidance records it from scattered disturbed sites in the state. Its ability to root at low stem joints can make a plant appear more persistent than its annual life cycle suggests. Regional occurrence should be checked independently of the different common names used for signalgrasses.

styela-plicata.summary: The pleated tunicate is a solitary sea squirt that often grows in crowded groups on docks, hulls and aquaculture equipment. Each individual filters water through its own two openings. Long-distance transport by vessels has blurred its original distribution, and its native region remains uncertain. Southern California harbors support introduced populations, but a confident worldwide origin should not be inferred from an old regional field guide.

paraserianthes-lophantha.summary: Plume albizia is a shrub or small tree with finely divided foliage and pale bottlebrushlike flower clusters. Also known as plume acacia or brush wattle, it has escaped cultivation in parts of coastal California, where Cal-IPC lists it on its Watch list. Its behavior elsewhere varies with climate and habitat. An ornamental specimen and a reproducing population beyond cultivation deserve different management decisions.

sphaericus-pinguis.summary: The plump spider beetle is a small beetle associated in published accounts with stored organic material, including dried plant collections. Some references use the name Sphaericus gibboides, which the Natural History Museum treats as a synonym. Reports from a museum or pantry should be checked carefully: several unrelated beetles can emerge from dried goods, and the common name does not establish which species is present.

potato-mop-top-virus.summary: Potato mop-top virus affects the quality of potato tubers, sometimes leaving internal blemishes even when the crop above ground looks healthy. It is carried through soil by Spongospora subterranea, the organism that also causes powdery scab. These are related problems but not interchangeable diagnoses: powdery scab can occur without the virus. Preventing contaminated soil and planting material from entering clean production areas is especially important.

neophyllaphis-podocarpi.summary: Podocarpus aphid forms small colonies on tender growth of podocarpus, a common ornamental shrub in warm parts of the United States. Its bluish purple color makes a colony noticeable against the narrow green leaves. Feeding can affect new growth, but finding aphids is a reason to inspect the plant and its condition, not an automatic reason for a broad insecticide application. Another Neophyllaphis species occurs on the same ornamentals.

narcissus-poeticus.summary: Poet's narcissus is a perennial bulb grown for fragrant white flowers with a small, brightly edged center. It can persist around old gardens and has naturalized along roadsides, in fields and in waste places in parts of North America. A long-lived clump is not necessarily evidence of rapid spread. Like other daffodils, it should be kept separate from edible bulbs and plants gathered for food.

conium-maculatum.summary: Poison hemlock is a highly poisonous biennial that often grows along roads, ditches, streams and disturbed field edges. In its first season it forms a leafy rosette; later it sends up a tall, branching flowering stem. All parts are unsafe to eat, and contamination of hay or other feed creates a risk for livestock. Its resemblance to edible members of the carrot family makes casual foraging particularly dangerous.

hypoestes-phyllostachya.summary: Polka-dot plant is a small tropical perennial grown for leaves splashed with pink, red or white. It is often kept indoors or used as seasonal bedding, but warm conditions can allow it to persist beyond a garden. Florida's current IFAS assessment predicts high invasion risk and does not recommend it there. That assessment is a regional planting recommendation, not proof that every houseplant is causing ecological damage.

brassicogethes-viridescens.summary: This pollen beetle is associated with flowering plants and is especially relevant to canola and other brassica crops. Adults seek pollen, while the crop's growth stage influences the significance of their feeding. Beetles visiting open flowers are not equivalent to beetles damaging unopened buds. Older literature may place the species in Meligethes, and it should not be confused with every small dark beetle found inside a blossom.

polyalthia-suberosa.summary: Polyalthia suberosa is an Asian shrub or small tree in the custard-apple family. Its name refers to the corky bark that develops on older growth. Botanical accounts describe it from forest and thicket habitats, including dry forests and streamside sites. A Bishop Museum report documented a naturalized Oahu tree collected in 2008. That limited record does not establish widespread invasion. Do not borrow the identity or behavior of the much taller ornamental formerly called Polyalthia longifolia.

branchiomma-coheni.summary: Branchiomma coheni is a marine feather-duster worm that lives in a tube and extends a crown of fine feeding branches into the water. It is native to the Pacific coast of Mexico and Central America. Researchers found it at a Tampa Bay marina in both 2012 and 2014, supporting establishment there. The available synthesis reports no demonstrated impacts for this species, so its introduction should not be presented as proof of ecological damage.

euwallacea-fornicatus.summary: The polyphagous shot hole borer is a tiny ambrosia beetle that excavates galleries in wood and cultivates fungi for food. The beetle and its associated fungi can damage trees, including ornamentals and native hardwoods in California. Its name once covered several nearly identical species, so older reports need care: Florida's tea shot hole borer is now treated as Euwallacea perbrevis, a different species.

eragrostis-japonica.summary: Pond lovegrass is a fine-flowered grass in a group whose species can be difficult to distinguish without mature heads. Botanical treatments describe it as an annual or sometimes a short-lived perennial, reflecting variation across its broad range. It is native to tropical and subtropical parts of the Old World and occurs in disturbed or wet settings elsewhere. Its common name should not be read as a requirement that it grow submerged.

callitriche-stagnalis.summary: Pond water-starwort is a small aquatic plant that can form mats of stems and floating leaf rosettes in quiet water. It reproduces by seed and vegetative growth, and plant material can be carried with wet equipment. Introduced populations occur in parts of the United States, but several native water-starworts look very similar. Correct identification is especially important before disturbing a pond or clearing a shoreline.

papaver-cambricum.summary: Welsh poppy is a tap-rooted perennial with yellow or orange flowers, often grown in cool, partly shaded gardens. It is native to western Europe and was long known as Meconopsis cambrica. The name Papaver cambricum is accepted by Kew. Its familiar garden presence should be distinguished from a documented naturalized population, and a plant appearing outside a border is not automatically a serious invasive threat.

ficus-rubiginosa.summary: Port Jackson fig, or rusty fig, is an Australian evergreen tree planted for shade and sometimes grown as bonsai. Mature trees can develop a broad crown and substantial supporting roots. Its suitability depends on available space, climate and local conditions. A cultivated tree's large size or vigorous roots should not be confused with evidence that the species is spreading invasively in every region where it is planted.

phytophthora-lateralis.summary: Phytophthora lateralis is a water mold that causes serious root disease in Port-Orford-cedar, also called Lawson cypress. It has damaged native cedar populations in southwestern Oregon and northwestern California. The pathogen can travel in contaminated soil and water, making muddy equipment and drainage routes important pathways. It is funguslike but is not a true fungus, and a declining cedar can have several other causes.

thespesia-populnea.summary: Portia tree is a tropical coastal tree with glossy, heart-shaped leaves and hibiscuslike flowers. It has a long history of cultivation and a broad tropical distribution. In central and southern Florida, introduced populations are a concern in coastal habitats, including mangrove edges and sheltered beaches. Current IFAS guidance treats it as invasive in those regions, while its northern Florida assessment differs.

calendula-officinalis.summary: Pot marigold is a familiar garden annual with yellow or orange daisy-shaped flower heads. Despite the common name, it belongs to Calendula rather than Tagetes, the genus containing many other garden marigolds. It can reseed in cultivated ground, sometimes reappearing where a previous planting has disappeared. Volunteers in a flower bed are usually a garden-management question, not evidence of a landscape-scale invasion.

psylliodes-affinis.summary: This potato flea beetle is a small leaf beetle associated with wild and cultivated members of the nightshade family. European sources describe adults feeding on foliage and larvae feeding on roots. The common name is shared or confused with other potato-associated flea beetles, especially Epitrix species. A report of potato flea beetle damage should therefore include the scientific identification before a species-specific management plan is chosen.

phthorimaea-operculella.summary: Potato tuber moth is most damaging during its caterpillar stage, when it tunnels through potato foliage, stems or tubers. Exposed tubers and cracks in the soil give females access to places where eggs can be laid. The insect can also develop on other nightshade crops, including tomato. Risk varies with region, weather and crop handling, and damage may continue in poorly protected storage.

bromus-sterilis.summary: Poverty brome, also called barren or sterile brome, is an introduced annual grass of fields and disturbed ground. The word sterile is misleading in everyday use: the plant produces seed and can reproduce readily. It is also treated as Anisantha sterilis in some botanical works. A mature flowering head is much more informative than the soft green leaves when separating it from other annual bromes.

praxelis-clematidea.summary: Praxelis is a fast-growing herb with clusters of lilac or blue-purple flower heads. Native to South America, it has become a weed in Florida, including ornamental production areas. It can flower while still relatively young and produce many small seeds that travel on wind, clothing, animals and equipment. Its resemblance to familiar blue-flowered plants has contributed to overlooked introductions.

symphytum-asperum.summary: Prickly comfrey is a coarse perennial with bristly foliage and hanging clusters of tubular flowers. It has been grown as an ornamental and is one parent of Russian comfrey, the hybrid Symphytum x uplandicum. That relationship makes names on old garden plants particularly unreliable. Comfreys contain pyrrolizidine alkaloids, so a plant's history of medicinal or forage use should not be treated as assurance that it is safe to consume.

lactuca-serriola.summary: Prickly lettuce is an upright annual weed that often begins as a low rosette before sending up a branching flowering stem. It grows in disturbed soil and can be troublesome in grain crops, particularly where established plants survive harvest and produce more seed. Despite its relationship to cultivated lettuce, an unidentified roadside plant should not be treated as food or used to make herbal preparations.

acacia-verticillata.summary: Prickly moses is an Australian wattle with densely arranged, sharply pointed foliage. It is usually a shrub or small tree, and it has naturalized outside its native range, including New Zealand. Its compact prickly form can resemble several other spiny shrubs. An overseas weed designation is useful context, but it does not establish the status or management priority of an unidentified American planting.

kali-ryanii.summary: This tumbleweed is better known in recent research as Salsola ryanii. It arose through hybridization between Salsola tragus and Salsola australis and carries additional sets of chromosomes. Researchers have documented its expansion in California. It is therefore a distinct biological entity, not simply another spelling of ordinary Russian thistle. The shared common name makes casual records difficult to interpret without specialist identification.

salsola-tragus.summary: Russian thistle is a branching annual associated with dry, disturbed ground across much of the western United States. Young plants are soft, but mature plants become rigid and prickly; dry plants can break loose and tumble with the wind. Several related species share this habit, so not every tumbleweed is Salsola tragus. Roadsides, bare lots and poorly covered field margins can provide recurring places for establishment.

carex-spicata.summary: Prickly sedge is a tufted sedge with compact clusters of small flowers and fruits near the stem tip. It belongs to a group of Carex species that can look almost identical in a casual photograph. The common name is also used inconsistently among related sedges. Mature fruiting material and the leaf collar are much more useful than a broad view of a grassy clump.

datura-inoxia.summary: Downy thorn-apple is a bushy plant with large white trumpet flowers and spiny seed capsules. Many references spell its name Datura innoxia, the spelling accepted by Kew. Its native range includes Texas and Mexico, so it should not be described as foreign everywhere in the United States. All parts are hazardous if eaten, and the attractive flowers do not make it a safe plant for home remedies.

caesalpinia-pulcherrima.summary: Pride-of-Barbados is a tropical flowering shrub or small tree, also called dwarf poinciana or red bird of paradise. It is widely cultivated for orange, red and yellow flowers and finely divided foliage. Florida's current IFAS assessment does not consider it a problem species in the state, so its presence in a garden is not an automatic reason for removal. Local escape behavior still deserves observation.

selenicereus-pteranthus.summary: Princess-of-the-night is a climbing or trailing cactus grown for very large pale flowers. Its long stems can scramble over supports and produce aerial roots. Botanical accounts record escapes in Florida, and IFAS currently places the species in its Caution category. That calls for attention to local spread and planting choices rather than assuming every cultivated night-blooming cactus is the same species.

paulownia-tomentosa.summary: Princess tree is a fast-growing deciduous tree introduced from China for ornament and timber. Its winged seeds can reach disturbed ground, rocky slopes, forest openings and even cracks around buildings. Large leaves make young plants conspicuous, while mature trees are most noticeable when pale purple flowers open before the new foliage. In regions where it escapes, early recognition prevents a small seedling from becoming a difficult tree-removal job.

myzus-ligustri.summary: Privet aphid is a tiny sap-feeding insect associated with privet shrubs and hedges. Its feeding can roll leaves into narrow tubes and leave yellow spotting, sometimes making new growth look untidy. Specialist accounts record it as introduced in North America. The damage is usually limited enough that an otherwise healthy hedge does not need treatment simply because a few curled leaves are present.

galega-officinalis.summary: Goatsrue is a perennial legume that can form persistent patches in moist pasture, ditches and other disturbed ground. It was once promoted as forage, but it is toxic to livestock and should never be introduced for grazing. Its clusters of pale pea-shaped flowers can resemble several harmless or native legumes, making careful identification essential before a pasture or wetland is treated.

panicum-miliaceum.summary: Proso millet is both a cultivated grain and a source of weedy populations. The wild forms can be troublesome in corn and other summer crops, especially when seed travels with harvesting or tillage equipment. A volunteer from birdseed or a planted grain crop does not automatically behave like the most persistent wild biotypes. Management should reflect what the population is doing in that particular field.

lindernia-procumbens.summary: Lindernia procumbens is a small wet-ground plant with delicate pale flowers. True L. procumbens is an Old World species that resembles the American Lindernia dubia. Similar names and small flowers can complicate older records, and a historical occurrence should not be treated as proof of a current established population. A record carrying the name therefore needs more scrutiny than a simple map dot.

polygonum-aviculare.summary: Prostrate knotweed is the low, wiry plant often found in hard-used lawn edges, paths and cracks where soil has become compacted. It usually grows as an annual and can survive routine mowing by staying close to the ground. Its name refers to the joints along its slender stems. It is very different from the tall, cane-forming Japanese knotweed, so their control approaches should not be confused.

amaranthus-albus.summary: Tumble pigweed is a bushy summer annual whose dried stems can break free and roll, scattering seed. It occurs in disturbed ground and cultivated settings, but its native range includes parts of the southern United States and northeastern Mexico. Being a crop weed and being nonnative are separate questions. Its relatively small leaves and pale branching stems give it a different appearance from tall pigweeds with prominent seed spikes.

parlatoria-proteus.summary: Proteus scale, also called orchid parlatoria scale or variable chaff scale, is a small armored scale insect found on many kinds of ornamental plants. It has been recorded as a pest of orchids in Florida and can travel with infested nursery material. Its broad host range means an orchid association is a clue, not a reliable identification. The insect can be overlooked because its protective cover resembles a tiny patch of plant debris.

tribulus-terrestris.summary: Puncturevine is a low-growing summer annual best known for the hard, sharp burs called goatheads. Those fruits can injure paws and bare feet and puncture bicycle tires. The plant favors warm, disturbed ground and can keep producing new seedlings through summer. Livestock may also be poisoned by eating the foliage, so grazing is not a suitable way to clear a patch.

melaleuca-quinquenervia.summary: Melaleuca, or broad-leaved paperbark, is an evergreen tree native to Australasia that became a major invader of southern Florida wetlands. Dense stands replace native plant communities and change the structure of places that formerly supported open marsh or diverse woodland. Florida management has combined repeated removal with carefully evaluated biological control. Trees left as seed sources can undermine that continuing work.

amaranthus-blitum.summary: Livid amaranth, also called purple pigweed, is a summer annual found in disturbed ground, crop fields and nursery settings. It can spread from bed edges into containers, making early inspection useful where plants are being moved or sold. Its low, branching growth often looks different from the tall pigweeds familiar in farm fields. The name Amaranthus lividus appears in older references to this plant.

corbicula-largillierti.summary: Purple Asian clam is a freshwater clam name applied to some introduced Corbicula populations. Recent studies disagree over whether Corbicula largillierti is a distinct species or belongs within Corbicula fluminea. North American specimens reported under the name therefore need careful review. A purple shell interior does not settle their identity. Keep the original identification, collection location and supporting specimen together rather than treating every Asian clam as this species.

lamium-purpureum.summary: Purple deadnettle is a small introduced annual often seen in lawns, garden beds and disturbed ground during cool weather. It commonly starts growing in autumn and flowers early the following season, although timing varies with climate. The reddish upper leaves can make a patch stand out before the small flowers are noticed. It provides nectar for insects, and whether a patch needs attention depends on the site rather than its presence alone.

brachypodium-distachyon.summary: Purple false brome, also called annual false brome, is a small annual grass from the Mediterranean region and nearby parts of Eurasia. It grows in dry, open or disturbed places and can become locally abundant in California. Dense growth leaves persistent dry material that can interfere with native seedlings and add to fine fuels. It is different from the perennial false brome that is the focus of some woodland weed-control programs.

digitalis-purpurea.summary: Purple foxglove is a familiar garden plant that can establish beyond cultivation, especially in moist disturbed ground, roadsides and forest openings. It usually begins as a leafy rosette before producing a tall flowering stalk. In some coastal regions, dense patches replace other vegetation. All parts are poisonous if eaten, so identifying a plant correctly matters even where it is an intentional garden planting rather than an unwanted escape.

passiflora-edulis.summary: Purple granadilla, or passionfruit, is a vigorous climbing vine grown for its fruit. In warm regions it can escape cultivation, and Hawaiian guidance describes naturalized vines that overgrow shrubs and trees. Birds and other animals carry the seeds after feeding on fruit. Its usefulness as a crop does not prevent escape, but risk assessments and behavior can differ among locations and cultivated forms.

lythrum-salicaria.summary: Purple loosestrife is a perennial wetland plant that can form dense stands along marshes, shorelines, ditches and streambanks. Established plants produce many flowering stems and large amounts of tiny seed, allowing disturbed wet ground to fill quickly. Dense stands can crowd out native wetland vegetation. A report is especially useful when plants are still scattered, before a small occurrence becomes difficult to manage.

molinia-caerulea.summary: Purple moorgrass is a perennial grass native to parts of Europe, western Asia and nearby regions. It is planted ornamentally and has been recorded outside cultivation in parts of North America, including New England. Its airy flowering stems can be attractive in a garden, but an observation should distinguish a maintained planting from self-sown plants beyond it. An introduced occurrence alone does not establish that the grass is causing local ecological damage.

cyperus-rotundus.summary: Purple nutsedge is a persistent perennial sedge of gardens, crop fields and other disturbed ground in warm regions. Much of the plant is underground: rhizomes connect chains of tubers that can produce new shoots after the visible leaves are removed. This is why a patch may return after ordinary weeding. It can become troublesome in cultivated soil, but recognizing its growth system is more useful than treating it as an unusually fast-growing lawn grass.

cortaderia-jubata.summary: Purple pampas grass, also called jubatagrass, forms large tussocks on coastal bluffs, dunes and disturbed ground. Introduced as an ornamental and for erosion control, it can spread far beyond a planting through windblown seed. Seeds can develop without fertilization, so one isolated plant can still produce an expanding population. Dense stands can displace lower vegetation and make access or restoration work difficult.

lepidosaphes-beckii.summary: Purple scale is an armored scale insect most familiar on citrus. It feeds on leaves, twigs and fruit, often in cooler, shaded parts of the canopy. Heavy patches can cause leaf loss or twig dieback, while natural enemies keep many populations below damaging levels. The brownish-purple structures visible on a plant are protective covers; the insect itself sits underneath. Finding a few old covers is not the same as finding an active outbreak.

linaria-purpurea.summary: Purple toadflax is a European perennial cultivated for its slender flowering stems. On Hawaii Island, BIISC reports that a garden escape entered dry native forest near Oceanview and that the known population was eradicated. Slender stems and many small flowers give it a light, airy appearance, but established plants have a persistent rootstock. It should not be confused with yellow toadflax or Dalmatian toadflax simply because the common names overlap; evidence and management for those species are not interchangeable.

lepidium-heterophyllum.summary: Purpleanther field pepperweed is a small mustard whose identification depends more on its fruits than its common name. The intended name here is Lepidium heterophyllum Benth., also recorded as Lepidium smithii. A different name with the same spelling has been applied to another pepperweed, so checking the author and underlying specimen is important when comparing databases. A matching search result is not always a matching species.

cyperus-sanguinolentus.summary: Purpleglume flatsedge is a tufted sedge recorded from wet ground, streambanks and disturbed roadsides. Its native range extends through parts of Africa, Asia and Australia, with introduced records in several southeastern states and Hawaii. Older references may call it Pycreus sanguinolentus. Those distribution records help place an observation in context, but do not by themselves show that a particular patch is damaging a wetland.

verbena-bonariensis.summary: Purpletop vervain is a South American garden plant with tall, open stems and clusters of small purple flowers. It can self-sow beyond a planting, but the name has often been confused with Verbena incompta, a similar plant with less conspicuous flowers. Older records may therefore need rechecking. A flower photograph is particularly valuable because the long flower tube is one of the best clues to the narrower species concept.

verbena-incompta.summary: Verbena incompta shares the common name purpletop vervain with a more familiar garden species, Verbena bonariensis. The two were long confused, so older reports can describe a broader group than the name now implies. This South American plant occurs in roadsides, fields and other disturbed places. North Carolina botanists map specimens reidentified specifically as V. incompta, while acknowledging that older bonariensis records still need sorting. Its precise local identity matters before transferring impact claims or control advice from another vervain.

odhneripisidium-moitessierianum.summary: Pygmy peaclam is a very small freshwater bivalve native to Europe and parts of western Asia and recorded in the Great Lakes region. Older sources place it in Pisidium. Historical accounts suggest ship transport as a likely introduction pathway, but its ecological effects are not well established. A French reservoir study documented recovery after temporary drying, so drawdown should not be assumed to eliminate it. Its minute size and resemblance to other pea clams make ordinary shoreline photographs unreliable for identification.

protopulvinaria-pyriformis.summary: Pyriform scale is a sap-feeding soft scale found on avocado and other ornamental hosts. Unlike armored scales, its visible surface is the insect's own body rather than a separate removable shield. Feeding can leave sticky honeydew that supports black sooty mold. In California, it is more often encountered on landscape avocados than in commercial groves, and natural enemies commonly keep soft scales from becoming serious pests.

elymus-repens.summary: Quackgrass is a perennial grass that spreads through underground stems called rhizomes as well as seed. A patch can return after its visible leaves are removed because living pieces remain below the surface. It occurs in lawns, planting beds and open ground, where its spreading growth can compete with desired plants. The underground network is the main reason a quick mowing or shallow cultivation rarely resolves an established patch.

dreissena-bugensis.summary: Quagga mussels are small freshwater mussels that attach to surfaces and can also colonize soft lake bottoms. Dense populations filter food from the water and foul water-intake systems, boats and equipment. Their microscopic young can travel in retained water even when no adult mussels are visible. Some references use Dreissena rostriformis bugensis for the same mussel, so both names can appear in monitoring records.

daucus-carota.summary: Wild carrot, or Queen Anne's lace, is a European plant now widespread along roadsides and in fields and disturbed ground. It commonly develops a leafy rosette before producing a taller flowering stem, then reproduces through seed. Its white flower heads may look familiar, but several dangerous plants in the carrot family have a similar outline. This profile should not be used to decide whether a wild root or leaf is safe to eat.

filipendula-ulmaria.summary: Queen of the meadow, also called meadowsweet, is a Eurasian perennial grown for its fragrant cream-colored flowers. It has escaped cultivation in parts of North America, particularly in moist habitats. Underground rhizomes let a patch expand and recover after its shoots are cut. Its presence should be recorded separately from native Filipendula or Spiraea species, some of which share similar common names.

selenicereus-grandiflorus.summary: Queen of the night is a climbing or scrambling cactus with spectacular flowers that open at night. The name is also used for unrelated-looking night-flowering cacti, so a garden label alone may not identify this species. Selenicereus grandiflorus comes from tropical American regions and is cultivated elsewhere. A planted specimen, an old surviving cutting and a self-sustaining escape need to be distinguished when describing its local occurrence.

syagrus-romanzoffiana.summary: Queen palm is a South American ornamental with arching feather-like leaves and large clusters of orange fruit. Birds and other animals can carry its seeds away from plantings, allowing seedlings to appear in nearby vegetation. Florida's current assessment advises caution and preventing escape. That recommendation is regional: an ornamental palm in a managed landscape is not automatically evidence of ecological damage at that exact site.

petrea-volubilis.summary: Queen's wreath, or sandpaper vine, is a tropical American woody climber grown for hanging purple flower clusters. Much of the long-lasting color comes from the enlarged calyx around each flower, which remains after the true flower falls. Florida's assessment currently regards it as low invasion risk and not a documented problem species. That is an important distinction from simply treating every introduced ornamental in a catalog as harmful.

gliricidia-sepium.summary: Gliricidia is a tropical legume tree widely planted for living fences, shade and other agricultural uses. Branch cuttings can establish readily, and mature pods split to scatter seeds. Its behavior varies markedly by region: USDA guidance describes invasive populations in some tropical countries while noting a low-risk assessment in Hawaii. Its useful agricultural role and its capacity to escape both belong in a clear local account.

trifolium-arvense.summary: Rabbit-foot clover is a small annual clover with soft, fuzzy flower heads. Introduced from Eurasia, it is often found in dry sandy ground, fields and other open, disturbed places. Its delicate appearance is unlike the broad-leaved lawn clovers many people recognize. It can be part of a disturbed-site plant community without every occurrence indicating substantial ecological harm, so local habitat and land-use goals matter.

nepeta-racemosa.summary: Raceme catmint is a perennial garden plant native from eastern Turkey to northwestern Iran. It forms leafy clumps with blue-purple flowers and has introduced records in parts of North America. Nursery names are especially confusing here: some familiar catmints are hybrids, and the same cultivar may be placed under different names in horticultural references. That uncertainty can affect whether a record belongs to this species and whether seed spread is expected.

chloris-radiata.summary: Radiate fingergrass is an annual grass of open and disturbed ground, with a seed head made of fine branches radiating from the stem tip. Its geographic status needs care: Flora of North America considers a Florida origin possible, while other sources describe it as introduced there. A historic Oregon record came from ship ballast and was not evidence of a continuing population. These differences should remain visible instead of becoming a blanket nonnative label.

phyllotreta-punctulata.summary: Phyllotreta punctulata is a tiny dark flea beetle recorded as introduced in North America. Adults are associated especially with plants in the mustard family. The name is easily confused with Psylliodes punctulata, a different flea beetle that appears in many crop guides. Advice or distribution for that other genus cannot be transferred simply because the species epithet is the same.

silene-flos-cuculi.summary: Ragged robin is a perennial wet-meadow plant from Europe and Asia, introduced through cultivation and other pathways. Its bright pink flowers have deeply divided petals that give them a ragged appearance. In some northeastern US conservation areas it is treated as an emerging invasive plant, and early reports help managers locate small populations before they expand. Its status in its native range is different from its behavior after introduction.

samanea-saman.summary: Rain tree, also called monkeypod, is a large tropical American tree planted around the world for shade and timber. Its wide, umbrella-shaped crown can become a prominent landscape feature. Introduced populations have naturalized in many tropical regions, and invasion of native vegetation has been reported in places including Hawaii. A valued shade tree and an escaping population are different situations that need different decisions.

cadra-figulilella.summary: Raisin moth is a small moth whose larvae feed on ripening, drying and stored fruit, especially raisins. Infestations can begin before storage and continue among stored products, where feeding and contamination reduce their value. An adult moth near a cupboard or drying tray is a reason to inspect the material, but it does not by itself prove that every package is infested or identify this species.

turnera-ulmifolia.summary: Yellow alder is a small tropical shrub with bright yellow flowers; despite the name, it is not an alder tree. It is planted ornamentally and can appear outside gardens in warm regions. Its Florida history has been reassessed: older references sometimes treated it as native, while newer state evidence supports introduction. UF/IFAS currently recommends caution and managing plantings to prevent escape, rather than treating every planting as an established invasion.

boehmeria-nivea.summary: Ramie is a perennial shrub or subshrub cultivated for the strong fibers in its stems. Originally from Asia, it has been introduced to warm regions elsewhere, including parts of the United States. Upright stems arise from underground rhizomes, so an old planting can persist or expand even after repeated cutting. Although it belongs to the nettle family, ramie does not have the stinging hairs associated with familiar stinging nettles.

campanula-rapunculoides.summary: Creeping bellflower is a Eurasian perennial once planted for its purple flowers and now troublesome in many North American gardens and other disturbed places. It spreads by seed and by persistent underground stems and storage roots. A few leaves returning after weeding can belong to a much larger root system, which explains why removing only the visible shoots often gives a misleading sense of progress.

brassica-napus.summary: Brassica napus includes important oilseed and vegetable crops. Canola refers to particular crop varieties, not a separate wild species. Seed lost during harvest or transport can produce volunteer plants in later crops or along routes and field edges. These volunteers may compete with a desired crop, but a cultivated field should not be counted as an invasive population merely because the species is introduced.

ceratocystis-fimbriata.summary: Ceratocystis fimbriata is a fungus associated with black rot of sweetpotato, but the name has also been used broadly for a complex of related fungi on other hosts. That history matters here. The fungi now recognized as major causes of rapid ohia death in Hawaii are Ceratocystis lukuohia and C. huliohia, not simply interchangeable names for C. fimbriata. Host and laboratory identification need to stay attached to each record.

angiostrongylus-cantonensis.summary: Rat lungworm is a parasitic roundworm whose life cycle involves rats and snails or slugs. People can become infected by accidentally or deliberately swallowing infected hosts, including small gastropods hidden in produce. Infection can affect the brain and spinal cord. A snail or slug cannot be declared infected or safe from its appearance, and finding one nearby does not mean that a person has been infected.

sesbania-punicea.summary: Red sesbania is a South American shrub planted for orange-red flowers and now invasive in some wet habitats. It can form dense thickets along streams and other water margins, crowding existing vegetation. Its winged pods contain seeds that may remain dormant for years, so removing a stand does not immediately remove the potential for new plants. Seeds and other plant parts should not be eaten.

bromus-briziformis.summary: Rattlesnake brome is an annual grass introduced from the Caucasus and nearby parts of western Asia. It grows in roadsides, waste ground and other disturbed sites, including some overgrazed areas. Its broad, dangling spikelets are distinctive among many common grasses. It should not be assigned the fire behavior or management of red brome or cheatgrass simply because all three have been placed in Bromus.

crotalaria-retusa.summary: Rattleweed is an upright tropical legume with yellow flowers and inflated pods. It grows in disturbed places and is cultivated in some regions, but its local ecological significance varies. UF/IFAS does not currently identify it as a documented problem species in Florida. That does not make its seeds safe: they contain toxic compounds, so the plant should not be treated as a harmless edible pea or used as an improvised animal feed.

heterosiphonia-japonica.summary: This red seaweed is now generally called Dasysiphonia japonica; Heterosiphonia japonica is an older name still used in research and records. Native to the northwestern Pacific, it has spread to European and northwestern Atlantic coasts. It can grow on rocks, shellfish gear and other surfaces, and large accumulations can affect coastal habitats. Reports of harmful blooms concern particular settings and should not be read as a claim that every small patch causes a fish kill.

caulacanthus-ustulatus.summary: Caulacanthus ustulatus is a small turf-forming red seaweed whose name has been used for more than one biological species. Many introduced populations described under this name on the Pacific coast are now treated as Caulacanthus okamurae. That distinction matters when connecting a photograph, location or ecological study to this profile. A historical label should not silently become proof that true C. ustulatus occurs at the same place today.

amaranthus-cruentus.summary: Red amaranth is an annual plant cultivated for grain, leafy produce and ornamental flower heads. It also appears outside cultivation, including introduced records in California. Its agricultural and cultural uses are part of its story, and a crop planting should not be described as an invasive outbreak. Escaped plants need to be assessed in their actual setting rather than assigned the behavior of another pigweed species.

adenanthera-pavonina.summary: Red beadtree is a tropical tree recognized by the bright red seeds exposed when its pods open. It has been planted as an ornamental and has escaped in warm regions. Florida sources document it in conservation areas where it can replace native vegetation. Those local observations are more informative than assuming every tree with colorful seeds has the same impact everywhere it is grown.

bromus-rubens.summary: Red brome is an introduced annual grass of dry and disturbed landscapes, especially important in parts of the southwestern United States. After wet periods it can produce abundant growth that later dries into fine fuel, helping fire spread between shrubs in places where vegetation was formerly more widely spaced. Its abundance changes with rainfall and disturbance, so one season's appearance does not describe every year or habitat.

scantius-aegyptius.summary: Mediterranean red bug is a small seed-feeding true bug established in parts of the southwestern United States.
