Large groups can gather on annual weeds or move toward developed areas as those plants dry. The sight of hundreds of bright insects can be alarming, but the available California accounts emphasize nuisance aggregations rather than major economic damage. Its presence should not be confused with proof of a serious crop or health threat.

silene-dioica.summary: Red campion is a European perennial introduced to parts of North America, sometimes as a garden escape. Male and female flowers occur on separate plants. It is closely related to white campion, and the two can hybridize where they grow together, producing plants with intermediate features. This means flower color is useful evidence but should not be the only basis for identifying a plant.

trifolium-pratense.summary: Red clover is a short-lived perennial widely grown for forage and as a cover crop. It supports nitrogen-fixing bacteria in root nodules and can improve soil fertility in managed rotations. It also escapes into lawns and other open ground. Whether it is a useful planting or an unwanted competitor depends on the site, so a record should distinguish an intended crop from spontaneous plants in a conservation area.

phoenicococcus-marlatti.summary: Red date scale is a small insect associated especially with date palms. It can remain hidden beneath white wax in protected parts of the plant, making a casual look at the outer foliage unreliable. Infested palms and planting material can carry it to new locations. Historical interceptions and eradications should be distinguished from currently established populations when interpreting a distribution record.

festuca-rubra.summary: Red fescue is a fine-leaved perennial grass found in lawns, meadows, dunes and open woodland. The name covers a variable group that includes native North American populations as well as widely planted turf forms. A patch therefore needs more context than the name alone: its location, planting history and botanical variety can change how it should be understood. In the Black Hills, range specialists have recently noted spreading red fescue in disturbed meadows and forest, while gardeners elsewhere deliberately use selected forms as turf.

glycaspis-brimblecombei.summary: Red gum lerp psyllid is an Australian sap-feeding insect that has spread to eucalyptus plantings in California and other warm regions. Its young feed beneath tiny pale shelters called lerps. Heavy populations can cause premature leaf drop, weakening affected trees, while sticky honeydew supports dark sooty mold on leaves and surfaces below. River red gum and several related eucalyptus species are particularly important hosts. A tree with scattered old lerps does not necessarily have an active infestation requiring treatment.

galeopsis-ladanum.summary: Red hempnettle is an annual member of the mint family introduced from Eurasia. In northeastern North America it is recorded from waste ground, old ballast sites and sandy places, including locations near the Atlantic coast. Its pink-red flowers can make a small patch stand out among roadside plants. Despite the name, it is not a true nettle. Several other hempnettles occur in the same broad region, and identifying the species is more useful than assuming every pink-flowered mint has the same behavior or management needs.

solenopsis-invicta.summary: Red imported fire ants are South American ants established across much of the southern United States. Their colonies can occupy lawns, pastures, disturbed ground and other open sites, bringing them close to people and animals. Workers defend a disturbed nest rapidly and can sting repeatedly. A mound deserves a cautious approach, but its shape alone does not identify the species: native fire ants, black imported fire ants and hybrids can look similar. The right response begins with identification and the location of the colony.

eucalyptus-sideroxylon.summary: Red ironbark is an Australian eucalyptus planted for shade and ornamental interest in California and other suitable climates. Its deeply furrowed, dark bark gives a mature tree a very different appearance from the smooth trunks of many familiar gums. California records include naturalized occurrences as well as street and garden trees. Those settings should be distinguished: an old planted specimen is not evidence that a woodland population is expanding. Seedlings beyond a planting are especially useful when evaluating whether a tree is escaping locally.

strobilanthes-alternata.summary: Red ivy is a creeping tropical ornamental grown for metallic leaves with purple undersides. Strobilanthes alternata is also sold as Hemigraphis alternata or Hemigraphis colorata. Its status in Hawaii needs care: older lists called it naturalized, but a 2025 Bishop Museum reassessment found no evidence of self-sustaining populations. A spreading garden bed therefore deserves observation without assuming that every record represents an established wild population. Following its stems back toward a planted bed can help explain what an apparent escape represents.

lumbricus-rubellus.summary: Red marshworm is a European earthworm found widely in North America, including gardens and forests. Lumbricus rubellus feeds near the surface and can alter the leaf litter and upper soil on which woodland plants depend. This matters especially in northern forests whose ecosystems developed without terrestrial earthworms after glaciation. The familiar idea that worms always improve soil does not fit every habitat. Moving bait or worm-filled soil can introduce them to places where their feeding changes the forest floor.

raoiella-indica.summary: Red palm mite is a minute, flattened mite that feeds on leaf undersides of palms and some other tropical plants. Raoiella indica has spread through the Caribbean and into Florida, with infested nursery stock and cut foliage providing routes for movement. Heavy feeding can turn a green palm leaflet yellow and eventually brown. Those symptoms resemble nutritional problems and other diseases, so a discolored palm should not be diagnosed from leaf color alone. Finding and identifying the mites is the important next step.

passiflora-manicata.summary: Red passionflower is a robust South American climbing vine grown for scarlet flowers. Passiflora manicata is native to the northern Andes and is recorded as naturalized in Hawaii. Its flowers can be confused with those of other red passionflowers in gardens, making the leaves and smaller flower structures important. A vine growing over a fence is not necessarily behaving like one spreading through adjacent forest. When evaluating an apparent escape, note both the plant and its connection to nearby cultivation.

matsucoccus-resinosae.summary: Red pine scale is a tiny insect associated with serious decline of red pine in parts of the northeastern United States. Matsucoccus resinosae appears in older accounts; modern references generally place it under Matsucoccus matsumurae, also called Japanese pine bast scale. Its feeding can contribute to pockets of tree mortality. In Maine, red pine is the affected native tree, while other native pine species growing alongside it may remain healthy. That host pattern is useful, but it does not replace a diagnosis.

spergularia-rubra.summary: Red sand-spurry is a small Eurasian herb that has been present in North America since at least the nineteenth century. Spergularia rubra often grows on disturbed ground, paths and open fields. Unlike several sand-spurries associated with salty shores, it also occurs well away from saline places. In New England it is introduced throughout the region. Its presence in a pavement crack or disturbed lawn does not by itself indicate a threat to surrounding natural vegetation. A careful identification is useful before deciding whether any action is needed.

centaurea-calcitrapa.summary: Purple starthistle is a Mediterranean-region weed with conspicuously armed flower heads. Centaurea calcitrapa grows in disturbed ground, roadsides and grazing land, where its spiny heads can interfere with access and pasture use. Plants may flower in their first year or spend longer as a rosette before producing a branched flowering stem. It spreads by seed, including seed carried with contaminated produce, soil and equipment. Local abundance and management priorities vary, so a newly found patch deserves confirmation and attention before it seeds.

centranthus-ruber.summary: Red valerian is a Mediterranean ornamental that readily seeds beyond gardens in some regions. Centranthus ruber also appears under the newer name Valeriana rubra. Its rounded flower clusters brighten walls, rocky slopes and disturbed coastal ground, especially in climates with relatively cool summers. In parts of the western United States and Hawaii it occurs outside cultivation. The feathery fruits can be carried by wind, so a tidy-looking parent plant may have offspring well beyond its bed. Local setting matters when deciding whether to retain a planting.

solenopsis-invicta-x-richteri.summary: Hybrid imported fire ants arise from interbreeding between red imported fire ants and black imported fire ants. Solenopsis invicta x richteri occurs in parts of the southeastern United States where the parental populations have met. These ants can build substantial soil mounds and defend colonies with painful stings. A hybrid colony is not a harmless intermediate between the two parents. However, a red-brown ant or a large mound cannot establish hybrid identity, and ordinary management decisions usually begin with confirming that imported fire ants are present.

aratinga-erythrogenys.summary: Red-masked parakeet is a green, long-tailed parrot native to Ecuador and Peru. Aratinga erythrogenys is an older scientific name; current references generally use Psittacara erythrogenys. Birds from the pet trade have formed free-living populations outside their native range, including California and Hawaii. Their loud calls and social flocks make them conspicuous in urban landscapes. An introduced flock can be worth documenting without assuming that every individual is a recent escape or that every population has the same ecological effects.

melanoides-tuberculatus.summary: Red-rim melania, often sold as Malaysian trumpet snail, is a warm-water snail associated with the aquarium trade. Its name appears as both Melanoides tuberculata and Melanoides tuberculatus in references. Native populations occur across parts of Africa and Asia; introduced populations occupy springs, streams and other suitable waters in the United States. The snails graze on fine organic material and algae and may become very abundant. A quiet aquarium population can be a source of introductions if snails, plants or bottom material are released outdoors.

pycnonotus-jocosus.summary: Red-whiskered bulbul is a fruit-eating songbird native to southern Asia and introduced to places including Florida, California and Hawaii. Pycnonotus jocosus often uses gardens, orchards and other open wooded settings. In Hawaii it can damage cultivated fruit and spread seeds of invasive plants, including miconia and ivy gourd. Its significance depends strongly on location: preventing movement to another island is a different task from observing an established population on Oahu. A clear sighting record can therefore be valuable even when the bird looks familiar.

selenothrips-rubrocinctus.summary: Redbanded thrips is a small leaf-feeding insect found in tropical and subtropical regions, including Florida and Hawaii. Selenothrips rubrocinctus attacks a range of plants, with mango, avocado and ornamental trees among its hosts. Feeding can leave leaves silvery, bronze or brown, and severe infestations may cause considerable foliage damage. The common name refers most clearly to the immature stages. Seeing damaged leaves without the insects is not enough to distinguish it from other thrips or from unrelated causes of leaf discoloration.

xyleborus-glabratus.summary: Redbay ambrosia beetle is a tiny Asian beetle associated with laurel wilt, a serious disease of trees in the laurel family. Xyleborus glabratus carries the fungus into wood as it bores galleries where the beetles cultivate fungi for food. Redbay and sassafras are important affected native trees in the southeastern United States. The beetle and disease are connected but are not the same organism, and other ambrosia beetles may also occur in dying trees. Moving infested wood can carry the problem beyond its natural rate of spread.

coptodon-zillii.summary: Redbelly tilapia is an African and Middle Eastern cichlid introduced to waters outside its native range for several purposes, including aquatic-plant control. Coptodon zillii appears in older literature as Tilapia zillii. In suitable warm waters it can consume substantial vegetation and change habitat used by other fishes. United States reports require care because some historical identifications may represent similar tilapias or hybrids. A fish with a reddish belly is therefore a useful lead, not a complete identification. Local fisheries staff can help establish what is actually present.

escallonia-rubra.summary: Red escallonia is an evergreen South American shrub often planted as a hedge. Escallonia rubra is native to Chile and neighboring Argentina and includes several variable forms. Some garden plants have escaped cultivation in temperate regions, but a maintained hedge and an independently reproducing wild population are different situations. In Hawaii, naturalization records include the large-flowered variety macrantha. The broader species name can appear on garden labels without indicating which variety or cultivated form is present, so labels are a starting point rather than a complete identification.

escallonia-rubra-var-macrantha.summary: Large-flowered red escallonia is a Chilean shrub grown for glossy foliage and red to pink flowers. Escallonia rubra var. macrantha is recognized as a variety in botanical accounts, although some references describe it within a broader Escallonia rubra. Bishop Museum records distinguish naturalization on Hawaii Island from cultivation on Oahu, and New Zealand records also document naturalization. These distinctions matter: a planted hedge and a wild population are different situations. Keep the variety name attached to a verified observation, rather than assuming every red-flowered escallonia belongs here.

strobilanthes-reptans.summary: Strobilanthes reptans is a low, spreading tropical herb also known by the older name Hemigraphis reptans. It is native to Malesia and parts of the western Pacific and has been introduced elsewhere, including Hawaii and parts of the southeastern United States. In Hawaii it is a naturalized lawn weed and also occurs in disturbed moist vegetation. Its creeping habit allows a small patch to extend through rooted stems. That growth form makes it easy to overlook as ordinary groundcover until it reaches places where it is unwanted.

crassocephalum-crepidioides.summary: Thickhead is an African annual herb that has become a widespread weed in tropical regions. Crassocephalum crepidioides grows on disturbed slopes, roadsides and other open sites, including locations in Hawaii. Its reddish flower tips and later fluffy seed heads can be conspicuous above surrounding vegetation. The plant belongs to the daisy family, but its heads lack the broad outer petals of a typical garden daisy. A small newly disturbed patch can look different over a short period as green plants flower and then release their light fruits.

necrobia-rufipes.summary: Redlegged ham beetle is a small metallic beetle associated with dried animal products and other stored foods rich in protein or fat. Necrobia rufipes occurs widely around the world and can infest cured meats, dried fish, pet food, copra and related products. It also scavenges and preys on other insects, so finding adults does not necessarily identify the original source of an infestation. In a storehouse or pantry, the useful question is which product or hidden residue is supporting its life cycle.

oenothera-glazioviana.summary: Garden evening-primrose is a tall, yellow-flowered plant widely grown and escaped from cultivation. Oenothera glazioviana probably arose in Europe from hybridization between North American evening-primroses, rather than representing a straightforward wild European species. It occurs in gardens, roadsides and disturbed fields in the United States, including New England. Its large flowers open toward evening, while the plant may spend an earlier season as a basal rosette. A flowering roadside plant can therefore look very different from the low rosette that preceded it.

necrobia-ruficollis.summary: Redshouldered ham beetle is a small scavenging and predatory beetle associated with dry animal material. Necrobia ruficollis occurs on dried fish and other preserved animal products as well as animal remains. It feeds both on decaying material and on other insects found there. A beetle encountered outdoors on carrion has a different significance from repeated discoveries in a food-storage room. Finding the material supporting the beetles is more useful than treating every metallic beetle as a pantry pest.

erodium-cicutarium.summary: Redstem filaree is a low-growing introduced herb common in open, disturbed places across much of the United States. Erodium cicutarium often grows as a winter annual in California, producing a leafy rosette before flowering and setting its distinctive long-beaked fruits. It occurs in pastures, roadsides, gardens and crop fields, and its importance varies with the site. In some natural communities it competes with native annual plants. In a working landscape, the response should account for both the existing vegetation and how readily seed can arrive again.

agrostis-gigantea.summary: Redtop is a perennial grass introduced for pasture, erosion control and turf. Agrostis gigantea can persist along wet field edges, ditches and disturbed shores, where underground stems help it form a dense cover. Its reddish flowering heads give the species its common name, although color varies with conditions. A useful erosion-control planting can become unwanted where it spreads into a native wet meadow. Management therefore depends on the purpose of the site and the plants that would replace it, rather than on the grass's name alone.

glyceria-maxima.summary: Reed manna grass is a tall Eurasian wetland grass that can form dense stands along ditches, ponds and slow-moving water. Glyceria maxima spreads through rhizomes and can crowd out other wetland vegetation. Introduced populations occur in parts of the northern United States, including Wisconsin and New England. The ornamental variegated form belongs to the same species and should not be assumed incapable of spreading. Early recognition is valuable because a small rooted patch is a more manageable problem than a continuous stand along a watercourse.

lilium-regale.summary: Regal lily is a Chinese bulbous perennial grown for large, fragrant trumpet-shaped flowers. Lilium regale comes from rocky slopes and river valleys in Sichuan and has long been cultivated well beyond that native range. A flowering clump in an old garden may persist after the surrounding planting has disappeared. Persistence at a former homesite should be distinguished from seedlings spreading into nearby vegetation. The common names royal lily and trumpet lily are shared loosely in horticulture, so the scientific identity is worth checking before interpreting an apparent escape.

rotylenchulus-parvus.summary: Rotylenchulus parvus is a microscopic plant-parasitic nematode associated with roots and their surrounding soil. It was first described from sugarcane soil in Mauritius and has been reported from several crops, including cotton, corn and sweet potato. In the United States, records include southern states and California's Imperial Valley. It belongs to the reniform nematode group, but should not be assumed to have the same crop effects or management responses as the better-known Rotylenchulus reniformis. The exact species and crop matter when interpreting a laboratory result.

bromus-catharticus.summary: Rescuegrass is a South American grass grown as forage and also encountered as a weed in disturbed ground and crops. Bromus catharticus can behave as an annual, biennial or short-lived perennial depending on climate and growing conditions. Its presence in a pasture may reflect deliberate planting, while seedlings in a vegetable field or restoration area may be unwanted. The same species therefore needs different decisions in different settings. Its broad, flattened seed heads are useful for recognizing it among the many brome grasses found in open landscapes.

amphibalanus-reticulatus.summary: Reticulated barnacle is a warm-water barnacle native to the Indo-Pacific and spread widely by shipping. Amphibalanus reticulatus attaches to hard surfaces such as hulls, pilings, rocks and shellfish. It has been recorded in the Gulf of Mexico and Hawaii, where its abundance and shore position vary among sites. The adults remain fixed in place, but boats can carry whole fouling communities between harbors. Its main practical significance is therefore connected to movement and maintenance of vessels and equipment as well as to local coastal observations.

trifolium-resupinatum.summary: Persian clover is a cool-season annual legume used as a cover crop and forage. Trifolium resupinatum is native from the Mediterranean region into western Asia and has been introduced widely, including much of the United States. It can provide useful cover and flowers for insects in managed systems, but plants that set seed may become weeds in a following crop. A patch may therefore be intentional, a volunteer from an earlier planting, or an escape. Its agricultural use should not be confused with a claim that it belongs in every natural area.

rabbit-hemorrhagic-disease-virus.summary: Rabbit hemorrhagic disease is caused by closely related lagoviruses, including RHDV2, which affects domestic rabbits and wild rabbits and hares. RHDV2 has spread through many parts of the United States since its detection in wild populations in 2020. It is not known to infect people, but people can carry contaminated material between rabbit populations on footwear, clothing or equipment. The disease name covers more than one viral type, so a laboratory result should specify which virus was identified rather than treating every historical outbreak as RHDV2.

macaca-mulatta.summary: Rhesus macaque is an Asian monkey with an introduced free-ranging population around Silver Springs in Florida. Macaca mulatta lives in social groups and uses both trees and the ground. Its adaptability and history of being fed by people can bring monkeys close to visitors, boats and developed areas. A macaque that approaches confidently is still a wild animal. Feeding changes that relationship and can encourage aggressive behavior, so keeping distance is the most useful way to protect both people and the monkeys.

chloris-gayana.summary: Rhodes grass is an African perennial grass widely planted for grazing and hay in warm regions, including parts of the United States. Chloris gayana can form leafy tufts and spreading runners, with substantial variation among cultivars. It tolerates conditions that make it useful in agriculture, but it can also spread beyond a planted area and crowd other vegetation. A productive pasture and an unwanted patch at the edge of native habitat call for different decisions. Its history as a forage crop does not remove the need to watch where it grows.

massilieurodes-chittendeni.summary: Rhododendron whitefly is a small sap-feeding insect found on rhododendrons in North America and Europe. Massilieurodes chittendeni is still called Dialeurodes chittendeni in many gardening references. Its geographic origin remains uncertain, with sources differing over an Asian or North American origin. The practical concern in a garden is the condition of the host plant and the extent of feeding, rather than assuming that every occurrence represents a newly introduced pest. Smooth-leaved rhododendrons and their hybrids can be especially attractive hosts.

chrysomyxa-rhododendri.summary: Chrysomyxa rhododendri is a rust fungus associated with rhododendrons and spruce, especially Norway spruce in European mountain forests. It can cause conspicuous needle discoloration and premature needle loss. Similar rusts occur on North American rhododendrons and spruces, but they are not automatically this species. Older names in the Chrysomyxa ledi complex have been applied differently, and modern North American guidance distinguishes other fungi, including C. reticulata and C. piperiana. A rusty leaf therefore needs a careful diagnosis before it is interpreted as an introduced European rust.

paspalum-malacophyllum.summary: Ribbed paspalum is a perennial South American grass that has been introduced to several warm regions, including parts of the United States. Paspalum malacophyllum is recorded as naturalized on Maui, while some Hawaiian specimens from other islands represent cultivation. That distinction matters when interpreting a map or an old collection label. The plant can form substantial clumps in disturbed vegetation, but a record from an agricultural trial does not show that it escaped or caused ecological damage at that site.

oryza-sativa.summary: Asian rice is a major food crop, and Oryza sativa includes both cultivated varieties and troublesome weedy forms. Weedy rice grows among planted rice, competes with the crop and can shed seed before harvest. The name red rice refers to reddish bran in some forms, but not every weedy type has the same hull or grain color. The species as a whole should not be treated as an invasive weed: the practical problem is an unwanted, reproducing rice population in a particular field or agricultural setting.

piptatherum-miliaceum.summary: Smilo grass is a perennial bunchgrass from the Mediterranean region and nearby areas, introduced to California and other parts of the United States. Piptatherum miliaceum also appears as Stipa miliacea in California references and as Oloptum miliaceum in Kew's current treatment. It grows along roadsides, ditches and disturbed ground and can spread into riparian areas and canyons. Its tall, loose flowering heads may resemble an ornamental grass, so plants at the edge of a garden can go unnoticed until several clumps have developed.

tetraneura-fusiformis.summary: Tetraneura fusiformis is a name used in a taxonomically difficult group of aphids associated with elm galls and grass roots. Recent research treats it tentatively as a synonym of Tetraneura akinire, while older literature often linked it with T. nigriabdominalis. Those changing names can make historical host and distribution records hard to compare. The group includes aphids living out of sight on roots as well as gall-forming stages on particular elms. A record called rice root aphid should not automatically be assigned to this exact name.

tetrapanax-papyrifer.summary: Rice paper plant is a large-leaved East Asian shrub grown for a bold tropical appearance. Tetrapanax papyrifer is associated with Taiwan and has long been cultivated in China. The name refers to paperlike sheets made from its stem pith; it is not the rice crop. In gardens, its most important spreading behavior is the production of new shoots from underground growth. A single ornamental stem can therefore become a wider colony even where cold weather kills the aboveground foliage back.

cyperus-iria.summary: Rice flatsedge is a warm-season annual sedge associated with moist disturbed ground and crop fields. Cyperus iria is native to Old World tropical and subtropical regions and is established in parts of the United States. It can grow quickly and produce abundant seed, sometimes allowing more than one generation in a favorable season. In rice and other crops, small plants may be overlooked until their branched flower heads rise above the leaves. It is a seed-producing annual, so management differs from that of perennial nutsedges with persistent underground tubers.

bromus-diandrus.summary: Ripgut brome is an introduced cool-season annual grass common in many western United States landscapes. Bromus diandrus grows in disturbed ground, fields and grasslands, where it can compete with other vegetation and contribute dry fuel after it matures. Its sharp, long-awned florets can injure grazing animals. The green young grass and the dry seed-bearing plant present very different management problems, making timing important. A patch is easiest to address before the stiff fruits are dispersed through surrounding vegetation or carried away on equipment and animals.

bromus-diandrus-var-rigidus.summary: Rigid brome is a long-awned annual grass from the Mediterranean region and neighboring areas. Bromus diandrus var. rigidus is a historical name; Kew treats it as a synonym of the separate species Bromus rigidus. Other treatments have combined the two more broadly. This naming difference matters because records labeled ripgut brome may include more than one botanical concept. When comparing a local plant with a distribution record or control study, retain the scientific name used by that source rather than assuming all records describe an identical grass.

eucalyptus-camaldulensis.summary: River red gum is a large Australian eucalyptus naturally associated with waterways and alluvial soils. Eucalyptus camaldulensis has been planted widely for shade, shelter and timber. In southern California it can establish outside plantings and crowd native vegetation in some locations. Its behavior should be assessed locally: a managed urban tree and a reproducing stand along a stream present different concerns. Several subspecies and cultivated forms exist, so one photograph or a familiar bark color may not represent the full range of the species.

casuarina-cunninghamiana.summary: River sheoak is an Australian tree planted outside its native range as an ornamental and windbreak. Casuarina cunninghamiana is one of several Australian pines that have naturalized in Florida. Despite the common name, it is not a true pine: its needlelike greenery consists mostly of slender branchlets, with tiny leaves arranged at their joints. Different Casuarina species and hybrids occur in Florida, and their spread and identification should be considered separately. A tree called Australian pine on a property may not belong to this exact species.

lepidium-ruderale.summary: Roadside pepperweed is a small Eurasian mustard that turns up in disturbed ground, including roadsides, rail corridors, gardens, and waste places. It is an annual or biennial rather than a woody shrub. North American floras record it across scattered parts of the continent, and it occurs throughout New England. Its inconspicuous flowers make it easy to overlook until the upper stems carry rows of tiny fruits. A roadside occurrence is a reason to check the plant carefully, rather than assume every pepperweed there is the same species.

taraxacum-erythrospermum.summary: Rock dandelion, also called red-seeded dandelion, is a Eurasian perennial established in North America. It grows in sunny disturbed places such as lawns, roadsides, grasslands, and parking areas. Regional floras record it from the Pacific Northwest and eastern states, including North Carolina, where it is more frequent in the mountains and Piedmont than near the coast. Like other dandelions, it produces a low leaf rosette, yellow flower heads, and wind-carried fruits. The useful distinction is often visible only after a flower head has matured.

columba-livia.summary: Rock pigeons are familiar birds of cities, farms, bridges, and grain-handling facilities. North American populations descend from birds introduced from the Old World, including domestic pigeons that escaped or were released. Buildings provide sheltered ledges resembling their ancestral cliff nesting sites, while spilled grain and discarded food support large flocks. Their presence is often simply part of urban bird life. Problems arise where repeated roosting leaves heavy accumulations of droppings, blocks building equipment, or contaminates stored food. Reducing those opportunities is the practical starting point.

consolida-ajacis.summary: Rocket larkspur is a garden annual that has escaped cultivation in many parts of North America. It is also known as Delphinium ajacis. Floras describe it in old homesites, drainage ditches, roadsides, railroad margins, and other disturbed places. The upright flowering stems make it conspicuous in summer, particularly when several plants have reseeded together. An escaped flower patch does not establish that it is damaging surrounding vegetation, but it is useful to record whether plants are persisting beyond a garden or spreading along disturbed ground.

palaemon-elegans.summary: Rockpool shrimp is a small coastal shrimp native to the eastern Atlantic and adjacent seas. In North America, the first documented introduced population was found at Salem, Massachusetts, in 2010. Subsequent surveys have recorded it at additional New England sites. It occupies shallow rocky habitats, pools, and artificial structures such as marina surfaces. Ecological effects reported elsewhere include changes in native shrimp communities, but those observations should not be treated as proof of the same effects at every American shoreline. Local observations are most useful when the animal's identity and location are well documented.

agdestis-clematidea.summary: Rockroot is a perennial, partly woody climbing plant also grown as an ornamental vine. Agdestis clematidea is the sole species in its genus, a useful point when consulting older floras that place the genus in different plant families. Kew places its native range from central Texas to Nicaragua and records introductions in Florida and Puerto Rico. Its large storage structure and climbing stems give it a very different habit from the upright pokeweeds with which older classifications grouped it. An established garden vine and an independently spreading population should be documented separately.

cotoneaster-horizontalis.summary: Rockspray cotoneaster is a low, spreading shrub from western China, widely grown for its neatly layered branches and bright red fruit. Its common name is also used for another species, Cotoneaster microphyllus, so a nursery label alone may not settle the identity. Plants can spread several feet outward while remaining comparatively low. European assessments recognize invasive behavior in some settings, but that regional experience should be distinguished from an individual American garden planting. The most useful local observation is whether new plants are appearing beyond the area where the shrub was intentionally installed.

calotropis-procera.summary: Rooster tree, also called small crownflower, is a large shrub or small tree that has naturalized on several Hawaiian islands. It is a plant of warm climates, with substantial pale leaves and distinctive waxy flowers. Hawaiian records have sometimes confused it with the related giant crownflower, Calotropis gigantea, making a careful identification particularly useful before reporting a new population. Bishop Museum records show that its island status is not uniform. A cultivated specimen, a few nearby seedlings, and a spreading stand are different observations worth recording clearly.

phytophthora-tentaculata.summary: Phytophthora tentaculata is a water mold that causes root, crown, and stem disease in nursery plants. Its detection in California native-plant nurseries and restoration plantings is especially concerning because infected stock can carry a root pathogen into a site being restored. California reports include sticky monkeyflower, coffeeberry, toyon, and sage. The organism was first described from ornamental plants in Germany; its name does not mean that all nursery root rot is caused by this species. A plant may look stressed for several reasons, and a laboratory diagnosis is essential.

rhizoecus-hibisci.summary: Root mealybug, Rhizoecus hibisci, is also treated under the name Ripersiella hibisci. Unlike the conspicuous mealybugs on leaves and stems, it usually feeds below ground, around the roots of potted plants. An infestation may travel unnoticed with nursery stock because the foliage can initially show little change. The name does not restrict it to hibiscus. Inspecting the root ball is therefore more useful than searching only the plant's shoots. Other root mealybugs occur in American nurseries, and a species determination matters when a new shipment or unusual infestation is involved.

phytophthora-pseudocryptogea.summary: Phytophthora pseudocryptogea is a root-infecting water mold recognized through studies of the Phytophthora cryptogea species complex. California records include nursery and landscape detections in several coastal and nearby counties. Reported hosts span woody ornamentals and food crops, so the plant involved is important evidence but does not identify the pathogen. Root and collar rot can interfere with water uptake and lead to decline even when soil is moist. Its recent taxonomic separation also means that an older record of P. cryptogea cannot automatically be relabeled as this species.

phytophthora-quercina.summary: Phytophthora quercina is a water mold associated with fine-root disease and decline in oaks. It was described from European oaks and is one of several organisms investigated in complex oak-decline problems. A declining oak may also be affected by drought, unsuitable irrigation, root disturbance, or other pathogens. This species should not be confused with Phytophthora ramorum, the cause of sudden oak death. American survey literature has referred to a P. quercina-like organism; that wording is important and should not be shortened into a confirmed record of P. quercina.

meloidogyne-mali.summary: Meloidogyne mali is a root-knot nematode first described from apple in Japan. Despite that association, its host range includes other woody and herbaceous plants, and European investigations have involved elms. The name Meloidogyne ulmi was later placed in synonymy with it. Reports document a United States detection in 2016, but that limited record should not be taken to mean that the nematode occurs throughout American orchards or landscapes. Rooted plants and the soil surrounding them deserve particular attention when tracing a possible introduction.

abrus-precatorius.summary: Rosary pea is a high-climbing woody vine established in peninsular Florida. Its slender stems twine through surrounding vegetation, and its brilliant red-and-black seeds have long attracted attention. Those seeds are highly poisonous and should never be treated as playthings or craft supplies. In Florida natural areas, the vine is managed as an invasive plant. A small plant is easier to address before it climbs into surrounding shrubs and produces mature pods, but the seed hazard makes careful handling and containment particularly important.

cotoneaster-salicifolius.summary: Willowleaf cotoneaster is an evergreen ornamental shrub native to western China. It belongs to the rose family, but it is not a rose: Cotoneaster salicifolius has simple leaves and small flowers followed by clusters of red fruit. Garden forms vary considerably in size, from low-growing selections to large arching shrubs. That variation can make a planted cultivar look different from a botanical description of the species. Where plants appear beyond cultivation, a clear record of the surrounding planting and the form of the escaped plant helps establish what is happening locally.

macrosiphum-rosae.summary: Rose aphids gather on the soft new growth and flower buds of roses. Their colonies can appear quickly during a flush of growth, but a few aphids usually cause little lasting damage. Larger populations may distort young leaves or slow shoot development. Sticky honeydew can attract ants and support dark sooty mold on surfaces beneath the colony. Several aphid species use roses, so a pink or green insect on a rose is not automatically Macrosiphum rosae. Observing the plant's condition and the insects together gives a better basis for deciding whether action is needed.

sitobion-fragariae.summary: Sitobion fragariae is better known as the blackberry-grass aphid. Its life cycle can connect brambles and other rose-family plants with grasses, including cultivated cereals. That movement between hosts explains why the plant on which it is found is useful evidence, but not a complete identification. European research identifies it as a vector of barley yellow dwarf virus, even where direct feeding causes little injury. The common name rose aphid is ambiguous and can also refer to quite different insects. A confirmed species and an assessment of the affected crop are needed before attributing damage to this aphid.

trifolium-hirtum.summary: Rose clover is a hairy annual clover introduced from the Mediterranean region and grown in some American forage systems. Its role varies with place and land use: a planted pasture legume and an unwanted plant in a conservation grassland require different decisions. Florida's assessment does not currently regard it as a documented problem species, while California resources evaluate its occurrence in natural vegetation. The rounded rosy flower heads are conspicuous in season, but identification should include the leaves and hairs rather than flower color alone.

clerodendrum-bungei.summary: Rose glorybower is an Asian ornamental shrub that can spread beyond a garden through underground shoots. A single planting may gradually produce a colony, making it troublesome in beds or along property edges. Florida records document scattered escapes, but the state's university account distinguishes that garden nuisance from broader environmental damage, which it does not document. The plant was formerly on a Florida invasive-plant council list and later removed. This is a useful reminder to judge local spread and current guidance rather than assume every vigorous ornamental has the same ecological effect.

rhodomyrtus-tomentosa.summary: Rose myrtle is an evergreen shrub from eastern and southeastern Asia that has become invasive in central and southern Florida. It can form dense thickets in native pinelands, crowding surrounding vegetation. Its pink flowers and purple fruits helped make it an ornamental introduction, but fruit-eating wildlife can move its seeds beyond gardens. A shrub in a natural area deserves attention before it becomes part of a larger stand. Florida accounts also note vigorous resprouting after fire, so burning a patch should not be assumed to remove the problem.

melinis-repens.summary: Rose natalgrass is an introduced grass recognizable by its airy pink seed heads. Originally promoted as a forage plant in Florida, it now occurs across much of the state and can interfere with native vegetation in scrub, sandhill, and other open habitats. Its appearance changes as the hairy flower clusters age from pink or purple to pale gray. It spreads readily by windborne seed, so a small roadside or trail-edge patch can supply seed to neighboring ground. Individual plants may persist, although seed production is the main route emphasized in Florida accounts.

aulacaspis-rosae.summary: Rose scale is an armored scale insect found on roses and caneberries. The insects live beneath small protective covers attached to the plant, so an infestation can look more like a coating on the stem than a group of moving animals. Heavy populations deserve attention, but old covers may remain after insects have died. Checking whether scales are alive and whether the plant is declining helps avoid unnecessary treatment. Other scale insects also occur on roses, and a white crust on a cane is not enough to establish the species.

pelargonium-capitatum.summary: Rose-scented geranium is a low, spreading South African pelargonium with aromatic foliage and pink flowers. Its native habitat includes coastal dunes and low hillsides, and botanical records list it as introduced in California. Garden plants sold under the name may be hybrids, which complicates identification outside cultivation. A scented leaf is therefore a clue to a group of ornamentals, not proof of this species. Documenting flowers and the whole plant is particularly helpful when assessing a possible escape from a nearby garden.

agrilus-cuprescens.summary: Rose stem girdler is a small introduced beetle whose larvae tunnel inside rose, raspberry, and blackberry canes. It has become a notable cane pest in parts of Utah, where infested stems can weaken, wilt, or break. The name is misleading if taken to mean it feeds only on roses. Damage is caused mainly by the concealed larvae rather than the visible adult beetles. A cane that snaps at a swelling provides a useful place to investigate, although other borers and cane diseases can also cause dieback.

metopolophium-dirhodum.summary: Rose-grass aphid, often called rose-grain aphid, uses roses and a range of grasses, including small-grain crops. On cereals it can resemble greenbug, but the distinction matters: rose-grain aphids generally cause much less direct feeding injury. They can transmit barley yellow dwarf virus, so crop condition, season, and local disease risk still matter when assessing a colony. European accounts describe movement between roses and grasses, while the details of overwintering vary with climate. Finding aphids on a rose does not by itself explain a problem in a nearby grain field.

nipponaclerda-biwakoensis.summary: Roseau cane scale is an Asian sap-feeding insect associated with Phragmites australis in Louisiana wetlands. It is a scale insect, despite sometimes being called a mealybug. Investigations have linked heavy infestations with stress in roseau cane stands, although wetland dieback has multiple interacting causes. In the Mississippi River Delta, these stands can provide cover and help stabilize marsh sediment, so their decline has consequences beyond the individual plant. This setting differs from places where an introduced Phragmites lineage is itself being controlled; the local wetland context matters.

dysaphis-plantaginea.summary: Rosy apple aphid is an early-season pest of apple trees. Colonies develop as buds and leaves expand, and their feeding can curl young foliage around the insects. That shelter makes established colonies harder to reach and helps explain why early inspection matters. The life cycle commonly includes summer movement to plantains and a return to apple in autumn. A curled apple leaf can also have other causes, so open it carefully and inspect the inhabitants before deciding which pest is involved. The timing of activity follows local tree development rather than a single nationwide calendar.

poa-trivialis.summary: Rough bluegrass is a cool-season perennial grass that can occur in lawns, pasture, and moist disturbed ground. In turf it may form patches with a different color and growth pattern from the intended lawn. The plant spreads through creeping aboveground stems, called stolons, so controlling seed production alone does not address an established patch. It is also used deliberately in some turf systems, making the management goal important. A pale or uneven area of lawn should be examined closely before it is attributed to rough bluegrass rather than watering, disease, or another grass.

adiantum-hispidulum.summary: Rough maidenhair is a fern naturalized on the main Hawaiian Islands. It grows on the ground and can be common in shaded vegetation. Its delicate-looking fronds do not make it harmless in every setting: Hawaiian conservation managers have identified it as a concern around some rare-plant sites, while also noting that effective control can be difficult. Management priorities therefore depend on the particular habitat and the plants nearby. It reproduces as a fern, with spores rather than flowers or seeds, so an apparent flowerless plant may still be fully mature.

neogobius-melanostomus.summary: Round goby is a bottom-dwelling fish native to the Black, Caspian, and Azov sea region and their tributaries. Introduced populations are established in the Great Lakes, where the fish can compete with native bottom dwellers and consume invertebrates, fish eggs, and small fish. It also becomes prey for larger animals, making its effects part of a changing food web rather than a single simple interaction. Preventing movement to new waters is especially important because effective population-wide removal from natural water bodies is not available.

juncus-compressus.summary: Roundfruit rush is a Eurasian rush introduced into North America. In New England it has been recorded in disturbed salty ground, including road shoulders, ditches, and railroad margins. Elsewhere in its introduced range it can occur in calcareous wetlands. These habitats contain many native rushes and sedges, so a grasslike plant beside a salted road should not be identified by location alone. Mature fruit and tiny flower parts provide the most useful evidence, especially when distinguishing it from saltmarsh rush and other similar species.

delonix-regia.summary: Royal poinciana is a broad-crowned tree native to Madagascar and planted in warm American landscapes for its vivid red-orange flowers. In frost-free settings it can become much wider than it is tall, providing light, dappled shade beneath fine foliage. Florida assessments distinguish the southern region, where plantings should be managed to prevent escape, from northern and central Florida, where it has not been treated as a problem species in the cited assessment. Its ornamental use and a nearby self-sown population should therefore be considered separately.

enchylaena-tomentosa.summary: Ruby saltbush is a small Australian shrub associated with dry and sometimes saline landscapes. Its colorful fleshy fruits and narrow succulent leaves give it a distinctive appearance. Botanical records list introductions outside Australia, but those records do not establish how it behaves at a particular American site. A cultivated shrub and a self-sustaining patch beyond a garden are different observations. When documenting a plant, note whether it is alone or accompanied by younger individuals and whether the surrounding ground is maintained, disturbed, or natural vegetation.

gymnocephalus-cernua.summary: Ruffe is a small Eurasian fish introduced into the Great Lakes, first detected near the St. Louis River in 1986. It lives near the bottom and feeds on aquatic invertebrates and other small prey. Introduced populations can compete with native fish for food, making prevention of further spread a priority. The scientific name also appears as Gymnocephalus cernuus in agency materials. An unfamiliar small perchlike fish in a bait container deserves a careful look, since accidental movement with bait can carry fish between waters.

rosa-rugosa.summary: Rugosa rose is an eastern Asian shrub planted widely for its flowers, tough foliage, and tolerance of coastal conditions. Along parts of the northeastern coast it has escaped into dunes and other shore habitats, where underground growth can create dense thickets. Both seeds and pieces of the spreading underground stems can travel in water. Its management importance is therefore especially strong near vulnerable coastal vegetation. A garden rose inland and a spreading dune colony are different situations, and local guidance should shape the response.

aleurodicus-rugioperculatus.summary: Rugose spiraling whitefly is an introduced tropical insect first reported in Florida in 2009. It can occur on palms and a range of woody plants, producing conspicuous wax and sticky honeydew. Dark sooty mold may then coat leaves, cars, patios, or plants beneath an infested tree. These effects can be a substantial nuisance without necessarily killing the host. An egg spiral on a surface does not prove that the insect can complete development there: females sometimes lay eggs on unsuitable plants and even on objects such as windows or vehicles.

chondrilla-juncea.summary: Rush skeletonweed is a perennial or sometimes biennial weed with a deep root system and a highly branched, nearly leafless flowering form. Introduced from southern Europe, it occurs in western American roadsides, rangelands, fields, and other disturbed open ground. Its early rosette can blend in with other yellow-flowered members of the sunflower family. Later, the wiry flowering stems make the name skeletonweed more understandable. Both seed production and regrowth from roots complicate management, so a patch deserves attention before machinery or soil disturbance carries it farther.

elaeagnus-angustifolia.summary: Russian olive is a thorny shrub or small tree introduced as an ornamental, windbreak, and bank-stabilization plant. It has escaped along streams, floodplains, and roadsides in parts of the western United States. Birds carry its fruits, helping seedlings appear beyond the original planting. In affected riparian areas, management often focuses on restoring a more diverse native plant community. Its value as cover or food for some wildlife does not remove the need to assess that local habitat change, and removal planning should consider what will replace the trees.

diuraphis-noxia.summary: Russian wheat aphid is a small cereal-feeding insect that can injure wheat and barley as it feeds. Unlike several other common grain aphids, it can produce visible damage at relatively low abundance, so species identification matters when scouting. Its American importance varies by region and year. California guidance describes substantial declines from earlier outbreaks, while Oklahoma accounts emphasize the Panhandle. Neither history means that every field requires treatment. Crop stage, actual infestation, and local advice should guide decisions.

psathyrostachys-juncea.summary: Russian wildrye is a long-lived, cool-season bunchgrass introduced for pasture and conservation plantings in the northern and intermountain West. USDA materials describe its use in Montana and Wyoming, especially where drought tolerance and a long grazing season are useful. Established plants have extensive roots and can compete strongly with other vegetation. That characteristic can be desirable in a managed pasture and undesirable where native plant diversity is the objective. Its presence should be interpreted in the context of planting history rather than treated automatically as an invasive outbreak.

puccinia-modiolae.summary: Puccinia modiolae is a rust fungus associated with Carolina bristlemallow and other members of the mallow family. A North American study documented it along the Gulf Coast, including Louisiana and Texas, and considered an introduction from South America likely. The same study added hollyhock and common mallow to its reported host range. Those records should not be confused with the much more familiar hollyhock rust, Puccinia malvacearum. Several rust species can occur on related hosts, and the host name alone does not determine which fungus is present.

uromyces-transversalis.summary: Uromyces transversalis is one of the fungi that cause gladiolus rust. Current USDA guidance identifies it as established in the United States and distinguishes it from other gladiolus rust fungi that remain a plant-health concern. This distinction matters because older information may describe responses that no longer apply to this species. Rust spores can travel on wind and with flowers, stems, and contaminated plant material. A grower who sees suspicious leaf lesions should seek a diagnosis before deciding how to handle a planting or shipment.

puccinia-pelargonii-zonalis.summary: Pelargonium rust is a leaf disease of zonal pelargoniums, the familiar bedding plants often called geraniums. It is caused by Puccinia pelargonii-zonalis. The host distinction matters: this account concerns zonal pelargoniums rather than every plant sold as a geranium. In greenhouse collections, infected plants can introduce the fungus before obvious symptoms appear. Repeated infections can yellow leaves and cause them to fall, weakening the plant. Humid conditions and prolonged leaf wetness favor the disease, so prevention includes how plants are arranged and watered as well as inspection of new stock.

arhopalus-rusticus.summary: Rust pine borer is a longhorn beetle associated with conifer wood. Its range and taxonomic history require care: North American taxonomic records include native populations and subspecies, while introduced populations have also been reported in South America. It should therefore not be presented as a uniformly foreign pest throughout the United States. European accounts describe larvae developing in dead conifer wood and adults visiting fallen logs and stumps. Finding a beetle near a woodpile is not, by itself, evidence that it killed a living tree.

dysaphis-apiifolia.summary: Rusty banded aphid, also called hawthorn-parsley aphid, is among the aphids encountered on celery. Related accounts include other carrot-family plants such as parsley, fennel, and carrot. In celery production, dense aphid colonies can interfere with growth and contaminate harvested stalks with insects, cast skins, and honeydew. Several species may be present, so a management decision should begin with the crop and the actual infestation rather than the common name. The species belongs to a difficult group whose members can be hard to separate even with close examination.

bromus-secalinus.summary: Rye brome, also called true cheat, is a winter annual grass that can be troublesome in wheat. In Oklahoma it grows on a seasonal schedule similar to winter wheat, making it difficult to separate from the crop through routine management alone. Competition, harvest interference, and contaminated grain can all matter to producers. The common name cheat should not be confused with cheatgrass, which usually means downy brome, Bromus tectorum. Several annual bromes occur together, and a mature flowering specimen is often the best starting point for identification.

carex-secalina.summary: Rye sedge is a Eurasian sedge documented as naturalized in southeastern New York. A 2012 study reported seven North American populations at that time, mainly in highly disturbed urban habitats, including salt-influenced ground. That historical count is not a current distribution estimate. In its native range the species also occupies damp or wet, often saline soils. The researchers did not consider it demonstrably invasive in North America then, but recommended monitoring because of its potential seed production. A new observation is useful evidence, particularly when accompanied by mature fruit.

tilletia-walkeri.summary: Ryegrass bunt is a fungal disease caused by Tilletia walkeri. It affects ryegrass seed and became particularly important in American diagnostic work because its spores resemble those of the Karnal bunt fungus, Tilletia indica. Surveys in southeastern wheat fields found T. walkeri on annual ryegrass growing among the crop; the study did not find bunted wheat seed or T. indica. That distinction matters when interpreting a contaminated grain sample. A spore detected among wheat grains does not necessarily mean that the wheat itself is infected.

phenacoccus-graminicola.summary: Ryegrass mealybug is a small plant-feeding insect recorded on grasses and several other plant groups. Older American literature may call it Phenacoccus graminosus, a name now treated as a synonym of Phenacoccus graminicola. California records are well established in the taxonomic literature. Its origin should be handled carefully, and an old collection record does not by itself establish whether a population is native. Reports of pasture damage elsewhere should not be transferred automatically to an American lawn or field. Finding a mealybug and explaining a patch of declining grass are separate steps.

nandina-domestica.summary: Sacred bamboo, or nandina, is an Asian shrub widely planted for its foliage and persistent red fruit. Despite the common name, it is a member of the barberry family rather than a true bamboo. In parts of the Southeast it has escaped into woods and floodplains, where spreading plants can form dense patches. Seeds carried by wildlife and growth from underground stems both contribute. Cultivars differ in fruit production, so a compact garden selection may behave differently from a heavily fruiting shrub; current local recommendations remain important when choosing replacements.

nelumbo-nucifera.summary: Sacred lotus brings enormous round leaves and pink or white flowers to shallow, quiet water. This Asian ornamental can escape water gardens and establish colonies in ponds, marshes, and lake margins in the United States. Underground rhizomes allow a planting to expand well beyond its original pot or shoreline position. Dense growth can crowd the water surface, but a patch of lotus should not automatically be treated as this introduced species: American lotus is native to parts of the country.

onobrychis-viciifolia.summary: Sainfoin is a perennial forage legume introduced from Eurasia and deliberately grown for hay and pasture in parts of the western United States. Its pink flower spikes make a field look quite different from alfalfa. Wyoming and Montana extension specialists describe it as an agricultural crop with useful forage qualities, not simply an unwanted plant wherever it occurs. An isolated roadside plant and a managed forage stand therefore call for different decisions.

tragopogon-porrifolius.summary: Purple salsify is a biennial herb historically cultivated for its root and now found outside gardens. A first-year plant can disappear into surrounding grass because its leaves are long and narrow. In its flowering year, the purple heads and large fluffy seed balls are much easier to notice. Several introduced salsifies occur in the United States, so the familiar common name does not identify a single species.

tamarix-ramosissima.summary: Saltcedar is a woody shrub or small tree associated with river corridors, reservoirs, and other moist places in the arid West. Its fine foliage and pink flower sprays can be attractive, but established stands complicate riparian restoration. Many North American plants called Tamarix ramosissima are hybrids with Tamarix chinensis. Research on that mixed population is often more relevant to a western saltcedar stand than a precise species label based only on appearance.

halogeton-glomeratus.summary: Halogeton is a small annual weed of dry, salty, disturbed ground in the Great Basin and other parts of the western United States. Introduced from Eurasia, it can occupy road edges, livestock trails, and degraded rangeland where perennial vegetation is sparse. Its most immediate practical concern is livestock poisoning: the foliage contains soluble oxalates, and sheep and cattle can be seriously affected. Risk varies with the animals, plant condition, and available forage.

echium-plantagineum.summary: Salvation jane, also called Paterson's curse, is a Mediterranean annual or biennial that has become a pasture and roadside weed in several regions, including parts of the western United States. The purple flowers can make a stand look like a desirable wildflower planting. However, its seeds move with hay, soil, vehicles, and agricultural materials, and the plant contains alkaloids that can harm livestock. Horses are particularly important to protect from contaminated forage.

alternanthera-ficoidea.summary: Slender joyweed is a small tropical American herb in the amaranth family. The name Alternanthera ficoidea has also been used broadly in horticulture for colorful bedding plants. That history matters when matching a garden plant to a botanical name: foliage sold under one label may belong to a different, closely related joyweed. A Florida assessment under this name applies to the plant concept assessed there, not automatically to every joyweed sold under a similar label.

calophyllum-brasiliense.summary: Santa Maria is an evergreen tropical American tree with dense foliage and small white flowers. Its native range includes Mexico, Central and South America, and parts of the Caribbean, including Puerto Rico. Trees cultivated in Florida under this name require particular care in identification because some records and landscape references concern the Antillean taxon, treated as Calophyllum brasiliense var. antillanum or Calophyllum antillanum. A name used in a nursery is not always a precise statement of botanical identity.

parthenium-hysterophorus.summary: Santa Maria feverfew, often called ragweed parthenium, is a branching annual of disturbed ground, fields, and nursery areas. It belongs to the tropical and subtropical American flora, and the limits of its native range in the southern United States have been interpreted differently. Elsewhere it is a serious agricultural invader. Its practical significance at a particular site comes from crop competition, seed movement, and the potential for allergic skin or respiratory reactions, rather than from a single nationwide label.

brachypeplus-basalis.summary: The Australian sap beetle, Brachypeplus basalis, is an introduced beetle found in stored honey bee hive equipment in Oregon and in pollen stores in California. Those associations matter to beekeepers, but they do not make it the small hive beetle, Aethina tumida, which has a different pest history. Oregon's first report concerned stored equipment rather than active colonies. Its presence alone therefore does not explain a struggling colony or prove that it damaged the comb.

manilkara-zapota.summary: Sapodilla is an evergreen fruit tree native to tropical America and widely cultivated in warm regions. In southern Florida, escaped trees can establish in hammocks, where dense seedlings and mature crowns interfere with native vegetation. The same tree may therefore be a valued orchard crop in one setting and an unwanted escape in another. Fallen fruit and wildlife movement are important links between a planted tree and seedlings appearing beyond the garden.

vigna-hosei.summary: Sarawak bean is a creeping or climbing tropical legume used as ground cover and green manure in plantations. It has also become naturalized in Hawaii, where botanical records document occurrences beyond its original plantings. A dense ground-cover planting can be useful in a managed agricultural setting while still needing containment at its edges. Its ability to produce pods close to the ground makes a quick inspection of the visible flowers an incomplete check for seed.

severe-acute-respiratory-syndrome-relate.summary: SARS-CoV-2 is the virus that causes COVID-19. It belongs to a broader coronavirus species now called Betacoronavirus pandemicum; the older species name severe acute respiratory syndrome-related coronavirus should not be read as a synonym for SARS-CoV-2 alone. This distinction separates the virus responsible for COVID-19 from related viruses discussed in taxonomy and wildlife research. For someone concerned about a possible infection, the useful next step is appropriate testing and health advice rather than trying to identify a virus from symptoms.

oryzaephilus-surinamensis.summary: The sawtoothed grain beetle is a small stored-food insect found in grain, cereal products, and other dry goods. Adults and larvae can develop in stored material, so seeing a few beetles on a pantry shelf may point to an infested package nearby. In bulk grain, heavy infestations can contribute to heating and deterioration. The closely related merchant grain beetle often occurs in similar settings, and the two are easily confused.

soybean-dwarf-virus.summary: Soybean dwarf virus infects legumes and has been documented in U.S. forage plants as well as in research involving soybean. Its name can suggest that every infected plant will be conspicuously dwarfed, but symptoms and host relationships differ among virus strains. Studies in Illinois found the virus in several clovers, emphasizing that its ecology extends beyond a soybean field. It is distinct from soybean mosaic virus and from viruses sometimes described with similar stunt or dwarf names.

duplachionaspis-divergens.summary: Duplachionaspis divergens is an armored scale associated with grasses, including ornamental grasses and sugarcane. It has been documented in Florida and other Gulf Coast states. A colony can be easy to overlook because the insects resemble small pale marks attached to a blade. Confirming the insect matters before linking it to thinning or yellowing grass, since turf and ornamental grasses can decline for many unrelated reasons.

eriococcus-insignis.summary: The scale historically called Eriococcus insignis is now treated in ScaleNet as Anophococcus insignis, with Acanthococcus insignis appearing in other references. It is a felt scale associated with grasses and a range of other plants. A New York population was originally described under the name Eriococcus saratogensis and later placed in synonymy. These name changes can make old records look like several different insects when they concern the same taxonomic concept.

eriococcus-pittospori.summary: Pittosporum eriococcin is a small felt scale described from California as Eriococcus pittospori and now generally placed in Acanthococcus. The original collection came from Pittosporum tenuifolium in San Francisco. A later illustrated collection was taken from Coprosma repens in the same city in 1973. These records help explain why a scale on pittosporum or Coprosma is worth documenting, but the host alone cannot identify it. Its original home remains uncertain.

fiorinia-japonica.summary: Coniferous fiorinia scale is an armored scale found on several kinds of conifers. U.S. records include the mid-Atlantic region and California, where infestations have occurred on residential trees and nursery plants. Feeding can produce yellow stippling, needle loss, and reduced growth, although the severity varies. Its history includes confusion with other Fiorinia species, so reports based only on a host list or a common name need care.

hypogeococcus-pungens.summary: Hypogeococcus pungens is a name that has been applied to several closely related South American mealybugs. Recent research distinguishes the narrow species associated with the amaranth family from a separate, still-unnamed cactus-feeding species with several lineages. A cactus-feeding member of this complex has harmed native cacti in Puerto Rico. That makes the identity especially important: a mealybug used against invasive cacti elsewhere should not automatically be treated as the same organism as the Puerto Rican pest.

morganella-longispina.summary: Maskell scale is a tiny armored scale recorded from many woody plants in warm regions. Original specimen studies include insects collected on oleander in Bermuda and Jamaica, alongside a separate Queensland account. Its native origin remains uncertain. A broad host list does not mean every plant or U.S. location experiences serious damage. When inspecting a suspect plant, look for living insects and a matching pattern of injury rather than assuming every dark scale cover represents an active problem.

parlatoria-theae.summary: Tea parlatoria scale is an armored scale found on tea and other woody plants. Dutch plant inspectors have identified it on imported boxwood, maples and other ornamentals from East Asia, illustrating how it can travel with nursery stock. An interception does not establish that the insect became established outdoors. Older U.S. reports also need care because related Parlatoria species have sometimes been confused. Its common name should not be used to identify every scale found on tea.

microcosmus-squamiger.summary: The scaly tunicate is a solitary sea squirt native to Australia and introduced to parts of the U.S. West Coast. It attaches to hard surfaces in harbors and coastal waters, including structures and vessel hulls. Many individuals can gather closely together even though each remains a separate animal. Dense fouling has affected shellfish culture in some invaded regions, making equipment and vessel movement important opportunities to prevent further spread.

hybosorus-roei.summary: This scarab relative is better known as Hybosorus illigeri. In 2021, the International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature conserved that name over older names including Hybosorus roei. The insect has been collected in Florida pasture surveys, but being caught near cattle dung does not establish that it feeds on dung or harms livestock. Research on the group includes predatory behavior by this species, so it should not automatically be treated like a root-feeding lawn grub.

pyracantha-coccinea.summary: Scarlet firethorn is a thorny ornamental shrub native to Europe and temperate Asia. White spring flowers and clusters of red fruits make it a familiar hedge plant. Birds can carry the seeds away from gardens, and escapes occur in suitable habitats, including parts of California. Regional assessments differ in how they describe its risk: a prediction of invasion potential is not the same as proof of widespread damage at every planted site.

malachius-aeneus.summary: The scarlet malachite beetle is a small flower-associated beetle introduced to North America from the western Palearctic region. Historical records place it in parts of the northern United States and southern Canada. It is also a conservation concern in Britain, illustrating why a species' significance depends on location. Finding an introduced beetle on a flower does not by itself show that the plant is being damaged or that control is needed.

pseudococcus-calceolariae.summary: Scarlet mealybug, also called citrophilus mealybug, is a sap-feeding insect associated with citrus and other plants. It has a long history in California citrus, where natural enemies can keep populations low. A white waxy colony therefore deserves inspection rather than an automatic spray. Mealybugs can hide among closely touching fruit and protected plant surfaces, and their honeydew can support dark sooty mold.

emilia-coccinea.summary: Scarlet tasselflower is a flowering herb with bright orange to red heads, often encountered as an ornamental. It belongs to a group of similar Emilia species whose names can be confused in gardens and weed records. In particular, Florida tasselflower, Emilia fosbergii, and lilac tasselflower, Emilia sonchifolia, are not interchangeable with this species. A red tassel-like flower is a useful clue, but it is not a complete identification. The cited Florida extension comparison reports that this exact species had not been documented there.

tripleurospermum-inodorum.summary: Scentless false mayweed, also called scentless chamomile, is a daisy-like weed of disturbed land and agricultural fields. Its finely divided foliage can make a young patch look delicate, but established plants compete with crops and can interfere with harvesting. Plants may behave as annuals, biennials, or short-lived perennials depending on conditions. Reproduction by seed makes preventing mature heads especially important.

gremmeniella-abietina.summary: Gremmeniella abietina is the fungus associated with Scleroderris canker, a disease of conifers that can kill shoots and damage nursery or plantation trees. Different strains have different histories and effects in North America. Red and Scots pine plantations are among the settings described in U.S. forest-health literature. A browning pine is not automatically infected, but a cluster of affected shoots deserves investigation before nursery plants or branches are moved elsewhere.

cytisus-scoparius.summary: Scotch broom is a European shrub that has escaped cultivation and spread through sunny disturbed ground, roadsides, pastures, and open woodland in parts of North America. Its bright yellow flowering display can conceal a persistent management problem: established shrubs are difficult to remove, and seeds can remain available for later germination. A newly found plant at the edge of an infestation is usually easier to address than an old, densely branched stand.

onopordum-acanthium.summary: Scotch thistle is a large Eurasian thistle that can make pastures, roadsides, and access routes difficult to use. Its pale, woolly foliage and heavily armed stems distinguish a mature stand from many ordinary roadside weeds. Plants commonly begin as broad rosettes before producing tall flowering stems. Removing a young rosette is much less demanding than working through a mature spiny plant, and preventing seed production is central to long-term control.

pinus-sylvestris.summary: Scots pine is a Eurasian conifer widely planted in North America for landscapes, windbreaks, and Christmas trees. It has naturalized in parts of the United States, particularly in northern regions. Its role depends on the site: a maintained specimen tree is different from seedlings spreading into an open habitat that managers are trying to conserve. Naturalization alone does not establish the same ecological impact everywhere.

cronartium-pini.summary: Scots pine blister rust is a fungal disease associated especially with hard pines in Europe and Asia. The name Cronartium pini now includes forms formerly separated as Cronartium flaccidum and Peridermium pini. One form alternates between pine and other plants, while another spreads directly between pines. This is different from assuming that all pine blister rusts have the same hosts or life cycle. A 2024 California assessment reports no North American disease records; older uncertain reports do not establish a current US occurrence.

solanum-tampicense.summary: Scrambling nightshade, also called wetland nightshade or aquatic soda apple, is a sprawling prickly shrub that has invaded Florida wetlands. Long stems clamber through surrounding vegetation and can form difficult, tangled thickets. It occurs around cypress swamps, stream margins, and other wet habitats, although it is not a plant of permanently submerged conditions. Pieces of stem can establish new growth, so careless cutting and disposal can spread the problem.

talipariti-tiliaceum.summary: Sea hibiscus is a tropical coastal shrub or small tree also widely known as Hibiscus tiliaceus. Its broad leaves and large yellow flowers make it easy to notice along wet coastal margins. Regional origin needs care: Florida treatments distinguish the introduced variety tiliaceum from a related variety, pernambucense, native to Puerto Rico and parts of tropical America. Advice for an escaped Florida planting should not automatically be applied to every sea hibiscus population.

didemnum-vexillum.summary: Didemnum vexillum is a colonial sea squirt that can spread across rocks, shellfish, dock structures, and other submerged surfaces. Colonies consist of many tiny animals embedded in a shared covering. It has established on both U.S. coasts and can alter bottom habitats or foul aquaculture equipment. Genetic evidence points toward a northwestern Pacific origin, but the exact limits of its native range remain less certain than its introduced occurrence in North America.

verbena-litoralis.summary: Seashore vervain is an upright tropical American herb that has naturalized widely, including across the main Hawaiian Islands.
