Despite its common name, it is not restricted to a narrow strip beside the sea. In Hawaii it occurs in moist or wet pastures, disturbed forest, and other altered sites, where it can displace forage and native vegetation. The base may become somewhat woody as the plant persists.

hordeum-marinum.summary: Seaside barley is a small annual grass associated with saline ground. It is native to the Mediterranean region and has been introduced elsewhere. The common names sea barley, barley grass, and Mediterranean barley have been used inconsistently for several Hordeum species, so an awned grass at the coast should not be assigned this name automatically. Its occurrence can also reflect the soil conditions of a site rather than establish that it is causing ecological damage.

calibrachoa-parviflora.summary: Seaside petunia is a small, low-growing plant with miniature pink to purple trumpet flowers. It also appears in older references as Petunia parviflora. Its North American status deserves regional care: California botanical resources treat it as native, while Kew's global checklist places California and other U.S. areas in its introduced range. That disagreement makes automatic removal from natural habitat inappropriate without local botanical advice.

carex-diluta.summary: Carex diluta is a Eurasian sedge documented as introduced in Montana, including moist alkaline meadow habitat. It is not simply another name for every pale sedge in a wet pasture. Sedges are a diverse and important part of many native wetland communities, and this species can be difficult to recognize without mature fruit. A new observation is most useful when it includes a precise location and enough detail for a botanist to verify it.

phoenix-reclinata.summary: Senegal date palm is an African palm commonly planted for its arching fronds and clusters of leaning trunks. In southern Florida it has escaped cultivation and is assessed as invasive, while its role in its African native range is very different. A mature clump can occupy much more space than a young nursery plant suggests. New shoots and seedlings around an established planting deserve attention before they develop into difficult-to-access growth.

neurolaena-lobata.summary: Sepi, Neurolaena lobata, is a tropical American shrub or subshrub also known by several regional names, including salve bush. Its native range includes Puerto Rico and much of the Caribbean and tropical mainland Americas. It has been introduced to Hawaii and other Pacific islands. That geography matters: a plant can belong to the local flora in one U.S. jurisdiction and be introduced in another, without those facts alone establishing the same management need.

senna-occidentalis.summary: Coffee senna, also called Senna occidentalis or formerly Cassia occidentalis, is an American plant now widespread in warm regions. It occurs around disturbed ground and agricultural areas. Its seeds can contaminate feed, and veterinary studies have documented serious poisoning in cattle and poultry. The common name coffee senna is not an invitation to use the seeds as a drink or home remedy.

campanula-poscharskyana.summary: Serbian bellflower is a low, spreading perennial grown in rock gardens, borders, and along walls. It comes from the Balkan region and can expand through runners and trailing growth. A planting that starts as a small cushion may gradually occupy neighboring pockets of soil. Horticultural descriptions sometimes call that behavior invasive, but garden spread and demonstrated damage in U.S. natural habitat are different questions.

lespedeza-cuneata.summary: Sericea lespedeza is an Asian perennial legume once widely planted for forage, erosion control, and wildlife cover. In parts of the central and eastern United States, it has spread into grasslands and other open habitats, where dense growth competes with native vegetation. Its deep root system and persistent seed supply make an established stand difficult to eliminate. Young plants and scattered outliers are valuable priorities before a larger patch forms.

nassella-trichotoma.summary: Serrated tussock is a South American perennial grass that has caused major pasture and native-vegetation problems in countries where it is established. Its dense tufts and abundant wind-moved seed make prevention important. U.S. records need particularly careful interpretation: some widely repeated records trace to contaminated seed shipments rather than confirmed growing populations. A suspected plant should therefore be documented and checked, not treated as proof that a state is already broadly infested.

alternanthera-sessilis.summary: Sessile joyweed is a creeping herb of wet disturbed places, ditches, pond margins, and cultivated ground. It can also grow in less saturated soil, so its presence is not limited to standing water. Florida plant-health guidance describes introduced populations in the southeastern United States and notes that stems root at their joints. Both seeds and rooted pieces can contribute to movement, including through garden or aquarium material.

coccinella-septempunctata.summary: The sevenspotted lady beetle is a European aphid predator that became established in North America after repeated introductions and an apparently accidental establishment in New Jersey. It can help suppress aphids in crops and gardens. At the same time, research and long-term observations have raised concerns about changes in native lady-beetle communities where introduced species become abundant. These two roles are compatible: a useful predator can still alter the community around it.

paederia-cruddasiana.summary: Sewer vine is a twining Asian vine that has escaped into Florida vegetation. It can climb over shrubs and other plants, while stems touching the ground root at nodes and create new points of growth. It is closely related to skunkvine, Paederia foetida, and has often been confused with that species. Both the living vine and discarded stem pieces deserve attention when a patch is being managed.

oxalis-exilis.summary: Shady woodsorrel is a small creeping perennial with yellow flowers and three-part leaves. Despite the common name, it also grows in lawns, gardens and disturbed open places. It is native to Australia and New Zealand, where it can be an ordinary part of the local flora. A plant reported elsewhere needs careful identification because several yellow-flowered woodsorrels have very similar foliage, and their native ranges and underground structures differ.

galinsoga-quadriradiata.summary: Shaggy soldier, also called hairy galinsoga, is a short-lived annual weed of vegetable plots, nursery containers and other disturbed ground. Its small daisy-like flowers are easy to overlook, but a plant can begin replenishing the seed supply while it is still modest in size. Repeated attention to young plants is more useful than waiting for a large patch to develop. It is closely related to smallflower galinsoga, which often grows in similar places.

crotalaria-incana.summary: Shakeshake, or fuzzy rattlepod, is an upright herb or small subshrub with yellow flowers and conspicuously hairy seedpods. Botanical accounts record it as naturalized on many Hawaiian islands. Its wider native range includes tropical regions on more than one continent, so the meaning of an occurrence depends on the location. It is one of several plants called rattlebox, a shared name that is not enough to identify the species or choose a pasture-management response.

fraxinus-uhdei.summary: Shamel ash is a large tree planted for shade, timber and landscape use. Native to Mexico and Central America, it has spread beyond plantings in places including Hawaii, where the university's weed-risk guidance advises against introducing it into new areas. Winged seeds allow new trees to appear away from the original planting. An isolated seedling is much easier to address than a mature tree beside a building or among native vegetation.

mimosa-pudica.summary: Sensitive plant is a low, prickly herb whose finely divided leaves fold when disturbed. That familiar movement makes it popular as a novelty plant, but it can also establish in lawns, roadsides and pastures in warm regions. Hawaiian accounts describe extensive naturalization, and Florida's current assessment predicts a high invasion risk. The moving leaves are a useful clue, not proof of identity: other sensitive plants can respond in a similar way.

leucanthemum-x-superbum.summary: Shasta daisy is a garden hybrid grown for large white flower heads with yellow centers. It is related to oxeye daisy, but the two names should not be treated as interchangeable. Different cultivars vary in size and form, and a planted clump is different from a population reproducing beyond a garden. Botanical records describe occasional garden escapes, while local guidance often makes a clearer distinction between this hybrid and the more widely invasive oxeye daisy.

lucilia-cuprina.summary: The sheep blow fly is a metallic fly whose larvae can cause flystrike, a serious skin infestation of sheep. It is especially important in Australian and South African livestock systems; the mix of flies involved in North American cases differs. A green fly near an animal does not establish which species is present. The immediate priority when maggots are found on a living animal is veterinary care, followed by identification and prevention.

alpinia-zerumbet.summary: Shell ginger is a large, clump-forming ornamental grown for arching foliage and hanging flower clusters. It spreads locally through underground rhizomes and is also propagated by dividing them. Its appearance outside a bed deserves attention, but it should not automatically be treated like every invasive ginger. Florida's assessment currently lists this species as not a documented problem across its zones. Conditions and management priorities can differ elsewhere.

capsella-bursa-pastoris.summary: Shepherd's purse is a small annual mustard common in disturbed soil, garden beds and agricultural ground. Many plants begin as a low rosette in cool weather, survive winter and send up flowering stems the following season. The distinctive seedpods explain the common name: they resemble tiny flattened purses or hearts. A few scattered plants are usually a straightforward garden-management issue, while repeated seed production can keep a patch returning.

diolcus-variegatus.summary: This small shield-backed bug was documented as established around Homestead in southern Florida after collections in 2001. The original report linked adults and young bugs to false mallow, Malvastrum corchorifolium, where they fed on the fruits. It was already known from the Caribbean. That history helps explain an identification, but a past collection does not show that the insect is currently present at every nearby site or that it damages unrelated garden plants.

mezium-affine.summary: The shiny spider beetle is a tiny scavenger associated with dry stored materials. Its rounded body and long legs can make it look more like a spider than a beetle. Museum pest specialists recognize it as a potential collection pest, but finding one does not show that a whole collection or pantry is infested. The useful next step is to identify the insect and locate the material it came from.

lyrodus-takanoshimensis.summary: Lyrodus takanoshimensis is a shipworm: a marine clam with a long, soft body that lives inside wood. The small shells at its front end help it excavate a tunnel, while the rest of the animal remains sheltered within the timber. Despite its name and wormlike appearance, it is a bivalve. A damaged piling or piece of driftwood cannot be assigned to this species simply because shipworm tunnels are present. A 2026 study sequenced an identified Japanese specimen; that finding does not confirm a US population.

ardisia-elliptica.summary: Shoebutton ardisia is an evergreen shrub or small tree introduced to Florida as an ornamental. Birds eat its dark fruits and can carry the seeds into nearby vegetation. In invaded Florida habitats, dense growth can crowd the understory and shade other plants. Its behavior there differs from its role in its native Asian range, where it is part of coastal vegetation. Location matters when deciding what an observation means.

erodium-brachycarpum.summary: Shortfruit storksbill is a small annual of disturbed ground, native to parts of the Mediterranean region and Canary Islands. Botanical records list it as introduced in several US states, including California and Oregon. It belongs to a group of similar storksbills whose long fruit beaks are often more useful for identification than their flowers. The common name can be misleading: the complete fruit, including its beak, is not especially short.

hirschfeldia-incana.summary: Shortpod mustard, also called summer mustard, is a branching yellow-flowered plant of roadsides, grasslands and disturbed shrublands. Unlike some annual mustards, it can survive for more than one season. In California, rapid growth and shading can interfere with native vegetation, including in recently burned areas. Cal-IPC rates its regional impact as moderate. Its persistence means that a patch deserves follow-up even after flowering stems have been cut.

phalaris-brachystachys.summary: Shortspike canarygrass is a tufted annual grass with a compact, egg-shaped flower head. It is native to a broad region from Macaronesia and the Mediterranean toward Iran. Several canarygrasses occur outside their native ranges, but they differ greatly in growth form and behavior. This species should not inherit the wetland impacts or rhizome-based management advice often associated with perennial reed canarygrass. Its identification begins with the mature flowering head. A 2016 USDA assessment reports California naturalization while questioning a Texas record.

graphium-euwallaceae.summary: Graphium euwallaceae is a microscopic fungus associated with the polyphagous shothole borer in California. Researchers recovered it from beetles and their tunnels in several tree species, including avocado and California sycamore. It is one member of a beetle-fungus association, not a diagnosis that can be made from a dark mark on bark. The practical concern for a tree owner is recognizing a possible infestation and arranging an appropriate inspection. An independent German greenhouse study confirmed the fungus with morphology and four genetic markers in 2026.

paracremonium-pembeum.summary: Paracremonium pembeum is a fungus associated with the polyphagous shothole borer. Researchers first described it from California beetle tunnels and tested it on cut shoots. A separate Israeli avocado experiment found that it did not persist in living wood as the principal Fusarium associate did, although it remained viable in dead wood. That distinction helps explain why finding a beetle-associated fungus is not the same as proving it caused a tree's decline. An affected tree needs its own diagnosis.

gypsophila-elegans.summary: Annual baby's-breath is a small flowering plant grown in gardens and included in some flower-seed mixtures. It comes from a region extending from southern Ukraine toward northwestern Iran. Its airy white or pink flowers resemble those of other baby's-breath species, but this annual should not be confused with the larger perennial baby's-breath involved in well-known dune invasions. A garden planting and a self-sustaining wild population are also different kinds of records.

crotalaria-spectabilis.summary: Showy rattlebox is an introduced yellow-flowered plant of open fields, roadsides and disturbed agricultural ground in the southeastern United States. It was historically planted for soil improvement, but escaped plants can compete with pasture vegetation. Its greatest practical concern around livestock is toxicity: plant material can remain dangerous after drying and may enter hay or contaminated feed. A flowering patch near a pasture deserves prompt identification and attention.

lespedeza-bicolor.summary: Shrubby lespedeza is an East Asian shrub introduced for purposes including erosion control and wildlife plantings. It can spread beyond those plantings into open ground and woodland edges, where dense growth interferes with other vegetation and young trees. Its woody structure separates it from the smaller bushclovers that may grow nearby. A planting that once served a practical purpose can therefore need attention when seedlings begin appearing in surrounding habitat.

spermacoce-verticillata.summary: Whitehead broom, also called shrubby false buttonweed, is a perennial with small white flower clusters along its stems. It has become troublesome in some south Florida pastures and hayfields, even though UF's broader natural-area assessment does not currently classify it as a documented problem species. Those accounts address different settings. A plant can be difficult to manage in a working pasture without having the same effect in every habitat where it grows. Authorities also disagree about whether it is native to Florida, so that regional status needs separate review.

fuchsia-paniculata.summary: Paniculate fuchsia is a large ornamental shrub or small tree from Mexico and Central America. Instead of the familiar large hanging flowers of many garden fuchsias, it carries sprays of much smaller rosy-purple blooms. Kew lists introductions in places including California and Hawaii. That broad distribution record does not tell us whether a particular plant was cultivated, escaped or forming a persistent wild population, so the setting of an observation matters.

ipomoea-carnea-ssp-fistulosa.summary: Bush morning-glory is a tropical American perennial grown for its large pink flowers. Unlike many familiar morning-glories, it can form a woody shrub, although branches may sprawl or climb. It has escaped cultivation in Florida, where it is prohibited and can occupy both terrestrial and wet settings. Its attractive flowers should not obscure the importance of checking the plant's local status before moving cuttings or adding it to a garden.

senna-siamea.summary: Siamese cassia, or kassod tree, is a yellow-flowered Asian tree planted widely for shade and ornamental use in warm regions. Older records often call it Cassia siamea. It can become a substantial tree with a dense crown, so an occurrence should be described as a planted tree, nearby seedling or wild-growing stand rather than simply marked present. Those distinctions help explain whether the tree is reproducing beyond cultivation at a particular site.

ulmus-pumila.summary: Siberian elm is a fast-growing Asian tree widely planted for its tolerance of difficult conditions. Wind-carried seeds can produce many seedlings along roads, streambanks, grasslands and other open sites. In parts of the United States, these recruits form dense growth that displaces other vegetation. An established shade tree and a spreading population around it present different management decisions, especially where removing a large tree could affect buildings or people.

caragana-arborescens.summary: Siberian peashrub is a hardy Asian shrub or small tree long used in northern windbreaks, hedges and wildlife plantings. It can escape into woodland edges, forests and other habitats beyond those plantings. Its pods release seeds as they ripen, creating new plants around an established hedge. The concern is not simply that a shrub survives a cold winter, but that it begins replacing the vegetation outside the area where it was planted.

scilla-siberica.summary: Siberian squill is a small bulb-forming plant whose blue flowers appear early in spring. It has been planted in lawns and woodland gardens, but can spread beyond them through seeds and new bulbs. Minnesota extension asks people to report populations in unmanaged areas so its wild distribution can be understood more clearly. A blue carpet in a garden and a spreading patch among native spring plants are worth recording differently.

senna-tora.summary: Foetid senna is a yellow-flowered tropical plant often called sicklepod, a name also used for the closely related Senna obtusifolia. The two have a long history of confusion in botanical and agricultural records. For a US observation, resolving that identity is more useful than applying the familiar sicklepod name immediately. Information about the widespread agricultural weed S. obtusifolia should not automatically be attached to S. tora.

viburnum-sieboldii.summary: Siebold viburnum is a large Japanese shrub or small tree planted for its white flowers and colorful fruit. Birds can carry seeds beyond gardens, and escaped plants have formed dense understory growth at some eastern US sites. A Pennsylvania preserve documented long-established plants shading native vegetation. That local history shows why seedlings around an old ornamental planting are worth checking, without implying that every cultivated viburnum behaves identically.

phaseolus-lunatus.summary: Lima bean is a widely cultivated food crop native to tropical America. Depending on the variety and growing conditions, it can form a compact bush or a climbing plant and may persist for more than one season in warm climates. Its presence in a vegetable plot is not evidence of an invasion. An escaped plant becomes a different kind of observation when it reproduces beyond cultivation, especially where vines extend into nearby unmanaged vegetation.

lagascea-mollis.summary: Silkleaf is a small member of the daisy family found in open disturbed ground. Its native range includes much of tropical America, while botanical accounts distinguish introduced populations in places such as Puerto Rico. That geography is important: a weedy appearance does not make the plant nonnative everywhere. The small pale flower clusters and softly hairy leaves are more useful starting points than assuming a regional status from the common name.

grevillea-robusta.summary: Silk oak is an Australian tree with fernlike foliage and orange-yellow flowers. Despite its common name, it is not a true oak. It has been widely planted for shade, timber and reforestation, including in Hawaii, where escaped trees have become a concern in natural forests. Florida's horticultural assessment describes a different regional situation. The surrounding habitat and evidence of seedlings matter more than treating every ornamental silk oak as the same management problem.

neyraudia-reynaudiana.summary: Burma reed is a tall, clump-forming Asian grass that has invaded parts of south Florida, including pine rocklands. Large feathery flower heads release wind-carried seeds, while pieces of its underground stems can travel with soil and construction equipment. Cutting away the tall growth does not necessarily remove the plant: living rhizomes can send up new shoots. Its size and persistence make early attention to small outlying clumps especially useful.

dichanthium-sericeum.summary: Silky bluegrass, also called Queensland bluegrass, is a tufted grass native across parts of the Indo-Pacific and Australia. It includes forms with different life spans, so describing every plant as a long-lived perennial would be misleading. Botanical sources list introductions in several US states. Those records establish a need for careful identification, not proof that this grass has the same impacts as other introduced grasses called bluestem or bluegrass.

hypophthalmichthys-molitrix.summary: Silver carp is a large East Asian fish introduced to the United States for uses including plankton control. Escaped populations have spread through many river systems. These efficient filter feeders can reduce food available to native plankton-eating fish, and startled adults can leap from the water, creating a hazard for boaters. An observation should identify the actual waterbody; a regional map does not mean every nearby lake contains silver carp.

potentilla-argentea.summary: Silver-leaved cinquefoil is a Eurasian perennial recorded across much of temperate North America. Its most useful field clue is the pale, densely hairy underside of the leaves, rather than the small yellow flowers shared with many other cinquefoils. It can occur in open and disturbed places, but the importance of a particular patch depends on the habitat and neighboring vegetation. Identification should come before a decision to remove an unfamiliar cinquefoil.

abies-alba.summary: European silver fir is a large evergreen conifer native to European mountain regions. It is grown as an ornamental and in collections outside that range. Its pale needle undersides explain the silver-fir name, but several North American trees have similar common names and foliage. A planted specimen should not be mistaken for evidence of a spreading wild population. Reports are most useful when they distinguish a labeled landscape tree from seedlings established beyond a planting.

aira-caryophyllea.summary: Common silver-hairgrass is a delicate introduced grass with a loose, airy flowering head. It is recorded in disturbed places, grasslands and woodland edges in New England, and is also widespread in California grasslands. Widespread occurrence does not by itself show severe ecological harm. California's 2006 inventory described its apparent impacts as negligible, a useful reminder to describe the plant's actual local abundance rather than assume that every patch is a major threat.

croton-argenteus.summary: Silver July croton is a small, hairy herb from tropical America. It belongs to the spurge family and is different from the brightly colored ornamental commonly sold as croton. Botanical accounts describe it from disturbed habitats, but its local status needs to be checked against the exact species and place. Several crotons are native in the United States, so confirm an unfamiliar hairy plant before deciding whether it belongs at the site or needs attention.

acacia-dealbata.summary: Silver wattle is an Australian tree planted for its soft-looking foliage and masses of yellow flowers. It has escaped cultivation in California, where land managers remove it from some natural areas. Long-lived seeds and shoots from damaged roots can make an established stand harder to manage than a single small seedling. A roadside planting and a colony spreading into nearby habitat should therefore be recorded separately.

acacia-retinodes.summary: Wirilda is an Australian shrub or small tree grown beyond its native range as an ornamental. Older references used Acacia retinodes for a broader group that now includes separate species, notably Acacia provincialis and Acacia uncifolia. That change matters when interpreting reports of escape: an old nursery name may not identify the plant under today's narrower definition. California introduction records deserve that extra check before claims about spread or harm are attached to them.

cotoneaster-pannosus.summary: Silverleaf cotoneaster is a Chinese ornamental shrub that has escaped into coastal California scrub, grassland and woodland. Birds and other animals carry its abundant fruits away from gardens, allowing seedlings to appear well beyond a hedge. A large shrub can be persistent after cutting, so management needs to include returning shoots and younger plants around it. The name also covers an identification challenge: several cultivated cotoneasters look very similar.

polygonum-argyrocoleon.summary: Silver-sheath knotweed is a small annual herb found in disturbed ground, especially in parts of the southwestern United States. It is not the tall, bamboo-like knotweed that forms large streamside thickets. Its slender flowering shoots and tiny flowers can make it easy to overlook among other weeds. A record should describe the plant and setting directly, without borrowing the much greater impacts or specialized treatment advice associated with Japanese knotweed.

cotoneaster-simonsii.summary: Himalayan cotoneaster is an introduced ornamental shrub recorded along the Pacific coast from British Columbia into California. It grows in places including thickets, forest openings, shorelines and grasslands. Birds can carry its bright fruits from planted shrubs into surrounding vegetation. Overseas weed assessments describe dense stands that interfere with other plants, but a US report should still document the local stand and habitat rather than assume the same impact everywhere.

sparganium-erectum.summary: Exotic bur-reed is an emergent wetland plant that can form dense colonies along shallow water. The name needs particular care: older botanical treatments sometimes included North American broadfruit bur-reed within Sparganium erectum. US identification guidance separates that native relative from the Eurasian plant addressed here. A broad leaf and a round, prickly-looking fruit head are therefore reasons to investigate, not enough evidence to remove a wetland plant.

gamochaeta-simplicicaulis.summary: Simple-stem cudweed is a small woolly herb whose inconspicuous flower clusters can be mistaken for several other cudweeds. Botanical sources place its native range in tropical America and record it beyond that range, including North America. Accurate naming is important because similar plants have often been grouped under older Gnaphalium names. A weed report from a South American crop field does not establish the same impact in a US natural area.

vitex-trifolia.summary: Three-leaf chastetree is an introduced shrub or small tree found in coastal and disturbed habitats in central and southern Florida. It was planted as an ornamental, including forms with variegated foliage. Florida's invasive-plant assessment places it among species increasing in abundance or frequency, rather than treating that category as proof of severe harm at every site. Its scientific name is important because other plants called chastetree or beach vitex have different habits and regional status.

luffa-acutangula.summary: Angled luffa is a climbing vegetable crop also called ridged gourd or Chinese okra. Despite that last name, it is a member of the cucumber family, not the okra plant. Its long fruits have strong lengthwise ribs, unlike smooth luffa grown for similar uses. Florida extension describes it as a cultivated warm-season crop. A plant growing on a trellis is not evidence of harmful spread, although self-sown vines outside a planting are worth documenting.

sirex-noctilio.summary: Sirex woodwasp is an introduced pine-associated insect established in parts of eastern North America. Females place eggs, a wood-decaying fungus and toxic mucus into trees; together these can weaken or kill the host. Stressed or crowded pines are particularly important to watch. Its severe effects in some overseas plantations should not be treated as a prediction for every US forest, but moving infested wood can carry the insect to a new area.

agave-sisalana.summary: Sisal hemp is the large, architectural agave once planted for the strong fibers in its leaves. In warm places, an old planting can keep expanding long after its original purpose has disappeared. New plants form around the parent and on its towering flower stalk, giving this succulent more than one way to persist. Florida sources describe escaped plants in coastal uplands, scrub and pine rockland. A planted specimen is not, by itself, evidence that surrounding natural habitat is invaded.

brachypodium-sylvaticum.summary: Slender false brome is a perennial bunchgrass that can make a woodland floor look freshly green while other grasses have faded. In parts of the Pacific Northwest, that attractive appearance hides a serious management problem: dense patches can replace the varied plants beneath trees and along trails. It also grows in open ground, so shade alone will not keep it contained. Seeds travel with people, animals and equipment, making trail edges and work routes useful places to notice a new patch.

alopecurus-myosuroides.summary: Slender meadow foxtail is better known to cereal growers as black-grass. It is an annual grass whose narrow flower heads can rise above a crop, especially where many plants have established together. In British arable fields it is an important competitor for light, water and nutrients. Its presence in a species catalog does not mean every meadow or American farm has the same problem. The setting matters: a confirmed weed patch in a crop needs a different response from an unidentified grass beside a path.

avena-barbata.summary: Slender oat is an annual wild oat with loose, nodding flower heads that move easily in the breeze. Introduced from Eurasia, it grows in fields, roadsides and other open, disturbed places in western North America. California lists it as an invasive plant, although a pasture, a roadside and a native grassland may have different management priorities. The dry heads are distinctive, but several wild oats occur together, and recognizing this particular species requires a closer look than its overall graceful shape.

thylacodes-vandyensis.summary: This worm-snail is a reminder that a snail does not always carry a neatly coiled shell around with it. Thylacodes vandyensis lives attached to a hard surface inside an irregular tube and feeds with mucus nets extended into the surrounding water. It was described from the artificial reef formed by the sunken USNS General Hoyt S. Vandenberg off the Florida Keys. Researchers considered it a likely non-native arrival, but its original home and wider distribution remained uncertain in the material reviewed.

cyperus-gracilis.summary: Slimjim flatsedge is a small, fine-leaved sedge that can pass for a delicate lawn grass. It is native to eastern Australia and New Caledonia, and has also been cultivated as a ground cover elsewhere. A Hawaiian botanical account records it as sparingly naturalized after planting. That history calls for checking where a plant is growing, rather than treating every tuft as an invasive threat. The reviewed sources describe its botany more clearly than any harmful effects in the United States.

arthraxon-hispidus.summary: Small carpgrass, also called hairy jointgrass or small carpetgrass, is an annual grass introduced from Asia. It can form conspicuous patches along moist edges and other disturbed ground. The spreading growth and numerous seeds make a modest-looking patch worth noticing before it fills more space. Its broad little leaves give it a different texture from many lawn grasses. In a restoration area, the important question is whether a confirmed population is expanding into the vegetation people are trying to protect.

geranium-pusillum.summary: Small geranium is one of the little crane's-bills that can appear among short grass, on open ground and around cultivated places. Its flowers are easy to overlook, while its rounded, divided leaves often attract more attention. It belongs to the true geraniums, rather than the large-flowered bedding plants commonly sold under that name. Several closely related species share this modest appearance. The sources reviewed support careful identification, but they do not justify treating every occurrence as a serious ecological invasion.

pycnoderes-vanduzeei.summary: Pycnoderes vanduzeei is a small plant bug reported from the Caribbean and parts of tropical America, with an established population documented in central and southern Florida. The Florida account identifies dayflower and spiderwort as reported hosts. That is useful information for looking for the insect, but a host record does not tell us how much injury it causes. The common name 'small green plant bug' is too broad to distinguish this species from the many other small bugs a gardener might find.

aethina-tumida.summary: Small hive beetle is a bee-colony pest whose larvae can turn stored pollen and honey into a fermenting, slimy mess. Adults may be present in a hive without causing obvious trouble, so a single beetle is not the same as a damaging larval infestation. The insect is native to sub-Saharan Africa and is established in much of the United States. Beekeepers are most concerned when beetles reproduce in comb that the bees cannot adequately defend, including stored equipment and honey awaiting extraction.

atrichonotus-taeniatulus.summary: Small lucerne weevil is a broad-nosed weevil associated with damage to lucerne, also known as alfalfa, and other pasture plants. Adults feed above ground, while the larvae work around roots below the soil surface. That split life cycle means a few notched leaves may reveal only part of what is happening. Agricultural accounts from Argentina and Western Australia document the insect, but those reports do not establish its presence or importance on an individual American farm.

synanthedon-myopaeformis.summary: Small red-belted clearwing is also called apple clearwing moth, a name that points to its best-known host. The caterpillars live beneath the bark of fruit trees, so their activity can be much less obvious than leaf feeding. The moth occurs in Europe and has been documented in Canadian orchards. Finding an unfamiliar clearwing near an apple tree deserves a careful look, but several other clearwing moths also visit gardens, and a flying adult alone does not establish an orchard infestation.

physokermes-hemicryphus.summary: Small spruce bud scale is a sap-feeding insect that can hide in plain sight on spruce branches. Mature females resemble small brown buds at the base of new growth, so a tree may carry them for some time before anyone recognizes the problem. Feeding produces sticky honeydew that can support black sooty mold. Heavy populations may stunt shoots or damage lower branches, but scattered scales do not automatically mean the tree needs an insecticide treatment. Authorities disagree about whether it is native to North America, so its regional origin should not be assumed from a sighting.

sisymbrium-loeselii.summary: Small tumbleweed mustard is an upright mustard also known as false London-rocket or tall hedge mustard. It is associated with open, disturbed places such as roadsides, rubble and gaps in paving. The name can make it sound interchangeable with other tumble mustards, but it is a separate species and should be identified on its own features. The botanical sources reviewed describe its form and habitat; they do not establish a particular ecological impact at a site in the United States.

lygodium-microphyllum.summary: Small-leaf climbing fern, often called Old World climbing fern, grows in a way that surprises people expecting a fern to stay near the ground. Its long, twining fronds climb over shrubs and into trees, forming blankets of growth. In Florida natural areas, those blankets can smother vegetation and carry fire upward into tree canopies. It spreads by tiny windborne spores as well as continued growth from its underground stems, making isolated new patches especially valuable to report.

tradescantia-fluminensis.summary: Small-leaf spiderwort is a trailing South American perennial that can turn damp, shaded ground into a thick green carpet. Soft stems root wherever their nodes meet the soil, so a broken piece can become a new patch. Garden escapes and dumped clippings are therefore important to prevent. Florida's university assessment identifies invasive behavior in the northern and central parts of the state. The effect of a particular planting still depends on its setting, and a contained houseplant is different from an expanding woodland mat.

ranunculus-parviflorus.summary: Smallflower buttercup is a short annual buttercup with flowers so modest that its leaves and developing fruits may be easier to notice. It is native to the Mediterranean region and has become naturalized elsewhere, including documented sites in Kansas. That record confirms that the species can occur outside cultivation, but it does not show that every population is spreading aggressively or causing ecological harm. Careful identification is particularly useful because several small buttercups share rounded leaves and tiny yellow flowers.

tamarix-parviflora.summary: Smallflower tamarisk is a deciduous shrub or small tree with fine, feathery-looking branches and clouds of pale pink flowers. It has been planted as an ornamental and is included in California's invasive-plant inventory. Tamarisks are often discussed together, but their identities and effects should not be treated as interchangeable. A species-level photograph or a general saltcedar story cannot tell you exactly how this tree is behaving along a particular stream. Local vegetation, water conditions and planting history all matter.

impatiens-parviflora.summary: Smallflower touch-me-not, also called small balsam or small-flowered jewelweed, is an annual plant with little pale yellow flowers. It is native to parts of Asia and has spread widely in Europe, often in shaded habitats. Washington also treats it as a weed of concern. The familiar touch-me-not appearance can be misleading where native jewelweeds grow, so a suspected patch deserves a careful identification before plants are pulled. Small flowers and finely toothed leaves are more useful clues than the common name.

buddleja-madagascariensis.summary: This smokebush is a sprawling shrub from Madagascar, also known as orange buddleia or Madagascar butterfly bush. Its long branches can scramble through surrounding vegetation, and Hawaiian guidance documents it invading mesic to humid forests. It is a different plant from the familiar purple-flowered butterfly bush, and it is also unrelated to the ornamental Cotinus commonly called smokebush. Those shared names make the scientific name especially helpful when checking a nursery plant or reporting an escape.

periplaneta-fuliginosa.summary: Smokybrown cockroach is a large, glossy cockroach often associated with outdoor shelter around buildings. It can live in leaf litter, tree cavities, wood piles and gutters, then turn up in garages, attics or other protected spaces. Adults are capable fliers and are attracted to lights at night. Seeing one indoors is unpleasant, but it does not by itself reveal where the population is living. Finding the shelter and entry route is usually more informative than repeatedly treating the room where one appeared.

bromus-inermis.summary: Smooth brome is a cool-season perennial grass widely planted for hay, pasture and erosion control. Its usefulness in those settings explains why it is so familiar across much of North America. The same ability to form a dense sod can be a problem where it spreads into native grassland. It grows from underground stems as well as seed, so an established patch is more than the visible flowering stems. Management should start with the purpose of the land and the identity of the grass.

hypochaeris-glabra.summary: Smooth cat's ear is a small yellow-flowered herb that can look like a delicate dandelion from a few steps away. It usually grows as an annual, with a low leaf rosette and slender flowering stems. Introduced from Europe, it is recorded in the Washington flora and has naturalized elsewhere. Its presence is not enough to establish a serious ecological problem. The most useful first step is to separate it from rough cat's ear and other yellow-flowered members of the daisy family.

digitaria-ischaemum.summary: Smooth crabgrass is a warm-season annual familiar in lawns, garden edges and other disturbed ground. It grows low and branches near the base, often filling gaps where the intended vegetation is thin. Much of the next season's population comes from seed, which makes preventing seed production and improving cover useful parts of management. It is a turf weed, but its appearance does not mean the surrounding landscape has an ecological emergency. A response can be matched to the size and purpose of the space.

crepis-capillaris.summary: Smooth hawksbeard is a short-lived, yellow-flowered plant that often appears in lawns, roadsides and other open, disturbed places. It begins with a rosette and later sends up branching stems carrying many small flower heads. European in origin, it has naturalized in other regions. Several hawksbeards and cat's-ears share this general look, so identifying it is more useful than treating every small yellow daisy as the same weed. The reviewed floras describe its biology without establishing a universal need for removal.

alternanthera-paronychioides.summary: Smooth joyweed is a low, mat-forming plant with small pale flower clusters tucked close to its leaves. Its native range includes tropical and subtropical America, which makes location essential to understanding an observation in the United States. Kew lists Puerto Rico within its native range and several continental US states as introductions. The name also belongs to a genus containing very different species, so the severe aquatic impacts associated with alligatorweed should not be attached to smooth joyweed without evidence.

crotalaria-pallida.summary: Smooth rattlebox is an upright member of the pea family with leaves divided into three leaflets and clusters of flowers followed by conspicuous pods. It is recorded from disturbed ground, fallow fields and roadsides in the southeastern United States. Some regional accounts identify those plants more narrowly as the variety obovata. That distinction matters when a catalog contains both the species and a variety: they are overlapping taxonomic records, not automatically two separate invaders at the same location.

crotalaria-pallida-var-obovata.summary: This smooth rattlebox record refers specifically to Crotalaria pallida variety obovata, rather than to the species in its broadest sense. It is an erect, short-lived plant found in disturbed ground, and North Carolina's flora assigns its smooth rattlebox populations to this variety. Florida's assessment currently advises preventing escape while reassessment continues. The variety and the broader species can describe the same individual plant, so observations should retain the most precise identification actually supported by the specimen.

sporobolus-indicus.summary: Smutgrass is a tough, perennial bunchgrass often noticed as wiry clumps standing above a pasture or lawn. Florida pasture guidance treats it as an important weed, while botanical sources disagree about the northern limits of its native range. That uncertainty does not prevent managing a damaging pasture population, but it does make a blanket 'foreign invader' label unhelpful. Small smutgrass also needs to be separated from giant smutgrass, a related species with a different scientific name.

sigmoidotropis-speciosa.summary: Snail flower is a twining member of the pea family whose flower shape is more distinctive than its common name. Older references may call it Vigna speciosa or Phaseolus speciosus; these names refer to the same taxonomic lineage now placed in Sigmoidotropis. It is a plant of tropical America, with botanical records describing it as a climbing herb. The reviewed sources establish its identity but do not demonstrate a particular invasive impact in the United States. Other vines sold as snail vine or corkscrew vine may be different species.

achillea-ptarmica.summary: Sneezewort, listed here under the common name sneezeweed, is a perennial Achillea with loose clusters of white flower heads. It is also grown as a garden flower, so a plant beside an old house may have a planting history worth investigating. This is not one of the Helenium species that also carry the name sneezeweed. Shared common names are especially unhelpful when people are looking up a plant's effects or deciding whether it belongs in a meadow.

cerastium-tomentosum.summary: Snow in summer is the silvery, low-growing perennial often planted over the edge of a wall or along a rock garden. Its pale foliage and white flowers can make a bright patch even in a small space. It spreads by runners and has escaped cultivation in some places, including documented records at Sleeping Bear Dunes National Lakeshore. That does not make every maintained planting equally troublesome; climate and nearby habitat influence how readily it expands beyond a garden.

breynia-disticha.summary: Snowbush is a tropical shrub grown mainly for its patterned foliage. Kew now treats Breynia disticha as a synonym of Phyllanthus nivosus. Green, white and sometimes pink-toned leaves can make it look as though the branch tips have been lightly dusted with snow. Despite names such as Hawaiian snowbush, its native range is in the southwestern Pacific, including New Caledonia and Vanuatu. It is widely used ornamentally, and the reviewed sources describe cultivation more clearly than ecological harm. A garden shrub should not be called an invader simply because it appears in this catalog.

rubus-niveus.summary: Snowpeaks raspberry is also known as Mysore or hill raspberry. It is a prickly, sprawling bramble introduced to Hawaii for ornamental and food use, where it can form dense thickets that exclude other plants and make forest access difficult. Birds and mammals can carry the seeds after eating the fruit, while vegetative growth expands established patches. Similar problems are documented in the Galapagos. Those regional impacts are more informative than assuming all raspberries, or every occurrence of this one, behave alike.

bromus-hordeaceus.summary: Soft brome, also called soft chess, is an annual grass introduced from Europe and widespread in many western North American grasslands and disturbed places. Its compact, softly hairy flower heads are a familiar part of spring vegetation. The name covers several subspecies, and different references draw those boundaries differently. A record identified only as Bromus hordeaceus should remain at that level. It should not be silently reassigned to a subspecies simply because that form is common nearby.

bromus-hordeaceus-ssp-divaricatus.summary: This record is for the divaricatus subspecies of soft brome, a narrower identification than the general Bromus hordeaceus entry. Botanical references have used several names for plants in this group, so the original identification and the reference used to make it are worth preserving. A subspecies name helps describe variation within soft brome; it does not by itself establish a distinct local impact or a different control program. The evidence reviewed here is strongest for taxonomy and recognition.

bromus-hordeaceus-ssp-hordeaceus.summary: This is the typical subspecies of soft brome, a name used when a plant has been identified more precisely than Bromus hordeaceus alone. It belongs to a variable grass group whose subspecies can overlap in outward appearance. Current Kew taxonomy recognizes this subspecies, and regional keys distinguish its mature flowering heads. That taxonomic detail is useful for a botanical record, but it should not turn a general soft-brome observation into a confirmed subspecies record without the necessary mature material.

pulvinaria-citricola.summary: Pulvinaria citricola is a soft scale insect whose scientific name has changed as researchers clarified its anatomy. Older references may place it in Takahashia or Saissetia. Those names are useful when tracing a specimen or publication, but they do not make it the same insect as the citrus pest commonly called citricola scale, Coccus pseudomagnoliarum. The material reviewed for this profile is primarily taxonomic, so it supports a careful identification route more strongly than a claim about local damage. This profile follows the 1909 name; a Japanese palace survey separately recorded it on satsuma in 2010.

pulvinaria-urbicola.summary: Urbicola soft scale is a plant-feeding insect with a broad host range, including many unrelated shrubs and trees. It has been documented on tropical islands and in other warm regions, and researchers consider outbreaks potentially damaging. Its cottony egg sacs can be more conspicuous than the females themselves. A white patch on a leaf is still only a clue: several scales and mealybugs look similar, and an exact species name matters before an observation is used to explain a plant's decline.

ruellia-simplex.summary: Softseed wild petunia is more often sold as Mexican petunia or Britton's wild petunia. It is a flowering perennial that has been widely planted because it tolerates many garden conditions. In Florida it can spread into natural areas and form dense stands. Seed-producing plants disperse through capsules, while creeping lateral roots allow established clumps to expand. Even a sterile cultivar can spread vegetatively, so a seedless label does not remove the need to watch the edge of a planting.

zeuxine-strateumatica.summary: Soldier's orchid is a small, ground-growing orchid that can turn up where a much showier flower would seem out of place: a lawn, a shrub border, or even a crack in pavement. Native to Asia, it has naturalized in parts of the southeastern United States and Hawaii. Its ability to occupy disturbed ground makes it worth documenting, but finding one plant does not establish that it is damaging the surrounding habitat. An orchid identification matters before deciding whether to remove it.

pimpinella-saxifraga.summary: Burnet saxifrage is a perennial member of the carrot family, despite a name that suggests a saxifrage. It grows in grassy and disturbed places, where its pale flower clusters can blend into the summer vegetation. University of Minnesota Extension identifies it as an invader of disturbed grasslands and woodlands and notes that abundant seed helps it colonize open ground. That regional concern is useful context, rather than a reason to assume that every white-flowered plant nearby belongs to this species.

sorghum-arundinaceum.summary: This wild sorghum is closely related to the sorghum grown for grain and forage. Some floras recognize Sorghum arundinaceum as a species; others place it within Sorghum bicolor as subsp. verticilliflorum. This account concerns the wild form, rather than every cultivated sorghum plant. Different names on two lists may describe the same plant and should not be counted as two separate findings. An observation should also explain whether the grass was deliberately planted or appeared on its own.

sorghum-bicolor.summary: Sorghum is an important cultivated grass, grown for grain, fodder and other uses. An intentionally planted crop is different from an unwanted volunteer outside the field. The broader species also includes wild forms, some listed separately under names such as Sorghum arundinaceum. This account covers that broader crop-and-wild context without treating the names as additional occurrences. A garden or roadside observation should explain whether the plant was sown, persisted from an earlier crop, or appeared without planting.

stenodiplosis-sorghicola.summary: Sorghum midge is a tiny fly whose larvae feed where a sorghum grain should develop. A flowering field can look promising while damage is beginning inside its flowers; later, affected heads contain empty or poorly developed grains. The vulnerable period is flowering, so the timing of an observation matters more than simply seeing small flies near a crop. Midge pressure can build through successive plantings, and susceptible late crops may face greater risk. This is a crop-monitoring problem that calls for timely, local advice.

prunus-cerasus.summary: Sour cherry is a familiar fruit tree with a second life beyond orchards and gardens. It can produce seedlings outside the planting area and send up suckers that develop into a thicket. That tendency deserves attention near a meadow, woodland edge or other place where a planted tree is meant to stay contained. It does not make every orchard tree an ecological problem. The useful distinction is between a maintained planting and new stems spreading into ground where they were not intended.

eragrostis-plana.summary: South African lovegrass is a dense perennial bunchgrass from southern Africa. Its tough clumps can be easy to overlook among other pasture or roadside grasses, especially before flowering. Botanical accounts describe it as a poor grazing grass and document introductions outside its native range. The Flora of North America records it from waste areas beside livestock lots in South Carolina. Those records are useful leads, but they do not establish that the species is widespread or causing the same problems throughout the United States.

hydrellia-wirthi.summary: The South American rice miner is a small fly whose young feed inside developing rice leaves. Damage may be much easier to notice than the insect itself: leaves emerge with pale scars and may tear, leaving the plants looking ragged. Extension reports documented injury in Louisiana and Texas rice during the early 2000s. Those reports establish a real crop association, while the importance of the insect in any present-day field still needs local assessment. Other rice insects can leave superficially similar marks.

elodea-callitrichoides.summary: South American waterweed is a submerged perennial native to southern South America and introduced in parts of Europe. Its slender leafy stems can resemble other waterweeds closely enough that distribution records have been confused. A U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service review specifically questioned a reported Washington occurrence because it lacked corroboration and could represent another Elodea. A name in a database is therefore not enough to announce that this species is established in a U.S. waterbody.

bipolaris-maydis.summary: Bipolaris maydis is the fungus responsible for southern corn leaf blight. It survives in infected crop material, and spores can move with wind and splashing rain when conditions favor infection. Warm, damp weather helps the disease develop. Its history includes the severe 1970 epidemic associated with a particularly susceptible type of corn, but that history should not be used to predict the outcome of every modern field infection. Hybrid resistance, crop conditions and the particular fungal race all affect the practical risk.

callosobruchus-maculatus.summary: The southern cowpea weevil is a small seed beetle that can turn an apparently sound bag of dried cowpeas into a source of emerging adults. Its young develop inside individual seeds, so the damage often remains hidden until neat round exit holes appear. Infestations can begin on legumes in the field and continue in warm storage. The important setting is therefore a seed lot or pantry, rather than a tree or wooden building. Finding adults near a cupboard should prompt a careful check of stored beans, peas, lentils, and other dried legumes.

nezara-viridula.summary: The southern green stink bug feeds by piercing plant tissue, with developing fruit, pods, and seeds particularly vulnerable. In vegetable gardens and farms, feeding can leave hard discolored spots or misshapen produce. It uses many host plants, and adults can shelter through colder weather before returning to growing crops. The species is established in warm parts of the United States, but a green shield-shaped insect is not automatically this pest. Some similar bugs have different feeding habits, and the crop's condition matters more than the presence of a single wandering adult.

culex-quinquefasciatus.summary: The southern house mosquito is a brown mosquito whose larvae develop in standing water, often where organic material has accumulated. Around homes, overlooked containers, catch basins, and poorly sealed septic systems can provide breeding sites. Females feed at night on birds and mammals; males feed on plant sugars. This species can transmit West Nile and St. Louis encephalitis viruses, although seeing a mosquito does not establish that it carries either virus. Local mosquito surveillance is the useful guide to current activity and response.

wahlenbergia-marginata.summary: Southern rockbell is a slender bellflower that can be easy to miss until its small blue flowers rise above nearby grass. Botanical accounts describe it as a perennial, with much of its foliage concentrated close to the ground. It occurs in open or disturbed settings, and Hawaiian collections document naturalized plants. A plant growing beside a trail is not, by itself, evidence of serious ecological damage. This entry is best used to recognize and document the species while local status and management needs are checked.

meloidogyne-incognita.summary: Southern root-knot nematode is a microscopic plant parasite that feeds inside roots. It belongs to a group capable of damaging many vegetables, field crops, and ornamentals. Infested plants may grow unevenly, yellow, or wilt despite adequate soil moisture because their damaged roots cannot supply the shoots normally. These aboveground signs resemble several other problems, including nutrient shortages and root disease. The useful first step is to examine roots and obtain a diagnosis, rather than assume that every weak patch needs more fertilizer or water.

pterygoplichthys-anisitsi.summary: Southern sailfin catfish, also called Parana sailfin catfish, is a South American armored catfish sold in the aquarium trade under names such as snow-king plecostomus. Its natural range includes the Paraguay and middle Parana river systems. Eschmeyer's current fish catalog treats Pterygoplichthys anisitsi as a synonym of P. ambrosettii; older references retain anisitsi. USGS records nonnative collections in Florida and Texas, but a collection record does not establish that a population still survives at that place. Aquarium names can also cover more than one species. A large armored fish seen in a local waterway therefore needs a careful identification before a species-level report is accepted.

emex-australis.summary: Southern threecornerjack is a sprawling annual with hard, three-spined fruits that can catch on footwear, tires, and animals. It is also called doublegee or spiny emex; some current authorities use the name Rumex hypogaeus. Native to southern Africa, it is a troublesome crop and pasture weed in parts of Australia. Those regional accounts explain its spread and recognition, but they do not establish its current status in a particular American county. The woody fruits are the feature most likely to bring an overlooked plant to someone's attention.

aphis-glycines.summary: Soybean aphid is a sap-feeding insect whose numbers can change quickly during the growing season. It spends winter as eggs on buckthorn, then moves to soybean, where many generations can develop without mating. Feeding colonies can weaken plants and leave sticky honeydew that supports sooty mold. Outbreaks vary considerably among fields and years, so finding a few aphids does not mean a damaging infestation is inevitable. Regular field scouting gives a much better basis for action than the first insect seen on a leaf.

phakopsora-meibomiae.summary: This entry concerns Phakopsora meibomiae, one of two fungi called soybean rust. It is generally the milder pathogen and must not be confused with Phakopsora pachyrhizi, the more damaging Asian soybean rust fungus. Both infect living plant tissue, and their similar appearance makes the common disease name insufficient for identification. Sources describe P. meibomiae from the Americas, including Puerto Rico. That history should not be converted into a claim that it occurs in every soybean-growing region or causes the losses associated with its better-known relative.

centella-asiatica.summary: Spadeleaf, often called gotu kola, is a creeping perennial in the carrot family. Its stems can root as they extend, creating low patches of rounded leaves. The name needs particular care in North America: some references place American Centella erecta within Centella asiatica, while other treatments distinguish the plants. Kew gives C. asiatica an Old World and western Pacific native range. This disagreement means that a familiar lawn or wet-ground plant should not be declared introduced or invasive from the catalog name alone.

merremia-tuberosa.summary: Spanish arborvine is a vigorous climbing plant also known as wood rose. Older references use Merremia tuberosa, while recent Florida assessments call it Distimake tuberosus. Its yellow flowers and decorative dried fruits helped carry it into gardens and floral arrangements. In Hawaii, officials describe an aggressive vine that can cover and smother other vegetation. Florida's assessment also identifies a high invasion risk. Those concerns are tied to warm regions where it can persist; they should not be treated as evidence that every planted vine has escaped.

spartium-junceum.summary: Spanish broom is a woody shrub with upright green shoots and bright yellow flowers. Introduced as an ornamental, it can form dense stands on disturbed ground and compete with other vegetation. Its long-lived seed bank makes an established patch a continuing management task, even after the mature shrubs are gone. It is one of several plants called broom, and their appearances and local requirements differ. A careful identification is particularly useful where Spanish broom is uncommon but other broom species are widespread.

mimusops-elengi.summary: Spanish cherry is a tropical evergreen tree also called tanjong or bullet wood. Despite its English name, it belongs to the sapodilla family rather than the cherry genus Prunus. It is planted for a rounded crown, dense foliage, and strongly fragrant small flowers. Singapore's botanical records describe it as a familiar roadside tree, while regional Asian floras document native populations. These uses and records explain why it may appear in collections or warm-climate gardens; they do not establish an invasive impact in the United States.

erica-lusitanica.summary: Spanish heath is a tall evergreen shrub that escaped ornamental planting in parts of the Pacific coast. Its fine foliage and masses of pale flowers can make it resemble a large garden heather, but it can develop dense stands in suitable moist, acidic settings. Oregon and California agencies document concern along roadsides, rights of way, and other open habitats. The plant produces many tiny seeds, so preventing new colonies is an important part of management. Regional reports should not be read as a nationwide distribution map.

melicoccus-bijugatus.summary: Spanish lime, also called genip, quenepa, or mamoncillo, is a tropical fruit tree in the soapberry family. It is related to lychee and longan rather than citrus. Native to northern South America, it has a long history of cultivation around the Caribbean and in southern Florida. A Virgin Islands flora also records naturalized plants. This combination of cultivation and escape makes site context important: an orchard tree, an old homestead planting, and a self-sown tree in surrounding vegetation should not be recorded as the same kind of occurrence.

lindernia-antipoda.summary: Sparrow false pimpernel is a small creeping herb associated with moist ground, stream margins, and other wet places. Asian botanical accounts describe slender stems that branch near the base and can root at lower nodes. Its flowers are modest enough that a patch may first be noticed as low green growth between taller plants. The species occurs naturally across parts of Asia and Australia. Its presence in a global plant catalog does not establish a harmful invasion or a current local record in the United States.

sweet-potato-chlorotic-stunt-virus.summary: Sweet potato chlorotic stunt virus, abbreviated SPCSV, infects sweetpotato and can travel in planting material as well as through whitefly feeding. An infected vine may show only mild symptoms, yet the virus can contribute to much more serious disease when another sweetpotato virus is present. The combination with sweet potato feathery mottle virus is known as sweetpotato virus disease. This distinction matters: a mild-looking source plant is not necessarily suitable for producing clean slips, and the severity of a mixed infection should not be attributed to SPCSV alone.

atriplex-patula.summary: Spear saltbush, also known as spreading atriplex or spearscale orache, is an annual of fields and disturbed ground. Despite its name, it is not a woody saltbush shrub. Regional botanical treatments record it as introduced in New England, where it can occur in human-disturbed habitats. Its relationship to similar oraches makes identification more demanding than the common name suggests. In particular, not every spear-shaped leaf beside a road belongs to this species, and occurrence alone is not a measure of ecological impact.

mentha-spicata.summary: Spearmint is a familiar aromatic garden herb that spreads by underground stems and can root where stems touch moist soil. A small planting can therefore become a broad patch without relying entirely on seed. Botanical records document naturalized plants in damp places such as ditches and water margins. The same growth that makes it useful in a kitchen garden can make it difficult to keep within a border. A cultivated clump and an escaped population should still be distinguished when reporting its occurrence.

caiman-crocodilus.summary: The spectacled caiman is a crocodilian native to Central and South America and established in parts of southeastern Florida. It is associated especially with freshwater canals and lakes. Florida managers work to detect and remove nonnative caimans while protecting native alligators and American crocodiles, which can be confused with them. A sighting therefore calls for a clear location and professional identification. It does not call for approaching the animal, and a small individual should not be assumed to be harmless.

sphaeropsis-sapinea.summary: Sphaeropsis blight is a pine disease often described in extension literature as Diplodia tip or shoot blight. The fungus has appeared under several names, including Sphaeropsis sapinea and Diplodia pinea. It can persist in apparently healthy tissue as well as dead material, with damage becoming more conspicuous after drought, hail, or other stress. Austrian, Scots, and red pines are among familiar susceptible hosts. A brown branch tip is a reason to investigate, but not proof of this fungus: insects, weather injury, and other diseases can produce similar dieback.

gynandropsis-gynandra.summary: Spiderwisp is an annual herb with conspicuous projecting flower parts that give its flower clusters a loose, whiskery appearance. Botanical references also call it Cleome gynandra, and Kew currently treats Gynandropsis gynandra as a synonym of that name. It occurs widely in tropical regions and has a history of cultivation as well as spontaneous growth. Name changes can scatter records between databases, so an older label is useful evidence rather than something to discard. These botanical records do not establish a damaging invasive population at a particular American site.

pomacea-diffusa.summary: The spike-topped applesnail is a South American freshwater snail familiar in the aquarium trade. It was formerly treated as Pomacea bridgesii diffusa, and aquarium labels may still confuse it with Pomacea bridgesii or simply call it a mystery snail. USGS records nonnative collections in the United States, but individual records vary in age and do not demonstrate that every reported population remains established. The distinctions among apple snails matter because their feeding behavior and impacts differ. Claims about a destructive apple-snail species should not be transferred to this one by common name. A New Zealand study independently identified a wild specimen and aquarium specimens using DNA; its single river find did not prove establishment.

tragus-berteronianus.summary: Spiked bur grass is a small annual grass whose flowering head carries tiny hooked structures. These can attach to fur or clothing, helping move the plant's reproductive parts beyond the original patch. Regional African flora records describe it on sandy ground and in open sunny settings, with stems sometimes spreading near the base before turning upward. Its short stature can make it easy to overlook among taller grasses. A specimen-based record is useful for identification, but it is not evidence that the species causes a particular level of harm in an American landscape.

veronica-spicata.summary: Spiked speedwell is an herbaceous perennial widely grown for upright spikes of small flowers. It is quite different in appearance from the low, creeping speedwells that can appear as lawn weeds. Garden selections vary in flower color and height, and many plants offered under the broader name Veronica are cultivars or hybrids. A flowerbed label is therefore useful context, but it does not prove that a nearby self-sown plant belongs to the same species. The sources reviewed here support recognition and cultivation, rather than a general claim of invasive harm.

pomacea-bridgesii.summary: The name spiketop apple snail is often used loosely in the aquarium trade. This entry is specifically for Pomacea bridgesii, a name that has frequently been applied to the separate species Pomacea diffusa. A US Fish and Wildlife screening document highlights that confusion and cautions that trade identifications can be unreliable. The practical consequence is simple: a purchased mystery snail is not a verified record of this species. Occurrence reports and impact descriptions need their scientific identity checked before they are combined.

spinacia-oleracea.summary: Spinach is the familiar cool-season leafy crop, Spinacia oleracea. It is grown for foliage and responds to increasing heat and day length by sending up flowering stems, a process gardeners call bolting. That change can make an abandoned crop look quite unlike the low leafy plant sold in markets. Cultivation is the central context for this entry: finding spinach in a garden or agricultural record does not establish an invasive problem. Volunteer seedlings and plants persisting outside a crop should be documented separately from deliberate plantings.

oceanaspidiotus-spinosus.summary: Spined scale insect is an armored scale found on a broad range of plants. A New Zealand study documented it on kiwifruit and noted other hosts including avocado, citrus, and several fruit crops. That study did not describe it as a major pest of all those hosts, although its presence could matter for movement of produce. This distinction is important: a host record identifies a plant the insect can use, not a guarantee of serious damage. Local identification and plant condition should guide any response.

amaranthus-spinosus.summary: Spiny amaranth is an annual pigweed that can grow in fields, gardens, pastures, and disturbed ground. Its sharp stem spines make it particularly unpleasant to encounter while weeding or moving through a mature patch. Like other annual pigweeds, it reproduces by seed, so plants left to mature can add to future weed problems. It also resembles several other amaranths that require different management decisions. Confirming the species is useful before treating a crop infestation or interpreting a report of a resistant pigweed.

xanthium-spinosum.summary: Spiny cocklebur is a branching annual with two different kinds of prickly structures: sharp spines on the stems and hooked burrs enclosing the seeds. It grows in disturbed places including fields, farmyards, floodplains, and water margins. Burrs can tangle in animal coats or wool and move with people and equipment. Washington's weed program also warns that seeds and very young seedlings can poison livestock. The practical concern is to prevent exposure and spread, while confirming the plant rather than relying on the word cocklebur alone.

carduus-acanthoides.summary: Spiny plumeless thistle is a biennial that begins as a low rosette and later sends up a tall, branching flowering stem. It favors disturbed ground, pastures, fields, and road margins. Dense infestations can replace desirable forage and make grazing difficult. The plant is introduced from Europe and temperate Asia, but the response to a sighting should reflect local conditions and rules. Native thistles also provide wildlife habitat, so identifying the plant before removing a whole patch is especially important.

sonchus-asper.summary: Spiny sowthistle is an annual weed that can move quickly from a low leaf rosette to a flowering stem. It is common in disturbed ground, gardens, roadsides, and agricultural settings. Yellow flower heads eventually become small white seed heads, allowing the fruits to travel on air currents. Its prickly leaves account for the thistle name, but it belongs to a different group from the purple-flowered true thistles. The useful management window is before seed release, especially where several generations or repeated flushes can appear in mild weather.

emex-spinosa.summary: Spiny threecornerjack is a prickly-fruited herb also known as lesser jack and, in newer botanical treatments, Rumex spinosus. It originates from the Mediterranean region and is recorded as an introduced plant in several parts of Australia. Its hard fruits can be troublesome in pasture and cultivation. It should be kept separate from southern threecornerjack, Emex australis, which is now often called Rumex hypogaeus. Similar common names can hide meaningful differences in fruit size, growth habit, and the interpretation of older records.

daphnia-lumholtzi.summary: This waterflea is a tiny freshwater crustacean, not a biting flea. Daphnia lumholtzi has become established in many United States waters after originating in warmer regions of Africa, Asia, and Australia. Its conspicuous spines can make it harder for some young fish to eat, potentially changing food-web relationships. Studies do not all find the same degree of impact, so local effects should not be overstated. The common name spiny waterflea is also used for other crustaceans, making the scientific name essential when comparing reports.

ranunculus-muricatus.summary: Spinyfruit buttercup is an annual buttercup whose most useful identifying feature appears after the yellow flowers fade. Its fruits have conspicuous projections, unlike the smoother fruits of many similar buttercups. Floristic accounts record it in damp disturbed places, cropland, and sometimes water margins, including naturalized occurrences outside its original range. The flowers can blend into a mixed patch of small yellow weeds. A record should therefore include mature fruits whenever possible, and should not be assigned from flower color alone.

costus-pulverulentus.summary: Spiral ginger is a tropical perennial grown for its leafy stems and bright flower heads. Costus pulverulentus belongs to the spiral-ginger family and develops from rhizomes. Botanical garden sources place its native range in Mexico, Central America, and South America. The name spiral ginger is shared with other Costus species, so a nursery name alone is not enough for an exact record. In Singapore the species is described as cultivated, a useful reminder that a plant collection entry is not the same as evidence of naturalization.

eryngium-foetidum.summary: Spiritweed is better known in many gardens as culantro or sawtooth coriander. It is a tropical American herb in the carrot family, grown in other warm regions and capable of seeding itself. Its long, sharply toothed leaves look quite unlike the finely divided foliage of common coriander. That distinction is useful when interpreting planting records, because several unrelated herbs share coriander-based common names. Cultivation and self-seeding explain how it can appear around gardens, but they do not establish a damaging invasive population at every location.
