amaranthus-dubius.summary: Spleen amaranth is an annual herb native to Mexico and tropical America. It has been grown and moved beyond that range, and regional floras also record it as a weed of disturbed places. The name is less familiar than the plant's resemblance to other pigweeds, which can make reports uncertain. It is particularly similar in overall form to spiny amaranth, but lacks that species' paired stem spines. Its occurrence in a cultivated or disturbed setting should not automatically be treated as evidence of harmful invasion.

galeopsis-bifida.summary: Splitlip hempnettle is an annual mint-family plant recorded in fields, meadows, and disturbed ground in northern North America. It is closely related to common or brittle-stemmed hempnettle, Galeopsis tetrahit, and older records sometimes combine them. The common name refers to the shape of the flower's lower lip rather than to a nettle sting. Because the two species are so similar without flowers, a summer photograph can be much more informative than a spring seedling or an autumn stem.

lymantria-dispar.summary: Spongy moth is a forest insect whose caterpillars can strip leaves from trees during outbreaks. Oaks and many other woody plants can be affected, and repeated defoliation adds stress to trees already coping with drought or other injury. The established European form in much of the eastern United States has one generation each year. Egg masses survive the winter on bark and many outdoor objects, creating a route for people to move the insect. Older sources use the former common name gypsy moth.

macrognathus-siamensis.summary: Spotfin spiny eel is an elongated freshwater fish also sold as a peacock eel. It comes from Southeast Asian river systems, including the Mekong and Chao Phraya basins. Despite its eel-like shape, its small dorsal spines and extended snout distinguish it from familiar true eels. USGS lists nonnative collections in Florida, but a collection is not proof of a widespread or self-sustaining population. Aquarium trade names are also variable, so reports should retain photographs and the scientific name used by the identifier. Thai researchers have also studied captive spawning and nursery rearing of this species.

therioaphis-trifolii.summary: Spotted alfalfa aphid is a small sap-feeding insect that can damage susceptible alfalfa, especially young plants. Feeding introduces substances that stunt growth, and honeydew can leave foliage sticky and support dark fungal growth. Resistant cultivars and natural enemies have made a substantial difference in management, but resistance is not a reason to stop scouting. This profile concerns the alfalfa-feeding form commonly treated as Therioaphis trifolii maculata; EPPO and some crop guides use Therioaphis maculata. The broader T. trifolii name also covers other host-associated forms.

lamium-maculatum.summary: Spotted henbit is more often called spotted deadnettle, a low perennial groundcover grown for patterned leaves and small flowers. Its trailing stems can root where they contact the soil, allowing a planting to widen beyond its original edge. It favors shaded garden settings and can persist around old plantings. Regional advice varies: Maryland extension has recorded some spread into natural areas and advises caution, while other horticultural sources emphasize garden use. That difference calls for local judgment rather than a blanket claim that every patch is invasive.

centaurea-stoebe.summary: Spotted knapweed is a taprooted perennial or biennial that can spread from roads, gravel areas, and field margins into grasslands and other open habitats. Dense patches compete with desirable plants and reduce the value of pasture. The name refers to dark markings on the bracts beneath each flower head, not spots on the petals. North American sources have used several scientific names for this plant, including Centaurea maculosa and C. biebersteinii. Records under those names need interpretation rather than automatic counting as different species.

centaurea-stoebe-ssp-micranthos.summary: Spotted knapweed is a persistent plant of open disturbed ground and grasslands in North American management accounts. The name Centaurea stoebe subsp. micranthos is still used in older guides; Kew and the updated California assessment place it under C. stoebe subsp. australis. These accounts describe the same subspecies under different names. A record identified only as Centaurea stoebe still needs its original determination checked before it is assigned to this subspecies.

spotted-lanternfly.summary: Spotted lanternfly is a sap-feeding planthopper introduced from Asia. It can gather in large numbers on woody plants, producing sticky honeydew that supports sooty mold and creates a nuisance beneath infested trees. Grapevines are a particularly important crop concern. Research-based guidance distinguishes that damage from the more limited effects often seen on established landscape trees. The insect is also an efficient hitchhiker: eggs laid on outdoor objects can move long distances with vehicles, equipment, and household goods.

limax-maximus.summary: The spotted leopard slug is a large land slug with a pale gray-brown body patterned in darker spots and bands. It occurs in human-modified settings and has been introduced beyond its original range, including California. The striking pattern makes it memorable, but a slug's presence does not establish that it caused nearby plant damage. Species differ in their habits, and native slugs can share the same garden or woodland edge. Identification and a direct look at feeding are more useful than treating every slug as the same pest.

impatiens-balsamina.summary: Spotted snapweed is the garden plant usually called garden balsam or rose balsam. It is an annual grown for colorful flowers that sit close to the stem, followed by capsules that scatter seed when ripe. It can naturalize in disturbed places, but it must not be confused with Himalayan balsam, Impatiens glandulifera, a different species with a different invasion history. Florida's assessment currently does not consider garden balsam a problem species there. That regional conclusion is useful context, not a guarantee about every climate or site.

tilapia-mariae.summary: Spotted tilapia is an African cichlid established in Florida and associated with introductions through the ornamental-fish trade. Newer references often call it Pelmatolapia mariae, while older records and this catalog use Tilapia mariae. It inhabits a range of freshwater settings, including canals, ditches, rivers, and lakes. Reports from outside Florida vary in certainty, and some historical records have been questioned because of misidentification. A fish sold as tilapia or observed in a warm spring should therefore not be assigned to this species without supporting evidence.

drosophila-suzukii.summary: Spotted-wing drosophila is a small vinegar fly that can infest ripening soft fruit while it still looks suitable for harvest. Females use a serrated egg-laying structure to cut into thin fruit skins, allowing larvae to develop inside berries and other susceptible fruit. That ability distinguishes it from many familiar fruit flies associated mainly with damaged or overripe produce. Damage may become apparent only after picking, when apparently sound fruit softens. Frequent harvest and prompt handling are therefore important alongside monitoring in the planting.

stictocardia-tiliifolia.summary: Spottedheart is a tropical climbing plant in the morning-glory family, with broad, heart-shaped leaves and large funnel-shaped flowers. It can grow as a substantial woody creeper in coastal thickets and forest margins. The name is a useful reminder to examine the tiny dark glands beneath its leaves. Floras document this plant across tropical regions, but those records do not establish that a particular American planting is invasive or that a nearby wild vine belongs to this species.

urochloa-reptans.summary: Sprawling signalgrass is a low, branching grass whose stems can lie along the ground and root at their lower joints. Botanical accounts place its native range from the Arabian Peninsula through parts of Asia to the Pacific and record introductions elsewhere in the tropics. It is associated with roadsides and disturbed ground. Finding it in a weedy patch is useful information, but neither a tropical distribution map nor a species-list entry demonstrates serious ecological damage at a particular United States site.

torilis-arvensis.summary: Spreading hedgeparsley is an upright herb in the carrot family that can turn a walk through grass or woodland edges into a session of picking burrs from clothing. Its small fruits carry gripping bristles, allowing animals and people to move seed beyond the original patch. It is an introduced weed in parts of the United States, with invasive-management guidance in California and Wisconsin. Its delicate white flowers can blend into other roadside plants, making fruiting material especially useful for confirmation.

erysimum-repandum.summary: Spreading wallflower, also called bushy wallflower, is a small cool-season mustard found in fields, pasture, turf, and other disturbed ground. It grows upright and produces pale yellow flowers followed by long, narrow seedpods. Agricultural identification guides describe it as a winter annual weed, so its timing can overlap a winter grain crop or newly established turf. Kew and the New England flora identify it as a Eurasian plant introduced to North America. Its presence in a field does not by itself show that it is causing a serious local problem.

chloris-divaricata.summary: Spreading windmill grass is also known as slender chloris, a name that suits its fine leaves and delicate, radiating seed heads. Australian floras describe a perennial grass growing in loose tufts, sometimes with short runners, and occurring on varied soils including periodically flooded ground. Its native status in Australia is well supported. That does not answer whether a United States observation represents an established introduction, a planted specimen, or a misidentified windmill grass, and its effects in the surrounding habitat need a local assessment.

asparagus-aethiopicus.summary: Sprenger's asparagus fern is a flowering plant, despite the fern-like appearance of its soft green sprays. This South African ornamental has escaped gardens in Florida, where birds carry its red fruits into surrounding vegetation. Its persistent below-ground growth makes an established patch harder to remove than the airy stems suggest. Florida's assessment distinguishes regions: it recommends caution in the north and identifies the plant as invasive in central and southern Florida. Those findings should not be extended automatically to every climate.

draba-verna.summary: Spring draba is a tiny, early-flowering member of the mustard family, often noticed as a dusting of white flowers over thin turf or disturbed soil. Also called spring whitlowgrass, it is not a grass. It can emerge in fall or early spring and finish its short life cycle before many taller plants become conspicuous. Its abundance can look alarming, but Ontario's crop guide reports no yield impact even in cereal fields where it occurs. Local growing conditions and the planting's purpose matter.

schizaphis-graminum.summary: The spring green aphid is usually called greenbug in crop-management guides. It feeds on grasses, including wheat and sorghum, and its saliva can injure leaves beyond the tiny puncture made while feeding. Colonies may produce patches of yellowing or reddish plants, and the aphid can transmit barley yellow dwarf virus. Damage depends on the crop, plant stage, weather, and natural enemies; seeing a few green aphids does not by itself establish that treatment is needed.

carp-sprivivirus.summary: Spring viraemia of carp is a contagious viral disease affecting carp and certain other freshwater fish. Koi and common carp are especially relevant to pond owners, but apparently healthy fish can also carry the virus. Outbreaks often occur as water warms in spring. The older name Carp sprivivirus is now linked to the species Sprivivirus cyprinus; disease guidance commonly calls it spring viremia of carp virus. Keep these names together in health records so a name change is not mistaken for a separate disease.

elatobium-abietinum.summary: Spruce aphid, often called green spruce aphid, is a small sap-feeding insect associated mainly with spruce trees. Its feeding can cause older needles to yellow, brown, and fall, sometimes leaving a tree with the current year's needles while older growth looks thin. Damage can be particularly noticeable after spring feeding and may be concentrated low in the crown. Similar-looking needle loss has other causes, so a sparse spruce should be examined for insects before anyone attributes the problem to this aphid.

euphorbia-esula-ssp-tommasiniana.summary: The name Euphorbia esula subsp. tommasiniana has been used for different plants. In a narrow treatment, it refers to Euphorbia tommasiniana, a perennial native to northeastern Italy. Broader leafy-spurge accounts have also applied the name to plants now treated as Euphorbia saratoi. A 2026 herbarium review in central Italy reassigned historical tommasiniana specimens to saratoi, illustrating why the original specimen matters. Older North American records need the same care: their name alone does not establish which spurge was present or which invasive-species guidance applies.

myllocerus-undatus.summary: Sri Lankan weevil is a small, pale, mottled beetle that chews leaves on many ornamental and food plants. It appears under the older name Myllocerus undatus and the subspecies name M. undecimpustulatus undatus. A recent study of Sri Lankan museum specimens explicitly links the names and provisionally retains the subspecies rank while further comparisons are needed. Leaf notches may draw attention to feeding, but they do not identify the beetle. Look for the insect itself before deciding how to respond.

stachys-arvensis.summary: Staggerweed is a small annual in the mint family, also known as field woundwort. Its weak stems and pale flowers can make it easy to overlook among other winter and spring weeds. Floras record it in cultivated ground, roadsides, and disturbed places outside its European native range. The common name has been associated with suspected livestock illness in Australian accounts, but that is not a diagnosis for an animal or proof that every local patch presents the same risk.

jasminum-multiflorum.summary: Star jasmine in this entry means Jasminum multiflorum, a climbing or sprawling shrub also called downy jasmine. It is grown for clusters of white, star-shaped flowers and has soft hairs on its young growth. Common names are a trap here because several unrelated ornamentals are sold as star jasmine. The reviewed Florida assessment describes this species as low invasion risk and not currently documented as a problem species there. A healthy garden planting should be evaluated in that regional context before any removal is considered.

ornithogalum-umbellatum.summary: Star of Bethlehem is a spring-flowering bulb that can persist and multiply in lawns and garden beds long after the original planting is forgotten. New bulbs form around the old ones, so a small tuft can become a scattered colony. Its leaves disappear for much of the year, making an apparently cleared site deceptive. Maryland extension identifies it as an escaped ornamental weed and emphasizes removing the underground bulbs, not merely cutting the leaves that happen to be visible in spring.

cynodon-plectostachyus.summary: Stargrass is a name used for several closely related tropical forage grasses, and Cynodon plectostachyus has a particularly confusing history in agricultural literature. A specialist forage account warns that many older records under this name actually concern other Cynodon species. The plant intended here is a perennial with spreading above-ground runners and upright flowering shoots. A field planted for forage, an escaped patch, and a different grass carrying the same common name need to be distinguished before ecological or livestock claims are attached.

nitellopsis-obtusa.summary: Starry stonewort is a large, plant-like green alga that can form dense underwater growth in lakes and other quiet waters. It has stems and branchlets to the eye, but it lacks the vascular system of a true flowering plant. Introduced North American populations can interfere with recreation and compete with other aquatic vegetation. Small fragments and reproductive bulbils can travel on boats and equipment, making prevention especially important. A tangled mass of green growth, however, is not enough to identify it.

vinsonia-stellifera.summary: Stellate scale is a tiny sap-feeding insect whose wax covering can look surprisingly like a miniature starfish on a leaf. The catalog uses Vinsonia stellifera, while current taxonomic sources also place it under Ceroplastes stellifer. It has been recorded from numerous tropical and subtropical host plants. Heavy scale feeding can weaken plants, but a single waxy spot should be identified before it is treated as a damaging infestation. The host plant and location are important parts of that identification.

puccinia-graminis.summary: Stem rust is a fungal disease of grasses, including important cereal crops. The species Puccinia graminis contains host-specialized forms, so a wheat stem-rust account does not mean every strain attacks every grass. In susceptible crops, infection can interfere with grain filling and weaken stems. Windborne spores allow disease to arrive from distant fields, while weather and cultivar resistance strongly influence its progress. This is a crop-disease identification problem rather than something that can be judged from a weed's presence alone.

erodium-stephanianum.summary: Stephen's stork's bill is a small herb in the geranium family with divided leaves and the long, beaked fruits that give stork's bills their name. Botanical sources describe it from Asia and record occasional introductions elsewhere, including sites associated with imported grain. An isolated introduced plant is not the same as a spreading ecological threat. A useful record includes the habitat, nearby planting or grain handling, and mature material that lets a botanist distinguish it from other stork's bills.

clerodendrum-chinense.summary: Stickbush, also called glory tree or Chinese glory bower, is a shrub grown for dense clusters of fragrant white to pale pink flowers. Double-flowered garden forms can look like little bouquets of roses. It spreads strongly through root suckers and can form thickets in warm, moist regions. This behavior has caused problems in parts of the Pacific and Caribbean. Florida's botanical account explicitly says comparable negative impacts have not yet been documented there, an important limit on how broadly the plant should be described.

cerastium-glomeratum.summary: Sticky chickweed is a small annual that can form low patches in lawns, beds, fields, and disturbed ground. Its pale, hairy foliage and small white flowers often appear during the cooler part of the growing season. It spreads by seed rather than by the persistent growth of a perennial mouse-ear chickweed. That difference matters when planning control: preventing another seed crop is more useful than assuming every chickweed patch has the same life cycle or underground structure.

solanum-sisymbriifolium.summary: Sticky nightshade is a conspicuously prickly herb from South America that may grow as an annual or short-lived perennial. It has deeply cut leaves, pale star-shaped flowers, and red ripe berries. Records outside its native range include disturbed ground and sites associated with imported grain; it has also been cultivated for particular agricultural uses. Those different settings matter. A documented roadside occurrence does not establish widespread ecological harm, and a planted crop should not be mistaken for an unmanaged invasion.

senecio-viscosus.summary: Sticky ragwort, also known as sticky groundsel, is a small annual or occasionally biennial herb found on disturbed, often sandy or gravelly ground. Its glandular hairs make stems, leaves, and flower stalks feel sticky, and the plant can have a noticeable odor. It is distinct from the larger tansy ragwort despite the shared common name. Botanical accounts document an introduced Eurasian weed in parts of North America, but the evidence reviewed here does not establish severe impact or a special control requirement at every site.

ageratina-adenophora.summary: Sticky snakeroot is more widely known in weed-management guides as Crofton weed. It is a shrubby perennial from Mexico and Central America that can form dense growth along moist forest edges, drainage lines, and disturbed sites. Australian agencies document substantial pasture and environmental problems, and Florida's assessment lists it as prohibited there. Regional legal status and observed impacts should still be checked locally. Its white flower clusters can resemble several other members of the aster family, including native plants.

urtica-dioica-ssp-dioica.summary: This entry concerns European stinging nettle, Urtica dioica subsp. dioica, not every nettle growing in North America. Native nettles are treated in some floras as Urtica gracilis and in others as subspecies of Urtica dioica. That naming overlap makes broad records difficult to interpret. The European plant is a tall perennial with spreading underground growth and stinging hairs. A patch beside a stream or woodland edge should be identified carefully before anyone assumes it is an introduced weed that needs removal.

eragrostis-cilianensis.summary: Stinkgrass is a summer annual that forms tufts in fields, pasture, hay ground, and other disturbed places. Its gray-green seed heads can be more conspicuous than the foliage, and the plant has a characteristic unpleasant odor. It reproduces by seed, so a patch can return even though individual plants do not persist as a perennial root system. Agricultural sources describe it as a weed in several settings; the practical need for control depends on the crop or planting and the amount present.

anthemis-cotula.summary: Stinking chamomile, also called mayweed chamomile, is a branching annual with small daisy-like flowers and finely divided leaves. It is a troublesome crop weed in parts of the Pacific Northwest and also occurs along roadsides and on disturbed ground. Plants may emerge in fall or spring, allowing different cohorts to appear within one growing cycle. Its familiar chamomile appearance can be misleading: this is not a plant to identify casually for tea, and the strong odor is only one clue.

jacobaea-vulgaris.summary: Stinking willie is more commonly called tansy ragwort, a yellow-flowered plant that can be a serious concern in pastures. It often begins as a leafy rosette and later produces tall flowering stems, though its life cycle can extend beyond two years. The plant is poisonous to livestock and can contaminate forage. It should be distinguished from common tansy and native yellow-flowered plants before control. Its older scientific name, Senecio jacobaea, still appears in many reliable management guides.

paederia-foetida.summary: Stinkvine, often called skunkvine, is a perennial twining vine from Asia that has established in parts of the southeastern United States and Hawaii. It can run across the ground or climb over shrubs and trees, shading the vegetation beneath it. Its unpleasant smell when damaged explains several common names, but the odor should not replace a careful botanical identification. Persistent woody bases and rooting stems help it recover after superficial cutting, so a cleared canopy does not necessarily mean the plant has been eliminated.

dittrichia-graveolens.summary: Stinkwort is a sticky, strongly scented annual that grows into a many-branched plant with numerous small yellow flower heads. It favors open, disturbed ground such as roadsides, abandoned fields, and overgrazed pasture. California weed specialists describe it as a management concern, and overseas agencies also document crop and livestock problems. Its late-season appearance can surprise people who thought a site was clear earlier in the year. The plant's oily hairs can irritate skin, so close observation is preferable to bare-handed handling.

aglossa-caprealis.summary: The stored grain moth, Aglossa caprealis, is also called the small tabby or fungus moth. Its larvae can live among damp grain residues, hay, decaying plant material, and fungi, so the source of an indoor sighting may be less obvious than an open food package. A moth resting on a wall is not proof that sound grain is infested. The surrounding storage conditions and the presence of larvae or silk are more informative than the adult's common name.

calyptocarpus-vialis.summary: Straggler daisy, often called horseherb, is a low-growing perennial with small yellow flowers and a habit of spreading through lawns and open ground. It is native in at least part of Texas and is deliberately used as a groundcover there. Botanical research indicates that some occurrences farther from its southern range may be more recent expansions or introductions. That history calls for regional care: a plant spreading in a lawn is not automatically an invasive alien, and a listing among weeds does not override its native status.

psidium-cattleianum.summary: Strawberry guava is a shrub or small tree whose attractive fruit helped carry it far beyond its tropical American origin. In places such as Hawaii and Florida, it can form dense stands that shade other vegetation. Animals disperse its seeds, while suckering allows established plants to expand locally. Red-fruited and yellow-fruited forms occur, so fruit color alone does not settle the identification. A productive garden tree can still seed into nearby habitat, making its surroundings part of the management picture.

acleris-comariana.summary: Strawberry tortrix is a small moth whose caterpillars feed on strawberry and some related plants. Larvae shelter in folded or silk-bound leaves, where feeding may go unnoticed until foliage is opened. Danish field studies document larvae and their natural enemies in strawberry crops. Their findings do not set a treatment threshold for every garden or farm. A rolled strawberry leaf can house several different insects, so neither the crop nor the shelter identifies this species by itself.

muntingia-calabura.summary: Strawberrytree here means Muntingia calabura, also called Jamaican cherry or Panama berry, rather than an Arbutus species sold under the same common name. It is a small tropical American tree with spreading, drooping branches and small red fruits. Cultivation and naturalization need to be distinguished: Kauai surveys from 2015-2017 documented plants establishing outside cultivation, including along irrigation ditches and disturbed agricultural ground. That dated evidence supports escape potential, but does not quantify current impacts throughout Hawaii or the mainland.

schoenoplectus-triqueter.summary: Streambank bulrush is a perennial wetland sedge also known as triangular club-rush. In the Pacific Northwest, the Burke Herbarium records it as introduced from Eurasia in the freshwater tidal zone of the lower Columbia River. That is a specific regional occurrence, not a reason to treat every bulrush along a waterway as an invader. Wetland sedges are often difficult to identify and can be important parts of shoreline habitat, so a suspect record needs more than a distant photograph of green stems.

cytisus-striatus.summary: Striated broom is more often called Portuguese broom, a woody shrub with green stems, yellow pea-shaped flowers, and hairy seedpods. It is one of several introduced brooms addressed by California weed-management guidance. Mature stands can leave a persistent seed reserve, so removing the shrubs may be followed by a flush of seedlings. Correct identification matters because Scotch, French, and Spanish broom have similar silhouettes but differ in leaves, stem ridges, flower placement, and pod shape.

amphibalanus-amphitrite.summary: The striped acorn barnacle is a warm-water fouling organism that attaches to hard surfaces such as rocks, shells, docks, and vessel hulls. Shipping has helped move it around the world, and its original range is difficult to reconstruct because related barnacles have often been confused under similar names. Local effects vary: a fouling species can be established without causing the same level of damage in every harbor. Smithsonian's Chesapeake account, for example, describes limited economic impact there.

phyllotreta-striolata.summary: Striped flea beetle is a tiny jumping beetle associated with cabbage-family crops. Adults chew small pits and holes in leaves, and very young seedlings or transplants can suffer much more than established plants. The term flea beetle describes several species rather than a single pest. A few holes on older leaves do not necessarily indicate damaging pressure, so the crop's size, fresh injury, and the number of active beetles should be considered together before deciding on control.

ferrisia-virgata.summary: Striped mealybugs can travel unnoticed on nursery plants. Their white wax and dark back markings draw attention, but older Ferrisia virgata reports combined several species that researchers later separated. A 2021 Florida study used genetic markers to confirm this particular species among mealybugs on cacao. That is stronger evidence than a historical host list, though it does not identify every striped colony on another crop. Check the living insects and plant condition before deciding whether a colony needs treatment.

trichodorus-viruliferus.summary: Trichodorus viruliferus is a microscopic plant-parasitic nematode that feeds from outside roots. Its feeding near growing root tips can interrupt normal elongation, leaving shortened, swollen roots. The species is also recorded as a vector of tobacco rattle virus. That combination makes diagnosis more involved than simply finding damaged roots: the nematode and a possible virus are separate things to test. The reviewed species account emphasizes western European records, so it does not establish current occurrence or crop losses in a particular American field.

trifolium-subterraneum.summary: Subterranean clover is an introduced annual legume deliberately grown in some pasture systems. Its unusual seed habit explains its name: after flowering, the developing burr is pressed toward or into the soil. Seed carried over between seasons allows a suitable stand to reappear without annual sowing. A pasture planting and an unwanted patch outside cultivation call for different decisions. Its presence alone does not establish harmful invasion. Soil, seasonal moisture, and the variety grown all influence how well this clover fits a particular farm or landscape.

coptotermes-gestroi.summary: The Asian subterranean termite can damage structural wood and also occupy trees and other woody material in warm regions. Colonies are hidden, so the first noticeable evidence may be a shelter tube, damaged timber, or winged termites around a building. Its similarity to the Formosan subterranean termite makes species confirmation useful, not merely academic. University of Hawaii surveys document an expanding distribution on Oahu, and the researchers explain that differences in foraging can affect how bait treatments are designed. Those local findings should not be read as a nationwide distribution map.

hypostomus-plecostomus.summary: The common pleco label does not reliably identify Hypostomus plecostomus. A modern study clarified this South American fish's identity in the Guianas, and a later Canje River survey recorded it in its native region. Many introduced American Hypostomus populations remain less securely identified. An aquarium label or an old occurrence name therefore needs checking before it becomes a species-level record. Findings about a different armored catfish, including its environmental effects, should not automatically be assigned to this one.

trifolium-dubium.summary: Suckling clover, also called small hop clover, is a little annual legume with yellow flowers. It often fits between grasses in lawns and other open ground, and Mississippi State describes it as a volunteer component of pasture. Its low stature makes it easy to overlook until small yellow heads appear across a patch. This is a European plant naturalized elsewhere, but that history does not mean every occurrence warrants control. In a lawn, pasture, or conservation area, the useful question is what it is doing at that particular site.

sorghum-x-drummondii.summary: Sudangrass is an annual forage grass associated with the Sorghum x drummondii complex. Farmers grow it and related hybrids for livestock feed, so an occurrence may be an intentional crop rather than an invading weed. The name also needs care: commercial sorghum-sudangrass hybrids are not all the same material as traditional sudangrass. Its most immediate management concern in a forage setting can be feed safety. Young or stressed sorghum-family plants may present prussic-acid hazards, and drought can also create nitrate concerns; a green-looking stand does not demonstrate that it is safe to graze.

sudden-oak-death.summary: Sudden oak death is a disease caused by the water mold Phytophthora ramorum. It has killed large numbers of susceptible trees in parts of coastal California and southern Oregon, but the same pathogen can cause a different-looking leaf or twig disease on other hosts. A shrub with infected leaves and an oak with a trunk canker do not play identical roles in the disease cycle. This host variation is why moving apparently ordinary nursery plants or contaminated material can matter even when no dying oak is nearby.

aspidiella-sacchari.summary: Sugar cane root scale is a small armored scale insect that can live in sheltered parts of its host, including beneath leaf sheaths and near the base of stems. Despite the common name, it is not confined to exposed roots, and published host records extend beyond sugarcane. California's pest assessment describes it as a sugarcane pest in the Caribbean and Florida but notes that it is usually a minor pest. Finding a few scales therefore calls for identification and inspection, rather than an assumption that severe crop loss is inevitable.

diatraea-saccharalis.summary: Sugarcane borer is a moth whose caterpillars feed on grasses and tunnel inside stalks. In sugarcane, this can reduce stalk weight and sugar yield, and injury near a young shoot's growing point can kill the shoot. The importance of the insect differs among production regions: Louisiana guidance treats it as a major crop pest, while Florida reports substantial historical suppression associated with natural enemies. That difference matters when deciding whether a sighting calls for routine monitoring or an urgent crop-management response.

perkinsiella-saccharicida.summary: Sugarcane delphacid is a small sap-feeding planthopper associated with sugarcane. Perkinsiella saccharicida has become established outside its original range, including Hawaii and Florida. It can transmit Fiji disease, but finding the insect does not establish that the disease is present. Florida extension guidance reports little economic damage from the insect there and specifically distinguishes that situation from disease outbreaks elsewhere. The useful question is whether a correctly identified population is damaging the crop or carrying a pathogen, rather than whether any hopper is present.

dicranoctetes-saccharella.summary: Sugarcane leafminer is a tiny moth whose caterpillars feed inside cane leaves. The name Dicranoctetes saccharella appears in older accounts; modern treatments place it in Elachista. A Louisiana survey following its discovery there in 2006 found mines on a minority of sampled stalks, mainly on older foliage, with substantial parasitism. That study did not consider it an economic threat under the conditions observed. A leafmine is therefore worth documenting, but it is not by itself evidence that a crop needs treatment.

eucalyptus-cladocalyx.summary: Sugar gum is a South Australian eucalyptus planted for shelter, shade and timber. It can also establish beyond plantings, including in parts of coastal California. That distinction matters: a mature planted tree and a group of self-sown seedlings tell different stories about spread. California resources identify sugar gum as a plant to watch, making nearby self-sown seedlings especially useful observations to record and follow. Its local effects should be assessed directly rather than borrowed from blue gum or another eucalyptus species.

potentilla-recta.summary: Sulfur cinquefoil is a long-lived Eurasian perennial that can form dense patches in open grasslands, pastures and disturbed ground. It grows from a substantial root crown and produces many seeds, allowing a small infestation to persist after the first visible plants are removed. Its pale yellow flowers are attractive, but it can displace other vegetation and reduce the usefulness of pasture. Native cinquefoils grow in many of the same settings, so careful identification comes before any removal.

cosmos-sulphureus.summary: Sulphur cosmos is a warm-season annual grown for its yellow and orange flower heads. Native to Mexico and nearby parts of Central America, it has escaped cultivation in several regions of the United States. It readily reseeds, which can be useful in a garden but deserves attention when seedlings appear beyond the intended bed. An escaped plant is not automatically evidence of severe ecological harm. The location, persistence and extent of spread help distinguish a few garden volunteers from a population needing closer review.

avocado-sunblotch-viroid.summary: Avocado sunblotch is caused by a viroid, a small infectious RNA rather than an insect or a conventional virus. It can reduce fruit quality and tree performance, yet some infected trees show no obvious symptoms. Those quiet infections matter when buds, grafts or nursery plants are shared. A tree that looks healthy is not necessarily suitable propagation stock. The disease is associated with avocado, and its presence should be established through plant-health testing rather than inferred from a discolored fruit alone.

tithonia-rotundifolia.summary: Mexican sunflower is a warm-season ornamental grown for its bright orange flowers. Tithonia rotundifolia is often visited by butterflies and other flower-feeding insects, but a useful garden plant can still produce seedlings beyond its intended bed. Its name is easily confused with Tithonia diversifolia, a different Mexican sunflower with a different invasion history. A Florida flora explicitly separates the annual species from its perennial relative. This profile should not turn reports about its larger relative into a claim that this species causes the same problems throughout the United States.

crotalaria-juncea.summary: Sunn hemp is a fast-growing annual legume used as a cover crop and green manure. Despite its common name, it is not cannabis. Fields of Crotalaria juncea are often intentional agricultural plantings, so a photograph of a crop is not evidence of an invasive population. Seed production and persistence depend on the cultivar, climate and planting date. Its use as forage also needs care: guidance for a selected cultivar should not be applied to every sunn hemp seed lot or to other Crotalaria species.

eugenia-uniflora.summary: Surinam cherry is an evergreen shrub or small tree introduced as a hedge and fruit plant. In central and southern Florida it can escape into natural areas, where dense growth competes with native vegetation and limits regeneration. Birds and mammals carry its seeds away from cultivated plants. Regional context matters: Florida guidance identifies the strongest concern in the south and uses caution categories farther north. A clipped garden hedge and a spreading population in a hammock should be recorded separately, even when both belong to the same species.

ipomoea-aquatica.summary: Water spinach is a trailing wetland vine also cultivated as a vegetable under names such as kangkong and ong choy. When it escapes into suitable waterways, it can crowd other plants and spread beyond the place where it was grown. Cultivation and possession rules vary by jurisdiction; Texas, for example, includes it among regulated aquatic species. An edible use does not make releasing it into a pond or ditch appropriate. A record should distinguish a managed crop from plants growing freely along a waterway.

eucalyptus-robusta.summary: Swamp mahogany is an Australian eucalyptus planted for timber, shelter and shade in warm regions. In Hawaii, forestry accounts describe regeneration through both seedlings and shoots from cut stumps after disturbance. Florida assessments identify a high predicted invasion risk, which is a risk evaluation rather than proof that every listed county has an established wild population. A useful observation records whether a tree was planted, whether younger trees are appearing beyond it, and whether those recruits persist in surrounding vegetation.

lobularia-maritima.summary: Sweet alyssum is a low flowering plant widely used along garden edges and in containers. It comes from the Mediterranean region and can reseed outside cultivation. A California field flora documents it in waste places and along roadsides, but those records do not establish severe ecological effects at every site. Some plants are short-lived escapes close to a planting; others may continue producing seedlings. Recording that distinction helps separate an ornamental occurrence from a population that is maintaining itself without gardening.

clematis-terniflora.summary: Sweet autumn clematis is a woody climbing vine introduced as an ornamental. It can escape into forest margins, stream edges and disturbed ground, covering nearby vegetation with dense growth. Its abundant white flowers are followed by wind-carried fruits, helping new plants appear away from a garden. Native clematis vines can flower at a similar time and look remarkably alike from a distance. Correct identification is especially important before removing a vine from a streamside or woodland edge.

ocimum-basilicum.summary: Sweet basil is a familiar culinary herb with many cultivars selected for leaf color, scent and size. It is grown widely in gardens and commercially, and occasional plants escape near cultivation. In New England, botanical accounts describe these escapes as likely short-lived. That is different from evidence of persistent ecological damage. A basil plant beside a garden should be recorded as cultivated or escaped as appropriate, rather than automatically labeled an established invasive population.

laurus-nobilis.summary: Bay laurel is a Mediterranean evergreen grown for its aromatic leaves and as a hedge or container plant. Records outside its native range include California, but a record of a nonnative tree does not by itself show that it is spreading or damaging habitat. Planted specimens can remain for many years. For this species, the most useful field detail is whether young plants are appearing independently beyond a maintained garden, rather than simply whether a mature tree is present.

lonicera-fragrantissima.summary: Winter honeysuckle is a Chinese shrub grown for fragrant flowers that open when few other garden shrubs are blooming. It has escaped into woodlands and disturbed places in parts of the southern and eastern United States. Dense growth can limit light and space for native plants and tree seedlings. Its seasonal behavior differs from some other invasive honeysuckles, so advice or photographs labeled only bush honeysuckle should be checked against the species rather than copied without qualification.

prunus-avium.summary: Sweet cherry is a Eurasian fruit tree that is widely cultivated and occasionally escapes into surrounding landscapes. An orchard tree, an old homestead planting and a self-sown tree in woodland represent different kinds of records. This distinction matters when deciding whether a population is spreading. The available botanical accounts support naturalization in parts of the United States, but they do not establish the same ecological impact everywhere. Native cherries and other planted cherry species should not be grouped under this name without identification.

foeniculum-vulgare.summary: Common fennel is a tall perennial herb that can form dense stands in disturbed grassland, coastal scrub and other open habitats. Once established, its root crown can survive cutting, while abundant seed helps maintain the population. California management accounts describe effects on native plant recovery. The culinary name can be confusing: some regulatory treatments exclude bulbing Florence fennel, so a vegetable bed and a wild stand should not automatically receive the same interpretation. Local guidance should determine whether a particular planting or population is a management priority.

elsinoe-australis.summary: Sweet orange scab is a citrus disease caused by the fungus Elsinoe australis. It produces corky blemishes on fruit and can reduce marketability, while severe early infection can distort fruit or contribute to premature drop. The fungus moves with infected plant material and locally with water splash. It is different from the more widespread citrus scab caused by Elsinoe fawcettii. Similar names and overlapping symptoms make laboratory confirmation important, especially when a finding could affect plant-movement requirements.

artemisia-annua.summary: Annual wormwood, also called sweet Annie, is an aromatic Eurasian herb introduced across much of North America. It occurs in gardens, roadsides and other disturbed ground. Unlike perennial wormwoods that return from established underground structures, this species completes its life cycle in one growing season and persists through seed. Some regional accounts describe escaped plants as short-lived at a particular site. A record therefore needs context about repeated recruitment and habitat, rather than assuming a lasting invasion from one tall plant.

anthoxanthum-odoratum.summary: Sweet vernalgrass is a small, early-flowering grass introduced from Eurasia. It grows in hayfields, pastures, roadsides and some natural grasslands, where its early growth can make it conspicuous before other grasses flower. Its sweet smell is familiar in drying hay, but that smell does not make a plant native sweetgrass. Whether a patch warrants removal depends on the habitat and the plants it is replacing. A pasture occurrence and a spreading population in a native meadow deserve different management decisions.

viola-odorata.summary: Sweet violet is a low-growing garden perennial introduced from Europe and nearby regions. It can persist around old plantings and spread into lawns, disturbed ground and woodland edges. A violet patch is not automatically an invasive population: many North American violets are native, and cultivated flowers may remain close to their original planting. Regional floras document sweet violet outside gardens, but the evidence reviewed here does not establish the same ecological effects across all locations. Confirming the species comes before deciding what to remove.

silene-armeria.summary: Sweet William catchfly is a European garden flower that has escaped cultivation in parts of North America. It is also treated under the scientific name Atocion armeria, so records using either name need to be matched carefully. It usually grows as an annual or biennial in disturbed ground, roadsides and former gardens. Botanical records establish that escapes occur; they do not by themselves show serious ecological harm at every site. This plant should not be confused with native catchflies or with the separate garden species called sweet William.

rosa-rubiginosa.summary: Sweetbriar rose is a thorny shrub introduced from Europe and widely associated with old plantings, roadsides and open ground. It can spread by seed and vegetative growth, forming difficult thickets in suitable settings. Its importance varies by region, and a watch-list entry should not be mistaken for a statewide removal requirement. Native roses support wildlife and can look similar from a distance. A reliable identification is therefore an important part of deciding whether a rose patch is an unwanted introduction or a plant worth protecting.

lathyrus-odoratus.summary: Sweet pea is a Mediterranean ornamental grown for fragrant flowers, often on fences or garden supports. It is generally an annual, unlike some perennial plants that share the name pea. Finding it beside a garden does not establish an invasive population, and the sources reviewed here do not support a uniform claim of ecological harm. Cultivated plants, discarded garden material and plants reproducing away from cultivation should be recorded separately. This flowering ornamental is also different from the peas grown for food.

ipomoea-batatas.summary: Sweetpotato is a familiar food crop and an ornamental vine in the morning glory family. Plants selected for colorful leaves and plants selected for useful storage roots belong to the same species, but they do not necessarily perform well for both purposes. Trailing stems can cover a surprising amount of ground during warm weather. Its appearance in a planted bed is evidence of cultivation, not proof of ecological invasion; a useful observation records whether the vine was planted or appeared independently outside a garden.

cereus-repandus.summary: Cereus repandus is a large, branching cactus often called apple cactus. The catalog name sweetpotato cactus should not be read as a connection to the sweetpotato vine. Mature plants can become tree-sized, with upright fleshy columns and conspicuous flowers that open at night. Kew accepts the species and places its native range in the southern Caribbean and northern South America. Horticultural sources use older names and sometimes conflicting origin accounts, so a cultivated cactus label deserves checking before it becomes a wild-species record.

bemisia-tabaci.summary: Sweetpotato whitefly is the name commonly used for Bemisia tabaci, a group of extremely similar whiteflies associated with many crops and ornamentals. The name covers a cryptic species complex rather than one easily recognized biological unit. Feeding can discolor or distort leaves, and some members transmit damaging plant viruses. Sticky honeydew and the dark mold growing on it are often the first noticeable signs. The host plant and local growing conditions matter when judging risk; a cloud of white insects alone does not establish which member is present.

dianthus-barbatus.summary: Sweet William is a familiar cottage-garden flower, usually grown as a biennial or a short-lived perennial. Compact clusters of pink, red, purple, or white blooms can persist as conspicuous traces of old planting. Many cultivars have been selected, including small plants and double flowers, so a garden escape may look different from a field-guide illustration. The evidence reviewed here establishes its horticultural identity but does not establish harmful invasion throughout the United States. A record should distinguish a maintained border, an abandoned planting, and self-sown plants.

anguillicoloides-crassus.summary: The eel swimbladder nematode is an internal parasite of freshwater eels. It is native to eastern Asia and has been introduced into other regions, including North America. Eels acquire infection by eating infected small crustaceans or other hosts in the food web; the worms eventually occupy the swimbladder. This organ helps regulate buoyancy, so infection can be important even when the eel looks ordinary from the outside. Evidence of infection is not, by itself, proof that the parasite caused a local eel-population decline.

chloris-barbata.summary: Swollen fingergrass is a warm-climate grass with a distinctive crown of fingerlike flowering branches. It commonly occupies disturbed, open ground, including roadsides and sandy places. Published accounts disagree about its original range: Singapore's botanical account places its origin in tropical America, while Kew treats the tropical and subtropical Old World as native. That disagreement should not be hidden behind a single global label. For a US observation, check the identification and the regional flora before deciding whether the population is an unwanted introduction.

macrothelypteris-torresiana.summary: This large, soft-textured fern is sometimes listed simply as swordfern, a name also used for quite different ferns. Macrothelypteris torresiana forms a tuft of broad, finely divided fronds and readily colonizes disturbed sites where conditions suit it. In 2026, the University of Florida assessment places it in the high invasion risk category throughout Florida using a predictive screening tool. That is a regional risk conclusion, not a claim that every fern with this common name is invasive or that measured damage has been documented at every site.

acer-pseudoplatanus.summary: Sycamore maple is a large deciduous tree introduced from Europe and western or central Asia. It has been planted for shade and can produce seedlings beyond managed landscapes. University of Connecticut documents an invasive tendency in that state, making nearby woodland edges worth checking when mature planted trees are present. The common name can confuse observers: this is a maple, not the American sycamore. Its behavior varies with location, and a street tree should be distinguished from a reproducing population in a natural area.

acacia-longifolia.summary: Sydney golden wattle is an Australian shrub or small tree with bright yellow flower spikes. It has been cultivated well beyond its native range, and a California risk assessment describes naturalized populations and the potential for troublesome thickets. Its numerous hard-coated seeds can persist in the soil, so removing a mature plant may not end the problem. This long follow-up period is an important practical distinction from a short-lived garden volunteer. Regional evidence matters; the plant's name alone does not establish the condition of a particular site.

zygophyllum-fabago.summary: Syrian bean-caper is a fleshy, branching plant of dry, disturbed ground, including rocky roadsides and gravelly areas. It is introduced from Eurasia and can compete with native vegetation and agricultural plants. Washington treats it as a serious noxious weed, so a suspected new patch there deserves prompt attention from the county weed program. Its spread is not confined to seed: underground growth and root fragments can also produce plants. That makes casual digging or moving contaminated soil a poor first response to an unfamiliar infestation.

compsilura-concinnata.summary: Compsilura concinnata is a parasitoid fly introduced into North America for control of spongy moth and other caterpillar pests. Its larvae develop inside caterpillars, eventually killing their hosts. The difficulty is its broad host range: native moths can also be attacked. A central Virginia experiment documented parasitism of luna moth caterpillars, while a separate Canadian field study found it using several native hosts. These findings justify concern about unintended effects, but they do not show that every local moth decline has the same cause.

stenhomalus-taiwanus.summary: Taiwan slender longhorned beetle is an Asian wood-associated beetle recorded in the southern United States. California's 2016 assessment describes larvae feeding in young stems and branches of two Zanthoxylum species, including Sichuan pepper and Japanese prickly ash. The same assessment emphasizes uncertainty about which hosts the beetle uses in the United States. That uncertainty matters: it would be misleading to portray it as a proven major forest pest, or to assume that every pepper plant showing branch damage contains this insect.

pittosporum-pentandrum.summary: Taiwanese cheesewood is an Asian tree cultivated as an ornamental in warm climates. Its behavior is a good example of why regional evidence matters. Kauai surveys documented naturalized populations and recommended continued mapping, while the University of Florida's 2026 assessment does not currently consider it a problem species there. Those findings can coexist; neither should be turned into a nationwide verdict. An observation is most informative when it separates a planted tree from seedlings or saplings established beyond the planting.

albizia-procera.summary: Tall albizia, also called white siris, is a substantial Asian and Australian tree grown for timber, shade, and other uses. A long, pale trunk and a light, spreading crown can make mature trees conspicuous. Historical New York Botanical Garden treatment documents cultivated plants in southern Florida, but that is not evidence of widespread ecological invasion. It is also important not to transfer the impacts of other trees commonly called albizia to this species. Local establishment and impact require records tied to the correct scientific name.

schedonorus-arundinaceus.summary: Tall fescue is a cool-season perennial grass widely planted for lawns, pasture, and erosion control. Those useful roles do not prevent it from becoming a problem in prairie restoration and other natural habitats. Dense surviving stands can compete with the plants a restoration is intended to recover. Illinois Extension notes that old pasture fescue can be difficult to remove when land is converted to prairie or wildflowers. The appropriate response depends on the site's purpose; managing an existing lawn is different from restoring a native grassland.

hieracium-piloselloides.summary: Tall hawkweed is a yellow-flowered perennial associated with open, often nutrient-poor ground. In Washington it is one of the nonnative hawkweeds that can interfere with grassland and disturbed-site recovery. A patch may be easy to overlook among dandelions until its taller, branching flower stems become apparent. King County asks residents to report it and provides site-specific management advice. Because native and introduced hawkweeds can be difficult to distinguish, a correct species identification is an essential first step rather than an optional detail.

ipomoea-purpurea.summary: Tall morning-glory is an annual climbing vine grown for its showy, funnel-shaped flowers. It can also become a weed in crops and disturbed ground, where stems wind around surrounding plants and complicate removal. The University of Florida currently gives it a high invasion risk rating based on predictive assessment, while California guidance describes practical problems in agricultural settings. These are regional findings, not a claim that every ornamental vine is causing ecological damage. Seed production and volunteers beyond the planting are useful things to watch.

arrhenatherum-elatius.summary: Tall oatgrass is a cool-season perennial introduced as a pasture and revegetation grass. It now grows beyond cultivation in many regions. Its height and dense growth can be a particular problem where managers are trying to recover shorter native prairie plants. Federal refuge planning in Oregon documents interference with upland prairie and oak-savanna restoration, while Washington's natural heritage assessment rates its ecological impact as moderate. Those regional assessments are more informative than treating all tall roadside grasses as equally harmful.

sisymbrium-altissimum.summary: Tall tumblemustard, also called Jim Hill mustard, is an introduced mustard of open and disturbed ground. It grows in agricultural land, roadsides, grasslands, and disturbed rangeland, including sites recovering after fire. A mature plant develops a loose, much-branched top that can break away and tumble, scattering seed as it moves. That dispersal habit helps explain why preventing mature seed production matters. Its presence signals a plant worth identifying and managing in context, not proof that it alone caused a site's poor condition.

chloris-elata.summary: Tall windmill grass needs a careful identity and origin check before it is treated as an unwanted introduction. The catalog uses Chloris elata, while Kew accepts the newer name Stapfochloa elata. More importantly, authoritative records disagree about its status in the continental United States: USDA GRIN and a South Florida conservation account treat it as native in Florida, while the older-name USDA PLANTS profile codes it as introduced. That conflict is material to management and cannot be resolved by the common name alone.

tamarindus-indica.summary: Tamarind is a tropical tree long cultivated for the tangy pulp surrounding its seeds. Its broad crown and fine-textured foliage also make it a familiar shade tree. Widespread cultivation complicates a simple account of its original range, although botanical sources generally associate its origin with Africa. In Florida, the current assessment displays not-a-problem conclusions, but marks the central and southern assessments incomplete. That is a reason to describe the evidence carefully, not to convert a common food and landscape tree into a proven invasive threat.

lathyrus-tingitanus.summary: Tangier pea is an annual climbing or scrambling legume associated with the Mediterranean region. It has become naturalized elsewhere, including California, where it may occur beyond gardens and along disturbed edges. Its bright pea-shaped flowers can make a patch look like an intentional planting, but the setting and presence of seedlings matter. Naturalization establishes that a plant can persist outside cultivation; it does not by itself establish the scale of ecological harm. Local impact and management evidence for this species remains less complete than its botanical description.

tarophagus-colocasiae.summary: Taro planthopper is a small sap-feeding insect associated especially with taro, Colocasia esculenta. Groups feed on leaves and their stalks, and heavy infestations can contribute to yellowing and wilting. The species was documented in Florida in 2015, but the economic importance of its establishment there remains uncertain in the reviewed Extension account. Older literature also needs care: a former broad species concept was divided into three Tarophagus species in 1989. Disease-vector or host claims from those older accounts cannot automatically be assigned to this species.

eucalyptus-globulus.summary: Tasmanian bluegum is a very tall Australian eucalyptus planted extensively in California. Some coastal stands have expanded into adjacent vegetation, while others have remained stable or declined, so the history of an individual grove matters. California's detailed assessment emphasizes that spread usually occurs around existing plantings rather than through frequent new populations far away. This is a reason to inspect grove edges and regeneration, not to assume every old planted tree is actively invading. Mature trees also require management decisions that account for their scale and surroundings.

rytidosperma-semiannulare.summary: Tasmanian wallaby grass is a tufted perennial native to southeastern Australia. It belongs to a difficult group of small grasses whose names have changed repeatedly in floras and collection records. Older references may call it Danthonia semiannularis or Notodanthonia semiannularis. Hawaiian records need particular care: a recent Bishop Museum checklist explains that some reports under Rytidosperma semiannulare were misapplied to Rytidosperma biannulare. A name on an older island list therefore cannot establish which species is present today or what impact it has.

lonicera-tatarica.summary: Tatarian honeysuckle is a large deciduous shrub whose spring flowers and summer berries helped make it a familiar ornamental. Outside its Eurasian home range, it has become an invasive woodland and edge plant in parts of North America. Its early leafing and abundant seed production help it occupy space needed by other vegetation. Birds can move the berries beyond the original hedge, so a tidy planting can still be a source for scattered shrubs nearby.

atriplex-tatarica.summary: Tatarian orache is an annual plant of disturbed ground, including roadsides, fields, sandy soils, and some salt-affected places. Its native range extends across parts of Europe and Asia, and botanical treatments record it as alien in North America. A dusty or silvery appearance can make the plant stand out among greener roadside weeds. Those records establish an introduced plant, however, not a nationwide ecological emergency or proof that a particular roadside population is spreading into intact habitat.

osmia-taurus.summary: The Taurus mason bee is an Asian bee now established in the eastern United States. It was first documented here in 2002, after the related hornfaced bee had been deliberately introduced for pollination. Researchers studying Mid-Atlantic bee collections found that Taurus mason bees increased while several native mason bees declined. That pattern raises a serious conservation question, but it does not by itself prove that this one species caused every decline. These bees still visit flowers and should not be confused with a swarming household pest.

aegilops-tauschii.summary: Tausch's goatgrass is a small annual relative of wheat with an outsized agricultural history. It contributed part of the genetic ancestry of bread wheat and remains valuable to crop researchers. It can also behave as a crop weed: studies document weedy populations in northern China's wheat-growing regions. Flora of North America records only a limited set of United States localities in its treatment. Neither its importance overseas nor its relationship to wheat establishes a widespread American infestation.

paratrechina-fulva.summary: The tawny crazy ant is now usually called Nylanderia fulva; Paratrechina fulva is an older scientific combination retained in this catalog. Native to South America, it has established troublesome populations in the southern United States. Large numbers can occupy gardens, buildings, and equipment, and their rapid, irregular movements explain the common name. Their impact is more than an occasional ant on a counter: dense populations can interfere with outdoor activities and electrical equipment and alter other insect communities.

dysmicoccus-wistariae.summary: Taxus mealybug is a sap-feeding insect most closely associated with yews in northeastern United States landscapes and nurseries. Colonies can hide in branch forks and protected parts of the plant, making the insects easier to overlook than the sticky honeydew or dark sooty mold they encourage. Dogwood and several other woody hosts are also reported. Published accounts disagree about generation timing in different regions, so a fixed calendar date is a poor substitute for checking the actual plants.

camellia-sinensis.summary: Tea is the evergreen shrub behind familiar green, black, white, and oolong teas. Different processing methods and cultivated varieties account for much of that diversity. In a garden it is a leafy shrub or small tree, not automatically an invasive plant because it originated in Asia. The University of Florida's assessment classifies Camellia sinensis as low invasion risk in Florida. That is a regional assessment, not a promise that every planting will behave identically in every climate.

tetranychus-kanzawai.summary: Tea red spider mite, also called Kanzawa spider mite, feeds on far more than tea. Published accounts include hydrangea, strawberry, and other crops, while California guidance describes infestations on citrus. The tiny mites feed on plant tissue and produce webbing that can become conspicuous on fruit and foliage. Host use and damage vary among populations and growing conditions. A red mite on a leaf is therefore neither a dependable identification nor proof that a serious regional outbreak has begun.

fiorinia-theae.summary: Tea scale is a small armored scale insect that often reveals itself on camellias as yellow blotches above and a crowded coating below the leaves. Despite its name, camellias and hollies are important landscape hosts in the southeastern United States. Heavy infestations can reduce growth and flowering, while lightly infested plants may remain vigorous. Several overlapping generations can occur, and damaged leaves may stay on the shrub after the insects have died. Appearance alone is therefore a poor measure of treatment success.

euwallacea-perbrevis.summary: Tea shot hole borer is a tiny ambrosia beetle associated with fungal partners inside wood. In southern Florida, Euwallacea perbrevis and the fungi it carries are linked to branch dieback in avocado. It belongs to a group whose names have changed as researchers separated similar-looking species. Older records labeled Euwallacea fornicatus may concern a different member of that group, so damage reports from California cannot automatically be assigned to this Florida beetle.

hyblaea-puera.summary: The teak defoliator is a moth whose caterpillars can consume much of a teak leaf, leaving its main framework behind. Forestry accounts from Asia describe repeated generations and damaging outbreaks on teak and other hosts. North American moth resources also recognize Hyblaea puera, but a tropical forestry pest account does not establish that every American observation is an invasive outbreak. Its regional origin, host relationship, and actual damage should be assessed separately from its presence on a species list.

eucalymnatus-tessellatus.summary: Tessellated scale is a soft scale insect often associated with palms and other tropical ornamental plants. Florida accounts also identify mango and crepe-jasmine as hosts. Colonies feed on plant sap and can contribute honeydew that supports dark sooty mold, making foliage look dirtier than the small insects themselves suggest. Greenhouses can support overlapping generations. The species can reproduce without mating, so a small introduction on a plant deserves attention even when no males are found.

psammonobiotus-communis.summary: Psammonobiotus communis is a microscopic shelled amoeba associated with the spaces between wet sand grains. It is far too small to recognize during an ordinary beach walk. Great Lakes records have prompted questions about introduction from other regions, but its arrival date and original range remain uncertain. Limited historical sampling leaves open the possibility that it was present long before scientists first recorded it. A database entry should therefore not be read as proof of a recent invasion or visible environmental damage.

psammonobiotus-dziwnowi.summary: Psammonobiotus dziwnowi is a minute testate amoeba, an organism that lives within a constructed shell. It was named in 2005 after earlier material had been reported without a species name. Records include Baltic coastal habitat and Great Lakes beach sediments. Those findings are scientifically interesting, but the available account reports little or no evidence of significant Great Lakes economic effects. Its native origin and the timing of its arrival remain uncertain because these microscopic communities have received relatively little historical study.

nicotiana-plumbaginifolia.summary: Tex-mex tobacco is an herbaceous tobacco that begins with a basal rosette and later sends up flowering stems. Floras describe it as annual or occasionally biennial and document naturalized populations in disturbed sites outside its home region. Indian botanical accounts associate it with roadsides, canal banks, and cultivated ground. The common name does not identify every small wild tobacco, and its occurrence in a weed list does not establish serious ecological impact at a particular United States site.

eragrostis-atrovirens.summary: Thalia lovegrass is a perennial bunchgrass native across parts of the tropical and subtropical Old World. Its slender stems and many small spikelets give the flowering plant a more delicate appearance than a broad-leaved pasture grass. Botanical accounts place it in grasslands, along rivers, and in other open habitats. Those habitat records are useful for recognition, but they do not establish a demonstrated invasion problem or a tested control program for every American location where the name appears.

hyparrhenia-hirta.summary: Thatching grass, widely called Coolatai grass in Australia, is a tough perennial that forms dense tussocks. Australian agencies document its ability to invade pastures and natural vegetation, including sites with little obvious disturbance. Drought and fire tolerance make established stands difficult to manage, while hairy seeds can travel on animals, clothing, and machinery. These are well-documented regional concerns. They should guide careful assessment elsewhere without turning an Australian weed designation into an automatic legal or ecological classification for a United States site.

puccinia-suaveolens.summary: Thistle rust is a fungus associated with Canada thistle, Cirsium arvense. Much of the North American literature calls it Puccinia punctiformis; current biological-control material also uses Puccinia suaveolens. This is not simply another weed to remove. Researchers study the fungus because systemic infection can weaken the thistle's underground system and reduce growth. That potential does not mean every rusty thistle is infected by this species or that an infection will eliminate a patch without other management.

elaeagnus-pungens.summary: Thorny olive is an evergreen shrub often planted as a hedge, but its long shoots can also scramble into neighboring trees. Native to East Asia, it has escaped cultivation in the southeastern United States. Florida's assessment identifies it as invasive and does not recommend planting it. Shade tolerance helps it persist beyond sunny garden edges, and animals can carry its seeds away from the original hedge. A clipped appearance therefore does not necessarily mean the plant is contained.

veronica-filiformis.summary: Threadstalk speedwell makes low mats of small rounded leaves and pale blue flowers. It is a creeping perennial familiar in lawns and ornamental beds, where slender stems root at their joints. North American plants often produce little or no viable seed, so pieces of rooted stem can matter more than a seed crop. A patch may lose leaves in hot, dry weather and then revive when conditions improve. Temporary browning should not be mistaken for complete removal.

mollugo-cerviana.summary: Threadstem carpetweed is a small annual with fine, branching stems and narrow leaves. Modern botanical treatments often place it in Hypertelis as Hypertelis cerviana, while older floras use Mollugo cerviana. The name change matters when searching records, because apparently different entries may describe the same plant. Floras associate it with open grassland, riverbanks, gardens, and disturbed soil. Its small size and weedy setting do not by themselves establish significant ecological damage or justify removing every similar plant.

allium-triquetrum.summary: Threecorner leek is a bulb-forming perennial that can create dense seasonal patches after escaping gardens. Its narrow leaves and nodding white flowers are attractive, but established colonies can be difficult to separate from the many small bulbs beneath them. Australian weed guidance documents dense stands that displace native ground vegetation, especially in moist shady sites. Its significance in the United States depends on local conditions and records; an overseas designation does not establish a nationwide rule for every garden.

desmodium-triflorum.summary: Threeflower ticktrefoil is a low, wiry legume whose stems spread over the ground and can root at their lower joints. It often blends into short vegetation until its small pea-like flowers or jointed fruits become visible. Modern treatments also use the name Grona triflora. Floras document it across tropical regions and in disturbed habitats, but that broad distribution does not mean every occurrence is harmful or that a United States lawn patch deserves an invasive-species label.

malvastrum-coromandelianum.summary: Threelobe false mallow is an upright, branching member of the mallow family with small yellow flowers. It can grow as an annual or persist longer, and botanical accounts document it in disturbed tropical and subtropical habitats. Its leaves are not always conspicuously three-lobed despite the common name. A roadside plant with a yellow mallow flower may belong to several different species, and neither a weedy appearance nor a foreign-sounding scientific name establishes that it is locally invasive.

eleusine-tristachya.summary: Threespike goosegrass is a small perennial grass from South America that can establish in lawns, gravelly ground, and other disturbed places. Its short stature makes it easy to overlook until the compact finger-like seed heads appear. The name suggests three branches, but plants can have two to four. Agricultural accounts from Argentina describe crop competition, while New Zealand records concern scattered naturalized populations. Those different contexts should not be collapsed into a single claim of severe impact everywhere.

scirtothrips-dorsalis.summary: Chilli thrips is a tiny introduced insect that damages tender plant growth rather than merely gathering harmlessly inside flowers. It has become a concern on ornamental plants and crops in parts of the southern United States and California. Feeding can discolor and distort young leaves and shoots, reducing a plant's ability to grow normally. Blueberry guidance from Georgia describes its importance to southeastern fruit production. The effect depends on the host and infestation, so a curled leaf alone is not a diagnosis.

thrips-palmi.summary: Melon thrips is a warm-climate crop pest that can also persist in protected growing spaces. It spread from Southeast Asia to many tropical and subtropical regions, with United States records including Hawaii and Florida. Vegetables such as eggplant and cucurbits can suffer feeding damage, but host suitability is not identical across all vegetables. In particular, tomato should not be assumed to support the same populations simply because several other thrips attack it. Greenhouse conditions can make a local risk different from the outdoor climate.

thrips-parvispinus.summary: Thrips parvispinus, often called short-spined or pepper thrips, is an emerging pest of ornamental plants and crops. It was confirmed in Florida in 2020, and later reports document spread associated with plant commerce. Texas extension describes specimens from hibiscus and pepper that were confirmed by a specialist in 2025. Such records deserve attention, but an interception at a retailer and an established outdoor population are different findings. The plant's source and location matter when interpreting a report.

dracocephalum-thymiflorum.summary: Thymeleaf dragonhead is a small herb in the mint family, with modest bluish flowers rather than the large blooms of ornamental dragonheads.
