Its close relative, white prunicola scale, can occur on similar hosts and is more likely in some northern settings, so the two should not be merged without identification.

eucalyptus-pulchella.summary: White peppermint is a fine-leaved eucalyptus native to Tasmania, where it belongs to dry forests and woodlands. It is also grown as an ornamental tree elsewhere. A cultivated tree, a naturalized seedling and an invasive stand are different situations; the sources reviewed here do not establish broad United States ecological impacts for this particular eucalyptus. Claims about blue gum or other large eucalypts should not be transferred to it simply because they share a genus.

populus-alba.summary: White poplar is a Eurasian tree planted for shade and its pale foliage. In parts of North America it spreads beyond old plantings through root suckers, forming colonies along roads, fields and woodland edges. Several stems in a patch may therefore be connected underground rather than representing separate seedlings. That growth pattern explains why cutting down one trunk can leave the colony in place or encourage additional shoots.

pseudaulacaspis-prunicola.summary: White prunicola scale is an introduced armored scale often found on cherry laurel and related ornamental plants. Its waxy cover protects the insect while it feeds on stems. Dense populations can contribute to poor growth and branch dieback, although a few old covers do not necessarily mean a plant has an active, damaging infestation. Checking the insects underneath is more useful than treating every white mark on the bark.

stromatinia-cepivora.summary: Onion white rot is caused by Stromatinia cepivora, also widely described as Sclerotium cepivorum. It attacks garlic, onions and other alliums, rotting roots and bulbs. The fungus leaves tiny resting bodies in soil that can survive for many years without a crop. Moving contaminated planting stock, soil or equipment can establish a problem in a previously clean bed, which makes prevention more useful than relying on a short crop rotation.

amylostereum-areolatum.summary: Amylostereum areolatum is a wood-decay fungus closely associated with woodwasps. Female Sirex noctilio can introduce it into pine wood while laying eggs, and the fungus helps support the developing larvae. Tree injury involves the insect, its secretions and the fungus together; white rot alone is not evidence of this particular association. Research has also found distinct fungal strains with native North American woodwasps, so it is inaccurate to label every occurrence a newly introduced Sirex infestation.

melilotus-albus.summary: White sweetclover is a tall, branching legume introduced from Eurasia and now widespread in open, disturbed habitats. It can produce dense growth along roads, riverbanks and grasslands. Its ability to fix nitrogen and produce persistent seed helps it occupy places where maintaining native plant communities is a priority. It is also a cultivated forage and bee plant, so management depends on the setting rather than its presence alone.

reseda-alba.summary: White upright mignonette is a Mediterranean-region herb that has been grown ornamentally and recorded outside cultivation in North America. It can behave as an annual or persist longer from a woody base. Its presence in a plant catalog documents an introduced plant, not proof that it is displacing native vegetation everywhere it occurs. Local spread and impacts need to be assessed separately from identification.

salix-alba.summary: White willow is a large Eurasian willow planted in landscapes and found along wet, disturbed places outside cultivation. Like other willows, it can grow readily from cuttings, which matters when branches or planting material are moved near waterways. It also belongs to a group with many native species and cultivated hybrids. A willow along a stream should not be removed solely because it has pale foliage or a spreading crown.

cronartium-ribicola.summary: White pine blister rust is a fungal disease that can damage or kill susceptible white pines. It cycles between pines and alternate hosts, commonly currants and gooseberries, rather than passing directly from one pine to the next. On a pine, the fungus can grow from infected needles into branches and eventually the trunk. A branch infection and a trunk infection have different consequences, so locating the canker matters when deciding what to do.

phyllorhiza-punctata.summary: White-spotted jellyfish is a large coastal jellyfish introduced to several regions outside its likely western Pacific origin. It can form dense seasonal gatherings in estuaries and lagoons, sometimes interfering with fishing gear and consuming plankton. A bloom can appear and disappear without showing the whole population history, because the visible swimming stage is only part of its life cycle. Local reports are most useful when they include dates and approximate abundance.

brotogeris-versicolurus.summary: White-winged parakeet is a small South American parrot whose introduced populations have been documented in urban areas outside its native range. Historical records sometimes used the name canary-winged parakeet for birds now separated into white-winged and yellow-chevroned parakeets. Those older reports cannot always be assigned confidently to one species. A single free-flying bird also does not establish that a local breeding population exists. A 2023 study followed two Puerto Rican populations through four years of roost counts, supplying local population evidence rather than a trend for every mainland city.

aleuroglandulus-subtilis.summary: Aleuroglandulus subtilis is a small whitefly associated especially with aroids such as caladiums, elephant ears and related ornamental plants. It has a long documented history in Florida and was confirmed in Hawaii after earlier tentative collections. Infestations can be conspicuous on leaf undersides, but regional experience differs: Florida observations include parasitized colonies, while early Hawaiian reports described plants carrying substantial populations. This is not interchangeable with every pest called whitefly.

naupactus-minor.summary: Naupactus minor is one of several closely related whitefringed beetles introduced from South America. In this group, adults feed above ground while larvae feed around roots, where injury can be harder to notice. The species has documented introductions in the southeastern United States, but many practical accounts discuss the whole beetle group together. A crop-loss claim for another whitefringed beetle should not automatically become a species-specific claim for this one. A separate Brazilian study identified this species on soybean plants; that observation does not supply a United States crop-loss threshold.

naupactus-peregrinus.summary: Naupactus peregrinus is a South American whitefringed beetle recorded as introduced in the United States. Its flightless adults can be found on vegetation, but the root-feeding larvae are often the more consequential stage in the whitefringed-beetle group. Reports that identify only the group cannot establish which species caused a particular injury. Keeping the specimen identity attached to the observation helps prevent similar-looking weevils from being merged in the record. Original Brazilian sampling identified N. peregrinus on soybean, providing a specific host observation without measuring its impact in a US field.

thunbergia-fragrans.summary: White thunbergia, also called whitelady or sweet clock-vine, is a climbing plant from Asia that has escaped ornamental cultivation. It can scramble over neighboring vegetation. Florida's assessment identifies a high predicted invasion risk, while its accompanying status assessment reports that it was not considered a problem species at that assessment stage. Those are different kinds of evidence: a risk prediction is a reason for caution, not proof of severe damage at every existing planting.

drymaria-cordata.summary: Drymaria cordata is a low, spreading herb also called tropical chickweed or whitesnow. It often occurs in moist, shaded lawns, gardens and disturbed ground. Its broad tropical distribution has led to conflicting accounts of where it is native, including differences among references for the southeastern United States. The local origin and habitat context should therefore be checked before treating every patch as a new invasive occurrence.

lepidium-draba.summary: Whitetop, also called hoary cress, is a perennial mustard that can form dense patches from an extensive root system. It competes with grasses and other vegetation in pastures, roadsides and disturbed open ground. A flowering patch may be only the visible part of a larger underground colony. This is why removing stems without addressing continued root growth often gives only temporary relief.

bifora-radians.summary: Wild bishop is a small annual in the carrot family, associated with fields and other disturbed ground in its Eurasian range. North American records are occasional rather than evidence of a widespread, uniformly harmful invasion. In crop-growing regions overseas it can occur among other annual weeds, but those reports do not by themselves establish its present effect in a United States county. A well-documented new observation is more useful than an assumed impact.

macroptilium-lathyroides.summary: Wild bushbean, also called phasey bean, is a tropical American legume used in some places as forage or a cover crop. Outside its native range it can escape into open and coastal habitats. Florida observers have documented dense stands in parts of the Keys, and the state's assessment advises against planting because of invasion risk. That regional evidence is more informative than assuming that a useful forage plant is harmless or that every planted crop is an invasion.

anthriscus-sylvestris.summary: Wild chervil is a Eurasian member of the carrot family that can form dense growth along roadsides, fields and woodland edges. It usually lives for two years or a little longer. Established roots can produce renewed growth, while seeds allow patches to expand. It can crowd other plants and reduce the usefulness of pasture or hay, making early recognition valuable before a small roadside population becomes a larger management problem.

cosmos-caudatus.summary: Wild cosmos is a tropical American herb also cultivated as ulam raja in parts of Southeast Asia. Its pink flower heads and divided foliage can resemble familiar garden cosmos, but this is a particular species rather than a name for any cosmos growing outside a flowerbed. Flora of North America documents it in the Florida Keys within its treatment area. That record does not establish broad United States ecological harm.

corchorus-tridens.summary: Wild jute, also called horn-fruited jute, is an annual herb in the mallow family. It occurs in disturbed ground and cultivated fields across warmer regions of the world. Its United States history needs care: Flora of North America includes New Jersey and Pennsylvania from database records but describes the plant as probably rare or an occasional arrival, with abundance unknown. Those entries should not be presented as proof of a currently established, damaging population.

avena-fatua.summary: Wild oat is a cool-season annual grass that is especially troublesome in small-grain crops. It competes with the crop and can leave seeds mixed into harvested grain. Populations differ in emergence timing and herbicide susceptibility, so a treatment that works in one field may not work in another. It also occurs along roads and in grasslands; its presence there needs to be assessed in the context of the habitat rather than assigned the same impact as a crop infestation.

pastinaca-sativa.summary: Wild parsnip is a Eurasian plant that has spread into North American roadsides, fields and other sunny habitats. It begins as a low leafy rosette and later sends up a flowering stem. Dense populations can replace other vegetation, but the immediate concern for someone encountering it is its sap: skin exposed to the sap and then sunlight can develop serious irritation and blisters. Avoid handling an unfamiliar patch while trying to identify it.

raphanus-raphanistrum.summary: Wild radish is a mustard-family weed of fields, gardens and other disturbed ground. It usually grows as an annual, producing a leafy rosette before flowering. In crops it can compete for resources and return many seeds to the soil. Identification becomes less straightforward where it grows with cultivated radish: the two can hybridize, and their offspring may not fit a simple field-guide description. A precise record is better than assigning every roadside radish to this species.

saccharum-spontaneum.summary: Wild sugarcane is a perennial grass used in sugarcane breeding that has escaped cultivation in some warm regions. It can spread by windborne seed and by living stem or underground fragments, forming persistent stands. Research in Panama shows how it can interfere with forest recovery and return after fire. Those findings help explain concern about the species, while United States reports need to be tied to their actual locations rather than assumed across the country.

quadraspidiotus-gigas.summary: Willow scale is a small armored insect also called poplar scale or aspen scale. Current taxonomic records place it in Diaspidiotus as D. gigas, although much useful research retains Quadraspidiotus gigas. Its host name can be misleading: Colorado observations describe damaging infestations on aspen trunks and large branches. Poorly situated street trees have been particularly vulnerable there. Research in northern China also documented severe injury to planted poplars, but that regional experience does not establish the insect's origin or severity everywhere in North America.

eragrostis-superba.summary: Wilman lovegrass is an African perennial grass introduced into the United States, including Arizona. It forms upright bunches rather than a creeping sod, and its broad, flattened seed clusters give it a different texture from many fine-headed lovegrasses. The University of Arizona records it on rocky slopes, sandy flats and roadsides. It has also been used as a forage grass elsewhere. These uses and occurrences establish an introduced grass, but they do not by themselves demonstrate that every roadside clump is causing ecological damage.

lolium-rigidum.summary: Wimmera ryegrass is an annual grass of Mediterranean origin that has been cultivated for pasture and can also become a troublesome crop weed. Wimmera began as a cultivar name and is now often used more broadly for Lolium rigidum. It grows as a tuft and completes its life cycle through seed. In California, original experiments have confirmed glyphosate resistance in particular populations. That finding makes repeated treatment failure worth investigating; it does not mean that every plant of this species is resistant.

rubus-phoenicolasius.summary: Wine raspberry, often called wineberry, is an introduced bramble whose red-haired canes can form tangled patches along woodland edges and other disturbed places. Its attractive fruit helps explain its history in gardens, but it has escaped cultivation in the eastern United States. Maryland Extension advises against planting it because it can crowd native vegetation. Birds and other animals can carry the seeds away from an established patch, so an abandoned planting may matter well beyond the original garden boundary.

euonymus-alatus.summary: Winged burning bush is a deciduous Asian shrub widely planted for its vivid red autumn leaves. Outside gardens it can establish in woodland, including shaded sites, and birds distribute its seeds. Minnesota's natural resources agency and Pennsylvania Extension describe it as an invasive shrub in their regional guidance. A neatly clipped hedge can still be a seed source, so the relevant question is not simply whether it stays within its planting bed. Nearby seedlings and fruiting branches are worth checking.

euonymus-fortunei-var-fortunei.summary: This record preserves the name Euonymus fortunei var. fortunei, the typical variety of wintercreeper. Kew accepts that name, but the boundaries among wintercreeper varieties have changed between botanical treatments. A Texas taxonomic study explains how nursery selections and variable leaf forms have made older names difficult to apply consistently. The variety should therefore not be given a separate invasion history simply by copying every report about the wider species. A garden label is useful evidence of planting history, but it is not a verified identification of a wild plant.

euonymus-fortunei-var-radicans.summary: The name Euonymus fortunei var. radicans appears in older plant records and horticulture for wintercreeper, but authorities do not all treat it the same way. Nesom's taxonomic discussion groups radicans names at species level, while USDA's germplasm database retains a record under var. radicans. That disagreement matters when deciding whether two records represent distinct plants or different names for the same taxonomic concept. This entry keeps the supplied identity visible while the name is reviewed; it does not establish a separate introduced range or distinct level of harm for radicans.

euonymus-fortunei.summary: Wintercreeper is an evergreen woody vine that can spread across the ground and climb trees or structures. An ornamental planting can become a persistent woodland problem: Missouri's conservation agency describes dense growth that displaces native ground vegetation, particularly around Kansas City and St. Louis. The plant can extend through rooting stems, while fruiting growth supplies seeds that animals may carry. An independent field study documented naturalized wintercreeper in Texas as well.

berberis-julianae.summary: Wintergreen barberry is a dense evergreen shrub from China, grown for its glossy foliage and formidable spines. Its yellow flowers are followed by dark, bluish-black fruit, and leaves may develop bronze or purple winter tones. It belongs to the same genus as several troublesome introduced shrubs, but that relationship is not enough to assign their impacts to this species. The University of Florida assessment currently records it as not a problem species in Florida, with impacts undocumented. That is a regional assessment, not a guarantee about every planting or climate.

west-nile-virus.summary: West Nile virus is a mosquito-borne virus, not a plant or an animal that can be recognized in the field. Mosquitoes acquire it from infected birds and can pass it to people through bites. Most infected people develop no symptoms, but some become ill and a smaller number develop serious disease affecting the nervous system. Public-health surveillance, rather than the presence of mosquitoes alone, establishes local activity. For example, New York's program tests trapped mosquitoes and investigates suspected human infections through its public-health laboratories.

albizia-lebbeck.summary: Woman's tongue is a broad-crowned tropical tree named for the sound of its dry, rattling pods. Albizia lebbeck has been planted as an ornamental and has escaped in Florida, where it can produce dense groups of seedlings and root sprouts. UF/IFAS describes invasion of vulnerable habitats including Florida Keys hammocks and pine rocklands. That concern is tied to particular warm regions and habitats; it should not be expanded into an unsupported claim that every tree throughout the United States poses the same threat.

poa-nemoralis-var-nemoralis.summary: Wood bluegrass is a tufted perennial of shaded woodland. This entry concerns its typical form, called Poa nemoralis var. nemoralis or subsp. nemoralis in different treatments. Botanical references distinguish that introduced North American concept from native relatives, but a general wood-bluegrass observation is not automatically identified to this level. A shaded location or a Poa label alone does not show that a patch is an invasive weed. Record the name actually determined and the flora used to identify it.

oxyporus-subulatus.summary: This wood-inhabiting fungus needs a careful name check. Oxyporus subulatus was described from Thailand, later appeared as Flavodon subulatus, and was transferred to Irpex subulatus in a 2022 scientific treatment. New Zealand's organism register instead places the name under Irpex spiculifer. Meanwhile, Florida researchers discuss wood decay associated with ambrosia beetles under the Flavodon name. Those connections are important evidence, but their taxonomic boundaries should be reconciled before attaching every regional observation to this catalog entry.

chelura-terebrans.summary: Chelura terebrans is a tiny marine amphipod associated with wood submerged in seawater. It often occupies timber already worked by gribbles, the wood-boring isopods called Limnoria. Smithsonian's invasion synthesis records introduced populations on both North American coasts, while treating a European native origin as probable rather than certain. Damage concerns focus on wooden maritime structures. Independent laboratory research also supports the amphipod's ability to digest wood, adding to older accounts that emphasized its close association with other borers.

limnoria-pfefferi.summary: Limnoria pfefferi is a marine wood-boring isopod, or gribble, recorded from timber and mangrove roots. Smithsonian treats it as Indo-Pacific in origin and introduced in the tropical western Atlantic. However, its Florida evidence consists of three Miami Beach specimens from 1950. Continued establishment is inferred from Caribbean records, not confirmed by a recent Florida survey in that account.

cardamine-flexuosa.summary: Woodland bittercress is a small mustard associated with damp woods, stream margins and other moist ground in its European range. It can behave as an annual, biennial or short-lived perennial. Its name has also been used too broadly: plants once called Asian Cardamine flexuosa are now distinguished as Cardamine occulta. That revision matters for nursery weeds and introduced records. An older report using the flexuosa name cannot automatically tell us which species was present, so this account keeps the identity question separate from assumptions about harm.

myosotis-sylvatica.summary: Woodland forget-me-not is a Eurasian flowering plant widely grown in gardens and naturalized in parts of North America. It can behave as a biennial or perennial and renew a patch through seed. Wisconsin field observations document escapes in woods, openings, roadsides and around old homesites. Its small blue flowers are appealing, but a garden border that repeatedly seeds into nearby woodland deserves attention. Those regional observations support watching escapes; they do not establish that every planted variety causes the same impact in every state.

senecio-sylvaticus.summary: Woodland ragwort is an annual herb that can appear abundantly after disturbance, including timber harvest in the Pacific Northwest. It grows from seed rather than building a persistent woody framework. An Oregon field experiment found a dramatic rise followed by a sharp decline within three growing seasons. That result is a useful caution: a conspicuous flush does not necessarily predict permanent dominance, and the study did not support a simple explanation that other plants had crowded it out. Management should consider what the whole recovering plant community is doing.

cyperus-entrerianus.summary: Woodrush flatsedge, also called deep-rooted sedge, can build a substantial clump in a wet ditch or field margin. This perennial comes from tropical and subtropical parts of the Americas and is introduced in the southeastern United States. Its underground rhizomes help established plants persist, while seeds and broken rhizomes can travel with disturbed soil and equipment. North Carolina Extension reports displacement of native vegetation, and Harris County's restoration guide treats it as an undesirable plant in poorly drained sites.

arctium-tomentosum.summary: Woolly burdock is a Eurasian biennial that has become established in scattered parts of North America. Its broad leaves and purple flower heads can look familiar even where this particular burdock is uncommon. Disturbed fields, roadside edges and open woodland are typical places to look. The mature heads become burrs that catch on fur or clothing, carrying seeds away from the parent plant. Records establish its presence, but the sources reviewed do not establish the same ecological impact at every North American site.

carthamus-lanatus.summary: Woolly distaff thistle, often called saffron thistle, is a spiny annual of pastures and disturbed ground. It begins as a low leafy plant before sending up branched flowering stems. In Australian grazing country, dense stands reduce useful pasture and the sharp foliage can injure livestock. It has also occurred in Oklahoma, where Extension describes historical infestations that were eradicated. Those regional accounts justify watching for new patches without assuming that every yellow thistle is this species.

opuntia-tomentosa.summary: Woollyjoint pricklypear is a large, branching cactus whose flattened pads have an unusually soft-looking surface. It is native to Mexico, where researchers have studied its seeds in volcanic scrubland. In parts of Australia it forms troublesome thickets that compete with pasture and native plants and obstruct access. Detached pieces can establish new plants, and seed dormancy adds another reason to keep watching a cleared site. These Australian impacts should not be read as proof of the same behavior throughout the United States.

dysphania-aristata.summary: The plant filed here as Dysphania aristata is a small annual of sandy, disturbed ground, also treated under the name Teloxys aristata. Its airy branches and inconspicuous flowers make it easy to overlook among other small weeds. North American floristic accounts describe it as an introduction from Asia. The common name wormseed is especially unhelpful: it is shared with quite different plants and does not establish an identification, a medicinal use or an invasive impact.

erysimum-cheiranthoides.summary: Wormseed wallflower is a modest yellow-flowered mustard found in fields and other disturbed places. New England flora treats it as introduced, but northern origin interpretations differ. Alaska's current nonnative list includes it, while a 2010 University of Alaska Anchorage river survey questioned its nonnative status and considered the northern complex likely native or a mixture of native and introduced plants. Those conflicting regional treatments are a reason to check local status, not to assume that every northern riverbank population needs removal. Identification and the actual effect of a patch should guide the response.

pachyrhizus-erosus.summary: Yam bean is the climbing vegetable better known as jicama. Despite its common name, it is a legume rather than a true yam. It comes from Mexico and Central America and is grown for its swollen storage root. Singapore's botanical account records it there as cultivated, while Australia's tropical flora notes occasional escapes around agricultural land. Those records support a crop-and-escape context, not a blanket claim that jicama is an invasive plant wherever it is grown.

scutellonema-bradys.summary: Yam nematode is a microscopic plant parasite associated with dry rot of true yams, especially in tropical production systems. It can remain active inside harvested tubers, so damage may worsen during storage as well as in the field. Infected pieces saved for planting can carry the nematode into the next crop. Most of the evidence reviewed concerns African yam production; it does not establish that an unexplained damaged tuber in a U.S. garden has this pest.

medicago-sativa-ssp-falcata.summary: Yellow alfalfa is a perennial forage legume with a long history in cold, relatively dry farming regions. The USDA treats it as Medicago sativa subspecies falcata, also known as Medicago falcata, and describes naturalized populations in parts of South Dakota. Its branching roots and persistent crown support repeated growth. A plant outside a field is therefore worth documenting, but the USDA guide does not identify this forage as an established environmental problem. Its presence alone is not a reason to launch weed control.

lamium-galeobdolon.summary: Yellow archangel can brighten a shady garden and then spread well beyond its intended bed. This perennial groundcover comes from Europe and Asia. In Washington, escaped plantings form dense mats in woodland edges, greenbelts and streamside areas, crowding other low-growing plants. Its creeping stems root where they touch suitable soil, and broken stems can start new patches. Dumped hanging baskets and garden waste have helped it reach natural areas, so disposal is an important part of managing it.

bothriochloa-ischaemum.summary: Yellow bluestem is an introduced perennial grass whose attractive seed heads can hide a difficult pasture or prairie problem. It was brought to the United States for forage and is one of the grasses often grouped as Old World bluestems. Texas vegetation accounts describe its King Ranch form, variety songarica, as a conspicuous or dominant component of some coastal prairie communities. Kansas guidance also warns that yellow bluestem can spread aggressively and suppress more desirable vegetation. Different Old World bluestem species should still be identified separately.

setaria-helvola.summary: The name Setaria helvola needs clarification before this record can describe a single grass confidently. Kew currently places that name under Setaria italica, the foxtail millet complex, while an older treatment cited on the same page linked it with Setaria pumila. A North American floristic portal also presents yellow-foxtail material under helvola. The catalog's common name, yellow bristlegrass, cannot resolve that disagreement. Assigning a definite origin, invasive impact or treatment to this entry would risk describing the wrong plant.

dypsis-lutescens.summary: Yellow butterfly palm is the familiar clumping palm often grown indoors or in warm-climate gardens. Its accepted name in current botanical sources is Chrysalidocarpus lutescens; Dypsis lutescens remains a widely encountered synonym. Native to Madagascar, it produces multiple slender stems rather than one solitary trunk. That habit can make a mature planting broad and dense, but a spreading garden clump is not, by itself, evidence of an invasive population. The sources reviewed chiefly describe cultivation and identification.

aedes-aegypti.summary: The yellow fever mosquito is a small mosquito closely associated with people and water-holding containers. Females often seek human blood and can transmit viruses including dengue, yellow fever, chikungunya and Zika. Finding the mosquito does not establish that those viruses are circulating locally; current health-department information is needed for that. Its use of buckets, planters, tanks and similar small habitats makes prevention around homes especially useful, even where there is no nearby pond or marsh.

iris-pseudacorus.summary: Yellow flag iris can make a striking display along a pond, but it is an invasive wetland plant in several parts of the United States. Native to Europe, western Asia and northern Africa, this perennial spreads through both seeds and thick underground rhizomes. Established clumps can expand into dense stands that crowd wetland vegetation. North Carolina Extension warns about its rapid growth in wet sites, while Wisconsin guidance describes the difficulty of removing the persistent rhizomes.

peltophorum-pterocarpum.summary: Yellow flame is a large shade tree with a broad crown, finely divided foliage and conspicuous yellow flower clusters. It is native across parts of tropical Asia to northern Australia, including Singapore, where wild populations have conservation value. It is also planted as an ornamental in other warm regions. UF guidance describes it as not a problem species in Florida at the time of that publication. Those differing settings are a good reason to distinguish a cultivated tree from a documented invasive population.

nymphoides-peltata.summary: Yellow floating heart is a rooted aquatic perennial that spreads leaves across the surface of still or slowly moving water. Introduced through water gardening, it can form mats that crowd native aquatic plants and interfere with recreation. New plants can develop from broken plant material, and seeds provide another route of reproduction. Research also shows that individual flowers are short-lived, so a patch may look quite different on two visits even while its floating foliage remains conspicuous.

hedychium-flavescens.summary: Yellow ginger is a tall perennial that builds its stems from a spreading network of thick rhizomes. It is grown for its pale, fragrant flowers, but has escaped cultivation in places including Hawaii and New Zealand. Hawaiian agency guidance describes yellow ginger as weedy particularly at forest edges and in wet habitats. In New Zealand, discarded garden material and moved rhizome fragments are important pathways. The large underground mass can persist after the visible shoots have been cut.

parentucellia-viscosa.summary: Yellow glandweed is an upright, sticky-haired annual of damp grassland and seasonally wet ground. It is a root hemiparasite: it can draw resources from neighboring plants while also making its own food, and it can grow without a host. California assessments describe invasion of coastal wetland prairies and some mountain pastures, while rating its overall impact as limited. That rating does not mean every patch is harmless, nor does a yellow flower in a wet meadow establish that this species is present.

phyllostachys-aureosulcata.summary: Yellow groove bamboo is a running bamboo, spreading through underground rhizomes rather than staying in a compact clump. A planted screen can therefore send up shoots well beyond the original row, including into adjoining woodland or a neighbor's garden. North Carolina extension identifies it as invasive and warns that dense stands can exclude native vegetation. The relevant issue is the connected underground colony, not simply the height of a few visible canes. Cutting the tops once does not remove that colony.

malachra-alceifolia.summary: Yellow leafbract is a coarse, hairy mallow with small yellow flowers gathered among conspicuous leafy bracts. Kew places the species' native range from Mexico through tropical America, including Caribbean islands, and records introductions in Hawaii and other islands. Its name needs particular care in Florida: conservation accounts identify Malachra alceifolia as a historically misapplied name for the native Malachra urens. A Florida record under the old label should not automatically be treated as an introduced population of this species.

reseda-lutea.summary: Yellow mignonette is a leafy, branching herb with slender spikes of small pale flowers. It grows in disturbed ground, roadsides, and agricultural settings, and botanical sources record it outside its Mediterranean-to-Asian native range. Calflora lists it as a nonnative perennial in California. Those records establish an introduction, but do not by themselves demonstrate severe ecological damage across the United States. Its quiet appearance also makes it easy to confuse with the related plant called weld, especially when the leaves are missing from a photograph.

cyperus-esculentus.summary: Yellow nutsedge is a perennial sedge that can be a stubborn garden or crop weed, even where it belongs to the regional flora. California's agriculture department explicitly recognizes it as native there, and botanical research describes geographically distinct wild forms as well as the cultivated tiger-nut crop. A nationwide alien-invader label would therefore be misleading. Its practical persistence comes from underground rhizomes and tubers that survive after the leaves disappear. Moving infested soil can carry that problem into another planting.

trisetum-flavescens.summary: Yellow oatgrass, also called golden oatgrass, is a tufted perennial whose flowering heads develop a bright, shiny appearance. It is native to Europe and the Mediterranean region and has been recorded as introduced in North America and Australasia. The common name can suggest a familiar forage crop, but it is a different grass from cultivated oats. The sources reviewed support recognition and naturalization; they do not establish that every American occurrence is a major invader or that it is appropriate for every pasture.

globodera-rostochiensis.summary: Golden potato cyst nematode is a microscopic root-feeding roundworm whose lasting legacy is hidden in soil. After a female dies, her hardened body forms a cyst protecting hundreds of eggs, which can remain viable for decades. Potatoes may grow poorly in patches, but low populations can escape notice for years. The pest is native to the South American Andes and is regulated in the United States and Canada. Preventing soil movement is central because an apparently clean truck or seed shipment can still carry contaminated dirt.

barbarea-vulgaris.summary: Yellow rocket is a mustard that often spends its first season as a low, glossy rosette before sending up bright yellow flower clusters. It commonly behaves as a winter annual or biennial, although some plants persist longer. Roadsides, field margins, and other disturbed ground provide opportunities for its seed-producing life cycle. Its conspicuous spring color makes it easy to notice, but several native and introduced mustards flower at similar times. The useful first question is which plant is present, not whether every yellow patch needs the same treatment.

tragopogon-dubius.summary: Yellow salsify, also called western salsify or goatsbeard, begins with leaves that can pass for grass and later produces a striking globe of windborne seeds. It is introduced in North America and can be weedy on roadsides, pasture, and rangeland. Montana extension describes plants that often take two to four years to flower and then die after producing seed. Wildlife also uses the plant, so its presence is not a simple measure of habitat value; dense stands and local competition deserve their own assessment.

aonidiella-citrina.summary: Yellow scale is an armored scale insect associated especially with citrus leaves and fruit. A settled female remains beneath a small protective cover, while young crawlers can move to new feeding sites. Its history should not be confused with the similar California red scale: UC IPM notes that yellow scale has not been observed in California in recent years and is more readily controlled by natural enemies. An old regional pest record is therefore not evidence that a current orchard problem is this species.

galium-verum.summary: Yellow bedstraw is a perennial that spreads from creeping underground stems and carries many tiny golden flowers above narrow leaves. It is native to Eurasia and introduced in North America, where regional floras record it in fields, meadows, and disturbed places. The plant is also known as lady's bedstraw. Its traditional uses are part of its history, not a reason to introduce it to a natural meadow or a guarantee that every unidentified bedstraw is suitable for food or household use.

centaurea-solstitialis.summary: Yellow starthistle is a deep-rooted plant that can turn open ground into a difficult, spiny stand. It usually grows as a winter annual in California, building a rosette before branching and flowering as the season advances. In invaded western rangelands it competes with desirable vegetation, reduces access, and presents a serious poisoning risk to horses. Its seeds sustain future generations after the standing plants die. Early recognition is much easier to act on than a field full of mature spiny flowerheads.

melanaphis-sacchari.summary: The name yellow sugarcane aphid usually refers to Sipha flava, a different insect from Melanaphis sacchari. This account concerns M. sacchari, ordinarily called the sugarcane aphid. There is a second naming issue: older work often combined it with the sorghum aphid, Melanaphis sorghi, but original molecular and body-measurement research supports their separation. An outbreak described under an older shared name cannot automatically establish the host range, spread, or treatment response of M. sacchari in its narrower sense.

melilotus-officinalis.summary: Yellow sweetclover is a tall, branching legume with slender clusters of small yellow flowers. It has been cultivated for forage and soil improvement, but it also spreads into roadsides, disturbed prairie, and other open ground. It commonly grows as a biennial, establishing leafy growth first and flowering in its second season, although annual forms occur. In a restoration site, a productive stand can compete with the vegetation being restored. Its agricultural usefulness does not make it an appropriate addition to every native grassland.

acanthogobius-flavimanus.summary: Yellowfin goby is an introduced bottom-associated fish established in California estuaries and connected waters. Its diet includes small invertebrates and fish, with prey changing as the goby grows. Field research in the lower Mokelumne River found strong seasonal differences in catches, a reminder that one visit does not describe the whole population. The species' occurrence and feeding habits are well documented, but claims about effects on a particular native fish need evidence from that place rather than an assumption that every introduced goby has identical impacts.

dioscorea-sansibarensis.summary: Zanzibar yam is a vigorous African climbing vine that grows from substantial underground tubers and also makes aerial bulbils. Those bulbils can fall and start new plants, allowing a cultivated vine to spread without a conspicuous crop of flowers. It is naturalized in Singapore, and UF/IFAS rates it as a high invasion risk in Florida. The current Florida assessment distinguishes predicted risk from documented local status; the risk rating should not be rewritten as proof of the same impact everywhere.

dreissena-polymorpha.summary: Zebra mussels are small freshwater mollusks that attach to hard surfaces with strong threads and can build dense colonies on boats, pipes, rocks, and native mussels. They filter plankton from the water, changing food availability even when the water looks clearer. Their spread has an easily missed stage: microscopic larvae, called veligers, can travel in retained water long before an adult shell is visible. Preventing that transfer is more useful than waiting until a dock or intake is covered.

podranea-ricasoliana.summary: Podranea ricasoliana is a vigorous woody climber commonly called pink trumpet vine or Port St Johns creeper. The name Zimbabwe creeper needs care: South African botanical accounts also apply it to Podranea brycei, so the common name alone cannot establish the species. UF/IFAS currently gives P. ricasoliana a high predictive invasion-risk rating in Florida while its status assessment says it is not presently considered a problem species. Those are different kinds of evidence, and neither should be silently substituted for the other.
